name: Water
scoreRationale: Water is the benchmark for a benign ingredient; it is only harmful at extreme intakes far beyond anything in a product.
summary: Water is the base of most drinks, lotions, shampoos and cleaners. It dissolves the other ingredients so they can be spread, rinsed or absorbed evenly.

overview: Water is a small, bent molecule (H₂O): one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms at an angle of about 104.5°. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself, so the molecule is polar, with a partial negative charge on the oxygen and partial positive charges on the hydrogens.

That polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other and with ions and other polar molecules. It is why water dissolves salt, sugar and acids so well (its nickname is the “universal solvent”), why it boils at an unusually high 100 °C for such a light molecule, and why ice floats: in the solid, molecules lock into an open hexagonal lattice that is less dense than the liquid.
profile.function: Formulators use water as the continuous phase of emulsions, the carrier for water-soluble actives, and the diluent that sets a product's concentration and texture.

mechanisms.title: Dissolving and transporting nutrients
mechanisms.chemical: Water is a polar molecule, which means its electric charge is spread unevenly: the oxygen end carries a slight negative charge and the two hydrogen ends carry slight positive charges. When a crystal of salt drops into water, the water molecules turn so that their oppositely charged ends face each ion, oxygen toward positive ions such as Na⁺ and hydrogen toward negative ions such as Cl⁻. Each ion ends up wrapped in a cluster of water molecules called a hydration shell. Forming these shells releases energy, and that energy helps pull the ions away from the crystal one by one. Polar molecules such as sugar dissolve in a similar way, by forming hydrogen bonds, weak attractions between a hydrogen on one molecule and an oxygen or nitrogen on another. Oils have no charged regions for water to grab, which is why they don't dissolve.
mechanisms.biological: Because so many substances dissolve in it, water is the body's delivery system. Blood plasma, the liquid part of blood, is about 90 percent water; it carries dissolved glucose, salts and hormones to every organ, and red blood cells are swept along in it. Inside each cell, water is the medium in which nearly all chemical reactions happen, since molecules have to move around and bump into each other in order to react. Waste products dissolve too, and the kidneys filter the blood and flush water-soluble wastes such as urea out in urine. An adult loses roughly two to three liters of water a day through urine, sweat and breath, so it has to be replaced constantly from drinks and food.

mechanisms.title: Hydrating the skin barrier
mechanisms.chemical: The outermost layer of skin, the stratum corneum, is made of flattened dead cells packed with a tough protein called keratin and glued together by fatty substances. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with keratin and with a mix of small, water-attracting molecules in the skin known as natural moisturizing factor, which includes amino acids, urea and lactate. Tucked between the protein chains, water acts as a plasticizer, a substance that makes a material softer and more flexible by letting its long molecules slide past one another. It works the way a little water turns dry, crumbly clay into something you can bend. When the skin dries out, the protein chains pack tightly together and the layer becomes stiff.
mechanisms.biological: Well-hydrated skin stays flexible, so it can stretch as you move without cracking. The outer layer normally contains roughly 15 to 30 percent water, and when it drops much below about 10 percent the skin feels tight, looks dull and may flake. Dry indoor air, cold wind, long hot showers and harsh soaps all speed up the loss of water from the surface. Moisturizers fight this in two ways: humectants such as glycerin pull water into the skin, and occlusives such as petrolatum or oils form a film that slows evaporation. Plain water evaporates within minutes, which is why splashing your face without following with a moisturizer can leave it feeling drier than before.

mechanisms.title: Cooling the body
mechanisms.chemical: Turning liquid water into vapor means breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold neighboring water molecules together, and that takes energy. The amount needed is called the heat of vaporization, and for water it is about 2,260 joules for every gram, among the highest of any common liquid. That is more than five times the energy needed to heat the same gram of water all the way from freezing to boiling. The energy has to come from somewhere, so when water evaporates from a surface it takes heat from that surface. This is why a wet surface always cools as it dries.
mechanisms.biological: Your body uses this chemistry as its main way to get rid of extra heat. When your core temperature rises during exercise or on a hot day, the brain signals millions of sweat glands in the skin to release a watery fluid. As each gram of sweat evaporates, it carries about 2,260 joules of heat away from the skin, cooling the blood flowing just underneath. Sweat that drips off without evaporating doesn't cool you, which is why humid days feel so much hotter: the air is already full of water vapor, so sweat evaporates slowly. Sweating a lot without drinking leads to dehydration, which shrinks blood volume and makes it even harder for the body to stay cool.

reactions.title: Autoionization
reactions.summary: Even perfectly pure water is not made only of H₂O molecules. At any moment, a tiny fraction of the molecules have passed a proton, the nucleus of a hydrogen atom, to a neighbor. The molecule that gains the proton becomes a hydronium ion (H₃O⁺), and the one that loses it becomes a hydroxide ion (OH⁻). The ions quickly recombine while new pairs form elsewhere, so their numbers stay balanced in what chemists call an equilibrium. This constant, tiny exchange is the reason the pH scale exists at all, and it explains why pure water is called neutral.

steps.name: Proton transfer
steps.text: A hydrogen atom on one water molecule is attracted to a lone pair, a pair of electrons not being used in a bond, on the oxygen of a neighboring molecule. The hydrogen's proton jumps across and leaves its electron behind. This happens because molecules in a liquid are always jostling and colliding with each other.

steps.name: Ion pair
steps.text: The molecule that gained the proton becomes hydronium (H₃O⁺), which carries a positive charge. The molecule that lost it becomes hydroxide (OH⁻), which carries a negative charge. Atoms or molecules that carry an electric charge are called ions.

steps.name: Equilibrium
steps.text: The two ions attract each other and recombine almost instantly, so very few exist at once. At 25 °C only about 1 water molecule in 555 million is split this way at any moment, which works out to 10⁻⁷ moles of each ion per liter. A mole is simply a counting unit chemists use for very large numbers of particles.

reactions.result: This is where pH 7 comes from. The pH number is the negative logarithm of the hydronium concentration, so 10⁻⁷ moles per liter gives a pH of 7, which is called neutral. Acids add extra hydronium and push the pH below 7, while bases add hydroxide and push it above 7. Each step on the scale is a tenfold change, so lemon juice at pH 3 has ten thousand times more hydronium than pure water.

reactions.title: Hydrolysis
reactions.summary: Hydrolysis means “splitting with water.” In this reaction a water molecule breaks a chemical bond in another molecule, and the water's own atoms end up attached to the two pieces. It is one of the most common reactions in both biology and everyday products. Your digestive system depends on it to break fats, proteins and starches into pieces small enough to absorb. The same reaction can slowly break down ingredients in water-based lotions, shampoos and drinks while they sit on a shelf. That is why many products need careful pH control, preservatives and sometimes an expiration date.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: The oxygen in water has lone pairs of electrons that are drawn toward atoms with a partial positive charge. In an ester, the carbon of the C=O group (the carbonyl carbon) is electron-poor, because the oxygen atoms around it pull electrons away. Water's oxygen moves in and begins to form a bond with that carbon.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: With a new bond forming, the carbon can't keep all of its old bonds, so the bond between the carbonyl carbon and the ester's second oxygen breaks. The molecule falls into two pieces. One piece takes water's OH and becomes a carboxylic acid, and the other takes water's H and becomes an alcohol.

steps.name: Catalysis
steps.text: On its own, water reacts slowly with most bonds. Acids, bases, heat or enzymes such as lipases speed the reaction up enormously by making the carbon more attractive to water or making water a stronger attacker. Anything that speeds up a reaction without being used up is called a catalyst.

reactions.result: Hydrolysis is how your body digests fats, proteins and starches into pieces it can absorb. In products, it is one reason old lotions can separate, change smell or turn sour, because some ingredients have been split into new substances. Keeping products at the right pH and away from heat slows hydrolysis down.

regulatory.status: Tap water must meet National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for over 90 contaminants.
Bottled water is regulated as a food with a standard of identity and quality.
Listed as Aqua (INCI); cosmetic water is typically purified by deionization or reverse osmosis to remove minerals and microbes.

hazards.title: Water intoxication (hyponatremia)
hazards.summary: Drinking water is almost never dangerous, but drinking a very large amount in a short time can be. The risk shows up in unusual situations: endurance athletes who drink far more than they sweat out, drinking contests, or certain medical conditions. It has nothing to do with the water in foods, drinks or personal-care products used normally. The medical name, hyponatremia, means “too little sodium in the blood.” The kidneys of a healthy adult can usually remove about 0.8 to 1 liter of water per hour, so the danger comes from outpacing them for several hours.
hazards.chemical: Blood contains dissolved sodium at a tightly controlled concentration of about 135 to 145 millimoles per liter. Concentration means how much of a substance is dissolved in a given volume, so adding lots of plain water without adding sodium dilutes it. If someone drinks water faster than their kidneys can get rid of it, roughly 0.8 to 1 liter per hour, the extra water stays in the blood. Blood sodium then falls below about 135 millimoles per liter. Neither the water nor the sodium is harmful on its own; the problem is the change in their ratio.
hazards.biological: Cell membranes let water pass through freely by osmosis, the movement of water from a more dilute solution toward a more concentrated one. When the blood becomes more dilute than the fluid inside cells, water flows into the cells and they swell like water balloons. Most organs can stretch a little, but the brain is enclosed by the skull and has very little room to expand. Swelling brain cells raise the pressure inside the head, causing headache, nausea and confusion, and in severe cases seizures or coma. Treatment involves limiting water and, in hospital, carefully raising blood sodium again.

hazards.title: Microbial growth in products
hazards.summary: Water is what lets bacteria, yeast and mold live in lotions, shampoos and foods. A completely dry product, like a powder or a pure oil, is a poor home for microbes, but anything containing water can support them. Contamination is the reason water-based products contain preservatives and why opened products have a recommended time limit for use. Dipping fingers into a jar or keeping a product in a warm, steamy bathroom makes contamination more likely. Most of the time the result is just spoilage, but occasionally it can cause infections.
hazards.chemical: Microbes need liquid water to run their metabolism: nutrients must be dissolved before they can be absorbed, and nearly all the chemical reactions inside a cell take place in water. Food scientists measure how much water is actually available to microbes with a number called water activity, which runs from 0 for bone dry to 1 for pure water. Water that is tightly held by sugar, salt or other dissolved substances is less available, which is why jam and salted meat resist spoilage. Most bacteria need a water activity above about 0.9, while many molds can grow at lower levels. Lotions and shampoos typically have a water activity close to 1.
hazards.biological: If microbes get into a water-based product and nothing controls them, they multiply and can reach millions of cells per gram. Some contaminants, such as the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa, can cause skin infections or serious eye infections, especially if a contaminated product is used near the eyes or on broken skin. People with weakened immune systems are at higher risk. Preservatives work by damaging microbial membranes or enzymes, keeping microbe numbers low throughout the product's life. Manufacturers check this by deliberately adding microbes to a sample and confirming that the preservatives kill them, a process called challenge testing.

profile.dosage: There is no meaningful risk from the water in foods, drinks or personal-care products. Healthy kidneys can clear roughly 0.8 to 1 liter of water per hour, and the body's thirst signals normally keep intake balanced with losses. Problems from drinking too much generally require several liters taken within a few hours, which is why most reported cases involve marathon runners, military training or drinking contests. U.S. health guidelines suggest that adults take in about 2.7 to 3.7 liters of water a day from all sources, including food, with more needed in heat or during exercise. The practical rule is to drink when thirsty, and during long exercise to replace what you sweat rather than drink as much as possible.

myths.claim: "Aqua" is a cheap filler that dilutes a product.
myths.consensus: Water is the solvent that lets actives dissolve, spread and absorb evenly; most lotions and cleansers could not exist without it.

myths.claim: Alkaline or "structured" water has special health effects.
myths.consensus: Stomach acid neutralizes drinking water's pH within minutes, and claims about restructured water have no support in physical chemistry.

environment.persistence: Not applicable: water is part of the natural hydrologic cycle.
environment.notes: The environmental cost of water in products is mostly the energy used to purify, heat and ship it.

synthesis.title: The natural water cycle
synthesis.summary: Earth's water is recycled, not manufactured. Almost all of it has been on the planet since early in its history, moving between oceans, air, ice, rivers, soil and living things. The water in your glass has probably fallen as rain, flowed down rivers and been part of plants and animals many times over. No factory makes new water for products; it is collected, cleaned and reused. The sun is the engine that drives the whole cycle.
synthesis.mechanism: The sun's energy warms the surface of oceans, lakes and soil, and the fastest-moving water molecules escape into the air as vapor, a process called evaporation. Dissolved salts and minerals can't evaporate, so they stay behind, which is why rain is fresh even though most of it comes from the salty ocean. As warm, moist air rises, it cools, and the vapor condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds. When the droplets merge and grow heavy enough, they fall as rain or snow. This is the same process as distillation in a laboratory, where a liquid is boiled and its vapor is cooled and collected to separate it from impurities, only carried out on the scale of a whole planet.
synthesis.significance: Rainwater is nearly pure, but groundwater dissolves minerals from the rocks it seeps through. The calcium and magnesium picked up this way are what make water “hard.”

synthesis.title: Purification for cosmetics and labs
synthesis.summary: Water used in cosmetics, medicines and laboratories is purified far beyond ordinary tap water. Tap water is safe to drink, but it contains dissolved minerals, traces of chlorine and occasionally microbes. Those can react with ingredients, weaken preservatives or leave deposits. Manufacturers therefore remove almost everything except H₂O, producing what is labeled “purified,” “deionized” or “distilled” water. On an ingredient list it usually appears simply as water or aqua.
synthesis.mechanism: Purification combines several techniques, each removing a different kind of impurity. Reverse osmosis pushes water at high pressure through a membrane whose pores are so small that dissolved ions, which travel wrapped in bulky shells of water molecules, can't fit through. Ion exchange then removes the ions that slip past: the water flows over resin beads that grab positive metal ions and release hydrogen ions (H⁺) in their place, while other beads grab negative ions and release hydroxide ions (OH⁻). The H⁺ and OH⁻ immediately combine to form more water, so what remains is very pure. A final step, such as ultraviolet light or an extremely fine filter, kills or removes any microbes left.
steps: Filters remove sand, rust and other particles.
Reverse osmosis pushes the water through a membrane that holds back most dissolved salts.
Ion-exchange resins swap the remaining ions for H⁺ and OH⁻, which combine into water (deionization).
Ultraviolet light or a very fine filter kills or removes microbes.
synthesis.significance: Removing calcium, iron and other metal ions keeps products stable and stops these ions from weakening preservatives or reacting with other ingredients.

citations.title: [Biotransformation of dimethylnitrosamine].
citations.abstract: NDMA, one of the most widely occurring carcinogenic compounds in the environment, is present in human food (meat, vegetables, cheese and alcohol beverages), in drinking water, in drugs, in cosmetics, in tobacco and its smokes. Furthermore NDMA may be synthesized from nitrates and nitrites and endogen or exogen amines. Since the first observations of MAGEE and BARNES in 1956 on the carcinogenicity of NDMA, this compound was reported to be carcinogenic in a large number of animal species including mammals, birds, amphibia and fish. NDMA requires metabolic activation for its cytotoxic and carcinogenic actions. The major activation step is believed to be the oxygenation of the alpha-carbon catalysed by a Cytochrome P-450-dependent enzyme system commonly know as NDMA-demethylase. Studies on the enzymology of NDMA metabolism show that some Cytochrome P-450 isozymes exhibit significant NDMA-demethylase activity only at high NDMA concentrations. The form of P-450 inducible by factors such as, fasting, diabetes, ethanol consumption and pretreatment with acetone, pyrazole or isopropanol has the higher affinity for NDMA. The gene coding for this isozyme belongs tho the P-450 II E subfamily. Because NDMA-demethylase activity is decreased by monoamine oxidase inhibitors, some authors have suggested a possible role of MAO in NDMA demethylation. This view is not supported by others who don't find evidence for an involvement of MAO in NDMA metabolism. Likewise, there are contradictory reports about the existence of some NDMA demethylase activity in cytosol, nuclei and mitochondria. NDMA demethylation, followed by nonenzymatic cleavage of the hydroxylated methyl group gives formaldehyde and methyldiazohydroxide and then leads to the formation of, a methonium ion, which is able to methylate nucleophilic sites of cellular macromolecules such as, proteins, RNA and DNA. A lot of studies suggest the existence of an alternative pathway to the formation of a methylating agent, denitrosation. Although the nature of mechanisms of denitrosation is not completely known, authors think that the formation of nitrite may represent a detoxification pathway rather than an activation pathway.

citations.title: [Importance of Helicobacter pylori in the pathogenesis of gastric cancer. Experimental models in rodents].
citations.abstract: Unlabelled: We found that the seroprevalence in Cancer Institute of H. pylori infection was significantly more frequent in gastric cancer than in age- and gender-matched controls. This study suggested an epidemiological link between H. pylori infection and gastric cancer. H. pylori exhibits a complex system of enzymes which serve a range of functions. Toxic effects are produced by urease (UR), phospholipase (PL) and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH). We embarked on an exploration of the enzyme activities of H. pylori infected patients using a TLC-autoradioluminography. This method has a wide dynamic range and could offer an analytical technique for studying a radioactive compound and its enzymes in H. pylori infected mucosa. Biopsies samples taken from 21 gastric cancer patients and 95 controls were studied. Although high activity of UR indicates well the presence of H. pylori impairment, activities of ADH and PL reflects more the chronicity of mucosal damage in both groups. Clearly, the enzyme profile showed in our study reflects the "physiological" adaptations behind chronic injured mucosal changes but its relation to gastric cancer and H. pylori needs further study. There is an urgent need to understand the carcinogenesis process using animal models. We performed previous study for to explore the effect of H. pylori infection on N- methyl-N-nitrosourea-induced (MNU) gastric carcinogenesis in mice C57BL/6 mice were administered broth culture of H. pylori and given MNU in drinking water. In terms of the incidence of neoplasms development was increase in the MNU group pre-infected with H. pylori. That findings showed that C57BL/6 mice-infected model is well suited for investigating the bacteria promoter effect in the gastric carcinogenesis. Finally another rodent model study (still in process) showed rapid development of hyperplastic gastritis with gastric erosions in H. pylori-infected MTH1 knockout mice. We sought to further evaluate MTH1 knockout mice as potential test animal for carcinogenesis. Conclusion: It is suggested that H. pylori infection is an important risk factor for the development of gastric cancer. The possibility that this organism acts etiologically, exerting its effect over long period of time, is biologically plausible. However, the role of H. pylori per se in that process is still a matter of discussion. The various enzymes of H. pylori discussed in this paper support colonization, and are perhaps important for epithelial damage, they could contribute to the stimulation and modulation of the chronic inflammatory response, but its relation to gastric cancer and H. pylori needs further study. Finally H. pylori in C57BL/6 and knockout mice showed excellent colonization at two months and six months after infection there was adenomatous, hyperplastic and ulcerative changes. Those findings showed that both mice-infected models are well suited for investigating the bacteria promoter effect in the gastric carcinogenesis.

citations.title: Dermatological and environmental toxicological impact of the sunscreen ingredient oxybenzone/benzophenone-3.
citations.abstract: Oxybenzone (Benzophenone-3) is an emerging human and environmental contaminant used in sunscreens and personal care products to help minimize the damaging effects of ultraviolet radiation. The Center for Disease Control fourth national report on human exposure to environmental chemicals demonstrated that approximately 97% of the people tested have oxybenzone present in their urine, and independent scientists have reported various concentrations in waterways and fish worldwide. Oxybenzone can also react with chlorine, producing hazardous by-products that can concentrate in swimming pools and wastewater treatment plants. Moreover, adverse reactions could very well be increased by the closed loop of ingesting fish contaminated with oxybenzone and/or washing the ingredient off our bodies and having it return in drinking water as treatment plants do not effectively remove the chemical as part of their processing protocols. In humans, oxybenzone has been reported to produce contact and photocontact allergy reactions, implemented as a possible endocrine disruptor and has been linked to Hirschsprung's disease. Environmentally, oxybenzone has been shown to produce a variety of toxic reactions in coral and fish ranging from reef bleaching to mortality. Lastly, with the rise in skin cancer rates and the availability of more effective sunscreen actives such as micronized zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, serious doubts about the relative prevention benefit of personal care products containing oxybenzone must be raised and compared with the potential negative health and environmental effects caused by the accumulation of this and other chemicals in the ecosystem.

citations.title: Climate change and allergic diseases in children and adolescents.
citations.abstract: Introduction: The Anthropocene is used to describe the most recent period where major disruptions in Earth's system processes have resulted from humanity's increasing ecological footprint. Climate change affects the social and environmental determinants of good health, such as clean air, stable ecosystems, safe drinking water, and sufficient and safe food, and they seem to be closely related to air pollution. Objectives: This article aims to review the evidence of how extreme weather events and indoor and outdoor pollution are associated with insufficient lung growth in early life, changes in lung function, and the increase in respiratory infections, favoring the development of allergic respiratory diseases. Material and methods: Non-systematic review of English, Spanish, and Portuguese articles published in the last ten years in databases such as PubMed, EMBASE, and SciELO. The terms used were air pollution OR climate changes OR smoke, AND health OR allergic disease. Results: Climate change and air pollution are the leading contributors to health emergencies around the world. On a global scale, those most at risk of adverse health effects associated with climate change include children, the elderly, and other vulnerable groups. Climate change and air pollution have adverse impacts on respiratory allergies, and the mechanisms are complex and interactive. Conclusion: Health professionals must receive information and education necessary to establish effective mitigation and adaptation strategies to minimize the effects of climate changes on the respiratory health of their patients.

citations.title: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances in the environment.
citations.abstract: Over the past several years, the term PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) has grown to be emblematic of environmental contamination, garnering public, scientific, and regulatory concern. PFAS are synthesized by two processes, direct fluorination (e.g., electrochemical fluorination) and oligomerization (e.g., fluorotelomerization). More than a megatonne of PFAS is produced yearly, and thousands of PFAS wind up in end-use products. Atmospheric and aqueous fugitive releases during manufacturing, use, and disposal have resulted in the global distribution of these compounds. Volatile PFAS facilitate long-range transport, commonly followed by complex transformation schemes to recalcitrant terminal PFAS, which do not degrade under environmental conditions and thus migrate through the environment and accumulate in biota through multiple pathways. Efforts to remediate PFAS-contaminated matrices still are in their infancy, with much current research targeting drinking water.
