name: Sugar
scoreRationale: Chemically benign, but added sugar is one of the clearest dietary risks: excess intake drives dental caries and contributes to weight gain and type 2 diabetes risk.
summary: Table sugar is a plant-derived disaccharide of glucose and fructose. It is safe in small amounts, but most people eat far more added sugar than health guidelines recommend.

physical.solubility: Very soluble in water (about 2,000 g/L at 25 °C); insoluble in oils
physical.phStability: Hydrolyzes in acid, especially when heated

overview: Sucrose, table sugar, is a disaccharide: one glucose ring and one fructose ring joined by a glycosidic bond between their most reactive carbons. Because both “reducing” ends are tied up in that bond, sucrose is a non-reducing sugar and is more chemically stable than glucose.

Its eight hydroxyl (–OH) groups make it extremely water-soluble (about 2 kilograms dissolves in a liter of water) and let it hold onto water in baked goods. Plants make sucrose in their leaves during photosynthesis and use it to move energy to roots, fruit and seeds.
profile.function: Provides sweetness, bulk and moisture retention, feeds yeast in bread, lowers the freezing point of ice cream, and browns during baking. In scrubs it acts as a dissolvable exfoliant.

mechanisms.title: Sweet taste
mechanisms.chemical: Sucrose has eight hydroxyl groups, oxygen–hydrogen (–OH) pairs that stick out from its two rings. On your tongue, taste cells carry a sweet-taste receptor made of two proteins, called T1R2 and T1R3, that fit together like a pair of cupped hands. The hydroxyl groups of sucrose form a precise pattern of hydrogen bonds, weak attractions between a hydrogen atom and a nearby oxygen or nitrogen, with matching spots inside the receptor. When enough of these bonds form, the receptor protein changes its shape slightly. That shape change is the chemical switch that starts the sweet signal. Other sweet molecules, including artificial sweeteners, work by fitting the same receptor in slightly different ways.
mechanisms.biological: Once the receptor changes shape, it sets off a chain of signaling molecules inside the taste cell, a relay called a signaling cascade. The chain ends with the cell releasing a chemical messenger that excites nearby nerve fibers. The nerves carry the message to the brain, which interprets it as sweetness and often as pleasure. Scientists think this system evolved because sweetness signaled energy-rich foods such as ripe fruit, which helped our ancestors survive. Today the same drive makes sugary foods very appealing even when we don't need the extra energy.

mechanisms.title: Digestion and blood sugar
mechanisms.chemical: Sucrose is too large to pass through the gut wall as it is. In the small intestine, an enzyme called sucrase-isomaltase, which sits on the surface of the cells lining the gut, breaks the glycosidic bond, the oxygen bridge that links the glucose ring to the fructose ring. It does this by hydrolysis, using a water molecule to split the bond. An enzyme is a protein that speeds up one particular reaction, and this one works in a fraction of a second. For every sucrose molecule, the result is one free glucose and one free fructose.
mechanisms.biological: Glucose crosses into the blood within minutes, raising blood sugar. The pancreas responds by releasing insulin, a hormone that tells muscle, fat and liver cells to take glucose in and use or store it. Fructose is absorbed by a different transporter called GLUT5 and travels mainly to the liver, where it is turned into glucose, stored as glycogen, or, when large amounts arrive often, converted into fat. Because table sugar has no fiber, protein or fat to slow its digestion, it raises blood sugar faster than foods like whole fruit. Over time, frequent large spikes put extra demand on the body's blood-sugar control system.

mechanisms.title: Tooth decay
mechanisms.chemical: Your mouth is home to hundreds of kinds of bacteria, and some of them, especially Streptococcus mutans, feed on sugar. They break sucrose down by fermentation, a way of getting energy without oxygen, and release lactic acid as waste. S. mutans also uses enzymes called glucosyltransferases to string the glucose halves of sucrose into long, sticky chains called glucans. These glucans act like glue, helping bacteria stick to teeth and to each other and building up the film known as plaque. Inside this film, the acid stays trapped against the tooth surface instead of being washed away by saliva.
mechanisms.biological: Tooth enamel is made mostly of hydroxyapatite, a hard mineral built from calcium and phosphate. When the pH at the tooth surface falls below about 5.5, which happens within minutes of eating sugar, hydrogen ions begin dissolving this mineral and pulling calcium and phosphate out of the enamel. Saliva slowly neutralizes the acid and brings minerals back, repairing early damage, but this takes around 20 to 30 minutes or longer. If sugar is eaten again and again throughout the day, the enamel never gets time to recover. Small weak spots then grow into holes, which are cavities, and fluoride in toothpaste helps by making enamel more resistant to acid and speeding up repair.

reactions.title: Inversion (hydrolysis)
reactions.summary: Sucrose can be split back into its two building blocks, glucose and fructose, in a reaction called inversion. It happens when sugar is heated with an acid, such as lemon juice or cream of tartar, or when it meets an enzyme called invertase. The name comes from how the sugar solution affects polarized light: sucrose rotates the light one way, while the glucose–fructose mixture rotates it the opposite way. Cooks use this reaction, often without knowing it, to keep candies and syrups smooth instead of grainy. Bees carry it out naturally when they make honey.

steps.name: Protonation
steps.text: An acid supplies a hydrogen ion (H⁺) that attaches to the oxygen atom bridging the two sugar rings, called the glycosidic oxygen. The added positive charge pulls electrons toward that oxygen and weakens the bonds around it. In the enzyme invertase, part of the protein does the same job as the acid.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: The weakened bond between the oxygen and the fructose side breaks. Glucose is released, and the fructose part is left behind as a reactive, positively charged fragment. A water molecule quickly attacks this fragment and completes it as a normal fructose molecule.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: The result is an equal mixture of glucose and fructose called invert sugar. No atoms are lost: one sucrose plus one water molecule become two simple sugars.

reactions.result: Invert sugar tastes slightly sweeter than sucrose and, more importantly, resists crystallizing, because a mix of two different sugars can't easily line up into orderly crystals. That keeps fondant, sorbet, fudge and jam smooth. Bees add invertase to flower nectar, which is mostly sucrose, and this is a key step in turning it into honey.

reactions.title: Caramelization
reactions.summary: Caramelization is what happens when sugar is heated on its own until it melts and turns brown. It is different from the browning of bread crusts or seared meat, which also needs proteins and is called the Maillard reaction. As the temperature climbs past about 160 °C, sucrose molecules begin to break apart, lose water and recombine into hundreds of new compounds. Some of these are brown, and many have strong smells and flavors: buttery, nutty, fruity and slightly bitter. The longer and hotter the heating, the darker and more bitter the result.

steps.name: Melting and splitting
steps.text: Above about 160 °C, sucrose crystals melt into a thick liquid. The heat gives the molecules enough energy to break the glycosidic bond, so much of the sucrose splits into glucose and fructose. These simpler sugars are more reactive than sucrose.

steps.name: Dehydration
steps.text: The sugars lose water molecules from their own structure, a type of reaction called dehydration. This rearranges them into new ring-shaped compounds such as hydroxymethylfurfural. These in-between molecules are highly reactive and don't last long.

steps.name: Polymerization
steps.text: The reactive fragments join together into larger and larger molecules, a process called polymerization. The large ones absorb light and look brown. Small ones escape as vapor and give caramel its aroma, including buttery-smelling diacetyl and nutty furans.

reactions.result: The same chemistry, carried out in factories with controlled heating and added reactants such as ammonia or sulfites, produces the caramel colors used in colas, soy sauce and gravies. At home, stopping the heating at the right moment decides whether you get a light, sweet caramel or a dark, bitter one.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; "Added Sugars" must be declared on the Nutrition Facts label.
Recommends free sugars below 10% of daily energy, ideally below 5% (about 25 g for adults).
Limit added sugars to less than 10% of calories from age 2; avoid them entirely before age 2.

hazards.title: Excess added sugar
hazards.summary: Sugar is not a poison, and a small amount in a balanced diet is fine. The concern is the large amount many people eat every day, often without noticing, from drinks, sweets and processed foods. Eating too much added sugar over months and years is linked to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver and tooth decay. Health agencies separate “added” or “free” sugars from the natural sugar inside whole fruit and milk, because the latter comes packaged with fiber, water and nutrients. The risk builds slowly, which is why guidelines focus on daily totals.
hazards.chemical: Free sugars, meaning sugars added to food plus those naturally present in honey, syrups and juice, are digested very quickly. Enzymes in the small intestine split sucrose into glucose and fructose within minutes, and both are absorbed almost at once. Whole foods slow this down: fiber forms a gel that holds sugar back in the gut, while protein and fat delay how fast the stomach empties. Without those brakes, a sugary drink delivers a large load of glucose and fructose to the blood and liver all at once. Sugar also supplies energy, measured in calories, without making people feel very full, so it's easy to take in more than the body needs.
hazards.biological: A rush of glucose triggers a large release of insulin from the pancreas to move the sugar out of the blood. When this happens many times a day for years, especially together with extra body fat and little exercise, cells can become less responsive to insulin, a condition called insulin resistance. The pancreas then has to work harder, and if it can't keep up, blood sugar stays high and type 2 diabetes develops. Meanwhile, large amounts of fructose arriving at the liver are partly turned into fat, which can build up inside the liver itself. Any extra calories that aren't burned are stored as body fat.

hazards.title: Dental caries
hazards.summary: Tooth decay, or dental caries, is one of the most common diseases in the world, and sugar is its main dietary cause. For teeth, how often you eat sugar matters more than how much you eat in one sitting. A dessert after a meal does less damage than the same amount of sugar sipped slowly from a drink over an afternoon. Brushing with fluoride toothpaste and limiting sugary snacks between meals greatly reduce the risk. Children are especially vulnerable because their enamel is still maturing.
hazards.chemical: Every time sugar enters the mouth, bacteria in dental plaque ferment it and release acid, mainly lactic acid. The pH at the tooth surface drops within a few minutes and stays low for roughly 20 to 30 minutes. During that time, hydrogen ions from the acid react with hydroxyapatite, the calcium phosphate mineral of enamel, and pull calcium and phosphate ions out of it, a process called demineralization. Once the sugar is gone, saliva washes away the acid and supplies fresh calcium and phosphate that can rebuild the surface. That rebuilding is called remineralization.
hazards.biological: Enamel is constantly losing and regaining minerals, and whether a tooth stays healthy depends on which side wins. With sugar a few times a day, saliva has time to repair the damage between acid attacks. With constant sipping or snacking, the pH stays low for most of the day and repair never catches up. Chalky white spots appear first, then the weakened surface collapses into a cavity, a hole that can reach the softer dentin and eventually the nerve beneath. At that stage the tooth can't heal itself and needs a filling.

profile.dosage: A teaspoon of sugar (about 4 grams) in a recipe is trivial; what matters is the total over a day. The World Health Organization recommends keeping free sugars below 10 percent of daily energy, and ideally below 5 percent, which is about 25 grams, or six teaspoons, for an adult. A single 12-ounce can of regular soda contains about 39 grams of sugar, already more than that ideal limit. Sweetened drinks, candy, breakfast cereals, flavored yogurts and baked goods supply most added sugar, and U.S. Nutrition Facts labels now list “Added Sugars” on their own line. Sugar inside whole fruit and plain milk does not count toward these limits.

myths.claim: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
myths.consensus: Double-blind trials, summarized in a 1995 JAMA meta-analysis, found no effect of sugar on children's behavior; expectations shape what parents observe.

myths.claim: "Natural" sugars like coconut sugar or raw cane sugar are healthier.
myths.consensus: They are still mostly sucrose and count as added sugar; trace minerals are nutritionally negligible.

environment.persistence: Not persistent; rapidly consumed by microbes.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Non-toxic, though large spills can deplete oxygen in waterways as microbes consume it.
environment.notes: Cane cultivation drives land-use change and field burning in some regions.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis (photosynthesis)
synthesis.summary: Every grain of table sugar was originally made by a plant using sunlight. Plants capture energy from light and store it in the chemical bonds of sugars, starting from nothing more than carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil. Sucrose is the form in which many plants send that stored energy from their leaves to the rest of the plant. Sugar cane and sugar beets are simply plants that store unusually large amounts of it. The whole process is called photosynthesis.
synthesis.mechanism: Inside leaf cells are tiny green structures called chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll, the pigment that absorbs light. The light's energy is used to split water and to charge up energy-carrying molecules called ATP and NADPH. These power a loop of reactions called the Calvin cycle, in which an enzyme named RuBisCO attaches carbon dioxide from the air onto an existing sugar, building three-carbon sugar units. Some of these units are exported into the surrounding cell fluid, where other enzymes assemble them into two larger sugars, UDP-glucose and fructose-6-phosphate. The enzyme sucrose-phosphate synthase joins these two together, and a second enzyme snips off the phosphate group, releasing sucrose.
synthesis.significance: Sucrose is the plant's transport sugar: stable, non-reducing (so it doesn't react easily with other molecules) and easy to pump through the phloem, the plant's sap-carrying tubes, to fruit, roots and seeds.

synthesis.title: Industrial extraction
synthesis.summary: Sugar refineries don't make sucrose; they extract and purify the sucrose that sugar cane and sugar beets have already made. Cane is a tall tropical grass and beets are root vegetables grown in cooler climates, but the sugar from both is chemically identical. The challenge is separating pure sucrose from everything else in the plant juice, including fibers, proteins, minerals and colored compounds. The process relies on dissolving, filtering, evaporating and crystallizing. The leftovers include molasses, which is used in food, animal feed and fermentation.
synthesis.mechanism: First the sugar is released into water: cane is crushed between heavy rollers, while beets are sliced into thin strips and soaked in hot water. The juice is cloudy with impurities, so lime (calcium hydroxide) is added and then carbon dioxide gas is bubbled through it. The two react to form calcium carbonate, chalk-like particles that trap proteins, colored compounds and other impurities as they settle, leaving a clearer juice. That juice is boiled under vacuum, which lowers its boiling point so the sugar doesn't burn, until it becomes a thick syrup. Tiny sugar crystals are added as seeds, and sucrose molecules from the syrup build onto them, growing larger crystals. Finally, centrifuges spin the mixture so fast that the dark liquid, molasses, is flung away from the white crystals.
synthesis.significance: Brown sugar is usually white sugar with a little molasses added back, which gives it color, moisture and flavor.

citations.title: Glycosyltransferases: structures, functions, and mechanisms.
citations.abstract: Glycosyltransferases catalyze glycosidic bond formation using sugar donors containing a nucleoside phosphate or a lipid phosphate leaving group. Only two structural folds, GT-A and GT-B, have been identified for the nucleotide sugar-dependent enzymes, but other folds are now appearing for the soluble domains of lipid phosphosugar-dependent glycosyl transferases. Structural and kinetic studies have provided new insights. Inverting glycosyltransferases utilize a direct displacement S(N)2-like mechanism involving an enzymatic base catalyst. Leaving group departure in GT-A fold enzymes is typically facilitated via a coordinated divalent cation, whereas GT-B fold enzymes instead use positively charged side chains and/or hydroxyls and helix dipoles. The mechanism of retaining glycosyltransferases is less clear. The expected two-step double-displacement mechanism is rendered less likely by the lack of conserved architecture in the region where a catalytic nucleophile would be expected. A mechanism involving a short-lived oxocarbenium ion intermediate now seems the most likely, with the leaving phosphate serving as the base.

citations.title: Complete biosynthesis of QS-21 in engineered yeast.
citations.abstract: QS-21 is a potent vaccine adjuvant and remains the only saponin-based adjuvant that has been clinically approved for use in humans1,2. However, owing to the complex structure of QS-21, its availability is limited. Today, the supply depends on laborious extraction from the Chilean soapbark tree or on low-yielding total chemical synthesis3,4. Here we demonstrate the complete biosynthesis of QS-21 and its precursors, as well as structural derivatives, in engineered yeast strains. The successful biosynthesis in yeast requires fine-tuning of the host's native pathway fluxes, as well as the functional and balanced expression of 38 heterologous enzymes. The required biosynthetic pathway spans seven enzyme families-a terpene synthase, P450s, nucleotide sugar synthases, glycosyltransferases, a coenzyme A ligase, acyl transferases and polyketide synthases-from six organisms, and mimics in yeast the subcellular compartmentalization of plants from the endoplasmic reticulum membrane to the cytosol. Finally, by taking advantage of the promiscuity of certain pathway enzymes, we produced structural analogues of QS-21 using this biosynthetic platform. This microbial production scheme will allow for the future establishment of a structure-activity relationship, and will thus enable the rational design of potent vaccine adjuvants.

citations.title: Complementary Feeding: A Position Paper by the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) Committee on Nutrition.
citations.abstract: Unlabelled: This position paper considers different aspects of complementary feeding (CF), focussing on healthy term infants in Europe. After reviewing current knowledge and practices, we have formulated these recommendations: Timing: Exclusive or full breast-feeding should be promoted for at least 4 months (17 weeks, beginning of the 5th month of life) and exclusive or predominant breast-feeding for approximately 6 months (26 weeks, beginning of the 7th month) is a desirable goal. Complementary foods (solids and liquids other than breast milk or infant formula) should not be introduced before 4 months but should not be delayed beyond 6 months. Content: Infants should be offered foods with a variety of flavours and textures including bitter tasting green vegetables. Continued breast-feeding is recommended alongside CF. Whole cows' milk should not be used as the main drink before 12 months of age. Allergenic foods may be introduced when CF is commenced any time after 4 months. Infants at high risk of peanut allergy (those with severe eczema, egg allergy, or both) should have peanut introduced between 4 and 11 months, following evaluation by an appropriately trained specialist. Gluten may be introduced between 4 and 12 months, but consumption of large quantities should be avoided during the first weeks after gluten introduction and later during infancy. All infants should receive iron-rich CF including meat products and/or iron-fortified foods. No sugar or salt should be added to CF and fruit juices or sugar-sweetened beverages should be avoided. Vegan diets should only be used under appropriate medical or dietetic supervision and parents should understand the serious consequences of failing to follow advice regarding supplementation of the diet. Method: Parents should be encouraged to respond to their infant's hunger and satiety queues and to avoid feeding to comfort or as a reward.

citations.title: Ultra-processed foods, allergy outcomes and underlying mechanisms in children: An EAACI task force report.
citations.authors: Berni Canani, Carucci, Coppola et al.
citations.abstract: Background: Consumption of ultra-processed foods [UPFs] may be associated with negative health outcomes. Limited data exist regarding the potential role of UPFs in the occurrence of allergic diseases. The underlying mechanisms underpinning any such associations are also poorly elucidated. Methods: We performed a systematic review and narrative evidence synthesis of the available literature to assess associations between UPF consumption and pediatric allergy outcomes (n = 26 papers), including data on the association seen with the gut microbiome (n = 16 papers) or immune system (n = 3 papers) structure and function following PRISMA guidelines. Results: Dietary exposure to fructose, carbonated soft drinks, and sugar intake was associated with an increased risk of asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergies in children. Commercial baby food intake was associated with childhood food allergy. Childhood intake of fructose, fruit juices, sugar-sweetened beverages, high carbohydrate UPFs, monosodium glutamate, UPFs, and advanced glycated end-products (AGEs) was associated with the occurrence of allergic diseases. Exposure to UPFs and common ingredients in UPFs seem to be associated with increased occurrence of allergic diseases such as asthma, wheezing, food allergies, atopic dermatitis, and allergic rhinitis, in many, but not all studies. Conclusion: More preclinical and clinical studies are required to better define the link between UPF consumption and the risk of allergies and asthma. These observational studies ideally require supporting data with clearly defined UPF consumption, validated dietary measures, and mechanistic assessments to definitively link UPFs with the risk of allergies and asthma.

citations.title: Modification of extracellular matrix proteins by oxidants and electrophiles.
citations.abstract: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is critical to biological architecture and determines cellular properties, function and activity. In many situations it is highly abundant, with collagens and elastin being some of the most abundant proteins in mammals. The ECM comprises of multiple different protein species and sugar polymers, with both different isoforms and post-translational modifications (PTMs) providing a large variety of microenvironments that play a key role in determining tissue structure and health. A number of the PTMs (e.g. cross-links) present in the ECM are critical to integrity and function, whereas others are deleterious to both ECM structure and associated cells. Modifications induced by reactive oxidants and electrophiles have been reported to accumulate in some ECM with increasing age. This accumulation can be exacerbated by disease, and in particular those associated with acute or chronic inflammation, obesity and diabetes. This is likely to be due to higher fluxes of modifying agents in these conditions. In this focused review, the role and effects of oxidants and other electrophiles on ECM are discussed, with a particular focus on the artery wall and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Modifications generated on ECM components are reviewed, together with the effects of these species on cellular properties including adhesion, proliferation, migration, viability, metabolic activity, gene expression and phenotype. Increasing data indicates that ECM modifications are both prevalent in human and mammalian tissues and play an important role in disease development and progression.

name: Salt
scoreRationale: Essential in small amounts, but typical diets exceed recommended sodium, which raises blood pressure in many people. In cosmetics it is a harmless thickener.
summary: Salt seasons and preserves food and thickens shampoos. The body needs sodium, but most people eat roughly 50% more than recommended.

physical.phStability: Neutral and stable at all pH values

overview: Sodium chloride is an ionic compound. Sodium gives up one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that attract each other strongly. The ions stack into a cubic crystal lattice in which every sodium is surrounded by six chlorides, and every chloride by six sodiums, which is why salt grains are tiny cubes.

When salt dissolves, water's partial charges pull the lattice apart into separate, water-coated ions. Those free ions are what you taste, what lets salt water conduct electricity, and what your nerves use to send signals.
profile.function: Enhances flavor, controls fermentation in bread, preserves by lowering water activity, and in shampoos thickens surfactant mixtures by packing micelles into worm-like shapes.

mechanisms.title: Nerve and muscle signaling
mechanisms.chemical: Every cell membrane contains a protein machine called the sodium–potassium pump. Using energy from ATP, the cell's energy currency, it pushes three sodium ions (Na⁺) out of the cell for every two potassium ions (K⁺) it brings in. Because it moves charged particles unevenly, the pump builds up two things at once: a large difference in sodium concentration across the membrane and a small electrical voltage, with the inside of the cell negative compared with the outside. This stored difference is like water held behind a dam, ready to rush through when a gate opens. The gates are channel proteins that let only sodium through when they open.
mechanisms.biological: When a nerve cell receives a strong enough signal, sodium channels in its membrane open and Na⁺ ions rush in, pulled by the negative inside and pushed by the concentration difference. The flood of positive charge flips the voltage across that patch of membrane, which opens the channels in the next patch, so the change travels along the nerve like a falling row of dominoes. This traveling wave is called an action potential. Muscle fibers, including heart muscle, use the same system to trigger each contraction. Every heartbeat, movement and thought depends on it, which is why the body keeps the sodium level in the blood within a narrow range.

mechanisms.title: Salty taste
mechanisms.chemical: When salt dissolves in saliva, it separates into sodium ions (Na⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻). Some taste cells on the tongue carry a protein called the epithelial sodium channel, or ENaC, a narrow tunnel through the cell membrane that lets sodium ions pass. Because sodium is positively charged, its entry changes the electrical voltage across the taste cell's membrane. This is an unusually direct way of tasting: instead of a molecule fitting into a receptor and changing its shape, the ion itself carries the signal into the cell. Other positive ions, such as potassium, fit the channel less well, which is one reason salt substitutes taste different.
mechanisms.biological: The incoming positive charge makes the taste cell more electrically active, so it releases chemical messengers that excite the nerve fibers connected to it. The brain reads this as “salty.” At low to moderate concentrations salt tastes pleasant, which encourages people and animals to seek out sodium, an essential mineral the body cannot make for itself. At very high concentrations other taste pathways kick in and salt starts to taste unpleasant, which helps prevent overdoing it. Our liking for salt is also shaped by habit: people who cut back for a few weeks often find their taste adjusts and foods start to taste saltier.

mechanisms.title: Blood pressure
mechanisms.chemical: Sodium is the main dissolved particle in the fluid outside our cells, including blood plasma. The total concentration of dissolved particles in a fluid is called its osmolality, and the body works hard to keep it constant. When we eat extra salt, the sodium concentration in the blood rises slightly. Sensors in the brain notice this and trigger thirst along with the release of a hormone that tells the kidneys to hold onto water. The extra water dilutes the sodium back to normal, but it also increases the total volume of fluid inside the blood vessels.
mechanisms.biological: With more fluid filling the same vessels, the pressure inside them rises, much like pumping more air into a tire. Over time, a high-salt diet may also affect hormones and make the walls of blood vessels stiffer. Not everyone responds the same way: some people, described as salt-sensitive, show a large rise in blood pressure with salt, and this is more common in older adults and in people with high blood pressure or kidney disease. Randomized controlled trials, in which people are assigned by chance to eat more or less salt, show that cutting sodium lowers blood pressure. High blood pressure, in turn, raises the risk of strokes and heart attacks.

mechanisms.title: Preserving food
mechanisms.chemical: When salt dissolves, each sodium and chloride ion gathers a shell of water molecules around itself, called a hydration shell. Water locked into these shells isn't free to move around or take part in other processes. Food scientists measure how much free water is left using water activity, a number that runs from 0 to 1. Enough salt can push the water activity of a food below the level most bacteria need to grow, which is around 0.91. This is the same idea that lets sugar preserve jam.
mechanisms.biological: Microbes are wrapped in a membrane that water can cross. When a bacterium sits in a very salty environment, the water inside the cell is more dilute than the water outside, so water flows out of the cell by osmosis, the movement of water toward a more concentrated solution. The cell shrinks and dries out, and its internal chemistry slows down or stops. Most disease-causing and spoilage bacteria cannot grow under these conditions. This is the principle behind curing ham, salting fish, pickling vegetables in brine and making cheese, methods people have relied on for thousands of years.

reactions.title: Dissolving
reactions.summary: Dissolving salt in water looks simple, but at the scale of atoms it is a tug-of-war. In a salt crystal, positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions are held together by strong electrical attractions called ionic bonds. Water molecules are polar, meaning one end is slightly negative and the other slightly positive, so they can tug on these ions. When the pull between water and the ions is strong enough, the crystal comes apart. Strictly speaking, dissolving is a physical change rather than a chemical reaction, because no new substances form: evaporate the water and you get the salt back.

steps.name: Attraction
steps.text: Water molecules crowd around the crystal and turn so that their slightly negative oxygen ends face the positive sodium ions and their slightly positive hydrogen ends face the negative chloride ions. Ions at the corners and edges of the crystal have the fewest neighbors holding them in place, so they are pulled away first.

steps.name: Separation
steps.text: As soon as an ion breaks free, it is surrounded by a shell of water molecules, called a hydration shell. The shell stops the ion from rejoining the crystal and lets it spread evenly through the water. This continues layer by layer until the whole crystal is gone or the water can hold no more.

steps.name: Entropy
steps.text: Breaking up the crystal takes in slightly more energy than forming the hydration shells gives back, so the water gets a little cooler. The process still happens because the ions become far more spread out and disordered, an increase in what scientists call entropy. Left alone, natural systems tend to move toward greater disorder.

reactions.result: Dissolving salt cools water very slightly, and salty water freezes at a lower temperature than pure water, because the dissolved ions get in the way of water molecules locking into ice crystals. This freezing-point depression is why salt is spread on icy roads. The matching effect on boiling point is too small to matter when you salt pasta water; that salt is there for flavor.

reactions.title: Chlor-alkali electrolysis
reactions.summary: Electrolysis means using electricity to drive a chemical reaction that would not happen on its own. When an electric current passes through a concentrated solution of salt in water, called brine, it produces three valuable chemicals at once: chlorine gas, hydrogen gas and sodium hydroxide, also known as lye or caustic soda. This chlor-alkali process is one of the largest operations in the chemical industry and uses enormous amounts of electricity. Two metal or carbon plates called electrodes sit in the brine and are connected to a power supply. The positive electrode is called the anode and the negative one the cathode.

steps.name: Oxidation at the anode
steps.text: Negative chloride ions (Cl⁻) are attracted to the positive anode, where each one gives up an electron. Losing electrons is called oxidation. Two chlorine atoms that have lost their extra electrons pair up into a molecule of chlorine gas (Cl₂), which bubbles off and is collected.

steps.name: Reduction at the cathode
steps.text: At the negative cathode, water molecules gain electrons, which is called reduction. Each water molecule that gains an electron splits, releasing hydrogen gas (H₂) and leaving behind a hydroxide ion (OH⁻). The hydrogen is collected as a useful byproduct.

steps.name: Separation
steps.text: A special membrane between the two sides lets positive sodium ions (Na⁺) cross over to join the hydroxide ions, forming sodium hydroxide solution. The membrane blocks chlorine from mixing with the sodium hydroxide, because the two would otherwise react with each other. Keeping them apart lets each product be collected pure.

reactions.result: From plain salt water, industry gets chlorine for disinfecting drinking water and making PVC plastic, sodium hydroxide for soap, paper and aluminum production, and hydrogen. Household bleach is made by deliberately letting the chlorine and sodium hydroxide react together. That makes salt the starting point for a huge range of everyday products.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; FDA issued voluntary sodium-reduction targets for processed foods in 2021.
Recommends under 2 g of sodium (5 g of salt) per day for adults.
Limit sodium to under 2,300 mg per day for ages 14 and up.

hazards.title: High blood pressure from excess sodium
hazards.summary: For most people, the health risk from salt comes from eating too much of it every day for years, not from any single food or meal. High salt intake is one of the leading dietary risk factors for high blood pressure, which usually has no symptoms but quietly strains the heart and blood vessels. Most of the salt people eat is already in processed and restaurant foods such as bread, cheese, cured meats, soups and snacks, not added from the shaker. People with high blood pressure, kidney disease or a family history of heart disease benefit most from cutting back. Eating more potassium-rich foods like fruit, vegetables and beans also helps offset sodium's effect.
hazards.chemical: When sodium intake stays high day after day, the body keeps holding extra water to keep blood sodium at its normal concentration, so blood volume stays slightly raised. High sodium also seems to make the smooth muscle in artery walls tighter and the walls themselves stiffer over time. Both changes increase the resistance the heart has to pump against. Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing on artery walls, so more volume plus more resistance means higher pressure. The kidneys normally get rid of excess sodium, but in salt-sensitive people they do so less efficiently.
hazards.biological: Years of high blood pressure damage the delicate inner lining of arteries, making it easier for fatty plaques to build up and for vessels to narrow, harden or burst. The heart muscle thickens from working harder, which can eventually weaken it. Small blood vessels in the brain, eyes and kidneys are especially vulnerable. This is why high blood pressure raises the risk of stroke, heart attack, heart failure and kidney disease. Because blood pressure usually causes no symptoms until damage is done, health agencies set daily sodium targets for everyone, not only for people who already have high blood pressure.

hazards.title: Acute salt poisoning
hazards.summary: Eating a very large amount of salt at once can be dangerous, although it is rare. Cases mostly involve small children who swallow salt or very salty liquids, people who drink seawater, or old-fashioned home remedies that use salt water to make someone vomit. Just a couple of teaspoons can be dangerous for a toddler, whose body is small. The symptoms come from a sudden rise in the sodium level of the blood. Emergency treatment carefully restores the body's water balance.
hazards.chemical: Swallowing a large amount of salt quickly floods the blood with sodium faster than the kidneys can remove it. Blood sodium then rises above its normal range of about 135 to 145 millimoles per liter, a condition called hypernatremia. The concentration of dissolved particles in the blood becomes much higher than the concentration inside the body's cells. Water always tends to move toward the more concentrated side of a membrane, and in this case that means out of the cells and into the blood.
hazards.biological: As water leaves by osmosis, cells throughout the body shrink. Brain cells are especially affected, and as the brain shrinks it can pull on the small blood vessels that connect it to the skull, sometimes tearing them and causing bleeding. Early symptoms include intense thirst, vomiting and irritability, followed by confusion, muscle twitching and, in severe cases, seizures. Treatment means giving water back slowly and carefully, because correcting sodium too quickly can make brain cells swell. This is why vomiting should never be induced with salt water.

profile.dosage: The World Health Organization recommends that adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which is 5 grams of salt, or about one teaspoon; the global average is roughly double that. In the United States, about 70 percent of dietary sodium comes from processed and restaurant foods, so the salt shaker plays only a small part. Food labels list sodium in milligrams, and a useful rule of thumb is that 5 percent of the Daily Value or less per serving is low, while 20 percent or more is high. Harm from any single product is unlikely. What matters is the total across all meals, every day.

myths.claim: Sea salt and pink Himalayan salt are healthier than table salt.
myths.consensus: By weight they contain about the same sodium; trace minerals are negligible, and they usually lack the iodine added to table salt.

myths.claim: Salt in shampoo damages hair.
myths.consensus: At the 1–2% used for thickening, sodium chloride is not shown to harm hair; the idea mostly comes from marketing for salt-free products.

environment.persistence: Chloride does not break down and accumulates in fresh water.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Road-salt runoff raises chloride levels that can harm freshwater organisms.

synthesis.title: Solar evaporation of seawater
synthesis.summary: One of the oldest ways to make salt is simply to let the sun dry up seawater. Seawater is about 3.5 percent dissolved salts, most of it sodium chloride. In warm, sunny, windy places, seawater is let into large, shallow ponds called salt pans and left to evaporate over weeks or months. As the water disappears, the dissolved salts become more and more concentrated until they come out as crystals. The method uses almost no fuel, since the sun and wind do the work.
synthesis.mechanism: Every dissolved substance has a limit to how much can stay dissolved in a given amount of water, called its solubility. As the sun evaporates water from the ponds, the remaining brine gets more concentrated, and each salt crystallizes out when its concentration passes its own limit. Salt makers move the brine through a series of ponds so that different salts settle out in different places. The least soluble salts, such as calcium carbonate and calcium sulfate (gypsum), crystallize first. Sodium chloride crystallizes next, in the later ponds, where it is raked or scooped up. The very soluble magnesium and potassium salts stay dissolved in the leftover liquid, called bittern, which is drained away.
synthesis.significance: This is fractional crystallization: separating a mixture of substances by how soluble they are, a technique chemists also use in the lab to purify compounds.

synthesis.title: Mining and vacuum evaporation
synthesis.summary: Most of the world's salt comes not from today's oceans but from ancient seas that dried up millions of years ago. Their salt was buried under layers of rock, forming thick underground beds of rock salt. Some of it is mined directly with machinery, much like coal, and is used mostly for de-icing roads. Table salt is usually made by dissolving underground salt in water and then purifying it. These methods supply the huge, steady amounts of salt that industry needs.
synthesis.mechanism: In solution mining, water is pumped down a well into a salt bed, where it dissolves the salt and becomes brine, which is then pumped back to the surface. The brine is treated to remove calcium and magnesium and then boiled in a series of closed containers called vacuum pans. Lowering the air pressure inside the pans lowers the temperature at which water boils, so less energy is needed, and the steam from one pan is even used to heat the next. As the water boils off, fine, uniform salt crystals form. They are collected, dried and sometimes mixed with an anti-caking agent so they pour freely.
synthesis.significance: Adding a little iodine, usually as potassium iodide, to table salt prevents iodine deficiency, which can cause goiter and harm brain development in children. Salt iodization is considered one of history's most successful public-health measures.

citations.title: Bile salt biotransformations by human intestinal bacteria.
citations.abstract: Secondary bile acids, produced solely by intestinal bacteria, can accumulate to high levels in the enterohepatic circulation of some individuals and may contribute to the pathogenesis of colon cancer, gallstones, and other gastrointestinal (GI) diseases. Bile salt hydrolysis and hydroxy group dehydrogenation reactions are carried out by a broad spectrum of intestinal anaerobic bacteria, whereas bile acid 7-dehydroxylation appears restricted to a limited number of intestinal anaerobes representing a small fraction of the total colonic flora. Microbial enzymes modifying bile salts differ between species with respect to pH optima, enzyme kinetics, substrate specificity, cellular location, and possibly physiological function. Crystallization, site-directed mutagenesis, and comparisons of protein secondary structure have provided insight into the mechanisms of several bile acid-biotransforming enzymatic reactions. Molecular cloning of genes encoding bile salt-modifying enzymes has facilitated the understanding of the genetic organization of these pathways and is a means of developing probes for the detection of bile salt-modifying bacteria. The potential exists for altering the bile acid pool by targeting key enzymes in the 7alpha/beta-dehydroxylation pathway through the development of pharmaceuticals or sequestering bile acids biologically in probiotic bacteria, which may result in their effective removal from the host after excretion.

citations.title: Marine enzymes.
citations.abstract: Marine enzyme biotechnology can offer novel biocatalysts with properties like high salt tolerance, hyperthermostability, barophilicity, cold adaptivity, and ease in large-scale cultivation. This review deals with the research and development work done on the occurrence, molecular biology, and bioprocessing of marine enzymes during the last decade. Exotic locations have been accessed for the search of novel enzymes. Scientists have isolated proteases and carbohydrases from deep sea hydrothermal vents. Cold active metabolic enzymes from psychrophilic marine microorganisms have received considerable research attention. Marine symbiont microorganisms growing in association with animals and plants were shown to produce enzymes of commercial interest. Microorganisms isolated from sediment and seawater have been the most widely studied, proteases, carbohydrases, and peroxidases being noteworthy. Enzymes from marine animals and plants were primarily studied for their metabolic roles, though proteases and peroxidases have found industrial applications. Novel techniques in molecular biology applied to assess the diversity of chitinases, nitrate, nitrite, ammonia-metabolizing, and pollutant-degrading enzymes are discussed. Genes encoding chitinases, proteases, and carbohydrases from microbial and animal sources have been cloned and characterized. Research on the bioprocessing of marine-derived enzymes, however, has been scanty, focusing mainly on the application of solid-state fermentation to the production of enzymes from microbial sources.

citations.title: Complementary Feeding: A Position Paper by the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) Committee on Nutrition.
citations.abstract: Unlabelled: This position paper considers different aspects of complementary feeding (CF), focussing on healthy term infants in Europe. After reviewing current knowledge and practices, we have formulated these recommendations: Timing: Exclusive or full breast-feeding should be promoted for at least 4 months (17 weeks, beginning of the 5th month of life) and exclusive or predominant breast-feeding for approximately 6 months (26 weeks, beginning of the 7th month) is a desirable goal. Complementary foods (solids and liquids other than breast milk or infant formula) should not be introduced before 4 months but should not be delayed beyond 6 months. Content: Infants should be offered foods with a variety of flavours and textures including bitter tasting green vegetables. Continued breast-feeding is recommended alongside CF. Whole cows' milk should not be used as the main drink before 12 months of age. Allergenic foods may be introduced when CF is commenced any time after 4 months. Infants at high risk of peanut allergy (those with severe eczema, egg allergy, or both) should have peanut introduced between 4 and 11 months, following evaluation by an appropriately trained specialist. Gluten may be introduced between 4 and 12 months, but consumption of large quantities should be avoided during the first weeks after gluten introduction and later during infancy. All infants should receive iron-rich CF including meat products and/or iron-fortified foods. No sugar or salt should be added to CF and fruit juices or sugar-sweetened beverages should be avoided. Vegan diets should only be used under appropriate medical or dietetic supervision and parents should understand the serious consequences of failing to follow advice regarding supplementation of the diet. Method: Parents should be encouraged to respond to their infant's hunger and satiety queues and to avoid feeding to comfort or as a reward.

citations.title: Buffering Capacity.
citations.abstract: Each biological system possesses a widely unrecognized buffer system to maintain acid-base balance to a specific pH. Our lives are dependent on the functioning of buffer systems. A buffer system is a solution that resists a change in pH when acids or bases are added. The skin possesses a fairly high buffer capacity, which is determined by the amount of H+ or OH- ions that is needed until the pH value of a solution changes by the unit 1. Buffers contain a weak or medium strong acid (base) and the corresponding salt. Buffers that show a pKa in the range of the Stratum corneum surface pH are most important for the skin. Buffer capacity is reduced both in baby skin and in aged skin. External factors, water, and detergent may reduce the local buffer capacity because of the elution of buffer chemicals leading to increased pH and irritative contact dermatitis. Inflammatory diseases, including atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, and acne vulgaris, which show an increased pH should probably also have reduced buffer capacities. For the treatment of the skin diseases and in aged skin, emollient with a pH that is slightly more acidic than the average normal pH and an appropriate buffer capacity should be preferably used.

citations.title: Plastic Degradation by Extremophilic Bacteria.
citations.abstract: Intensive exploitation, poor recycling, low repeatable use, and unusual resistance of plastics to environmental and microbiological action result in accumulation of huge waste amounts in terrestrial and marine environments, causing enormous hazard for human and animal life. In the last decades, much scientific interest has been focused on plastic biodegradation. Due to the comparatively short evolutionary period of their appearance in nature, sufficiently effective enzymes for their biodegradation are not available. Plastics are designed for use in conditions typical for human activity, and their physicochemical properties roughly change at extreme environmental parameters like low temperatures, salt, or low or high pH that are typical for the life of extremophilic microorganisms and the activity of their enzymes. This review represents a first attempt to summarize the extraordinarily limited information on biodegradation of conventional synthetic plastics by thermophilic, alkaliphilic, halophilic, and psychrophilic bacteria in natural environments and laboratory conditions. Most of the available data was reported in the last several years and concerns moderate extremophiles. Two main questions are highlighted in it: which extremophilic bacteria and their enzymes are reported to be involved in the degradation of different synthetic plastics, and what could be the impact of extremophiles in future technologies for resolving of pollution problems.
