name: Citric Acid
scoreRationale: A natural metabolite with an exceptional safety record; the main caveat is enamel erosion from frequent acidic drinks.
summary: Citric acid gives lemons their sourness. Made by fermentation, it adds tartness, adjusts pH and captures metal ions in foods, cosmetics and descalers.

physical.solubility: Very soluble in water; soluble in ethanol

overview: Citric acid is a six-carbon molecule carrying three carboxylic acid groups (–COOH) and one hydroxyl group (–OH). Each carboxylic acid group can release a proton, so citric acid is a triprotic weak acid, with pKa values of about 3.1, 4.8 and 6.4.

Those three carboxylate arms can wrap around a metal ion like a claw, a property called chelation (from the Greek chele, claw), which makes citric acid useful far beyond adding sourness. It is also central to life: every cell that breathes oxygen makes and breaks down citrate in the Krebs cycle.
profile.function: Adds tartness, lowers pH to help preservatives work, chelates metals that would otherwise catalyze spoilage, and dissolves limescale in cleaners.

mechanisms.title: Energy metabolism (the Krebs cycle)
mechanisms.chemical: Every cell that uses oxygen runs a loop of chemical reactions called the Krebs cycle, also known as the citric acid cycle, inside tiny structures called mitochondria. The loop begins when an enzyme called citrate synthase joins a two-carbon fragment, carried by a molecule named acetyl-CoA, onto a four-carbon molecule called oxaloacetate, producing six-carbon citrate. Over the next several steps, other enzymes rearrange the citrate and remove two of its carbons as carbon dioxide (CO₂), the gas we breathe out. Along the way they strip off electrons and hand them to carrier molecules. At the end of the loop, oxaloacetate has been rebuilt, ready to start again.
mechanisms.biological: The electrons collected during the cycle are passed along a chain of proteins in the mitochondria, and the energy they release is used to make ATP, the molecule cells use to power almost everything they do. The two-carbon fragments that feed the cycle come from breaking down sugars, fats and proteins in food, which is why the Krebs cycle is called the central hub of metabolism. Because our cells make and use citrate constantly, the citric acid in fruit and processed food is nothing foreign to the body. It is absorbed and fed into this same pathway or excreted. Your own metabolism handles far more citrate every day than any food adds.

mechanisms.title: Sour taste
mechanisms.chemical: Acids are substances that release hydrogen ions (H⁺), also called protons, when dissolved in water. Citric acid can release up to three protons per molecule, but it is a weak acid, meaning only a small share of its molecules let go of a proton at any moment. Sour-sensing taste cells on the tongue have a channel protein called OTOP1, a tiny pore that lets protons pass into the cell. When citric acid is in your mouth, protons flow through these pores and make the inside of the taste cell more acidic. Uncharged citric acid molecules can also slip into the cell and release their protons once inside.
mechanisms.biological: As the inside of the taste cell becomes more acidic, the cell's electrical state changes and it fires a signal to nerves that carry it to the brain, which reads it as sour. Sourness helps animals detect unripe fruit and spoiled food, both of which tend to be acidic. At moderate levels, sourness makes food taste fresh and bright, and it balances sweetness, which is why lemonade needs both sugar and acid. Because citric acid is a weak acid, it tastes tart rather than harsh, and the taste fades quickly as saliva neutralizes it. That clean sourness is why it is the most widely used acid in foods and drinks.

mechanisms.title: Exfoliation (as an alpha-hydroxy acid)
mechanisms.chemical: Citric acid belongs to a family called alpha-hydroxy acids, or AHAs: molecules with a hydroxyl group (–OH) on the carbon right next to an acid group. The outermost layer of skin is made of dead, flattened cells joined by protein connections called desmosomes, which work like rivets. At low pH, acids weaken the ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds that hold these protein rivets together, and citrate may also grab some of the calcium ions that help keep them stable. With the rivets loosened, dead cells separate from each other more easily. The lower the pH and the higher the concentration, the stronger the effect.
mechanisms.biological: Skin naturally sheds its dead outer cells, but the process can slow down, leaving the surface rough or dull. When an acid loosens the connections between dead cells, they are shed faster, so the surface looks smoother and more even. With regular use, AHAs may also encourage the deeper skin to renew itself. Citric acid, however, is a milder exfoliant than glycolic or lactic acid and is less often used for this purpose. In most cosmetics it appears in tiny amounts, below 1 percent, simply to set the product's pH so that the other ingredients stay stable.

mechanisms.title: Antioxidant helper
mechanisms.chemical: Metal ions such as iron (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺) and copper (Cu²⁺) are powerful catalysts for oxidation, the reaction in which oxygen attacks fats, vitamins and colors and breaks them down. They can trigger the formation of free radicals, highly reactive molecules with an unpaired electron that start chain reactions of damage. Citric acid's three carboxylate groups can wrap around a metal ion and hold it from several sides at once, like a claw. This grip is called chelation, and the bundle it forms is called a complex. A metal that is chelated can't easily take part in reactions, so it stops speeding up oxidation.
mechanisms.biological: By locking up stray metal ions, citric acid slows the processes that make oils taste rancid, colors fade and vitamins lose potency. In packaged foods and cosmetics, that means a longer shelf life and fresher flavor or scent. Citric acid also helps true antioxidants such as vitamin C and vitamin E last longer, because they no longer get used up fighting metal-driven reactions. That is why it is often called a synergist, a helper that makes other ingredients more effective. It is one of the cheapest and safest ways to protect a product from oxygen.

reactions.title: Neutralization with baking soda (the bath-bomb reaction)
reactions.summary: When an acid meets a base, they react and cancel out each other's properties in a reaction called neutralization. Citric acid and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) are a classic pair: mix them in water and they fizz hard as carbon dioxide gas forms. The reaction powers bath bombs, effervescent vitamin tablets, some antacids and many kitchen science experiments. Surprisingly, the two powders can sit mixed together for months without reacting, as long as they stay dry. Water is needed because it lets the molecules break apart into ions that can move around and meet.

steps.name: Proton donation
steps.text: In water, citric acid releases hydrogen ions (protons), up to three from each molecule. Bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) from the baking soda are good at accepting protons. Each bicarbonate picks up one proton.

steps.name: Carbonic acid
steps.text: A bicarbonate ion that has accepted a proton becomes carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). Carbonic acid is unstable and can't stay in that form for long. It is the same substance that forms briefly in fizzy drinks.

steps.name: Gas release
steps.text: Carbonic acid quickly breaks apart into water and carbon dioxide gas. The carbon dioxide forms bubbles that rise and escape, producing the fizz. What stays dissolved is sodium citrate, a mild salt.

reactions.result: The products are harmless: sodium citrate, water and carbon dioxide. Because the dry powders don't react, bath bombs and effervescent tablets stay stable until they hit water. Bakers rely on a similar acid-plus-bicarbonate reaction in baking powder to make cakes rise.

reactions.title: Chelation and descaling
reactions.summary: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium, which leave white, crusty deposits called limescale in kettles, coffee makers, showerheads and dishwashers. Limescale is mostly calcium carbonate, the same mineral found in chalk and limestone. Citric acid removes it in two ways at once: it dissolves the scale with acid, and then it grabs the freed calcium so the scale can't re-form. That makes it a popular, food-safe descaler. The same ability to hold onto calcium is why it is used as a water softener in eco-friendly detergents.

steps.name: Acid attack
steps.text: Protons from citric acid react with the calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) in the scale. The carbonate part turns into carbonic acid, which breaks down into water and carbon dioxide gas, so you may see small bubbles as descaling begins. This leaves calcium ions (Ca²⁺) free in the water.

steps.name: Binding
steps.text: Citrate, the form of citric acid that has lost its protons, has three negatively charged carboxylate groups. These can wrap around a positively charged calcium ion and grip it from several sides at once, forming a stable bundle called a complex. This grabbing action is chelation.

steps.name: Clearing
steps.text: Because the calcium is now held by citrate, it can't easily recombine with carbonate to form new scale. The calcium citrate complexes stay dissolved and are rinsed away with the water.

reactions.result: This is how citric acid descales kettles and why it softens water in detergents, where free calcium would otherwise react with soap and reduce its cleaning power. It works more gently than strong acids and is safe to use around food surfaces.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe with no limit beyond good manufacturing practice.
Authorized as E330 at quantum satis (no numerical limit).
Acceptable daily intake "not limited".
Safe in cosmetics in the present practices of use and concentration.

hazards.title: Tooth enamel erosion
hazards.summary: Acidic foods and drinks, including citrus juices, sodas, sports drinks and sour candies, can slowly wear away tooth enamel when consumed often. This is called dental erosion, and it differs from cavities because no bacteria are involved, just the direct effect of acid on teeth. An occasional sour drink is not a problem, but frequent sipping throughout the day can thin enamel over years. Simple habits reduce the risk a lot. Drinking acidic drinks with meals or through a straw, rinsing with water afterward and waiting before brushing all help.
hazards.chemical: Tooth enamel is made mostly of hydroxyapatite, a crystal of calcium, phosphate and hydroxide. When the pH at the tooth surface falls below about 5.5, hydrogen ions from the acid react with the phosphate and hydroxide in the crystal, and calcium ions break loose. Citric acid adds a second effect: citrate grabs those freed calcium ions by chelation, pulling them away so the crystal dissolves faster than it would with acid alone. This is why citric acid is more erosive than some other acids at the same pH. Saliva normally brings calcium and phosphate back, but only if it is given time.
hazards.biological: Erosion removes a thin layer of enamel with each acid exposure, and unlike bone, enamel can't regrow once it is lost. As it thins, teeth may look more yellow because the dentin underneath shows through, and edges can become see-through or chip. When dentin is exposed, its tiny tubes lead toward the nerve, so hot, cold or sweet foods can cause sharp sensitivity. Brushing right after an acidic drink can scrub away enamel that the acid has softened, which is why dentists suggest waiting about 30 minutes. Fluoride toothpaste helps make the surface more resistant.

hazards.title: Eye and skin irritation when concentrated
hazards.summary: Pure citric acid powder and strong solutions can sting the eyes and irritate skin, especially skin that is cut or chapped. This mostly matters when handling the concentrated chemical, for example as a powdered descaler or in homemade cleaning recipes. In finished foods and cosmetics it is used at around 0.1 to 1 percent, where it is harmless. Getting lemon juice in a paper cut gives a good sense of the same sting. Rinsing with plenty of water solves the problem.
hazards.chemical: A concentrated citric acid solution has a low pH, often below 2, meaning it contains a lot of hydrogen ions. Proteins hold their working shapes partly through charged groups and hydrogen bonds, and a flood of hydrogen ions disrupts these, making the proteins unfold, a process called denaturation. The surface of the eye and broken skin have little protection against this. Intact skin is covered by a tough, fatty outer layer that blocks much of the acid, so it is far less sensitive. The effect depends on concentration, so diluting the acid quickly weakens it.
hazards.biological: When surface cells are irritated, nerve endings send pain signals, producing stinging or burning. The damaged cells release chemical signals that widen blood vessels, so the area turns red and may water or swell. In the eye this shows up as tearing, redness and blinking, the eye's way of flushing the irritant out. Because citric acid is a weak acid, this kind of irritation usually clears quickly after rinsing and doesn't cause lasting damage. Wearing gloves and avoiding splashes when handling the powder prevents it.

profile.dosage: Foods and cosmetics typically contain about 0.1 to 1 percent citric acid, mainly to add tartness or adjust pH. That is modest compared with nature: lemon juice is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid. Your own body also makes and breaks down large amounts of citrate every day in the Krebs cycle, so dietary citric acid simply joins that normal flow. Regulators such as the U.S. FDA classify it as generally recognized as safe, and international experts have not set any limit on daily intake. The realistic concerns are tooth erosion from very frequent acidic drinks and irritation from handling the pure powder.

myths.claim: Citric acid is made from toxic black mold.
myths.consensus: It is produced by fermenting sugar with Aspergillus niger, then purified; the final crystals contain no mold. A 2018 case series suggested reactions to residual impurities, but controlled studies have not confirmed this.

myths.claim: "Citric acid" on a label means the product contains citrus.
myths.consensus: Industrial citric acid comes from fermentation, not fruit, so it is generally safe for people with citrus allergies.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low; it is a preferred "green" alternative to phosphates and EDTA in detergents.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis (in citrus and every cell)
synthesis.summary: Citrus fruits like lemons and limes taste sour because they store large amounts of citric acid. They make it the same way every oxygen-breathing cell does, as part of the Krebs cycle, but they keep much of it instead of using it straight away. Lemons and limes contain the most, while oranges and grapefruit contain less, so they taste sweeter. Citric acid was first isolated from lemon juice in 1784 by the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele. For more than a century after that, lemons were the main commercial source.
synthesis.mechanism: Inside the mitochondria of fruit cells, the enzyme citrate synthase joins acetyl-CoA, a two-carbon unit made by breaking down sugar, with oxaloacetate, a four-carbon molecule, to form citrate. In most cells the citrate continues around the Krebs cycle and is broken down for energy. In the juice cells of citrus fruit, however, a large share of it is moved out of the mitochondria and pumped into the vacuole, a big storage compartment inside the cell. Pumps in the vacuole's membrane also use energy to move hydrogen ions in, making the vacuole very acidic. The trapped citric acid builds up until lemon juice is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid, with a pH of around 2.

synthesis.title: Industrial fermentation
synthesis.summary: Almost all the citric acid sold today is made not from lemons but by a mold. In the early 1900s scientists discovered that the black mold Aspergillus niger, the kind that sometimes appears on old onions, could produce large amounts of citric acid from sugar. Fermentation, using microbes to make useful chemicals, quickly replaced fruit as the main source. The mold is grown in huge steel tanks on cheap sugar sources such as molasses or corn syrup. More than two million tonnes are made this way each year.
synthesis.mechanism: Like all cells, the mold makes citrate in its Krebs cycle. Producers deliberately limit trace metals, especially iron and manganese. Aconitase, the enzyme that would normally carry citrate onward in the cycle, needs iron to work, and the metal shortages also shift the mold's metabolism in ways that favor making citrate. With plenty of sugar and oxygen and a low pH, citrate is produced faster than it is used, so it builds up and the mold pumps it out into the surrounding liquid. After several days the liquid is filtered to remove the mold, and lime (calcium hydroxide) is added so the citrate settles out as solid calcium citrate. Sulfuric acid then frees the citric acid, leaving calcium sulfate, or gypsum, behind.
synthesis.significance: Citric acid made by fermentation is chemically identical to the citric acid in lemons, and far cheaper than extracting it from fruit.

citations.title: Ischaemic accumulation of succinate controls reperfusion injury through mitochondrial ROS.
citations.abstract: Ischaemia-reperfusion injury occurs when the blood supply to an organ is disrupted and then restored, and underlies many disorders, notably heart attack and stroke. While reperfusion of ischaemic tissue is essential for survival, it also initiates oxidative damage, cell death and aberrant immune responses through the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS). Although mitochondrial ROS production in ischaemia reperfusion is established, it has generally been considered a nonspecific response to reperfusion. Here we develop a comparative in vivo metabolomic analysis, and unexpectedly identify widely conserved metabolic pathways responsible for mitochondrial ROS production during ischaemia reperfusion. We show that selective accumulation of the citric acid cycle intermediate succinate is a universal metabolic signature of ischaemia in a range of tissues and is responsible for mitochondrial ROS production during reperfusion. Ischaemic succinate accumulation arises from reversal of succinate dehydrogenase, which in turn is driven by fumarate overflow from purine nucleotide breakdown and partial reversal of the malate/aspartate shuttle. After reperfusion, the accumulated succinate is rapidly re-oxidized by succinate dehydrogenase, driving extensive ROS generation by reverse electron transport at mitochondrial complex I. Decreasing ischaemic succinate accumulation by pharmacological inhibition is sufficient to ameliorate in vivo ischaemia-reperfusion injury in murine models of heart attack and stroke. Thus, we have identified a conserved metabolic response of tissues to ischaemia and reperfusion that unifies many hitherto unconnected aspects of ischaemia-reperfusion injury. Furthermore, these findings reveal a new pathway for metabolic control of ROS production in vivo, while demonstrating that inhibition of ischaemic succinate accumulation and its oxidation after subsequent reperfusion is a potential therapeutic target to decrease ischaemia-reperfusion injury in a range of pathologies.

citations.title: Design of glycolysis.
citations.journal: Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci
citations.abstract: The design of the glycolytic pathway resulting from the continuous refinement of evolution is discussed with regard to three aspects. 1. Functional and structural properties of individual enzymes. The catalytic constants of the glycolytic enzymes are remarkably optimized; the turnover numbers are within one order of magnitude. The same is true for the molarities of catalytic centres in the cytosol, as is noted for yeast. Functional properties of the enzymes are reflected in their tertiary and quaternary structures. 2. Regulatory mechanisms of single enzymes. A classification of the various types of enzymic control mechanisms operating in the glycolytic pathway is given. In addition to the usual Michaelis-Menten saturation kinetics and the various types of inhibition there is control by positive and negative effectors based on oligomeric structures (fast acting, fine control) as well as regulation by chemical interconversion structures (fast acting, fine control) as well as regulation by chemical based on enzymes cascades (slow acting, very effective). 3. Functional and regulatory mechanisms of the whole glycolytic reaction pathway. A prominent feature is the high enzyme:substrate ratio, which guarantees fast response times. However, a quantitative treatment of the overall kinetics is limited by an incomplete knowledge of the enzymes' dynamic and chemical compartmentation as well as some of their control properties. From an analysis of the oscillatory state, certain control points in the glycolytic chain can be located that coincide with major branching points to other metabolic pathways. These points are controlled by fast-acting cooperative enzymes that operate in a flip-flop mechanism together with the respective antagonistic enzymes, preventing futile cycles. The gating enzymes leading to the glycogen store and the citric acid cycle are of the slow-acting but very effective interconvertible type. The combination of all the complex and intricate features of design yields a glycolytic network that enables the cell to respond to its various metabolic needs quickly, effectively and economically.

citations.title: Allergenic Ingredients in Facial Wet Wipes.
citations.abstract: Background: Allergic contact dermatitis commonly occurs on the face. Facial cleansing wipes may be an underrecognized source of allergens. Objective: The aim of this study was to determine the frequency of potentially allergenic ingredients in facial wet wipes. Methods: Ingredient lists from name brand and generic facial wipes from 4 large retailers were analyzed. Results: In the 178 facial wipes examined, a total of 485 ingredients were identified (average, 16.7 ingredients per wipe). Excluding botanicals, the top 15 potentially allergenic ingredients were glycerin (64.0%), fragrance (63.5%), phenoxyethanol (53.9%), citric acid (51.1%), disodium EDTA (44.4%), sorbic acid derivatives (39.3%), tocopherol derivatives (38.8%), polyethylene glycol derivatives (32.6%), glyceryl stearate (31.5%), sodium citrate (29.8%), glucosides (27.5%), cetearyl alcohol (25.8%), propylene glycol (25.3%), sodium benzoate (24.2%), and ceteareth-20 (23.6%)/parabens (23.6%). Of note, methylisothiazolinone (2.2%) and methylchloroisothiazolinone (1.1%) were uncommon. The top potential allergens of botanical origin included Aloe barbadensis (41.0%), chamomile extracts (27.0%), tea extracts (21.3%), Cucumis sativus (20.2%), and Hamamelis virginiana (10.7%). Conclusions: Many potential allergens are present in facial wet wipes, including fragrances, preservatives, botanicals, glucosides, and propylene glycol.

citations.title: Citrate pathophysiology and metabolism.
citations.abstract: By chelating ionized calcium, citrate allows extracorporeal circuit anticoagulation without a bleeding risk for the patient. Citrate anticoagulation is also associated with a reduced activation of leucocytes and platelets. Citrate clearance by citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle) is not modified by renal failure, but is reduced by about 50% in patients with cirrhosis. Toxic effects of citrate result from a decrease in plasma ionized calcium of the patient. The first side effect is a prolongation of the QT interval. Clinical signs of hypocalcemia and hypotension in humans appear below 0.9mmol/L of plasma ionized calcium.

citations.title: Metabolism in hyperthermophilic microorganisms.
citations.abstract: Hyperthermophilic microorganisms grow at temperatures of 90 degrees C and above and are a recent discovery in the microbial world. They are considered to be the most ancient of all extant life forms, and have been isolated mainly from near shallow and deep sea hydrothermal vents. All but two of the nearly twenty known genera are classified as Archaea (formerly archaebacteria). Virtually all of them are strict anaerobes. The majority are obligate heterotrophs that utilize proteinaceous materials as carbon and energy sources, although a few species are also saccharolytic. Most also depend on the reduction of elemental sulfur to hydrogen sulfide (H2S) for significant growth. Peptide fermentation involves transaminases and glutamate dehydrogenase, together with several unusual ferredoxin-linked oxidoreductases not found in mesophilic organisms. Similarly, a novel pathway based on a partially non-phosphorylated Entner-Doudoroff scheme has been postulated to convert carbohydrates to acetate, H2 and CO2, although a more conventional Embden-Meyerhof pathway has also been identified in one saccharolytic species. The few hypethermophiles known that can assimilate CO2 do so via a reductive citric acid cycle. Two S(o)-reducing enzymes termed sulfhydrogenase and sulfide dehydrogenase have been purified from the cytoplasm of a hyperthermophile that is able to grow either with or without S(o). A scheme for electron flow during the oxidation of carbohydrates and peptides and the reduction of S(o) has been proposed. However, the mechanisms by which S(o) reduction is coupled to energy conservation in this organism and in obligate S(o)-reducing hyperthermophiles is not known.

name: Ascorbic Acid
scoreRationale: An essential vitamin with a wide safety margin; very high supplement doses can upset the stomach.
summary: Vitamin C is an essential nutrient and antioxidant. In food it prevents browning; in serums it brightens skin and supports collagen.

physical.solubility: Freely soluble in water; poorly soluble in oils
physical.phStability: Most stable below pH 3.5; oxidizes quickly in air, light and heat

overview: Ascorbic acid is vitamin C: a small six-carbon molecule built around a five-membered ring that carries an enediol group, two –OH groups attached to a carbon–carbon double bond. That enediol gives up electrons easily, which makes vitamin C a strong reducing agent and antioxidant.

Most animals make their own vitamin C from glucose, but humans, other primates and guinea pigs lost the final enzyme (L-gulonolactone oxidase) to a mutation millions of years ago. We must eat it; without it, collagen falls apart and scurvy follows.
profile.function: Stops cut fruit and cured meats from discoloring, strengthens bread dough, fortifies foods, and in skincare acts as an antioxidant and brightening active.

mechanisms.title: Building collagen
mechanisms.chemical: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the body, the strong, rope-like material in skin, bones, tendons, gums and blood vessel walls. As new collagen chains are being made, two enzymes, prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, add hydroxyl groups (–OH) to some of the amino acids proline and lysine in the chain. Each of these enzymes has an iron atom at its center that must be in the Fe²⁺ form to work. During the reaction, that iron sometimes gets stuck in the inactive Fe³⁺ form. Vitamin C (ascorbate) donates an electron to turn it back into Fe²⁺, keeping the enzyme running.
mechanisms.biological: The added hydroxyl groups let three collagen chains twist tightly around each other into a triple helix and form hydrogen bonds that hold the helix together. Properly built collagen is remarkably strong, giving tissues their toughness and stretch. Without enough vitamin C, collagen is made poorly and falls apart easily at body temperature. The result is scurvy: gums swell and bleed, teeth loosen, old wounds reopen, small blood vessels leak and bruise, and the person feels exhausted. Scurvy killed huge numbers of sailors on long voyages until citrus fruit was found to prevent it.

mechanisms.title: Antioxidant defense
mechanisms.chemical: Free radicals are molecules with an unpaired electron, which makes them very reactive: they steal electrons from nearby molecules, damaging fats, proteins and DNA and turning those molecules into new radicals in a chain reaction. Vitamin C stops this by donating one of its own electrons to the radical, which neutralizes it. After giving up an electron, vitamin C becomes the ascorbyl radical, which is unusually stable and doesn't continue the chain. It can then give up a second electron and become dehydroascorbic acid. A substance that donates electrons in this way is called a reducing agent, or antioxidant.
mechanisms.biological: Vitamin C dissolves in water, so it protects the watery parts of cells and the fluid in blood. It also works as a teammate for vitamin E, a fat-soluble antioxidant that guards cell membranes: when vitamin E neutralizes a radical in the membrane, vitamin C can restore it by passing it an electron. Cells then use enzymes to recycle dehydroascorbic acid back into active vitamin C. Because the body keeps only limited stores and excretes any extra in urine, vitamin C needs to be eaten regularly. Fruits and vegetables are the main sources.

mechanisms.title: Iron absorption
mechanisms.chemical: Iron in plant foods such as beans, spinach and grains is mostly in the ferric form, Fe³⁺, which tends to form insoluble clumps in the less acidic environment of the small intestine. Iron that doesn't dissolve can't be absorbed. Vitamin C reduces ferric iron to ferrous iron, Fe²⁺, by handing it an electron. It can also bind iron into a soluble complex, keeping it dissolved as it moves from the acidic stomach into the intestine. Both actions leave more of the iron in a form the body can take up.
mechanisms.biological: The cells lining the small intestine absorb iron mainly through a transporter protein called DMT1, which only carries the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form. With vitamin C in the same meal, more iron reaches these transporters in a form they can use. Studies show that adding a vitamin C-rich food, such as orange juice, peppers or tomatoes, to a meal can raise iron absorption from plant foods several-fold. This matters most for vegetarians, vegans and others at risk of iron-deficiency anemia, a condition in which the blood carries less oxygen. Iron from meat, called heme iron, is absorbed by a different route and depends less on vitamin C.

mechanisms.title: Fading dark spots
mechanisms.chemical: Skin color comes from melanin, a pigment made by cells called melanocytes. The first and slowest step in making melanin is controlled by an enzyme called tyrosinase, which has copper atoms at its active site and converts the amino acid tyrosine into molecules that link up into melanin. Applied to skin at a low pH, ascorbic acid interferes with tyrosinase, partly by acting on its copper center, and it can also convert early intermediate molecules back before they join into pigment. The low pH matters because vitamin C passes through the skin best in its uncharged form. Serums typically use 10 to 20 percent.
mechanisms.biological: With less melanin being made, areas of extra pigment, such as sun spots or marks left after acne, gradually fade as pigmented skin cells are shed and replaced. Results take weeks to months, because the outer skin renews itself roughly every month. Vitamin C also supports collagen production in the deeper layer of skin and gives some antioxidant protection against sun damage. It doesn't replace sunscreen, which blocks the UV light that triggers extra melanin in the first place. Results in studies are real but modest, and a stable formula matters, since vitamin C breaks down quickly in air.

reactions.title: Oxidation (why vitamin C serums turn brown)
reactions.summary: Vitamin C protects other molecules by sacrificing itself: it gives away its electrons, which is a type of reaction called oxidation. That makes it an excellent antioxidant, but it also means vitamin C is used up whenever it meets oxygen, light or reactive metals. In a bottle of serum or a carton of juice, it slowly oxidizes over days or weeks. At first the change is invisible, but eventually the breakdown products turn yellow, then orange or brown. The color change is a handy sign that the vitamin C is losing its strength.

steps.name: First electron
steps.text: Ascorbate gives one electron to oxygen or a free radical. It becomes the ascorbyl radical, which has an unpaired electron but is stable enough not to cause damage. This step is what makes vitamin C an antioxidant.

steps.name: Second electron
steps.text: The ascorbyl radical gives up a second electron and a proton, forming dehydroascorbic acid. Up to this point the change can be reversed: in the body, enzymes can put the electrons back. In a bottle there are no such enzymes.

steps.name: Breakdown
steps.text: Dehydroascorbic acid is unstable in water. Its ring opens permanently, and it breaks into smaller molecules that react further to form yellow and brown compounds. Once this happens, the vitamin C can't be restored.

reactions.result: Light, heat, air and traces of metals such as copper and iron all speed this process up. That's why vitamin C serums come in dark, airtight bottles, why they often include stabilizers such as vitamin E and ferulic acid, and why a serum that has turned dark orange has lost much of its potency. Juice loses vitamin C faster once opened for the same reason.

reactions.title: Benzene formation with sodium benzoate
reactions.summary: In 2005 and 2006, testing found small amounts of benzene, a chemical known to cause cancer at high exposures, in some soft drinks. The cause turned out to be an unexpected reaction between two common ingredients: vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and the preservative sodium benzoate. Neither ingredient is benzene, and they rarely react, but under certain conditions vitamin C helps produce highly reactive radicals that can knock a piece off benzoate. The amounts formed were tiny, measured in parts per billion. The discovery led manufacturers to reformulate their drinks.

steps.name: Radical generation
steps.text: Vitamin C reduces trace amounts of copper or iron ions in the drink, putting them into a reactive form. These metal ions react with oxygen dissolved in the drink and produce hydroxyl radicals (•OH), among the most reactive molecules known. The dot in •OH marks the unpaired electron.

steps.name: Decarboxylation
steps.text: A hydroxyl radical attacks benzoic acid, the active form of the preservative in acidic drinks, and helps remove its carboxyl group (–COOH) as carbon dioxide gas. Removing a carboxyl group is called decarboxylation.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: What remains is a bare benzene ring with nothing attached: a molecule of benzene. Heat and light supply extra energy that speeds up every step.

reactions.result: Storing drinks warm or in sunlight increases the amount formed. After the 2006 findings, manufacturers reformulated, often by removing one of the two ingredients, and most drinks now test below 5 parts per billion, the U.S. drinking-water limit for benzene. The episode is a reminder that safety testing has to consider how ingredients behave together.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a nutrient and preservative.
RDA 90 mg/day for men and 75 mg/day for women; tolerable upper intake level 2,000 mg/day.
Authorized as E300 at quantum satis.

hazards.title: Digestive upset at megadoses
hazards.summary: Vitamin C from food is safe, and so are normal supplement doses. Problems appear only with very large doses, usually from high-dose supplements or powders taken in the belief that more is better. The main effect is an upset stomach, cramps or diarrhea, which goes away once the dose is lowered. This is why health authorities set an upper limit of 2,000 milligrams a day for adults. There is little evidence that such megadoses give healthy people any extra benefit.
hazards.chemical: The intestine absorbs vitamin C using special transporter proteins, and there are only so many of them. At normal intakes nearly all of it is absorbed, but at doses of a gram or more the transporters become saturated, meaning they are all busy, and absorption drops sharply. The unabsorbed vitamin C stays dissolved inside the intestine. Dissolved particles attract water by osmosis, the movement of water toward a more concentrated solution. So the extra vitamin C draws water from the body into the gut.
hazards.biological: The extra water in the intestine makes stools looser and speeds them through the gut, causing diarrhea, cramps, bloating and nausea. This is the same way some laxatives work. The effect is temporary and stops once the dose is reduced. Any vitamin C that is absorbed beyond the body's needs is filtered out by the kidneys and leaves in urine, so the body doesn't stockpile it. Above about 2 grams a day, these side effects become common.

hazards.title: Kidney stones in susceptible people
hazards.summary: Taking high doses of vitamin C supplements every day for years may slightly raise the risk of kidney stones in some people. The link has been seen mainly in men, and especially in people who have had kidney stones before. Vitamin C from fruits and vegetables has not been linked to stones. People with a history of stones or kidney disease are usually advised to avoid high-dose supplements. For most people, the risk at normal intakes is negligible.
hazards.chemical: The body breaks down some of the vitamin C it absorbs, and one of the end products is oxalate. Oxalate is also found naturally in foods such as spinach, rhubarb and nuts. In urine, oxalate ions can combine with calcium ions to form calcium oxalate, a compound that dissolves very poorly in water. When the levels of calcium and oxalate in urine are high enough, the compound comes out of solution as tiny solid crystals. The more vitamin C is absorbed beyond the body's needs, the more oxalate is produced.
hazards.biological: Most of the time, tiny crystals are flushed out in urine without anyone noticing. In some people, though, they stick together and grow inside the kidney into a hard stone. A stone can sit quietly for years, but if it moves into the narrow tube that drains the kidney, it can cause intense pain, nausea and blood in the urine. Most kidney stones are made mainly of calcium oxalate. Drinking plenty of water keeps urine dilute and is one of the best ways to prevent them.

profile.dosage: Adults need about 75 milligrams of vitamin C a day for women and 90 milligrams for men, an amount easily reached by eating one orange (about 70 milligrams) plus some vegetables. Smokers need about 35 milligrams more, because smoking uses vitamin C up faster. The safe upper limit for adults is 2,000 milligrams a day, above which digestive upset becomes common. Food additives and cosmetics contribute only small amounts by comparison. Skin serums use 10 to 20 percent vitamin C at a pH below about 3.5, which can cause a brief tingle when applied.

myths.claim: Megadoses of vitamin C prevent colds.
myths.consensus: Cochrane reviews find regular supplements do not reduce how often the general population catches colds, though they slightly shorten their duration.

myths.claim: Vitamin C serum makes skin more sensitive to the sun.
myths.consensus: Unlike some acids it does not increase photosensitivity, and it is often paired with sunscreen for added antioxidant protection.

environment.persistence: Not persistent; oxidizes rapidly in air and water.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis
synthesis.summary: Almost all plants and most animals make their own vitamin C, so for them it isn't a vitamin at all. Dogs, cats, cows and rats, for example, produce it in their liver or kidneys from glucose. Humans, other apes and monkeys, guinea pigs, fruit bats and some birds have lost this ability, which is why we must get it from food. Plants make vitamin C in large amounts, especially in leaves and fruit, where it helps protect them from damage caused by strong sunlight. Citrus fruits, kiwis, strawberries and peppers are especially rich sources.
synthesis.mechanism: In animals that can make it, the process starts with glucose, a six-carbon sugar. A series of enzymes converts glucose into glucuronic acid, then into a molecule called L-gulonic acid, which is closed into a ring called L-gulonolactone. The final enzyme, L-gulonolactone oxidase, removes two hydrogen atoms to form ascorbic acid. Plants use a different route that also starts from glucose but passes through the sugars GDP-mannose and L-galactose. Different paths lead to the same product: the vitamin C molecule is identical whether it was made by a lemon, a dog or a factory.
synthesis.significance: Humans still carry a broken copy of the gene for L-gulonolactone oxidase, called a pseudogene, with the same disabling mutations as other primates. That shared damage is evidence that we inherited it from a common ancestor.

synthesis.title: Industrial two-step fermentation
synthesis.summary: Most vitamin C sold today is made in factories, largely in China, by combining chemical steps with fermentation by bacteria. The first industrial process was invented in 1933 by the Swiss chemist Tadeus Reichstein, and it used several chemical reactions and solvents. Modern factories have replaced most of those chemical steps with bacteria that carry out the same transformations more cleanly. The starting material is glucose from corn or other starchy crops. The final product is chemically identical to the vitamin C in fruit.
synthesis.mechanism: First, glucose is reacted with hydrogen gas over a nickel catalyst, a reaction called hydrogenation, which turns it into sorbitol, a sugar alcohol. Bacteria of the genus Gluconobacter then oxidize sorbitol into L-sorbose, a different sugar, by removing hydrogen from one specific carbon atom, something that is hard to do with ordinary chemistry because the molecule has many similar spots. In a second fermentation, other bacteria convert L-sorbose into 2-keto-L-gulonic acid. Treating this molecule with acid makes it close into a ring and rearrange into ascorbic acid. The product is then crystallized and purified.
synthesis.significance: This largely replaced Reichstein's original process, which needed more chemical steps and solvents.

citations.title: Recent progress on the characterization of aldonolactone oxidoreductases.
citations.abstract: L-Ascorbic acid (ascorbate, AsA, vitamin C) is essential for animal and plant health. Despite our dependence on fruits and vegetables to fulfill our requirement for this vitamin, the metabolic network leading to its formation in plants is just being fully elucidated. There is evidence supporting the operation of at least four biosynthetic pathways leading to AsA formation in plants. These routes use D-mannose/L-galactose, L-gulose, D-galacturonate, and myo-inositol as the main precursors. This review focuses on aldonolactone oxidoreductases, a subgroup of the vanillyl alcohol oxidase (VAO; EC 1.1.3.38) superfamily, enzymes that catalyze the terminal step in AsA biosynthesis in bacteria, protozoa, animals, and plants. In this report, we review the properties of well characterized aldonolactone oxidoreductases to date. A shared feature in these proteins is the presence of a flavin cofactor as well as a thiol group. The flavin cofactor in many cases is bound to the N terminus of the enzymes or to a recently discovered HWXK motif in the C terminus. The binding between the flavin moiety and the protein can be either covalent or non-covalent. Substrate specificity and subcellular localization differ among the isozymes of each kingdom. All oxidases among these enzymes possess dehydrogenase activity, however, exclusive dehydrogenases are also found. We also discuss recent evidence indicating that plants have both L-gulono-1,4-lactone oxidases and L-galactono-1,4-lactone dehydrogenases involved in AsA biosynthesis.

citations.title: A metallo-β-lactamase enzyme for internal detoxification of the antibiotic thienamycin.
citations.abstract: Thienamycin, the first representative of carbapenem antibiotics was discovered in the mid-1970s from soil microorganism, Streptomyces cattleya, during the race to discover inhibitors of bacterial peptidoglycan synthesis. Chemically modified into imipenem (N-formimidoyl thienamycin), now one of the most clinically important antibiotics, thienamycin is encoded by a thienamycin gene cluster composed of 22 genes (thnA to thnV) from S. cattleya NRRL 8057 genome. Interestingly, the role of all thn-genes has been experimentally demonstrated in the thienamycin biosynthesis, except thnS, despite its annotation as putative β-lactamase. Here, we expressed thnS gene and investigated its activities against various substrates. Our analyses revealed that ThnS belonged to the superfamily of metallo-β-lactamase fold proteins. Compared to known β-lactamases such as OXA-48 and NDM-1, ThnS exhibited a lower affinity and less efficiency toward penicillin G and cefotaxime, while imipenem is more actively hydrolysed. Moreover, like most MBL fold enzymes, additional enzymatic activities of ThnS were detected such as hydrolysis of ascorbic acid, single strand DNA, and ribosomal RNA. ThnS appears as a MBL enzyme with multiple activities including a specialised β-lactamase activity toward imipenem. Thus, like toxin/antitoxin systems, the role of thnS gene within the thienamycin gene cluster appears as an antidote against the produced thienamycin.

citations.title: Management of acute radiation dermatitis: A review of the literature and proposal for treatment algorithm.
citations.abstract: Radiation dermatitis is a common sequela of radiation therapy; up to 95% of patients will develop moderate-to-severe skin reactions. No criterion standard currently exists for the treatment of acute radiation-induced skin toxicity. It is therefore imperative to develop a greater understanding of management options available to allow clinicians to make informed decisions when managing radiation oncology patients. This literature review discusses the topical agents that have been studied for the treatment of acute radiation dermatitis, reviews their mechanisms of action, and presents a treatment algorithm for clinicians managing patients experiencing radiation dermatitis.

citations.title: The effects of vitamin C on respiratory, allergic and immunological diseases: an experimental and clinical-based review.
citations.abstract: Vitamin C is used in modern medicine supplements for treatment of various disorders associated with oxidative stress, inflammation and immune dysregulation. In this review article, experimental and clinical results regarding the effects of vitamin C on respiratory immunologic, and allergic diseases are reviewed. Various databases and appropriate keywords are used to search the effect of vitamin C on respiratory diseases until the end of May 2022. Books, theses and articles were included. These studies assessed the effects of vitamin C on respiratory disorders including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung infection and lung cancer. Vitamin C showed relaxant effect on tracheal smooth muscle via various mechanisms. The preventive effects of vitamin C were mediated by antioxidant, immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory mechanisms in the experimental animal models of different respiratory diseases. Some clinical studies also indicated the effect of vitamin C on lung cancer and lung infections. Therefore, vitamin C could be used a preventive and/or relieving therapy in respiratory diseases.

citations.title: Ocular oxidants and antioxidant protection.
citations.abstract: Oxidative damage and antioxidant protection in ocular tissues has not been reviewed recently. Metabolism in the eye is of increasing interest because the organ is highly susceptible to damage by sunlight, oxygen, various chemicals, and pollutants. Interest is expected to increase because of an aging Western world population and a continued depletion of stratospheric ozone. Hydrogen peroxide is discussed because it is both a byproduct and a source of free radical reactions and is normally present in the aqueous humor. The metabolism of reactive oxygen species by enzymes, nutrients, pigments, and low molecular weight scavengers is evaluated. Ascorbic acid, because of its high concentration in the eye, is thought to be a primary substrate in ocular protection; progress in determining the mechanisms by which it is recycled and maintained in the useful, reduced state is discussed. Recent information is included about antioxidants not previously known to be present in the eye, and some importance is placed on the properties of the vitreous humor and tear fluid because of the previous lack of emphasis on these.

name: Sodium Benzoate
scoreRationale: Well studied and low in toxicity, but it can form trace benzene with vitamin C under heat and light, and it was part of the additive mix linked to hyperactivity in some children.
summary: Sodium benzoate stops mold and yeast in acidic foods, drinks and cosmetics. It's considered safe at permitted levels, with a few chemistry caveats worth knowing.

physical.solubility: Very soluble in water (about 630 g/L); slightly soluble in ethanol

overview: Sodium benzoate is the sodium salt of benzoic acid: a flat benzene ring attached to a carboxylate group (–COO⁻ Na⁺). As a salt it dissolves easily in water, about 630 grams per liter.

Its preservative power depends on pH. Benzoic acid has a pKa of about 4.2, so in acidic foods and drinks (pH below 4.5) much of it exists as uncharged benzoic acid, the form that slips through microbial membranes. In neutral products it stays charged and works poorly, which is why it's used in sodas, pickles and sauces.
profile.function: Prevents yeast and mold spoilage in sodas, pickles, sauces and rinse-off cosmetics, extending shelf life once a product is opened.

mechanisms.title: Stopping yeast and mold (the pH trap)
mechanisms.chemical: Benzoic acid exists in two forms: an uncharged acid (C₆H₅COOH) and a charged ion called benzoate (C₆H₅COO⁻), and the balance between them depends on pH. In an acidic food or drink, most of it is in the uncharged form. Cell membranes are made of fatty molecules that block charged particles but let small uncharged molecules slip through, so uncharged benzoic acid diffuses into microbes easily. Inside the cell the pH is close to neutral, so the benzoic acid lets go of its proton (H⁺) and becomes the charged benzoate ion. Now charged, it can't get back out through the membrane, so it is trapped, while more benzoic acid keeps flowing in.
mechanisms.biological: As benzoic acid enters and drops its protons, the inside of the microbe becomes more acidic. Many of the cell's enzymes only work within a narrow pH range, and one important target is phosphofructokinase, a key enzyme in glycolysis, the pathway that breaks down sugar for energy. With glycolysis slowed, the cell makes less ATP, its energy currency. At the same time the microbe spends what energy it has left running pumps that push protons back out. Starved of energy, yeasts and molds stop growing, although they aren't always killed outright.

mechanisms.title: Clearance in the human body
mechanisms.chemical: When we eat sodium benzoate, it is absorbed quickly from the gut and carried to the liver. Inside the mitochondria of liver cells, an enzyme attaches benzoate to coenzyme A, a helper molecule, forming benzoyl-CoA. A second enzyme then joins this to glycine, the smallest amino acid, creating a new molecule called hippuric acid. Attaching a substance to another molecule to make it easier to remove is called conjugation. Hippuric acid is very water-soluble and is not toxic.
mechanisms.biological: The kidneys filter hippuric acid out of the blood efficiently, and it leaves the body in urine, usually within hours of eating benzoate. Because this route is fast, benzoate doesn't build up in the body at normal food levels. Doctors even use the same pathway as a treatment: babies with certain rare genetic diseases, called urea-cycle disorders, can't get rid of nitrogen properly, and ammonia builds up to dangerous levels. Giving sodium benzoate makes the body use up glycine, which contains nitrogen, and excrete it as hippuric acid, lowering ammonia. The name hippuric comes from the Greek word for horse, because it was first found in horse urine.

reactions.title: Activation in acidic food
reactions.summary: Sodium benzoate is sold as a salt, which dissolves easily in water but isn't the form that stops microbes. To work, it has to pick up a hydrogen ion and become benzoic acid, and that only happens when the surroundings are acidic. This is an example of an acid–base equilibrium: a reaction that runs in both directions at once, with the balance set by pH. Chemists use a number called the pKa to describe where that balance lies, and for benzoic acid it is about 4.2. At a pH equal to the pKa, exactly half the molecules are in each form.

steps.name: Acidic environment
steps.text: A soda at pH 3 contains many free hydrogen ions (H⁺), about ten times as many as a solution at pH 4. pH is a logarithmic scale, so each step down means ten times more acid. Many sauces, pickles and fruit drinks are similarly acidic.

steps.name: Equilibrium shift
steps.text: When hydrogen ions are plentiful, benzoate ions are more likely to grab one, so the balance shifts toward uncharged benzoic acid. At pH 3, more than 90 percent of the preservative is in the acid form. At pH 7, almost all of it would stay as the charged ion.

steps.name: Activation
steps.text: Only uncharged benzoic acid can pass through a microbe's fatty membrane and get trapped inside. So the lower the pH, the more of the preservative is in its active form, and the less is needed to prevent spoilage.

reactions.result: This is why sodium benzoate is paired with acidic products like sodas, fruit juices, salad dressings and pickles, and is rarely used in neutral foods such as milk or meat. Food scientists choose preservatives partly by matching each one's pKa to the product's pH.

reactions.title: Benzene formation
reactions.summary: Under a specific combination of conditions, benzoate can break down into small amounts of benzene, a chemical known to cause cancer with long-term, high-level exposure. The reaction needs vitamin C, traces of metal ions such as copper or iron, and oxygen, and it speeds up with heat and light. U.S. regulators first learned it could happen in soft drinks around 1990, and it became widely known after new testing in 2006. The amounts involved are very small, measured in parts per billion. It is an example of two individually safe ingredients interacting in an unexpected way.

steps.name: Trigger
steps.text: Vitamin C converts trace copper or iron ions in the drink into a reactive form. These metal ions react with dissolved oxygen and generate hydroxyl radicals (•OH), extremely reactive fragments with an unpaired electron.

steps.name: Decarboxylation
steps.text: A hydroxyl radical attacks benzoic acid and helps remove its carboxyl group (–COOH), which leaves as carbon dioxide. Removing a carboxyl group is called decarboxylation.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: What is left is a bare benzene ring, a molecule of benzene. The warmer the drink and the more light it gets, the faster the reaction runs and the more benzene forms.

reactions.result: After the 2006 findings, manufacturers reformulated many products, for example by removing vitamin C or switching preservatives, and most drinks now test below the U.S. drinking-water limit of 5 parts per billion. Storing drinks somewhere cool and dark also keeps benzene formation to a minimum.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a preservative.
Group acceptable daily intake of 0–5 mg/kg body weight (as benzoic acid).
Permitted preservative.
Was included in the Southampton additive mixture; the EU hyperactivity warning applies to the six dyes, not to benzoate.

hazards.title: Trace benzene in drinks
hazards.summary: The concern here is not sodium benzoate itself but the small amount of benzene that can form when it reacts with vitamin C inside a drink. Benzene is a known human carcinogen, but its harm is tied to high, long-term exposures, such as those once faced by workers in some industries. The trace amounts found in beverages are thousands of times lower than those workplace exposures. For comparison, people also breathe in benzene from car exhaust, gasoline fumes and cigarette smoke. Reformulation since 2006 has lowered levels in drinks even further.
hazards.chemical: Benzene forms only when several conditions line up: benzoate must be present together with vitamin C, traces of copper or iron must be there to make reactive radicals, and heat or light must speed things up. Remove any one of these and very little benzene forms. Benzene itself is a flat ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen. It is fairly unreactive but dissolves in fats, so once absorbed it can travel throughout the body. In the liver, enzymes convert it into reactive breakdown products, and those are what cause harm.
hazards.biological: Benzene's breakdown products are especially toxic to bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones where blood cells are made. They can damage DNA and interfere with the cells that develop into red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Long-term, high exposure, such as years of breathing benzene vapor at work, is linked to anemia and to leukemia, a cancer of the blood-forming cells. The amounts in reformulated drinks are below the limits set for drinking water, which are designed with large safety margins. Even so, regulators prefer to keep any exposure to a known carcinogen as low as possible.

hazards.title: Pseudo-allergic reactions
hazards.summary: A small number of people react to benzoates with hives, itching, flushing or, rarely, asthma symptoms. These reactions are more common in people who are sensitive to aspirin or who already have chronic hives. They are called pseudo-allergic because they look like allergies but don't involve the usual allergy antibodies. For people who notice a pattern, reading labels and avoiding benzoates usually solves the problem. For everyone else, sodium benzoate at food levels causes no reaction at all.
hazards.chemical: In a true allergy, the immune system makes antibodies called IgE that recognize one specific substance. In a pseudo-allergic reaction, benzoate seems to act more directly on mast cells, immune cells packed with granules of chemical messengers. Scientists don't know every detail, but the result is that the mast cells release their contents without any antibody being involved. That is why someone can react the very first time they meet the substance. The reaction depends on dose, so small amounts may cause nothing while larger amounts cause symptoms.
hazards.biological: Mast cells release histamine and other signals that widen small blood vessels and make them leaky. Fluid seeps into the skin and forms raised, itchy welts called hives, and the widened vessels cause flushing and warmth. In the airways, histamine can tighten the surrounding muscles and trigger wheezing in people with asthma. These symptoms usually appear within minutes to an hour and fade as histamine is cleared. Antihistamine medicines block histamine's effects and can relieve them.

hazards.title: Behavior in sensitive children (as part of mixtures)
hazards.summary: Some parents worry that food additives affect children's behavior. The best-known study, the 2007 Southampton trial in the U.K., tested drinks containing mixtures of artificial food colors together with sodium benzoate. It found a small increase in hyperactive behavior in some children who drank the mixtures compared with a look-alike drink with no additives. Because benzoate was always given along with the dyes, the study couldn't show whether benzoate alone had any effect. The findings led the European Union to require a warning label on foods containing those dyes, but not on benzoate.
hazards.chemical: Nobody knows exactly how additive mixtures might affect behavior, and the effect may differ from child to child. One idea is that some additives trigger the release of histamine, the same messenger involved in pseudo-allergic reactions, and that histamine in the brain affects attention and activity. Genetic differences in how quickly children break down histamine might explain why only some seem to respond. These ideas remain hypotheses. No clear chemical mechanism for benzoate on its own has been demonstrated.
hazards.biological: In the Southampton trial, about 300 children aged three and eight to nine drank either additive-containing drinks or identical-looking placebo drinks without knowing which was which, and their behavior was rated by parents, teachers and trained observers. On average, hyperactivity scores rose slightly with the additive drinks, though the effect was small and varied widely between children. The European Food Safety Authority reviewed the study and concluded it did not justify changing the safe intake levels for the additives. Parents who suspect a link can try removing the additives, ideally with a doctor's guidance, and watch for changes.

profile.dosage: Drinks usually contain less than 0.05 percent sodium benzoate, and regulators cap how much can be used. International food-safety experts have set an acceptable daily intake (ADI), the amount a person could eat every day for life without appreciable risk, of 5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. For a 60-kilogram adult that is about 300 milligrams a day, and typical intakes are well below it. Children who drink a lot of soft drinks have the highest exposures. Because the body converts benzoate to hippuric acid and excretes it within hours, it doesn't accumulate.

myths.claim: Sodium benzoate turns into benzene in your body.
myths.consensus: Benzene can form in the bottle under specific conditions (vitamin C, metals, heat, light), not in the body. The body converts benzoate to hippuric acid.

myths.claim: It causes ADHD.
myths.consensus: The 2007 Southampton study tested it mixed with dyes and found small behavioral effects in some children; the effect couldn't be pinned on benzoate, and it does not cause ADHD.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low toxicity to fish and invertebrates; EPA Safer Choice lists it as low concern.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Almost all sodium benzoate is made from toluene, a liquid chemical obtained from petroleum. Toluene is a benzene ring with a single methyl group (–CH₃) attached. Manufacturers convert that methyl group into a carboxylic acid group (–COOH), which turns toluene into benzoic acid, and then react the acid with a base to make the salt. The process is efficient and cheap. Benzoic acid made this way is identical to the benzoic acid some fruits produce.
synthesis.mechanism: Toluene is heated to about 150 °C while air is blown through it, together with small amounts of cobalt or manganese salts that act as catalysts. The reaction runs as a radical chain: the catalyst helps pull a hydrogen atom off the methyl group, leaving a radical, a molecule with an unpaired electron, which then reacts with oxygen from the air. Over several steps, the methyl carbon gains oxygen atoms until it becomes a carboxyl group, producing benzoic acid and water. The benzoic acid is purified by distillation and crystallization. Finally it is neutralized with sodium hydroxide, an acid–base reaction that swaps the acidic hydrogen for sodium and produces sodium benzoate and water.
synthesis.significance: Food-grade benzoate must meet strict purity limits for any leftover byproducts.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis in plants
synthesis.summary: Benzoic acid isn't only a factory chemical; many plants make it naturally. Cranberries, lingonberries, plums, cinnamon and cloves all contain it. Plants use it as a building block for other compounds and as part of their defense against microbes and insects. Some fermented dairy foods, such as yogurt, also contain small amounts produced by bacteria. This natural benzoic acid is one reason lingonberry jam keeps well without added preservatives.
synthesis.mechanism: Plants start with phenylalanine, one of the amino acids used to build proteins. An enzyme called phenylalanine ammonia-lyase removes the amino group from phenylalanine, producing cinnamic acid, which has a three-carbon side chain attached to a benzene ring. The plant then trims this side chain by two carbons in a sequence of steps similar to the way animals break down fatty acids. What remains is benzoic acid, with a single carbon in its carboxyl group attached to the ring. Plants can store benzoic acid as it is or attach it to sugars and other molecules.
synthesis.significance: Cranberries and lingonberries accumulate enough benzoic acid to help them resist spoilage.

citations.title: Artificial food additives: hazardous to long-term health?
citations.abstract: Many additives, some of which have no nutritional value, can be legally used in processed foods. They intensify colour, thicken, increase shelf life and enhance flavour. Regulatory authorities issue approvals as safe within acceptable quantitative limits. Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) contain combinations of all these additives and are particularly attractive to children.Many publications suggest that artificial colourants, benzoate preservatives, non-caloric sweeteners, emulsifiers and their degradation derivatives have adverse effects by increasing risks of mental health disorders, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome and potential carcinogenic effects.A systematic review has established that artificial azo dye food colourants (AFCs) and sodium benzoate preservative cause disturbed behaviour in children. AFCs and benzoates in animal models have neurotoxic properties through gut microbial generation of toxic metabolites. Observational studies show associations between high emulsifier intake and cardiovascular disease. Animal models and in vitro studies have highlighted neurotoxic, cytotoxic, genotoxic and carcinogenic effects. High intake of non-caloric sweeteners has been linked to cardiovascular disease and depression in adults and is linked to childhood obesity.Little research has focused on children who are the largest consumers of UPFs. Potentially, they are a ticking time bomb for adult obesity, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular diseases, mental health disorders and cancers. Based on risk/benefit analysis, azo dye AFCs should be banned. Benzoates, emulsifiers and sweeteners require assessment of quantitative limits and cumulative effects of combinations. Consumers purchasing UPFs require information through ingredient health warnings and recommendations to use natural unprocessed foods which have well-described health-promoting properties. Clinical characteristics: Citrullinemia type I (CTLN1) presents as a spectrum that includes a neonatal acute form (the "classic" form), a milder late-onset form (the "non-classic" form), a form in which women have onset of symptoms at pregnancy or post partum, and a form without symptoms or hyperammonemia. Distinction between the forms is based primarily on clinical findings, although emerging evidence suggests that measurement of residual argininosuccinate synthase enzyme activity may help to predict those who are likely to have a severe phenotype and those who are likely to have an attenuated phenotype. Infants with the acute neonatal form appear normal at birth. Shortly thereafter, they develop hyperammonemia and become progressively lethargic, feed poorly, often vomit, and may develop signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Without prompt intervention, hyperammonemia and the accumulation of other toxic metabolites (e.g., glutamine) result in increased ICP, increased neuromuscular tone, spasticity, ankle clonus, seizures, loss of consciousness, and death. Children with the severe form who are treated promptly may survive for an indeterminate period of time, but usually with significant neurologic deficits. Even with chronic protein restriction and scavenger therapy, long-term complications such as liver failure and other (rarely reported) organ system manifestations are possible. The late-onset form may be milder than that seen in the acute neonatal form, but commences later in life for reasons that are not completely understood. The episodes of hyperammonemia are similar to those seen in the acute neonatal form, but the initial neurologic findings may be more subtle because of the older age of the affected individuals. Women with onset of severe symptoms including acute hepatic decompensation during pregnancy or in the postpartum period have been reported. Furthermore, previously asymptomatic and non-pregnant individuals have been described who remained asymptomatic up to at least age ten years, with the possibility that they could remain asymptomatic lifelong. Diagnosis/testing: The diagnosis of CTLN1 is established in a proband with elevated plasma ammonia concentration (>150 µmol/L; may range to ≥2000-3000 µmol/L), elevated plasma citrulline concentration (usually >500 µmol/L), and absent argininosuccinate and/or by identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in ASS1 on molecular genetic testing. Management: Treatment of manifestations: Liver transplantation is the only known curative therapy and eliminates the need for dietary restriction. Transplantation is ideally performed in affected individuals who are younger than age one year (prior to the development of any neurocognitive impairment) but older than age three months and/or above 5 kg body weight. Daily routine treatment in those who have not undergone a liver transplantation includes lifelong protein restriction in conjunction with a metabolic nutritionist; nitrogen scavenger medications; arginine supplementation; consideration of carnitine supplementation in those with secondary carnitine deficiency; addressing increased energy/caloric demands through tube feedings (as needed); and routine treatment of developmental delay / intellectual disability. Acute inpatient treatment of a metabolic crisis includes addressing hyperammonemia through withholding of all protein intake for a maximum of 24 to 28 hours; pharmacologic nitrogen scavenger therapy; and consideration of dialysis (the most effective means of reducing plasma ammonia concentration rapidly). To address increased catabolism, administration of high-energy fluids (and insulin, as needed) and intravenous intralipids is typically required. However, care must be taken to avoid electrolyte imbalance and fluid overload, which can contribute to the development of increased intracranial pressure. The patient should be maintained on the dry side of fluid balance (approximately 85 mL/kg of body weight per day in infants and appropriate corresponding fluid restriction in children and adults). Prevention of secondary complications: Education of parents and caregivers such that diligent observation and management can be administered expediently in the setting of intercurrent illness or other catabolic stressors; written protocols for maintenance and emergency treatment should be provided to parents and primary care providers / pediatricians, and to teachers and school staff. For those affected individuals requiring any sedated procedure where a person cannot eat for an extended period of time, drug treatment should be switched to IV and nutrition with 10% glucose with age-appropriate electrolytes should be administered via IV to promote anabolism starting as soon as the patient is NPO. Surveillance: Follow up in a metabolic clinic with a qualified metabolic nutritionist and clinical biochemical geneticist is required. Measurement of growth parameters; evaluation of nutrition status and safety of oral intake; assessment for early warning signs of impending hyperammonemic episodes (mood changes, headache, lethargy, nausea, refusal to eat); review of dietary assessment; monitoring of developmental progress/educational needs; assessment of mobility and self-help skills; and measurement of carnitine levels (for those on sodium benzoate) at each visit. Plasma amino acid analysis at least every three months during the first year of life and every six to 12 months in the teenage/adult years (depending on clinical stability). Agents/circumstances to avoid: Excessive protein intake, prolonged fasting, and obvious exposure to communicable diseases. Evaluation of relatives at risk: It is important that at-risk sibs be identified as soon as possible, either through molecular genetic testing (if the pathogenic variants in the family are known) or measurement of plasma concentrations of ammonia and citrulline on the first day of life. Elevation of either above acceptable levels (ammonia >100 µmol/L or plasma citrulline >~100 µmol/L) is sufficient evidence to initiate treatment in a newborn. Pregnancy management: Because women with onset of severe symptoms during pregnancy or in the postpartum period have been reported, scrupulous attention needs to be paid to diet and medication during these periods. Genetic counseling: CTLN1 is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. At conception, each sib of an affected individual has a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier. Carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal testing for a pregnancy at increased risk are possible if the pathogenic variants in the family are known.

citations.title: Water is a preservative of microbes.
citations.abstract: Water is the cellular milieu, drives all biochemistry within Earth's biosphere and facilitates microbe-mediated decay processes. Instead of reviewing these topics, the current article focuses on the activities of water as a preservative-its capacity to maintain the long-term integrity and viability of microbial cells-and identifies the mechanisms by which this occurs. Water provides for, and maintains, cellular structures; buffers against thermodynamic extremes, at various scales; can mitigate events that are traumatic to the cell membrane, such as desiccation-rehydration, freeze-thawing and thermal shock; prevents microbial dehydration that can otherwise exacerbate oxidative damage; mitigates against biocidal factors (in some circumstances reducing ultraviolet radiation and diluting solute stressors or toxic substances); and is effective at electrostatic screening so prevents damage to the cell by the intense electrostatic fields of some ions. In addition, the water retained in desiccated cells (historically referred to as 'bound' water) plays key roles in biomacromolecular structures and their interactions even for fully hydrated cells. Assuming that the components of the cell membrane are chemically stable or at least repairable, and the environment is fairly constant, water molecules can apparently maintain membrane geometries over very long periods provided these configurations represent thermodynamically stable states. The spores and vegetative cells of many microbes survive longer in the presence of vapour-phase water (at moderate-to-high relative humidities) than under more-arid conditions. There are several mechanisms by which large bodies of water, when cooled during subzero weather conditions remain in a liquid state thus preventing potentially dangerous (freeze-thaw) transitions for their microbiome. Microbial life can be preserved in pure water, freshwater systems, seawater, brines, ice/permafrost, sugar-rich aqueous milieux and vapour-phase water according to laboratory-based studies carried out over periods of years to decades and some natural environments that have yielded cells that are apparently thousands, or even (for hypersaline fluid inclusions of mineralized NaCl) hundreds of millions, of years old. The term preservative has often been restricted to those substances used to extend the shelf life of foods (e.g. sodium benzoate, nitrites and sulphites) or those used to conserve dead organisms, such as ethanol or formaldehyde. For living microorganisms however, the ultimate preservative may actually be water. Implications of this role are discussed with reference to the ecology of halophiles, human pathogens and other microbes; food science; biotechnology; biosignatures for life and other aspects of astrobiology; and the large-scale release/reactivation of preserved microbes caused by global climate change.

citations.title: [Inherited hyperammonemia].
citations.abstract: Inherited hyperammonemia disorders are caused by specific enzymatic defects in the urea cycle or in metabolic pathways related to it. These disorders can be divided into the following groups: deficiencies of urea cycle enzymes, transport defects of dibasic amino acids, organic acidemias, defects in beta-oxidation of fatty acids, transient hyperammonemia of the newborn-probably a not genetically determined disorder. Manifestation of the mentioned disorders includes elevated serum ammonia level resulting in altered level of consciousness and/or persisted vomiting. Occurrence of irreversible neurologic sequelae depends mostly on the extent of hyperammonemic period. Differential diagnosis includes blood gas, anion gap, plasma amino acids analysis and urine organic acids analysis. In some cases specific tissue enzymes activity measurement is necessary. Dialysis, sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate and arginine are used in the treatment of acute hyperammonemia. In addition oral or rectal neomycin and/or lactulose can be used, which reduces intestinal ammonia production.
