name: Potassium Sorbate
scoreRationale: One of the gentlest preservatives; the body metabolizes it like a fatty acid. Rare skin reactions keep it from a top score.
summary: Potassium sorbate prevents mold and yeast in cheese, baked goods, wine and cosmetics. It is broken down by the body much like a dietary fat.

physical.phStability: Effective up to about pH 6.5; best below pH 5

overview: Potassium sorbate is the potassium salt of sorbic acid, a six-carbon fatty acid with two conjugated double bonds (CH₃–CH=CH–CH=CH–COOH). The alternating single and double bonds share electrons along the chain, which makes the molecule absorb UV light and react slowly with oxygen.

Like benzoate, it works best as the uncharged acid, but sorbic acid's higher pKa (4.76) means it keeps working up to about pH 6.5, so it suits cheese, baked goods and wine. Because it looks like a natural fatty acid, the body burns it for energy the same way it burns dietary fat.
profile.function: Inhibits molds and yeasts (less so bacteria) and stops wine from re-fermenting after bottling.

mechanisms.title: Inhibiting mold and yeast
mechanisms.chemical: Like benzoate, potassium sorbate works through its uncharged acid form, sorbic acid, which can pass through the fatty membrane of a microbe. Once inside, sorbic acid does more than acidify the cell. Its chain of alternating double bonds is reactive, and it can bond with sulfhydryl groups (–SH), sulfur-containing groups found in many enzymes. When these groups are blocked, the enzymes can no longer do their jobs. Sorbic acid also seems to disturb the cell membrane itself, interfering with the way nutrients are carried into the cell.
mechanisms.biological: With key enzymes slowed and nutrient transport disrupted, molds and yeasts can't produce enough energy to grow and divide. Molds are particularly sensitive, which is why sorbate is widely used on cheese, bread, cakes, dried fruit and wine, where mold and yeast are the main spoilage risks. Bacteria are less affected, so sorbate is usually combined with acidity, refrigeration or other preservatives. It slows growth more than it kills, so it works best in products that start out with few microbes. Food made under clean conditions and preserved with sorbate can stay mold-free for weeks longer.

mechanisms.title: Metabolized like a fat
mechanisms.chemical: Sorbic acid is a six-carbon chain with a carboxylic acid group at one end, which makes it look very much like the fatty acids found in food fats and oils. Inside cells, enzymes attach it to coenzyme A, a helper molecule that tags fatty acids for breakdown. It then enters beta-oxidation, the pathway that chops fatty acids into two-carbon pieces. Each round of beta-oxidation removes two carbons as acetyl-CoA. Sorbic acid's double bonds just need a couple of extra enzyme steps that cells already use for the unsaturated fats in our diet.
mechanisms.biological: The two-carbon pieces enter the Krebs cycle, the same energy pathway used for sugars and fats, and are broken down to carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy the body can use. In effect, the body treats sorbic acid like a tiny amount of dietary fat. Because it is completely broken down, it doesn't build up in tissues. This efficient metabolism is one reason sorbic acid is considered among the safest preservatives. Long-term studies in animals fed large amounts found no harmful effects at levels far above what people eat.

reactions.title: Acid–base equilibrium
reactions.summary: When potassium sorbate dissolves in food, it splits into potassium ions and sorbate ions. Sorbate is the charged form, which doesn't easily enter microbes. To become the active, uncharged sorbic acid, each sorbate ion has to pick up a hydrogen ion from its surroundings, and how often that happens depends on how acidic the food is. The reaction runs in both directions at once, so at any pH there is a balance between the two forms, called an equilibrium. Sorbic acid's pKa, the pH at which the two forms are balanced fifty-fifty, is 4.76.

steps.name: Dissolving
steps.text: Potassium sorbate is a salt, so it dissolves readily in water and separates into potassium ions (K⁺) and sorbate ions. The potassium plays no part in preserving. Sorbic acid itself dissolves poorly in water, which is why the salt form is the one added to food.

steps.name: Protonation
steps.text: In acidic food there are many hydrogen ions (H⁺) available. Sorbate ions pick them up and become uncharged sorbic acid. The more acidic the food, the more of the preservative ends up in this active form.

steps.name: Activity
steps.text: At pH 4.76, exactly half is sorbic acid; at pH 3.76 about 90 percent is, and at pH 5.76 only about 10 percent. Because sorbic acid's pKa is higher than benzoic acid's, sorbate keeps some of its active form in mildly acidic foods up to about pH 6.5.

reactions.result: That's why sorbate works well in wine, yogurt, cheese and baked goods, which are mildly acidic, but is weak in neutral foods. Food makers sometimes add a little citric or lactic acid to boost its effect.

reactions.title: Mold decarboxylation (the kerosene smell)
reactions.summary: Some molds have found a way to fight back against sorbate. Certain species, particularly of Penicillium, along with some yeasts, carry an enzyme that breaks sorbic acid down, turning it into a different chemical that no longer stops them. This reaction, called decarboxylation, releases carbon dioxide and leaves behind a small, smelly hydrocarbon. The smell is so distinctive that food scientists use it as a clue that the preservative has been defeated. It is most often noticed in cheese, cakes and marzipan.

steps.name: Resistant molds
steps.text: Resistant molds produce an enzyme that recognizes sorbic acid and works on it. This lets them grow on foods where the preservative would normally hold them back. Food that becomes heavily contaminated is more likely to contain these strains.

steps.name: Decarboxylation
steps.text: The enzyme removes the carboxyl group (–COOH) from sorbic acid, which leaves as carbon dioxide gas. What remains is a five-carbon hydrocarbon, a molecule made only of carbon and hydrogen, called 1,3-pentadiene.

steps.name: Off-odor
steps.text: 1,3-Pentadiene is volatile, meaning it evaporates easily, and it smells strongly of kerosene, paint thinner or plastic. Even tiny amounts are noticeable, so the food smells wrong before it looks moldy.

reactions.result: A kerosene-like smell on old cheese, cake or marzipan means resistant mold has been breaking down the preservative, and the food should be thrown away. Producers prevent it with good hygiene, so that resistant molds never get a foothold in the first place.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a chemical preservative.
Group ADI of 11 mg/kg body weight per day for sorbic acid and potassium sorbate.
Permitted preservative.

hazards.title: Occasional skin reactions
hazards.summary: Potassium sorbate is one of the gentlest preservatives, but in a small number of people it can cause mild skin reactions. These are mostly seen with creams and cosmetics, where it is applied directly to the skin, sometimes at higher concentrations than in food. The usual reaction is brief stinging, redness or itchy bumps where the product touched the skin, appearing within minutes and fading within an hour or so. True allergy, which involves immune memory, is uncommon. People who notice a reaction can simply choose products without it.
hazards.chemical: At higher concentrations, sorbic acid can directly trigger certain cells in the skin to release inflammatory messengers such as histamine and prostaglandins, without the immune system first having to learn to recognize it. Prostaglandins are signaling molecules that make blood vessels widen and nerves more sensitive. Because no prior exposure is needed, this can happen the very first time someone uses the product. The effect depends strongly on dose, so more concentrated products are more likely to cause it. Sorbic acid's mild acidity may also add to the sting on sensitive or broken skin.
hazards.biological: The released messengers widen small blood vessels in the skin, which causes redness, and make them slightly leaky, so fluid collects and forms small raised bumps called wheals. This is known as contact urticaria, a hive-like reaction limited to where the product touched. Nerves are stimulated too, producing stinging or itching. Because no immune memory is involved, the reaction doesn't grow stronger with repeated use the way an allergy can. It fades as the messengers are cleared away.

profile.dosage: Foods use about 0.025 to 0.2 percent potassium sorbate, and cosmetics up to about 0.6 percent. International food-safety experts have set an acceptable daily intake (ADI) of up to 25 milligrams per kilogram of body weight for sorbic acid and its salts, while European regulators chose a more cautious group ADI of 11 milligrams per kilogram in 2019. Typical intakes fall well within both limits. Because the body breaks sorbate down like a fatty acid, it doesn't accumulate. Skin reactions are the main concern, and they are uncommon and mild.

myths.claim: Potassium sorbate is a pesticide.
myths.consensus: It is a food preservative with a fatty-acid-like structure; it is not registered or used as a pesticide.

myths.claim: It damages DNA.
myths.consensus: Some cell studies used concentrations far above food levels; regulatory reviews by EFSA and JECFA found no genotoxic concern at permitted uses.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Sorbic acid for food use is made in chemical plants from two small, simple industrial chemicals, ketene and crotonaldehyde. Chemists worked out how to make it on a large scale in the 1950s, once its value as a mold inhibitor was clear. The sorbic acid is then converted to its potassium salt, because the salt dissolves far better in water and is easier to mix into foods and drinks. The finished product is a white powder or granules. It is chemically identical to sorbic acid from natural sources.
synthesis.mechanism: Ketene (CH₂=C=O) is a highly reactive gas that readily adds onto other molecules. With the help of a catalyst, it reacts with crotonaldehyde, a four-carbon molecule containing a double bond and an aldehyde group, and the products link together into a long chain called a polyester, a polymer whose units are connected by ester bonds. Treating this polyester with acid and water breaks those ester bonds by hydrolysis, releasing individual sorbic acid molecules with their characteristic chain of two alternating double bonds. The sorbic acid is purified by crystallization. It is then neutralized with potassium hydroxide, which swaps the acid's hydrogen for potassium and forms potassium sorbate and water.
synthesis.significance: The salt is used because it dissolves far better in water than sorbic acid itself.

synthesis.title: Natural origin
synthesis.summary: Sorbic acid takes its name from the rowan or mountain ash tree, Sorbus aucuparia, whose bright orange-red berries are where it was first found. In 1859 the German chemist August Wilhelm von Hofmann distilled oil from rowan berries, isolated a compound called parasorbic acid, and converted it into sorbic acid. For decades it remained a chemical curiosity. Its ability to stop mold wasn't recognized until about 80 years later, and it came into wide use as a food preservative in the 1950s. Today essentially all commercial sorbic acid is made synthetically.
synthesis.mechanism: Rowan berries don't contain much sorbic acid itself. Instead they contain parasorbic acid, a close relative in which the carbon chain is curled into a ring, a structure chemists call a lactone. Parasorbic acid is mildly toxic, gives raw rowan berries a harsh taste and can upset the stomach. When the berries are heated, or the compound is treated with acid or base, the ring opens and the molecule rearranges into straight-chain sorbic acid, which is far less toxic. That chemical change is what Hofmann used to obtain sorbic acid. It also explains why rowan berries are always cooked before being made into jelly.
synthesis.significance: Cooking rowan berries before eating them turns irritating parasorbic acid into harmless sorbic acid, an old kitchen habit with a chemical explanation.

citations.title: Preservatives and ocular surface disease: A review.
citations.abstract: Ocular surface disease (OSD) is a complex condition that can cause a range of symptoms (e.g, dryness, irritation, and pain) and can significantly impact the quality of life of affected individuals. Iatrogenic OSD, a common finding in patients with glaucoma who receive chronic therapy with topical ocular antihypertensive drugs containing preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride (BAK), has been linked to damage to the ocular surface barrier, corneal epithelial cells, nerves, conjunctival goblet cells, and trabecular meshwork. Chronic BAK exposure activates inflammatory pathways and worsens symptoms, compromising the success of subsequent filtration surgery in an exposure-dependent manner. In eyes being treated for glaucoma, symptomatic treatment of OSD may provide some relief, but addressing the root cause of the OSD often necessitates reducing or, ideally, eliminating BAK toxicity. Strategies to decrease BAK exposure in patients with glaucoma encompass the use of preservative-free formulations or drugs with alternative and less toxic preservatives such as SofZia®, Polyquad, potassium sorbate, or Purite®. Though the benefits of these alternative preservatives are largely unproven, they might be considered when financial constraints prevent the use of preservative-free versions. For patients receiving multiple topical preserved drugs, the best practice is to switch to nonpreserved equivalents wherever feasible, regardless of OSD severity. Furthermore, nonpharmacological approaches, including laser or incisional procedures, should be considered. This review explores the effects of BAK on the ocular surface and reviews strategies for minimizing or eliminating BAK exposure in patients with glaucoma in order to significantly improve their quality of life and prevent complications associated with chronic exposure to BAK.

citations.title: Intake of food additive preservatives and incidence of cancer: results from the NutriNet-Santé prospective cohort.
citations.authors: Hasenböhler, Javaux, Payen de la Garanderie et al.
citations.abstract: Objective: To investigate the association between intake of food additive preservatives and cancer incidence in a large prospective cohort. Design: Prospective cohort. Setting: French NutriNet-Santé cohort, 2009-23. Participants: 105 260 participants (≥15 years) without prevalent cancer who completed at least two 24 hour dietary records at baseline. Main outcome measures: Cumulative time dependent intake of preservatives, including those in industrial food brands, assessed using repeated 24 hour dietary records and evaluated through multiple composition databases and ad hoc laboratory assays in food products for the most frequently consumed additive-food pairs. Associations between intake of three categories of preservatives (defined as sex specific thirds if preservative was consumed by at least a third of participants, otherwise defined as non-consumers and lower or higher consumers separated by the sex specific median) and cancer incidence were characterised using multivariable proportional hazards Cox models adjusted for potential confounders. Results: Mean age of participants was 42.0 years (standard deviation (SD 14.5) years), and 78.7% were women. 4226 participants received a diagnosis of incident cancer (mean follow-up 7.57 (SD 4.56) years), comprising 1208 breast, 508 prostate, 352 colorectal, and 2158 other cancers). Higher intakes of several preservatives were associated with higher cancer incidence: total non-antioxidants with overall cancer (hazard ratio for higher v non-consumers or lower consumers 1.16 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.07 to 1.26); absolute risk of cancer at age 60 years, respectively, 13.3%, 12.1%) and breast cancer (1.22 (1.05 to 1.41); 5.7%, 4.8%); total sorbates, specifically potassium sorbate, with overall cancer (1.14 (1.04 to 1.24); 13.4%, 11.8%) and breast cancer (1.26 (1.07 to 1.49); 5.7%, 4.6%); total sulfites with overall cancer (1.12 (1.02 to 1.24); 13.4%, 11.9%); potassium metabisulfite with overall cancer (1.11 (1.03 to 1.20); 13.5%, 12.0%) and breast cancer (1.20 (1.04 to 1.38); 5.7%, 4.9%); sodium nitrite with prostate cancer (1.32 (1.02 to 1.70); 4.2%, 3.4%); potassium nitrate with overall cancer (1.13 (1.05 to 1.23); 14.0%, 12.0%) and breast cancer (1.22 (1.05 to 1.41); 5.9%, 4.8%); total acetates with overall cancer (1.15 (1.06 to 1.25); 14.3%, 12.2%) and breast cancer (1.25 (1.07 to 1.45); 6.1%, 4.9%); acetic acid with overall cancer (1.12 (1.01 to 1.25); 14.4%, 12.4%); and sodium erythorbate with overall cancer (1.12 (1.04 to 1.22); 13.5%, 11.9%) and breast cancer (1.21 (1.04 to 1.41); 5.7%, 4.8%). 11 of the 17 individually studied preservatives were not associated with cancer incidence. Conclusion: Multiple positive associations between intake of preservatives widely used in industrial foods and higher cancer incidence (overall, breast, and prostate) were observed in this large prospective cohort. Epidemiology based on health effect biomarkers and experimental research are needed to gain insight into outcome pathways. If confirmed, these new data call for the re-evaluation of regulations governing the food industry's use of these additives, to improve consumer protection. In the meantime, the findings support recommendations for consumers to favour freshly made, minimally processed foods. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03335644.

citations.title: A novel ophthalmic latanoprost 0.005% nanoemulsion: a cytotoxicity study.
citations.authors: Tau, Passerini, Del Papa et al.
citations.abstract: Background: Benzalkonium chloride (BAK), the most commonly used preservative in anti-glaucoma eye drops, inflicts damage to the ocular surface. A novel anti-glaucoma formulation that avoids the use of BAK has been developed. The aim of this study was to evaluate the cytotoxicity of this formulation and to compare it with an ophthalmic solution containing BAK. Methods: Two different latanoprost eye drops were used: one ophthalmic solution (LSc) containing BAK 0.02% and one ophthalmic nanoemulsion (LNe) with a soft preservative (potassium sorbate 0.18%). Human epithelial conjunctival cells were incubated for 15, 30, and 60 min with either LSc or LNe. The cytotoxicity was determined by MTT assay. Cell death was measured by flow cytometry using annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide. Results: The values of cell viability and proliferation obtained from cells exposed to LNe were between 80 and 90% relative to the control group, whereas values obtained from cells exposed to LSc were around 30% at all study times (p < 0.05 at 15 and 30 min; p < 0.01 at 60 min). The percentage of viable cells decreased significantly when cells were incubated with LSc compared with cells incubated with LNe at all the study times, while the percentage of cells in late apoptosis/necrosis increased significantly in cells exposed to LSc compared to LNe. Conclusions: The new latanoprost nanoemulsion is significantly less cytotoxic on human conjunctival cells than LSc. These results suggest that the new formulation might be gentler on the eye surface than currently available BAK-preserved latanoprost solutions.

citations.title: Surface activity and foaming properties of saponin-rich plants extracts.
citations.abstract: Saponins are amphiphilic glycosidic secondary metabolites produced by numerous plants. So far only few of them have been thoroughly analyzed and even less have found industrial applications as biosurfactants. In this contribution we screen 45 plants from different families, reported to be rich in saponins, for their surface activity and foaming properties. For this purpose, the room-temperature aqueous extracts (macerates) from the alleged saponin-rich plant organs were prepared and spray-dried under the same conditions, in presence of sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate as preservatives and drying aids. For 15 selected plants, the extraction was also performed using hot water (decoction for 15 min) but high temperature in most cases deteriorated surface activity of the extracts. To our knowledge, for most of the extracts this is the first quantitative report on their surface activity. Among the tested plants, only 3 showed the ability to reduce surface tension of their solutions by more than 20 mN/m at 1% dry extract mass content. The adsorption layers forming spontaneously on the surface of these extracts showed a broad range of surface dilational rheology responses - from null to very high, with surface dilational elasticity modulus, E' in excess of 100 mN/m for 5 plants. In all cases the surface dilational response was dominated by the elastic contribution, typical for saponins and other biosurfactants. Almost all extracts showed the ability to froth, but only 32 could sustain the foam for more than 1 min (for 11 extracts the foams were stable during at least 10 min). In general, the ability to lower surface tension and to produce adsorbed layers with high surface elasticity did not correlate well with the ability to form and sustain the foam. Based on the overall characteristics, Saponaria officinalis L. (soapwort), Avena sativa L. (oat), Aesculus hippocastanum L. (horse chestnut), Chenopodium quinoa Willd. (quinoa), Vaccaria hispanica (Mill.) Rauschert (cowherb) and Glycine max (L.) Merr. (soybean) are proposed as the best potential sources of saponins for surfactant applications in natural cosmetic and household products.

name: High Fructose Corn Syrup
scoreRationale: Metabolically similar to sugar, but it signals sugar-sweetened, ultra-processed products; a major source of added sugar in American diets.
summary: HFCS is a liquid sweetener made from corn starch. It behaves much like table sugar in the body; the real issue is how much added sugar it delivers.

identity.composition: HFCS-42 (42% fructose, ~53% glucose) for foods; HFCS-55 (55% fructose, ~42% glucose) for soft drinks; about 24% water.

overview: High fructose corn syrup isn't a single molecule but a water solution of two simple sugars, glucose and fructose. Both have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆, but they are structural isomers: glucose is an aldose, with its carbonyl group at carbon 1, and usually forms a six-membered ring; fructose is a ketose, with its carbonyl at carbon 2, and often forms a five-membered ring.

Fructose tastes sweeter than glucose, so converting part of corn's glucose into fructose makes a cheap liquid sweetener as sweet as table sugar. The common grades are HFCS-42 (42% fructose), used in foods, and HFCS-55, used in soft drinks.
profile.function: Sweetens, retains moisture, prevents crystallization and browns well; being liquid it mixes easily into drinks.

mechanisms.title: How the liver handles fructose
mechanisms.chemical: Glucose and fructose contain the same atoms but are handled differently by the body. Glucose can be used by almost every cell, and its breakdown is controlled at an early step by an enzyme called phosphofructokinase, which acts like a brake: when a cell already has enough energy, this enzyme slows down. Fructose, by contrast, is mostly taken up by the liver, where an enzyme called fructokinase quickly attaches a phosphate group to it, forming fructose-1-phosphate. This molecule joins the energy pathway at a point after the phosphofructokinase brake. As a result, fructose flows into the liver's metabolism without the usual control.
mechanisms.biological: When fructose arrives in moderate amounts, as in a piece of fruit, the liver simply turns it into glucose, stores it as glycogen or burns it for energy. But when large amounts arrive often, mostly from sweetened drinks, the unregulated flow supplies more building blocks than the liver needs. The excess is turned into fat through a process called de novo lipogenesis, which means “making new fat.” Some of this fat is sent into the blood as triglycerides, and some stays in the liver. Over time this can contribute to fatty liver and less healthy blood-fat levels, which is why health guidelines focus on limiting sugary drinks.

mechanisms.title: Liquid calories and fullness
mechanisms.chemical: In a drink, sugar is already dissolved, so the body doesn't need to chew or break down any food structure to get to it. Liquids also leave the stomach quickly, especially when they contain no protein, fat or fiber. Protein and fat trigger hormones that slow stomach emptying, and fiber forms a gel that holds food back, but a soft drink has none of these. The sugar reaches the small intestine and is absorbed within minutes. The body receives a large dose of energy, measured in calories, very quickly.
mechanisms.biological: The brain judges how full we are partly from signals sent by the stomach and intestine, such as stretching and the release of fullness hormones. Liquid sugar produces weaker fullness signals than the same number of calories in solid food. Studies that track what people eat show that they usually don't eat less later to make up for the calories they drank. Over weeks and months, those extra calories add up. This helps explain why sugary drinks are more strongly linked to weight gain than solid sugary foods.

reactions.title: Turning starch into glucose
reactions.summary: High fructose corn syrup starts as corn starch, which is made of thousands of glucose units linked into long chains. To make a sweet syrup, those chains have to be cut into individual glucose molecules. This is done with enzymes, proteins that speed up specific reactions, in a process similar to what happens when you chew bread long enough that it starts to taste slightly sweet. Each cut uses up a water molecule, so the overall reaction is hydrolysis. The result is a clear syrup that is mostly glucose.

steps.name: Gelatinization
steps.text: Starch in corn is packed into tight granules that enzymes can't easily reach. Heating the starch in water makes the granules swell and burst as water molecules push between the chains. The chains loosen and unwind into a thick paste, giving the enzymes access.

steps.name: Liquefaction
steps.text: An enzyme called alpha-amylase cuts the long starch chains at random points along their length, turning them into shorter fragments called dextrins. This turns the thick paste thin and runny. Industrial alpha-amylases come from heat-loving bacteria, so they can work at the high temperatures used in this step.

steps.name: Saccharification
steps.text: A second enzyme, glucoamylase, works from the ends of the shorter chains, snipping off one glucose unit at a time. After a day or two, more than 95 percent of the starch has become glucose. The word saccharification comes from the Latin word for sugar.

reactions.result: The product is ordinary corn syrup, which is mostly glucose. Glucose is only about 70 to 75 percent as sweet as table sugar, so this syrup alone can't replace sugar in drinks without changing their taste. That's why the next step converts some of the glucose into sweeter fructose.

reactions.title: Isomerization: glucose into fructose
reactions.summary: Glucose and fructose are isomers, meaning they have exactly the same atoms, C₆H₁₂O₆, arranged differently. Fructose tastes considerably sweeter than glucose, so converting part of the glucose into fructose makes the syrup as sweet as table sugar. The conversion is done by an enzyme called glucose isomerase, which rearranges the atoms without adding or removing any. Learning to do this cheaply on a large scale transformed the sweetener industry. Nothing new is attached to the sugar; it is a rearrangement that also happens inside living cells.

steps.name: Ring opening
steps.text: In water, glucose molecules exist mostly as closed six-membered rings, but they briefly open into straight chains and then close again. The enzyme works on the open-chain form, in which glucose has an aldehyde group: a carbon double-bonded to oxygen at the very end of the chain (carbon 1).

steps.name: Rearrangement
steps.text: Glucose isomerase, fixed onto small beads packed in a column so it can be reused for months, moves a hydrogen atom from carbon 2 to carbon 1. This shifts the double-bonded oxygen from carbon 1 to carbon 2, turning the aldehyde into a ketone, a carbonyl group partway along the chain. The molecule is now fructose, which closes into its own ring.

steps.name: Enrichment
steps.text: The reaction runs in both directions, so it settles at a balance of about 42 percent fructose and 50 percent glucose, plus some other sugars. To make a sweeter syrup, a separation technique called chromatography pulls out a stream that is about 90 percent fructose. This is blended with the 42 percent syrup to make HFCS-55, the grade used in soft drinks.

reactions.result: Enzyme engineering made HFCS cheap enough to replace sugar in most American soft drinks by the mid-1980s. Nutritionally, HFCS-55 is very close to table sugar, which becomes half glucose and half fructose once digested. Its advantages for manufacturers are price and the fact that it is already a liquid.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; the FDA rejected renaming it "corn sugar" in 2012.
Sold as glucose-fructose syrup or isoglucose; production quotas ended in 2017.

hazards.title: Added sugar in sweetened drinks
hazards.summary: High fructose corn syrup is sometimes described as worse than ordinary sugar, but most research suggests the real concern is the total amount of added sugar people consume, not HFCS being uniquely harmful. HFCS and table sugar provide nearly the same mix of glucose and fructose. In the United States, HFCS is especially common in soft drinks, so it has become associated with the health problems of drinking too many sugary beverages. Those problems include weight gain, type 2 diabetes and tooth decay. Choosing water or unsweetened drinks most of the time lowers the risk whichever sugar a product contains.
hazards.chemical: HFCS-55 contains about 55 percent fructose and 42 percent glucose, while table sugar splits into exactly half of each during digestion. The difference is small, and in the body the two sweeteners produce very similar blood sugar and insulin responses. The main chemical difference is that in HFCS the two sugars are already separate, while sucrose must first be split by an enzyme, but that enzyme works so fast that it makes little practical difference. What matters most is that both deliver a lot of quickly absorbed sugar with no fiber or nutrients alongside it.
hazards.biological: Drinking large amounts of sugary drinks regularly adds many calories that don't make people feel full, which contributes to weight gain. Frequent large sugar loads also put extra demand on the body's insulin system and are linked to a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. Sugary drinks bathe the teeth in sugar that mouth bacteria turn into acid, causing cavities. Large studies that follow people for years find that those who drink more sugary beverages have higher rates of these conditions. The effects come from the sugar itself, so they apply just as much to drinks sweetened with cane sugar.

hazards.title: Liver fat with high fructose intake
hazards.summary: Eating large amounts of fructose regularly, mostly from sweetened drinks, can encourage fat to build up in the liver. This condition, long known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and now often called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, has become very common and affects roughly a quarter of adults worldwide. Fructose is not the only cause: extra calories, inactivity and genetics all play a part. The fructose in whole fruit isn't a concern, because fruit contains relatively little and comes with fiber and water. The issue is large, frequent doses of added sugar.
hazards.chemical: In the liver, fructose is tagged with a phosphate by fructokinase and enters the energy pathways after the main checkpoint that normally controls sugar breakdown. This means the liver can't easily slow fructose processing down when it already has enough energy. The extra carbon atoms from fructose are converted into acetyl-CoA, the starting material for building fatty acids. Fructose also appears to switch on genes that increase the liver's fat-making machinery. The new fatty acids are assembled into triglycerides, the main storage form of fat.
hazards.biological: Some of the triglycerides made in the liver are packaged into particles and released into the blood, raising blood triglyceride levels, which is a risk factor for heart disease. The rest can collect as fat droplets inside liver cells. A little liver fat is harmless, but large amounts can lead to inflammation, liver cell damage and eventually scarring called fibrosis. The good news is that fatty liver is often reversible: cutting back on sugary drinks, losing excess weight and exercising can reduce liver fat within weeks to months. Doctors can detect it with blood tests and ultrasound scans.

profile.dosage: A 20-ounce bottle of regular soda sweetened with HFCS can contain about 65 grams of sugar. That is more than double the World Health Organization's ideal limit of about 25 grams of free sugars a day for adults, and above the U.S. guideline of keeping added sugars under 10 percent of calories, which is about 50 grams on a 2,000-calorie diet. Because HFCS behaves almost exactly like table sugar in the body, it counts toward the same added-sugar limits. Small amounts in sauces, breads or condiments contribute relatively little; sweetened drinks are by far the biggest source. Swapping them for water or unsweetened drinks is the most effective way to cut intake.

myths.claim: HFCS is far worse than table sugar.
myths.consensus: HFCS-55 is 55% fructose versus 50% in sucrose; controlled studies show similar effects at equal doses. The problem is total added sugar.

myths.claim: HFCS contains mercury.
myths.consensus: A 2009 report found traces in some samples from older chlor-alkali caustic soda; manufacturers use mercury-free processes.

environment.notes: Tied to large-scale corn monoculture and fertilizer runoff.

synthesis.title: Industrial wet milling and enzyme processing
synthesis.summary: High fructose corn syrup is made from field corn through a series of physical and enzyme-based steps. The process was developed in the 1960s and scaled up in the 1970s, mostly in the United States, where corn was plentiful and cheap and sugar imports were restricted. Each step either separates parts of the corn kernel or uses enzymes to reshape the starch. The finished syrup is simply a mixture of the sugars glucose and fructose dissolved in water. Byproducts such as corn oil, gluten and fiber are sold for food and animal feed.
synthesis.mechanism: First, corn kernels are soaked in warm water containing a little sulfur dioxide for a day or two, which softens them and loosens the starch from the protein. The soaked kernels are ground and separated by weight and size, a process called wet milling, into germ (which yields corn oil), fiber, protein and pure starch. The starch is cooked in water and treated with alpha-amylase and then glucoamylase, enzymes that break it down into glucose. The glucose syrup flows through columns packed with immobilized glucose isomerase, enzyme fixed onto solid beads, which converts part of it to fructose. Finally the syrup is cleaned with activated carbon, which soaks up colors and off-flavors, and with ion-exchange resins, which remove minerals, then evaporated to the right thickness.
steps: Corn is soaked (steeped) to loosen the starch from the rest of the kernel.
Wet milling separates germ, fiber, protein and starch.
Two enzymes break the starch down into glucose syrup.
Immobilized glucose isomerase converts about 42 percent of the glucose to fructose.
Carbon filtering, ion exchange and evaporation purify and concentrate the syrup.
synthesis.significance: Japanese researcher Yoshiyuki Takasaki developed the industrial glucose-isomerase process in the 1960s.

citations.title: Dietary Fructose and Fructose-Induced Pathologies.
citations.abstract: The consumption of fructose as sugar and high-fructose corn syrup has markedly increased during the past several decades. This trend coincides with the exponential rise of metabolic diseases, including obesity, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes. While the biochemical pathways of fructose metabolism were elucidated in the early 1990s, organismal-level fructose metabolism and its whole-body pathophysiological impacts have been only recently investigated. In this review, we discuss the history of fructose consumption, biochemical and molecular pathways involved in fructose metabolism in different organs and gut microbiota, the role of fructose in the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases, and the remaining questions to treat such diseases.

citations.title: Molecular aspects of fructose metabolism and metabolic disease.
citations.abstract: Excessive sugar consumption is increasingly considered as a contributor to the emerging epidemics of obesity and the associated cardiometabolic disease. Sugar is added to the diet in the form of sucrose or high-fructose corn syrup, both of which comprise nearly equal amounts of glucose and fructose. The unique aspects of fructose metabolism and properties of fructose-derived metabolites allow for fructose to serve as a physiological signal of normal dietary sugar consumption. However, when fructose is consumed in excess, these unique properties may contribute to the pathogenesis of cardiometabolic disease. Here, we review the biochemistry, genetics, and physiology of fructose metabolism and consider mechanisms by which excessive fructose consumption may contribute to metabolic disease. Lastly, we consider new therapeutic options for the treatment of metabolic disease based upon this knowledge.

citations.title: Sugar consumption, metabolic disease and obesity: The state of the controversy.
citations.abstract: The impact of sugar consumption on health continues to be a controversial topic. The objective of this review is to discuss the evidence and lack of evidence that allows the controversy to continue, and why resolution of the controversy is important. There are plausible mechanisms and research evidence that supports the suggestion that consumption of excess sugar promotes the development of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) both directly and indirectly. The direct pathway involves the unregulated hepatic uptake and metabolism of fructose, leading to liver lipid accumulation, dyslipidemia, decreased insulin sensitivity and increased uric acid levels. The epidemiological data suggest that these direct effects of fructose are pertinent to the consumption of the fructose-containing sugars, sucrose and high fructose corn syrup (HFCS), which are the predominant added sugars. Consumption of added sugar is associated with development and/or prevalence of fatty liver, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, hyperuricemia, CVD and T2DM, often independent of body weight gain or total energy intake. There are diet intervention studies in which human subjects exhibited increased circulating lipids and decreased insulin sensitivity when consuming high sugar compared with control diets. Most recently, our group has reported that supplementing the ad libitum diets of young adults with beverages containing 0%, 10%, 17.5% or 25% of daily energy requirement (Ereq) as HFCS increased lipid/lipoprotein risk factors for CVD and uric acid in a dose-response manner. However, un-confounded studies conducted in healthy humans under a controlled, energy-balanced diet protocol that enables determination of the effects of sugar with diets that do not allow for body weight gain are lacking. Furthermore, recent reports conclude that there are no adverse effects of consuming beverages containing up to 30% Ereq sucrose or HFCS, and the conclusions from several meta-analyses suggest that fructose has no specific adverse effects relative to any other carbohydrate. Consumption of excess sugar may also promote the development of CVD and T2DM indirectly by causing increased body weight and fat gain, but this is also a topic of controversy. Mechanistically, it is plausible that fructose consumption causes increased energy intake and reduced energy expenditure due to its failure to stimulate leptin production. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) of the brain demonstrates that the brain responds differently to fructose or fructose-containing sugars compared with glucose or aspartame. Some epidemiological studies show that sugar consumption is associated with body weight gain, and there are intervention studies in which consumption of ad libitum high-sugar diets promoted increased body weight gain compared with consumption of ad libitum low- sugar diets. However, there are no studies in which energy intake and weight gain were compared in subjects consuming high or low sugar, blinded, ad libitum diets formulated to ensure both groups consumed a comparable macronutrient distribution and the same amounts of fiber. There is also little data to determine whether the form in which added sugar is consumed, as beverage or as solid food, affects its potential to promote weight gain. It will be very challenging to obtain the funding to conduct the clinical diet studies needed to address these evidence gaps, especially at the levels of added sugar that are commonly consumed. Yet, filling these evidence gaps may be necessary for supporting the policy changes that will help to turn the food environment into one that does not promote the development of obesity and metabolic disease.

citations.title: Mediterranean diet: The role of long-chain ω-3 fatty acids in fish; polyphenols in fruits, vegetables, cereals, coffee, tea, cacao and wine; probiotics and vitamins in prevention of stroke, age-related cognitive decline, and Alzheimer disease.
citations.abstract: The mechanisms of action of the dietary components of the Mediterranean diet are reviewed in prevention of cardiovascular disease, stroke, age-associated cognitive decline and Alzheimer disease. A companion article provides a comprehensive review of extra-virgin olive oil. The benefits of consumption of long-chain ω-3 fatty acids are described. Fresh fish provides eicosapentaenoic acid while α-linolenic acid is found in canola and soybean oils, purslane and nuts. These ω-3 fatty acids interact metabolically with ω-6 fatty acids mainly linoleic acid from corn oil, sunflower oil and peanut oil. Diets rich in ω-6 fatty acids inhibit the formation of healthier ω-3 fatty acids. The deleterious effects on lipid metabolism of excessive intake of carbohydrates, in particular high-fructose corn syrup and artificial sweeteners, are explained. The critical role of the ω-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid in the developing and aging brain and in Alzheimer disease is addressed. Nutritional epidemiology studies, prospective population-based surveys, and clinical trials confirm the salutary effects of fish consumption on prevention of coronary artery disease, stroke and dementia. Recent recommendations on fish consumption by pregnant women and potential mercury toxicity are reviewed. The polyphenols and flavonoids of plant origin play a critical role in the Mediterranean diet, because of their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of benefit in type-2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, stroke and cancer prevention. Polyphenols from fruits and vegetables modulate tau hyperphosphorylation and beta amyloid aggregation in animal models of Alzheimer disease. From the public health viewpoint worldwide the daily consumption of fruits and vegetables has become the main tool for prevention of cardiovascular disease and stroke. We review the important dietary role of cereal grains in prevention of coronary disease and stroke. Polyphenols from grapes, wine and alcoholic beverages are discussed, in particular their effects on coagulation. The mechanisms of action of probiotics and vitamins are also included.

name: Aspartame
scoreRationale: Safe for most people within the ADI, but IARC's 2023 "possibly carcinogenic" classification, the phenylalanine warning and the WHO advice against sweeteners for weight control keep it in the middle.
summary: Aspartame is a low-calorie sweetener about 200 times sweeter than sugar. Regulators consider it safe within daily limits, but people with PKU must avoid it.

physical.phStability: Most stable at pH 4.3; breaks down with heat or in neutral/alkaline conditions

overview: Aspartame is the methyl ester of a dipeptide: two amino acids, aspartic acid and phenylalanine, joined by a peptide bond, with a methyl group capping phenylalanine's carboxyl end. Each building block is an ordinary part of dietary protein.

It is about 200 times sweeter than sugar, so tiny amounts replace a spoonful of sugar with almost no calories. The trade-off is fragility: heat, time and neutral pH break the molecule apart, so diet drinks slowly lose their sweetness and aspartame is rarely used for baking.
profile.function: Provides sugar-like sweetness with almost no calories in diet sodas, yogurts, gum and tabletop sweeteners.

mechanisms.title: Sweetness without the sugar
mechanisms.chemical: Aspartame works on the same sweet-taste receptor as sugar, a pair of proteins called T1R2 and T1R3 on the surface of taste cells. Its shape lets it slip into a pocket of the receptor and grip it far more tightly than sucrose does, using hydrogen bonds plus attractions between its oily phenylalanine ring and oily patches inside the receptor. A molecule that binds tightly only needs to be present at a low concentration to switch a receptor on. Aspartame activates the receptor at roughly one two-hundredth of the concentration sugar needs, which is why it is described as about 200 times sweeter. Small changes to its structure, even flipping one part into its mirror image, can make it taste bitter or tasteless instead.
mechanisms.biological: Once activated, the receptor sends the brain the same “sweet” signal that sugar does, so food and drinks taste sweet. Aspartame is made of the same building blocks as protein, and like protein it provides about 4 calories per gram. But because so little is needed, those calories are negligible: a can of diet soda contains roughly 200 milligrams, which adds up to less than one calorie. That is how diet drinks taste sweet with almost no energy. Some people notice a slightly different aftertaste or a sweetness that lingers longer than sugar's, because the molecule grips and releases the receptor differently.

mechanisms.title: Digested into familiar molecules
mechanisms.chemical: In the small intestine, enzymes break aspartame apart using water, a reaction called hydrolysis. An esterase, an enzyme that cuts ester bonds, removes the methyl group as methanol. Peptidases, enzymes that cut the bonds between amino acids, then split the remaining two-part molecule into aspartic acid and phenylalanine. By weight, aspartame yields roughly 50 percent phenylalanine, 40 percent aspartic acid and 10 percent methanol. Essentially none of the original aspartame reaches the bloodstream intact.
mechanisms.biological: The three products are absorbed and handled exactly like the same molecules from ordinary food. Aspartic acid and phenylalanine are amino acids found in every protein you eat, from milk to beans, and a normal serving of those foods supplies far more of them than a diet drink. Methanol is converted in the liver into formaldehyde and then quickly into formic acid, which is processed further. Fruits and vegetables release methanol naturally too, and a glass of tomato juice provides more of it than a can of diet soda. Because the amounts are small and travel through normal pathways, they don't build up.

mechanisms.title: Phenylalanine and PKU
mechanisms.chemical: Normally, a liver enzyme called phenylalanine hydroxylase adds a hydroxyl group (–OH) to phenylalanine, converting it into another amino acid, tyrosine. People with phenylketonuria (PKU) inherit two faulty copies of the gene for this enzyme, so it works poorly or not at all. Phenylalanine from food then can't be converted and builds up in the blood. Some of it is diverted into other molecules called phenylketones, which give the disease its name. Since aspartame is about half phenylalanine by weight, it adds to this load.
mechanisms.biological: High levels of phenylalanine interfere with brain development, partly by crowding out other amino acids that the brain needs to make chemical messengers such as dopamine and serotonin. Untreated PKU causes severe intellectual disability. Today, newborns in many countries are tested for PKU with a heel-prick blood test in their first days of life, and babies who have it follow a strict low-phenylalanine diet from then on. That diet limits high-protein foods and avoids aspartame. This is why every product containing aspartame must carry the warning “Phenylketonurics: contains phenylalanine.”

reactions.title: Hydrolysis during digestion
reactions.summary: Aspartame is held together by two kinds of bonds that water can break: an ester bond, which attaches the methyl group, and a peptide bond, which joins the two amino acids. In the body these bonds are broken by digestive enzymes, the same way the proteins in food are digested. Breaking a bond with water is called hydrolysis, and each break uses up one water molecule. It all happens in the small intestine, so intact aspartame isn't absorbed into the blood. What the body actually receives are three small, familiar molecules.

steps.name: Ester hydrolysis
steps.text: An enzyme called an esterase attacks the ester bond at the phenylalanine end and adds water across it. The methyl group leaves as methanol (CH₃OH), and the phenylalanine end becomes an ordinary carboxylic acid. This removes the part of the molecule most responsible for its sweetness.

steps.name: Peptide hydrolysis
steps.text: A peptidase, one of the enzymes that normally digests protein, cuts the peptide bond joining aspartic acid to phenylalanine. Again, water is added across the bond. The result is two separate amino acids.

steps.name: Absorption
steps.text: Aspartic acid and phenylalanine are carried into the cells lining the intestine by the same transporters that absorb amino acids from food. From there they join the body's general pool of amino acids, used for building proteins or burned for energy. The methanol is absorbed and processed by the liver.

reactions.result: Nothing unusual is left behind, which is why regulators evaluate aspartame's breakdown products alongside the sweetener itself. Because those products are identical to molecules from ordinary food, the body already has well-worn ways of handling them.

reactions.title: Cyclization (why diet drinks go flat in taste)
reactions.summary: Aspartame is less stable than sugar, and one reason is that it can react with itself. Over time, especially when warm, one end of the molecule bends around and attacks the other end, forming a ring. A reaction that turns a chain into a ring is called cyclization. The ring-shaped product doesn't fit the sweet receptor, so it has no sweet taste at all. This is why diet sodas slowly lose sweetness in storage and why aspartame is a poor choice for baking.

steps.name: Internal attack
steps.text: The free amino group (–NH₂) at the aspartic acid end has a lone pair of electrons. Because the molecule is flexible, this group can swing around and reach the carbonyl carbon of the ester at the phenylalanine end, which is electron-poor. The amino group attacks that carbon and begins forming a new bond.

steps.name: Methanol leaves
steps.text: As the new carbon–nitrogen bond forms, that carbon has to give up one of its existing bonds. The methoxy group (–OCH₃) leaves and picks up a hydrogen to become methanol. The molecule is now joined end to end.

steps.name: Ring formation
steps.text: The product is a six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms, called a diketopiperazine. Its shape is completely different from aspartame's, so it doesn't activate the sweet receptor. The change can't be undone.

reactions.result: Heat and long storage speed this reaction up, so old diet sodas taste less sweet, and most of the aspartame in a batter would break down in the oven. Manufacturers who need heat stability choose sweeteners such as sucralose instead. The diketopiperazine itself has been studied and is considered safe at the levels that form.

regulatory.status: Approved as a general-purpose sweetener.
Reaffirmed the ADI of 40 mg/kg body weight after reviewing cancer data.
Group 2B "possibly carcinogenic to humans" based on limited evidence; a hazard label, not a measure of risk at normal intake.
Conditionally advises against non-sugar sweeteners for long-term weight control.

hazards.title: IARC “possibly carcinogenic” classification
hazards.summary: In 2023, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified aspartame as “possibly carcinogenic to humans,” its Group 2B. This category signals a possible hazard backed by limited evidence, and it also contains things like aloe vera extract and pickled vegetables. IARC does not consider how much of something people actually consume. At the same time, a separate expert committee of the World Health Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization, called JECFA, reviewed the same evidence and left the acceptable daily intake unchanged. Put simply, the evidence was judged too weak to show harm at normal intakes.
hazards.chemical: The main evidence came from a few observational studies in people and from animal experiments. Lifetime studies in rats from one Italian research institute reported more tumors in animals fed aspartame, but other scientists criticized their methods, and other animal studies have not found the same effect. Some laboratory studies have suggested that aspartame or its breakdown products might cause oxidative stress, an imbalance in which reactive oxygen molecules damage cells. However, aspartame itself never reaches the blood intact, and its breakdown products are the same as those from ordinary foods. No clear chemical mechanism for cancer at normal doses has been shown.
hazards.biological: IARC's job is to ask whether something could cause cancer under any circumstances, while JECFA's job is to work out a safe level of intake. JECFA concluded there was no convincing evidence of harm at the existing acceptable daily intake of 40 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day. For a 70-kilogram adult that is about 2,800 milligrams daily, roughly the amount in 9 to 14 cans of diet soda every day for life. Most people consume far less. Researchers continue to study long-term effects, and some health groups advise moderation simply because of the remaining uncertainty.

hazards.title: Danger for people with PKU
hazards.summary: For most people aspartame poses no particular risk, but for people born with phenylketonuria (PKU) it is a real hazard. PKU affects roughly 1 in 10,000 to 15,000 babies and is caused by an inherited problem with the enzyme that processes phenylalanine. People with PKU must strictly limit phenylalanine from every source throughout their lives. Aspartame is a hidden source in diet drinks, chewing gum and some medicines, which is why it has to be labeled. With early diagnosis and a careful diet, people with PKU grow up healthy.
hazards.chemical: Aspartame is about 50 percent phenylalanine by weight, which is released during digestion as free phenylalanine. In most people, the liver enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase converts extra phenylalanine into tyrosine, another amino acid. People with PKU lack a working version of this enzyme. So almost all the phenylalanine they eat, beyond what the body uses to build proteins, accumulates in the blood. A single can of diet soda can therefore use up a meaningful part of their tightly limited daily allowance.
hazards.biological: When blood phenylalanine stays high, it enters the brain and crowds out other amino acids the brain needs to make neurotransmitters, the chemical messengers between nerve cells. In babies and young children, whose brains are still developing, this can cause permanent intellectual disability, seizures and behavior problems. In adults, high levels can cause trouble concentrating, mood changes and headaches. This is why newborns are screened and why products containing aspartame must state “Phenylketonurics: contains phenylalanine.” Women with PKU need especially careful control during pregnancy to protect the baby's brain.

profile.dosage: The acceptable daily intake (ADI), the amount considered safe to eat every day for life, is 40 milligrams per kilogram of body weight according to JECFA and European regulators, and 50 milligrams per kilogram according to the U.S. FDA. For a 70-kilogram adult, reaching JECFA's limit would take roughly 9 to 14 cans of diet soda every day, depending on the brand, and most people consume a small fraction of that. The methanol released from a can of diet soda is less than from a glass of fruit or tomato juice. People with phenylketonuria are the exception and must avoid aspartame. Because aspartame breaks down when heated or stored warm, products containing it keep their sweetness best when kept cool.

myths.claim: Aspartame is proven to cause cancer.
myths.consensus: IARC's 2B label means limited evidence (the same category as aloe vera extract). JECFA found no reason to change the safe daily limit.

myths.claim: Aspartame turns into formaldehyde and poisons you.
myths.consensus: Methanol from aspartame is metabolized like the larger amounts naturally present in fruits and vegetables.

synthesis.title: Chemical peptide coupling
synthesis.summary: Aspartame was discovered by accident in 1965, when a chemist working on an ulcer drug licked his finger and noticed it tasted sweet. Making it means joining two amino acids, aspartic acid and phenylalanine methyl ester, with a peptide bond. The challenge is that aspartic acid has two carboxylic acid groups and one amino group, all of which could react. If the bond forms at the wrong spot, the product tastes bitter instead of sweet. Chemists therefore use protecting groups, temporary chemical caps, to control which part reacts.
synthesis.mechanism: First, aspartic acid's amino group is protected, for example by converting it into an N-formyl group, so it can't react with itself. The protected aspartic acid is turned into an anhydride, a reactive form in which its two acid groups are activated. This activated molecule is mixed with phenylalanine methyl ester, whose free amino group attacks one of the activated carbonyl carbons and forms the peptide bond. Reaction conditions are tuned so the bond forms mainly at aspartic acid's alpha carboxyl group, the one next to the amino group. Finally, the protecting group is removed with acid, and the bitter-tasting isomer formed at the other carboxyl group is separated out.
synthesis.significance: Small structural differences change taste completely: linking the amino acids through the wrong carboxyl group gives a bitter molecule, not a sweet one.

synthesis.title: Enzymatic coupling
synthesis.summary: An alternative way to make aspartame uses an enzyme instead of protecting-group chemistry to form the peptide bond. Enzymes are extraordinarily selective: they react only at specific positions and only with one mirror-image form of a molecule. This avoids the bitter isomer and other unwanted products. The enzyme used is thermolysin, which comes from a heat-loving bacterium. Enzymatic processes like this are often called green chemistry because they produce less waste.
synthesis.mechanism: Thermolysin is a protease, an enzyme that normally cuts peptide bonds by adding water to them. But reactions can run in reverse when conditions favor the products. Manufacturers use high concentrations of the starting materials and arrange for the product to come out of solution as an insoluble salt, which pulls the reaction toward forming the bond rather than breaking it. The enzyme joins protected aspartic acid to phenylalanine methyl ester, reacting only at the correct carboxyl group and only with the L-forms of the amino acids, the forms found in nature. The protecting group is removed afterward to give pure aspartame.
synthesis.significance: Enzymes give a level of control over 3D structure that is difficult to achieve with ordinary chemical reagents.

citations.title: Sweetener aspartame aggravates atherosclerosis through insulin-triggered inflammation.
citations.abstract: Consumption of artificial sweeteners (ASWs) in various foods and beverages has been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). However, molecular mechanisms underlying ASW-associated CVD remain unknown. Here, we show that consumption of 0.15% aspartame (APM) markedly increased insulin secretion in mice and monkeys. Bilateral subdiaphragmatic vagotomy (SDV) obliterated APM-elevated blood insulin levels, demonstrating crucial roles of parasympathetic activation in regulation of insulin secretion. Incessant APM feeding of ApoE-/- mice aggravated atherosclerotic plaque formation and growth via an insulin-dependent mechanism. Implantation of an insulin-slow-release pump in ApoE-/- mice exacerbated atherosclerosis. Whole-genome expression profiling discovered that CX3CL1 chemokine was the most upregulated gene in the insulin-stimulated arterial endothelial cells. Specific deletion of a CX3CL1 receptor, Cx3cr1 gene, in monocytes/macrophages completely abrogated the APM-exacerbated atherosclerosis. Our findings uncover a novel mechanism of APM-associated atherosclerosis and therapeutic targeting of the endothelial CX3CL1-macrophage CX3CR1 signaling axis provides an approach for treating atherosclerotic CVD.
