citations.title: Aspartame Safety as a Food Sweetener and Related Health Hazards.
citations.abstract: Aspartame is the methyl-ester of the aspartate-phenylalanine dipeptide. Over time, it has become a very popular artificial sweetener. However, since its approval by the main food safety agencies, several concerns have been raised related to neuropsychiatric effects and neurotoxicity due to its ability to activate glutamate receptors, as well as carcinogenic risks due to the increased production of reactive oxygen species. Within this review, we critically evaluate reports concerning the safety of aspartame. Some studies evidenced subtle mood and behavioral changes upon daily high-dose intake below the admitted limit. Epidemiology studies also evidenced associations between daily aspartame intake and a higher predisposition for malignant diseases, like non-Hodgkin lymphomas and multiple myelomas, particularly in males, but an association by chance still could not be excluded. While the debate over the carcinogenic risk of aspartame is ongoing, it is clear that its use may pose some dangers in peculiar cases, such as patients with seizures or other neurological diseases; it should be totally forbidden for patients with phenylketonuria, and reduced doses or complete avoidance are advisable during pregnancy. It would be also highly desirable for every product containing aspartame to clearly indicate on the label the exact amount of the substance and some risk warnings.

citations.title: Artificial sweeteners and cancer risk: Results from the NutriNet-Santé population-based cohort study.
citations.abstract: Background: The food industry uses artificial sweeteners in a wide range of foods and beverages as alternatives to added sugars, for which deleterious effects on several chronic diseases are now well established. The safety of these food additives is debated, with conflicting findings regarding their role in the aetiology of various diseases. In particular, their carcinogenicity has been suggested by several experimental studies, but robust epidemiological evidence is lacking. Thus, our objective was to investigate the associations between artificial sweetener intakes (total from all dietary sources, and most frequently consumed ones: aspartame [E951], acesulfame-K [E950], and sucralose [E955]) and cancer risk (overall and by site). Methods and findings: Overall, 102,865 adults from the French population-based cohort NutriNet-Santé (2009-2021) were included (median follow-up time = 7.8 years). Dietary intakes and consumption of sweeteners were obtained by repeated 24-hour dietary records including brand names of industrial products. Associations between sweeteners and cancer incidence were assessed by Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for age, sex, education, physical activity, smoking, body mass index, height, weight gain during follow-up, diabetes, family history of cancer, number of 24-hour dietary records, and baseline intakes of energy, alcohol, sodium, saturated fatty acids, fibre, sugar, fruit and vegetables, whole-grain foods, and dairy products. Compared to non-consumers, higher consumers of total artificial sweeteners (i.e., above the median exposure in consumers) had higher risk of overall cancer (n = 3,358 cases, hazard ratio [HR] = 1.13 [95% CI 1.03 to 1.25], P-trend = 0.002). In particular, aspartame (HR = 1.15 [95% CI 1.03 to 1.28], P = 0.002) and acesulfame-K (HR = 1.13 [95% CI 1.01 to 1.26], P = 0.007) were associated with increased cancer risk. Higher risks were also observed for breast cancer (n = 979 cases, HR = 1.22 [95% CI 1.01 to 1.48], P = 0.036, for aspartame) and obesity-related cancers (n = 2,023 cases, HR = 1.13 [95% CI 1.00 to 1.28], P = 0.036, for total artificial sweeteners, and HR = 1.15 [95% CI 1.01 to 1.32], P = 0.026, for aspartame). Limitations of this study include potential selection bias, residual confounding, and reverse causality, though sensitivity analyses were performed to address these concerns. Conclusions: In this large cohort study, artificial sweeteners (especially aspartame and acesulfame-K), which are used in many food and beverage brands worldwide, were associated with increased cancer risk. These findings provide important and novel insights for the ongoing re-evaluation of food additive sweeteners by the European Food Safety Authority and other health agencies globally. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03335644.

citations.title: Neurophysiological symptoms and aspartame: What is the connection?
citations.abstract: Aspartame (α-aspartyl-l-phenylalanine-o-methyl ester), an artificial sweetener, has been linked to behavioral and cognitive problems. Possible neurophysiological symptoms include learning problems, headache, seizure, migraines, irritable moods, anxiety, depression, and insomnia. The consumption of aspartame, unlike dietary protein, can elevate the levels of phenylalanine and aspartic acid in the brain. These compounds can inhibit the synthesis and release of neurotransmitters, dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, which are known regulators of neurophysiological activity. Aspartame acts as a chemical stressor by elevating plasma cortisol levels and causing the production of excess free radicals. High cortisol levels and excess free radicals may increase the brains vulnerability to oxidative stress which may have adverse effects on neurobehavioral health. We reviewed studies linking neurophysiological symptoms to aspartame usage and conclude that aspartame may be responsible for adverse neurobehavioral health outcomes. Aspartame consumption needs to be approached with caution due to the possible effects on neurobehavioral health. Whether aspartame and its metabolites are safe for general consumption is still debatable due to a lack of consistent data. More research evaluating the neurobehavioral effects of aspartame are required.

name: Sucralose
scoreRationale: Approved and mostly unabsorbed, but emerging research on gut microbes, a genotoxic impurity and heating by-products warrants caution.
summary: Sucralose is a chlorinated sugar about 600 times sweeter than sugar. Most of it passes through the body unchanged; newer studies raise open questions.

physical.phStability: Stable over a wide pH range and during most cooking

overview: Sucralose is sucrose with three of its hydroxyl (–OH) groups replaced by chlorine atoms, and one carbon of the glucose half flipped into its mirror-image configuration. Those changes make it about 600 times sweeter than sugar.

The chlorine atoms also make the molecule unrecognizable to the enzyme that digests sucrose, so it passes through the body mostly unchanged and provides essentially no calories. Carbon–chlorine bonds are strong, so sucralose survives most cooking and even wastewater treatment.
profile.function: Adds zero-calorie sweetness to drinks, baked goods, protein powders and flavored lip products.

mechanisms.title: Intense sweetness
mechanisms.chemical: Sucralose is made from sucrose by replacing three of its hydroxyl groups (–OH) with chlorine atoms. Chlorine atoms are larger than hydroxyl groups and repel water, so they change both the molecule's shape and the way it interacts with the sweet-taste receptor, the T1R2/T1R3 protein pair on taste cells. These changes let sucralose settle into the receptor's binding pocket much more snugly than sugar can. A molecule that binds tightly switches the receptor on even at very low concentrations. As a result, sucralose is roughly 600 times sweeter than sucrose.
mechanisms.biological: The activated receptor sends the brain the same message as sugar, so the taste is clean and sugar-like, without the bitter aftertaste of some older sweeteners. Because it is so potent, only a few milligrams are needed to match a teaspoon of sugar, which is why packets of sucralose sweetener are mostly filler such as maltodextrin. Sucralose provides essentially no calories, since the body doesn't break it down for energy. The sweet taste may still trigger a small insulin release in some people, a reflex called the cephalic phase insulin response, though studies disagree on whether this matters. For most people, sucralose has no measurable effect on blood sugar.

mechanisms.title: Passing through undigested
mechanisms.chemical: Ordinary sucrose is split by an enzyme in the small intestine called sucrase, which recognizes the exact shape of the bond connecting glucose to fructose. In sucralose, the chlorine atoms change the shape around that bond, so the enzyme can't grip it or split it. The chlorinated molecule also isn't recognized by the transporter proteins that carry sugars across the gut wall. Small molecules can sometimes slip through cell membranes on their own, but sucralose's structure makes this inefficient. So very little of it is absorbed.
mechanisms.biological: About 85 percent of the sucralose you eat passes through the intestines and leaves unchanged in feces. Of the small amount that is absorbed, most is filtered out by the kidneys and leaves in urine within about a day. Because the body doesn't break it down for energy, it adds no calories. It also doesn't accumulate in body fat, since it dissolves in water rather than oil. Studies that tracked labeled sucralose through the bodies of volunteers confirmed this pattern.

mechanisms.title: Possible effects on gut microbes
mechanisms.chemical: Because most sucralose isn't absorbed, it travels on to the colon, the last section of the intestine, where trillions of bacteria live. These bacteria meet it at much higher concentrations than any other part of the body does. Laboratory studies suggest sucralose may affect the growth of some bacterial species more than others. Some research also suggests gut bacteria can modify a small portion of it, for example producing traces of sucralose-6-acetate. How much these interactions matter at normal intakes is still being worked out.
mechanisms.biological: Gut bacteria help digest food, train the immune system and produce useful substances, so changes in their balance could, in theory, affect health. A few human studies have reported shifts in gut bacteria, and small changes in how blood sugar responds to glucose, after people consumed sucralose for several weeks. Other studies have found no such effects. The results vary with the dose, the length of the study and the people taking part. Scientists consider this an emerging area, and no firm conclusions about health effects have been reached.

reactions.title: Selective chlorination (how it's made)
reactions.summary: Making sucralose requires swapping exactly three of sucrose's eight hydroxyl groups for chlorine atoms while leaving the other five untouched. That is tricky, because all eight hydroxyl groups are chemically similar and a chlorinating reagent can't tell them apart on its own. Chemists solve this with a strategy called protection: they temporarily block the groups they don't want to react, carry out the reaction, and then remove the blocks. Along the way, the 3D arrangement of atoms at one carbon is flipped. Hitting exactly the right three positions is what turns sugar into a high-intensity sweetener.

steps.name: Protection
steps.text: The hydroxyl group at carbon 6 of the glucose ring is capped with an acetyl group, forming an ester that won't react with the chlorinating reagent. This position is the most exposed and would otherwise react first. Capping it steers the next reaction toward the positions chemists want.

steps.name: Chlorination
steps.text: A chlorinating reagent replaces the hydroxyls at three positions, carbon 4 on the glucose ring and carbons 1' and 6' on the fructose ring, with chlorine atoms. At carbon 4 the chlorine comes in from the opposite side, so that carbon's 3D arrangement flips. This inversion turns the glucose ring into a galactose-shaped ring, which is part of why digestive enzymes don't recognize sucralose.

steps.name: Deprotection
steps.text: The acetyl cap at carbon 6 is removed with a mild base, restoring the original hydroxyl group. The finished sucralose is then purified by crystallization to remove byproducts and molecules that were chlorinated in the wrong places.

reactions.result: Selective protection is a core strategy in organic synthesis: block what you don't want to react, then unblock it afterward. Without it, the reaction would produce a messy mixture of molecules chlorinated in the wrong places. One leftover from incomplete deprotection, sucralose-6-acetate, is now being studied as an impurity.

reactions.title: Breakdown at baking temperatures
reactions.summary: Sucralose is often marketed as suitable for cooking and baking, and it is far more heat-stable than aspartame. Research has found, however, that at very high temperatures, especially with fats or glycerol present, it can begin to break down. As it decomposes, it can release chlorine-containing compounds. This mainly matters for baking or frying at high temperatures, not for drinks or sprinkling on food. Regulators are reviewing the evidence.

steps.name: Heating
steps.text: Above about 120 °C, and more so at typical oven temperatures of 180 °C or higher, sucralose molecules gain enough energy for their bonds to start breaking. Fats, oils or glycerol in the mixture seem to speed this up. Dry heat and long baking times make it worse.

steps.name: Dechlorination
steps.text: The carbon–chlorine bonds begin to break, releasing hydrogen chloride (HCl), the molecule that forms hydrochloric acid in water. The remaining sugar skeleton breaks down further, a little like ordinary sugar browning.

steps.name: Byproducts
steps.text: The released chlorine can react with glycerol, which comes from fats, forming chloropropanols, chlorinated molecules with three carbon atoms. Some of these, such as 3-MCPD, are a concern because they harm the kidneys in animal studies.

reactions.result: Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment advises against heating sucralose to high temperatures, as in baking or frying, until more is known. In drinks and foods that aren't heated strongly, this reaction doesn't happen. The finding is a reminder that an ingredient's safety can depend on how it is used.

regulatory.status: Approved as a general-purpose sweetener (1999).
Authorized as E955.
Conditionally advises against non-sugar sweeteners for weight control.

hazards.title: Sucralose-6-acetate
hazards.summary: Sucralose-6-acetate is a closely related molecule that can be present as an impurity left over from manufacturing, and small amounts may also form from sucralose in the gut. It drew attention after a 2023 laboratory study reported that it damaged DNA in human cells grown in dishes. The amounts in commercial sucralose are small, and the study did not involve people. It is an open scientific question rather than an established risk. Further research and regulatory review are under way.
hazards.chemical: Sucralose-6-acetate is sucralose with an acetyl group still attached at carbon 6, the position that is temporarily protected during manufacturing. If the protecting group isn't completely removed, some molecules keep it. In the 2023 study, researchers exposed cultured human cells to sucralose-6-acetate and saw breaks in their DNA strands, which suggests it is genotoxic, meaning it can damage genetic material. They also reported changes in the activity of genes linked to inflammation. Cells in a dish, however, lack many of the protective systems of a whole body.
hazards.biological: DNA damage can, in principle, lead to mutations if cells fail to repair it, which is why genotoxicity tests are part of safety evaluations. But whether sucralose-6-acetate reaches the body's cells at levels that could do this from normal sucralose intake is unknown. The amounts measured in commercial sucralose were small, and absorption from the gut is limited. No study in people has shown harm. Regulators have noted the findings and may re-review sucralose as more data become available.

hazards.title: Heating byproducts
hazards.summary: This concern applies only to cooking with sucralose at high temperatures, such as baking or frying, not to drinks, table use or most packaged foods. When strongly heated with fats or glycerol, sucralose can break down and release chlorine that forms chloropropanols. These compounds also form naturally when some other foods are processed at high heat. Some chloropropanols have shown harmful effects in animal studies at high doses. Regulators are assessing how much might form during home baking.
hazards.chemical: At high temperatures the carbon–chlorine bonds in sucralose can break, releasing chlorine, mostly as hydrogen chloride. Fats are built from glycerol joined to fatty acids, and free glycerol is present in many foods. Chlorine can replace hydroxyl groups on glycerol, forming chloropropanols such as 3-MCPD (3-monochloropropane-1,2-diol). How much forms depends on the temperature, the heating time and the other ingredients. Scientists are still measuring how much forms under realistic baking conditions.
hazards.biological: In animal studies, high doses of 3-MCPD over long periods damaged the kidneys and affected male fertility, and it is classified as possibly carcinogenic. Regulators have therefore set a tolerable daily intake for 3-MCPD from all foods combined. People already take in small amounts from refined vegetable oils and some processed foods. Whether baking with sucralose adds meaningfully to that exposure isn't clear yet. The cautious advice is to avoid using sucralose in recipes baked at high temperatures.

profile.dosage: A single packet of sucralose sweetener contains about 12 milligrams of sucralose mixed with a bulking agent. The U.S. FDA has set an acceptable daily intake of 5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, and international experts (JECFA) a higher 15 milligrams per kilogram, so a 60-kilogram adult could have about 300 milligrams a day even under the stricter limit. That is roughly 25 packets, or the amount in several cans of diet soda, every day. Typical intakes are far below these limits. The open questions concern high-temperature baking and the impurity sucralose-6-acetate rather than everyday use.

myths.claim: Sucralose is basically sugar, so it's natural.
myths.consensus: It starts as sugar but is chemically chlorinated; the body does not recognize it as sugar.

myths.claim: Zero-calorie sweeteners spike insulin just like sugar.
myths.consensus: Most trials show no acute blood-sugar spike; some show subtle changes in insulin response when combined with carbohydrates.

environment.persistence: Highly persistent; passes through wastewater treatment largely intact.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Low acute toxicity, but it is now widespread in rivers and groundwater.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis from sucrose
synthesis.summary: Sucralose starts life as ordinary table sugar. It was discovered in 1976 by researchers at a British sugar company and Queen Elizabeth College in London who were making chlorinated sugars as possible chemical building blocks. According to the well-known story, a young researcher misheard a request to “test” a compound as “taste” it, and found it intensely sweet. It was approved for use in the United States in 1998. Today it is one of the most widely used sweeteners in the world.
synthesis.mechanism: Sucrose is first treated so that its hydroxyl group at carbon 6 is capped with an acetyl group, protecting it from the next step. The protected sucrose is then reacted with a chlorinating reagent of a type known as a Vilsmeier reagent, which swaps three specific hydroxyl groups for chlorine atoms. Reaction conditions, temperature and the bulky shape of the reagent help it reach the intended positions. Next, the acetyl protecting group is removed with a base. The crude sucralose is then purified by repeated crystallization, which separates it from partly chlorinated sugars and other byproducts.
synthesis.significance: The same strong carbon–chlorine bonds that resist digestion also resist wastewater treatment, so sucralose is now detected in rivers and coastal waters worldwide and is used as a tracer for sewage.

citations.title: Sucralose: From Sweet Success to Metabolic Controversies-Unraveling the Global Health Implications of a Pervasive Non-Caloric Artificial Sweetener.
citations.abstract: Sucralose is a food additive initially used to mitigate glycemic peaks and calorie intake in patients with diabetes and obesity. Although sucralose has been considered safe for human consumption, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued a global alert in 2023 concerning the potential health implications of this artificial sweetener. This review aims to comprehensively explore the effects of sucralose intake on human health by understanding sucralose absorption, metabolism, and excretion. We also outline the role of the sweet taste 1 receptor 3 (T1R3) in mediating sucralose-dependent signaling pathways that regulate satiety, incretin release, and insulin response. Finally, we discuss the impact of sucralose on microbiome dysbiosis, inflammatory response origin, liver damage, and toxicity. Gaining a deeper understanding of the manifold effects of sucralose on human physiology will help promote further studies to ensure its consumption is deemed safe for a broader population, including children, adolescents, and pregnant women.

citations.title: Toxicological and pharmacokinetic properties of sucralose-6-acetate and its parent sucralose: in vitro screening assays.
citations.journal: J Toxicol Environ Health B Crit Rev
citations.abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the toxicological and pharmacokinetic properties of sucralose-6-acetate, a structural analog of the artificial sweetener sucralose. Sucralose-6-acetate is an intermediate and impurity in the manufacture of sucralose, and recent commercial sucralose samples were found to contain up to 0.67% sucralose-6-acetate. Studies in a rodent model found that sucralose-6-acetate is also present in fecal samples with levels up to 10% relative to sucralose which suggest that sucralose is also acetylated in the intestines. A MultiFlow® assay, a high-throughput genotoxicity screening tool, and a micronucleus (MN) test that detects cytogenetic damage both indicated that sucralose-6-acetate is genotoxic. The mechanism of action was classified as clastogenic (produces DNA strand breaks) using the MultiFlow® assay. The amount of sucralose-6-acetate in a single daily sucralose-sweetened drink might far exceed the threshold of toxicological concern for genotoxicity (TTCgenotox) of 0.15 µg/person/day. The RepliGut® System was employed to expose human intestinal epithelium to sucralose-6-acetate and sucralose, and an RNA-seq analysis was performed to determine gene expression induced by these exposures. Sucralose-6-acetate significantly increased the expression of genes associated with inflammation, oxidative stress, and cancer with greatest expression for the metallothionein 1 G gene (MT1G). Measurements of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and permeability in human transverse colon epithelium indicated that sucralose-6-acetate and sucralose both impaired intestinal barrier integrity. Sucralose-6-acetate also inhibited two members of the cytochrome P450 family (CYP1A2 and CYP2C19). Overall, the toxicological and pharmacokinetic findings for sucralose-6-acetate raise significant health concerns regarding the safety and regulatory status of sucralose itself.

citations.title: Artificial sweeteners and cancer risk: Results from the NutriNet-Santé population-based cohort study.
citations.abstract: Background: The food industry uses artificial sweeteners in a wide range of foods and beverages as alternatives to added sugars, for which deleterious effects on several chronic diseases are now well established. The safety of these food additives is debated, with conflicting findings regarding their role in the aetiology of various diseases. In particular, their carcinogenicity has been suggested by several experimental studies, but robust epidemiological evidence is lacking. Thus, our objective was to investigate the associations between artificial sweetener intakes (total from all dietary sources, and most frequently consumed ones: aspartame [E951], acesulfame-K [E950], and sucralose [E955]) and cancer risk (overall and by site). Methods and findings: Overall, 102,865 adults from the French population-based cohort NutriNet-Santé (2009-2021) were included (median follow-up time = 7.8 years). Dietary intakes and consumption of sweeteners were obtained by repeated 24-hour dietary records including brand names of industrial products. Associations between sweeteners and cancer incidence were assessed by Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for age, sex, education, physical activity, smoking, body mass index, height, weight gain during follow-up, diabetes, family history of cancer, number of 24-hour dietary records, and baseline intakes of energy, alcohol, sodium, saturated fatty acids, fibre, sugar, fruit and vegetables, whole-grain foods, and dairy products. Compared to non-consumers, higher consumers of total artificial sweeteners (i.e., above the median exposure in consumers) had higher risk of overall cancer (n = 3,358 cases, hazard ratio [HR] = 1.13 [95% CI 1.03 to 1.25], P-trend = 0.002). In particular, aspartame (HR = 1.15 [95% CI 1.03 to 1.28], P = 0.002) and acesulfame-K (HR = 1.13 [95% CI 1.01 to 1.26], P = 0.007) were associated with increased cancer risk. Higher risks were also observed for breast cancer (n = 979 cases, HR = 1.22 [95% CI 1.01 to 1.48], P = 0.036, for aspartame) and obesity-related cancers (n = 2,023 cases, HR = 1.13 [95% CI 1.00 to 1.28], P = 0.036, for total artificial sweeteners, and HR = 1.15 [95% CI 1.01 to 1.32], P = 0.026, for aspartame). Limitations of this study include potential selection bias, residual confounding, and reverse causality, though sensitivity analyses were performed to address these concerns. Conclusions: In this large cohort study, artificial sweeteners (especially aspartame and acesulfame-K), which are used in many food and beverage brands worldwide, were associated with increased cancer risk. These findings provide important and novel insights for the ongoing re-evaluation of food additive sweeteners by the European Food Safety Authority and other health agencies globally. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03335644.

citations.title: Biological fate of low-calorie sweeteners.
citations.abstract: With continued efforts to find solutions to rising rates of obesity and diabetes, there is increased interest in the potential health benefits of the use of low- and no-calorie sweeteners (LNCSs). Concerns about safety often deter the use of LNCSs as a tool in helping control caloric intake, even though the safety of LNCS use has been affirmed by regulatory agencies worldwide. In many cases, an understanding of the biological fate of the different LNSCs can help health professionals to address safety concerns. The objectives of this review are to compare the similarities and differences in the chemistry, regulatory status, and biological fate (including absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) of the commonly used LNCSs: acesulfame potassium, aspartame, saccharin, stevia leaf extract (steviol glycoside), and sucralose. Understanding the biological fate of the different LNCSs is helpful in evaluating whether reports of biological effects in animal studies or in humans are indicative of possible safety concerns. Illustrations of the usefulness of this information to address questions about LNCSs include discussion of systemic exposure to LNCSs, the use of sweetener combinations, and the potential for effects of LNCSs on the gut microflora.

citations.title: Effect of Non-Nutritive Sweeteners on the Gut Microbiota.
citations.abstract: The human gut microbiota, a complex community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, consists of more than 1500 species distributed in more than 50 different phyla, with 99% of bacteria coming from about 30-40 species. The colon alone, which contains the largest population of the diverse human microbiota, can harbor up to 100 trillion bacteria. The gut microbiota is essential in maintaining normal gut physiology and health. Therefore, its disruption in humans is often associated with various pathological conditions. Different factors can influence the composition and function of the gut microbiota, including host genetics, age, antibiotic treatments, environment, and diet. The diet has a marked effect, impacting the gut microbiota composition, beneficially or detrimentally, by altering some bacterial species and adjusting the metabolites produced in the gut environment. With the widespread use of non-nutritive sweeteners (NNS) in the diet, recent investigations have focused on their effect on the gut microbiota as a mediator of the potential impact generated by gastrointestinal-related disturbances, such as insulin resistance, obesity, and inflammation. We summarized the results from pre-clinical and clinical studies published over the last ten years that examined the single effects of the most consumed NNS: aspartame, acesulfame-K, sucralose, and saccharin. Pre-clinical studies have given conflicting results for various reasons, including the administration method and the differences in metabolism of the same NNS among the different animal species. A dysbiotic effect of NNS was observed in some human trials, but many other randomized controlled trials reported a lack of significant impacts on gut microbiota composition. These studies differed in the number of subjects involved, their dietary habits, and their lifestyle; all factors related to the baseline composition of gut microbiota and their response to NNS. The scientific community still has no unanimous consensus on the appropriate outcomes and biomarkers that can accurately define the effects of NNS on the gut microbiota.

name: Caffeine
scoreRationale: Moderate intake is safe for most adults, but it is a psychoactive stimulant with sensitivity, sleep, pregnancy and overdose caveats.
summary: Caffeine is the world's most widely used stimulant. Up to about 400 mg a day is fine for most healthy adults; energy drinks can pack a lot of it.

physical.solubility: Moderately soluble in water (about 22 g/L), highly soluble in hot water

overview: Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) is a purine alkaloid: two fused nitrogen-containing rings, the same skeleton as the DNA bases adenine and guanine, decorated with three methyl groups. Plants make it as a natural pesticide that deters and poisons insects feeding on their leaves and seeds.
Its shape closely mimics adenosine, a molecule your brain uses as a “sleep pressure” signal. That resemblance is the key to how caffeine keeps you awake.
profile.function: Adds bitterness and stimulant effect to colas and energy drinks; in eye creams it constricts blood vessels to reduce puffiness temporarily.

mechanisms.title: Blocking adenosine (the alertness effect)
mechanisms.chemical: Adenosine is a small molecule your brain uses as a signal of tiredness. It works by fitting into receptor proteins on the surface of nerve cells, called A1 and A2A receptors, like a key fitting a lock. Caffeine has a similar shape, with two fused rings and nitrogen atoms in the right places, so it fits into the same locks. But it doesn't turn them; it just sits there and blocks adenosine from getting in. A molecule that occupies a receptor without activating it is called an antagonist, and because caffeine and adenosine compete for the same spot, caffeine is called a competitive antagonist.
mechanisms.biological: During waking hours, adenosine slowly builds up in the brain as a byproduct of energy use, and as it binds its receptors it dampens nerve activity, creating “sleep pressure.” When caffeine blocks those receptors, the brakes ease off and other signaling systems, including dopamine and glutamate, become more active, so you feel more awake and focused. The effect begins within about 15 to 45 minutes of a drink. People who use caffeine every day gradually make more adenosine receptors, so they need more caffeine for the same effect, which is called tolerance. If they suddenly stop, those extra receptors are left unblocked, causing withdrawal headaches and tiredness for a few days.

mechanisms.title: Tightening blood vessels
mechanisms.chemical: Adenosine also acts on receptors in the smooth muscle wrapped around blood vessels, where it tells the muscle to relax so the vessels widen. When caffeine blocks these receptors, that relaxing signal is lost. The muscle tightens slightly and the vessels narrow, a change called vasoconstriction. This happens in the brain and the skin, among other places. The effect lasts a few hours, for as long as caffeine remains in the blood.
mechanisms.biological: Some headaches involve widened blood vessels in the head, so narrowing them can help, which is why caffeine is included in some pain relievers for headaches and migraines. Caffeine also helps the body absorb those medicines faster. In skincare, caffeine is added to eye creams, where it may briefly reduce puffiness by narrowing blood vessels and reducing fluid in the area. The effect is temporary and modest. On the flip side, a person who drinks caffeine daily can get a rebound headache after skipping it, because the vessels widen again.

mechanisms.title: Liver metabolism
mechanisms.chemical: Caffeine is broken down mostly in the liver by an enzyme called CYP1A2, a member of the large cytochrome P450 family that processes many drugs and other foreign substances. The enzyme removes one methyl group (–CH₃) at a time from caffeine's nitrogen atoms, a reaction called demethylation. About 80 percent of caffeine becomes paraxanthine, and the rest becomes theobromine (the stimulant in chocolate) and theophylline (once used as an asthma drug). These are broken down further and excreted in urine. How fast CYP1A2 works varies from person to person because of genes and lifestyle.
mechanisms.biological: The time it takes for half the caffeine in your blood to be cleared is called its half-life, and for most adults it is about 3 to 7 hours. That means a coffee at 4 p.m. can leave about half its caffeine in your body at 9 p.m. Pregnancy and some medications, including certain birth control pills and antibiotics, slow CYP1A2 down, so caffeine lasts much longer. Smoking speeds the enzyme up, so smokers clear caffeine faster. Newborn babies have very little CYP1A2, so caffeine can stay in their bodies for days.

reactions.title: Decaffeination with supercritical carbon dioxide
reactions.summary: Taking caffeine out of coffee is harder than it sounds, because a coffee bean contains hundreds of flavor molecules that you want to keep. One of the cleanest methods uses carbon dioxide, the same gas that makes drinks fizzy, in an unusual state called a supercritical fluid. Under high pressure and moderate heat, carbon dioxide behaves partly like a gas and partly like a liquid, so it can seep into beans and dissolve caffeine. It is selective, removing caffeine while leaving most of the flavor behind. Afterward the carbon dioxide simply turns back into gas, leaving no solvent in the beans.

steps.name: Soaking
steps.text: Green, unroasted coffee beans are moistened with water or steam so they swell. Water opens up the bean's structure and helps caffeine move out of the plant cells. Caffeine leaves wet beans much more easily than dry ones.

steps.name: Supercritical CO₂
steps.text: Carbon dioxide is pumped into a sealed steel vessel and brought above 31 °C and 74 bar, about 74 times normal air pressure. Past this point, called the critical point, there is no difference between the liquid and gas forms. The resulting supercritical fluid flows into tiny spaces like a gas but dissolves substances like a liquid.

steps.name: Selective extraction
steps.text: Caffeine molecules dissolve into the supercritical carbon dioxide and are carried out of the beans. Most larger flavor molecules and sugars don't dissolve well in it, so they stay behind. The process runs for hours, until at least about 97 percent of the caffeine is gone.

steps.name: Recovery
steps.text: The caffeine-rich carbon dioxide is passed through water or activated charcoal, which captures the caffeine. The cleaned carbon dioxide is recycled back into the vessel. The beans are dried and then roasted as usual.

reactions.result: Decaf coffee isn't completely caffeine-free; a cup typically still has a few milligrams. The recovered caffeine is purified and sold to soft-drink, energy-drink and supplement makers, so very little goes to waste.

reactions.title: Demethylation in the liver
reactions.summary: Your liver takes caffeine apart step by step, removing its three methyl groups one at a time. Each removal is a small chemical reaction carried out by the enzyme CYP1A2, and each step produces a molecule that is still mildly stimulating. This is why caffeine's effects fade gradually over hours instead of switching off suddenly. Removing a methyl group is called demethylation. The final products are excreted in urine, along with a little unchanged caffeine.

steps.name: Oxidation
steps.text: CYP1A2 holds caffeine in its active site and uses oxygen and an iron atom to add an oxygen atom to one of the methyl groups attached to a nitrogen. This turns the methyl group into a hydroxymethyl group (–CH₂OH), which is unstable. Most often the methyl group at position 3 is targeted first.

steps.name: Removal
steps.text: The unstable group breaks away from the nitrogen as formaldehyde (CH₂O), leaving a hydrogen behind in its place. Other enzymes quickly convert the formaldehyde into formic acid and then carbon dioxide. The amounts are tiny and the body handles them routinely.

steps.name: Products
steps.text: Losing one methyl group turns caffeine into paraxanthine, theobromine or theophylline, depending on which one was removed. These are called dimethylxanthines because they have two methyl groups left. They are demethylated and oxidized further into molecules such as methyluric acids, which the kidneys excrete.

reactions.result: This is why the effects of a cup of coffee fade over several hours rather than minutes. Because paraxanthine and the other products are mild stimulants too, they stretch caffeine's effects out a little. Differences in CYP1A2 activity help explain why some people can drink coffee at night and sleep fine while others can't.

regulatory.status: GRAS in cola-type beverages; FDA cites 400 mg/day as not generally associated with adverse effects for healthy adults.
Single doses up to 200 mg and 400 mg/day are safe for adults; 200 mg/day in pregnancy.
Drinks over 150 mg/L must state "High caffeine content" and that they are not recommended for children or pregnant women.

hazards.title: Caffeine toxicity
hazards.summary: Ordinary coffee, tea and soft drinks rarely cause caffeine poisoning, because you would have to drink an enormous amount quickly. Serious and fatal cases almost always involve pure caffeine powder or concentrated pills, where one spoonful can contain many times a safe dose. Energy drinks combined with other caffeine sources can also push some people into unpleasant symptoms, especially young people and those with heart conditions. The U.S. FDA has warned against selling bulk caffeine powder to consumers for this reason. Anyone with a racing heart, chest pain or seizures after taking caffeine needs emergency care.
hazards.chemical: At normal doses, caffeine's main effect is blocking adenosine receptors. At very high blood levels it starts acting on other targets too. It inhibits phosphodiesterases, enzymes that break down a messenger molecule called cyclic AMP, so cAMP builds up inside cells and ramps up their activity. It also triggers the release of calcium from storage compartments inside muscle cells, and calcium is the signal that makes muscles contract. Together, these effects push heart and nerve cells into overdrive.
hazards.biological: The heart may beat very fast and irregularly, a dangerous condition called an arrhythmia, and blood pressure can rise. Overstimulated nerves cause tremors, agitation and, in severe cases, seizures. Vomiting, confusion and low potassium in the blood are also common. Toxic effects can appear at around 1.2 grams of caffeine taken quickly, and around 10 grams can be fatal for an adult. A single teaspoon of pure caffeine powder can contain about 3 grams or more, which is why these powders are so dangerous.

hazards.title: Sleep disruption and dependence
hazards.summary: For regular users, the most common downside of caffeine isn't danger but disrupted sleep and mild dependence. Because caffeine lingers in the body for hours, an afternoon coffee or energy drink can still be active at bedtime. Many people don't notice how much it affects the quality of their sleep, even if they fall asleep without trouble. Daily users also become dependent, meaning they feel tired, irritable or headachy without it. Both effects reverse with gradual changes in intake.
hazards.chemical: Caffeine's half-life of about 3 to 7 hours means that after a 200-milligram coffee at 3 p.m., roughly 100 milligrams may still be circulating in the evening. That caffeine keeps occupying adenosine receptors, blocking the tiredness signal adenosine is meant to send. With daily use, nerve cells respond by making more adenosine receptors, trying to restore their normal sensitivity. This adaptation is the chemical basis of tolerance. It also sets up withdrawal, because without caffeine all those extra receptors are fully activated by adenosine.
hazards.biological: Caffeine late in the day delays falling asleep and reduces deep, slow-wave sleep, the stage most important for feeling rested. Poor sleep makes people tired the next day, so they reach for more caffeine, starting a cycle. When regular users stop suddenly, unblocked adenosine receptors and widening blood vessels cause withdrawal: headaches, sleepiness, low mood and trouble concentrating, usually starting 12 to 24 hours after the last dose and lasting a few days. Cutting back gradually avoids most of these symptoms. Many sleep experts suggest no caffeine for at least six hours before bed.

hazards.title: Pregnancy
hazards.summary: Health agencies recommend that pregnant people limit caffeine to no more than about 200 milligrams a day, roughly one or two cups of coffee. That is lower than the 400 milligrams considered safe for other adults. The concern is that very high caffeine intake during pregnancy has been linked in some studies to lower birth weight and a higher risk of miscarriage, though the evidence is debated. Caffeine is also found in tea, chocolate, soft drinks and some medicines, so every source counts. Moderate intake is generally considered safe.
hazards.chemical: Caffeine is a small molecule that dissolves in both water and fat, so it crosses the placenta easily and reaches the fetus at about the same concentration as in the mother's blood. During pregnancy, the mother's CYP1A2 enzyme slows down, especially in the later months, so caffeine's half-life can stretch to 10 hours or more. The fetus has almost no working CYP1A2 of its own to break caffeine down. As a result, caffeine lingers far longer in both mother and baby than in a non-pregnant adult.
hazards.biological: In the fetus, caffeine can affect heart rate and may narrow blood vessels in the placenta, possibly reducing blood flow. Large studies have found links between high caffeine intake and slightly lower birth weight, although it's hard to separate caffeine's effect from other lifestyle factors. Because of that uncertainty and the slow clearance, health authorities take a cautious approach. Staying under 200 milligrams a day is considered a safe margin. Caffeine also passes into breast milk, and some breastfed babies become fussy when their parent drinks a lot of it.

profile.dosage: A typical cup of brewed coffee has about 95 milligrams of caffeine, a cup of black tea about 45, a 12-ounce cola about 35, and a 16-ounce energy drink anywhere from 150 to 300. For healthy adults, up to about 400 milligrams a day is generally considered safe, and the guideline during pregnancy is 200 milligrams. Teenagers are often advised to stay under about 100 milligrams a day. Toxic effects can appear around 1.2 grams taken quickly, an amount that is hard to reach with drinks but easy with pure powder, where a single teaspoon can exceed it. Sensitivity varies a lot between people, so how you feel is a useful guide.

myths.claim: Coffee dehydrates you.
myths.consensus: Moderate habitual intake has only a mild diuretic effect; caffeinated drinks still count toward daily fluids.

myths.claim: Caffeine stunts growth.
myths.consensus: There is no evidence that caffeine affects height.

environment.persistence: Moderately persistent; a common marker of human wastewater in rivers.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis in plants
synthesis.summary: Caffeine is made naturally by more than 60 plant species, including coffee, tea, cacao, guaraná, yerba mate and kola nut. Plants don't make it to keep anyone awake. Caffeine is bitter and toxic to many insects, so it protects leaves and seeds from being eaten. Fallen leaves can also release caffeine into the soil, where it may slow the growth of competing seedlings. Curiously, small amounts in the nectar of coffee and citrus flowers seem to help bees remember the flowers and come back to them.
synthesis.mechanism: Plants build caffeine from xanthosine, a molecule closely related to the building blocks of DNA and RNA. Enzymes called N-methyltransferases add methyl groups (–CH₃) one at a time to nitrogen atoms on the molecule. Each methyl group is supplied by a donor molecule called S-adenosylmethionine, a kind of molecular delivery truck for methyl groups that all living cells use. After the first methyl group is added, another enzyme snips off the sugar part of the molecule. The sequence runs from xanthosine to 7-methylxanthosine, then 7-methylxanthine, then theobromine (with two methyl groups), and finally caffeine (with three).
synthesis.significance: Coffee and tea evolved their caffeine-making enzymes independently, a striking example of convergent evolution, where different species arrive at the same solution separately.

synthesis.title: Recovery and laboratory synthesis
synthesis.summary: The caffeine added to soft drinks, energy drinks and pills comes from two sources: it is recovered while decaffeinating coffee and tea, or it is built from scratch in chemical plants. Synthetic caffeine is cheaper and is made in large quantities, much of it in China and India. Both sources produce exactly the same molecule. Labels usually just say “caffeine” either way. The popularity of energy drinks has made synthetic caffeine a major product.
synthesis.mechanism: Recovered caffeine is collected from the water, charcoal or solvent used in decaffeination and purified by crystallization. Synthetic caffeine is assembled from simple starting materials. One classic method, the Traube purine synthesis, begins with dimethylurea, a small molecule with two nitrogen atoms already carrying methyl groups, and reacts it with a derivative of malonic acid to build the first ring. Further steps add nitrogen and carbon atoms and close the second ring, forming theophylline or a similar molecule. A final methylation step adds the third methyl group to give caffeine.
synthesis.significance: Natural and synthetic caffeine are the same molecule. Isotope analysis, which detects tiny differences in the proportions of heavier and lighter carbon atoms, is the only way to tell them apart.

citations.title: Metabolism and Mechanism of Human Cytochrome P450 Enzyme 1A2.
citations.abstract: Human cytochrome P450 enzyme 1A2 (CYP1A2) is one of the most important cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes in the liver, accounting for 13% to 15% of hepatic CYP enzymes. CYP1A2 metabolises many clinical drugs, such as phenacetin, caffeine, clozapine, tacrine, propranolol, and mexiletine. CYP1A2 also metabolises certain precarcinogens such as aflatoxins, mycotoxins, nitrosamines, and endogenous substances such as steroids. The regulation of CYP1A2 is influenced by many factors. The transcription of CYP1A2 involves not only the aromatic hydrocarbon receptor pathway but also many additional transcription factors, and CYP1A2 expression may be affected by transcription coactivators and compression factors. Degradation of CYP1A2 mRNA and protein, alternative splicing, RNA stability, regulatory microRNAs, and DNA methylation are also known to affect the regulation of CYP1A2. Many factors can lead to changes in the activity of CYP1A2. Smoking, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon ingestion, and certain drugs (e.g., omeprazole) increase its activity, while many clinical drugs such as theophylline, fluvoxamine, quinolone antibiotics, verapamil, cimetidine, and oral contraceptives can inhibit CYP1A2 activity. Here, we review the drugs metabolised by CYP1A2, the metabolic mechanism of CYP1A2, and various factors that influence CYP1A2 metabolism. The metabolic mechanism of CYP1A2 is of great significance in the development of personalised medicine and CYP1A2 target-based drugs.

citations.title: Human cytochrome P4501A2.
citations.abstract: CYP1A2, a member of the cytochrome P450 superfamily (CYPs), is involved in the metabolic activation of several carcinogens, among them aromatic and heterocyclic amines, nitroaromatic compounds, mycotoxins and estrogens. Several drugs are also metabolized by CYP1A2. Individual differences in CYP1A2 activity may thus influence individual susceptibility to cancer risk and the therapeutic efficacy of some drugs. In humans, CYP1A2 has been detected only in the liver, where it seems to be regulated by at least two mechanisms, one controlling constitutive levels of expression and another regulating inducibility. Wide interindividual differences in CYP1A2 activity have been described. They may be due to factors such as gender, race, genetic polymorphisms, and exposure to inducers. Higher activity has been shown in men than in women. Wide variation across racial/ethnic groups has been reported. Overall, slow and intermediate CYP1A2 metabolizers represent about 50% of Caucasians, while their frequency in Japanese subjects seems to be much lower. No nucleotide differences that could explain the phenotypic variability of the CYP1A2 gene have been found in any exons, exon-intron junctions, or 5'-flanking regions of the gene. However, two genetic variants have been identified which seem to be associated with CYP1A2 inducibility only. Induction of CYP1A2 activity has been reported as a consequence of cigarette smoking, dietary factors, several drugs, chronic hepatitis, and exposure to polybrominated biphenyls and 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin. Several epidemiological studies have been conducted into the relationship between CYP1A2 activity, alone or in combination with other CYPs, and cancer risk. In the absence of a genotypic assay, only the CYP1A2 phenotype can be assessed at present. Many compounds have been tested as in vitro probes to assess CYP1A2 activity in humans. Currently, caffeine has the best potential for use in epidemiological studies: metabolites of caffeine after coffee consumption are measured as an index of CYP1A2 activity. Variable results have been obtained with caffeine-based methods, the use of some caffeine metabolite ratios having given bimodal or trimodal distributions while others have suggested normal or unimodal distributions. Although the epidemiological studies are limited because only phenotyping data are available, there is a suggestion of increased risk of colon cancer and bladder cancer in subjects with rapid CYP1A2 activity. A higher level of 4-aminobiphenyl-haemoglobin adducts has also been found in moderate smokers with rapid CYP1A2 phenotype than in subjects with slow activity.

citations.title: Caffeine: cognitive and physical performance enhancer or psychoactive drug?
citations.abstract: Caffeine use is increasing worldwide. The underlying motivations are mainly concentration and memory enhancement and physical performance improvement. Coffee and caffeine-containing products affect the cardiovascular system, with their positive inotropic and chronotropic effects, and the central nervous system, with their locomotor activity stimulation and anxiogenic-like effects. Thus, it is of interest to examine whether these effects could be detrimental for health. Furthermore, caffeine abuse and dependence are becoming more and more common and can lead to caffeine intoxication, which puts individuals at risk for premature and unnatural death. The present review summarizes the main findings concerning caffeine's mechanisms of action (focusing on adenosine antagonism, intracellular calcium mobilization, and phosphodiesterases inhibition), use, abuse, dependence, intoxication, and lethal effects. It also suggests that the concepts of toxic and lethal doses are relative, since doses below the toxic and/or lethal range may play a causal role in intoxication or death. This could be due to caffeine's interaction with other substances or to the individuals' preexisting metabolism alterations or diseases.

citations.title: Doping and respiratory system.
citations.abstract: Historically many different drugs have been used to enhance sporting performances. The magic elixir is still elusive and the drugs are still used despite the heavy adverse effects. The respiratory system is regularly involved in this research probably because of its central location in the body with several connections to the cardiovascular system. Moreover people are aware that O2 consumption and its delivery to mitochondria firstly depend on ventilation and on the respiratory exchanges. The second step consists in the tendency to increase V'O2 max and to prolong its availability with the aim of improving the endurance time and to relieve the fatigue. Many methods and substances had been used in order to gain an artificial success. Additional oxygen, autologous and homologous transfusion and erythropoietin, mainly the synthetic type, have been administered with the aim of increasing the amount of oxygen being delivered to the tissues. Some compounds like stimulants and caffeine are endowed of excitatory activity on the CNS and stimulate pulmonary ventilation. They did not prove to have any real activity in supporting the athletic performances. Beta-adrenergic drugs, particularly clenbuterol, when administered orally or parenterally develop a clear illicit activity on the myosin fibres and on the muscles as a whole. Salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol and formoterol are legally admitted when administrated by MDI in the treatment of asthma. The prevalence of asthma and bronchial hyperactivity is higher in athletes than amongst the general population. This implies that clear rules must be provided to set a correct diagnosis of asthma in the athletes and a correct therapy to align with the actual guidelines according to the same rights of the "other" asthmatic patients.

citations.title: Caffeine effects on systemic metabolism, oxidative-inflammatory pathways, and exercise performance.
citations.abstract: Caffeine, a xanthine alkaloid compound, is consumed widely and daily by humans, as it is present in several regular beverages such as tea, coffee, soda beverages, and some drugs. Its consumption triggers arousal and alertness, improves mood, and causes the release of catecholamines, which induce beneficial effects on human behavior. Nonetheless, caffeine has been related to other beneficial effects such as antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions that are extremely important to human health, altering the cellular redox and inflammatory status in a dose-dependent manner. Caffeine intake has also shown ergogenic effects, which are attributed to different factors, such as enhanced substrate utilization, fatigue delay, and alertness. As such, caffeine has been consumed by athletes from different sports modalities, with positive and negative effects declared. Although peripheral tissues such as the heart, skeletal muscle, and adipocytes are also impacted, there is a deficit of recognized mechanisms in systemic metabolism when compared to caffeine action in the central nervous system. This review summarizes the most relevant classical and current literature available regarding the use of caffeine in different metabolic situations, such as oxidative and inflammatory status, as well as anaerobic and aerobic physical exercises. Here, we identified the non-central nervous system caffeine mechanisms modulation, as most are still unknown or controversial, highlighting its influence in the peripheral system and its essential and crucial impacts on the human's organism adaptation.

name: Phosphoric Acid
scoreRationale: Safe as used, but frequent colas are linked to enamel erosion and, in women, lower bone density; concentrated forms in cleaners are corrosive.
summary: Phosphoric acid gives colas their tang and powers rust removers. It's fine in moderation, but acidic sodas are hard on teeth.

overview: Phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) has a phosphorus atom at the center of a tetrahedron of four oxygens: one double-bonded oxygen and three –OH groups. Each –OH can release a proton, so it is a triprotic acid, strong enough to give colas a pH around 2.5 but much weaker than hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
Its conjugate bases, phosphate ions, are everywhere in biology: in the backbone of DNA, in ATP (the cell's energy currency), and in the calcium phosphate mineral that makes up bones and teeth.
profile.function: Provides sharp acidity in colas, adjusts pH in cosmetics, and converts rust in toilet and metal cleaners.

mechanisms.title: Sharp, tangy acidity
mechanisms.chemical: Phosphoric acid has three hydrogen atoms it can release as hydrogen ions (H⁺), but it gives them up one at a time, and the first comes off much more easily than the other two. Chemists describe this with pKa values, and the first one is about 2.1, which means that first proton is released fairly readily. In a cola, phosphoric acid brings the pH down to around 2.5, more acidic than orange juice. The released hydrogen ions are what switch on the sour-sensing taste cells on your tongue. Unlike citric acid, phosphoric acid has no fruity flavor of its own.
mechanisms.biological: Sour-taste cells detect hydrogen ions through a channel called OTOP1 and send a “sour” signal to the brain. In colas, phosphoric acid provides a sharp, clean tang that balances the large amount of sugar, which would otherwise taste cloying. Because it doesn't add fruity notes, it suits cola's spicy, vanilla-like flavor better than citric acid would. The low pH also makes it hard for bacteria and molds to grow in the drink. That acidity is part of why sodas can sit on store shelves for months.

mechanisms.title: Enamel erosion
mechanisms.chemical: Tooth enamel is made of hydroxyapatite, Ca₅(PO₄)₃OH, a hard crystal of calcium, phosphate and hydroxide ions. At a pH of 2 to 3 there are so many hydrogen ions that they react with the phosphate and hydroxide parts of the crystal. Hydroxide becomes water, and phosphate becomes hydrogen phosphate, which no longer holds calcium tightly. With its framework weakened, calcium ions dissolve away from the surface. In effect, the acid is taking the crystal apart from the outside in.
mechanisms.biological: Each sip of cola softens the outer surface of the enamel for a while. Saliva then neutralizes the acid with bicarbonate, a natural buffer, and supplies calcium and phosphate that can partly rebuild the surface. If someone sips cola throughout the day, their teeth spend most of the time under acid attack and repair can't keep up. Over years, the enamel thins, which can make teeth sensitive and more yellow-looking. Drinking with meals, using a straw and rinsing with water afterward all reduce contact time.

mechanisms.title: Bone mineral balance
mechanisms.chemical: Calcium and phosphate are the two main ingredients of bone mineral, and the body keeps their levels in the blood carefully balanced. When phosphate intake is high and calcium intake is low, that balance shifts. The parathyroid glands, four tiny glands in the neck, respond by releasing parathyroid hormone. This hormone raises blood calcium, partly by releasing calcium from the skeleton. Over long periods, that could in theory weaken bones.
mechanisms.biological: In the Framingham Osteoporosis Study, women who drank cola every day had lower bone mineral density in the hip than women who drank it less than once a month, even after accounting for other factors. Other carbonated drinks didn't show the same link, which points to something specific about cola, possibly phosphoric acid or caffeine. Part of the effect, though, may simply be that people who drink a lot of cola drink less milk and miss out on calcium. Other studies have found mixed results. Overall, it's a reason to treat cola as an occasional drink and to get enough calcium.

reactions.title: Rust conversion
reactions.summary: Rust is iron oxide, a flaky, crumbly substance that forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. Because it is porous and loose, rust lets more air and water reach the metal underneath, so the rusting keeps spreading. Phosphoric acid can turn this weak layer into a tougher, protective coating. Products sold as rust converters, and some metal cleaners, rely on this reaction. It's a nice example of an acid that doesn't just dissolve something but changes it into something more useful.

steps.name: Dissolving
steps.text: Hydrogen ions from phosphoric acid attack the iron oxide (Fe₂O₃) on the metal's surface. They react with the oxide ions, forming water and freeing iron ions (Fe³⁺). This loosens the rust and exposes the metal underneath.

steps.name: Precipitation
steps.text: The freed iron ions combine with phosphate ions from the acid to form iron phosphate (FePO₄). Iron phosphate is insoluble, meaning it doesn't dissolve in water. So it comes out of solution as a solid and sticks to the surface.

steps.name: Passivation
steps.text: The iron phosphate forms a thin, tight, dark layer that seals the surface. It is far less porous than rust, so oxygen and water can't easily reach the metal beneath. Making a metal surface less reactive like this is called passivation.

reactions.result: This is how “rust converter” products and some toilet and metal cleaners work. The iron phosphate layer also gives paint something to grip. Car makers use a related process, called phosphating, to protect steel before painting it.

reactions.title: Phosphate buffering
reactions.summary: A buffer is a mixture that resists changes in pH when an acid or a base is added. Phosphates form one of the most important buffers in biology. Because phosphoric acid releases its three protons one at a time, at three different pH values, its partly ionized forms can soak up or release hydrogen ions as needed. The pair of forms present around pH 7 is especially useful, because that is close to the pH inside living cells. Buffers are also used in foods, medicines and laboratories to keep pH steady.

steps.name: Stepwise ionization
steps.text: Phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) releases its first proton around pH 2.1 to form H₂PO₄⁻, its second around pH 7.2 to form HPO₄²⁻, and its third around pH 12.4 to form PO₄³⁻. Each step is harder than the last, because pulling a positive proton off an ion that is already negative takes more effort.

steps.name: Buffer pair
steps.text: Near pH 7.2, a solution contains a mixture of H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻. One form can donate a proton and the other can accept one. Together they act like a sponge for both acid and base.

steps.name: Balance
steps.text: If acid is added, the extra H⁺ is taken up by HPO₄²⁻, turning it into H₂PO₄⁻, so the pH barely changes. If a base is added, its OH⁻ is neutralized by a proton from H₂PO₄⁻. Only when one of the two forms runs out does the pH begin to change quickly.

reactions.result: The phosphate buffer is one of the main systems keeping the pH inside your cells stable, which is vital because enzymes only work within narrow pH ranges. Food manufacturers use phosphate salts for the same reason, to hold the pH of processed foods steady.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Authorized as E338 with maximum levels by food category; EFSA set a group ADI for phosphates in 2019.
Danger: causes severe skin burns and eye damage (H314) when concentrated.

hazards.title: Corrosive when concentrated
hazards.summary: The phosphoric acid in food is extremely dilute: a cola contains only about 0.05 percent. The concentrated acid sold to manufacturers, typically 75 to 85 percent, is a different matter and can cause serious burns. Household rust removers and some toilet cleaners contain 10 to 30 percent and should be handled with gloves and eye protection. The danger lies in the concentration, not in the chemical itself. Swallowing concentrated acid can badly injure the mouth, throat and stomach.
hazards.chemical: Concentrated phosphoric acid packs a large amount of acid into a small amount of water. When it touches tissue, it lowers the pH sharply, which makes proteins unfold, a process called denaturation. It also pulls water out of tissue, because concentrated acid strongly attracts water, and that damages cells further. Proteins in the skin and eyes lose their structure and stop working. Phosphoric acid acts somewhat more slowly than some strong acids, but prolonged contact still causes burns.
hazards.biological: On skin, contact causes redness and pain and, with longer exposure, burns and blisters. In the eye it can damage the cornea, the clear front layer, so it must be rinsed out immediately with plenty of water for at least 15 minutes. Breathing in mist from the concentrated acid irritates the nose, throat and lungs. Swallowing it can burn the lining of the digestive tract. These hazards are why products with high concentrations carry warning labels and why the industrial acid is handled by trained workers.

hazards.title: Dental erosion from frequent soft drinks
hazards.summary: Regularly sipping colas and other acidic soft drinks can slowly wear away the enamel on your teeth. This is dental erosion, a chemical process that doesn't involve bacteria. One drink causes no lasting harm, but frequent exposure over months and years adds up. Diet colas are just as acidic as regular ones, so they also erode enamel, even though they don't feed cavity-causing bacteria. Teenagers and young adults who drink a lot of soda are among those most affected.
hazards.chemical: Colas have a pH around 2.5, well below the critical level of about 5.5 at which tooth enamel starts to dissolve. Each exposure lets hydrogen ions react with the calcium phosphate crystals of enamel, releasing calcium and phosphate and softening the surface. Phosphoric acid is an effective erosive acid, although some studies suggest citric acid, common in fruit-flavored drinks, is even more erosive because it also grabs calcium. Holding the drink in your mouth or swishing it around increases contact time and the damage. Cold drinks are slightly less erosive than warm ones.
hazards.biological: Saliva slowly neutralizes acid and helps repair softened enamel by supplying calcium and phosphate, but that takes time. With frequent sips, enamel loses more than it can rebuild, and the surface gradually thins. As it wears down, the yellowish dentin underneath shows through more, and teeth can become sensitive to hot, cold and sweet foods. Thin enamel is also easier to chip and more vulnerable to decay. Since enamel can't regrow, prevention matters: drinking soda with meals, using a straw, rinsing with water afterward and waiting about 30 minutes before brushing.

profile.dosage: A cola contains only about 0.05 percent phosphoric acid, which supplies roughly 40 to 60 milligrams of phosphorus per 12-ounce can. That is small next to the 1,000 milligrams or more of phosphorus most adults get each day from meat, dairy, grains and beans, and far below the adult upper limit of 4,000 milligrams a day. The more practical concerns are tooth erosion from frequent sipping and the chance that heavy cola drinking replaces milk and other sources of calcium. Concentrated forms are another story: rust removers and toilet cleaners can contain 10 to 30 percent and call for gloves, goggles and good ventilation.

myths.claim: A cola will dissolve a tooth overnight.
myths.consensus: Erosion takes repeated exposure over time; saliva buffers acids between sips.

myths.claim: Phosphoric acid in soda leaches calcium from your bones.
myths.consensus: The bone link is modest and may partly reflect cola replacing milk in the diet.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Phosphate runoff drives algal blooms; phosphates were phased out of U.S. laundry and dishwasher detergents for this reason.

synthesis.title: Wet process (fertilizer grade)
synthesis.summary: Most of the world's phosphoric acid is made from phosphate rock, a mineral mined in places such as Morocco, China and Florida. The rock is treated with sulfuric acid in a method called the wet process. It produces large amounts of acid cheaply, but the product carries impurities from the rock, such as fluoride and traces of heavy metals. For that reason, most wet-process acid goes into fertilizers, which supply crops with phosphorus, an essential nutrient. With extra purification, some of it can be upgraded to food grade.
synthesis.mechanism: Phosphate rock is mostly fluorapatite, a calcium phosphate mineral that also contains fluoride. The rock is ground into a fine powder and mixed with concentrated sulfuric acid. Sulfuric acid is the stronger acid, so it hands its protons to the phosphate, turning it into phosphoric acid. At the same time, calcium from the rock combines with sulfate to form calcium sulfate, which crystallizes with water as gypsum. Because gypsum barely dissolves, it can be filtered off, leaving impure phosphoric acid in solution, while some of the fluoride escapes as hydrogen fluoride gas that has to be captured.
synthesis.equation: Ca5(PO4)3F + 5 H2SO4 + 10 H2O → 3 H3PO4 + 5 CaSO4·2H2O + HF
synthesis.significance: This acid carries impurities such as fluoride and heavy metals, so it's used mainly for fertilizers. Every tonne of acid also leaves behind several tonnes of gypsum waste, called phosphogypsum.

synthesis.title: Thermal process (food grade)
synthesis.summary: Foods, drinks and electronics need very pure phosphoric acid. The traditional way to make it is the thermal process, which first produces pure elemental phosphorus and then burns it. This method uses a lot of electricity, so it costs more than the wet process. Today some food-grade acid is instead made by carefully purifying wet-process acid. Either way, the final product has to meet strict purity standards.
synthesis.mechanism: Phosphate rock is mixed with coke, a nearly pure form of carbon made from coal, and silica (sand), then heated to about 1,500 °C in an electric arc furnace. At that temperature the carbon strips oxygen away from the phosphate, releasing phosphorus as a vapor, while the silica combines with calcium to form a molten slag that is drained off. The phosphorus vapor is cooled and collected as white phosphorus. It is then burned in air to form tetraphosphorus decoxide (P₄O₁₀), a white powder that reacts eagerly with water. Absorbing that powder in water produces pure phosphoric acid.
synthesis.significance: The high purity makes it suitable for foods, drinks and electronics.

citations.title: Phosphodiester models for cleavage of nucleic acids.
citations.abstract: Nucleic acids that store and transfer biological information are polymeric diesters of phosphoric acid. Cleavage of the phosphodiester linkages by protein enzymes, nucleases, is one of the underlying biological processes. The remarkable catalytic efficiency of nucleases, together with the ability of ribonucleic acids to serve sometimes as nucleases, has made the cleavage of phosphodiesters a subject of intensive mechanistic studies. In addition to studies of nucleases by pH-rate dependency, X-ray crystallography, amino acid/nucleotide substitution and computational approaches, experimental and theoretical studies with small molecular model compounds still play a role. With small molecules, the importance of various elementary processes, such as proton transfer and metal ion binding, for stabilization of transition states may be elucidated and systematic variation of the basicity of the entering or departing nucleophile enables determination of the position of the transition state on the reaction coordinate. Such data is important on analyzing enzyme mechanisms based on synergistic participation of several catalytic entities. Many nucleases are metalloenzymes and small molecular models offer an excellent tool to construct models for their catalytic centers. The present review tends to be an up to date summary of what has been achieved by mechanistic studies with small molecular phosphodiesters.

citations.title: Aging of adhesive interfaces treated with benzalkonium chloride and benzalkonium methacrylate.
citations.abstract: Inhibition of endogenous dentin matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) within incompletely infiltrated hybrid layers can contribute to the preservation of resin-dentin bonds. This study evaluated the bond stability of interfaces treated with benzalkonium chloride (BAC) and benzalkonium methacrylate (MBAC), and the inhibitory properties of these compounds on dentin MMP activity. Single-component adhesive ALL-BOND UNIVERSAL, modified with BAC or MBAC at concentrations of 0, 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0%, was used for microtensile bond strength (μTBS) evaluation after 24 h, 6 months, and 1 yr. Beams produced from human dentin were treated with 37% phosphoric acid, dipped in 0.5% BAC, 1.0% BAC, or water (control) for 60 s, and then incubated in SensoLyte generic MMP substrate to determine MMP activity. A significant decrease in the μTBS after 6 months and 1 yr was observed for the control group only. No significant differences among groups were shown at 24 h. After 6 months and 1 yr, the control group demonstrated significantly lower μTBS than all treatment groups. When applied for 60 s, 0.5% BAC inhibited total MMP activity by 31%, and 1.0% BAC inhibited total MMP activity by 54%. Both BAC and MBAC contributed to the preservation of resin-dentin bonds, probably because of their inhibitory properties of endogenous dentin proteinases.

citations.title: Chlorhexidine in endodontics.
citations.abstract: Chemical auxiliary substances (CAS) are essential for a successful disinfection and cleanness of the root canals, being used during the instrumentation and if necessary, as antimicrobial intracanal medicaments. Different CAS have been proposed and used, among which sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl), chlorhexidine (CHX), 17% EDTA, citric acid, MTAD and 37% phosphoric acid solution. CHX has been used in Endodontics as an irrigating substance or intracanal medicament, as it possesses a wide range of antimicrobial activity, substantivity (residual antimicrobial activity), lower cytotoxicity than NaOCl whilst demonstrating efficient clinical performance, lubricating properties, rheological action (present in the gel presentation, keeping the debris in suspension); it inhibits metalloproteinase, is chemically stable, does not stain cloths, it is odorless, water soluble, among other properties. CHX has been recommended as an alternative to NaOCl, especially in cases of open apex, root resorption, foramen enlargement and root perforation, due to its biocompatibility, or in cases of allergy related to bleaching solutions. The aim of this paper is to review CHX's general use in the medical field and in dentistry; its chemical structure, presentation form and storage; mechanism of action; antimicrobial activity including substantivity, effects on biofilms and endotoxins, effects on coronal and apical microbial microleakage; tissue dissolution ability; interaction with endodontic irrigants; effects on dentin bonding, metalloproteinases and collagen fibrils; its use as intracanal medicament and diffusion into the dentinal tubules; its use as disinfectant agent of obturation cones; other uses in the endodontic therapy; and possible adverse effects, cytotoxicity and genotoxicity.

citations.title: Design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of liver-targeting phosphoric acid thyroid hormone receptor agonists for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis.
citations.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) represents a progressive stage of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and is characterized by steatosis, inflammation, hepatocyte ballooning, and fibrosis. Resmetirom, a thyroid hormone receptor β (THR-β) agonist, is the first drug approved by the FDA for the treatment of MASH. The beneficial effects of THR-β agonists on lipid levels primarily result from their action on THR-β in the liver, whereas adverse effects, including impacts on cardiac and bone health, are mediated through thyroid hormone receptor α (THR-α). In this study, we report the discovery of a series of liver-targeting phosphoric acid thyroid hormone receptor agonists that merge the pharmacophores THR-β agonists VK2809 and resmetirom. Further optimization led to compound 29a, which exhibited significant cholesterol-lowering effects in a cholesterol-fed rat model and demonstrated favorable targeting properties, with primary distribution in liver and kidney tissues. Compound 29a, which had excellent PK properties and a good safety profile, showed potent anti-MASH effects in HFD-CCl4-induced mice MASH model. Collectively, these findings suggest that compound 29a holds considerable promise for the treatment of MASH and other inflammatory and fibrotic diseases.

citations.title: Atroposelective Synthesis of N-Arylated Quinoids by Organocatalytic Tandem N-Arylation/Oxidation.
citations.abstract: Diarylamines and related scaffolds are ubiquitous atropisomeric chemotypes in biologically active natural products. However, the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of these axially chiral compounds remains largely unexplored. Herein, we report that a BINOL-derived chiral phosphoric acid (CPA) successfully catalyzed the atroposelective coupling of quinone esters and anilines through direct C-N bond formation to afford N-aryl quinone atropisomers with an unprecedented intramolecular N-H-O hydrogen bond within a six-membered ring in good yields and enantioselectivities with the quinone ester as both the electrophile and the oxidant. A gram-scale experiment demonstrated the utility of this synthetic protocol. Moreover, this methodology provides a platform for the synthesis of structurally diverse secondary amine atropisomers by nucleophilic addition.
