name: Monosodium Glutamate
scoreRationale: Decades of controlled research find no consistent harm at normal intakes; it contains a third of the sodium of table salt.
summary: MSG adds savory umami flavor. It's chemically the same glutamate found in tomatoes and parmesan, and controlled studies don't support the old "MSG symptom" fears.

overview: Monosodium glutamate is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, one of the 20 amino acids that build proteins. Glutamic acid has two carboxylic acid groups and one amino group; in MSG, one carboxyl group has traded its proton for a sodium ion.

When food proteins are broken down by cooking, aging or fermentation, free glutamate is released, which is why parmesan, ripe tomatoes, soy sauce and broths taste savory. MSG delivers that same free glutamate in a pure, concentrated form.
profile.function: Boosts savory, meaty (umami) flavor in soups, snacks, sauces and seasonings, allowing less salt overall.

mechanisms.title: Umami taste
mechanisms.chemical: Glutamate is detected by a taste receptor made of two proteins, T1R1 and T1R3, related to the sweet receptor. Free glutamate, meaning glutamate that isn't locked inside a protein chain, fits into a pocket of T1R1 shaped like a Venus flytrap, which closes around it. Molecules called ribonucleotides, such as inosinate (found in meat and fish) and guanylate (found in mushrooms), bind to a neighboring spot on the same receptor. When they do, they help hold the flytrap shut, making the receptor far more responsive to glutamate. This teamwork, called synergy, can multiply the strength of the umami signal several times over.
mechanisms.biological: The activated receptor sends a signal through taste nerves to the brain, which reads it as umami, a savory, meaty, satisfying taste. Umami is thought to signal the presence of protein, an essential nutrient. Besides adding flavor, it increases saliva and can make food seem fuller and longer-lasting in the mouth. It is the reason broth, aged cheese, ripe tomatoes and soy sauce taste so rich. Breast milk is also rich in free glutamate, so people meet this taste from the very start of life.

mechanisms.title: Fuel for the gut lining
mechanisms.chemical: When we eat glutamate, whether from MSG or from the protein in food, it is taken up by the cells lining the small intestine, called enterocytes. These cells absorb glutamate through amino-acid transporters and use it as one of their main fuels. Inside the cells, enzymes convert glutamate into α-ketoglutarate, a molecule that feeds into the Krebs cycle, the central energy-producing pathway. Through this route, glutamate's carbon atoms are burned for energy and leave as carbon dioxide. Some glutamate is also used to make other molecules, such as the amino acids alanine and proline and the antioxidant glutathione.
mechanisms.biological: Because the gut lining burns so much of it, most dietary glutamate never reaches the bloodstream in large amounts. Only when very large doses are eaten on an empty stomach do blood levels rise noticeably, and then only briefly. The brain is protected further by the blood–brain barrier, a tightly sealed layer of cells around the brain's blood vessels that strictly controls what gets in. The brain makes its own glutamate, where it acts as a major neurotransmitter, and doesn't rely on glutamate from food. This is why MSG in food doesn't act on the brain the way glutamate released by nerve cells does.

mechanisms.title: A lower-sodium seasoning
mechanisms.chemical: MSG contains sodium, but much less than table salt. By weight, MSG is about 12 percent sodium, while sodium chloride is about 39 percent sodium. The difference arises because the glutamate part of MSG is much heavier than the chloride part of salt, so a gram of MSG holds fewer sodium ions. Both add savory or salty taste, but through different receptors on the tongue. Glutamate's umami taste makes food seem flavorful even when it contains less salt.
mechanisms.biological: Studies have found that replacing part of the salt in dishes such as soups, sauces and stir-fries with MSG can cut total sodium by roughly a quarter to a third without people liking the food less. This matters because most people eat more sodium than recommended, which raises their risk of high blood pressure. The savory taste of glutamate partly makes up for the lower saltiness. The approach doesn't work for every food, and MSG still contributes some sodium. But it is one practical tool for reducing sodium while keeping food appealing.

reactions.title: Dissociation in food
reactions.summary: MSG is a salt, a compound made of a positive ion and a negative ion held together by their opposite charges. Like table salt, it only works once it dissolves, whether in saliva or in the moisture of food. Dissolving separates it into sodium ions and glutamate ions, and it is the free glutamate ion that our taste buds detect. This is exactly the same free glutamate that forms naturally when proteins in foods break down. Your tongue cannot tell whether glutamate came from a tomato or from a shaker of MSG.

steps.name: Dissolving
steps.text: When MSG crystals touch water, water molecules surround the sodium and glutamate ions and pull them apart. The ions spread out evenly through the liquid. This happens almost instantly because MSG dissolves very easily in water.

steps.name: Free glutamate
steps.text: The released glutamate ion carries a negative charge at the pH of food and saliva. In this free form it can reach the umami receptors on taste cells. Glutamate that is still bonded inside a protein chain can't fit into the receptor, which is why raw meat tastes less savory than cooked or aged meat.

steps.name: Synergy
steps.text: When inosinate or guanylate are also present, they bind next to glutamate on the receptor and boost its response. With these helpers, much less glutamate produces the same savory intensity. Food manufacturers sometimes blend small amounts of these ribonucleotides with MSG for this reason.

reactions.result: This synergy is why pairings like Japanese dashi (kombu seaweed rich in glutamate plus bonito fish rich in inosinate) or tomato sauce with parmesan taste so intensely savory. Cooks around the world discovered these combinations long before anyone understood the chemistry.

reactions.title: The Maillard reaction
reactions.summary: The Maillard reaction is a family of chemical reactions between amino acids and sugars that happens when food is heated. It produces the brown color and rich flavor of toast, roasted meat, fried onions and coffee. Glutamate, like other amino acids, can take part. The reaction is named after the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912. It runs fastest at high temperatures in fairly dry conditions, which is why searing meat browns it but boiling does not.

steps.name: Condensation
steps.text: When food is heated, the amino group (–NH₂) of glutamate reacts with the carbonyl group of a reducing sugar such as glucose. The two molecules join and release a molecule of water, a type of reaction called condensation. The product is an unstable compound called a glycosylamine.

steps.name: Rearrangement
steps.text: The glycosylamine rearranges its atoms into a more stable structure called an Amadori compound. No atoms are added or removed in this step; bonds just shift around. The Amadori compound is the starting point for many further reactions.

steps.name: Flavor and color
steps.text: With continued heating, Amadori compounds break apart and react in many different ways, producing hundreds of small molecules with strong aromas, such as pyrazines (roasted, nutty) and furans (caramel-like). Some fragments join into large brown polymers called melanoidins, which give browned food its color.

reactions.result: Amino acids and sugars reacting together create the flavors of toast, roasted meat, chocolate and fried onions. Each amino acid produces a slightly different set of aromas, which is part of why different foods brown with such different flavors.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; must be labeled as monosodium glutamate.
ADI "not specified" (the safest category).
Group ADI of 30 mg/kg body weight per day for glutamates.

hazards.title: Reported sensitivity
hazards.summary: For decades, MSG was blamed for a cluster of symptoms, including headache, flushing and sweating, once nicknamed “Chinese restaurant syndrome.” The label came from a 1968 letter to a medical journal and spread widely despite little evidence, and it is now recognized as reflecting prejudice against Asian food. Carefully controlled studies have not supported the idea that MSG in normal amounts causes these symptoms. A small number of people may get mild, short-lived symptoms after large doses on an empty stomach. Regulators worldwide consider MSG safe.
hazards.chemical: Glutamate is mostly burned as fuel by the cells lining the gut, so normal amounts in food barely change blood levels. When large amounts, several grams, are taken without food, blood glutamate can rise briefly, because there is nothing to slow its absorption. Scientists have looked for a way that this rise could cause headaches or flushing, but no consistent mechanism has been found. The brain is shielded from blood glutamate by the blood–brain barrier. Glutamate from MSG is chemically identical to the glutamate in tomatoes, cheese and breast milk.
hazards.biological: In double-blind trials, neither the participants nor the researchers knew who got MSG and who got a placebo. Under those conditions, symptoms appeared inconsistently and weren't reliably linked to MSG. A few studies found slightly more mild symptoms, such as headache or muscle tightness, after doses of 3 grams or more without food, which is far more than a typical serving. These symptoms were brief and caused no lasting harm. Expectations strongly shape how people feel, which may explain why some report reactions when they believe they have eaten MSG.

hazards.title: Sodium contribution
hazards.summary: Although MSG contains less sodium than salt, it still adds some, and that sodium counts toward your daily total. People carefully limiting sodium for blood pressure or kidney reasons should take it into account. In processed foods, MSG is often used alongside salt rather than instead of it, so total sodium can still be high. The sodium figure on the Nutrition Facts label gives the full picture. Used as a partial replacement for salt, though, MSG can help lower sodium intake.
hazards.chemical: Each MSG molecule contains one sodium ion. Because glutamate is a fairly heavy ion, sodium makes up only about 12 percent of MSG's weight. So each gram of MSG supplies about 120 milligrams of sodium, compared with about 390 milligrams in a gram of table salt. Inside the body, sodium from MSG behaves exactly like sodium from salt. It dissolves into the blood and is regulated by the kidneys.
hazards.biological: Sodium is vital for nerve signals and fluid balance, but most people eat more than they need. High intake over many years contributes to high blood pressure, which raises the risk of heart disease and stroke. A teaspoon of MSG, about 4 grams, contains roughly 500 milligrams of sodium, about a fifth of the recommended daily limit for adults. Most people consume far less MSG than that. As with salt, the overall daily total matters more than any single food.

profile.dosage: Most people eat about 0.5 to 1 gram of added MSG a day, while they get far more glutamate, roughly 10 grams or more, bound up in the protein of ordinary foods. International food-safety experts (JECFA) have given MSG an acceptable daily intake of “not specified,” the category for substances of very low concern, and the U.S. FDA considers it generally recognized as safe. In controlled studies, symptoms appeared only in some people and only after 3 grams or more on an empty stomach. Each gram of MSG contributes about 120 milligrams of sodium. As a seasoning a little goes a long way: about half a teaspoon flavors a pound of meat or several servings of vegetables.

myths.claim: "Chinese Restaurant Syndrome" proves MSG is harmful.
myths.consensus: The idea began with a 1968 letter to a medical journal; double-blind studies have not reproduced consistent reactions, and the narrative carried xenophobic undertones.

myths.claim: MSG is artificial.
myths.consensus: It is made by fermentation, and the glutamate is identical to that in tomatoes, parmesan, mushrooms and breast milk.

synthesis.title: Bacterial fermentation
synthesis.summary: Nearly all MSG today is made by fermentation, using bacteria to turn sugar into glutamic acid in a process much like brewing. The main microbe is Corynebacterium glutamicum, a soil bacterium found in Japan in 1956 because of its remarkable ability to pour out glutamate. It is grown in huge tanks on sugar cane or sugar beet molasses, corn starch or tapioca. The glutamate it makes is identical to the glutamate in tomatoes or cheese. Millions of tonnes are produced every year, making it one of the largest-volume fermentation products in the world.
synthesis.mechanism: Like all cells, Corynebacterium glutamicum runs the Krebs cycle, which produces a molecule called α-ketoglutarate. An enzyme then adds an amino group, taken from ammonia, to α-ketoglutarate, converting it into glutamate. Normally the bacteria keep their glutamate inside and use it to build proteins. But when producers limit biotin, a vitamin the bacteria need to build healthy cell membranes, the membranes become leaky. Glutamate then streams out into the surrounding broth while the cells keep making more. Afterward, glutamic acid is crystallized out of the broth by adjusting the pH and neutralized with sodium hydroxide to make MSG.
synthesis.significance: This 1950s Japanese discovery made MSG cheap and launched the industrial fermentation of amino acids.

synthesis.title: Original extraction
synthesis.summary: MSG was discovered in 1908 by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda, who wanted to know what gave kombu seaweed broth, a staple of Japanese cooking, its distinctive savory taste. He boiled down large amounts of the broth and isolated crystals of glutamic acid. He found that its sodium salt, MSG, had a strong, pleasant savory taste and was easy to handle. Ikeda named the taste “umami,” from a Japanese word meaning delicious. The next year, MSG went on sale in Japan under the brand name Ajinomoto, meaning “essence of taste.”
synthesis.mechanism: Ikeda extracted glutamate by evaporating kombu broth and separating its components by crystallization, taking advantage of differences in how well each substance dissolves. Early industrial production didn't use seaweed, which contained too little glutamate to be practical. Instead, factories took wheat gluten, a protein rich in glutamic acid, and boiled it with hydrochloric acid. The acid broke the peptide bonds holding the protein together, a reaction called hydrolysis, releasing all of its amino acids. Glutamic acid was then separated from the mixture by crystallization and neutralized to make MSG. This method was slow and costly, and fermentation replaced it in the 1950s and 1960s.
synthesis.significance: Umami was accepted as a fifth basic taste, alongside sweet, sour, salty and bitter, after its receptor was discovered in the early 2000s.

citations.title: Flavor potentiators.
citations.abstract: This review provides extensive presentation and evaluation of data relative to flavor potentiation, including the historical, chemical, organoleptic, metabolic, physiological, and consumptive properties of the commonly available flavor potentiators, which are primarily monosodium glutamate and 5'-nucleotides. In addition, their food occurrences, mode of action, manufacturing procedures, and methods of analyses will be discussed. Also, attention will be given to miscellaneous compounds that possess flavor potentiating properties.

citations.title: Crossreacting drugs and chemicals.
citations.abstract: Aspirin and nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) exert their clinical effect through inhibition of prostaglandin H synthases 1 and 2, also known as cyclooxygenase. This shared effect of COX-inhibition is also the mechanism for shared adverse effects. Much of our understanding of cross-reacting drugs and chemicals with aspirin comes from studying asthmatics with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD). Aspirin exacerbated respiratory disease is characterized by recalcitrant sinusitis/polyposis, asthma and precipitation of asthma after ingestion of aspirin and most NSAIDs. Cross-reactions between ASA and NSAIDs occur with first exposure unlike IgE-mediated allergic drug reactions. Cross-reactions between aspirin and other drugs are dependent upon inhibition of the cyclooxygenase-1 isoenzyme. Desensitization to aspirin will result in cross-desensitization to all NSATDs that inhibit COX-1. Despite reports in the literature, there does not appear to he cross-reactions between food coloring, hydrocortisone succinate and monosodium glutamate in individuals with aspirin exacerbated respiratory disease. The new highly selective cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors are well tolerated in AERD asthmatics who have not been desensitized to aspirin. Because low-dose ASA exerts a cardioprotective effect by irreversible inhibition of COX-1, AERD patients who are at risk for coronary artery disease should be considered for aspirin desensitization.

citations.title: Ultra-processed foods, allergy outcomes and underlying mechanisms in children: An EAACI task force report.
citations.authors: Berni Canani, Carucci, Coppola et al.
citations.abstract: Background: Consumption of ultra-processed foods [UPFs] may be associated with negative health outcomes. Limited data exist regarding the potential role of UPFs in the occurrence of allergic diseases. The underlying mechanisms underpinning any such associations are also poorly elucidated. Methods: We performed a systematic review and narrative evidence synthesis of the available literature to assess associations between UPF consumption and pediatric allergy outcomes (n = 26 papers), including data on the association seen with the gut microbiome (n = 16 papers) or immune system (n = 3 papers) structure and function following PRISMA guidelines. Results: Dietary exposure to fructose, carbonated soft drinks, and sugar intake was associated with an increased risk of asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergies in children. Commercial baby food intake was associated with childhood food allergy. Childhood intake of fructose, fruit juices, sugar-sweetened beverages, high carbohydrate UPFs, monosodium glutamate, UPFs, and advanced glycated end-products (AGEs) was associated with the occurrence of allergic diseases. Exposure to UPFs and common ingredients in UPFs seem to be associated with increased occurrence of allergic diseases such as asthma, wheezing, food allergies, atopic dermatitis, and allergic rhinitis, in many, but not all studies. Conclusion: More preclinical and clinical studies are required to better define the link between UPF consumption and the risk of allergies and asthma. These observational studies ideally require supporting data with clearly defined UPF consumption, validated dietary measures, and mechanistic assessments to definitively link UPFs with the risk of allergies and asthma.

citations.title: The restaurant syndromes.
citations.abstract: The Restaurant syndromes can be caused by five major factors: food allergens, sulfites, monosodium glutamate (MSG), tartrazine, and scombroidosis (and other seafood poisoning). A history of atopy and ingestion of known food allergens such as peanuts, egg, fish, and walnuts, together with positive results of skin tests or RAST to these foods, will favor a diagnosis of food allergy. Allergic reactions to peanuts have produced fatalities in minutes through an IgE mediated reaction. An extremely rapid onset (minutes) of symptoms consisting of flushing, bronchospasm and hypotension is consistent with a sulfite reaction. Burning, pressure, and tightness or numbness in the face, neck, and upper chest following ingestion of Chinese food favors a diagnosis of adverse reaction to MSG. Also, development of late onset bronchospasm (up to 14 hours) may be related to MSG reactions. Bronchospasm and urticaria in a patient with a history of aspirin intolerance suggests tartrazine sensitivity. If everyone ingesting a fish meal develops flushing, urticaria, pruritus, gastrointestinal complaints, or bronchospasm, this implies scombroidosis, ciguatera, or other seafood poisoning. Finally, severe headache or hypertension can result from ingestion of naturally occurring amines, such as tyramine (cheese, red wine) and phenylethylamine (chocolate). A double-blind oral challenge test may be the only way of confirming the diagnosis for most of the etiological factors of the Restaurant syndromes. The treatment of choice for acute reaction is epinephrine followed by antihistamine. Proper labeling and avoidance of these ingredients in sensitive individuals are the best preventive measures.

citations.title: Drug-pyridoxal phosphate interactions.
citations.journal: Q Rev Drug Metab Drug Interact
citations.abstract: In this review it has been pointed out that vitamin B6 and its vitamers can be involved in many interactions with a number of drugs, as well as with the actions of various endocrines and neurotransmitters. Nutritional deficiencies, especially of vitamins and proteins, can affect the manner in which drugs undergo biotransformation, and thereby may also modify the therapeutic efficacy of certain drugs. The differences between nutritional vitamin B6 deficiency and the hereditary disorder producing pyridoxine dependency are discussed. In addition to a pyridoxine deficiency being able to adversely affect drug actions, the improper supplementation with vitamin B6 can in some instances also adversely affect drug efficacy. A decrease by pyridoxine in the efficacy of levodopa used in the treatment of Parkinsonism is an example. The interrelationships and enzymatic interconversions among pyridoxine vitamers, both phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated, are briefly discussed, particularly regarding their pharmacokinetic properties. The ways in which the normal biochemical functions of vitamin B6 may be interfered with by various drugs are reviewed. (1) The chronic administration of isoniazid for the prevention or treatment of tuberculosis can produce peripheral neuropathy which can be prevented by the concurrent administration of pyridoxine. An acute toxic overdose of isoniazid causes generalized convulsions, and the intravenous administration of pyridoxine hydrochloride will prevent or stop these seizures. (2) The acute ingestion of excessive monosodium glutamate will, in some individuals, cause a group of symptoms including among others headache, weakness, stiffness, and heartburn, collectively known as the 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome.' These symptoms can be prevented by prior supplementation with vitamin B6. The beneficial effect is ascribed to the correction of a deficiency in the activity of glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase, an enzyme that is dependent on pyridoxal phosphate. Some interesting relationships are pointed out between vitamin B6, picolinic acid, and zinc. It is postulated that the intestinal absorption of zinc is facilitated by picolinic acid, a metabolite of tryptophan. The derivation of picolinic acid from tryptophan depends on the action of the enzyme kynureninase, which is dependent on pyridoxal phosphate; therefore, the adequate absorption of zinc is indirectly dependent on an adequate supply of vitamin B6. The formation of pyridoxal phosphate, on the other hand, appears to be indirectly dependent on Zn2++ which activates pyridoxal kinase.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 400 WORDS) This review examines the interaction of pyridoxal phosphate with select neuroendocrine and neuropharmacological systems and their health related therapeutic implications. Nutritional deficiencies, particularly of vitamins and proteins, can affect the manner in which drugs undergo biotransformation and thus may modify the therapeutic efficacy of certain drugs. In addition to pyridoxine deficiency adversely affecting drug actions, improper supplementation with viatmin B6 can in some instances also adversely affect drug efficacy. A decrease by pyridocxine in the efficacy of levodopa used in the treatment of Parkinsonism is an example. The interrelationships and enzymatic interconversions amony pyridoxine vitamers, both phosphorylated and nonphosphorylated, are briefly discussed, particularly concerning their pharmacokinetic properties. The chronic administration of isoniazid for the prevention or treatment of tuberculosis can produce peripheral neuropathy which can be prevented by the concurrent administration of pyridoxine. An acute toxic overdose of isoniazid causes generalized convulsions, and the intravenous administration of pryidoxine hydrochloride prevents or stops these seizures. The acute ingestion of excessive monosodium glutamate will, in some persons, cause a group of symptoms, including headache, weakness, stiffness, and heartburn, collectively known as the "Chinese Restaurant Syndrome." These symptoms can be prevented by prior supplementation with vitamin B6. It is postulated that the intestinal absorption of zinc is facilitated by picolinic acid, a metabolite of tryptophan. The derivation of picolinic acid from tryptophan depends on the action of the enzyme kynureninase, which is dependent on pyridoxal phosphate. Therefore, the adequate absorption of zinc is indirectly dependent on an adequate supply of vitamin B6. The formation of pyridoxal phospate appears to be indirectly dependent on Zn2++ which activates pyridoxal kinase. Treatment with daily pyridoxine can reverse a state of depression induced in women who take oral contraceptives (OCs). 1 hypothesis to explain this effect is that the OC is somehow causing a deficiency of seroton serotonin in the brain and that the vitamin B6 helps to overcome this deficiency through the stimulation of 5-hydroxytryptophan decarboxylase by pyridoxal phosphate. In sum, the stimulation of 5-hydroxytryptophan decarboxylase by pyridoxal phosphate. In sum, pyridoxal phosphate in physiological concentrations seems to function as an endogenous "down regulator" of several receptor sites, including estrogen, progesterone, and androgen.

name: Red 40
scoreRationale: Legal and within ADI for most people, but linked to hyperactivity in some children, carries an EU warning label, and is being phased out of U.S. school foods.
summary: Red 40 is the most-used synthetic food dye in the U.S. It's purely cosmetic, and evidence that it affects some children's behavior is driving new restrictions.

physical.phStability: Stable across food pH; resists light and heat

overview: Allura Red AC (Red 40) is an azo dye: two aromatic ring systems connected by an azo bridge (–N=N–). The azo group links the rings into one long conjugated system of alternating double bonds, which absorbs blue-green light (around 504 nm) so we see red.

Two sulfonate groups (–SO₃⁻ Na⁺) make the dye very water-soluble and keep it from being absorbed well in the gut. Food makers favor it because it is cheap, bright and stable to heat, light and acid, unlike many natural red pigments.
profile.function: Colors candy, drinks, cereals, snacks and cosmetics a bright, consistent red with no flavor or nutritional role.

mechanisms.title: Why it looks red
mechanisms.chemical: White light, like sunlight, is a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow. Allura Red's molecule contains a long chain of alternating single and double bonds running across its rings and the azo bridge, called a conjugated system. In such a system, electrons are spread out over many atoms and can absorb energy from light. Allura Red's electrons absorb light with a wavelength of about 504 nanometers, which is blue-green, and jump up to a higher energy level. The length and shape of the conjugated system decide exactly which wavelength gets absorbed.
mechanisms.biological: When white light hits a food colored with Allura Red, the blue-green part is absorbed and the rest is reflected or passes through. Our eyes and brain see the mix of remaining wavelengths as red, the complementary color of blue-green. Cone cells in the retina, which respond to red, green and blue light, send signals that the brain combines into the color we perceive. Because only tiny amounts of dye are needed to absorb enough light, foods can be colored with just a few parts per million. That intensity is part of what makes synthetic dyes so cheap to use.

mechanisms.title: Breakdown by gut bacteria
mechanisms.chemical: Allura Red is poorly absorbed in the small intestine because its sulfonate groups give it a negative charge and make it dissolve readily in water, so it passes on to the colon. There, bacteria produce enzymes called azoreductases that break the azo bond (–N=N–), the bridge between the dye's two halves. They do this by adding hydrogen atoms, a type of reaction called reduction. The dye splits into two separate molecules, each with an amino group (–NH₂) and a sulfonate group. These are called sulfonated aromatic amines.
mechanisms.biological: Most of the breakdown products are poorly absorbed, because their sulfonate groups keep them charged, so they leave the body in feces. The sulfonate groups also make these amines far less toxic than unsulfonated aromatic amines, some of which are known to cause cancer. Laboratory studies show that gut bacteria can break Allura Red down within hours. Researchers are still studying whether these products have subtler effects on the gut lining or on the bacteria themselves. Current evidence suggests they are largely harmless at normal intakes.

mechanisms.title: Behavior in sensitive children
mechanisms.chemical: No single biological mechanism has been established for how synthetic dyes might affect behavior. One idea is that some children are sensitive to histamine, a messenger molecule, and that additives may trigger histamine release that affects the brain. Another is that the dyes or their breakdown products interfere with neurotransmitters, the chemicals nerve cells use to communicate. Differences in genes or gut bacteria could explain why only some children seem to be affected. These ideas are still being tested.
mechanisms.biological: In the 2007 Southampton study in the U.K., children drank juice containing either a mixture of synthetic dyes plus the preservative sodium benzoate or a look-alike placebo, without knowing which. Some of the children showed a small rise in hyperactive behavior after the dye mixtures. Since then, a 2021 review by California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment concluded that synthetic food dyes can affect behavior in some children. The effects are generally small and vary from child to child. They don't mean dyes cause ADHD, but they may worsen symptoms in sensitive children.

mechanisms.title: Gut inflammation in mice
mechanisms.chemical: In a 2022 study, researchers fed mice Allura Red for several weeks. They found it increased production of serotonin, a signaling molecule, by specialized cells in the lining of the gut called enterochromaffin cells. In the gut, serotonin affects how the intestine moves, what it secretes and how the immune system responds. The dye also seemed to change the makeup of the gut bacteria. These effects depended on long-term exposure, not a single dose.
mechanisms.biological: Mice exposed to Allura Red were more susceptible to experimentally induced colitis, a model of inflammatory bowel disease in which the colon becomes inflamed. The rise in gut serotonin appeared to be part of the cause. However, mouse studies don't always predict what happens in people, and the doses relative to body weight may differ from typical human exposure. Researchers are now investigating whether similar effects occur in humans. For now it remains an early laboratory finding rather than an established human risk.

reactions.title: Diazotization and azo coupling (how it's made)
reactions.summary: Most synthetic dyes, including Allura Red, are made by joining two aromatic molecules with an azo bridge (–N=N–). This takes two classic steps, first developed in the 19th century during the boom in synthetic dyes. In the first step, an aromatic amine is turned into a reactive molecule called a diazonium ion. In the second, the diazonium ion attaches itself to another aromatic molecule. The reactions run in water, usually in the cold, and they are the foundation of the whole azo-dye industry.

steps.name: Diazotization
steps.text: An aromatic amine, cresidine-4-sulfonic acid, is mixed with sodium nitrite and acid near 0 °C. The acid and nitrite form nitrous acid, which reacts with the amine's –NH₂ group and converts it into a diazonium group (–N₂⁺). The cold is essential because diazonium ions fall apart quickly when warm.

steps.name: Azo coupling
steps.text: The diazonium ion is hungry for electrons, so it attacks an electron-rich aromatic ring, here a naphthol called Schaeffer's salt. It replaces a hydrogen atom on that ring in a reaction called electrophilic aromatic substitution. The two ring systems are now linked by an –N=N– bridge.

steps.name: Isolation
steps.text: Adding a lot of salt makes the dye less soluble, so it comes out as a solid, a technique called salting out. The dye is filtered, purified to remove leftover starting materials and impurities, and dried into a powder.

reactions.result: The new –N=N– bridge joins the two rings into one long conjugated system, which is what creates the color. By changing the starting amine and the coupling partner, chemists can make thousands of different azo dyes in nearly every color.

reactions.title: Azo reduction
reactions.summary: The azo bridge (–N=N–) that gives Allura Red its color can be broken by adding electrons and hydrogen atoms, a type of reaction called reduction. When the bridge breaks, the long conjugated system is cut in two and the color disappears. This happens in our intestines, where bacteria do it with enzymes, and it can also be done with chemicals or in wastewater treatment. The reaction matters both for understanding what happens to dyes in the body and for removing them from the environment. It is essentially the coupling reaction run backward.

steps.name: Electron transfer
steps.text: Bacterial enzymes called azoreductases take electrons from a carrier molecule, NADH, and hand them to the azo group. The two nitrogen atoms in the double bond accept those electrons. This weakens the bond between them.

steps.name: Intermediate
steps.text: After the first two electrons and two hydrogen ions are added, the –N=N– double bond becomes a single bond with a hydrogen on each nitrogen (–NH–NH–), called a hydrazo group. This intermediate is colorless because the conjugated system has been interrupted.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: Adding two more electrons and hydrogens breaks the nitrogen–nitrogen bond completely. The molecule splits into two separate aromatic amines, each with an –NH₂ group where the bridge used to be.

reactions.result: The same reaction lets bacteria in wastewater treatment plants decolorize azo dyes from industrial waste. Chemists also use it to work out the structure of an unknown azo dye: reducing it and identifying the two amines reveals the original building blocks.

regulatory.status: Certified color additive; FDA announced in 2025 a plan to phase out petroleum-based dyes, relying largely on industry commitments.
Authorized as E129 but foods must carry the warning "may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children".
The School Food Safety Act (2024) bans Red 40 in public-school foods from the end of 2027.
ADI 0–7 mg/kg body weight.

hazards.title: Hyperactivity in sensitive children
hazards.summary: Synthetic food dyes, including Allura Red, don't cause ADHD, but research suggests they can increase hyperactive behavior in some sensitive children. The effect was seen in controlled trials, especially the 2007 Southampton study, which used mixtures of dyes. Average effects were small, but some children seemed to react much more strongly than others. This evidence has led to policy changes in several places. Many parents choose to limit dyed foods as a precaution.
hazards.chemical: The underlying mechanism remains unclear. Researchers have proposed that dyes might trigger histamine release or affect neurotransmitter systems in the brain, but neither has been proven. Because the dyes are poorly absorbed, it's also possible that their breakdown products, or their effects on gut bacteria, play a role. Genetic differences, for example in how quickly children clear histamine, may explain why some are affected and others aren't. Studying these effects is hard because behavior is shaped by so many factors.
hazards.biological: In trials where children didn't know whether their drink contained dyes, parents and teachers rated some children as more hyperactive after the dye drinks. The European Union responded by requiring foods containing certain dyes to carry the warning “may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.” In the United States, California passed a law in 2024 that removes six synthetic dyes, including Red 40, from food served in public schools. Many food companies have reformulated products to use natural colors instead.

hazards.title: Manufacturing impurities
hazards.summary: Making synthetic dyes from petroleum chemicals can leave behind small amounts of unwanted byproducts. Some of these, certain aromatic amines in particular, are known or suspected to cause cancer. That is why food dyes are strictly regulated and tested. In the United States, Allura Red is one of a small group of color additives that the FDA must certify batch by batch. Certification keeps impurities at tiny, carefully controlled levels.
hazards.chemical: The reactions that make Allura Red start from aromatic amines, molecules made of a benzene ring carrying an amino group. If the starting materials aren't pure, or if side reactions occur, small amounts of amines can remain in the final dye. For Allura Red, the main one is leftover p-cresidine, the starting amine, which has caused cancer in animals at high doses; benzidine, a related amine linked to bladder cancer in dye workers decades ago, is another impurity regulators watch for in azo dyes. Traces of metals such as lead and arsenic from raw materials are also possible. Purification steps are designed to remove them.
hazards.biological: FDA chemists test a sample from every batch of certified dye sold in the United States, checking that impurities fall below strict limits measured in parts per million or less. Only batches that pass can be used in food, drugs or cosmetics. These limits are set far below levels that would cause harm. As a result, the amount of impurities anyone eats from food dyes is extremely small. Batch certification of food colors has been required in the U.S. since 1938.

profile.dosage: International experts (JECFA) have set an acceptable daily intake for Allura Red of up to 7 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, the amount considered safe to eat every day for life. Average intakes are below this, but children who eat a lot of brightly colored candy, cereals and drinks can approach several milligrams per kilogram on some days. A single serving of a red drink or candy may contain tens of milligrams. In the U.S., Red 40 must be listed by name on ingredient labels, so it is easy to spot. Families who want to limit it can choose products colored with natural pigments such as beet juice or paprika.

myths.claim: Red 40 is made from bugs.
myths.consensus: That's carmine (cochineal). Red 40 is synthesized from petroleum-derived chemicals.

myths.claim: Red 40 causes ADHD.
myths.consensus: It doesn't cause ADHD, but evidence suggests it can worsen hyperactive behavior in some sensitive children.

environment.persistence: Moderately persistent; azo dyes resist aerobic breakdown.

synthesis.title: Petrochemical synthesis
synthesis.summary: Allura Red is made entirely from chemicals derived from petroleum, as are most synthetic food dyes. It was introduced by the Allied Chemical Corporation in the early 1970s (the “AC” in its name stands for Allied Chemical) and became the main red food dye in the U.S. after Red No. 2 was banned in 1976. Its manufacture uses classic azo-dye chemistry. The final product is a dark red powder that dissolves easily in water. It is stable in light, heat and acid, which natural red colors often are not.
synthesis.mechanism: The process starts with cresidine-4-sulfonic acid, an aromatic amine with a sulfonate group that will help the finished dye dissolve in water. It is chilled in water with acid and treated with sodium nitrite, turning its amino group into a reactive diazonium ion. This solution is then slowly added to a second chemical, 6-hydroxy-2-naphthalenesulfonic acid, a two-ring aromatic compound that also carries a sulfonate group. The diazonium ion attacks the electron-rich ring, linking the two molecules through an azo bridge (–N=N–). The resulting dye is collected as its disodium salt, washed to remove impurities and dried.
synthesis.significance: Every batch sold in the U.S. is chemically tested and certified by the FDA before use.

citations.title: Squid pen chitin chitooligomers as food colorants absorbers.
citations.abstract: One of the most promising applications of chitosanase is the conversion of chitinous biowaste into bioactive chitooligomers (COS). TKU033 chitosanase was induced from squid pen powder (SPP)-containing Bacillus cereus TKU033 medium and purified by ammonium sulfate precipitation and column chromatography. The enzyme was relatively more thermostable in the presence of the substrate and had an activity of 93% at 50 °C in a pH 5 buffer solution for 60 min. Furthermore, the enzyme used for the COS preparation was also studied. The enzyme products revealed various mixtures of COS that with different degrees of polymerization (DP), ranging from three to nine. In the culture medium, the fermented SPP was recovered, and it displayed a better adsorption rate (up to 96%) for the disperse dyes than the water-soluble food colorants, Allura Red AC (R40) and Tartrazne (Y4). Fourier transform-infrared spectroscopic (FT-IR) analysis proved that the adsorption of the dyes onto fermented SPP was a physical adsorption. Results also showed that fermented SPP was a favorable adsorber and could be employed as low-cost alternative for dye removal in wastewater treatment.

citations.title: Food dyes as P-glycoprotein modulators.
citations.abstract: The drug transporter P-glycoprotein (P-gp) is often investigated in drug-interaction studies because the activity is modulated by a wide variety of xenobiotics including drugs, herbal products, and food components. In this study, we tested six common arylsulfonate food dyes-allura red, carmoisine, ponceau 4R, quinolone yellow, sunset yellow, and tartrazine-as activators and inhibitors of P-gp activity in vitro. The dyes were studied as P-gp activators by measuring ATPase activity in P-gp-expressing membranes. Compared to verapamil, a known activator of P-gp, the six food dyes showed no stimulatory activity. The potential for these six food dyes to act as P-gp inhibitors was tested in an intracellular efflux assay with P-gp-expressing cells. Compared to GF120918, a known P-gp inhibitor, there was no inhibitory activity for these six food dyes. The six food dyes tested do not interact with P-gp in vitro and, therefore, are unlikely cause clinical drug-food dye interactions. Further investigation is necessary to determine whether these food dyes could interact with other drug transporters.

citations.title: Food Safety and Health Concerns of Synthetic Food Colors: An Update.
citations.abstract: The toxicity of food additives is widely studied and concerns many consumers worldwide. Synthetic food colors are often considered an unnecessary risk to consumer health. Since the European Food Safety Authority's (EFSA) re-evaluation between 2009 and 2014, the body of scientific literature on food colors has grown, and new evaluations are being published by the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA). Therefore, this narrative review aims to review the toxicological data that have become available since 2014. The reviewed colors are Quinoline Yellow, Sunset Yellow, Azorubine, Amaranth, Ponceau 4R, Erythrosine, Allura Red, Patent Blue, Indigo Carmine, Brilliant Blue FCF, Green S, Brilliant Black, Brown HT, and Lithol Rubine BK. Tartrazine was not included in this paper; the overwhelming amount of recent data on Tartrazine toxicity requires more space than this review can provide. The issues regarding the toxicity of synthetic food colors and real population exposures are being regularly examined and reviewed by relevant authorities, such as the EFSA and JECFA. The current ADI limits set by the authorities are mostly in agreement, and they seem safe. However, the EFSA and JECFA assessments of some of the colors are more than a decade old, and new evidence will soon be required.

citations.title: Health safety issues of synthetic food colorants.
citations.abstract: Increasing attention has been recently paid to the toxicity of additives used in food. The European Parliament and the Council published the REGULATION (EC) No. 1333/2008 on food additives establishing that the toxicity of food additives evaluated before 20th January 2009 must be re-evaluated by European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The aim of this review is to survey current knowledge specifically on the toxicity issues of synthetic food colorants using official reports published by the EFSA and other available studies published since the respective report. Synthetic colorants described are Tartrazine, Quinoline Yellow, Sunset Yellow, Azorubine, Ponceau 4R, Erythrosine, Allura Red, Patent Blue, Indigo Carmine, Brilliant Blue FCF, Green S, Brilliant Black and Brown HT. Moreover, a summary of evidence on possible detrimental effects of colorant mixes on children's behaviour is provided and future research directions are outlined.

name: Yellow 5
scoreRationale: Must be named on U.S. labels due to intolerance reactions, carries the EU hyperactivity warning, and is included in new school-food bans.
summary: Yellow 5 is a synthetic lemon-yellow dye. A small number of people react to it, and it's part of the dye group linked to hyperactivity in some children.

physical.phStability: Stable in acidic foods; good light fastness

overview: Tartrazine (Yellow 5) is a lemon-yellow azo dye built from a pyrazolone ring and two sulfonated benzene rings, linked by an azo group (–N=N–). Its conjugated system absorbs violet-blue light (about 427 nm), so we see yellow.
Its sulfonate groups make it water-soluble and poorly absorbed. Mixed with a blue dye such as Brilliant Blue, it makes the bright greens of candies and sports drinks.
profile.function: Colors soft drinks, candies, chips, pickles, soaps and cosmetics yellow or, mixed with blue, green.

mechanisms.title: Why it looks yellow
mechanisms.chemical: Tartrazine's molecule has a conjugated system, a chain of alternating single and double bonds, running through its pyrazolone ring, the azo bridge (–N=N–) and a benzene ring. Electrons in this system are spread over many atoms and can absorb energy from light. Tartrazine's conjugated system is arranged differently from Allura Red's, so its electrons absorb light of a shorter wavelength, around 427 nanometers, which is violet-blue. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy. By changing the length and shape of a dye's conjugated system, chemists can shift which color it absorbs.
mechanisms.biological: When white light shines on tartrazine, the violet and blue parts are absorbed and the remaining wavelengths, mainly green, yellow, orange and red, reach our eyes. The brain blends them into the perception of bright lemon yellow. Because yellow and blue are complementary, mixing tartrazine with a blue dye such as Brilliant Blue FCF absorbs light at both ends of the spectrum and leaves green. That is how the vivid greens of candies, sports drinks and some pickles are made. Tartrazine also colors some medicines and cosmetics.

mechanisms.title: Intolerance reactions
mechanisms.chemical: In a small number of people, tartrazine appears to trigger mast cells, immune cells that store chemical messengers such as histamine, to release their contents. Unlike a true allergy, this doesn't involve IgE antibodies, the proteins that recognize specific allergens, so it is called a pseudo-allergic reaction. Tartrazine may also affect the production of inflammatory molecules called leukotrienes, in a way similar to aspirin. The exact mechanism isn't fully understood. The reaction depends on how much is eaten.
mechanisms.biological: When mast cells release histamine and other messengers, small blood vessels widen and leak fluid, causing hives, itching and swelling of the skin. In people with asthma, the airways can tighten, leading to wheezing or an asthma attack. Many people who react to tartrazine are also sensitive to aspirin, which hints at a shared pathway. Symptoms usually appear within minutes to hours of eating the dye. Avoiding foods and medicines that contain tartrazine prevents the reactions.

mechanisms.title: Gut bacterial breakdown
mechanisms.chemical: Like other azo dyes, tartrazine is poorly absorbed in the small intestine, because its sulfonate and carboxylate groups make it strongly charged and very water-soluble. When it reaches the colon, bacteria produce azoreductase enzymes that break the azo bond (–N=N–) by adding hydrogen atoms. This splits tartrazine into two smaller molecules: sulfanilic acid and an aminopyrazolone. Both have amino groups where the azo bridge used to be. The breakdown destroys the dye's color.
mechanisms.biological: The breakdown products are themselves poorly absorbed and mostly leave in feces, while the small amounts that are absorbed are removed in urine. Sulfanilic acid is a fairly harmless compound that doesn't build up in the body. Studies in animals and people show that tartrazine and its breakdown products don't accumulate in tissues. This is part of why regulators consider tartrazine safe at typical intakes for most people. Research continues into how azo dyes interact with the gut bacteria that break them down.

reactions.title: Azo coupling (how it's made)
reactions.summary: Tartrazine is made by the same two-step azo chemistry used for most synthetic dyes: diazotization followed by azo coupling. The first molecule, sulfanilic acid, is turned into a reactive diazonium ion. It then attaches to the second molecule, a pyrazolone, forming an azo bridge between them. Choosing a pyrazolone as the partner, instead of a naphthol like the one used for Allura Red, is what makes the dye yellow rather than red. The reactions are carried out in cold water.

steps.name: Diazotization
steps.text: Sulfanilic acid, a benzene ring carrying an amino group and a sulfonate group, is treated with sodium nitrite and acid near 0 °C. Nitrous acid formed in the mixture converts the amino group into a diazonium group (–N₂⁺). This makes the molecule highly reactive toward electron-rich partners.

steps.name: Coupling
steps.text: The diazonium ion is added to a solution of a sulfophenyl pyrazolone carboxylic acid. The pyrazolone ring has an electron-rich carbon atom that the diazonium ion attacks, forming a new nitrogen–carbon bond. The two halves are now joined by an –N=N– bridge.

steps.name: Salt formation
steps.text: The product is neutralized with sodium hydroxide to form its trisodium salt, meaning three sodium ions balance its three negative charges. The dye is then salted out, filtered, purified and dried into a yellow-orange powder.

reactions.result: The pyrazolone ring changes the conjugated system compared with naphthol-based dyes, shifting absorption toward shorter wavelengths, so the dye looks yellow instead of red. Small structural changes like this let chemists tune dyes to almost any color.

regulatory.status: Certified color; must be declared by name on labels because of intolerance reports.
Authorized as E102 with the mandatory hyperactivity warning label.
Banned in public-school foods from the end of 2027 (AB 2316).

hazards.title: Intolerance in a small minority
hazards.summary: A small minority of people react to tartrazine with hives, itching or, rarely, asthma attacks. Because these reactions can be serious for people with asthma, U.S. labels must list “Yellow 5” or “FD&C Yellow No. 5” by name rather than just “artificial color,” a rule in place since 1981. People who know they react can easily avoid it by reading labels. For the vast majority of people, tartrazine causes no reaction at all. Reactions are more common among people who are also sensitive to aspirin.
hazards.chemical: In sensitive people, tartrazine triggers mast cells to release histamine and other inflammatory messengers without involving IgE antibodies. Because this pseudo-allergic activation doesn't need prior exposure, it can happen the first time someone eats the dye. Some evidence suggests tartrazine acts on the same inflammatory pathway as aspirin, increasing the production of leukotrienes, molecules that make airways tighten. The reaction depends on dose, so small amounts may cause no symptoms at all. The exact chemical trigger remains uncertain.
hazards.biological: Histamine released from mast cells widens small blood vessels in the skin and makes them leak, producing raised, itchy welts called hives and sometimes swelling. In the airways, histamine and leukotrienes make the muscles tighten and the lining swell, which can cause wheezing or an asthma attack in susceptible people. Estimates suggest well under 1 in 1,000 people are affected. Reactions usually fade once the dye has been cleared from the body. Antihistamines and asthma medicines can relieve the symptoms.

hazards.title: Hyperactivity in sensitive children
hazards.summary: Tartrazine was one of the dyes in the mixtures tested in the 2007 Southampton study, which found small increases in hyperactive behavior in some children. As with other dyes, it doesn't cause ADHD, but it may affect behavior in sensitive children. Because it was only tested as part of mixtures, its individual effect isn't known. The European Union now requires a warning label on foods that contain it. Some manufacturers have replaced it with natural yellows such as turmeric or annatto.
hazards.chemical: No mechanism by which tartrazine might affect behavior has been established. Proposed explanations include histamine release that could affect the brain, or effects on how nutrients are absorbed, but the evidence for either is limited. Because tartrazine is poorly absorbed, any effects might also run through gut bacteria or the dye's breakdown products. Genetic differences may help explain why only some children respond. More research is needed to understand the chemistry involved.
hazards.biological: In the Southampton trial, children who drank juice containing dye mixtures with tartrazine were rated as more hyperactive, on average, by parents and teachers than when they drank a placebo. The effect varied a lot from child to child. Based on this study, the EU requires foods containing tartrazine to carry the warning “may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.” Regulators did not change the acceptable daily intake, judging the evidence too limited for that. Parents who suspect a sensitivity can choose dye-free foods.

profile.dosage: International experts (JECFA) have set an acceptable daily intake for tartrazine of up to 10 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, the amount considered safe every day for life. Typical exposures are lower, although children who eat a lot of brightly colored foods have the highest intakes. A colored drink or candy usually contains a few to tens of milligrams. In the U.S., it must appear as “Yellow 5” on ingredient lists, and in the EU as E102. People with aspirin sensitivity or asthma who notice reactions are the main group advised to avoid it.

myths.claim: Yellow 5 lowers sperm count.
myths.consensus: This long-running rumor about neon sodas has no supporting human evidence.

myths.claim: Yellow 5 is banned in Europe.
myths.consensus: It is permitted in the EU, but products must carry a warning about children's activity and attention.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Tartrazine was first made in 1884 by the Swiss chemist Johann Heinrich Ziegler, at a time when chemists were racing to invent new synthetic dyes. Today it is produced from petroleum-derived chemicals in large chemical plants. It is one of the most widely used yellow food colors in the world. In the U.S., every batch has to be certified by the FDA. In Europe it is labeled E102.
synthesis.mechanism: Sulfanilic acid, an aromatic amine with a sulfonate group, is first converted into a diazonium ion by treating it with sodium nitrite and acid at low temperature. The diazonium ion is then coupled with 1-(4-sulfophenyl)-3-carboxy-5-pyrazolone, a ring-shaped molecule with an electron-rich carbon that the diazonium ion attacks. This forms the azo bridge linking the two parts of the dye. Adding sodium hydroxide converts the product into its trisodium salt. It is then purified by salting out, filtering and washing, and dried into a powder.
synthesis.significance: Tartrazine's name comes from tartaric acid, used in Ziegler's original 1884 synthesis.

citations.title: Experimental and theoretical study of dyes adsorption process on chitosan-based cryogel.
citations.abstract: In this research, the adsorption of three synthetic dyes dissolved in an aqueous solution on chitosan cryogel beads (Q-C-EGDE) was compared. The effect of the pH of the solution on the adsorption capacity of each dyes was analyzed. Furthermore, the kinetics and adsorption isotherms were compared, at temperatures of 283.15 K, 303.15 K and 323.15 K, and the kinetic and adsorption equilibrium data were fitted to three mathematical models, respectively. The biosorbent was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), the nitrogen physisorption BET method and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The characterization results show that the cryogel is composed of low-surface, macroporous, porous grooved walls. The functional groups that took part in the adsorption were mainly amino groups (NH3+). When comparing the adsorption capacities, it was found that the dyes adsorb in the following order Blue 1 > Red 2 > Yellow 5 reaching capacities from 1600 mg/L to 850 mg/L. The results of the adsorption and mathematical modelling suggest that the process is regulated mainly by physisorption and is largely limited by mass transfer mechanisms within the cryogel, where the electrostatic charges present affect adsorption. The latter was corroborated by the Monte Carlo simulation.

citations.title: Enhanced decolorization of dyes by an iron modified clay and thermodynamic parameters.
citations.abstract: The sorption processes of red 5 (R5) and yellow 5 (Y5) dyes by iron modified and sodium bentonite in aqueous solutions was evaluated. The modified clay was prepared, conditioned and characterized. The sodium clay did not remove any of either dye. The sorption kinetics and isotherms of R5 and Y5 dyes by iron modified clay were determined. The maximum removal percentages achieved were 97% and 98% for R5 and Y5, respectively, and a contact time of 72 h; the experimental data were best adjusted to Ho model. The isotherms of both dyes were best adjusted to the Langmuir model and the maximum adsorption capacities of the modified clay were 11.26 mg/g and 5.28 mg/g for R5 and Y5, respectively. These results indicate that adsorption processes have a high probability to be described as chemisorption on a homogeneous material. Temperature range between 283 and 213 K does not affect the adsorption of Y5 by the iron modified clay, but the adsorption process of R5 was affected, and the thermodynamic parameters could be calculated, which indicate a chemisorption mechanism.

citations.title: Toxicology of food dyes.
citations.abstract: Background: Food dyes, synthesized originally from coal tar and now petroleum, have long been controversial because of safety concerns. Many dyes have been banned because of their adverse effects on laboratory animals or inadequate testing. Conclusions: This review finds that all of the nine currently US-approved dyes raise health concerns of varying degrees. Red 3 causes cancer in animals, and there is evidence that several other dyes also are carcinogenic. Three dyes (Red 40, Yellow 5, and Yellow 6) have been found to be contaminated with benzidine or other carcinogens. At least four dyes (Blue 1, Red 40, Yellow 5, and Yellow 6) cause hypersensitivity reactions. Numerous microbiological and rodent studies of Yellow 5 were positive for genotoxicity. Toxicity tests on two dyes (Citrus Red 2 and Orange B) also suggest safety concerns, but Citrus Red 2 is used at low levels and only on some Florida oranges and Orange B has not been used for several years. The inadequacy of much of the testing and the evidence for carcinogenicity, genotoxicity, and hypersensitivity, coupled with the fact that dyes do not improve the safety or nutritional quality of foods, indicates that all of the currently used dyes should be removed from the food supply and replaced, if at all, by safer colorings. It is recommended that regulatory authorities require better and independent toxicity testing, exercise greater caution regarding continued approval of these dyes, and in the future approve only well-tested, safe dyes.

citations.title: HC Yellow 5.
citations.abstract: The Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety reviewed updated information that has become available since their original assessment from 2007, along with updated information regarding product types, and frequency and concentrations of use, and reaffirmed their original conclusion that HC Yellow 5 is safe as a hair dye ingredient in the practices of use and concentration as described in this report.

citations.title: Application of the IOC Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Clinical Assessment Tool version 2 (CAT2) across 200+ elite athletes.
citations.abstract: Objective: This cross-sectional retrospective and prospective study implemented the 2023 International Olympic Committee Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Clinical Assessment Tool version 2 (CAT2) to determine the current severity of REDs (primary outcome) and future risk of bone stress injuries (BSI, exploratory outcome) in elite athletes. Methods: Female (n=143; 23.3±4.3 years) and male (n=70; 23.1±3.7 years) athletes (performance tier 3 (52%), tier 4 (36%), tier 5 (12%)) participated in a baseline CAT2 (with minor modifications) assessment, including a self-report questionnaire (menstrual function (females), BSI, Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q)), bone mineral density (BMD via DXA) and fasted blood analysis (triiodothyronine (T3), testosterone, cholesterol). Athletes were assigned a green, yellow, orange or red light via CAT2. The prospective risk of new self-report of physician-diagnosed BSI was assessed over a subsequent 6-24 months. Results: REDs prevalence was 55% green, 36% yellow, 5% orange and 4% red light. The CAT2 identified a greater prevalence of amenorrhoea and BSI and lower T3, testosterone and BMD (p<0.01) in red, orange and yellow (those with REDs) versus green light. ORs for a prospective self-reported BSI (majority physician diagnosed) were greater in orange vs green (OR 7.71, 95% CI (1.26 to 39.83)), in females with severe amenorrhoea (OR 4.6 (95% CI 0.98 to 17.85)), in males with low sex drive (OR 16.0 (95% CI 4.79 to 1038.87)), and athletes with elevated EDE-Q global scores (OR 1.45 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.97)). Conclusion: The CAT2 has high validity in demonstrating current severity of REDs, with increased future risk of self-reported BSI in athletes with a more severe REDs traffic light category.

name: Caramel Color
scoreRationale: Plain caramel (class I) is benign, but ammonia-process caramels (classes III/IV, used in colas) contain 4-MEI, a possible carcinogen now kept low under California rules.
summary: Caramel color gives colas, sauces and gravies their brown hue. Most types are harmless; the ammonia-made kinds contain a by-product regulators limit.

identity.composition: Complex mixture of polymers from heated carbohydrates. Class I (plain), II (caustic sulfite), III (ammonia) and IV (sulfite-ammonia).

physical.phStability: Classes are matched to product pH (class IV for acidic colas)

overview: Caramel color is a complex mixture of brown polymers made by heating sugars under controlled conditions. Unlike a single dye molecule, it contains thousands of different molecules, from small flavor compounds to large colored polymers called melanoidins.

Manufacturers sort it into four classes by what is added during heating: plain (I), caustic sulfite (II), ammonia (III) and sulfite-ammonia (IV). The additives control the particles' electric charge, which matters: a cola needs a negatively charged caramel (class IV) that won't clump in its acidic environment.
profile.function: Provides consistent brown color in colas, soy sauce, beer, gravy, baked goods and some hair and skin products.

mechanisms.title: Why it's brown
mechanisms.chemical: When sugar is heated strongly, its molecules lose water and break into small, reactive fragments. These fragments link together into larger and larger molecules with long chains of alternating single and double bonds, called conjugated systems. Large conjugated molecules absorb light across much of the visible spectrum, but they absorb blue and violet light more strongly than red. Because caramel color is a mixture of thousands of such molecules of different sizes, it absorbs a broad sweep of wavelengths. The largest of these brown polymers are called melanoidins.
mechanisms.biological: With blue light absorbed most and red light least, the light that reaches our eyes is weighted toward red, orange and yellow, which together look brown. Darker caramels contain more and bigger polymers, so they absorb more light overall. Manufacturers measure color strength as “tinctorial power,” how much light a standard solution absorbs. Caramel color gives colas, dark beers, soy sauce, gravies and baked goods a consistent brown appearance. At the amounts used, it adds very little flavor.

mechanisms.title: Matching the charge
mechanisms.chemical: Caramel color isn't a single substance dissolved in water but a suspension of tiny particles called colloids, so small that they stay spread out instead of sinking. These particles carry an electric charge on their surfaces, and the charge depends on the chemicals added during heating. Ammonia compounds tend to give a positive charge, while sulfite compounds give a negative one. Particles with the same charge repel each other, which keeps them evenly dispersed. If they meet substances with the opposite charge, they can clump together and settle.
mechanisms.biological: To keep the color evenly spread through a product, the caramel's charge has to suit the product's chemistry. Colas are very acidic and contain negatively charged ingredients, so they need negatively charged class IV caramel; a positively charged caramel would clump and form sediment. Beer and soy sauce contain positively charged proteins, so they use positively charged class III caramel. Matching the charge prevents haze, sediment and color loss during storage. This is why food makers pick a specific class of caramel for each product.

mechanisms.title: 4-MEI in animal studies
mechanisms.chemical: When caramel is made with ammonia compounds (classes III and IV), the ammonia reacts with small fragments of broken-down sugar such as methylglyoxal, a molecule with two reactive carbonyl groups. This reaction forms small ring-shaped molecules called imidazoles, which contain two nitrogen atoms. One of these is 4-methylimidazole, or 4-MEI. It is a byproduct, not something added on purpose. Similar reactions produce small amounts of 4-MEI in roasted coffee and grilled foods.
mechanisms.biological: In a long-term study by the U.S. National Toxicology Program, mice fed high doses of 4-MEI for two years developed more lung tumors, while rats did not. Because of that study, the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies 4-MEI as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B). The doses in the mouse study were far higher than what people get from food and drink. Regulators such as the FDA and the European Food Safety Authority have concluded that 4-MEI at typical exposures is not a health concern. Manufacturers have nonetheless reduced it as a precaution.

reactions.title: Ammonia caramel chemistry
reactions.summary: Ammonia caramels (classes III and IV) are made by heating sugar with ammonia compounds, and the reactions involved resemble the Maillard reaction that browns bread and roasted meat. Heat breaks sugar into small, reactive pieces, ammonia contributes nitrogen atoms, and the fragments join into large colored molecules. Hundreds of different compounds form at once. The process is carefully controlled to reach the desired color and charge while limiting unwanted byproducts such as 4-MEI. Small changes in time, temperature or pH can noticeably change the outcome.

steps.name: Fragmentation
steps.text: As the sugars are heated, they lose water and break apart into small, highly reactive pieces called dicarbonyls, molecules with two carbon–oxygen double bonds. Methylglyoxal is one example. These fragments react quickly with whatever is nearby.

steps.name: Ring formation
steps.text: Ammonia reacts with the dicarbonyl fragments, adding nitrogen atoms and closing them into small rings called imidazoles. One of these is 4-methylimidazole (4-MEI). Other nitrogen-containing rings, such as pyrazines, also form and contribute to the aroma.

steps.name: Polymerization
steps.text: Many of the reactive fragments, with and without nitrogen, link up into very large, complex molecules called melanoidins. Their long conjugated systems absorb light and give the deep brown color. They also carry the surface charge that determines how the caramel behaves in a drink or sauce.

reactions.result: Controlling time, temperature and reactants lets manufacturers minimize 4-MEI while hitting a target color. Since 2012, makers of class IV caramel for colas have changed their processes to cut 4-MEI levels dramatically.

regulatory.status: Color additive exempt from certification.
4-MEI is listed; beverages over 29 µg/day exposure need a warning, which led major colas to reduce 4-MEI levels in 2012.
Set ADIs of 100–300 mg/kg body weight depending on class.

hazards.title: 4-MEI byproduct
hazards.summary: The main health question about caramel color concerns 4-methylimidazole (4-MEI), a byproduct formed in ammonia-process caramels (classes III and IV), which are used in colas, beers and soy sauces. Plain caramel (class I) doesn't contain it. In 2011 California added 4-MEI to its Proposition 65 list of chemicals known to the state to cause cancer, which requires warning labels above a set exposure level. Major cola makers responded in 2012 by changing their caramel recipes to reduce 4-MEI. Today's exposure is far below the levels that caused effects in animal studies.
hazards.chemical: 4-MEI forms when ammonia reacts with sugar fragments such as methylglyoxal during heating. How much forms depends on the temperature, the heating time, the pH and the ratio of sugar to ammonia. By adjusting these conditions, manufacturers can make caramel with much less 4-MEI while keeping the same color. 4-MEI dissolves easily in water, so it ends up in the drinks and sauces the caramel colors. It also forms in small amounts when other foods, such as coffee, are roasted.
hazards.biological: In mice given very high doses of 4-MEI over their lifetime, lung tumors increased, but similar effects weren't seen in rats. IARC therefore classifies it as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), based on limited evidence in animals and none in people. The U.S. FDA and the European Food Safety Authority have concluded that 4-MEI at the levels found in foods is not a safety concern. California's Proposition 65 safe-harbor level for 4-MEI is 29 micrograms per day. After reformulation, a can of cola typically contains well under that amount.

profile.dosage: How much caramel color a person eats depends mostly on how much cola, dark beer, soy sauce and gravy they consume. International experts have set high acceptable daily intakes for caramel colors, in the range of 100 to 300 milligrams per kilogram of body weight depending on the class and the agency, reflecting their low toxicity. Typical intakes are well below these limits. The main concern, 4-MEI, has been greatly reduced in U.S. colas since 2012, when manufacturers changed their processes in response to California's Proposition 65. Plain caramel (class I) is essentially burnt sugar and contains no 4-MEI.

myths.claim: Caramel color is just burnt sugar.
myths.consensus: Class I is, but classes III and IV are made with ammonia compounds that create by-products like 4-MEI.

synthesis.title: Industrial cooking
synthesis.summary: Caramel color is made by cooking sugar under carefully controlled conditions, much like making caramel at home but on a vast scale and with precise chemistry. The starting material is usually glucose syrup from corn or wheat, or sucrose. Depending on the class of caramel, manufacturers add acids, alkalis, ammonium compounds or sulfites to steer the reactions. The batch is heated until it reaches the desired color and then cooled. The result is a dark brown liquid or powder used to color thousands of products.
synthesis.mechanism: Food-grade sugar syrup is heated, often under pressure, to temperatures above 120 °C in large stainless-steel reactors. As it heats, the sugar molecules lose water and break into reactive fragments that then join together into large brown polymers. Adding acids or bases speeds these reactions up. Adding ammonium compounds introduces nitrogen and gives the particles a positive charge (class III), adding sulfites gives a negative charge (class II), and using both produces negatively charged class IV. Throughout the process, technicians monitor the color intensity, and when the target is reached, the batch is cooled quickly to stop the reactions and then filtered.
synthesis.significance: Plain caramel (class I) is essentially burnt sugar; the other classes trade simplicity for stability in specific products.

citations.title: Mechanisms of Rebaudioside A Degradation and Ingredient-Sweetener Interactions in Beverages during Storage.
citations.abstract: The instability of rebaudioside A (Reb A) in food product applications during storage challenges their utilization. The pathways of Reb A degradation in aged acidic beverages were investigated. Three Reb A degradation compounds of known sensory importance were monitored, consisting of (1) a rearrangement, (2) a hydration, and (3) an epoxidation/rearrangement product. Using deuterium-labeled water (D2O) experiments, compounds 1-2 were reported to be generated by acid-catalyzed mechanisms involving the formation of a carbocation on carbon position 16, followed by either deprotonation via E1 elimination on C15 to form the more thermodynamically stable trisubstituted alkene (compound 1), or by the Markovnikov addition of water via SN1 substitution to form a tertiary alcohol (compound 2). Compound 3 was generated by epoxidation of the exomethylene at the C16-17 positions, followed by the opening and rearrangement of the ring to form a new alkene bond between C15-C16 and a primary alcohol on C17. Further analysis of the effect of beverage ingredients indicated the addition of caramel color significantly increased (p < 0.0001) the concentrations of compounds 1-2 compared to the aged control by 89 and 83%, respectively, whereas a specific coffee flavor and caramel color were reported to significantly reduce (p < 0.0001) the formation of compound 3 compared to the aged control during storage by 90 and 79%, respectively.

citations.title: Component of Caramel Food Coloring, THI, Causes Lymphopenia Indirectly via a Key Metabolic Intermediate.
citations.abstract: Caramel color is widely used in the food industry, and its many variations are generally considered to be safe. It has been known for a long time that THI (2-acetyl-4-(tetrahydroxybutyl)imidazole), a component of caramel color III, causes lymphopenia in animals through sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) lyase (S1PL) inhibition. However, this mechanism of action has not been fully validated because THI does not inhibit S1PL in vitro. To reconcile this situation, we examined molecular details of THI mechanism of action using "smaller" THI derivatives. We identified a bioactive derivative, A6770, which has the same lymphopenic effect as THI via S1PL inhibition. In the case of A6770 we observe this effect both in vitro and in vivo, and demonstrate that A6770 is phosphorylated and inhibits S1PL in the same way as 4-deoxypyridoxine. In addition, A6770 was detected in rat plasma following oral administration of THI, suggesting that A6770 is a key metabolic intermediate of THI.

citations.title: Food caramels: a review.
citations.abstract: Caramel, defined as coloring agent and as an antioxidant, is being used in several kinds of food products. It has been classified into 4 classes to satisfy the requirement of several food and beverage systems. The variation in its consistency owing to its basic content of milk solids, sugars, and fat has been studied. Several methods have been found to estimate the amount of color provided by caramel in food products. Various formulations have been cited for the production of caramel by eradicating the frequent areas of problems during its processing. Caramel has been used as a synthetic colorant replacer in the baking and beverage industries. Researchers have aimed to ascertain the contribution to the antioxidant activity of some caramel-containing soft drinks. The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) has established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) of Class I caramel color as "not specified"; that of Class II as 0-160 mg/kg body weight; that of Class III as 0-200 mg/kg body weight; and that of Class IV as 0-200 mg/kg body weight. This paper is an overview of the classification, physicochemical nature, formulations, coloring properties, antioxidant properties, and toxicity of caramel in different food systems.

citations.title: Caramel color safety - An update.
citations.abstract: Caramel color has been used in foods and beverages for over 150 years and is globally regulated as a color additive. The four distinct classes of caramel color (Plain Caramel, Sulfite Caramel, Ammonia Caramel, and Sulfite Ammonia Caramel) are well characterized and each have specifications that take into account processing variables including reactants that can give rise to low molecular weight constituents (e.g., 4-MeI and THI) that may have toxicological significance for evaluating safety.
