Extensive safety testing has been conducted with the different classes of caramel color and its constituents, including toxicokinetics, genotoxicity, subchronic toxicity, carcinogenicity, and reproductive/developmental toxicity studies. In addition, data is available on uses and use levels that have been used to estimate intakes of caramel colors and their constituents. No Observable Adverse Effect Levels (NOAEL) have been identified for all classes and Acceptable Daily Intakes have been established to ensure safety of use. Available studies support a conclusion that caramel colors are not genotoxic or carcinogenic, and exposure estimates indicate that intake of caramel colors and constituents do not pose undue safety risks. This update summarizes available relevant safety studies and authoritative reviews on caramel colors and its toxicologically important constituents, 4-MeI and THI.

citations.title: Formation of 4(5)-Methylimidazole in Aqueous d-Glucose-Amino Acids Model System.
citations.abstract: The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IRAC) has classified 4(5)-methylimidazole (4-MeI) as a group 2B possible human carcinogen. Thus, how 4-MeI forms in a D-glucose (Glu) amino acids (AA) model system is important, as it is how browning is affected. An aqueous solution of Glu was mixed individually in equimolar amounts at 3 concentrations (0.05, 0.1, and 0.15 M) with aqueous solutions of L-Alanine (Ala), L-Arginine (Arg), Glycine (Gly), L-Lysine (Lys), and L-Serine (Ser). The Glu-AA mixtures were reacted at 60, 120, and 160 °C for 1 h. The 4-MeI levels were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry after derivatization with isobutylchloroformate. No 4-MeI was formed at 60 °C for any treatment combination; however, at 120 °C and 0.05 M, Glu-Arg and Glu-Lys produced 0.13 and 0.14 mg/kg of 4-MeI. At 160 °C and 0.05 M all treatment combinations formed 4-MeI. At 160 °C and 0.15 M, the observed levels of Glu-Ala, Glu-Arg, Glu-Gly, Glu-Lys, and Glu-Ser were 0.21, 1.00, 0.15, 0.22, and 0.16 mg/kg. The AA type, reactant concentrations, and temperature significantly affected (P < 0.001) formation of 4-MeI as well as browning. Glu-Lys treatment in all combinations produced the most browning, but Glu-Arg produced the most 4-MeI. This method showed that foods processed using low temperatures may have reduced levels of 4-MeI.

name: Xanthan Gum
scoreRationale: Very well tolerated at the tiny amounts used; large doses act as a laxative, and it should not be given to premature infants.
summary: Xanthan gum is a fermentation-made fiber that thickens sauces, dressings, gluten-free baking and lotions using less than 1%.

identity.composition: High-molecular-weight polysaccharide: a cellulose backbone with trisaccharide side chains of mannose and glucuronic acid.

physical.solubility: Dissolves in hot or cold water to form viscous solutions
physical.phStability: Stable from pH 2 to 12 and through heating and freezing

overview: Xanthan gum is a polysaccharide: a long, cellulose-like backbone of glucose units with a three-sugar side chain (mannose, glucuronic acid, mannose) on every second glucose. Many side chains carry acetyl and pyruvate groups, and the glucuronic acid carries a negative charge.

In water, the side chains wrap around the backbone and stiffen it into a rod-like helix. Rigid rods tangle and trap water, so less than 1% xanthan can turn a thin liquid into a thick, pourable sauce, and it works whether the liquid is hot, cold, salty or acidic.
profile.function: Creates viscosity and suspends particles, keeping dressings from separating and replacing gluten's structure in gluten-free baking.

mechanisms.title: Shear thinning
mechanisms.chemical: Xanthan gum molecules are extremely long chains of sugars, and in water their side chains fold back along the main chain, turning each molecule into a stiff, rod-like helix. At rest, these long rods point in every direction and tangle with each other, trapping water between them, so the liquid is thick. When the liquid is stirred, squeezed or poured, the flow pulls the rods into line, all pointing the same way, like logs floating down a river. Lined-up rods slide past each other easily, so the liquid suddenly becomes much thinner. When the flow stops, the rods drift back into a tangle and the thickness returns, a behavior called shear thinning.
mechanisms.biological: Shear thinning is why a dressing thickened with xanthan pours easily from a shaken bottle but then clings to lettuce instead of pooling at the bottom of the bowl. Toothpaste works the same way: it flows when you squeeze the tube but sits still on the brush. In the mouth, chewing and swallowing thin the sauce out, so it feels smooth and light rather than gummy or slimy. Because xanthan is unaffected by heat, cold, salt and acid, it behaves the same in very different foods. That reliability also makes it valuable in gluten-free baking, where it helps hold batter together.

mechanisms.title: Helping people swallow safely
mechanisms.chemical: Thin liquids like water flow very fast and can split into separate streams in the mouth and throat. A small amount of xanthan gum makes a liquid flow more slowly and hold together as one cohesive mass, called a bolus. Because xanthan is shear-thinning, the thickened drink still feels smooth as it is swallowed. It also keeps a steady thickness when mixed with saliva, unlike starch-based thickeners, which enzymes in saliva break down. That stability keeps every mouthful predictable.
mechanisms.biological: Some people, such as those recovering from a stroke or living with Parkinson's disease or dementia, have dysphagia, meaning difficulty swallowing safely. For them, thin liquids can move faster than the muscles and reflexes that protect the airway can react, so liquid slips into the windpipe and lungs, a problem called aspiration. Aspiration can cause coughing, choking and a serious lung infection called aspiration pneumonia. Speech and language therapists prescribe drinks thickened to specific levels so that liquid moves slowly enough to swallow safely. Xanthan-based thickeners are widely used in hospitals and care homes for this purpose.

mechanisms.title: A fermentable fiber
mechanisms.chemical: Xanthan's backbone is made of glucose units joined by beta (β) glycosidic bonds, the same kind of bond found in cellulose. Human digestive enzymes can only break alpha (α) glycosidic bonds, the kind found in starch, so xanthan passes through the stomach and small intestine undigested. In the colon, some bacteria do have enzymes that can break it apart. They ferment parts of the gum, breaking it into smaller molecules for energy. This produces short-chain fatty acids, such as acetate and butyrate, along with gases.
mechanisms.biological: Like other dietary fiber, xanthan adds bulk to stool and holds water, which keeps stools softer. The short-chain fatty acids made by fermentation are a fuel for the cells lining the colon and may help keep the gut healthy. The gases produced, such as carbon dioxide and hydrogen, can cause bloating if large amounts are eaten. In amounts above about 15 grams a day, far more than any normal diet contains, xanthan acts as a laxative. At normal food levels, measured in fractions of a gram, these effects are negligible.

reactions.title: Gelling with locust bean gum
reactions.summary: On their own, neither xanthan gum nor locust bean gum forms a gel; each one simply thickens liquids. But when the two are mixed, heated and then cooled, they form an elastic, bouncy gel. This is an example of synergy, where two ingredients together do something neither can do alone. It happens because the chains of the two gums lock onto each other at certain points. Food scientists use this effect to make desserts, jellies and pet foods with a particular texture.

steps.name: Helix
steps.text: In solution, xanthan molecules form stiff helices because their side chains wrap around the main chain. Heating loosens these helices, and as the mixture cools they form again. The surface of each helix has regions where other molecules can attach.

steps.name: Binding
steps.text: Locust bean gum is a galactomannan, a chain of mannose sugars with some galactose branches. Parts of its chain have no branches and are smooth. As the mixture cools, these smooth stretches lie alongside the xanthan helices and stick to them through many weak attractions, mainly hydrogen bonds.

steps.name: Network
steps.text: Each locust bean gum chain can bind several different xanthan helices, and each helix can bind several locust bean gum chains. These connecting points, called junction zones, link everything into a three-dimensional network that traps water. The result is an elastic gel.

reactions.result: This synergy is used in some desserts, pet foods and gluten-free products to create a firm but springy texture. Because the bonds holding the network together are weak, the gel melts when heated and sets again when cooled. It shows how combining ingredients can create textures that neither could achieve alone.

reactions.title: Precipitation with alcohol (purification)
reactions.summary: When bacteria have finished making xanthan in a fermentation tank, the gum is dissolved in a huge volume of watery broth along with the bacteria and leftover nutrients. To collect it, manufacturers add alcohol, which makes the gum come out of solution as solid fibers. This works because of how differently xanthan interacts with water and with alcohol. It's the same trick used in the classroom experiment of pulling DNA out of a strawberry with cold alcohol. The alcohol is recovered afterward and reused.

steps.name: Pasteurize
steps.text: The broth is heated to kill the Xanthomonas bacteria and switch off their enzymes. Heating also helps the gum dissolve completely. The broth may be filtered to remove bits of bacterial cells.

steps.name: Lower polarity
steps.text: Isopropyl alcohol is mixed into the broth. Alcohol is less polar than water, meaning its molecules carry a weaker uneven charge. Xanthan's many charged and polar groups were comfortably surrounded by water molecules, but in the alcohol–water mixture they can't stay hydrated as well.

steps.name: Aggregate
steps.text: Without enough water around them, the xanthan chains start sticking to each other instead, clumping into fibrous strands that separate from the liquid. These fibers are collected by filtering or pressing, then dried and ground into a fine powder.

reactions.result: The alcohol is recovered by distillation and reused, and the finished xanthan contains only trace residues. The same principle, that adding alcohol makes large polar molecules drop out of water, is used to purify DNA, pectin and many other biological polymers.

regulatory.status: Approved food additive.
ADI "not specified"; FDA and EFSA advise against use in premature infants after thickener-associated necrotizing enterocolitis cases.

hazards.title: Not for premature infants
hazards.summary: Xanthan gum is considered safe for older children and adults, but it is avoided in premature babies. In 2011, the U.S. FDA warned parents and caregivers not to feed a xanthan-based thickening product to premature infants after reports of a serious intestinal illness. The concern is specific to babies born early, whose digestive systems are immature. It doesn't apply to xanthan in ordinary foods eaten by healthy children and adults. Thickeners for infants should only be used under medical guidance.
hazards.chemical: Xanthan isn't digested by human enzymes and reaches the large intestine intact, where bacteria ferment it. Fermentation produces gases, such as hydrogen and carbon dioxide, along with short-chain fatty acids. In adults the gut handles these products easily. In premature infants, the gut wall is thin and immature, and the bacteria living there differ from those in older children. Large amounts of fermentation products may stress this fragile environment.
hazards.biological: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a serious condition in which parts of the intestine become inflamed and the tissue starts to die. It mainly affects premature babies and can lead to surgery or death. The FDA's 2011 warning followed reports of NEC in premature infants who had been fed a xanthan-based thickener. Researchers suspect that fermentation of the gum in an immature gut, together with other factors, may have contributed, although the exact cause was never proven. As a precaution, xanthan-based thickeners are not given to premature infants.

hazards.title: Digestive effects at high doses
hazards.summary: In normal food, xanthan gum is used in tiny amounts, usually less than half a percent of a product, so it has no noticeable effect on digestion. Problems only appear with very large amounts, such as from supplements or products designed as laxatives. Then it can cause bloating, gas and loose stools. Those effects are similar to eating a lot of any fiber at once. Increasing fiber gradually and drinking enough water reduces them.
hazards.chemical: Because human enzymes can't break xanthan's β-glycosidic bonds, all of the gum reaches the colon undigested. There it holds onto water, making the colon's contents wetter and bulkier. Colon bacteria ferment part of the gum, producing gases such as hydrogen, carbon dioxide and sometimes methane. The more xanthan is eaten, the more water is held and the more gas is produced. That is why the effects depend on dose.
hazards.biological: Extra water and bulk in the colon soften stools and speed them through the intestine, which can cause loose stools or diarrhea when large amounts are eaten. The gases stretch the intestinal wall, causing bloating, discomfort and flatulence. In a 1980s study, adults who ate about 10 to 13 grams of xanthan a day for three weeks had bulkier, more frequent stools but no other harmful effects. Typical intakes from food are well under a gram a day. At those levels xanthan acts as a minor source of dietary fiber.

profile.dosage: Foods use about 0.05 to 0.5 percent xanthan gum, so a serving of salad dressing or sauce contains a fraction of a gram. International food-safety experts (JECFA) have given it an acceptable daily intake of “not specified,” their category for substances of very low concern, and the U.S. FDA permits it as a food additive. Laxative effects appear only above about 15 grams a day, far more than anyone eats in normal food. Gluten-free bakers commonly use about half a teaspoon to a teaspoon per cup of flour. The one clear exception is premature infants, who should not be given xanthan-based thickeners.

myths.claim: Xanthan gum is made from bacteria, so it's unsafe.
myths.consensus: Bacteria make it during fermentation, but the purified gum contains no living organisms.

synthesis.title: Bacterial fermentation
synthesis.summary: Xanthan gum is made by a bacterium called Xanthomonas campestris, which naturally produces it as a slimy coating around its cells. In nature, this slime helps the bacterium cling to plant leaves and protects it from drying out. Scientists at the U.S. Department of Agriculture discovered its usefulness in the 1950s while searching for new uses for corn sugar. Today it is made in large fermentation tanks, in a process much like brewing. It was approved for use in U.S. food in 1968.
synthesis.mechanism: The bacteria are grown in sterile tanks containing water, a sugar such as glucose or sucrose, a nitrogen source and minerals, while air is bubbled through to supply oxygen. As they feed on the sugar, the bacteria use enzymes to link sugar units into long xanthan chains and release them into the surrounding liquid. Over two to four days, the broth thickens as the gum builds up. After fermentation, the broth is pasteurized to kill the bacteria, and isopropyl alcohol is added to make the gum separate out. The solid gum is then dried and milled into a fine powder.
synthesis.significance: The same bacterium causes black rot on cabbage; its slime helps it cling to leaves.

citations.title: What makes Xanthomonas albilineans unique amongst xanthomonads?
citations.abstract: Xanthomonas albilineans causes leaf scald, a lethal disease of sugarcane. Compared to other species of Xanthomonas, X. albilineans exhibits distinctive pathogenic mechanisms, ecology and taxonomy. Its genome, which has experienced significant erosion, has unique genomic features. It lacks two loci required for pathogenicity in other plant pathogenic species of Xanthomonas: the xanthan gum biosynthesis and the Hrp-T3SS (hypersensitive response and pathogenicity-type three secretion system) gene clusters. Instead, X. albilineans harbors in its genome an SPI-1 (Salmonella pathogenicity island-1) T3SS gene cluster usually found in animal pathogens. X. albilineans produces a potent DNA gyrase inhibitor called albicidin, which blocks chloroplast differentiation, resulting in the characteristic white foliar stripe symptoms. The antibacterial activity of albicidin also confers on X. albilineans a competitive advantage against rival bacteria during sugarcane colonization. Recent chemical studies have uncovered the unique structure of albicidin and allowed us to partially elucidate its fascinating biosynthesis apparatus, which involves an enigmatic hybrid PKS/NRPS (polyketide synthase/non-ribosomal peptide synthetase) machinery.

citations.title: Natural Regenerative Hydrogels for Wound Healing.
citations.authors: Chelu, Calderon Moreno, Musuc et al.
citations.abstract: Regenerative hydrogels from natural polymers have come forth as auspicious materials for use in regenerative medicine, with interest attributed to their intrinsic biodegradability, biocompatibility, and ability to reassemble the extracellular matrix. This review covers the latest advances in regenerative hydrogels used for wound healing, focusing on their chemical composition, cross-linking mechanisms, and functional properties. Key carbohydrate polymers, including alginate, chitosan, hyaluronic acid, and polysaccharide gums, including agarose, carrageenan, and xanthan gum, are discussed in terms of their sources, chemical structures and specific properties suitable for regenerative applications. The review further explores the categorization of hydrogels based on ionic charge, response to physiological stimuli (i.e., pH, temperature) and particularized roles in wound tissue self-healing. Various methods of cross-linking used to enhance the mechanical and biological performance of these hydrogels are also examined. By highlighting recent innovations and ongoing challenges, this article intends to give a detailed understanding of natural hydrogels and their potential to revolutionize regenerative medicine and improve patient healing outcomes.

citations.title: Recent trends on gellan gum blends with natural and synthetic polymers: A review.
citations.abstract: Gellan gum (GG), a linear negatively charged exopolysaccharide,is biodegradable and non-toxic in nature. It produces hard and translucent gel in the presence of metallic ions which is stable at low pH. However, GG has poor mechanical strength, poor stability in physiological conditions, high gelling temperature and small temperature window.Therefore,it is blended with different polymers such as agar, chitosan, cellulose, sodium alginate, starch, pectin, polyanaline, pullulan, polyvinyl chloride, and xanthan gum. In this article, a comprehensive overview of combination of GG with natural and synthetic polymers/compounds and their applications in biomedical field involving drug delivery system, insulin delivery, wound healing and gene therapy, is presented. It also describes the utilization of GG based materials in food and petroleum industry. All the technical scientific issues have been addressed; highlighting the recent advancement.

citations.title: Polysaccharide-based nanofibers for pharmaceutical and biomedical applications: A review.
citations.authors: Priya, Batra, R N et al.
citations.abstract: Nanofibers are fibrous nanocarriers that can be synthesized from natural polymers, synthetic polymers, semiconducting materials, composite materials, and carbon-based materials. Recently, natural polysaccharides-based nanofibers are gaining attention in the field of pharmaceuticals and biomedical as these are biocompatible, biodegradable, non-toxic, and economic. Nanofibers can deliver a significant amount of drug to the targeted site and provide effective interaction of therapeutic agent at the site of action due to a larger surface area. Other important advantages of nanofibers are low density, high porosity, small pore size, high mechanical strength, and low cost. In this review, natural polysaccharides such as alginate, pullulan, hyaluronic acid, dextran, cellulose, chondroitin sulfate, chitosan, xanthan gum, and gellan gum are discussed for their characteristics, pharmaceutical utility, and biomedical applications. The authors have given particular emphasis to the several fabrication processes that utilize these polysaccharides to form nanofibers, and their recent updates in pharmaceutical applications such as drug delivery, tissue engineering, skin disorders, wound-healing dressings, cancer therapy, bioactive molecules delivery, anti-infectives, and solubility enhancement. Despite these many advantages, nanofibers have been explored less for their scale-up and applications in advanced therapeutic delivery.

citations.title: Xanthan gum in drug release.
citations.abstract: Controlled release is of vital relevance for many drugs; thus, there is a keen interest in materials that can improve the release profiles of formulations administered via buccal, transdermal, ophthalmic, vaginal, and nasal. The desirable effects of those materials include the improvement of stability, adhesiveness, solubility, and retention time. Hence, different synthetic and natural polymers are utilized to achieve these objectives. In this respect, xanthan gum is an anionic polysaccharide that can be obtained from Xanthomonas bacteria. It is a natural polymer broadly employed in numerous food products, lotions, shampoos, and dermatological articles. Furthermore, due to its physicochemical features, xanthan gum is growingly utilized for the development and improvement of drug delivery systems. In this regard, encouraging findings have been revealed by recent formulations for pharmaceutical applications, including antiviral carriers, antibacterial transporters, transdermal patches, vaginal formulations, and anticancer medications. In this article, we perform a concise description of the chemical properties of xanthan gum and its role as a modifier of drug release. Furthermore, we present an outlook of the state of the art of research focused on the utilization of xanthan gum in varied pharmaceutical formulations, which include tablets, films, hydrogels, and nanoformulations. Finally, we discuss some perspectives about the use of xanthan gum in these formulations.

name: Soy Lecithin
scoreRationale: A natural phospholipid mixture with a long safety record; trace soy protein matters only for highly sensitive allergy sufferers.
summary: Lecithin is a natural emulsifier from soybean oil that helps oil and water mix in chocolate, dressings and creams.

identity.composition: Mixture of phospholipids (phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylinositol), glycolipids and triglycerides.

physical.solubility: Disperses in water; soluble in oils

overview: Lecithin is a mixture of phospholipids, chiefly phosphatidylcholine. Each phospholipid has a glycerol backbone carrying two fatty-acid tails, which repel water, and a phosphate group linked to a small charged molecule such as choline, which loves water.
That two-faced (amphiphilic) structure is the same design as the phospholipids in every cell membrane. It lets lecithin sit at the boundary between oil and water and hold the two together.
profile.function: Stabilizes emulsions, reduces chocolate viscosity, prevents sticking in cooking sprays and softens skin in creams.

mechanisms.title: Emulsifying oil and water
mechanisms.chemical: Oil and water don't mix because water molecules are polar and cling strongly to each other, squeezing nonpolar oil molecules out of the way. Lecithin molecules have two personalities: two long fatty tails that are drawn to oil and a charged phosphate head that is drawn to water. A molecule like this is called amphiphilic, and when it helps oil and water mix it is called an emulsifier. At the boundary between oil and water, lecithin molecules line up with their tails poking into the oil and their heads sitting in the water. This lowers the tension between the two liquids, making it easier to break the oil into tiny droplets and keep them coated.
mechanisms.biological: Once each oil droplet is coated with lecithin, the charged heads on the outside make the droplets push each other away, so they don't merge back together. This keeps salad dressings, margarine and sauces smooth instead of separating into layers. In chocolate, lecithin coats the sugar particles so they slide past each other in the cocoa butter, which makes melted chocolate flow better and reduces the amount of expensive cocoa butter needed. When you eat these foods, the evenly spread fat feels smooth and creamy on the tongue. Without emulsifiers, many foods would feel greasy or grainy.

mechanisms.title: A source of choline
mechanisms.chemical: Phosphatidylcholine, the main component of lecithin, has a small molecule called choline attached to its phosphate group. In the digestive system, enzymes called phospholipases take the molecule apart, eventually releasing free choline. Choline is a small, positively charged molecule containing nitrogen. The liver can make a little choline on its own, but not enough to meet all the body's needs. So choline from food is considered an essential nutrient.
mechanisms.biological: The body uses choline to build phosphatidylcholine for its own cell membranes, the outer boundary of every cell. It also uses choline to make acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter that carries signals from nerves to muscles and is important for memory. In the liver, choline helps package fats for export; without enough of it, fat can build up in the liver. Eggs, meat, fish and soybeans are major dietary sources. The choline from lecithin used as a food additive is small but adds to the total.

mechanisms.title: Helping absorb dietary fat
mechanisms.chemical: In the small intestine, an enzyme from the pancreas called phospholipase A2 removes one of the two fatty-acid tails from phosphatidylcholine. What is left, lysophosphatidylcholine, has one tail and a large water-loving head, so it is shaped like a cone rather than a cylinder. Cone-shaped molecules are even better at curving around tiny droplets and gathering into small spheres. Together with bile salts from the liver, they form particles called micelles, only a few billionths of a meter across. Fats and fat-soluble vitamins dissolve in the oily center of these micelles.
mechanisms.biological: Fat can't be absorbed as big drops; it has to be broken into very small particles that can reach the surface of the intestinal cells. Micelles act like tiny delivery vehicles, ferrying fatty acids, cholesterol and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) across the watery layer that coats the gut wall. At the cell surface, their contents are released and absorbed. Without enough bile and phospholipids, fat passes through undigested, causing greasy stools and poor absorption of those vitamins. Lecithin in food supports this process, though the body's own bile supplies most of the phospholipids needed.

reactions.title: Forming an emulsion
reactions.summary: An emulsion is a mixture of two liquids that normally don't mix, with tiny droplets of one spread throughout the other. Mayonnaise, milk and creamy dressings are all emulsions. Emulsions naturally tend to separate, because oil droplets bump into each other, merge and rise to the top. An emulsifier such as lecithin slows this down by coating each droplet. Making an emulsion usually takes both an emulsifier and energy, such as whisking or blending, to break the oil into small droplets.

steps.name: Orientation
steps.text: When lecithin is mixed into oil and water, its molecules move to the boundary between the two liquids, where they are most comfortable. Their fatty tails dissolve into the oil and their charged phosphate heads stay in the water. This arrangement lowers the energy cost of having a boundary at all.

steps.name: Coating
steps.text: Whisking or blending breaks the oil into tiny droplets, creating a huge amount of new surface. Lecithin molecules quickly cover each droplet in a single layer, forming a protective coat. The smaller the droplets, the more emulsifier is needed to cover them all.

steps.name: Stabilizing
steps.text: The charged heads facing outward give every droplet a similar electric charge, so droplets repel each other when they come close. The coating also acts as a physical barrier. Together, these effects stop droplets from merging into bigger ones, so the emulsion stays smooth.

reactions.result: Mayonnaise works the same way, using lecithin from egg yolk to hold tiny drops of oil suspended in vinegar or lemon juice. Without the yolk, the oil and vinegar would separate within minutes. Many sauces and dressings depend on this principle.

reactions.title: Enzymatic modification
reactions.summary: Food technologists can change lecithin's properties by using enzymes to reshape its molecules. The most common change is removing one of the two fatty-acid tails from each phospholipid. This is the same reaction that happens naturally during digestion. The modified lecithin, called lysolecithin, behaves differently as an emulsifier. It is used in baked goods, instant drinks and animal feed.

steps.name: Hydrolysis
steps.text: Lecithin is mixed with water and a phospholipase enzyme, often made by microbes. The enzyme adds water across one of the ester bonds that holds a fatty acid to the glycerol backbone. This cuts that fatty acid free.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: The result, lysolecithin, has one fatty tail instead of two, plus a loose fatty acid. With only one tail, the molecule is cone-shaped, with a big head and a narrow tail.

steps.name: Effect
steps.text: Cone-shaped emulsifiers curve best around oil droplets floating in water, so lysolecithin favors oil-in-water emulsions. It also disperses more easily in water and holds up better under heat and salt. That makes it more effective in baked goods, drinks and instant powders.

reactions.result: Changing a molecule's shape changes which kind of emulsion it stabilizes. Two-tailed lecithin leans toward water-in-oil emulsions such as margarine, while one-tailed lysolecithin favors oil-in-water emulsions such as milky drinks. Chemists choose or create emulsifiers based on these shapes.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
ADI "not specified"; no safety concern at reported uses.
Declared as soy under FALCPA because trace soy protein may remain.

hazards.title: Trace soy protein
hazards.summary: Soy is one of the major food allergens, and some people worry that soy lecithin might trigger allergic reactions. Lecithin itself is a fat-like molecule, not a protein, and allergies are triggered by proteins. Refining removes most of the soy protein from lecithin, but tiny traces can remain. Most people with soy allergy eat foods containing soy lecithin without problems, though a few very sensitive people may react. U.S. labeling rules still require soy lecithin to be declared as soy.
hazards.chemical: Allergic reactions are triggered by specific proteins that the immune system mistakes for threats, and soybeans contain several such proteins. When lecithin is made from soybean oil, it is separated out of the oil as a gum and dried, while most of the soy protein stays behind in the soybean meal. Even so, small amounts of protein can be carried along, measured in parts per million. The amount varies from batch to batch. Sunflower lecithin is an alternative for people who want to avoid soy entirely.
hazards.biological: In people with soy allergy, the immune system makes IgE antibodies against soy proteins. When those proteins are eaten, they latch onto the antibodies sitting on mast cells, which then release histamine and other chemicals. That can cause symptoms ranging from hives and itching to, rarely, severe reactions. Because the amount of protein in lecithin is so small, it usually isn't enough to trigger a reaction. People with severe soy allergy should ask their doctor whether they need to avoid soy lecithin.

profile.dosage: Chocolate typically contains about 0.3 to 0.5 percent lecithin, and other foods use similarly small amounts, often well under a gram per serving. Lecithin is also sold as a supplement, and several grams a day are well tolerated. International experts (JECFA) have given it an acceptable daily intake of “not specified,” reflecting its very low toxicity, and the U.S. FDA considers it generally recognized as safe. The body handles lecithin like the phospholipids already present in eggs, meat and many plant foods. The main caution is for people with severe soy allergy, who may want to check with a doctor.

myths.claim: Soy lecithin disrupts hormones.
myths.consensus: Lecithin contains negligible isoflavones; the phytoestrogen debate concerns whole soy foods and supplements.

synthesis.title: Degumming soybean oil
synthesis.summary: Most lecithin is a byproduct of making clear cooking oil from soybeans. Crude soybean oil, pressed or extracted from the beans, contains about 2 to 3 percent phospholipids, which would make the oil cloudy and cause it to foam and darken when heated. Removing them, a step called degumming, produces both cleaner oil and lecithin. Lecithin is also made from sunflower seeds, rapeseed and eggs. Soy is the most common source simply because so much soybean oil is produced.
synthesis.mechanism: Crude soybean oil is warmed and mixed with a small amount of water, about 1 to 3 percent. The phospholipids in the oil have water-loving heads, so they soak up the water and swell into a sticky, gel-like mass called gum. Because this gum is denser than the oil and no longer dissolved in it, it can be separated. Large centrifuges spin the mixture very fast, flinging the heavier gum outward, away from the lighter oil. The gum is then dried under vacuum to remove the water, leaving lecithin, a brown, sticky liquid or powder.
synthesis.significance: Removing the gums keeps the oil from turning cloudy, and the gums become a useful product instead of waste.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis
synthesis.summary: Every plant and animal cell makes phosphatidylcholine, because it is a main building block of cell membranes. In your body, cells are constantly making new phospholipids to grow, divide and repair their membranes. The liver makes especially large amounts to package fats for transport in the blood. Soybeans, sunflower seeds and eggs are rich in phospholipids because seeds and yolks are built to support new life. The main route for making phosphatidylcholine is called the Kennedy pathway, after the biochemist Eugene Kennedy, who worked it out in the 1950s.
synthesis.mechanism: The Kennedy pathway builds phosphatidylcholine in three main steps. First, the enzyme choline kinase attaches a phosphate group to choline, using energy from ATP, to make phosphocholine. Next, phosphocholine is activated by combining with CTP, another energy-carrying molecule, forming CDP-choline. Finally, an enzyme transfers the phosphocholine part of CDP-choline onto diacylglycerol, a glycerol molecule already carrying two fatty acids. The finished phosphatidylcholine is inserted into membranes, where it forms part of the double layer that wraps around every cell.
synthesis.significance: Lecithin was first isolated from egg yolk in the 1840s; its name comes from the Greek lekithos, meaning yolk.

citations.title: Lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase.
citations.abstract: Cholesterol transport in circulation and its removal from tissues depends on the activity of lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). LCAT is a soluble enzyme that converts cholesterol and phosphatidylcholines (lecithins) to cholesteryl esters and lyso-phosphatidylcholines on the surface of high-density lipoproteins. This review presents key background information and recent research advances on the structure of human LCAT, its reactions and substrates, and the expression of the LCAT gene. While the three-dimensional structure of LCAT is not yet known, a partial model now exists that facilitates the study of structure-function relationships of the native enzyme, and of natural and engineered mutants. The LCAT reaction on lipoproteins consists of several steps, starting with enzyme binding to the lipoprotein/lipid surface, followed by activation of LCAT by apolipoproteins, binding of lipid substrates and the catalytic steps giving rise to the lipid products. Quantitative data are presented on the kinetic and equilibrium constants of some of the LCAT reaction steps. Finally, overexpression of the human LCAT gene in mice and rabbits has been used to examine the physiologic role of LCAT in vivo and its protective effect against diet induced atherosclerosis.

citations.title: Lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase: old friend or foe in atherosclerosis?
citations.abstract: Lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is a key enzyme that catalyzes the esterification of free cholesterol in plasma lipoproteins and plays a critical role in high-density lipoprotein (HDL) metabolism. Deficiency leads to accumulation of nascent preβ-HDL due to impaired maturation of HDL particles, whereas enhanced expression is associated with the formation of large, apoE-rich HDL(1) particles. In addition to its function in HDL metabolism, LCAT was believed to be an important driving force behind macrophage reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) and, therefore, has been a subject of great interest in cardiovascular research since its discovery in 1962. Although half a century has passed, the importance of LCAT for atheroprotection is still under intense debate. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the insights that have been gained in the past 50 years on the biochemistry of LCAT, the role of LCAT in lipoprotein metabolism and the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis in animal models, and its impact on cardiovascular disease in humans.

citations.title: Multi-liposomal containers.
citations.abstract: Small unilamellar liposomes, 40-60 nm in diameter, composed of anionic diphosphatidylglycerol (cardiolipin, CL(2-)) or phosphatidylcerine (PS(1-)) and zwitter-ionic egg yolk lecithin (EL) or dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), electrostatically complex with polystyrene microspheres, ca. 100 nm in diameter, grafted by polycationic chains ("spherical polycationic brushes", SPBs). Polymer/liposome binding studies were carried out using electrophoretic mobility (EPM), dynamic light scattering (DLS), fluorescence, conductometry, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and cryogenic transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) as the main analytical tools. By these means a remarkably detailed picture emerges of molecular events inside a membrane. The following are among the most important conclusions that arose from the experiments: (a) binding of liposomes to SPBs is accompanied by flip-flop of anionic lipids from the inner to the outer leaflet of the liposomal membrane along with lateral lipid segregation into "islands". (b) The SPB-induced structural reorganization of the liposomal membrane, together with the geometry of anionic lipid molecules, determines the maximum molar fraction of anionic lipid (a key parameter designated as ν) that ensures the structural integrity of liposomes upon complexation: ν=0.3 for liposomes with conically-shaped CL(2-) and ν=0.5 for liposomes with anionic cylindrically-shaped PS(1-). (c) The number of intact liposomes per SPB particle varies from 40 for (ν=0.1) to 13 (ν=0.5). (d) By using a mixture of liposomes with variety of encapsulated substances, multi-liposomal complexes can be prepared with a high loading capacity and a controlled ratio of the contents. (e) In order to make the mixed anionic liposomes pH-sensitive, they are additionally modified by 30 mol% of a morpholinocyclohexanol-based lipid that undergoes a conformational flip when changing pH. Being complexed with SPBs, such liposomes rapidly release their contents when the pH is reduced from 7.0 to 5.0. The results allow loaded liposomes to be concentrated within a rather small volume and, thereby, the preparation of multi-liposomal containers of promise in the drug delivery field.

citations.title: Functions of Intracellular Retinoid Binding-Proteins.
citations.abstract: Multiple binding and transport proteins facilitate many aspects of retinoid biology through effects on retinoid transport, cellular uptake, metabolism, and nuclear delivery. These include the serum retinol binding protein sRBP (aka Rbp4), the plasma membrane sRBP receptor Stra6, and the intracellular retinoid binding-proteins such as cellular retinol-binding proteins (CRBP) and cellular retinoic acid binding-proteins (CRABP). sRBP transports the highly lipophilic retinol through an aqueous medium. The major intracellular retinol-binding protein, CRBP1, likely enhances efficient retinoid use by providing a sink to facilitate retinol uptake from sRBP through the plasma membrane or via Stra6, delivering retinol or retinal to select enzymes that generate retinyl esters or retinoic acid, and protecting retinol/retinal from excess catabolism or opportunistic metabolism. Intracellular retinoic acid binding-proteins (CRABP1 and 2, and FABP5) seem to have more diverse functions distinctive to each, such as directing retinoic acid to catabolism, delivering retinoic acid to specific nuclear receptors, and generating non-canonical actions. Gene ablation of intracellular retinoid binding-proteins does not cause embryonic lethality or gross morphological defects. Metabolic and functional defects manifested in knockouts of CRBP1, CRBP2 and CRBP3, however, illustrate their essentiality to health, and in the case of CRBP2, to survival during limited dietary vitamin A. Future studies should continue to address the specific molecular interactions that occur between retinoid binding-proteins and their targets and their precise physiologic contributions to retinoid homeostasis and function.

citations.title: Myeloperoxidase: an oxidative pathway for generating dysfunctional high-density lipoprotein.
citations.abstract: Accumulation of low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-derived cholesterol by artery wall macrophages triggers atherosclerosis, the leading cause of cardiovascular disease. Conversely, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) retards atherosclerosis by promoting cholesterol efflux from macrophages by the membrane-associated ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) pathway. HDL has been proposed to lose its cardioprotective effects in subjects with atherosclerosis, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. One potential pathway involves oxidative damage by myeloperoxidase (MPO), a heme enzyme secreted by human artery wall macrophages. We used mass spectrometry to demonstrate that HDL isolated from patients with established cardiovascular disease contains elevated levels of 3-chlorotyrosine and 3-nitrotyrosine, two characteristic products of MPO. When apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I), the major HDL protein, was oxidized by MPO, its ability to promote cellular cholesterol efflux by ABCA1 was impaired. Moreover, oxidized apoA-I was unable to activate lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT), which rapidly converts free cholesterol to cholesteryl ester, a critical step in HDL maturation. Biochemical studies implicated tyrosine chlorination and methionine oxygenation in the loss of ABCA1 and LCAT activity by oxidized apoA-I. Oxidation of specific residues in apoA-I inhibited two key steps in cholesterol efflux from macrophages, raising the possibility that MPO initiates a pathway for generating dysfunctional HDL in humans.

name: Sodium Bicarbonate
scoreRationale: Extremely safe at normal uses; only large ingestions (as a home antacid) pose risks.
summary: Baking soda leavens baked goods, neutralizes odors, and scrubs gently. It's one of the safest multi-purpose household chemicals.

overview: Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) is made of sodium ions and bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻). Bicarbonate is amphoteric: it can accept a proton to become carbonic acid or give one up to become carbonate, so it neutralizes acids and resists strong bases.
When bicarbonate meets an acid, it releases carbon dioxide gas, the bubbles that make pancakes and cakes rise. The very same bicarbonate ion is the main pH buffer in your blood.
profile.function: Releases CO2 to raise dough, neutralizes acids and odors, softens water, and acts as a mild abrasive in toothpaste and cleaners.

mechanisms.title: Buffering blood pH
mechanisms.chemical: Your blood holds a balance of carbon dioxide (CO₂), carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) and bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻). An enzyme called carbonic anhydrase, found in red blood cells and many tissues, speeds up the reaction of CO₂ with water to form carbonic acid by about a million times. Carbonic acid quickly splits into a hydrogen ion and a bicarbonate ion, and the whole reaction can also run backward. When extra acid enters the blood, bicarbonate grabs the hydrogen ions and becomes carbonic acid, which turns back into CO₂ and water. A system like this, which soaks up acid or base and keeps pH steady, is called a buffer.
mechanisms.biological: Blood pH has to stay between 7.35 and 7.45; even small moves outside that range disrupt enzymes and nerve signals. The lungs control how much carbon dioxide you breathe out: breathing faster removes more CO₂, which lowers the amount of acid. The kidneys control how much bicarbonate is kept or sent out in urine, adjusting more slowly, over hours to days. Together these organs keep the bicarbonate buffer working. In emergencies such as severe acidosis from kidney failure or poisoning, doctors may give sodium bicarbonate directly into a vein.

mechanisms.title: Antacid
mechanisms.chemical: The stomach makes hydrochloric acid (HCl), with a pH as low as 1 to 2, to help digest food and kill microbes. When sodium bicarbonate is swallowed, its bicarbonate ions accept hydrogen ions from the acid in a neutralization reaction. Each bicarbonate becomes carbonic acid, which immediately breaks down into water and carbon dioxide gas. The chloride from the acid and the sodium from the bicarbonate are left dissolved together as sodium chloride, ordinary salt. The reaction is over within seconds.
mechanisms.biological: Heartburn happens when stomach acid splashes back up into the esophagus, the tube from the mouth to the stomach, and irritates its lining. Neutralizing the acid relieves the burning within minutes. The carbon dioxide produced collects in the stomach and usually escapes as a burp. Because bicarbonate works fast but doesn't last long, and because it adds sodium, it is meant for occasional use only. For frequent heartburn, medicines that reduce acid production are more appropriate.

mechanisms.title: Neutralizing odors
mechanisms.chemical: Many unpleasant smells come from acidic molecules that evaporate easily, such as butyric acid in sour milk and spoiled butter and isovaleric acid in sweaty socks. These are carboxylic acids, molecules with a –COOH group. When they meet bicarbonate, the bicarbonate takes the acid's hydrogen ion and the acid becomes a charged carboxylate ion paired with sodium, which is a salt. Salts are made of ions held tightly together by their charges, so they don't evaporate. The smelly acid has been turned from a volatile molecule into one that stays put.
mechanisms.biological: To smell something, its molecules have to travel through the air into your nose and bind to smell receptors there. Once an acidic odor molecule has become a salt, it stays in the fridge, carpet or shoe instead of drifting into the air. With fewer odor molecules reaching your nose, the smell fades. Baking soda works best on acidic smells and does little against basic ones such as ammonia or neutral ones. That is why an open box in the fridge helps with some smells but not all.

reactions.title: Leavening with acid
reactions.summary: Baking soda is a leavening agent, meaning it makes baked goods rise by producing gas bubbles. It does this by reacting with an acid in the batter, which releases carbon dioxide. The gas forms bubbles in the batter, and in the oven the heat expands those bubbles and sets the structure around them, giving a light, airy texture. Without leavening, cakes and pancakes would be dense and flat. Bakers have to balance the amount of baking soda against the amount of acid in a recipe.

steps.name: Proton transfer
steps.text: As the batter is mixed, acids in ingredients such as buttermilk, yogurt, lemon juice, brown sugar or the acid salts in baking powder hand hydrogen ions (H⁺) to bicarbonate ions. This starts as soon as the ingredients are wet and meet. The bicarbonate is acting as a base by accepting those protons.

steps.name: Carbonic acid
steps.text: Each bicarbonate ion that gains a proton becomes carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). Carbonic acid is unstable and can't hold together. It breaks apart almost immediately.

steps.name: Gas
steps.text: Carbonic acid splits into water and carbon dioxide gas. The CO₂ forms tiny bubbles trapped in the batter. In the oven, heat makes the gas expand, and the bubbles grow until the batter sets around them.

reactions.result: Baking powder packages baking soda together with a dry acid, so it only needs water and heat to work. Double-acting baking powder releases some gas when it gets wet and more once it is heated. Recipes that already contain acidic ingredients often use baking soda alone.

reactions.title: Thermal decomposition
reactions.summary: Baking soda can also produce gas without any acid at all, just by being heated. When it gets hot enough, bicarbonate ions react with each other and break down into carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. This is called thermal decomposition. It helps baked goods rise, but it leaves behind a different, more strongly basic substance. Using too much baking soda in a recipe can leave a noticeable aftertaste for this reason.

steps.name: Heating
steps.text: Above about 80 °C, and much faster above 200 °C, bicarbonate ions have enough energy to react with one another. Oven temperatures easily reach these levels. The heat breaks bonds within the bicarbonate ions.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: Two bicarbonate ions trade a proton, forming one carbonate ion, one water molecule and one carbon dioxide molecule. The CO₂ escapes as gas and the water leaves as steam.

steps.name: Residue
steps.text: Sodium carbonate, also called washing soda, is left behind. It is a stronger base than sodium bicarbonate, giving a pH of about 11 in water.

reactions.result: Too much baking soda without enough acid leaves sodium carbonate in the food, which tastes soapy and bitter and can tint baked goods yellow or green. That's why recipes balance baking soda with acidic ingredients. The same decomposition is put to work in some fire extinguishers, where the released CO₂ helps smother flames.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Authorized as E500(ii) at quantum satis.
Safe as used in cosmetics.

hazards.title: Large ingestions
hazards.summary: Sodium bicarbonate is safe in cooking and as an occasional antacid, but swallowing large amounts can be dangerous. Problems have occurred when people take baking soda over and over for indigestion, use it as a home remedy for other conditions, or try to use it to cheat drug tests. The risks include serious disturbances in the body's chemistry and, rarely, a ruptured stomach. Young children are also at risk if they swallow a lot. Antacid labels set daily limits for good reason.
hazards.chemical: A large dose of bicarbonate adds more base to the body than its buffering systems can quickly deal with. Blood pH rises above 7.45, a condition called metabolic alkalosis. At the same time, the sodium in baking soda raises blood sodium levels. The body responds by shifting potassium into its cells, which can lower the potassium in the blood. These changes upset the delicate balance that nerves and muscles rely on.
hazards.biological: Alkalosis and the related mineral imbalances can cause muscle twitching, cramps, nausea, confusion and an irregular heartbeat, and in severe cases seizures. People with heart or kidney problems are at greater risk because they can't easily get rid of extra sodium. In rare cases, taking baking soda after a very large meal has ruptured the stomach, because the carbon dioxide released couldn't escape from an overfilled stomach fast enough. Following antacid label directions avoids these problems. Large accidental swallows need medical help.

profile.dosage: Baking typically uses about a teaspoon of baking soda per recipe, shared among many servings. As an antacid, the usual adult dose is half a teaspoon dissolved in water, and labels limit use to a few doses a day, with lower limits for people over 60. One teaspoon contains about 1,200 milligrams of sodium, roughly half the recommended daily limit, so frequent use adds up quickly. Baking soda should not be taken on a very full stomach, used for more than two weeks without a doctor's advice, or given to young children without medical guidance. For cleaning and personal care, it is mild and safe.

myths.claim: Baking soda plus vinegar is a super cleaner.
myths.consensus: They neutralize each other into salty water; the fizz is only CO2. Each works better on its own.

myths.claim: Baking soda cures cancer by alkalizing the body.
myths.consensus: Blood pH is tightly regulated; diet cannot meaningfully change it, and this claim has caused harm.

environment.persistence: Not persistent; part of the natural carbonate cycle.

synthesis.title: The Solvay process
synthesis.summary: The Solvay process, developed by the Belgian chemist Ernest Solvay in the 1860s, made sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate cheap enough for everyday use. It uses three abundant raw materials: salt, limestone and ammonia. Before Solvay, soda was made by an older, much dirtier method that produced large amounts of toxic waste. The Solvay process is still used worldwide, especially where natural mineral deposits aren't available. It is a classic example of clever industrial chemistry that recycles its own reagents.
synthesis.mechanism: First, limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated to release carbon dioxide. Concentrated salt water, called brine, is saturated with ammonia gas, and then the carbon dioxide is bubbled through it. The ammonia makes the solution basic, which helps carbon dioxide dissolve and form bicarbonate ions. Sodium bicarbonate is the least soluble of the possible products, so it crystallizes out of the cold solution and is filtered off. The leftover ammonium chloride is treated with lime from the heated limestone to regenerate the ammonia, which goes back to the start of the process.
synthesis.equation: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O → NaHCO3 + NH4Cl
synthesis.significance: Ernest Solvay's 1860s process made soda chemicals cheap enough for everyday use.

synthesis.title: From trona ore
synthesis.summary: In the United States, most baking soda doesn't come from the Solvay process but from a natural mineral called trona. Huge deposits of trona lie underground in Wyoming's Green River Basin, left behind by an ancient lake that dried up about 50 million years ago. Trona is a natural combination of sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate. Mining and refining it uses less energy and creates less waste than the Solvay process. The U.S. is one of the world's largest producers of natural soda ash.
synthesis.mechanism: Trona ore is mined from deep underground beds, crushed and heated, which converts it into crude sodium carbonate. The sodium carbonate is dissolved in water, and the solution is filtered to remove insoluble rock and other impurities. The purified solution is then reacted with carbon dioxide gas. Carbon dioxide combines with the carbonate ions and water to form bicarbonate ions, and sodium bicarbonate crystallizes out because it is less soluble. The crystals are separated, washed and dried.
synthesis.significance: The same Wyoming deposits supply much of the world's soda ash for glassmaking and detergents.

citations.title: Pancreatic enzyme supplementation for patients receiving enteral feeds.
citations.abstract: Background: Pancreatic enzyme supplementation is an important part of management for a number of gastrointestinal conditions. For patients who are unable to swallow pancreatin capsules or granules, enteral feeding tubes can be used to administer the pancreatic enzyme. This presents challenges given the unique format of the pancreatic enzyme supplements, with common problems including tube blockage and loss of the enzyme's effect. Methods and results: A novel technique is described for administration of pancreatic enzyme via feeding tubes. For gastrically placed tubes, this involves opening the pancreatin capsules and suspending the enzyme microspheres in thickened acidic fluid (such as the mildly thickened or "nectar-thick" fruit juice used for dysphagia) for delivery into the feeding tube. This technique minimizes tube blockage by preventing the enzyme from clumping in the tube. For jejunally placed tubes, enzyme microspheres can be crushed and activated with sodium bicarbonate before flushing into the tube, or the activated enzyme mixture can be added to enteral feeds. Conclusions: Pancreatic enzyme supplementation can continue while patients receive enteral feeding. Using the described technique can help to avoid tube blockage and maintain optimal enzyme activity.

citations.title: Rhabdomyolysis.
citations.abstract: Rhabdomyolysis is a syndrome involving the breakdown of skeletal muscle causing myoglobin and other intracellular proteins and electrolytes to leak into the circulation. The development of rhabdomyolysis is associated with a wide variety of diseases, injuries, medications and toxins. While the exact mechanisms responsible for all the causes are not fully understood, it is clear that muscle damage can occur from direct injury or by metabolic inequalities between energy consumption and energy production. Rhabdomyolysis is diagnosed by elevations in serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK), and while there is no established serum level cut-off, many clinicians use five times the upper limit of normal ( approximately 1000 U/l). Rhabdomyolysis can be complicated by acute renal failure (occurring in 4%-33% of patients), compartment syndrome, cardiac dysrhythmias via electrolyte abnormalities, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. The mainstay of treatment is hospitalisation with aggressive intravenous fluid (IVF) resuscitation with the correction/prevention of electrolyte abnormalities. There are additional adjunctive therapies to IVF, such as alkalinisation of the urine with sodium bicarbonate, diuretic therapy or combinations of both; however the lack of large randomised control studies concerning the benefits of these treatments makes it difficult to make strong recommendations for or against their use in the treatment of rhabdomyolysis. Regardless of these controversies, the overall prognosis for rhabdomyolysis is favourable when treated with early and aggressive IVF resuscitation, and full recovery of renal function is common. Irrespective of the cause of rhabdomyolysis the mortality rate may still be as high as 8%. This is a comprehensive review of the pathophysiology, diagnosis, complications and treatment options for rhabdomyolysis.

citations.title: Complexities, Benefits, Risks, and Clinical Implications of Sodium Bicarbonate Administration in Critically Ill Patients: A State-of-the-Art Review.
citations.abstract: Sodium bicarbonate has been used in the treatment of different pathologies, such as hyperkalemia, cardiac arrest, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity, aspirin toxicity, acute acidosis, lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and adrenergic receptors' resistance to catecholamine in patients with shock. An ongoing debate about bicarbonate's efficacy and potential harm has been raised for decades because of the lack of evidence supporting its potential efficacy. Despite the guidelines' restrictions, sodium bicarbonate has been overused in clinical practice. The overuse of sodium bicarbonate could be because of the desire to correct the arterial blood gas parameters rapidly instead of achieving homeostasis by treating the cause of the metabolic acidosis. Moreover, it is believed that sodium bicarbonate may reverse acidosis-induced myocardial depression, hemodynamic instability, ventricular arrhythmias, impaired cellular energy production, resistance to catecholamines, altered metabolism, enzyme suppression, immune dysfunction, and ineffective oxygen delivery. On the other hand, it is crucial to pay attention to the potential harm that could be caused by excessive sodium bicarbonate administration. Sodium bicarbonate may cause paradoxical respiratory acidosis, intracellular acidosis, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, alkalosis, impaired oxygen delivery, cerebrospinal fluid acidosis, and neurologic dysfunction. In this review, we discuss the pathophysiology of sodium bicarbonate-induced adverse effects and potential benefits. We also review the most recent clinical trials, observational studies, and guidelines discussing the use of sodium bicarbonate in different pathologies. Sodium bicarbonate is a multifaceted medication that plays a crucial role in managing and treating diverse disease pathologies. This activity delves into the expansive applications of sodium bicarbonate, providing healthcare professionals with a nuanced understanding of its indications, mechanism of action, and contraindications. The program focuses on its pivotal role in treating conditions such as lactic acidosis and QRS prolongation, offering participants in-depth insights into therapeutic considerations, including dosing, toxicities, and relevant interactions. By examining sodium bicarbonate's adverse event profile, participants will be better equipped to ensure its effective utilization across a spectrum of clinical scenarios. This evidence-based activity aims to empower interprofessional healthcare team members with the essential knowledge to optimize sodium bicarbonate's potential to enhance patient outcomes.

citations.title: Perioperative Clinical Trials in AKI.
citations.abstract: To characterize current evidence and current foci of perioperative clinical trials, we systematically reviewed Medline and identified perioperative trials involving 100 or more adult patients undergoing surgery and reporting renal end points that were published in high-impact journals since 2004. We categorized the 101 trials identified based on the nature of the intervention and summarized major trial findings from the five categories most applicable to perioperative management of patients. Trials that targeted ischemia suggested that increasing perioperative renal oxygen delivery with inotropes or blood transfusion does not reliably mitigate acute kidney injury (AKI), although goal-directed therapy with hemodynamic monitors appeared beneficial in some trials. Trials that have targeted inflammation or oxidative stress, including studies of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, steroids, N-acetylcysteine, and sodium bicarbonate, have not shown renal benefits, and high-dose perioperative statin treatment increased AKI in some patient groups in two large trials. Balanced crystalloid intravenous fluids appear safer than saline, and crystalloids appear safer than colloids. Liberal compared with restrictive fluid administration reduced AKI in a recent large trial in open abdominal surgery. Remote ischemic preconditioning, although effective in several smaller trials, failed to reduce AKI in two larger trials. The translation of promising preclinical therapies to patients undergoing surgery remains poor, and most interventions that reduced perioperative AKI compared novel surgical management techniques or existing processes of care rather than novel pharmacologic interventions.

citations.title: Methanol poisoning.
citations.abstract: Methanol ingestion is an uncommon form of poisoning that can cause severe metabolic disturbances, blindness, permanent neurologic dysfunction and death. While methanol itself may be harmless, it is converted in vivo to the highly toxic formic acid. The diagnosis is sometimes elusive and requires a high index of suspicion. Because antidotal treatment is available it is important to recognize methanol poisoning promptly. The presence of metabolic acidosis associated with an increased anion gap and increased osmol gap are important laboratory findings. Specific therapeutic measures include correction of the metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate and administration of enteral or parenteral ethanol to competitively inhibit the metabolic breakdown of methanol to formic acid. Hemodialysis accelerates the elimination of both methanol and formic acid and also assists in correction of the metabolic acidosis. Experimental data suggests that administration of folic acid may be of benefit by hastening the metabolism of formic acid to carbon dioxide. Prompt institution of specific therapy can probably decrease the morbidity and mortality associated with this form of poisoning.

name: Carrageenan
scoreRationale: Approved worldwide, but ongoing debate about gut inflammation and EFSA's call for more data keep it in the middle.
summary: Carrageenan is a seaweed-derived thickener used in dairy alternatives, deli meats and toothpaste. Its gut effects remain debated.

identity.composition: Sulfated linear galactans (kappa, iota, lambda types) from red seaweeds.

physical.solubility: Soluble in hot water; kappa and iota form gels on cooling

overview: Carrageenans are long chains of galactose sugars with sulfate groups attached, extracted from red seaweeds. The three main types differ in how many sulfates they carry: kappa (one per repeating unit), iota (two) and lambda (three).

Sulfate groups are negatively charged, so carrageenan chains repel each other and attract positive ions. Kappa and iota chains twist into double helices that link into gels when the right ions are present, while heavily sulfated lambda stays liquid and simply thickens.
profile.function: Thickens and stabilizes plant milks, ice cream, chocolate milk and deli meats; binds toothpaste.

mechanisms.title: Ion-triggered gelling
mechanisms.chemical: Carrageenan chains are long and carry negatively charged sulfate groups. As a hot solution cools, kappa and iota carrageenan chains pair up and twist around each other into double helices. These helices are negatively charged, so they repel one another until positive ions come along. Potassium ions (K⁺) fit neatly between kappa-carrageenan helices and bridge them together tightly, while calcium ions (Ca²⁺) bridge iota helices more loosely. Lambda carrageenan carries so many sulfate groups that its chains can't form helices at all.
mechanisms.biological: These differences give each type its own texture. Kappa-carrageenan forms firm, brittle gels that can crack, useful in deli meats, pet foods and some jellies. Iota-carrageenan forms soft, elastic gels that bounce back, useful in puddings and dairy desserts. Lambda-carrageenan never gels and simply thickens liquids, giving chocolate milk and other drinks a creamy feel. By combining types, food makers can create almost any texture between a liquid and a solid.

mechanisms.title: Stabilizing milk
mechanisms.chemical: Milk contains tiny particles of casein, its main protein, clustered into structures called micelles. Although casein micelles are negatively charged overall, one of the casein proteins, kappa-casein, has a region that carries positive charges. Carrageenan's negative sulfate groups are attracted to these positive patches and bind to them. At the same time, carrageenan chains form a weak, invisible network running through the milk. Together, these interactions hold the casein and other particles in place.
mechanisms.biological: Without a stabilizer, cocoa powder in chocolate milk sinks to the bottom, and plant-based milks separate into watery and solid layers. Even 0.02 percent carrageenan, which is 200 milligrams per liter, makes a network strong enough to keep cocoa particles suspended. The drink stays smooth and evenly colored without shaking. Because the network is so weak, it doesn't make the drink noticeably thicker. This is why carrageenan appears in so many dairy and plant-based drinks.

mechanisms.title: The gut inflammation debate
mechanisms.chemical: Some laboratory studies, mainly in cells and animals, have found that carrageenan can activate a receptor called TLR4 on cells lining the gut. TLR4 normally detects molecules from bacteria and triggers an immune response. When it is activated, it switches on a signaling pathway called NF-κB, which tells cells to produce inflammatory messengers. Other researchers have argued that these results came from poligeenan, a degraded form not allowed in food, or from very high doses. How food-grade carrageenan might cause such effects remains debated.
mechanisms.biological: If carrageenan did trigger inflammation in the human gut, it could in theory worsen conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, in which the gut lining is chronically inflamed. A small study in people with ulcerative colitis found that those who avoided carrageenan had fewer relapses, but it was too small to be conclusive. Large regulatory reviews have found no clear evidence of harm at food levels. In 2018 the European Food Safety Authority kept carrageenan approved but asked for more data, particularly on infants. Research is ongoing.

reactions.title: Setting a gel
reactions.summary: Carrageenan gels form when a hot solution cools and melt again when heated, which is why they are called thermoreversible. That is different from egg white, which sets permanently when cooked. The gelling happens because carrageenan chains change shape as they cool and then link together with the help of positive ions. Understanding this lets food makers control a gel's firmness and melting point. It is similar to how gelatin sets, although here the chains are made of sugars rather than protein.

steps.name: Dissolving
steps.text: In hot water, above about 70 °C, carrageenan chains have enough energy to move freely as loose, tangled coils. In this state the solution is liquid. The chains don't hold any fixed shape.

steps.name: Helix formation
steps.text: As the solution cools, the chains slow down and pairs of them twist around each other into double helices held together by hydrogen bonds. This happens over a particular temperature range that depends on the type of carrageenan and the ions present. The helices are much stiffer than the loose coils.

steps.name: Bridging
steps.text: Positive ions such as potassium or calcium settle between neighboring helices, cancelling some of their negative charge and linking them together. Many helices join into a three-dimensional network that traps water in its spaces. The liquid has become a gel.

reactions.result: Because heat breaks the helices and bridges apart again, carrageenan gels melt when warmed and set again when cooled. This is useful in foods that are heated during processing and served cold, such as desserts and processed meats.

reactions.title: Acid degradation
reactions.summary: When carrageenan is exposed to strong acid and high heat for a long time, its long chains are broken into shorter and shorter pieces. This process is called acid hydrolysis. If the chains become very short, the material behaves differently and is no longer considered carrageenan. These short fragments are called poligeenan, or degraded carrageenan, and they are not permitted in food. Understanding this reaction is central to keeping food-grade carrageenan safe.

steps.name: Hydrolysis
steps.text: Hydrogen ions from the acid attack the glycosidic bonds, the oxygen bridges joining the sugar units in the chain. With heat supplying extra energy, water molecules split those bonds. Each break cuts one long chain into two shorter ones.

steps.name: Shortening
steps.text: With continued exposure, more and more bonds break and the average chain length falls. Food-grade carrageenan chains have molecular weights of hundreds of thousands of daltons. A dalton is a unit of mass roughly equal to one hydrogen atom.

steps.name: Poligeenan
steps.text: Below an average molecular weight of about 20,000 daltons, the fragments are called poligeenan. Poligeenan doesn't gel, and in animal studies it has caused inflammation and ulcers in the colon. It is a different substance from food-grade carrageenan.

reactions.result: This is why food-grade carrageenan must meet a minimum molecular weight and is produced with alkaline processing rather than strong acid. Most studies indicate that stomach acid is not strong or hot enough to turn food-grade carrageenan into meaningful amounts of poligeenan during digestion, although some researchers have questioned this.

regulatory.status: Approved food additive.
Temporary ADI of 75 mg/kg body weight per day while more data are gathered.
Remains allowed after a 2016 advisory board vote to remove it was not adopted.

hazards.title: Possible gut irritation
hazards.summary: Whether carrageenan irritates the human gut is debated. Most regulatory reviews, including those by the U.S. FDA and international experts, consider food-grade carrageenan safe at the levels used in food. However, some laboratory studies have raised concerns about inflammation, and some people with digestive conditions report feeling better without it. The evidence in humans is limited and inconsistent. People with inflammatory bowel disease who notice symptoms may choose to avoid it.
hazards.chemical: Some studies suggest that carrageenan can bind to and activate immune receptors, such as TLR4, on the surface of cells lining the gut. These receptors normally help detect bacteria, so activating them sets off inflammatory signals. Carrageenan might also affect the mucus layer that protects the gut lining, or shift the balance of gut bacteria. Critics of these studies point out that many used degraded carrageenan, very high doses or isolated cells. How relevant they are to people eating normal amounts is uncertain.
hazards.biological: In people with inflammatory bowel disease, such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, the gut lining is already inflamed and more sensitive. Some patients report fewer symptoms when they avoid foods containing carrageenan, and a small trial found fewer relapses in a carrageenan-free group. That evidence is too limited to prove cause and effect. Healthy people generally show no signs of harm. Because carrageenan is listed on ingredient labels, anyone who wants to avoid it can do so easily.

profile.dosage: Foods use about 0.01 to 1 percent carrageenan, typically a few hundred milligrams or less per serving. In 2018 the European Food Safety Authority set a temporary acceptable daily intake of 75 milligrams per kilogram of body weight and noted that people who eat a lot of dairy desserts, plant milks and processed meats might exceed it. International experts (JECFA) consider it safe in foods at current use levels, including in infant formula at regulated amounts, and it is approved as a food additive in the U.S. People with digestive conditions who notice symptoms can easily avoid it by reading labels.

myths.claim: Carrageenan is the same as poligeenan, a carcinogen.
myths.consensus: Poligeenan is a degraded, much smaller molecule; food-grade carrageenan has a specified minimum molecular weight.

environment.notes: Seaweed farming supports coastal communities in the Philippines and Indonesia.

synthesis.title: Alkaline extraction from seaweed
synthesis.summary: Carrageenan comes from red seaweeds, especially species called Kappaphycus and Eucheuma, which are farmed in warm, shallow seas. Its name comes from the Irish word carraigín, meaning “little rock,” for a red seaweed known as Irish moss that people in Ireland have used for centuries to thicken milk puddings. Today most carrageenan comes from seaweed farms in the Philippines, Indonesia and East Africa. The seaweed is harvested, dried and shipped to processing plants. Extraction uses hot water and alkali.
synthesis.mechanism: The dried seaweed is washed to remove sand and salt, then cooked in a hot solution of an alkali such as potassium or calcium hydroxide. The alkali does two jobs: it helps dissolve the carrageenan, and it chemically changes some of the galactose units in the chains into a ring form called 3,6-anhydrogalactose by removing a sulfate group. This change makes the chains better at forming helices, so the final gel is stronger. The hot extract is filtered to remove the seaweed remains, and then carrageenan is made to come out of solution by adding alcohol or potassium chloride. The solid is pressed, dried and milled into powder.
synthesis.significance: Seaweed farming for carrageenan supports coastal communities in the Philippines and Indonesia.

citations.title: Icariin modulates carrageenan-induced acute inflammation through HO-1/Nrf2 and NF-kB signaling pathways.
citations.abstract: Cellular inflammation has been recognized as the leading factor in numerous diseases, causing either cell death, organ-specific damage, or genesis of different cancers. Icariin, a flavonol glucoside, extracted from Herba Epimedii, offers various pharmacological activities, including reducing inflammation and an antioxidant effect. We aimed to evaluate the anti-inflammatory mechanisms of icariin focussing on both HO-1/Nrf2 and NF-kB pathways. Acute inflammation was induced in rats via carrageenan in this study. Icariin was injected in a dose of 50 mg/kg. Icariin significantly reduced paw swelling in carrageenan-injected animals. It also ameliorated carrageenan-induced paw histopathological alterations. Icariin significantly increased paw enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidants. It decreased paw lipid peroxidation. Icariin decreased paw levels of inflammatory cytokines and NF-kB. The immunohistochemical analysis showed that icariin significantly increased Nrf2 gene expression while decreasing NF-kB and COX-2 gene expression. RT-PCR analysis revealed that icariin injection significantly increased both Nrf2 and HO-1 expression of mRNA. The results of this study collectively show that icariin improved carrageenan-induced paw edema by modulating HO-1/Nrf2 and NF-ĸB signaling.

citations.title: Marine Polysaccharides: Occurrence, Enzymatic Degradation and Utilization.
citations.abstract: Macroalgae species are fast growing and their polysaccharides are already used as food ingredient due to their properties as hydrocolloids or they have potential high value bioactivity. The degradation of these valuable polysaccharides to access the sugar components has remained mostly unexplored so far.
