One reason is the high structural complexity of algal polysaccharides, but also the need for suitable enzyme cocktails to obtain oligo- and monosaccharides. Among them, there are several rare sugars with high value. Recently, considerable progress was made in the discovery of highly specific carbohydrate-active enzymes able to decompose complex marine carbohydrates such as carrageenan, laminarin, agar, porphyran and ulvan. This minireview summarizes these achievements and highlights potential applications of the now accessible abundant renewable resource of marine polysaccharides.

citations.title: Carrageenan: a review of its effects on the immune system.
citations.abstract: Carrageenans (kappa, lambda and iota) are sulphated polysaccharides isolated from marine algae that can markedly suppress immune responses both in vivo and in vitro. Impairment of complement activity and humoral responses to T-dependent antigens, depression of cell-mediated immunity, prolongation of graft survival and potentiation of tumour growth by carrageenans have been reported. The mechanism responsible for carrageenan-induced immune suppression is believed to be its selective cytopathic effect on macrophages. This property of carrageenan has led to its adoption as a tool for analysing the role of these cells in the induction and expression of immune reactivity. Systemic administration of carrageenan may, however, induce disseminated intravascular coagulation and inflict damage on both the liver and kidney. This is an important consideration in the interpretation of the effects of carrageenan in vivo and precludes its use as a clinical immune suppressant.

citations.title: Antioxidant modulation of sirtuin 3 during acute inflammatory pain: The ROS control.
citations.abstract: Oxidative stress induced post-translational protein modifications are associated with the development of inflammatory hypersensitivities. At least 90% of cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced in the mitochondria, where the mitochondrial antioxidant, manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), is located. MnSOD's ability to reduce ROS is enhanced by the mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacetylase sirtuin (SIRT3). SIRT3 can reduce ROS levels by deacetylating MnSOD and enhancing its ability to neutralize ROS or by enhancing the transcription of MnSOD and other oxidative stress-responsive genes. SIRT3 can be post-translationally modified through carbonylation which results in loss of activity. The contribution of post-translational SIRT3 modifications in central sensitization is largely unexplored. Our results reveal that SIRT3 carbonylation contributes to spinal MnSOD inactivation during carrageenan-induced thermal hyperalgesia in rats. Moreover, inhibiting ROS with natural and synthetic antioxidants, prevented SIRT3 carbonylation, restored the enzymatic activity of MnSOD, and blocked the development of thermal hyperalgesia. These results suggest that therapeutic strategies aimed at inhibiting post-translational modifications of SIRT3 may provide beneficial outcomes in pain states where ROS have been documented to play an important role in the development of central sensitization.

name: Vitamin E
scoreRationale: An essential nutrient and gentle antioxidant; only high-dose supplements carry risks.
summary: Vitamin E protects oils from going rancid and helps defend skin lipids against oxidation. It's among the safest antioxidants.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in oils and ethanol
physical.phStability: Stable, but oxidizes with light and air

overview: Vitamin E is a family of eight related molecules; the most biologically active is alpha-tocopherol. Each has a chromanol ring (a phenol fused to an oxygen-containing ring) attached to a long, oily 16-carbon tail.

The tail anchors the molecule inside fatty cell membranes, while the ring's –OH group sits near the membrane surface, ready to donate a hydrogen atom and stop chain reactions that would otherwise damage membrane fats.
profile.function: Prevents rancidity in oils and cosmetics and provides antioxidant and conditioning benefits for skin.

mechanisms.title: Chain-breaking antioxidant
mechanisms.chemical: Fats in cell membranes often contain several double bonds, and the carbon atoms between those double bonds hold their hydrogen atoms loosely. When a free radical steals one of these hydrogens, it starts a chain reaction: the damaged fat becomes a radical, reacts with oxygen to form a peroxyl radical, and then steals a hydrogen from the next fat molecule. Tocopherol stops the chain by donating the hydrogen atom from its own –OH group to the peroxyl radical. That turns the radical into a stable molecule called a hydroperoxide. The tocopherol is left as a tocopheroxyl radical, but its unpaired electron is spread across its aromatic ring, which makes it too stable to keep the chain going.
mechanisms.biological: Cell membranes contain many polyunsaturated fats, especially in nerve cells and red blood cells, and these fats are vulnerable to oxidation. Without protection, oxidation makes membranes leaky and stiff and damages the proteins embedded in them. Vitamin E sits inside the membrane itself, right where radicals form, ready to catch them. Severe vitamin E deficiency, which is rare and usually caused by problems absorbing fat, leads to nerve damage, muscle weakness and trouble with balance and vision. It can also make red blood cells burst more easily.

mechanisms.title: Recycled by vitamin C
mechanisms.chemical: After tocopherol neutralizes a radical, it becomes the tocopheroxyl radical, which can't protect anything until it is restored. At the surface of the membrane, where the fatty interior meets the watery surroundings, vitamin C (ascorbate) can reach it. Ascorbate donates a hydrogen atom, turning tocopherol back into its active form. The vitamin C becomes the ascorbyl radical, which is stable and is later recycled by enzymes. In this way one tocopherol molecule can be used again and again.
mechanisms.biological: Vitamin E dissolves in fats and works inside membranes, while vitamin C dissolves in water and works in the fluids inside and around cells. By passing electrons between them, the two vitamins form a team that covers both environments. Enzymes in the cell use other molecules, such as glutathione, to recycle vitamin C in turn. This chain of recycling helps explain why getting enough of several antioxidants together matters more than taking a large dose of one. Fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds supply both vitamins.

mechanisms.title: Protecting oils and skin
mechanisms.chemical: When vegetable oils and creams are exposed to light, heat and oxygen, radicals form and attack their fatty acids, the same chain reaction that happens in cell membranes. Added tocopherol intercepts these radicals by donating hydrogen atoms and stopping the chain. On labels it is often listed as “mixed tocopherols” or “vitamin E.” In skincare, tocopherol dissolves into the oily parts of the product and of the skin's surface. It also absorbs a little ultraviolet light, though nowhere near enough to replace sunscreen.
mechanisms.biological: By slowing oxidation, tocopherol keeps oils and creams from going rancid, which would change their smell and texture. On skin, it adds to the natural antioxidants in the outer layer, helping protect skin fats from damage by sunlight and pollution. However, controlled trials have found that rubbing vitamin E onto scars doesn't make them fade and can occasionally cause irritation or allergic reactions. In foods it acts as a natural preservative. The amounts used are small compared with what people get from nuts and seeds.

reactions.title: Stopping a radical chain reaction
reactions.summary: Fats and oils go rancid through a process called lipid peroxidation, a chain reaction driven by free radicals. A single radical can start a chain that damages hundreds of fat molecules, changing their smell, taste and color. Tocopherol is a chain-breaking antioxidant: it stops the chain partway through. Understanding this reaction explains why oils are sold in dark bottles and why antioxidants are added to foods. The same chemistry damages cell membranes inside the body.

steps.name: Initiation
steps.text: Light, heat or a metal ion pulls a hydrogen atom off a fatty acid, usually from a carbon between two double bonds. This creates a lipid radical (L•), which has an unpaired electron. Initiation is fairly rare, but it starts everything.

steps.name: Propagation
steps.text: The lipid radical quickly reacts with oxygen from the air, forming a lipid peroxyl radical (LOO•). This radical is reactive enough to steal a hydrogen atom from a neighboring fatty acid, becoming a lipid hydroperoxide but creating a brand-new lipid radical. That new radical repeats the cycle, so the chain keeps going.

steps.name: Termination
steps.text: Tocopherol (TOH) gives its hydrogen atom to the peroxyl radical faster than the radical can attack another fatty acid. The peroxyl radical becomes a stable hydroperoxide, and the tocopherol becomes a tocopheroxyl radical (TO•) that is too stable to continue the chain. The chain is broken.

reactions.result: One tocopherol molecule can stop a chain that would otherwise damage many fatty acids, which is why only small amounts of vitamin E are needed to protect oils and membranes. The hydroperoxides that do form can still break down into smelly compounds, so tocopherol slows rancidity rather than preventing it completely.

reactions.title: Being used up
reactions.summary: Antioxidants like vitamin E protect other molecules by sacrificing themselves, so they gradually get used up. Once all the tocopherol in an oil or a membrane has been consumed, the fats are no longer protected. In the body, vitamin C and other molecules can recycle vitamin E and extend its working life. In a bottle of oil, no such recycling happens. This explains why oils eventually go rancid even though they contain natural vitamin E.

steps.name: First oxidation
steps.text: When tocopherol donates a hydrogen atom to a radical, it becomes the tocopheroxyl radical. This radical is fairly stable but can no longer protect fats. In the body, vitamin C can turn it back into active tocopherol.

steps.name: Second oxidation
steps.text: Without vitamin C or another partner to recycle it, the tocopheroxyl radical reacts with another radical or with oxygen. This changes its structure further. It can no longer easily be restored.

steps.name: End product
steps.text: Eventually the ring of the tocopherol molecule opens, forming tocopherylquinone, a yellowish compound that can no longer act as an antioxidant. Tocopherylquinone may also contribute to color changes in old oils.

reactions.result: Oils go rancid once their tocopherol has been consumed. Storing oils somewhere cool and dark, in sealed bottles, slows the rate at which it is used up. Food manufacturers sometimes add extra tocopherols or vitamin C to extend shelf life.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a nutrient and preservative.
RDA 15 mg/day; upper limit 1,000 mg/day from supplements.
Safe as used in cosmetics.

hazards.title: Bleeding risk at high supplement doses
hazards.summary: Vitamin E from food and cosmetics poses no bleeding risk, but high-dose vitamin E supplements can interfere with blood clotting. The risk is greatest for people who also take blood-thinning medicines such as warfarin, or who are short of vitamin K. The U.S. upper limit for adults is 1,000 milligrams a day from supplements, partly for this reason. People scheduled for surgery are often told to stop high-dose vitamin E beforehand. Most people get enough vitamin E from a normal diet without supplements.
hazards.chemical: Blood clotting depends on several proteins, called clotting factors, that have to be chemically activated with the help of vitamin K. At high doses, vitamin E, or one of its breakdown products called tocopherylquinone, seems to interfere with the enzymes that recycle vitamin K. With less active vitamin K available, fewer clotting factors get switched on. Vitamin E may also make platelets, the tiny cell fragments that start a clot, less likely to clump together. Both effects slow down clotting.
hazards.biological: When blood clots more slowly, cuts bleed longer and bruises appear more easily. In people already taking anticoagulant drugs, which deliberately slow clotting, the extra effect of vitamin E could raise the risk of serious bleeding, including bleeding in the brain. Some large studies found a slight increase in a type of stroke caused by bleeding among people taking vitamin E supplements. This risk doesn't apply to vitamin E from foods like nuts and oils. People on blood thinners should talk to their doctor before taking supplements.

hazards.title: Prostate cancer risk with supplements
hazards.summary: Vitamin E supplements were once widely believed to prevent cancer and heart disease, but large trials haven't supported that. The SELECT trial, which followed more than 35,000 men, found that a high daily dose of vitamin E actually increased the risk of prostate cancer. This finding applies to supplements, not to vitamin E from food or skincare. It is an important example of how a nutrient that is essential in normal amounts can have unexpected effects at high doses. Most experts now advise against routine vitamin E supplements.
hazards.chemical: Why vitamin E supplements might raise prostate cancer risk is not known. One possibility is that high doses of alpha-tocopherol lower the levels of other forms of vitamin E, such as gamma-tocopherol, which may have protective effects of their own. Another idea is that antioxidants at high doses interfere with the body's normal use of reactive oxygen molecules, which help regulate cell growth and kill damaged cells. Vitamin E might also affect hormones or enzymes involved in how prostate cells grow. None of these explanations has been proven.
hazards.biological: In the SELECT trial, men took either 400 IU of synthetic vitamin E a day (about 180 milligrams), selenium, both, or a placebo. After several years, men taking vitamin E alone had about a 17 percent higher risk of prostate cancer than those on placebo, and the increase was still seen after they had stopped taking it. No benefit was found for preventing other cancers or heart disease. Based on this and other trials, health organizations recommend getting vitamin E from foods rather than supplements.

profile.dosage: Adults need about 15 milligrams of vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) a day, which is easy to get from nuts, seeds, vegetable oils and leafy greens; an ounce of almonds supplies about half. The amounts added to foods as antioxidants and to cosmetics are measured in milligrams and are not a concern. Problems are linked to long-term supplement doses of hundreds of international units a day, which have been associated with bleeding risk and, in the SELECT trial, prostate cancer. The U.S. upper limit for adults is 1,000 milligrams a day from supplements. Most health organizations recommend getting vitamin E from food.

myths.claim: Vitamin E oil erases scars.
myths.consensus: Controlled studies show no benefit over plain moisturizer, and some people develop contact dermatitis.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis in plants
synthesis.summary: Only plants, algae and some bacteria that carry out photosynthesis can make vitamin E; animals, including humans, have to get it from food. Plants make tocopherols mainly in their chloroplasts, where they protect the membranes involved in photosynthesis from damage by light and oxygen. Seeds are especially rich in tocopherols, which protect their stored oils from going rancid. That's why vegetable oils, nuts and seeds are the best dietary sources. Leafy greens supply smaller amounts.
synthesis.mechanism: Plants make vitamin E from two building blocks. The first is homogentisic acid, which provides the aromatic ring and is made from the amino acid tyrosine. The second is phytyl diphosphate, a long, oily chain related to the tail of the chlorophyll molecule. An enzyme joins the two, attaching the tail to the ring. Further enzymes add methyl groups to the ring and close a second, oxygen-containing ring, forming the chromanol structure. Depending on how many methyl groups are added and where, the plant makes alpha-, beta-, gamma- or delta-tocopherol.
synthesis.significance: Different plants make different mixtures: sunflower oil is rich in alpha-tocopherol, while soybean and corn oils contain mostly gamma-tocopherol.

synthesis.title: Extraction from vegetable oil
synthesis.summary: Natural vitamin E sold as a supplement or food additive mostly comes from refining vegetable oil, especially soybean oil. During refining, a step called deodorization removes unwanted smells and flavors from the oil. Tocopherols end up concentrated in the byproduct of this step. Rather than being wasted, that byproduct is processed to recover the vitamin E. Labels often call the result “mixed tocopherols” because it contains several forms.
synthesis.mechanism: During deodorization, steam is blown through hot vegetable oil under vacuum. Molecules that evaporate relatively easily, including odor compounds, free fatty acids and tocopherols, are carried away with the steam. When the vapor is cooled, they collect as a liquid called deodorizer distillate, which can be 10 percent or more tocopherols. This distillate is purified by molecular distillation, a gentle technique that separates molecules by how easily they evaporate at very low pressure. The result is a concentrated oil of mixed tocopherols.
synthesis.significance: Using a byproduct of oil refining makes natural vitamin E production more efficient and reduces waste.

synthesis.title: Chemical synthesis
synthesis.summary: Synthetic vitamin E is made in chemical plants from two building blocks, one providing the ring and one providing the tail. It is cheaper than natural vitamin E and is widely used in supplements, animal feed and fortified foods. On labels, synthetic vitamin E is often listed as “dl-alpha-tocopherol” or “all-rac-alpha-tocopherol,” while natural vitamin E is “d-alpha-tocopherol.” The difference lies in the 3D shape of the molecules. Synthetic and natural vitamin E contain the same atoms but are not all identical in shape.
synthesis.mechanism: The ring comes from trimethylhydroquinone, a benzene ring with two –OH groups and three methyl groups. The tail comes from isophytol, a long, oily alcohol assembled from smaller petrochemical building blocks. When the two are heated together with an acid catalyst, the tail attaches to the ring and a second ring closes, forming the chromanol structure in a single step. The product is usually converted into an ester, tocopheryl acetate, which keeps better in storage. In the body, the acetate group is removed to release active vitamin E.
synthesis.significance: Synthetic all-rac-alpha-tocopherol is a mix of eight stereoisomers, and only half of them are counted as active, so it is about half as potent per milligram as natural vitamin E.

citations.title: Several lines of antioxidant defense against oxidative stress: antioxidant enzymes, nanomaterials with multiple enzyme-mimicking activities, and low-molecular-weight antioxidants.
citations.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) are well recognized for playing a dual role, since they can be either deleterious or beneficial to biological systems. An imbalance between ROS production and elimination is termed oxidative stress, a critical factor and common denominator of many chronic diseases such as cancer, cardiovascular diseases, metabolic diseases, neurological disorders (Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases), and other disorders. To counteract the harmful effects of ROS, organisms have evolved a complex, three-line antioxidant defense system. The first-line defense mechanism is the most efficient and involves antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione peroxidase (GPx). This line of defense plays an irreplaceable role in the dismutation of superoxide radicals (O2•-) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). The removal of superoxide radicals by SOD prevents the formation of the much more damaging peroxynitrite ONOO- (O2•- + NO• → ONOO-) and maintains the physiologically relevant level of nitric oxide (NO•), an important molecule in neurotransmission, inflammation, and vasodilation. The second-line antioxidant defense pathway involves exogenous diet-derived small-molecule antioxidants. The third-line antioxidant defense is ensured by the repair or removal of oxidized proteins and other biomolecules by a variety of enzyme systems. This review briefly discusses the endogenous (mitochondria, NADPH, xanthine oxidase (XO), Fenton reaction) and exogenous (e.g., smoking, radiation, drugs, pollution) sources of ROS (superoxide radical, hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radical, peroxyl radical, hypochlorous acid, peroxynitrite). Attention has been given to the first-line antioxidant defense system provided by SOD, CAT, and GPx. The chemical and molecular mechanisms of antioxidant enzymes, enzyme-related diseases (cancer, cardiovascular, lung, metabolic, and neurological diseases), and the role of enzymes (e.g., GPx4) in cellular processes such as ferroptosis are discussed. Potential therapeutic applications of enzyme mimics and recent progress in metal-based (copper, iron, cobalt, molybdenum, cerium) and nonmetal (carbon)-based nanomaterials with enzyme-like activities (nanozymes) are also discussed. Moreover, attention has been given to the mechanisms of action of low-molecular-weight antioxidants (vitamin C (ascorbate), vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol), carotenoids (e.g., β-carotene, lycopene, lutein), flavonoids (e.g., quercetin, anthocyanins, epicatechin), and glutathione (GSH)), the activation of transcription factors such as Nrf2, and the protection against chronic diseases. Given that there is a discrepancy between preclinical and clinical studies, approaches that may result in greater pharmacological and clinical success of low-molecular-weight antioxidant therapies are also subject to discussion.

citations.title: alpha-Tocopheryl phosphate--an active lipid mediator?
citations.abstract: The vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol, alphaT) derivative, alpha-tocopheryl phosphate (alphaTP), is detectable in small amounts in plasma, tissues, and cultured cells. Studies done in vitro and in vivo suggest that alphaT can become phosphorylated and alphaTP dephosphorylated, suggesting the existence of enzyme(s) with alphaT kinase or alphaTP phosphatase activity, respectively. As a supplement in animal studies, alphaTP can reach plasma concentrations similar to alphaT and only a part is dephosphorylated; thus, alphaTP may act both as pro-vitamin E, but also as phosphorylated form of vitamin E with possibly novel regulatory activities. Many effects of alphaTP have been described: in the test tube alphaTP modulates the activity of several enzymes; in cell culture alphaTP affects proliferation, apoptosis, signal transduction, and gene expression; in animal studies alphaTP prevents atherosclerosis, ischemia/reperfusion injury, and induces hippocampal long-term potentiation. At the molecular level, alphaTP may act as a cofactor for enzymes, as an active lipid mediator similar to other phosphorylated lipids, or indirectly by altering membrane characteristics such as lipid rafts, fluidity, and curvature. In this review, the molecular and cellular activities of alphaTP are examined and the possible functions of alphaTP as a natural compound, cofactor and active lipid mediator involved in signal transduction and gene expression discussed.

citations.title: Allergenic Ingredients in Facial Wet Wipes.
citations.abstract: Background: Allergic contact dermatitis commonly occurs on the face. Facial cleansing wipes may be an underrecognized source of allergens. Objective: The aim of this study was to determine the frequency of potentially allergenic ingredients in facial wet wipes. Methods: Ingredient lists from name brand and generic facial wipes from 4 large retailers were analyzed. Results: In the 178 facial wipes examined, a total of 485 ingredients were identified (average, 16.7 ingredients per wipe). Excluding botanicals, the top 15 potentially allergenic ingredients were glycerin (64.0%), fragrance (63.5%), phenoxyethanol (53.9%), citric acid (51.1%), disodium EDTA (44.4%), sorbic acid derivatives (39.3%), tocopherol derivatives (38.8%), polyethylene glycol derivatives (32.6%), glyceryl stearate (31.5%), sodium citrate (29.8%), glucosides (27.5%), cetearyl alcohol (25.8%), propylene glycol (25.3%), sodium benzoate (24.2%), and ceteareth-20 (23.6%)/parabens (23.6%). Of note, methylisothiazolinone (2.2%) and methylchloroisothiazolinone (1.1%) were uncommon. The top potential allergens of botanical origin included Aloe barbadensis (41.0%), chamomile extracts (27.0%), tea extracts (21.3%), Cucumis sativus (20.2%), and Hamamelis virginiana (10.7%). Conclusions: Many potential allergens are present in facial wet wipes, including fragrances, preservatives, botanicals, glucosides, and propylene glycol.

citations.title: Selenium in biology.
citations.abstract: The role of Se in biology appears from the evidence now at hand to be as a catalyst par excellence. As unique prosthetic group of a variety of enzymes, presumably as Se(2-), Se functions with tocopherol to protect cell and organelle membranes from oxidative damage, to facilitate the union between oxygen and hydrogen at the end of the metabolic chain, and to transfer ions across cell membranes, in protein synthesis in erythrocytes and in liver organelles, in immunoglobulin synthesis, and in ubiquinone syntheses. As perhaps the most versatile and rapid nucleophile, Se is thought to amplify and orient SH in equilibrium -S-S-interactions involving glutathione and proteins. Its toxicity appears to be due to overaccumulation of selenite ions, which act as oxidants to inhibit SH interactions. Such toxicity is readily avoided or reversed in many ways. Although not yet recognized as essential for man, Se is clearly essential for many animal species and some microorganisms. As the active selenide, Se emerged as the target for many heavy metal toxicities; contrariwise, as a specific antidote against heavy metal toxicities. Despite all this, its unusual toxicity and the many preconceived notions about Se continue to confuse attitudes toward the safe uses of selenicals. From a suspected cause of cancer, Se metamorphosed, via evidence over many years, into something of possible anticancer value. Interrelations between Se, Vitamin E, the ubiquinones, and various chronic diseases appear as beckoning research areas. The reported veterinary values of Se-tocopherol combinations in animals, together with clinical evidence, plus human and animal evidence for safety, offer promise for intensive medical investigation. The historical confusion and misunderstandings regarding Se must be corrected, however, before advantage can be taken of its potential for human welfare. The many misjudgments about Se, ever since 1900 and more obviously since the 1930s, have involved other trace elements. Unrealistic regulations stemming from these misunderstandings prevail worldwide. Evidence suggests that, once the nutrition biochemistry and toxicology of Se is sufficiently understood and appreciated, major breakthroughs in agriculture, medicine, and public health can result. Much has been accomplished along these lines in New Zealand in animal agriculture, in the US and other countries in veterinary medicine, and in Mexico in human medicine.

citations.title: Detection of lipid peroxidation in equine spermatozoa based upon the lipophilic fluorescent dye C1l-BODIPY581/591.
citations.abstract: The lipophilic fluorescent probe, 4,4-difluoro-5-(4-phenyl-1 ,3-butadienyl)-4-bora-3a,4a-diaza-s-indacene-3-undecanoic acid (C11-BODIPY581/591) was used to evaluate changes in lipid peroxidation in equine spermatozoa during both short-term exposure to ferrous sulfate and sodium ascorbate in the presence of cumene hydroperoxide as well as during storage of spermatozoa at 5 degrees C for 48 hours. Peroxidation of C11-BODIPY581/591 was accompanied by a shift in fluorescence from red to green, and the relative amount of nonoxidized probe was determined as the ratio of red:(red + green) fluorescence as detected by either fluorescence microplate reader or by flow cytometry. The addition of Fe2SO4 (0 to 0.5 mM), low concentrations of sodium ascorbate, and the addition of cumene hydroperoxide increased peroxidation of C11-BODIPY581/591. The addition of high concentrations (10 or 20 mM) of sodium ascorbate or alpha-tocopherol reduced peroxidation of C11-BODIPY581/591 during short-term incubations. During storage at 5 degrees C in a skim milk-based extender, equine spermatozoa demonstrated a progressive decline in motility and a small but significant increase in lipid peroxidation based upon ratiometric analysis of C11-BODIPY581/591. The addition of Fe2SO4 increased lipid peroxidation in cooled spermatozoa in a dose-dependent fashion and decreased sperm motility. The addition of alpha-tocopherol, however, did not reduce lipid peroxidation during cooled semen storage. These data demonstrate that the lipophilic fluorescent probe C11-BODIPY581/591 is a useful measurement of lipid peroxidation in equine spermatozoa and that there is an increase in lipid peroxidation during cooled storage of equine spermatozoa that is increased in the presence of ferrous promoters.

name: Natural Flavors
scoreRationale: Generally safe, but the blend is undisclosed and can include carriers and processing aids that consumers cannot evaluate.
summary: "Natural flavors" are proprietary blends of flavor chemicals from plant or animal sources. They're usually safe, but you can't see what's inside.

identity.composition: Undisclosed blends of essential oils, extracts, distillates and fermentation products, often with carriers such as ethanol, propylene glycol or maltodextrin.

overview: “Natural flavors” isn't one substance; it's a legal category. In the U.S., a natural flavor is any flavoring derived from a plant, animal or microbial source by extraction, distillation, roasting, heating or fermentation, whose main purpose is flavor rather than nutrition.

A single natural flavor can contain dozens of aroma molecules (esters, aldehydes, terpenes and more) plus carriers such as ethanol or propylene glycol. Formulas are trade secrets, so they appear on labels as just two words.
profile.function: Adds or restores specific tastes and aromas lost in processing, at parts-per-million concentrations.

mechanisms.title: Smell does most of the work
mechanisms.chemical: Flavor molecules are usually small and volatile, meaning they evaporate easily and drift into the air. When you chew, these molecules are released and travel from the back of your mouth up into your nose, a route called retronasal smell. There they meet the lining of the nose, which carries about 400 different types of smell receptors, each a protein shaped to bind certain molecules. Each aroma molecule can activate several receptor types, and each receptor can respond to several molecules. The overall pattern of activated receptors is what identifies a particular smell.
mechanisms.biological: Smell receptor cells send their signals to the olfactory bulb in the brain, which combines them with taste signals from the tongue and with sensations such as texture and temperature. The brain merges all of this into what we experience as flavor. Taste on its own only detects five qualities: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Everything else, like the difference between strawberry and raspberry, comes from smell. That is why food tastes bland when your nose is blocked by a cold.

mechanisms.title: Molecules, not sources
mechanisms.chemical: The smell of a strawberry comes from a mixture of molecules, such as furaneol, which smells sweet and caramel-like, and ethyl butyrate, which smells fruity. A natural strawberry flavor contains these same kinds of molecules, but under U.S. rules they don't have to come from strawberries. They might be extracted from another plant or produced by microbes through fermentation, as long as the source is natural. What makes a flavor “natural” is where its molecules came from and how they were processed, not their chemical structure. A molecule of ethyl butyrate is identical whatever its source.
mechanisms.biological: Your smell receptors respond to the shape and chemical properties of molecules, not to where they came from. Identical molecules bind receptors in exactly the same way, so they smell and taste identical whether they came from a fruit, a fermentation tank or a laboratory. Your body also digests and processes them the same way. So the label “natural” doesn't tell you whether a flavor is healthier or safer than an artificial one. It tells you about the source, which matters to some people for other reasons.

reactions.title: Steam distillation
reactions.summary: Steam distillation is one of the oldest ways to capture flavors and fragrances from plants. It separates volatile aroma molecules from plant material using steam, without the high temperatures that might destroy them. This is how essential oils of mint, citrus, cinnamon and many other spices are made. The method takes advantage of the fact that oily aroma compounds and water don't mix. People have used it for more than a thousand years.

steps.name: Heating
steps.text: Steam is passed through plant material, such as citrus peel, mint leaves or crushed spices, packed into a still. The hot steam bursts the tiny oil glands in the plant tissue. Aroma molecules are released.

steps.name: Carrying
steps.text: The volatile aroma molecules evaporate and travel along with the steam. Because a mixture of water and oil boils at a lower temperature than the oil alone, the aroma molecules evaporate below their own boiling points, which protects them from heat damage.

steps.name: Separating
steps.text: The steam and aroma vapors flow into a cooled tube, where they condense back into liquid. Since oil and water don't mix, the aroma compounds form a separate oily layer, the essential oil, which floats on the water and can be collected.

reactions.result: This is how mint, citrus and many spice flavors are captured. The leftover water, called a hydrosol or floral water, also carries a little scent and is used in some products. Many natural flavors begin with an essential oil made this way.

reactions.title: Fermentation to natural vanillin
reactions.summary: Vanillin is the main flavor molecule in vanilla, but real vanilla beans are expensive and supply only a tiny share of world demand. Most vanillin is made synthetically, but companies that want a “natural” label need vanillin from a natural source. One solution is to have microbes make it from a natural starting material. This process, called bioconversion, uses enzymes inside microbes to change one molecule into another. The resulting vanillin can legally be called natural.

steps.name: Feedstock
steps.text: Ferulic acid, a compound found in the cell walls of plants such as rice bran and corn, is the starting material. Its structure is similar to vanillin's but with a longer side chain. It is extracted and purified from plant waste.

steps.name: Bioconversion
steps.text: Selected bacteria or fungi are fed ferulic acid. Their enzymes shorten its three-carbon side chain by two carbons in a series of steps. This leaves an aldehyde group: a carbon double-bonded to oxygen with a hydrogen attached.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: The result is vanillin, which is collected from the fermentation broth and purified. It is chemically identical to the vanillin in vanilla beans.

reactions.result: Because a microbe made it from a natural source, it can legally be called natural, even though it's the same molecule as synthetic vanillin. Real vanilla extract, by contrast, contains hundreds of other aroma molecules besides vanillin, which give it a richer flavor.

regulatory.status: Defined as flavor derived from plant or animal sources whose primary function is flavor, not nutrition.
Industry-led expert panel reviews flavor substances; critics note limited FDA oversight.

hazards.title: Undisclosed components
hazards.summary: Natural flavors are generally safe, but consumers can't see exactly what's in them. A natural flavor may contain dozens of aroma molecules plus solvents, preservatives and carriers, all listed under just two words. Flavor companies keep their formulas secret as trade secrets. This lack of transparency can be frustrating for people with rare sensitivities or dietary restrictions. Major food allergens, however, must still be declared by law.
hazards.chemical: A typical natural flavor might contain esters, aldehydes, terpenes, ketones and other aroma molecules, along with carriers such as ethanol, propylene glycol or triacetin that help spread and preserve them. Other ingredients, called incidental additives, may be present in very small amounts. Because flavors are used so sparingly, each component ends up at a very low level in the food. Many of the molecules used in natural flavors are also found in everyday foods. The exact mixture varies from product to product.
hazards.biological: Most people have no reaction to natural flavors. But a small number of people with rare sensitivities, for example to certain plant compounds or particular carriers, can't pin down a trigger because the components aren't listed. People following vegan, kosher or halal diets also can't always tell whether a natural flavor came from an animal source without contacting the manufacturer. In the U.S., the nine major allergens, such as milk, eggs, soy and wheat, must be declared even when they are part of a flavoring. People with concerns can ask manufacturers for more details.

profile.dosage: Natural flavors typically make up less than 0.1 percent of a food, and each individual aroma molecule is often present at just parts per million. In the U.S., most flavoring substances are evaluated by the expert panel of the Flavor and Extract Manufacturers Association (FEMA), and those recognized as generally safe can be used without separate FDA approval. International experts (JECFA) also evaluate many flavoring substances. Because the amounts are so small, the safety margins for most flavor molecules are very large. People with specific dietary or allergy concerns can contact the manufacturer about a particular flavoring.

myths.claim: "Natural flavors" means the product contains that fruit.
myths.consensus: Strawberry natural flavor can be derived from other natural sources; it need not come from strawberries.

myths.claim: Natural flavors are safer than artificial ones.
myths.consensus: Many natural and artificial flavor molecules are chemically identical; the difference is where they come from, not how safe they are.

synthesis.title: Extraction, distillation and fermentation
synthesis.summary: Natural flavors are created by flavor companies, often called flavor houses, that combine natural ingredients into blends with specific tastes. The blends are designed by flavorists, specialists who train for years to recognize hundreds of aroma molecules. They start from natural raw materials such as fruits, spices, herbs, meats and microbial cultures. Different techniques are used to extract or produce the flavor molecules they need. The finished flavor is often a complex mixture designed to taste exactly the same in every batch of a product.
synthesis.mechanism: Raw materials are processed in several ways. Solvent extraction soaks plant material in ethanol or another food-safe solvent to dissolve flavor molecules out of it. Supercritical carbon dioxide extraction uses CO₂ under high pressure to pull out delicate aromas without heat. Steam distillation separates volatile oils, and fermentation uses microbes to make flavor molecules or to transform natural starting materials into new ones. Flavorists then blend dozens of these components with carriers into a proprietary formula and test it in the food it is meant for.
synthesis.significance: The flavor industry's own expert panel (FEMA) reviews most flavor substances, which critics say gives the FDA limited oversight.

citations.title: Diacetyl formation by lactic bacteria.
citations.abstract: Some of the most widely used products in the food industry are flavour compounds. These products can be obtained either by chemical synthesis and therefore are called synthetic or by fermentation thus called natural flavors. There is a tendency towards the use of natural products by the consumer, therefore there is an increasing industrial interest in them. One of these products is diacetyl, an important component in the flavor of butter, although others, like acetoin, acetaldehyde and 2,3-butanediol play a role in the flavor, they are present in trace amounts. The mixture of all these compounds produced during the lactic acid fermentation in suitable proportions is what gives butter its characteristic flavor. The most common metabolic route that produces diacetyl is the one starting from pyruvate, in this case it seems that the biosynthesis is related to the presence of citrate in the medium. An alternative route for the production is from acetaldehyde, in this route citrate does not seem to intervene. In the present paper a review of the mechanisms of formation of diacetyl by lactic acid bacteria, as well as the most important factors that influence the biosynthesis of this metabolite is made.

citations.title: Mycobacterium smegmatis acyltransferase: The big new player in biocatalysis.
citations.abstract: After several decades during which proteases and after lipases took the biotransformation world scene as the predominant biocatalysts, a new, promising enzyme was discovered and characterized. The acyltransferase from Mycobacterium smegmatis (MsAcT) has in fact an extraordinary activity for a wide array of reactions, such as trans-esterification, amidation, trans-amidation and perhydrolysis, both in water and solvent media, giving rise to a series of interesting compounds including APIs (i.e., active pharmaceutical ingredients), natural flavors and fragrances, monomers for polymer synthesis, and peracids employed as disinfectants or antimicrobials. Although the most used acylating agent has been ethyl acetate (EtOAc), depending on the reaction type also acetamide, dimethyl carbonate and a variety of other esters, have been reported. The best yields were reached using very reactive donors such as vinyl or isopropenyl esters (almost complete conversion in rapid reaction times and water media for condensation reactions). In this review article the most innovative scientific advances on MsAcT, its mechanism and engineering are summarized, putting a particular focus on the different kind of processes (batch and flow) that it is possible to carry out using this enzyme as free or immobilized form. In conclusion, the author personal view on the unexplored reaction possibilities using MsAcT is reported as a window on the future of the topic.

citations.title: Biosynthesis of monoterpenoid and sesquiterpenoid as natural flavors and fragrances.
citations.abstract: Terpenoids are a large class of plant-derived compounds, that constitute the main components of essential oils and are widely used as natural flavors and fragrances. The biosynthesis approach presents a promising alternative route in terpenoid production compared to plant extraction or chemical synthesis. In the past decade, the production of terpenoids using biotechnology has attracted broad attention from both academia and the industry. With the growing market of flavor and fragrance, the production of terpenoids directed by synthetic biology shows great potential in promoting future market prospects. Here, we reviewed the latest advances in terpenoid biosynthesis. The engineering strategies for biosynthetic terpenoids were systematically summarized from the enzyme, metabolic, and cellular dimensions. Additionally, we analyzed the key challenges from laboratory production to scalable production, such as key enzyme improvement, terpenoid toxicity, and volatility loss. To provide comprehensive technical guidance, we collected milestone examples of biosynthetic mono- and sesquiterpenoids, compared the current application status of chemical synthesis and biosynthesis in terpenoid production, and discussed the cost drivers based on the data of techno-economic assessment. It is expected to provide critical insights into developing translational research of terpenoid biomanufacturing.

citations.title: Synthetic Biology of Terpenoid and Flavonoid Natural Food Additives: Research Progress and Future Challenges.
citations.abstract: Food additives play an indispensable role in food processing, in which they improve taste, flavor, and appearance. Terpenoid and flavonoid natural food additives (NFAs), mostly derived from plants, are believed to be healthier and greener. However, limited supply and low yield result in high production costs. The development of synthetic biology technologies opens the door for the bioproduction of terpenoid and flavonoid NFAs. This account summarizes the biosynthetic routes of representative terpenoid and flavonoid NFAs, highlighting recent progress in the bioproduction of natural flavors, sweeteners, and pigments. Particularly, the frontier metabolic engineering strategies that aim to improve the production of terpenoid and flavonoid NFAs are also systematically summarized, including engineering the supply of the precursor, promoter engineering strategies, engineering cofactor supply, enzyme engineering, subcellular organelle engineering, biosensor-based dynamic regulation, and microbial consortia engineering. Finally, the prospects and challenges of synthetic biology for the production of NFAs are discussed.

name: Artificial Flavors
scoreRationale: Individually evaluated flavor chemicals at tiny levels, but undisclosed blends and their presence in ultra-processed foods lower the score.
summary: Artificial flavors are synthesized flavor molecules, often identical to natural ones. They're used in tiny amounts but aren't individually listed.

identity.composition: Blends of synthesized flavor molecules (for example vanillin, ethyl butyrate, benzaldehyde) plus carriers.

overview: Artificial flavors are flavor molecules made by chemical synthesis rather than taken from a natural source. Many are identical to molecules found in nature, such as vanillin, benzaldehyde (almond) or ethyl butyrate (pineapple); others don't occur naturally but are evaluated as safe at the tiny amounts used.
Because they're made in a controlled way, synthetic flavors are consistent, affordable and don't depend on harvests. A single flavor blend may combine dozens of them.
profile.function: Delivers consistent, affordable flavor profiles that do not depend on crop quality.

mechanisms.title: Esters: fruit in a molecule
mechanisms.chemical: Esters are molecules formed by joining an acid and an alcohol, with a characteristic –COO– group linking the two parts. Small esters, with fewer than about ten carbon atoms, are volatile, meaning they evaporate easily and float into the air where we can smell them. The exact size and shape of an ester decides which of our roughly 400 types of smell receptors it fits and activates. Changing the length of the carbon chains on either side of the ester group changes the smell. Adding or removing a single carbon atom can turn one fruity smell into another.
mechanisms.biological: When we smell or taste an ester, the brain interprets the pattern of activated smell receptors as a specific aroma. Isoamyl acetate smells like banana, ethyl butyrate like pineapple, and methyl anthranilate like grape. Many fruits contain these same esters naturally, and they help give each fruit its characteristic smell. Flavorists blend several esters with other molecules to create fuller, more realistic fruit flavors. Artificial grape flavor is based on methyl anthranilate from Concord grapes, which is why it tastes different from the green and red grapes most people eat.

mechanisms.title: Same receptors as natural flavors
mechanisms.chemical: A molecule's smell depends entirely on its structure: the atoms it contains, how they are connected and its 3D shape. Synthetic vanillin, made from petroleum-derived chemicals or wood pulp, has exactly the same structure as vanillin from a vanilla bean. Smell receptors in the nose bind molecules according to their shape and chemical properties. Because the molecules are identical, they bind the same receptors in the same way. There is no chemical difference for a receptor to detect.
mechanisms.biological: A molecule of synthetic vanillin and one from a vanilla bean are indistinguishable to your nose and your body. Your gut absorbs them the same way, and your liver breaks them down by the same pathways. Real vanilla extract does taste different from artificial vanilla, but that's because the extract contains hundreds of other molecules besides vanillin. The difference is in the mixture, not in the vanillin itself. Scientists can only tell where a sample of vanillin came from by measuring rare, heavier forms of carbon atoms called isotopes.

reactions.title: Fischer esterification
reactions.summary: Fischer esterification is a classic reaction used to make esters, including many of the fruity molecules in artificial flavors. It joins a carboxylic acid and an alcohol and releases a molecule of water. The German chemist Emil Fischer described it in 1895. It needs an acid catalyst, such as sulfuric acid, and usually some heat. Many high school chemistry classes make fruity-smelling esters this way as a lab experiment.

steps.name: Activation
steps.text: An acid catalyst adds a hydrogen ion (H⁺) to the oxygen of the carboxylic acid's C=O group. This makes the carbon attached to that oxygen even more electron-poor, so it becomes an easier target for attack.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: The oxygen atom of the alcohol, which has spare pairs of electrons, attacks the electron-poor carbon. A new bond forms between them, creating a short-lived structure with four groups attached to that carbon.

steps.name: Elimination
steps.text: After hydrogen ions shuffle between the oxygen atoms, one of the acid's original –OH groups leaves as a water molecule. The remaining structure gives up a hydrogen ion, which regenerates the catalyst, and the ester is formed.

reactions.result: Butyric acid smells like rancid butter, but its ethyl ester, ethyl butyrate, smells like pineapple, which shows how small structural changes can completely transform a smell. The reaction is reversible, so chemists often remove water as it forms to push the reaction toward making more ester.

reactions.title: Making vanillin from guaiacol
reactions.summary: Most of the world's vanillin is made synthetically, and the most common method today starts from a chemical called guaiacol. Guaiacol is a benzene ring carrying an –OH group and a methoxy group (–OCH₃), and it can be made from petroleum-derived chemicals. The process adds the aldehyde group that gives vanillin its flavor. It is efficient and produces very pure vanillin. Vanilla beans could never come close to supplying the world's demand for vanilla flavor.

steps.name: Condensation
steps.text: Guaiacol reacts with glyoxylic acid, a small molecule containing both an aldehyde and an acid group, in a basic solution. The glyoxylic acid attaches to the ring opposite the –OH group, adding a two-carbon side chain. The product is called vanillylmandelic acid.

steps.name: Oxidation
steps.text: The side chain is oxidized, often with air and a metal catalyst. This turns the –CH(OH)– group next to the ring into a C=O group. The side chain is now a keto acid.

steps.name: Decarboxylation
steps.text: When the molecule is heated in acid, its carboxylic acid group (–COOH) breaks off as carbon dioxide gas. What remains on the ring is an aldehyde group (–CHO), and the molecule is now vanillin.

reactions.result: Vanilla beans can't come close to meeting world demand, so synthetic vanillin flavors most vanilla foods, at a tiny fraction of the cost of vanillin from beans. An older route made vanillin from lignin, a byproduct of papermaking.

regulatory.status: Permitted synthetic flavoring substances are listed in federal regulations; others are GRAS through FEMA review.
Removed seven synthetic flavors, including pulegone and benzophenone, from the permitted list.

hazards.title: Undisclosed blends
hazards.summary: Like natural flavors, artificial flavors usually appear on labels as a single term, even when they contain many different chemicals. Individual flavoring substances are evaluated for safety, but consumers can't see which ones are in a particular product. In 2018 the U.S. FDA removed seven synthetic flavoring substances from its list of permitted food additives after high-dose animal studies showed they could cause cancer. The decision rested on a legal rule rather than evidence of harm at the tiny amounts actually used. Still, it highlighted how little consumers know about specific flavor ingredients.
hazards.chemical: An artificial flavor blend may contain esters, aldehydes, ketones, alcohols and other synthetic molecules chosen to recreate or invent a taste. In the U.S., each substance must either be approved by the FDA or recognized as safe through expert review. The seven substances removed in 2018 were benzophenone, ethyl acrylate, eugenyl methyl ether, myrcene, pulegone, pyridine and styrene. In animal studies, very high doses of these substances caused tumors. A U.S. law called the Delaney Clause bans any food additive shown to cause cancer in animals, regardless of dose.
hazards.biological: The amounts of flavor chemicals in foods are tiny, usually parts per million, far below the doses that caused effects in animal studies. The FDA stated that the seven removed substances posed no risk to public health at the levels used, but the law required their removal. Most people experience no effects at all from artificial flavors. However, people with specific sensitivities can't easily identify a trigger when ingredients aren't listed. Some consumers avoid artificial flavors to limit their exposure to undisclosed chemicals.

profile.dosage: Artificial flavors are usually present at parts per million, meaning a gram of flavoring may flavor a kilogram or more of food. Each individual flavoring substance is evaluated for safety at these levels by the FDA, the FEMA expert panel or international experts (JECFA), and the safety margins are typically very large because so little is used. In the U.S., the Delaney Clause bans any additive shown to cause cancer in animals at any dose, which led to the 2018 removal of seven flavor substances. People who prefer to avoid artificial flavors can check ingredient labels.

myths.claim: Artificial flavors are made in labs, so they must be worse.
myths.consensus: Synthetic vanillin is the same molecule as vanillin from vanilla beans.

synthesis.title: Chemical synthesis
synthesis.summary: Artificial flavor molecules are made in chemical plants using standard organic chemistry reactions. The starting materials, called feedstocks, may come from petroleum or from plant sources such as wood, turpentine or plant oils. Each target molecule is made separately, purified to a high standard and then blended with others by flavorists. Because every molecule is made under controlled conditions, the flavors are consistent from batch to batch. They are also far cheaper than extracting flavors from natural sources.
synthesis.mechanism: Chemists choose a route for each flavor molecule based on its structure. Esters are made by Fischer esterification, joining an acid and an alcohol with an acid catalyst. Aldehydes, such as benzaldehyde, the main flavor of almond and cherry, can be made by oxidizing alcohols or other starting materials. Some molecules need several steps, each one adding or changing part of the structure. After each reaction the product is separated and purified, often by distillation or crystallization, to remove byproducts and leftover starting materials, and flavorists then blend dozens of these molecules into the final flavor.
synthesis.significance: Ferdinand Tiemann and Wilhelm Haarmann synthesized vanillin in 1874, launching the synthetic flavor industry.

citations.title: Common confounders of dietary elimination trials contain the antigens soy, pork, and beef.
citations.abstract: Nutritionists and dermatologists recommend avoiding flavored over-the-counter (OTC) products and medications during dietary elimination trials because those products are thought to contain common proteins that may confound the trial. The objective of this study was to determine if there are soy, pork, and beef antigens in flavored OTC products and medications and, if so, could those antigens be identified. Seven products, three OTC products and four veterinary therapeutics, were tested using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) for the presence of soy, pork, and beef antigens, in addition to positive and negative controls. All OTC test products produced ELISA results in agreement with their ingredient lists. ELISA testing of veterinary therapeutic products did not agree with either their ingredient lists or product inserts because of other ingredients not listed. Veterinarians should contact manufacturers of oral therapeutics prior to prescribing them to determine other ingredients. Likewise, manufacturers should be contacted regarding "natural and artificial flavors." Lastly, gelatin capsules may contain either beef or pork proteins and should not be administered during a trial. In conclusion, flavored medications contain the common antigens soy, pork, and beef although they may or may not be listed on the ingredient list or product insert.

citations.title: Yeast Fermentation at Low Temperatures: Adaptation to Changing Environmental Conditions and Formation of Volatile Compounds.
citations.abstract: Yeast plays a key role in the production of fermented foods and beverages, such as bread, wine, and other alcoholic beverages. They are able to produce and release from the fermentation environment large numbers of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). This is the reason for the great interest in the possibility of adapting these microorganisms to fermentation at reduced temperatures. By doing this, it would be possible to obtain better sensory profiles of the final products. It can reduce the addition of artificial flavors and enhancements to food products and influence other important factors of fermented food production. Here, we reviewed the genetic and physiological mechanisms by which yeasts adapt to low temperatures. Next, we discussed the importance of VOCs for the food industry, their biosynthesis, and the most common volatiles in fermented foods and described the beneficial impact of decreased temperature as a factor that contributes to improving the composition of the sensory profiles of fermented foods.

citations.title: Atmospheric isoprene and monoterpenes in a typical urban area of Beijing: Pollution characterization, chemical reactivity and source identification.
citations.abstract: Continuous observation of isoprene, α-pinene and β-pinene was carried out in a typical urban area of Beijing from March 2014 to February 2015, using an AirmoVOC online analyzer. Based on the analysis of the ambient level and variation characteristics of isoprene, α-pinene and β-pinene, the chemical reactivity was studied, and their sources were identified. Results showed that the concentrations of isoprene, α-pinene and β-pinene in the urban area of Beijing were lower than those in richly vegetated areas; the concentrations of isoprene were at a moderate level compared with those of previous studies of Beijing. Concentrations of isoprene, α-pinene and β-pinene showed different seasonal, monthly, daily and diurnal variations, and all of the three species showed higher level at night than those in the daytime as a whole, the variations of isoprene, α-pinene and β-pinene mainly influenced by emission of sources, photochemical reaction, and meteorological parameters. Isoprene was the largest contributor to the total OFP values than α-pinene and β-pinene. α-Pinene was the largest contributor to the total SOAFP values than isoprene and β-pinene in autumn, while isoprene was the largest one in other seasons. Isoprene, α-pinene and β-pinene were derived mainly from biological sources; and α-pinene level were also affected by industrial sources. To reduce the concentrations of isoprene, α-pinene and β-pinene, it is necessary to scientifically select urban green plant species, and more strict control measures should be taken to reduce the emission of α-pinene from industrial sources, such as artificial flavors and resins synthesis processes.

citations.title: The chemical jungle: today's beef industry.
citations.abstract: In the absence of effective federal regulation, the meat industry uses hundreds of animal feed additives, including antibiotics, tranquilizers, pesticides, animal drugs, artificial flavors, industrial wastes, and growth-promoting hormones, with little or no concern about the carcinogenic and other toxic effects of dietary residues of these additives. Illustratively, after decades of misleading assurances of the safety of diethylstilbestrol (DES) and its use as a growth-promoting animal-feed additive, the United States finally banned its use in 1979 some 40 years after it was first shown to be carcinogenic. The meat industry then promptly switched to other carcinogenic additives, particularly the natural sex hormones estradiol, progesterone, and testosterone, which are implanted in the ears of more than 90 percent of commercially raised feedlot cattle. Unlike the synthetic DES, residues of which can be monitored and use of which was conditional on a seven-day preslaughter withdrawal period, residues of natural hormones are not detectable, since they cannot be practically differentiated from the same hormones produced by the body. The relationship between recently increasing cancer rates and the lifetime exposure of the U.S. population to dietary residues of these and other unlabeled carcinogenic feed additives is a matter of critical public health concern.

name: Titanium Dioxide
scoreRationale: An effective, well-tolerated sunscreen filter on skin, but banned as a food additive in the EU over unresolved genotoxicity concerns, and its powder is a possible carcinogen when inhaled.
summary: Titanium dioxide is a bright white mineral pigment and sunscreen filter. On skin it's protective; in food and inhaled powders it's under scrutiny.

overview: Titanium dioxide (TiO₂) is a mineral of titanium and oxygen locked in a rigid crystal lattice; its common forms are rutile and anatase. Its refractive index (about 2.6 for rutile) is one of the highest of any common substance, so it bends and scatters light extremely strongly, making it intensely white and opaque.

It is also a semiconductor. Ultraviolet light carries enough energy to push its electrons across the band gap, which lets TiO₂ absorb UV radiation (useful in sunscreen) but can also generate reactive oxygen species, which is why cosmetic grades are coated.
profile.function: Makes candy coatings, frosting and toothpaste opaque white; in sunscreen it reflects, scatters and absorbs UV light.

mechanisms.title: Scattering light into whiteness
mechanisms.chemical: When light passes from one material into another, it bends, and the amount of bending is measured by the refractive index. Titanium dioxide has one of the highest refractive indices of any common material, about 2.6 for its rutile form, compared with about 1.5 for glass. When TiO₂ particles are mixed into paint, plastic or food, the big difference between the particles and their surroundings makes light bounce and scatter strongly at each particle's surface. Particles about 200 to 300 nanometers across, roughly half the wavelength of visible light, scatter all visible colors most efficiently. Because none of the colors is absorbed, essentially all of the light is scattered.
mechanisms.biological: When every color of visible light is scattered evenly back toward our eyes, we see the result as brilliant white. That's why TiO₂ is used to whiten paint, paper, plastics, toothpaste, sunscreen and some candies and frostings. Its strong scattering also makes it opaque, so it hides whatever is underneath. A thin layer of TiO₂ paint can cover a dark wall in fewer coats than other white pigments. In medicines, it makes tablets and capsules opaque, which can protect light-sensitive ingredients inside.

mechanisms.title: Blocking UV in sunscreen
mechanisms.chemical: Titanium dioxide is a semiconductor, a material whose electrons can jump up to a higher energy level if they absorb enough energy. The minimum energy needed, called the band gap, is about 3.0 to 3.2 electron volts for TiO₂. Ultraviolet light, with wavelengths shorter than about 400 nanometers, carries more energy than this, so it gets absorbed. Visible light carries less, so it passes. In sunscreens, TiO₂ is often ground into nanoparticles, which scatter much less visible light, so they look nearly clear on the skin while still absorbing UV.
mechanisms.biological: Ultraviolet radiation from the sun damages skin cells by breaking bonds in DNA and producing harmful reactive molecules. Over time this can cause sunburn, premature aging and skin cancer, including melanoma. By absorbing and scattering UV before it reaches living skin cells, TiO₂ cuts down that damage. It works mainly against UVB rays, which cause sunburn, and also blocks some UVA. Mineral sunscreens containing TiO₂ and zinc oxide are often recommended for sensitive skin because they rarely cause irritation.

mechanisms.title: Nanoparticles in food
mechanisms.chemical: Food-grade titanium dioxide, known in Europe as E171, contains particles of many sizes, and a share of them, by number sometimes a third or more, are smaller than 100 nanometers, which counts as nanoscale. Particles this small have a lot of surface area compared with their volume and can behave differently from larger ones. Studies have shown that a small proportion can cross the lining of the gut and enter the blood. Under some conditions, especially in light, TiO₂ particles can generate reactive oxygen species, molecules that can damage cells and DNA. In the dark of the gut, however, this light-driven effect is minimal.
mechanisms.biological: Animal studies found that small amounts of TiO₂ particles can accumulate in tissues such as the liver, spleen and intestinal lining. Some rodent studies suggested changes in the gut's immune cells and possible links to inflammation and precancerous changes in the colon, though the results were mixed. In 2021 the European Food Safety Authority concluded that it couldn't rule out that TiO₂ damages DNA, so it couldn't set a safe level. Based on that, the European Union banned TiO₂ as a food additive from 2022. Other regulators, including the U.S. FDA, have not found enough evidence to ban it.

reactions.title: Photocatalysis
reactions.summary: When titanium dioxide absorbs ultraviolet light, it doesn't just block it; it can also use that energy to drive chemical reactions on its surface. This is called photocatalysis, because light switches TiO₂ on as a catalyst. It produces highly reactive radicals that can break down organic molecules, including grime, bacteria and pollutants. The property is useful for self-cleaning surfaces but unwanted in sunscreens and cosmetics. Manufacturers control it by choosing the type of TiO₂ and coating the particles.

steps.name: Excitation
steps.text: A UV photon is absorbed by a TiO₂ particle, giving one of its electrons enough energy to jump across the band gap into a higher-energy level called the conduction band. This leaves behind a positively charged gap, called a hole, in the lower level. Both the electron and the hole can move through the crystal.

steps.name: Radicals
steps.text: At the particle's surface, the hole takes an electron from a water molecule, forming a hydroxyl radical (•OH). The excited electron passes itself to an oxygen molecule, forming superoxide (O₂•⁻). Both are extremely reactive.

steps.name: Oxidation
steps.text: These radicals attack organic molecules on the surface, such as grease, dirt or bacteria, breaking their bonds. Repeated attacks gradually break the molecules down into simpler substances, eventually carbon dioxide and water.

reactions.result: This powers self-cleaning glass and some air purifiers, where sunlight helps break down grime. Coating cosmetic TiO₂ with silica or alumina switches the effect off on your skin by keeping radicals from forming there. The rutile form of TiO₂ is also less photoactive than the anatase form, so it is preferred in sunscreens.

reactions.title: The chloride process
reactions.summary: The chloride process is one of the two main ways to purify titanium dioxide from its ore. It works by turning the titanium in the ore into a gas, purifying that gas, and then turning it back into solid TiO₂. This produces very pure, bright white pigment. The process was developed by the chemical company DuPont in the 1950s. Chlorine, the key reagent, is recycled and reused.

steps.name: Chlorination
steps.text: Rutile ore, which is mostly TiO₂, is mixed with coke (a form of carbon) and reacted with chlorine gas at about 1,000 °C. The carbon removes oxygen from the titanium and chlorine takes its place, forming titanium tetrachloride (TiCl₄). At that temperature TiCl₄ is a gas, so it separates from the leftover solid.

steps.name: Purification
steps.text: The TiCl₄ gas is cooled into a liquid and distilled to remove iron, vanadium and other metal chlorides formed from impurities in the ore. Because each chloride boils at a different temperature, they separate cleanly. The result is very pure TiCl₄.

steps.name: Oxidation
steps.text: The purified TiCl₄ is burned with pure oxygen at about 1,500 °C. This forms solid titanium dioxide particles and releases the chlorine again. By controlling the temperature and adding small amounts of other chemicals, manufacturers can make particles of the ideal size for scattering light.

reactions.result: Recycling the chlorine makes the process efficient and the product very pure. The chloride process now produces most of the world's high-grade TiO₂ pigment.

regulatory.status: No longer considered safe as a food additive; E171 banned in EU food since 2022.
Permitted color additive in food and a sunscreen active ingredient.
regulatory.limit: Up to 1% of food by weight (21 CFR 73.575); up to 25% in sunscreen

regulatory.status: Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic) based on inhalation of powder in rats.

hazards.title: Food additive concerns (EU ban)
hazards.summary: Titanium dioxide was banned as a food additive in the European Union in 2022, but it is still permitted in U.S. food at up to 1 percent by weight. It was used to make candies, frostings, chewing gum and some sauces and dairy products look whiter and brighter. The EU decision was based on uncertainty rather than proven harm: regulators couldn't rule out that its nanoparticles might damage DNA. Many food companies have since removed it from their products worldwide. It is still allowed in medicines and cosmetics in the EU.
hazards.chemical: Food-grade TiO₂ contains a mix of particle sizes, including nanoscale particles smaller than 100 nanometers. These tiny particles have a large surface area and may be able to cross the gut lining in small amounts. Studies in cells suggest TiO₂ particles may generate reactive oxygen species, which can damage DNA and cell membranes. They may also trigger inflammation in some immune cells. How much of this happens in the human body at normal intakes, though, is not well understood.
hazards.biological: The European Food Safety Authority reviewed the evidence in 2021 and concluded that it couldn't exclude the possibility that TiO₂ damages DNA, a property called genotoxicity. For substances that might damage DNA, regulators usually can't set a safe threshold, so EFSA concluded TiO₂ could no longer be considered safe as a food additive. No harm in people has been directly demonstrated. Agencies in the U.S., U.K. and Canada reviewed similar evidence and did not ban it. The disagreement shows how regulators can reach different conclusions from the same uncertain evidence.

hazards.title: Inhaled powder
hazards.summary: Breathing in large amounts of fine titanium dioxide powder over long periods may harm the lungs. This is mainly a concern for workers in factories that produce or handle TiO₂ powder. For consumers, the relevant products are loose powders, such as some makeup, and sprays. TiO₂ in lotions, creams and paints isn't a lung concern because it isn't breathed in. Choosing pressed rather than loose powders and using sprays in well-ventilated spaces reduces exposure.
hazards.chemical: When fine particles are breathed in, the smallest ones can travel deep into the lungs and reach the tiny air sacs called alveoli. TiO₂ particles are insoluble, meaning they don't dissolve in lung fluid. Immune cells called macrophages try to clear them by swallowing them up, but with heavy exposure they can become overloaded. The particles then stay in the lungs for a long time. Persistent particles can cause ongoing irritation and inflammation.
hazards.biological: In long-term studies, rats exposed to very high levels of TiO₂ dust developed chronic lung inflammation, and some developed lung tumors. Because of these results, the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies inhaled TiO₂ as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B). Studies of workers in TiO₂ factories haven't shown a clear rise in lung cancer, and rats may be especially sensitive to this kind of particle overload. Workplaces control exposure with ventilation and masks. For consumers, avoiding breathing in loose powders and sprays is a sensible precaution.

profile.dosage: In the United States, titanium dioxide may make up to 1 percent of a food's weight and is used in some candies, frostings and coatings; in the European Union it has been banned from food since 2022. Studies estimate that children have higher dietary exposure than adults, mainly from sweets. In sunscreens it is used at up to 25 percent and is not absorbed through intact skin. Mineral makeup and loose powders may contain it in a form that can be breathed in, so pressed powders and good ventilation reduce exposure. The key safety distinction is between swallowing it, putting it on skin and breathing it in.

myths.claim: Mineral sunscreens with TiO2 get into your bloodstream.
myths.consensus: Studies show it stays on the skin's surface; FDA absorption concerns focused on chemical filters like oxybenzone.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low for coated bulk grades; nanoparticle effects are under study.

synthesis.title: Chloride process
synthesis.summary: The chloride process is the main route for making high-purity titanium dioxide pigment today. It was developed by DuPont in the 1950s and produces very bright white pigment with consistent particle sizes. The process uses chlorine to turn titanium ore into a gas that can be purified by distillation. Afterward the chlorine is recovered and reused. It requires high-grade ores, such as rutile or upgraded ilmenite.
synthesis.mechanism: Titanium ore is ground, mixed with coke, a nearly pure form of carbon, and reacted with chlorine gas in a reactor at around 1,000 °C. The carbon removes oxygen from the ore as carbon dioxide, while chlorine bonds to the titanium to form titanium tetrachloride (TiCl₄), a volatile liquid that boils at 136 °C. The gaseous TiCl₄ is collected, cooled and distilled to separate it from other metal chlorides. The purified TiCl₄ is then burned in pure oxygen, forming fine TiO₂ particles and releasing the chlorine. Finally, the particles are coated with materials such as silica or alumina to improve their performance, then dried and milled.
synthesis.significance: The same titanium tetrachloride is also the starting point for making titanium metal, used in aircraft and medical implants.

synthesis.title: Sulfate process
synthesis.summary: The sulfate process is the older method for making titanium dioxide, first used commercially in the 1910s and 1920s. It starts with ilmenite, an ore containing both iron and titanium, and uses sulfuric acid to dissolve it. The process is simpler but produces more waste, particularly iron sulfate and dilute acid. It can make both the anatase and rutile forms of TiO₂. It is still widely used today, especially in China.
synthesis.mechanism: Ilmenite ore (FeTiO₃) is ground and digested, meaning dissolved, in hot concentrated sulfuric acid, producing a solution of titanium and iron sulfates. The solution is cooled so that iron sulfate crystallizes out and can be removed. Next, the solution is diluted and heated, which makes the titanium react with water and form solid hydrated titanium dioxide that settles out. This solid is filtered, washed and heated to about 900 °C in a kiln, a step called calcination, which drives off water and leftover acid and turns it into crystalline TiO₂. The product is then milled and treated to give it the right properties.
synthesis.significance: TiO₂ replaced toxic lead white in paints during the 20th century.

citations.title: In-Depth Characterization of the Clostridioides difficile Phosphoproteome to Identify Ser/Thr Kinase Substrates.
citations.authors: Garcia-Garcia, Douché, Giai Gianetto et al.
citations.abstract: Clostridioides difficile is the leading cause of postantibiotic diarrhea in adults. During infection, the bacterium must rapidly adapt to the host environment by using survival strategies. Protein phosphorylation is a reversible post-translational modification employed ubiquitously for signal transduction and cellular regulation. Hanks-type serine/threonine kinases (STKs) and serine/threonine phosphatases have emerged as important players in bacterial cell signaling and pathogenicity. C. difficile encodes two STKs (PrkC and CD2148) and one phosphatase. We optimized a titanium dioxide phosphopeptide enrichment approach to determine the phosphoproteome of C. difficile. We identified and quantified 2500 proteins representing 63% of the theoretical proteome. To identify STK and serine/threonine phosphatase targets, we then performed comparative large-scale phosphoproteomics of the WT strain and isogenic ΔprkC, CD2148, Δstp, and prkC CD2148 mutants. We detected 635 proteins containing phosphorylated peptides. We showed that PrkC is phosphorylated on multiple sites in vivo and autophosphorylates in vitro. We were unable to detect a phosphorylation for CD2148 in vivo, whereas this kinase was phosphorylated in vitro only in the presence of PrkC. Forty-one phosphoproteins were identified as phosphorylated under the control of CD2148, whereas 114 proteins were phosphorylated under the control of PrkC including 27 phosphoproteins more phosphorylated in the ∆stp mutant. We also observed enrichment for phosphothreonine among the phosphopeptides more phosphorylated in the Δstp mutant.
