Both kinases targeted pathways required for metabolism, translation, and stress response, whereas cell division and peptidoglycan metabolism were more specifically controlled by PrkC-dependent phosphorylation in agreement with the phenotypes of the ΔprkC mutant. Using a combination of approaches, we confirmed that FtsK was phosphorylated in vivo under the control of PrkC and that Spo0A was a substrate of PrkC in vitro. This study provides a detailed mapping of kinase-substrate relationships in C. difficile, paving the way for the identification of new biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

citations.title: Dysregulation of splicing proteins in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
citations.abstract: Signaling plays an important role in regulating all cellular pathways. Altered signaling is one of the hallmarks of cancers. Phosphoproteomics enables interrogation of kinase mediated signaling pathways in biological systems. In cancers, this approach can be utilized to identify aberrantly activated pathways that potentially drive proliferation and tumorigenesis. To identify signaling alterations in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), we carried out proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis of HNSCC cell lines using a combination of tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling approach and titanium dioxide-based enrichment. We identified 4,920 phosphosites corresponding to 2,212 proteins in six HNSCC cell lines compared to a normal oral cell line. Our data indicated significant enrichment of proteins associated with splicing. We observed hyperphosphorylation of SRSF protein kinase 2 (SRPK2) and its downstream substrates in HNSCC cell lines. SRPK2 is a splicing kinase, known to phosphorylate serine/arginine (SR) rich domain proteins and regulate splicing process in eukaryotes. Although genome-wide studies have reported the contribution of alternative splicing events of several genes in the progression of cancer, the involvement of splicing kinases in HNSCC is not known. In this study, we studied the role of SRPK2 in HNSCC. Inhibition of SRPK2 resulted in significant decrease in colony forming and invasive ability in a panel of HNSCC cell lines. Our results indicate that phosphorylation of SRPK2 plays a crucial role in the regulation of splicing process in HNSCC and that splicing kinases can be developed as a new class of therapeutic target in HNSCC.

citations.title: Safety of titanium dioxide nanoparticles in cosmetics.
citations.abstract: Titanium dioxide (TiO2 ) is widely used in a variety of products including cosmetics. TiO2 in its nanoparticle form (nano-TiO2 ) is now the only form used as an ultraviolet (UV) filter in sunscreens, but also in some day creams, foundations and lip balms. While its efficacy as a UV filter is proven in the prevention of skin cancers and sunburns, some concerns have been raised about its safety. Indeed, considering its small size, nano-TiO2 is suspected to penetrate dermal, respiratory or gastrointestinal barriers, disseminate in the body and therefore constitute a potential risk to the consumer. At the skin level, most studies performed in humans or animals showed that nano-TiO2 did not penetrate beyond the outer layers of stratum corneum to viable cells and did not reach the general circulation, either in healthy or in compromised skin. The Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) considers nano-TiO2 as a non-sensitizer and as mild- or non-irritant to skin and concludes in no evidence of carcinogenicity (supported by the European Chemicals Agency), mutagenicity or reproductive toxicity after dermal exposure to nano-TiO2 . According to the SCCS, nano-TiO2 from sunscreens does not present any health risk when applied on the skin at a concentration up to 25%. However, the SCCS does not recommend the use of nano-TiO2 in formulations that may lead to exposure of the consumer's lungs by inhalation (sprayable products and powders). Indeed, even if human data are sparse and inconsistent, lung inflammation was reported in animals. In 2016, the EU Cosmetic Regulation made nano-TiO2 as an authorized UV filter, except in products that could lead to exposure of the lungs. After oral exposure, nano-TiO2 absorption and toxicity are limited. The incidental oral exposure to nano-TiO2 contained in lip balms is thus not expected to induce adverse health effects.

citations.title: Sunscreens part 2: Regulation and safety.
citations.authors: Abdel Azim, Bainvoll, Vecerek et al.
citations.abstract: The second part of this CME article discusses sunscreen regulation and safety considerations for humans and the environment. First, we provide an overview of the history of the US Food and Drug Administration's regulation of sunscreen. Recent Food and Drug Administration studies clearly demonstrate that organic ultraviolet filters are systemically absorbed during routine sunscreen use, but to date there is no evidence of associated negative health effects. We also review the current evidence of sunscreen's association with vitamin D levels and frontal fibrosing alopecia, and recent concerns regarding benzene contamination. Finally, we review the possible environmental effects of ultraviolet filters, particularly coral bleaching. While climate change has been shown to be the primary driver of coral bleaching, laboratory-based studies suggest that organic ultraviolet filters represent an additional contributing factor, which led several localities to ban certain organic filters.

citations.title: Nanomaterials and neurodegeneration.
citations.authors: Migliore, Uboldi, Di Bucchianico et al.
citations.abstract: The increasing application of nanotechnology in various industrial, environmental, and human settings raises questions surrounding the potential adverse effects induced by nanosized materials to human health, including the possible neurotoxic and neuroinflammatory properties of those substances and their capability to induce neurodegeneration. In this review, a panel of metal oxide nanoparticles (NPs), namely titanium dioxide, silicon dioxide, zinc oxide, copper oxide, iron NPs, and carbon nanotubes have been focused. An overview has been provided of the in vitro and in vivo evidence of adverse effects to the central nervous system. Research indicated that these nanomaterials (NMs) not only reach the brain, but also can cause a certain degree of brain tissue damage, including cytotoxicity, genotoxicity, induction of oxidative stress, and inflammation, all potentially involved in the onset and progression of neurodegeneration. Surface chemistry of the NMs may play an important role in their localization and subsequent effects on the brain of rodents. In addition, NM shape differences may induce varying degrees of neurotoxicity. However, one of the potential biomedical applications of NMs is nanodevices for early diagnostic and novel therapeutic approaches to counteract age related diseases. In this context, engineered NMs were promising vehicles to carry diagnostic and therapeutic compounds across the blood-brain barrier, thereby representing very timely and attractive theranostic tools in neurodegenerative diseases. Therefore, a careful assessment of the risk-benefit ratio must be taken into consideration in using nanosized materials.

name: BHT
scoreRationale: Permitted at low levels, but mixed animal data (tumor promotion and inhibition) and possible endocrine effects keep it under review.
summary: BHT is a synthetic antioxidant that keeps cereals, fats and cosmetics from going rancid. Regulators allow it; some scientists want a fresh look.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in fats and oils

overview: BHT (butylated hydroxytoluene) is a phenol, a benzene ring carrying an –OH group, flanked on both sides by bulky tert-butyl groups. Chemists call it a hindered phenol: the big groups crowd around the –OH like bodyguards.

That crowding is the secret to its job. When BHT gives up the hydrogen of its –OH to stop a free radical, the radical left behind on BHT is shielded by the bulky groups and too stable to start new chain reactions. BHT dissolves in fats, so it protects oils, cereals and cosmetics from going rancid.
profile.function: Prevents oxidation of fats and oils in cereals, chewing gum and cosmetics.

mechanisms.title: Scavenging free radicals
mechanisms.chemical: When fats and oils are exposed to oxygen, free radicals form: molecules with an unpaired electron that set off chain reactions of damage. A peroxyl radical (ROO•), created when oxygen attacks a fat molecule, is a key link in that chain. BHT stops it by donating the hydrogen atom from its –OH group, which turns the peroxyl radical into a stable hydroperoxide. What's left on BHT is a phenoxyl radical, but its unpaired electron is spread out over the benzene ring, a stabilizing effect called resonance. On top of that, the two bulky tert-butyl groups on either side physically block the radical from reaching and attacking other molecules.
mechanisms.biological: By breaking the chain early, BHT keeps the fats in breakfast cereals, chewing gum, snack foods and cosmetics from oxidizing. Oxidized fats taste and smell rancid, like stale crackers or old cardboard, and can lose nutritional value. With BHT, products stay fresh for months. In cereals it is often added to the packaging liner rather than the food itself, and small amounts slowly migrate into the cereal. BHT is also used in rubber, plastics and jet fuel for the same reason.

mechanisms.title: Liver metabolism
mechanisms.chemical: When BHT is eaten, it is absorbed and carried to the liver, where a family of enzymes called cytochrome P450 work to make it easier to excrete. These enzymes add oxygen atoms to BHT's methyl group and tert-butyl groups. One product of this process is a quinone methide, a reactive molecule that can bond to proteins and other molecules in the cell. Most BHT and its breakdown products are eventually attached to other molecules and excreted in urine and feces. Because BHT dissolves in fat, though, small amounts can be stored in body fat.
mechanisms.biological: In rats and mice given high doses of BHT, the liver grew larger as it made extra enzymes to process the chemical. High doses also affected the thyroid gland and, in mice, the lungs. Some BHT breakdown products can bind to proteins in cells, which may explain some of these effects. These high-dose findings are why regulators set a relatively low acceptable daily intake for BHT compared with many other additives. At normal dietary levels, such effects are not expected.

mechanisms.title: Mixed animal cancer data
mechanisms.chemical: BHT's effects on cancer in animal studies are surprisingly mixed. When given before or alongside known cancer-causing chemicals, BHT sometimes reduced tumors, perhaps because it boosted the liver enzymes that detoxify carcinogens or because of its antioxidant activity. When given after a carcinogen, it sometimes increased tumors, possibly by encouraging damaged cells to grow. The outcome depended on the dose, the timing, the animal species and the organ studied. BHT itself doesn't appear to damage DNA directly.
mechanisms.biological: Because of these conflicting results, the International Agency for Research on Cancer lists BHT as “not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans” (Group 3), meaning there isn't enough evidence either way. The doses in animal studies were typically hundreds or thousands of times higher than what people eat. Some researchers have even studied BHT as a possible protective agent, though that hasn't been shown either. Regulators continue to allow it at low levels with safety margins. Some food companies have removed it anyway in response to consumer concern.

reactions.title: Hydrogen-atom transfer
reactions.summary: BHT protects fats through a reaction called hydrogen-atom transfer, in which it hands a single hydrogen atom, a proton together with an electron, to a free radical. This turns a dangerous, reactive radical into a stable molecule and stops the chain reaction of oxidation. BHT's special structure, with bulky groups guarding its reactive –OH, makes the radical it leaves behind unusually stable. Antioxidants built this way are called hindered phenols. Many antioxidants used in foods, plastics and fuels work on the same principle.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: As fat oxidizes, oxygen reacts with fat molecules to form peroxyl radicals (ROO•), which are reactive and want to steal a hydrogen atom. Normally they would take it from another fat molecule, keeping the chain going. Instead, a peroxyl radical collides with a BHT molecule.

steps.name: Transfer
steps.text: BHT's O–H bond is relatively weak, so it gives up its hydrogen atom easily. The peroxyl radical takes it and becomes a hydroperoxide (ROOH), a stable molecule that doesn't continue the chain. The fat molecules nearby are spared.

steps.name: Stabilization
steps.text: BHT is left as a phenoxyl radical with an unpaired electron on its oxygen. That electron spreads out over the benzene ring, which lowers its energy. The two large tert-butyl groups crowd around the oxygen and stop it from reacting with anything else.

reactions.result: Each BHT molecule can stop up to two radical chains before it is used up, because its phenoxyl radical can trap a second radical. So a small amount of BHT protects a large amount of fat. Eventually, though, all the BHT is consumed and oxidation picks up again.

reactions.title: Friedel–Crafts alkylation (how it's made)
reactions.summary: BHT is made by attaching two bulky tert-butyl groups to a simpler molecule called p-cresol, using a classic reaction called Friedel–Crafts alkylation. The reaction, developed by Charles Friedel and James Crafts in 1877, attaches carbon groups to aromatic rings. It works by generating a positively charged carbon fragment called a carbocation, which attacks the ring. Where the new groups attach is steered by the –OH group already on the ring. The same type of reaction is used to make many antioxidants for fuels, plastics and rubber.

steps.name: Carbocation
steps.text: Isobutylene, a small gas with a carbon–carbon double bond, is treated with an acid catalyst. The acid adds a hydrogen ion to the double bond, forming a tert-butyl carbocation, a carbon atom with only three bonds and a positive charge. This carbocation is very hungry for electrons.

steps.name: Substitution
steps.text: p-Cresol's –OH group pushes electrons into the benzene ring, making the positions right next to it especially electron-rich. The carbocation attacks one of these positions, and a hydrogen on the ring is replaced by the tert-butyl group. This is called electrophilic aromatic substitution.

steps.name: Repeat
steps.text: The reaction happens again on the other side of the –OH group, adding a second tert-butyl group. Now the –OH is flanked by two bulky groups and the BHT molecule is complete. The product is purified to remove molecules that picked up only one tert-butyl group.

reactions.result: The two bulky groups are what make BHT an effective antioxidant, shielding its radical from further reactions. The same reaction type is used to make many antioxidants for fuels, plastics and rubber.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
regulatory.limit: Up to 0.02% of the fat content (21 CFR 182.3173)

regulatory.status: ADI 0.25 mg/kg body weight per day.
Group 3 (not classifiable as to carcinogenicity).

hazards.title: Effects at high doses in animals
hazards.summary: The main safety concerns about BHT come from animal studies that used much higher doses than people normally eat. These studies found effects on the liver, thyroid, lungs and, in some cases, development. Regulators use such data to set an acceptable daily intake with a large safety margin. Because of these findings, some countries restrict BHT more than others, and some food companies have dropped it. For typical diets, exposure is well below the levels of concern.
hazards.chemical: At high doses, liver enzymes convert BHT into several breakdown products, including reactive quinone methides that can bind to proteins and may interfere with how they work. The liver also responds by making more of these enzymes, which can change how it handles other substances, including hormones and medicines. This enzyme boost, called induction, is one of the main effects seen in animals. BHT dissolves in fat, so with long-term high exposure some of it can build up in body fat. All of these effects depend strongly on dose.
hazards.biological: In rodents fed high doses, effects included enlarged livers, changes in thyroid hormones and, in mice, lung damage. Some studies also hinted at effects on hormone signaling. Starting from the highest dose that caused no effect in animals and dividing by a 100-fold safety factor, the European Food Safety Authority set an acceptable daily intake of 0.25 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. For a 60-kilogram adult that is 15 milligrams a day. Estimated human intakes are well below this.

hazards.title: Rare contact allergy
hazards.summary: BHT is used in many cosmetics, such as lipsticks, moisturizers and makeup, to keep their oils from going rancid. In rare cases, people develop an allergic skin reaction to it. This is called allergic contact dermatitis, and it involves the immune system learning to recognize the substance. BHT is considered a weak allergen, and reactions are uncommon. People who know they're allergic can check ingredient lists.
hazards.chemical: When BHT oxidizes, either in the product or on the skin, it can form reactive molecules such as quinone methides. These can form chemical bonds with proteins in the skin. A small molecule that becomes an allergen by attaching to a protein is called a hapten. The modified protein looks unfamiliar to the immune system. This is the same general mechanism behind many chemical skin allergies.
hazards.biological: In a sensitized person, immune cells in the skin recognize the BHT-modified proteins and trigger inflammation. That causes redness, itching, swelling and sometimes small blisters where the product was applied, usually appearing a day or two after contact. The reaction stays limited to the areas that touched the product. Once someone is sensitized, it can come back with every exposure. Dermatologists can identify the cause with patch testing.

profile.dosage: The European Food Safety Authority has set an acceptable daily intake for BHT of 0.25 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, about 15 milligrams a day for a 60-kilogram adult, and international experts (JECFA) set a similar limit. Foods that use it, such as cereals, snack foods and chewing gum, typically contain tens of parts per million, and sometimes it is added to the packaging rather than the food. Estimated human intakes are well below the ADI. Cosmetics use small amounts, usually well under 1 percent. People who want to avoid it can look for “BHT” or “butylated hydroxytoluene” on labels.

myths.claim: BHT is embalming fluid.
myths.consensus: BHT is an antioxidant; embalming uses formaldehyde. BHT is also used in some fuels and rubbers, which is where the rumor may come from.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic to aquatic life at higher concentrations.

synthesis.title: Industrial alkylation
synthesis.summary: BHT is made in chemical plants from two starting materials: p-cresol, a phenol carrying a methyl group, and isobutylene, a small hydrocarbon gas. Both come from petroleum or coal tar. The process uses Friedel–Crafts alkylation to attach the bulky tert-butyl groups that make BHT work. It was patented in 1947 and quickly adopted as an antioxidant for foods, rubber, plastics and fuels. Most BHT made today goes into non-food products.
synthesis.mechanism: p-Cresol is heated with isobutylene gas in the presence of an acid catalyst, such as sulfuric acid or an acidic resin. The acid converts isobutylene into tert-butyl carbocations, which attack the electron-rich positions on the p-cresol ring next to its –OH group. Two tert-butyl groups are added, one on each side. The crude product contains BHT along with some partly alkylated molecules and other byproducts. It is purified by distillation, which separates molecules by boiling point, and by crystallization, giving white crystals of food-grade BHT.
synthesis.significance: BHT was patented in 1947 and approved for food use in the U.S. in 1954.

citations.title: Platelet autophagic machinery involved in thrombosis through a novel linkage of AMPK-MTOR to sphingolipid metabolism.
citations.abstract: Basal macroautophagy/autophagy has recently been found in anucleate platelets. Platelet autophagy is involved in platelet activation and thrombus formation. However, the mechanism underlying autophagy in anucleate platelets require further clarification. Our data revealed that LC3-II formation and SQSTM1/p62 degradation were noted in H2O2-activated human platelets, which could be blocked by 3-methyladenine and bafilomycin A1, indicating that platelet activation may cause platelet autophagy. AMPK phosphorylation and MTOR dephosphorylation were also detected, and block of AMPK activity by the AMPK inhibitor dorsomorphin reversed SQSTM1 degradation and LC3-II formation. Moreover, autophagosome formation was observed through transmission electron microscopy and deconvolution microscopy. These findings suggest that platelet autophagy was induced partly through the AMPK-MTOR pathway. In addition, increased LC3-II expression occurred only in H2O2-treated Atg5f/f platelets, but not in H2O2-treated atg5-/- platelets, suggesting that platelet autophagy occurs during platelet activation. atg5-/- platelets also exhibited a lower aggregation in response to agonists, and platelet-specific atg5-/- mice exhibited delayed thrombus formation in mesenteric microvessles and decreased mortality rate due to pulmonary thrombosis. Notably, metabolic analysis revealed that sphingolipid metabolism is involved in platelet activation, as evidenced by observed several altered metabolites, which could be reversed by dorsomorphin. Therefore, platelet autophagy and platelet activation are positively correlated, partly through the interconnected network of sphingolipid metabolism. In conclusion, this study for the first time demonstrated that AMPK-MTOR signaling could regulate platelet autophagy. citations.title: The role of toxicological interactions in lung injury.
citations.abstract: Interactions between two or more toxic agents can produce lung damage by chemical-chemical interactions, chemical-receptor interactions or by modification, by a first agent, of the cell and tissue response to a second agent. Interactions may occur by simultaneous exposure and if exposure to the two agents is separated in time. Chemical-chemical interactions have been mostly studied in the toxicology of air pollutants, where it was shown that the untoward effect of certain oxidants may be enhanced in the presence of other aerosols. Interactions at the receptor site have been found in isolated perfused lung experiments. Oxygen tolerance may be an example, when pre-exposure to one concentration of oxygen mitigates later exposure to 100% oxygen by modifying cellular and enzymatic composition of the lung. Damage of the alveolar zone by the antioxidant butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) can be greatly enhanced by subsequent exposure to oxygen concentration which, otherwise, would have little if any demonstrable effect. The synergistic interaction between BHT and oxygen results in a resulting interstitial pulmonary fibrosis. Acute or chronic lung disease may then be caused not only by one agent, but very likely in many instances by the interaction of several agents.

citations.title: Final report on the safety assessment of BHT(1).
citations.abstract: BHT is the recognized name in the cosmetics industry for butylated hydroxytoluene. BHT is used in a wide range of cosmetic formulations as an antioxidant at concentrations from 0.0002% to 0.5%. BHT does penetrate the skin, but the relatively low amount absorbed remains primarily in the skin. Oral studies demonstrate that BHT is metabolized. The major metabolites appear as the carboxylic acid of BHT and its glucuronide in urine. At acute doses of 0.5 to 1.0 g/kg, some renal and hepatic damage was seen in male rats. Short-term repeated exposure to comparable doses produced hepatic toxic effects in male and female rats. Subchronic feeding and intraperitoneal studies in rats with BHT at lower doses produced increased liver weight, and decreased activity of several hepatic enzymes. In addition to liver and kidney effects, BHT applied to the skin was associated with toxic effects in lung tissue. BHT was not a reproductive or developmental toxin in animals. BHT has been found to enhance and to inhibit the humoral immune response in animals. BHT itself was not generally considered genotoxic, although it did modify the genotoxicity of other agents. BHT has been associated with hepatocellular and pulmonary adenomas in animals, but was not considered carcinogenic and actually was associated with a decreased incidence of neoplasms. BHT has been shown to have tumor promotion effects, to be anticarcinogenic, and to have no effect on other carcinogenic agents, depending on the target organ, exposure parameters, the carcinogen, and the animal tested. Various mechanism studies suggested that BHT toxicity is related to an electrophillic metabolite. In a predictive clinical test, 100% BHT was a mild irritant and a moderate sensitizer. In provocative skin tests, BHT (in the 1% to 2% concentration range) produced positive reactions in a small number of patients. Clinical testing did not find any depigmentation associated with dermal exposure to BHT, although a few case reports of depigmentation were found. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel recognized that oral exposure to BHT was associated with toxic effects in some studies and was negative in others. BHT applied to the skin, however, appears to remain in the skin or pass through only slowly and does not produce systemic exposures to BHT or its metabolites seen with oral exposures. Although there were only limited studies that evaluated the effect of BHT on the skin, the available studies, along with the case literature, demonstrate no significant irritation, sensitization, or photosensitization. Recognizing the low concentration at which this ingredient is currently used in cosmetic formulations, it was concluded that BHT is safe as used in cosmetic formulations.

citations.title: Safety aspects of food preservatives.
citations.abstract: The use of food preservatives, such as benzoic acid, nitrites, and sulphites, as antimicrobials, and butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA), butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT), ascorbic acid and tocopherols, as antioxidants, has probably changed food production patterns and eating habits more than has the use of any other class of food additive. These food preservative chemicals confer substantial benefits on man, not only by the preservation and increased palatability of food, but also by affording protection against the pathological effects of reactive oxygen species (ROS) which are associated with cancer, cardiovascular disease and aging. Nevertheless, although most preservatives are now considered to be without potential adverse effects and are classified as GRAS, there have been problems concerning the safety of some of these chemicals, including the possibility of allergies from benzoic acid and sulphites, the formation of carcinogenic nitrosamines from nitrites, and the possible rodent carcinogenicity of BHA and BHT. The mechanisms of this toxicity at high dosage, the roles of the cytochromes P450, and the generation and scavenging of ROS in the toxicity of these chemicals, are reviewed and discussed.

citations.title: Ionol (BHT) produces superoxide anion.
citations.abstract: In aqueous medium etiolated wheat seedlings release superoxide anion (O2*-). Interaction of a synthetic antioxidant, butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT, ionol), with oxygen in the aqueous medium is accompanied by O2*- formation. This suggests that under certain conditions BHT behaves as a prooxidant. A natural antioxidant, superoxide dismutase (SOD), and also a wound healing preparation, emulsified denatured placenta (EDP), do not exhibit the prooxidant properties. In contrast to BHT, they reduce O2*- production by the etiolated wheat seedling system.

name: Maltodextrin
scoreRationale: Safe, but it is a rapidly digested carbohydrate with a high glycemic index and a hallmark of ultra-processed foods.
summary: Maltodextrin is a starch-derived powder that adds body and carries flavors. It digests quickly into glucose.

identity.composition: Short chains of glucose units (dextrose equivalent below 20) from partial starch hydrolysis.

overview: Maltodextrin is a mixture of short chains of glucose, made by partially breaking down starch. Chains typically contain about 3–17 glucose units linked by α-1,4 bonds, with some α-1,6 branch points. Products are graded by “dextrose equivalent” (DE): below 20 is maltodextrin, above 20 is corn syrup solids.
Because its chains are short and branched, maltodextrin dissolves easily, tastes only faintly sweet and adds body without much flavor. Your digestive enzymes break it back into glucose very quickly.
profile.function: Adds bulk and mouthfeel, carries spray-dried flavors, and supplies quick energy in sports drinks.

mechanisms.title: Rapid digestion
mechanisms.chemical: Starch is broken down by enzymes called amylases, which are found in saliva and released by the pancreas into the small intestine. Amylases cut the α-1,4 bonds that link glucose units into chains. Maltodextrin's chains are much shorter than starch's, so they offer many more chain ends and exposed bonds for the enzymes to attack. Another enzyme, maltase, sitting on the surface of intestinal cells, finishes the job by splitting two-unit pieces into single glucose molecules. Because maltodextrin is already partly broken down and dissolves so easily, all of this happens very quickly.
mechanisms.biological: Glucose from maltodextrin is absorbed almost as fast as pure glucose, causing a rapid rise in blood sugar. Its glycemic index, a measure of how quickly a food raises blood sugar, can be higher than that of table sugar, which is half fructose. For endurance athletes this is useful: sports drinks and energy gels use maltodextrin to deliver energy quickly without tasting overly sweet. For people who aren't exercising, especially those with diabetes, rapid blood sugar spikes are less welcome. The effect depends on how much maltodextrin a food actually contains.

mechanisms.title: Carrying flavors
mechanisms.chemical: Maltodextrin is often used to turn liquid flavors into powders by spray-drying. A mixture of maltodextrin, water and tiny droplets of flavor oil is sprayed into hot air. As the water evaporates in a fraction of a second, the maltodextrin hardens into a solid, glassy shell around each flavor droplet. In this glassy state the molecules are packed so tightly that they barely move, so volatile flavor molecules are trapped inside. The shell also shields the flavor from oxygen, slowing down oxidation.
mechanisms.biological: When you eat a powdered seasoning, flavored chips or instant soup, the maltodextrin shell dissolves in your saliva and releases the trapped flavor molecules, which then reach your taste and smell receptors. This keeps flavors fresh in the package and lets them burst out when eaten. Because maltodextrin itself is almost tasteless, it doesn't get in the way of the flavor. It also adds bulk and helps powders pour without clumping. Many drink mixes, seasonings and supplements rely on it.

mechanisms.title: Gut microbiome questions
mechanisms.chemical: Most maltodextrin is digested and absorbed in the small intestine, but some can reach the large intestine, especially when large amounts are eaten. There, certain bacteria can use it as food. Laboratory studies have found that maltodextrin helps some bacteria, including certain strains of E. coli, form biofilms, sticky layers of bacteria that cling to surfaces. Maltodextrin may also affect the protective mucus layer lining the gut. These interactions are still being studied.
mechanisms.biological: In mouse and cell studies, maltodextrin has been linked to thinning of the intestinal mucus layer and to increases in bacteria associated with inflammation, which could in theory matter for conditions like inflammatory bowel disease. Some researchers have suggested it might weaken the gut's ability to fend off harmful bacteria. However, these findings come mainly from laboratory and animal work, and evidence in people is limited. The amounts used in studies may also differ from typical diets. This is an emerging area of research.

reactions.title: Partial starch hydrolysis
reactions.summary: Maltodextrin is made by breaking starch, a very long chain of glucose units, into shorter pieces, but not all the way down to single glucose molecules. The trick is to stop the reaction at just the right point. The degree of breakdown is measured by dextrose equivalent (DE), which describes how sweet and reactive the product is compared with pure glucose. Pure starch has a DE near 0 and pure glucose has a DE of 100. Maltodextrin falls between about 3 and 20.

steps.name: Gelatinization
steps.text: Starch granules from corn, potato, rice or another plant are mixed with water and heated. The heat makes the granules swell and burst, releasing their long chains into the water. This makes the chains reachable by enzymes.

steps.name: Cutting
steps.text: An enzyme called alpha-amylase is added, and it cuts α-1,4 bonds at random places along the starch chains. Each cut makes two shorter pieces. Over time the chains get shorter and shorter, producing a mixture of fragments of many different lengths.

steps.name: Stopping
steps.text: When the mixture reaches the target DE, the reaction is stopped by heating to destroy the enzyme or by adding acid. Timing is crucial, since letting it run longer produces more simple sugars such as glucose and maltose.

reactions.result: Stopping earlier gives longer chains (low DE: less sweet and more viscous); running longer gives shorter chains and sweeter syrups. This lets manufacturers make maltodextrins with different properties for different jobs.

reactions.title: Spray-drying encapsulation
reactions.summary: Spray-drying is a fast way to turn a liquid into a fine powder, and maltodextrin is one of the most common materials used in it. It is how powdered flavors, instant drinks and many nutritional supplements are made. The process relies on how quickly water evaporates from tiny droplets surrounded by hot air. Maltodextrin forms a protective shell around the flavor or nutrient. The same method makes powdered milk and instant coffee.

steps.name: Mixing
steps.text: Maltodextrin is dissolved in water, and a flavor oil or other ingredient is added and broken up into tiny droplets. The maltodextrin coats the droplets and thickens the mixture. The liquid is now ready to spray.

steps.name: Atomizing
steps.text: The mixture is pumped through a nozzle or a spinning disk that sprays it as a very fine mist into a chamber of hot air, often around 150 to 200 °C. The enormous surface area of the tiny droplets lets water evaporate almost instantly.

steps.name: Drying
steps.text: Water evaporates within seconds, and because evaporation cools the droplets, the flavor inside doesn't get too hot. The maltodextrin hardens into a glassy shell with the flavor trapped inside. The dry particles fall to the bottom of the chamber and are collected as powder.

reactions.result: Encapsulation protects sensitive ingredients from air and moisture, extending shelf life. When the powder is mixed with water or eaten, the shell dissolves and releases what it holds. The same method makes powdered milk, instant coffee and many dried vitamins.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.

hazards.title: High glycemic load
hazards.summary: Maltodextrin is digested very quickly, so foods or drinks that contain a lot of it can cause a sharp rise in blood sugar. This mainly matters in products where it is a major ingredient, such as sports drinks, protein powders, meal replacements and some snacks. In most foods it is present in small amounts as a thickener or carrier and has little effect. People with diabetes or insulin resistance should be aware of it. Checking the total carbohydrate figure on the Nutrition Facts label helps.
hazards.chemical: Maltodextrin's short glucose chains are broken down by amylases and maltase into glucose almost as quickly as pure glucose is absorbed. Its glycemic index, which compares how fast a food raises blood sugar against pure glucose, ranges from about 85 to over 100. Table sugar, which is half fructose, scores around 65. Glycemic load takes into account both the glycemic index and how much carbohydrate is eaten. Foods with a high glycemic load cause bigger blood sugar spikes.
hazards.biological: When blood sugar rises quickly, the pancreas releases a large amount of insulin to bring it back down. In people with diabetes, either not enough insulin is made or the body responds poorly to it, so blood sugar stays high for longer. Over years, frequently high blood sugar contributes to damage in the eyes, kidneys and nerves. Healthy people handle occasional spikes easily, but a diet heavy in rapidly digested carbohydrates is linked to a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. For athletes in the middle of long exercise, the quick energy is exactly what they need.

profile.dosage: In most foods, maltodextrin is used in small amounts, often a few percent or less, as a thickener, filler or flavor carrier, and it contributes few calories. The U.S. FDA considers it generally recognized as safe, with no set limit on daily intake. The main thing to watch is products where it is a major ingredient, such as sports drinks, energy gels, protein powders and meal replacements, which can contain tens of grams per serving. Like sugar, it provides about 4 calories per gram. People managing their blood sugar should count it as a rapidly digested carbohydrate.

myths.claim: Maltodextrin is worse than sugar.
myths.consensus: Its glycemic index is high, but most foods contain only small amounts.

synthesis.title: Enzymatic processing of starch
synthesis.summary: Maltodextrin is made from starch, the main energy store of plants, taken from crops such as corn, potato, rice, tapioca or wheat. In the United States most of it comes from corn. The starch is partly broken down by enzymes in a carefully controlled process. The result is a white, nearly flavorless powder that dissolves easily in water. It is one of the most widely used food ingredients, found in everything from salad dressings to sports drinks.
synthesis.mechanism: Purified starch is mixed with water into a slurry and heated to gelatinize it, meaning the granules swell and burst so their chains are released. Heat-stable alpha-amylase enzymes, often made by bacteria, are added to cut the long starch chains into shorter fragments. Technicians monitor the dextrose equivalent and stop the reaction by heating or changing the pH once the target is reached. The resulting syrup is filtered and cleaned with activated carbon and ion-exchange resins to remove impurities. Finally it is spray-dried into a fine white powder.
synthesis.significance: Wheat-derived maltodextrin is processed so thoroughly that it is considered gluten-free.

citations.title: Structural relationships among regulated and unregulated phosphorylases.
citations.abstract: Species and tissue-specific isozymes of phosphorylase display differences in regulatory properties consistent with their distinct roles in particular organisms and tissues. In this review, we compare crystallographic structures of regulated and unregulated phosphorylases, including maltodextrin phosphorylase (MalP) from Escherichia coli, glycogen phosphorylase from yeast, and mammalian isozymes from muscle and liver tissues. Mutagenesis and functional studies supplement the structural work and provide insights into the structural basis for allosteric control mechanisms. MalP, a simple, unregulated enzyme, is contrasted with the more complicated yeast and mammalian phosphorylases that have evolved regulatory sites onto the basic catalytic architecture. The human liver and muscle isozymes show differences structurally in their means of invoking allosteric activation. Phosphorylation, though common to both the yeast and mammalian enzymes, occurs at different sites and activates the enzymes by surprisingly different mechanisms.

citations.title: Biotechnological potential of novel glycoside hydrolase family 70 enzymes synthesizing α-glucans from starch and sucrose.
citations.abstract: Transglucosidases belonging to the glycoside hydrolase (GH) family 70 are promising enzymatic tools for the synthesis of α-glucans with defined structures from renewable sucrose and starch substrates. Depending on the GH70 enzyme specificity, α-glucans with different structures and physicochemical properties are produced, which have found diverse (potential) commercial applications, e.g. in food, health and as biomaterials. Originally, the GH70 family was established only for glucansucrase enzymes of lactic acid bacteria that catalyze the synthesis of α-glucan polymers from sucrose. In recent years, we have identified 3 novel subfamilies of GH70 enzymes (designated GtfB, GtfC and GtfD), inactive on sucrose but converting starch/maltodextrin substrates into novel α-glucans. These novel starch-acting enzymes considerably enlarge the panel of α-glucans that can be produced. They also represent very interesting evolutionary intermediates between sucrose-acting GH70 glucansucrases and starch-acting GH13 α-amylases. Here we provide an overview of the repertoire of GH70 enzymes currently available with focus on these novel starch-acting GH70 enzymes and their biotechnological potential. Moreover, we discuss key developments in the understanding of structure-function relationships of GH70 enzymes in the light of available three-dimensional structures, and the protein engineering strategies that were recently applied to expand their natural product specificities.

citations.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement.
citations.abstract: It is the position of the American College of Sports Medicine that adequate fluid replacement helps maintain hydration and, therefore, promotes the health, safety, and optimal physical performance of individuals participating in regular physical activity. This position statement is based on a comprehensive review and interpretation of scientific literature concerning the influence of fluid replacement on exercise performance and the risk of thermal injury associated with dehydration and hyperthermia. Based on available evidence, the American College of Sports Medicine makes the following general recommendations on the amount and composition of fluid that should be ingested in preparation for, during, and after exercise or athletic competition: 1) It is recommended that individuals consume a nutritionally balanced diet and drink adequate fluids during the 24-hr period before an event, especially during the period that includes the meal prior to exercise, to promote proper hydration before exercise or competition. 2) It is recommended that individuals drink about 500 ml (about 17 ounces) of fluid about 2 h before exercise to promote adequate hydration and allow time for excretion of excess ingested water. 3) During exercise, athletes should start drinking early and at regular intervals in an attempt to consume fluids at a rate sufficient to replace all the water lost through sweating (i.e., body weight loss), or consume the maximal amount that can be tolerated. 4) It is recommended that ingested fluids be cooler than ambient temperature [between 15 degrees and 22 degrees C (59 degrees and 72 degrees F])] and flavored to enhance palatability and promote fluid replacement. Fluids should be readily available and served in containers that allow adequate volumes to be ingested with ease and with minimal interruption of exercise. 5) Addition of proper amounts of carbohydrates and/or electrolytes to a fluid replacement solution is recommended for exercise events of duration greater than 1 h since it does not significantly impair water delivery to the body and may enhance performance. During exercise lasting less than 1 h, there is little evidence of physiological or physical performance differences between consuming a carbohydrate-electrolyte drink and plain water. 6) During intense exercise lasting longer than 1 h, it is recommended that carbohydrates be ingested at a rate of 30-60 g.h(-1) to maintain oxidation of carbohydrates and delay fatigue. This rate of carbohydrate intake can be achieved without compromising fluid delivery by drinking 600-1200 ml.h(-1) of solutions containing 4%-8% carbohydrates (g.100 ml(-1)). The carbohydrates can be sugars (glucose or sucrose) or starch (e.g., maltodextrin). 7) Inclusion of sodium (0.5-0.7 g.1(-1) of water) in the rehydration solution ingested during exercise lasting longer than 1 h is recommended since it may be advantageous in enhancing palatability, promoting fluid retention, and possibly preventing hyponatremia in certain individuals who drink excessive quantities of fluid. There is little physiological basis for the presence of sodium in n oral rehydration solution for enhancing intestinal water absorption as long as sodium is sufficiently available from the previous meal.

citations.title: Effect of Low-Dose Iron Supplementation on Early Development in Breastfed Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
citations.abstract: Importance: Breastfed infants are at risk of iron deficiency, which is associated with suboptimal development. There is a paucity of evidence on the effects of iron supplementation on child development, and current guidelines are divergent. Objective: To assess whether daily iron supplementation, 1 mg/kg, between 4 and 9 months in exclusively or predominantly breastfed infants improves psychomotor development at 12 months. Design, setting, and participants: This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted between December 2015 and May 2020 with follow-up through May 2023 in an outpatient setting in Poland and Sweden. Participants were healthy singleton infants born at term with birth weight greater than 2500 g who were exclusively or predominantly breastfed (>50%) and did not have anemia (hemoglobin >10.5 g/dL) at age 4 months. Exclusion criteria included major illness, congenital anomaly, food allergy, and difficulty communicating with caregivers. Interventions: Iron (micronized microencapsulated ferric pyrophosphate), 1 mg/kg, or placebo (maltodextrin) once daily from age 4 to 9 months. Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was psychomotor development assessed by motor score of Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development III at 12 months, adjusted for gestational age, sex, and maternal education. Secondary outcomes included cognitive and language scores at 12 months; motor, cognitive, and language scores at 24 and 36 months; iron deficiency (serum ferritin <12 ng/mL), and iron deficiency anemia (iron deficiency and hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL) at 12 months. Results: Of 221 randomized infants (111 female), 200 (90%) were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (mean [SD] age, 12.4 [0.8] months). Iron supplementation (n = 104) compared to placebo (n = 96) had no effect on psychomotor development (mean difference [MD] for motor score, -1.07 points; 95% CI, -4.69 to 2.55), cognitive score (MD, -1.14; 95% CI, -4.26 to 1.99), or language score (MD, 0.75; 95% CI, -2.31 to 3.82) at 12 months. There were no significant differences at 24 and 36 months. The intervention did not reduce the risk for iron deficiency (relative risk [RR], 0.46; 95% CI, 0.16 to 1.30) or iron deficiency anemia (RR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.05 to 12.46) at 12 months. Conclusion and relevance: No benefit was found with daily low-dose iron supplementation between 4 and 9 months with respect to psychomotor development, risk of iron deficiency, or iron deficiency anemia among breastfed infants in a setting of low risk of anemia. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02242188.

citations.title: An integrated network pharmacology approach reveals that Ampelopsis grossedentata improves alcoholic liver disease via TLR4/NF-κB/MLKL pathway.
citations.abstract: Background: Alcohol-related liver damage is the most prevalent chronic liver disease, which creates a heavy public health burden worldwide. The leaves of Ampelopsis grossedentata have been considered a popular tea and traditional herbal medicine in China for more than one thousand years, and possess anti-inflammatory, antioxidative, hepatoprotective, and antiviral activities. Purpose: We explored the protective effects of Ampelopsis grossedentata extract (AGE) against chronic alcohol-induced hepatic injury (alcoholic liver disease, ALD), aiming to elucidate its underlying mechanisms. Methods: Firstly, UPLC-Q/TOF-MS analysis and network pharmacology were used to identify the constituents and elucidate the potential mechanisms of AGE against ALD. Secondly, C57BL/6 mice were pair-fed the Lieber-DeCarli diet containing either isocaloric maltodextrin or ethanol, AGE (150 and 300 mg/kg/d) and silymarin (200 mg/kg) were administered to chronic ethanol-fed mice for 7 weeks to evaluate the hepatoprotective effects. Serum biochemical parameters were determined, hepatic and ileum sections were used for histologic examination, and levels of inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress in the liver were examined. The potential molecular mechanisms of AGE in improving ALD were demonstrated by RNA-seq, Western blotting analysis, and immunofluorescence staining. Results: Ten main constituents of AGE were identified using UPLC-Q/TOF-MS and 274 potential ALD-related targets were identified. The enriched KEGG pathways included Toll-like receptor signaling pathway, NF-κB signaling pathway, and necroptosis. Moreover, in vivo experimental studies demonstrated that AGE significantly reduced serum aminotransferase levels and improved pathological abnormalities after chronic ethanol intake. Meanwhile, AGE improved ALD in mice by down-regulating oxidative stress and inflammatory cytokines. Furthermore, AGE notably repaired damaged intestinal epithelial barrier and suppressed the production of gut-derived lipopolysaccharide by elevating intestinal tight junction protein expression. Subsequent RNA-seq and experimental validation indicated that AGE inhibited NF-κB nuclear translocation, suppressed IκB-α, RIPK3 and MLKL phosphorylation and alleviated hepatic necroptosis in mice. Conclusion: In this study, we have demonstrated for the first time that AGE protects against alcoholic liver disease by regulating the gut-liver axis and inhibiting the TLR4/NF-κB/MLKL-mediated necroptosis pathway. Therefore, our present work provides important experimental evidence for AGE as a promising candidate for protection against ALD.

name: Sodium Nitrite
scoreRationale: Prevents deadly botulism, but in processed meats it forms carcinogenic nitrosamines; processed meat is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen.
summary: Sodium nitrite cures bacon, ham and hot dogs, keeping them pink and safe from botulism. Cooking cured meat can create cancer-causing nitrosamines.

physical.phStability: Forms nitrous acid in acidic conditions

overview: Sodium nitrite (NaNO₂) is a salt of nitrous acid. The nitrite ion (NO₂⁻) is bent, with nitrogen in a middle oxidation state (+3), so it can either gain or lose electrons, which makes it chemically versatile and reactive.

In cured meat, nitrite does three jobs at once: it creates the pink color, adds the characteristic cured flavor, and, most importantly, blocks the growth of Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium that makes deadly botulinum toxin.
profile.function: Gives cured meats their pink color and flavor and inhibits Clostridium botulinum.

mechanisms.title: Pink cured color
mechanisms.chemical: Muscle contains a protein called myoglobin, which stores oxygen and has an iron atom at its center inside a ring-shaped structure called heme. The color of meat depends on what is attached to that iron: bright red with oxygen, purple without it, and brownish-gray when the iron is oxidized or the protein is cooked. In cured meat, nitrite is converted, partly with help from added vitamin C, into nitric oxide (NO). Nitric oxide binds tightly to the iron in myoglobin, forming red nitrosylmyoglobin. When the meat is cooked, the protein part unfolds but the nitric oxide stays attached to the heme, forming a stable pink pigment called nitrosyl hemochrome.
mechanisms.biological: That's why cooked ham, bacon, hot dogs and corned beef stay pink, while ordinary cooked pork or beef turns gray-brown. The pink color lasts a long time, which keeps cured meats looking appealing. Because nitric oxide is bound so tightly, the color resists fading during storage. Without nitrite, cured meats would look gray like cooked fresh meat. The same reaction between nitric oxide and heme proteins happens inside our own bodies, where NO acts as a signaling molecule.

mechanisms.title: Preventing botulism
mechanisms.chemical: Clostridium botulinum is a bacterium that forms tough spores, which can survive cooking and then grow in low-oxygen places such as vacuum-packed or canned meats. When the spores sprout into active bacteria, they produce botulinum toxin, one of the most powerful toxins known. Nitrite and the nitric oxide formed from it react with iron-sulfur proteins inside bacterial cells. These proteins are essential parts of the enzymes the bacteria use to produce energy, such as one called ferredoxin. When they are disabled, the bacteria can't make enough energy to grow.
mechanisms.biological: With their energy-producing enzymes blocked, C. botulinum spores can't sprout and turn into toxin-producing cells. Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine, the chemical messenger nerves use to tell muscles to contract, causing paralysis that can be fatal if it reaches the breathing muscles. Before nitrite curing was understood and controlled, botulism from cured meats was a serious problem; the name comes from the Latin botulus, meaning sausage. Nitrite's protection matters most in products like ham and sausages that are stored without oxygen. This is the main reason regulators allow nitrite despite its downsides.

mechanisms.title: Forming nitrosamines
mechanisms.chemical: In acidic conditions or at high temperatures, nitrite forms reactive nitrogen compounds called nitrosating agents, such as dinitrogen trioxide. These can transfer a nitroso group (–N=O) onto amines, nitrogen-containing molecules that come from the breakdown of proteins in meat. The products are N-nitrosamines. This can happen during cooking, especially high-heat frying of bacon, and also in the acidic stomach. Secondary amines, nitrogen atoms attached to two carbon groups, react most readily.
mechanisms.biological: N-nitrosamines themselves aren't very reactive, but liver enzymes called cytochrome P450 convert them into highly reactive molecules. These attach small carbon groups to DNA bases, a type of damage called alkylation, which can cause copying errors and mutations if not repaired. Many nitrosamines cause cancer in animal studies. Together with other factors, nitrosamine formation is part of why the World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies processed meat as carcinogenic to humans. Adding vitamin C to cured meats greatly reduces how many nitrosamines form.

mechanisms.title: The body's own nitrite
mechanisms.chemical: Vegetables such as spinach, beets, lettuce and celery contain large amounts of nitrate (NO₃⁻), which plants absorb from the soil. When you eat them, nitrate is absorbed into the blood, and some of it is concentrated into saliva. Bacteria living on the back of the tongue convert this nitrate into nitrite (NO₂⁻) by removing an oxygen atom, a reaction called reduction. When the nitrite-rich saliva is swallowed, stomach acid turns some of it into nitric oxide. This route is called the nitrate–nitrite–nitric oxide pathway.
mechanisms.biological: Nitric oxide made this way helps relax and widen blood vessels, which can lower blood pressure, and may help protect the stomach lining and kill harmful bacteria. Studies show that eating nitrate-rich vegetables like beets can lower blood pressure slightly. In fact, vegetables supply most of the nitrite people are exposed to, far more than cured meats. But vegetables also bring vitamin C, polyphenols and other antioxidants that limit nitrosamine formation. That is one reason nitrate from vegetables is considered beneficial while nitrite in processed meat is linked to cancer risk.

reactions.title: Nitrosamine formation
reactions.summary: Nitrosamines form when nitrite reacts with certain amines under acidic or hot conditions. This reaction is a key reason processed meats are linked to cancer, and food scientists have worked hard to reduce it. Frying bacon at high temperature is one of the main situations where nitrosamines form in food. Adding vitamin C or a closely related compound, erythorbate, to cured meats greatly reduces their formation. Understanding this reaction has led to safer curing practices.

steps.name: Acidification
steps.text: In acidic conditions, such as the stomach or meat being heated, nitrite ions (NO₂⁻) pick up a hydrogen ion and become nitrous acid (HNO₂). Nitrous acid is unstable and reactive. This is the first step toward nitrosamines.

steps.name: Nitrosating agent
steps.text: Two nitrous acid molecules can combine and lose a water molecule to form dinitrogen trioxide (N₂O₃), a powerful nitrosating agent. It easily hands an –N=O group to other molecules. This is the species that actually forms nitrosamines.

steps.name: Nitrosation
steps.text: N₂O₃ reacts with a secondary amine, a nitrogen atom bonded to two carbon groups, which comes from the breakdown of meat proteins. The –N=O group attaches to the amine's nitrogen, forming an N-nitrosamine. The high heat of frying speeds this up.

steps.name: Blocking
steps.text: Added ascorbate (vitamin C) or erythorbate reacts with nitrous acid faster than the amines can, reducing it to harmless nitric oxide. That cuts off the pathway before nitrosamines can form. Antioxidants in vegetables work the same way.

reactions.result: High-heat frying of bacon favors nitrosamines, which is why U.S. rules require bacon to contain added vitamin C or erythorbate and limit how much nitrite can be used. Cooking bacon at lower temperatures, or in a microwave, also reduces nitrosamine formation.

reactions.title: Developing cured color
reactions.summary: The pink color of cured meats develops through a series of reactions between nitrite and myoglobin, the red protein in muscle. It builds up over hours to days during curing and is completed by cooking. Scientists worked this out in the early 1900s, when they discovered that nitrite, not nitrate, was the real curing agent. The same process also creates the distinctive flavor of cured meat. Vitamin C speeds it up.

steps.name: Reduction
steps.text: Nitrite added to meat is reduced to nitric oxide (NO) by gaining an electron. This happens slowly on its own, but added ascorbate (vitamin C) or erythorbate speeds it up greatly by donating electrons. Natural reducing substances in the meat also help.

steps.name: Binding
steps.text: Nitric oxide binds tightly to the iron atom at the center of myoglobin's heme group, forming nitrosylmyoglobin. This compound is red, similar to fresh meat. The bond is very strong and isn't displaced by oxygen.

steps.name: Cooking
steps.text: When the meat is heated, the protein part of myoglobin unfolds, a process called denaturation. The nitric oxide stays attached to the heme, now surrounded by unfolded protein, forming nitrosyl hemochrome. This stable compound has the familiar pink color.

reactions.result: The same NO–iron chemistry is how nitric oxide sends signals in your blood vessels, where it binds to the iron in an enzyme and triggers the vessel wall to relax. In meat, it gives a lasting pink color that survives cooking and storage.

regulatory.status: Permitted in cured meats with limits; bacon must include ascorbate or erythorbate.
regulatory.limit: 200 ppm maximum in finished products (21 CFR 172.175)

regulatory.status: Processed meat is Group 1 (carcinogenic); ingested nitrite under conditions causing nitrosation is Group 2A.
Lowered maximum added nitrite levels in meat products.

hazards.title: Processed meat and colorectal cancer
hazards.summary: In 2015 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified processed meat, such as bacon, ham, hot dogs and salami, as a Group 1 carcinogen, meaning there is sufficient evidence that it causes cancer in people, specifically colorectal cancer. The category describes how strong the evidence is, not how dangerous the substance is; tobacco is also in Group 1, but processed meat is far less risky. The risk grows with the amount eaten regularly. Nitrite is one of several factors involved. Health organizations recommend eating little, if any, processed meat.
hazards.chemical: Several chemical processes may explain the link. Nitrite in processed meat can form N-nitrosamines and related compounds, either during cooking or inside the stomach and gut. Red and processed meats also contain heme, the iron-containing part of myoglobin, which can encourage nitroso compounds to form in the gut and can generate reactive molecules that damage the gut lining. High-temperature cooking produces other potential carcinogens as well, such as heterocyclic amines and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. All of these can damage DNA in the cells lining the colon.
hazards.biological: The cells lining the colon are constantly dividing to replace those shed from the surface, so DNA damage there can accumulate over time and contribute to cancer. Irritation from heme may also speed up cell division, giving more chances for mutations. IARC estimated that eating 50 grams of processed meat every day, about one hot dog or a few slices of ham, raises the risk of colorectal cancer by about 18 percent. Because colorectal cancer is common, that matters across a whole population. For an individual, the absolute risk remains relatively low.

hazards.title: Methemoglobinemia (acute poisoning)
hazards.summary: Swallowing a large amount of sodium nitrite can cause a dangerous condition called methemoglobinemia, in which the blood can't carry oxygen properly. Concentrated curing salts containing sodium nitrite have caused poisonings when mistaken for table salt or sugar. That's why curing salt, sold as “pink curing salt” or “Prague powder,” is dyed pink. Infants are especially vulnerable, which is one reason nitrate in drinking water is regulated. Because concentrated sodium nitrite has also been misused deliberately, some countries now restrict its sale.
hazards.chemical: Hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, contains iron in its ferrous form, Fe²⁺, which can bind oxygen. Nitrite is an oxidizing agent: it can pull an electron off that iron, converting it to the ferric form, Fe³⁺. Hemoglobin with ferric iron is called methemoglobin, and it can't bind oxygen. It also makes the remaining normal hemoglobin hold onto its oxygen more tightly, so less is released to the tissues. The body has an enzyme that converts small amounts of methemoglobin back, but a large dose overwhelms it.
hazards.biological: When more than about 10 to 20 percent of hemoglobin has become methemoglobin, the skin and lips turn bluish-gray, a sign called cyanosis. Higher levels cause headache, dizziness, a racing heart, shortness of breath and confusion as organs run short of oxygen. Very high levels, above about 70 percent, can be fatal. Doctors treat severe cases with a drug called methylene blue, which helps convert methemoglobin back to normal hemoglobin. Babies under six months are especially vulnerable because their enzyme for reversing methemoglobin is not yet fully developed.

profile.dosage: U.S. rules limit how much nitrite can be added to cured meats; for bacon the limit is 120 parts per million, and much of it is used up during curing, leaving tens of parts per million or less in the finished product. Bacon must also contain added vitamin C or erythorbate to curb nitrosamine formation. Most of the nitrite people are exposed to actually comes from vegetable nitrate converted by mouth bacteria, which arrives with protective antioxidants. International experts have set an acceptable daily intake for nitrite of 0.07 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. Cancer organizations recommend eating little, if any, processed meat.

myths.claim: "Uncured, no nitrates added" bacon is nitrite-free.
myths.consensus: It is cured with celery powder, a natural nitrate source that becomes the same nitrite.

environment.persistence: Converted to nitrate in the environment.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic to fish at elevated concentrations.

synthesis.title: Absorbing nitrogen oxides
synthesis.summary: Sodium nitrite is made industrially from nitrogen oxides, gases containing nitrogen and oxygen that are produced by burning ammonia. This process is closely tied to the manufacture of nitric acid, which is used to make fertilizers and explosives. The nitrogen oxides are captured in a basic solution that converts them into sodium nitrite. The product is purified and sold for curing meat, preventing corrosion and making dyes and medicines. Food-grade sodium nitrite must meet strict purity standards.
synthesis.mechanism: First, ammonia (NH₃) is burned with air over a platinum catalyst at about 900 °C, producing nitric oxide (NO) and water. Some of the nitric oxide reacts further with oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide (NO₂). A mixture of NO and NO₂ in roughly equal amounts is bubbled through a solution of sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate. The two gases react together with the base to form sodium nitrite and water. Any sodium nitrate formed as a byproduct is separated off, and the sodium nitrite is crystallized, dried and packaged.
synthesis.significance: The same burning of ammonia, called the Ostwald process, is the first step in making nitric acid for fertilizers.

synthesis.title: “Natural” curing with celery powder
synthesis.summary: Many processed meats labeled “uncured” or “no nitrites added” are actually cured with celery powder or celery juice instead of sodium nitrite. Celery naturally contains a lot of nitrate, which can be turned into nitrite. U.S. labeling rules require these products to say “uncured” along with “no nitrates or nitrites added except those naturally occurring in celery powder.” But the meat ends up containing nitrite that works exactly the same way. Some studies have found similar or even higher nitrite levels in these products.
synthesis.mechanism: Celery is grown and harvested, and its juice, rich in nitrate absorbed from the soil, is extracted. Bacteria, often a species called Staphylococcus carnosus, are added to the juice. These bacteria have an enzyme called nitrate reductase that removes an oxygen atom from nitrate, converting it into nitrite. After fermentation, the nitrite-rich juice is dried into a powder. Added to meat, this nitrite cures it exactly as sodium nitrite does, producing the pink color, cured flavor and protection against botulism.
synthesis.significance: The nitrite is chemically identical, which is why “no nitrites added” bacon still contains nitrite.

citations.title: Thymoquinone therapy remediates elevated brain tissue inflammatory mediators induced by chronic administration of food preservatives.
citations.abstract: Continuous exposure to preservatives such as nitrite salts has deleterious effects on different organs. Meanwhile, Nigella sativa oil can remediate such organ dysfunction. Here, we studied the effect of consumption of thymoquinone (TQ); the main component of Nigella sativa oil on the brain damage induced by sodium nitrite. Forty adult male rats were daily given oral gavage of sodium nitrite (80 mg/kg) with or without thymoquinone (50 mg/kg). Oxidative stress, cytokines of inflammation, fibrotic elements and apoptotic markers in brain tissue were measured. Exposure to sodium nitrite (SN) resulted in increased levels of malondialdehyde, TGF-β, c-reactive protein, NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β and caspase-3 associated with reduced levels of glutathione, cytochrome c oxidase, Nrf2 and IL-10. However, exposure of rats' brain tissues to thymoquinone resulted ameliorated all these effects. In conclusion, thymoquinone remediates sodium nitrite-induced brain impairment through several mechanisms including attenuation of oxidative stress, retrieving the reduced concentration of glutathione, blocks elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, restores cytochrome c oxidase activity, and reducing the apoptosis markers in the brain tissues of rats.

citations.title: Reaction of Dimethyl Trisulfide with Hemoglobin.
citations.abstract: Dimethyl trisulfide (DMTS) is a promising antidotal candidate for cyanide intoxication. DMTS acts as a sulfur donor in the conversion of cyanide to the less-toxic thiocyanate. The alternate reaction pathways of DMTS in the blood are not well understood. We report changes in the hemoglobin absorption spectrum upon reaction with DMTS. These changes closely match those induced by the known methemoglobin former, sodium nitrite. The kinetics of methemoglobin formation with DMTS is slower than with sodium nitrite. These results support the hypothesis that a potentially significant side-reaction of the therapeutically administered DMTS is the oxidization of hemoglobin to methemoglobin.

citations.title: Inorganic Salts and Antimicrobial Photodynamic Therapy: Mechanistic Conundrums?
citations.abstract: We have recently discovered that the photodynamic action of many different photosensitizers (PSs) can be dramatically potentiated by addition of a solution containing a range of different inorganic salts. Most of these studies have centered around antimicrobial photodynamic inactivation that kills Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria in suspension. Addition of non-toxic water-soluble salts during illumination can kill up to six additional logs of bacterial cells (one million-fold improvement). The PSs investigated range from those that undergo mainly Type I photochemical mechanisms (electron transfer to produce superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals), such as phenothiazinium dyes, fullerenes, and titanium dioxide, to those that are mainly Type II (energy transfer to produce singlet oxygen), such as porphyrins, and Rose Bengal. At one extreme of the salts is sodium azide, that quenches singlet oxygen but can produce azide radicals (presumed to be highly reactive) via electron transfer from photoexcited phenothiazinium dyes. Potassium iodide is oxidized to molecular iodine by both Type I and Type II PSs, but may also form reactive iodine species. Potassium bromide is oxidized to hypobromite, but only by titanium dioxide photocatalysis (Type I). Potassium thiocyanate appears to require a mixture of Type I and Type II photochemistry to first produce sulfite, that can then form the sulfur trioxide radical anion. Potassium selenocyanate can react with either Type I or Type II (or indeed with other oxidizing agents) to produce the semi-stable selenocyanogen (SCN)₂. Finally, sodium nitrite may react with either Type I or Type II PSs to produce peroxynitrate (again, semi-stable) that can kill bacteria and nitrate tyrosine. Many of these salts (except azide) are non-toxic, and may be clinically applicable.

citations.title: Clinical features and management of cyanide poisoning.
citations.abstract: The pathophysiology, clinical features, and management of cyanide toxicity are reviewed and sources of cyanide are listed. Cyanide is a deadly poison that is found in many foods and household and industrial products, including some that are readily available. Cyanide binds with cytochrome oxidase, the enzyme responsible for oxidative phosphorylation, and paralyzes cellular respiration. Because the tissues cannot use oxygen that is delivered, aerobic metabolism ceases. The signs and symptoms of cyanide poisoning reflect the extent of cellular hypoxia. Manifestations may include respiratory abnormalities (progressing from tachypnea and dyspnea to respiratory depression and apnea), hemodynamic instability, metabolic acidosis, and, possibly, local irritant effects after oral ingestion of cyanide. The mainstays of therapy are 100% oxygen and specific antidotes to cyanide. Sequential treatment with amyl nitrite by inhalation, intravenous sodium nitrite 3%, and intravenous sodium thiosulfate 25% is directed toward decreasing the amount of cyanide available for cellular binding. Nitrites convert hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which reacts with cyanide to form cyanomethemoglobin. Sodium thiosulfate serves as a source of sulfur groups, which are needed for conversion of cyanide to thiocyanate, a compound that is relatively less toxic and is excreted renally. Supportive care also is important. Cobalt EDTA, hydroxocobalamin, and aminophenols have also been used but are not considered standard treatments. Cyanide poisoning is a medical emergency that requires prompt recognition and immediate and aggressive treatment.

citations.title: Dietary Nitrate and Nitric Oxide Metabolism: Mouth, Circulation, Skeletal Muscle, and Exercise Performance.
citations.abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) is a gaseous signaling molecule that plays an important role in myriad physiological processes, including the regulation of vascular tone, neurotransmission, mitochondrial respiration, and skeletal muscle contractile function. NO may be produced via the canonical NO synthase-catalyzed oxidation of l-arginine and also by the sequential reduction of nitrate to nitrite and then NO. The body's nitrate stores can be augmented by the ingestion of nitrate-rich foods (primarily green leafy vegetables). NO bioavailability is greatly enhanced by the activity of bacteria residing in the mouth, which reduce nitrate to nitrite, thereby increasing the concentration of circulating nitrite, which can be reduced further to NO in regions of low oxygen availability. Recent investigations have focused on promoting this nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway to positively affect indices of cardiovascular health and exercise tolerance. It has been reported that dietary nitrate supplementation with beetroot juice lowers blood pressure in hypertensive patients, and sodium nitrite supplementation improves vascular endothelial function and reduces the stiffening of large elastic arteries in older humans. Nitrate supplementation has also been shown to enhance skeletal muscle function and to improve exercise performance in some circumstances. Recently, it has been established that nitrate concentration in skeletal muscle is much higher than that in blood and that muscle nitrate stores are exquisitely sensitive to dietary nitrate supplementation and deprivation. In this review, we consider the possibility that nitrate represents an essential storage form of NO and discuss the integrated function of the oral microbiome, circulation, and skeletal muscle in nitrate-nitrite-NO metabolism, as well as the practical relevance for health and performance.
