name: Palm Oil
scoreRationale: High in saturated fat, refining can create processing contaminants, and unsustainable plantations drive deforestation.
summary: Palm oil is the world's most-used vegetable oil, in foods, soaps and cosmetics. It's versatile but high in saturated fat and linked to deforestation.

identity.composition: Triglycerides with about 44% palmitic, 39% oleic, 10% linoleic and 5% stearic acid.

overview: Palm oil is mostly triglycerides: molecules with a glycerol backbone carrying three fatty acids. About half are saturated, mainly palmitic acid (a straight 16-carbon chain), and half unsaturated, mainly oleic acid (an 18-carbon chain with one kinked cis double bond).

Straight saturated chains pack tightly, so palm oil is semi-solid at room temperature, giving baked goods and spreads their texture without the trans fats of partially hydrogenated oils. Unrefined red palm oil gets its orange color from beta-carotene.
profile.function: Provides texture and shelf stability in baked goods and spreads, and is the base of soaps and many surfactants.

mechanisms.title: Texture from fatty-acid packing
mechanisms.chemical: Fats are made of molecules called triglycerides, each with three fatty-acid chains attached to a glycerol backbone. Saturated fatty acids such as palmitic acid have only single bonds between their carbon atoms, so their chains are straight and can line up closely, like pencils in a box. Unsaturated fatty acids such as oleic acid have a double bond that puts a kink in the chain and stops it packing tightly. Where straight chains pack tightly they form stable crystals, which makes a fat solid. Palm oil's mix of roughly half straight and half kinked chains leaves it semi-solid at room temperature.
mechanisms.biological: Palm oil's crystal structure gives baked goods, spreads and sweets a pleasing texture. Because its fatty-acid mix melts close to body temperature, it feels creamy and melts smoothly in the mouth. In pastries, layers of solid fat create flakiness, and in spreads it provides spreadability without needing trans fats. This is why palm oil replaced partially hydrogenated oils, which contained harmful trans fats, in many products. It turns up in close to half of all packaged supermarket products, from bread to shampoo.

mechanisms.title: Raising LDL cholesterol
mechanisms.chemical: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) particles carry cholesterol through the blood. The liver clears LDL using LDL receptors on the surface of liver cells, which grab LDL particles and pull them inside. Saturated fatty acids, palmitic acid in particular, reduce the number and activity of these receptors. With fewer receptors at work, LDL particles stay in the blood longer and LDL cholesterol rises. Unsaturated fatty acids, such as the oleic acid in olive oil, don't have this effect and may even boost receptor activity.
mechanisms.biological: Over many years, high LDL cholesterol can lead to fatty plaques building up in artery walls, a process called atherosclerosis. These plaques narrow the arteries and can rupture, triggering blood clots that cause heart attacks or strokes. Studies comparing oils show that palm oil raises LDL cholesterol more than unsaturated oils like olive, canola or sunflower oil, though less than butter. That is why health guidelines recommend swapping saturated fats for unsaturated ones. Palm oil is still a better choice than the trans fats it replaced in many products.

mechanisms.title: Beta-carotene in red palm oil
mechanisms.chemical: Unrefined palm oil is rich in carotenoids, especially beta-carotene, the same pigment that makes carrots orange. Beta-carotene has a long chain of alternating single and double bonds, a conjugated system that absorbs blue light, so it looks orange-red. In the intestine, an enzyme can split a beta-carotene molecule in half to make vitamin A. Red palm oil is one of the richest natural sources of beta-carotene. Refining, especially the bleaching and deodorizing steps, removes most of it.
mechanisms.biological: Vitamin A is essential for vision, especially in dim light, for a healthy immune system and for growth. Vitamin A deficiency is a major cause of preventable blindness in children in parts of the world. Red palm oil has been used in programs in India and parts of Africa to help prevent deficiency, particularly in children and pregnant women. Because beta-carotene dissolves in fat, it is well absorbed when eaten in oil. Most palm oil sold commercially, however, is refined and pale, having lost these carotenoids.

reactions.title: Saponification (making soap)
reactions.summary: Saponification is the reaction that turns fats and oils into soap. People have used it for thousands of years, and it involves heating fat with a strong base such as sodium hydroxide, also called lye. The base breaks the ester bonds that hold fatty acids to glycerol. The fatty acids become soap molecules, and glycerol is released as a byproduct. Palm oil is widely used in soapmaking because its fatty acids make hard, long-lasting bars.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: Hydroxide ions (OH⁻) from the lye attack the carbon atoms in the ester bonds linking each fatty acid to the glycerol backbone. These carbons are slightly positive because they are attached to two oxygen atoms. The hydroxide bonds to the carbon and the ester bond breaks.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: As each ester bond breaks, a fatty acid comes free of the glycerol. Once all three bonds have broken, glycerol is released as its own molecule with three –OH groups. Glycerol is valuable in cosmetics and foods.

steps.name: Soap
steps.text: Each fatty acid, now carrying a negatively charged carboxylate group, pairs with a sodium ion to form a fatty-acid salt. These salts are soap molecules, with a long oily tail and a charged, water-loving head that together let them trap grease in water.

reactions.result: Many bar soaps list “sodium palmate,” which is soap made from palm oil; it makes hard bars with a creamy lather. The same reaction happens slowly when fats meet strong cleaning products, which is how drain cleaners dissolve greasy clogs.

reactions.title: Refining contaminants
reactions.summary: Crude palm oil is refined to remove impurities, color and strong flavors, producing the pale, neutral oil used in most foods. One step, deodorization, uses very high temperatures. At those temperatures unwanted side reactions can create contaminants, notably glycidyl esters and 3-MCPD esters. These raised health concerns because of their effects in animal studies. Since the problem was identified, manufacturers have changed their processes to greatly reduce them.

steps.name: Deodorizing
steps.text: The oil is heated to about 230 to 260 °C under vacuum while steam is blown through it. This strips out volatile molecules responsible for unwanted smells and flavors, along with free fatty acids. The high temperature is needed to remove them efficiently.

steps.name: Side reactions
steps.text: At these temperatures, diglycerides, glycerol molecules carrying two fatty acids, can lose a fatty acid and close into a three-atom ring, forming glycidyl esters. If chloride is present, it can react with glycerides to form 3-MCPD esters. Palm oil naturally contains more diglycerides than other oils, so it tends to form more of these contaminants.

steps.name: Mitigation
steps.text: Manufacturers reduce these contaminants by washing out chloride before refining, deodorizing at lower temperatures for shorter times, and using fresher fruit that contains fewer diglycerides. Some contaminants can also be removed after refining.

reactions.result: Since the European Food Safety Authority's 2016 opinion on these contaminants, industry changes have sharply reduced glycidyl ester levels in refined palm oil. The EU has also set legal maximum levels for them in oils and infant foods.

regulatory.status: Maximum limits for glycidyl esters in vegetable oils since 2018.
The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil certifies deforestation-controlled supply chains.
Requires proof that palm oil is deforestation-free once it applies.

hazards.title: Higher LDL cholesterol
hazards.summary: Palm oil isn't toxic, but because it is high in saturated fat, eating a lot of it can raise LDL cholesterol compared with oils rich in unsaturated fat. This is a concern about overall diet rather than any single food. Palm oil is less harmful than the trans fats it replaced in many processed foods, but more likely to raise cholesterol than olive, canola or sunflower oil. Because it is in so many processed foods, people can eat a fair amount without realizing it. Health guidelines recommend limiting saturated fat overall.
hazards.chemical: About 44 percent of palm oil's fatty acids are palmitic acid, a saturated fat with 16 carbon atoms. Palmitic acid reduces the activity of LDL receptors in the liver, the proteins responsible for clearing LDL cholesterol from the blood. With fewer active receptors, LDL particles circulate longer and cholesterol levels rise. Palm oil also contains about 40 percent oleic acid, which partly offsets this effect. The overall impact depends on which fats palm oil is replacing in someone's diet.
hazards.biological: High LDL cholesterol is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis, the buildup of fatty plaques in artery walls that can lead to heart attacks and strokes. Studies show that replacing saturated fats like palm oil with unsaturated fats lowers LDL cholesterol and reduces heart disease risk. Health guidance recommends keeping saturated fat below 10 percent of daily calories, which for a 2,000-calorie diet is about 22 grams. A diet built around whole foods, with less processed food, naturally contains less palm oil.

hazards.title: Processing contaminants
hazards.summary: Refining palm oil at high temperatures can create contaminants called glycidyl esters and 3-MCPD esters. These form in many refined vegetable oils, but palm oil tends to have higher levels. They became a concern because animal studies showed possible health effects at high doses. The European Union now sets legal maximum levels for them. Infant formula, which often contains refined vegetable oils, has especially strict limits.
hazards.chemical: Glycidyl esters form during high-temperature deodorization when diglycerides, which palm oil contains in relatively large amounts, lose a fatty acid and close into a ring. During digestion, enzymes break glycidyl esters apart, releasing glycidol, a small, reactive molecule with a strained three-atom ring that can react with DNA. 3-MCPD esters form when chloride is present during refining, and they release 3-MCPD during digestion. Both glycidol and 3-MCPD are then absorbed into the body.
hazards.biological: In animal studies, glycidol caused tumors in several organs and can damage DNA, so IARC classifies it as probably carcinogenic to humans (Group 2A). 3-MCPD damaged the kidneys and affected male fertility in rats. Because glycidol may damage DNA, regulators aim to keep exposure as low as reasonably achievable. Babies fed formula were found to have relatively high exposure for their body weight, which is why formula limits are especially strict. Industry efforts have greatly reduced these contaminants since 2016.

profile.dosage: Palm oil appears in close to half of packaged supermarket products, from bread and cookies to margarine and instant noodles, usually as one of several fats. Health guidance recommends keeping saturated fat below 10 percent of daily calories, about 22 grams on a 2,000-calorie diet, and palm oil is roughly half saturated fat: a tablespoon contains about 7 grams. Using oils rich in unsaturated fat, such as olive or canola, for most cooking and limiting heavily processed foods keeps intake moderate. Refined oils sold in the EU must meet legal limits for glycidyl esters and 3-MCPD.

myths.claim: Red palm oil is a superfood.
myths.consensus: It is rich in beta-carotene and vitamin E, but it's still about 50% saturated fat.

environment.notes: Plantation expansion in Indonesia and Malaysia has destroyed rainforest habitat for orangutans and released peatland carbon.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis in the fruit
synthesis.summary: The oil palm, Elaeis guineensis, originally from West Africa, makes oil in two parts of its fruit: the fleshy outer layer, called the mesocarp, which yields palm oil, and the seed, which yields palm kernel oil. The two oils differ: palm kernel oil is much richer in saturated lauric acid, like coconut oil. Oil palms are the most productive oil crop, giving several times more oil per hectare than soybeans or sunflowers. The fruit takes about five to six months to develop. Its oil content rises rapidly in the final weeks of ripening.
synthesis.mechanism: Inside the fruit's cells, an enzyme complex called fatty acid synthase builds fatty acids from small two-carbon units supplied by acetyl-CoA, adding two carbons at a time until it reaches a 16-carbon chain, palmitic acid. Some palmitic acid is extended to 18 carbons, forming stearic acid, and an enzyme called a desaturase then inserts a double bond to make oleic acid. These fatty acids are attached one by one to a glycerol-3-phosphate backbone, forming triglycerides. The triglycerides collect in oil droplets in the cells of the fleshy mesocarp. When the fruit is ripe, oil makes up about half of the mesocarp's weight.
synthesis.significance: Because oil palms yield so much oil per hectare, replacing them with other oil crops would require far more farmland.

synthesis.title: Milling and refining
synthesis.summary: Turning palm fruit into cooking oil involves milling, which extracts crude oil, and refining, which cleans it up. Fresh fruit bunches have to be processed within about a day of harvest, because enzymes in the fruit start breaking down the oil. Indonesia and Malaysia together produce about 85 percent of the world's palm oil. Crude palm oil is a deep orange-red with a strong flavor. Refining turns it into a pale, neutral oil.
synthesis.mechanism: At the mill, fresh fruit bunches are steamed under pressure, which destroys the enzymes that would split fats into free fatty acids and loosens the fruit from the bunch. The fruit is mashed and pressed to squeeze out crude palm oil, which is clarified to remove water and fiber. At the refinery the oil is degummed with acid to remove phospholipids, bleached with clay that soaks up pigments and impurities, and deodorized with steam at high temperature to remove odors and free fatty acids. The refined oil can then be cooled slowly so that solid crystals form, separating it into liquid palm olein, used for cooking, and solid palm stearin, used in margarine and baking fats.
synthesis.significance: Plantation expansion has destroyed rainforest habitat; certification schemes such as RSPO aim to trace deforestation-free supply.

citations.title: Biobased adipic acid - The challenge of developing the production host.
citations.abstract: Adipic acid is a platform chemical, and is the most important commercial dicarboxylic acid. It has been targeted for biochemical conversion as an alternative to present chemical production routes. From the perspective of bioeconomy, several kinds of raw material are of interest including the sugar platform (derived from starch, cellulose or hemicellulose), the lignin platform (aromatics) and the fatty acid platform (lipid derived). Two main biochemical-based production schemes may be employed: (i) direct fermentation to adipic acid, or (ii) fermentation to muconic or glucaric acid, followed by chemical hydrogenation (indirect fermentation). This review presents a comprehensive description of the metabolic pathways that could be constructed and analyzes their respective theoretical yields and metabolic constraints. The experimental yields and titers obtained so far are low, with the exception of processes based on palm oil and glycerol, which have been reported to yield up to 50 g and 68 g adipic acid/L, respectively. The challenges that remain to be addressed in order to achieve industrially relevant production levels include solving redox constraints, and identifying and/or engineering enzymes for parts of the metabolic pathways that have yet to be metabolically demonstrated. This review provides new insights into ways in which metabolic pathways can be constructed to achieve efficient adipic acid production. The production host provides the chassis to be engineered via an appropriate metabolic pathway, and should also have properties suitable for the industrial production of adipic acid. An acidic process pH is attractive to reduce the cost of downstream processing. The production host should exhibit high tolerance to complex raw material streams and high adipic acid concentrations at acidic pH.

citations.title: Dietary Palmitic Acid Drives a Palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC15-YAP Feedback Loop Promoting Tumor Metastasis.
citations.abstract: Elevated uptake of saturated fatty acid palmitic acid (PA) is associated with tumor metastasis; however, the precise mechanisms remain partially understood, hindering the development of therapy for PA-driven tumor metastasis. The Hippo-Yes-associated protein (Hippo/YAP) pathway is implicated in cancer progression. Here it is shown that a high-palm oil diet potentiates tumor metastasis in murine xenografts in part through YAP. It is found that the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC15 is a YAP-regulated gene that forms a feedback loop with YAP. Notably, PA drives the ZDHHC15-YAP feedback loop, thus enforces YAP signaling, and hence promotes tumor metastasis in murine xenografts. In addition, it is shown that ZDHHC15 associates with Kidney and brain protein (KIBRA, also known as WW- and C2 domain-containing protein 1, WWC1), an upstream component of Hippo signaling, and mediates its palmitoylation. KIBRA palmitoylation leads to its degradation and regulates its subcellular localization and activity toward the Hippo/YAP pathway. Moreover, PA enhances KIBRA palmitoylation and degradation. It is further shown that combinatorial targeting of YAP and fatty acid synthesis exhibits augmented effects against metastasis formation in mice fed with a Palm diet. Collectively, these findings uncover a ZDHHC15-YAP feedback loop as a previously unrecognized mechanism underlying PA-promoted tumor metastasis and support targeting YAP and fatty acid synthesis as potential therapeutic targets in PA-driven tumor metastasis.

citations.title: Palm Oil on the Edge.
citations.abstract: Internationally recognized Spanish experts in the food industry, nutrition, toxicology, sustainability, and veterinary science met in Madrid on July 2018 to develop a consensus about palm oil (PO) as a food ingredient. Their aim was to provide a useful, evidence-based point of reference about PO. Scientific evidence about the role of PO in food safety, nutrition and sustainability was analyzed. Main conclusions were: (1) RSPO foundation responded to the environmental impact of palm crops. The Amsterdam Declaration pursues the use of 100% sustainable PO in Europe by 2020. Awareness about choosing sustainable products will help to maintain local economies and environments in the producing countries; (2) evidence shows that a moderate intake of PO within a healthy diet presents no risks for health. No evidence justifies any change fat intake recommendations; (3) food industry is interested in assuring safe, sustainable and high-quality products. The use of certified sustainable PO is increasing; and (4) there is no evidence associating PO consumption and higher cancer risk, incidence or mortality in humans. Tolerable daily intake (TDI) for toxic contaminants (2-and 3-monochloropropanediols (MCPDs), glycidyl esters (GEs)) have been established by JECFA and EFSA. Consequently, the European Commission has modified the Contaminants Regulation for GEs and it is still working on 3-MCPDs'.

citations.title: Anticancer properties of tocotrienols: A review of cellular mechanisms and molecular targets.
citations.authors: Montagnani Marelli, Marzagalli, Fontana et al.
citations.abstract: Vitamin E is composed of two groups of compounds: α-, β-, γ-, and δ-tocopherols (TPs), and the corresponding unsaturated tocotrienols (TTs). TTs are found in natural sources such as red palm oil, annatto seeds, and rice bran. In the last decades, TTs (specifically, γ-TT and δ-TT) have gained interest due to their health benefits in chronic diseases, based on their antioxidant, neuroprotective, cholesterol-lowering, anti-inflammatory activities. Several in vitro and in vivo studies pointed out that TTs also exert a significant antitumor activity in a wide range of cancer cells. Specifically, TTs were shown to exert antiproliferative/proapoptotic effects and to reduce the metastatic or angiogenic properties of different cancer cells; moreover, these compounds were reported to specifically target the subpopulation of cancer stem cells, known to be deeply involved in the development of resistance to standard therapies. Interestingly, recent studies pointed out that TTs exert a synergistic antitumor effect on cancer cells when given in combination with either standard antitumor agents (i.e., chemotherapeutics, statins, "targeted" therapies) or natural compounds with anticancer activity (i.e., sesamin, epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), resveratrol, ferulic acid). Based on these observations, different TT synthetic derivatives and formulations were recently developed and demonstrated to improve TT water solubility and to reduce TT metabolism in cancer cells, thus increasing their biological activity. These promising results, together with the safety of TT administration in healthy subjects, suggest that these compounds might represent a new chemopreventive or anticancer treatment (i.e., in combination with standard therapies) strategy. Clinical trials aimed at confirming this antitumor activity of TTs are needed.

citations.title: Overfeeding polyunsaturated and saturated fat causes distinct effects on liver and visceral fat accumulation in humans.
citations.abstract: Excess ectopic fat storage is linked to type 2 diabetes. The importance of dietary fat composition for ectopic fat storage in humans is unknown. We investigated liver fat accumulation and body composition during overfeeding saturated fatty acids (SFAs) or polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs). LIPOGAIN was a double-blind, parallel-group, randomized trial. Thirty-nine young and normal-weight individuals were overfed muffins high in SFAs (palm oil) or n-6 PUFAs (sunflower oil) for 7 weeks. Liver fat, visceral adipose tissue (VAT), abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), total adipose tissue, pancreatic fat, and lean tissue were assessed by magnetic resonance imaging. Transcriptomics were performed in SAT. Both groups gained similar weight. SFAs, however, markedly increased liver fat compared with PUFAs and caused a twofold larger increase in VAT than PUFAs. Conversely, PUFAs caused a nearly threefold larger increase in lean tissue than SFAs. Increase in liver fat directly correlated with changes in plasma SFAs and inversely with PUFAs. Genes involved in regulating energy dissipation, insulin resistance, body composition, and fat-cell differentiation in SAT were differentially regulated between diets, and associated with increased PUFAs in SAT. In conclusion, overeating SFAs promotes hepatic and visceral fat storage, whereas excess energy from PUFAs may instead promote lean tissue in healthy humans.

name: Lactic Acid
scoreRationale: A natural metabolite; in leave-on skincare at higher strengths it can irritate and increases sun sensitivity.
summary: Lactic acid is the tang in yogurt and a gentle exfoliating acid in skincare. It's produced naturally by your own muscles and skin.

overview: Lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) is a three-carbon molecule with a carboxylic acid group and a hydroxyl group on the neighboring carbon, making it an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA). Its middle carbon is chiral, so it exists as two mirror-image forms, L- and D-lactic acid; your muscles make the L-form.

It's the acid that sours milk into yogurt and cabbage into sauerkraut, and it builds up in hard-working muscles. On skin, it's one of the gentlest exfoliating acids, and its salt, sodium lactate, is part of the skin's own moisturizing system.
profile.function: Acidifies and preserves foods, exfoliates and hydrates skin, and descales in bathroom cleaners.

mechanisms.title: Energy when oxygen runs short
mechanisms.chemical: Cells break glucose down for energy in a series of reactions called glycolysis, which splits each glucose into two molecules of pyruvate and makes a small amount of ATP. Glycolysis also needs a helper molecule called NAD⁺, which picks up electrons along the way and becomes NADH. Normally NADH hands its electrons on to the mitochondria, which use oxygen to make much more ATP. When oxygen is in short supply, such as during intense exercise, that can't happen fast enough. Instead, an enzyme called lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH to convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates the NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep going.
mechanisms.biological: This lets muscles keep producing energy quickly during sprints and heavy effort, even when oxygen delivery can't keep up. Lactate isn't a waste product: the blood carries it to the heart, other muscles and the brain, which burn it as fuel. The liver can also turn lactate back into glucose and send it back to the muscles, a loop called the Cori cycle. Contrary to a common myth, lactic acid doesn't cause the soreness you feel a day or two after exercise; that comes from tiny injuries in the muscle fibers. The burning feeling during intense effort is linked to a buildup of hydrogen ions and other factors.

mechanisms.title: Gentle exfoliation
mechanisms.chemical: Lactic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA), a molecule with an –OH group on the carbon next to its acid group. The outermost layer of skin is made of dead cells held together by connections called desmosomes and by fatty substances. Below about pH 4, a good share of lactic acid is in its uncharged form, which can slip into that outer layer. There it weakens the ionic and hydrogen bonds holding dead cells together and may take away some of the calcium that stabilizes their connections. As a result, dead cells come loose more easily.
mechanisms.biological: When dead cells are shed faster, the skin surface becomes smoother and more even, and fine lines and dull patches can look less noticeable. Regular use can also improve rough skin and mild uneven pigmentation. Lactic acid molecules are larger than glycolic acid molecules, so they soak into skin more slowly, which makes them gentler and less likely to irritate. That's why lactic acid is often recommended for sensitive skin. It also appears in treatments for very dry, rough skin, such as keratosis pilaris.

mechanisms.title: Moisturizing
mechanisms.chemical: Sodium lactate, the salt of lactic acid, has a charged carboxylate group and a hydroxyl group, both of which attract water molecules through hydrogen bonds and electrical attraction. Substances that attract and hold water are called humectants. Sodium lactate is a natural part of the skin's natural moisturizing factor, a mix of water-attracting molecules inside the cells of the outermost skin layer. These molecules pull in water from the air and from deeper skin layers and hold it in place. Lactic acid itself works as a humectant too.
mechanisms.biological: By holding water in the outer layer of skin, sodium lactate keeps it soft and flexible so it can stretch without cracking. When skin is short of natural moisturizing factor, as in some dry-skin conditions, it becomes rough, flaky and prone to splitting. Lotions containing lactic acid or lactate salts help replace these molecules and improve hydration. Products with about 5 to 12 percent lactate are used to treat very dry skin and conditions such as ichthyosis. In this way lactic acid both moisturizes and gently exfoliates.

mechanisms.title: Preserving food
mechanisms.chemical: Lactic acid preserves food in two ways. First, it lowers the food's pH, and many spoilage and disease-causing bacteria can't grow below about pH 4.5. Second, uncharged lactic acid molecules can pass through bacterial cell membranes; inside, where the pH is near neutral, they release their protons and acidify the cell's interior, disrupting its enzymes and its energy supply. Lactic acid is produced naturally during fermentation by lactic acid bacteria, which tolerate the acidity they create. In effect, these friendly bacteria make their surroundings hostile to competitors.
mechanisms.biological: This is how fermentation has preserved food for thousands of years. In yogurt, sauerkraut, kimchi, pickles and sourdough, lactic acid bacteria convert sugars into lactic acid, which gives these foods their sour taste and keeps many harmful bacteria from growing. The acidity also changes texture, for example by making milk proteins clump into yogurt. Lactic acid is added directly to some foods as well, and it is used to rinse meat carcasses to reduce bacteria. Many fermented foods also contain live bacteria that may benefit gut health.

reactions.title: Lactic acid fermentation
reactions.summary: Lactic acid fermentation is how bacteria, and your own muscle cells, turn sugar into lactic acid without using oxygen. It is an ancient and widespread way of getting energy, used by microbes for billions of years. Humans have harnessed it for thousands of years to make yogurt, cheese, sauerkraut, pickles and sourdough. It produces only a little energy compared with breathing oxygen, but it is fast. In factories, it is used to make most of the world's lactic acid.

steps.name: Glycolysis
steps.text: A glucose molecule, with six carbon atoms, is broken down through ten enzyme-controlled steps into two molecules of pyruvate, each with three carbons. This releases enough energy to make two molecules of ATP. Meanwhile, two molecules of NAD⁺ pick up electrons and become NADH.

steps.name: Reduction
steps.text: The enzyme lactate dehydrogenase passes electrons from NADH to each pyruvate, converting it into lactate. This is called reduction because pyruvate gains electrons. Each glucose yields two lactates.

steps.name: Recycling
steps.text: Turning pyruvate into lactate converts NADH back into NAD⁺. Because glycolysis needs NAD⁺ to continue, recycling it lets glycolysis keep running without oxygen. That is the whole point of the process: keeping the energy supply going.

reactions.result: Lactobacillus bacteria use this to sour milk into yogurt: the lactic acid lowers the pH, which makes milk's casein proteins clump together and thicken. Similar bacteria ferment cabbage into sauerkraut and give sourdough its tang. In your muscles, the same process helps you sprint.

reactions.title: Polymerization into PLA plastic
reactions.summary: Lactic acid can be linked into long chains to make a plastic called polylactic acid, or PLA. PLA is made from renewable plant sugars, such as those from corn or sugarcane, rather than from petroleum. Under industrial composting conditions it breaks back down into lactic acid, which microbes then consume. It is used in 3D-printing filament, compostable cups and food packaging. However, PLA doesn't break down easily in home compost, soil or the ocean.

steps.name: Dimerizing
steps.text: Lactic acid molecules are first linked into short chains and then heated with a catalyst to form a ring made of two lactic acid units, called lactide. This step removes water. The lactide is purified to remove anything that would weaken the plastic.

steps.name: Ring opening
steps.text: Lactide is heated with a tin-based catalyst, which opens the ring. Each opened ring can then attach to another, so a chain grows. This is called ring-opening polymerization, and it lets very long chains form quickly.

steps.name: Polymer
steps.text: The chains grow to thousands of lactic acid units long, forming polylactic acid. The long chains tangle and pack together into a clear, strong plastic. Its properties depend on the chain length and on which mirror-image forms of lactic acid were used.

reactions.result: PLA is used in 3D-printer filament and compostable cups, and also in dissolvable surgical stitches, which slowly break down into lactic acid inside the body. Using just one mirror-image form of lactic acid makes stronger, more heat-resistant PLA.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe; recommends a sunburn alert on alpha-hydroxy acid cosmetics.
AHAs are safe at 10% or less, pH 3.5 or higher, with sun protection advised.

hazards.title: Increased sun sensitivity (AHAs)
hazards.summary: Skincare products containing alpha-hydroxy acids, including lactic acid, can make skin more prone to sunburn. This was found in studies sponsored by the U.S. FDA around the turn of the 2000s. The effect lasts while the product is in use and for about a week after stopping. Because of this, the FDA recommends that AHA products carry a sunburn alert. Daily sunscreen prevents the problem.
hazards.chemical: The outermost layer of skin, the stratum corneum, is made of dead cells that help scatter and absorb ultraviolet light. AHAs like lactic acid speed up the shedding of these cells, which makes this protective layer thinner. With less dead-cell material in the way, more ultraviolet radiation reaches the living cells underneath. UV light carries enough energy to damage DNA and other molecules in those cells. The thinner the outer layer, the more UV gets through.
hazards.biological: When UV light damages skin cells badly enough, some of them die, forming what scientists call sunburn cells. In the FDA-sponsored studies, people who had been using AHA products for several weeks developed more sunburn cells and burned more easily after a measured dose of UV. Over time, extra UV damage contributes to premature skin aging and raises the risk of skin cancer. That is why AHA products are labeled with advice to use sunscreen and limit sun exposure. Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen is recommended for anyone using them.

hazards.title: Irritation at high strength
hazards.summary: Lactic acid is one of the gentlest exfoliating acids, but at high concentrations or very low pH it can still irritate skin. This is more likely with products containing more than 10 percent lactic acid, with a pH below 3.5, or when they are used too often. People with sensitive skin, eczema or rosacea are more prone to it. Professional chemical peels use much higher concentrations under supervision. Starting with a lower strength and using it less often reduces the risk.
hazards.chemical: A low-pH product contains many hydrogen ions, and a high concentration of lactic acid pushes more acid molecules into the skin. Together they can break down the skin barrier more than intended, removing too many dead cells and disrupting the fatty layers between them. Water then escapes from the skin more easily, and irritants can penetrate deeper. Acid can also directly activate pain-sensing nerve endings. The lower the pH and the higher the concentration, the stronger the effect.
hazards.biological: When the skin barrier is disrupted, nerve endings fire, causing stinging or burning, and inflammatory signals widen blood vessels, causing redness. Overdoing exfoliation can lead to peeling, flaking and increased sensitivity. In darker skin tones, irritation sometimes leaves dark patches called post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. These effects usually fade once use is reduced or stopped. A plain moisturizer and sunscreen help the skin recover.

profile.dosage: Foods use under 1 percent lactic acid to add tartness or act as a preservative, and the U.S. FDA considers it generally recognized as safe with no set daily limit, since the body makes and uses lactate constantly. In skincare, U.S. safety reviews recommend that consumer products contain no more than 10 percent alpha-hydroxy acids at a pH of at least 3.5; most retail products use about 5 to 10 percent. Professional peels use higher concentrations under supervision. Daily sunscreen is recommended while using AHA products, and people with sensitive skin should start with lower strengths.

myths.claim: Lactic acid buildup causes next-day muscle soreness.
myths.consensus: Delayed soreness comes from muscle micro-damage; lactate clears within an hour and is used as fuel.

synthesis.title: Bacterial fermentation
synthesis.summary: Nearly all lactic acid made today comes from bacterial fermentation, the same process that makes yogurt but on an industrial scale. Bacteria such as Lactobacillus, or specially engineered microbes, are grown in large tanks on sugar from corn, sugarcane or beets. Fermentation makes lactic acid efficiently from renewable materials. About 90 percent of the world's lactic acid is produced this way. It goes into food, cosmetics, medicines and PLA plastic.
synthesis.mechanism: Bacteria are grown in sterile tanks containing glucose or sucrose, nutrients and water, kept warm. As they ferment the sugar they produce lactic acid, which lowers the pH. To keep the bacteria working, calcium carbonate or another base is added to neutralize the acid, forming calcium lactate. After fermentation the bacteria are filtered out, and the calcium lactate is treated with sulfuric acid, which frees the lactic acid and forms solid calcium sulfate that can be filtered away. The lactic acid is then purified by methods such as distillation, ion exchange or crystallization.
synthesis.significance: Fermentation produces a single mirror-image form, which matters for making high-quality PLA.

synthesis.title: Chemical synthesis
synthesis.summary: Before fermentation took over, lactic acid was made chemically from petroleum-derived starting materials. The route uses acetaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide, both produced from fossil fuels. Chemically, the result is the same lactic acid, but with an important difference in shape. Fermentation has largely replaced this method. A small amount is still made chemically.
synthesis.mechanism: Acetaldehyde, a small molecule with an aldehyde group, reacts with hydrogen cyanide, which adds across the aldehyde's carbon–oxygen double bond. This forms lactonitrile, a molecule carrying both a hydroxyl group and a nitrile group (–C≡N). The lactonitrile is then treated with strong acid and water, which converts the nitrile into a carboxylic acid group by hydrolysis, giving lactic acid and an ammonium salt. The lactic acid is purified by turning it into an ester, distilling that ester, and then splitting it back into lactic acid.
synthesis.significance: This route gives a 50:50 mix of both mirror-image forms (a racemic mixture), which is why fermentation replaced it.

citations.title: Reduction of hydrogen peroxide in gram-negative bacteria - bacterial peroxidases.
citations.abstract: Bacteria display an array of enzymes to detoxify reactive oxygen species that cause damage to DNA and to other biomolecules leading to cell death. Hydrogen peroxide is one of these species, with endogenous and exogenous sources, such as lactic acid bacteria, oxidative burst of the immune system or chemical reactions at oxic-anoxic interfaces. The enzymes that detoxify hydrogen peroxide will be the focus of this review, with special emphasis on bacterial peroxidases that reduce hydrogen peroxide to water. Bacterial peroxidases are periplasmic cytochromes with either two or three c-type haems, which have been classified as classical and non-classical bacterial peroxidases, respectively. Most of the studies have been focus on the classical bacterial peroxidases, showing the presence of a reductive activation in the presence of calcium ions. Mutagenesis studies have clarified the catalytic mechanism of this enzyme and were used to propose an intramolecular electron transfer pathway, with far less being known about the intermolecular electron transfer that occurs between reduced electron donors and the enzyme. The physiological function of these enzymes was not very clear until it was shown, for the non-classical bacterial peroxidase, that this enzyme is required for the bacteria to use hydrogen peroxide as terminal electron acceptor under anoxic conditions. These non-classical bacterial peroxidases are quinol peroxidases that do not require reductive activation but need calcium ions to attain maximum activity and share similar catalytic intermediates with the classical bacterial peroxidases.

citations.title: Arginine dihydrolase pathway in Lactobacillus buchneri: a review.
citations.authors: Manca de Nadra, Pesce de Ruiz Holgado, Oliver
citations.abstract: The arginine dihydrolase system was studied in homo- and hetero-fermentative lactic acid bacteria. This system is widely distributed in Betabacteria lactobacilli subgroup (group II in Bergey's Manual). It is generally absent in the Thermobacterium lactobacilli subgroup (group IA in Bergey's Manual) and also in the Streptobacterium subgroup (group IB in Bergey's Manual). It is present in some species of the genus Streptococcus (groups II, III and IV in Bergey's Manual). In Lactobacillus buchneri NCDO110 the 3 enzymes of the arginine dihydrolase pathway, arginine deiminase, ornithine transcarbamylase and carbamate kinase, were purified and characterized. Arginine deiminase was partially purified (68-fold); ornithine transcarbamylase was also partially purified (14-fold), while carbamate kinase was purified to homogeneity. The apparent molecular weight of the enzymes was 199,000, 162,000 and 97,000 for arginine deiminase, ornithine transcarbamylase and carbamate kinase respectively. For arginine deiminase, maximum enzymatic activity was observed at 50 degrees C and pH 6; for ornithine transcarbamylase it was observed at 35 degrees C and pH 8.5, and for carbamate kinase at 30 degrees C and pH 5.4. The activation energy of the reactions was determined. For arginine deiminase, delta G* values were: 8,700 cal mol-1 below 50 degrees C and 380 cal mol-1 above 50 degrees C; for ornithine transcarbamylase, the values were: 9,100 cal mol-1 below 35 degrees C and 4,300 cal mol-1 above 35 degrees C; for carbamate kinase, the activation energy was: 4,078 cal mol-1 for the reaction with Mn2+ and 3,059 cal mol-1 for the reaction with Mg2+.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 250 WORDS)

citations.title: Role of topical emollients and moisturizers in the treatment of dry skin barrier disorders.
citations.abstract: Emollients and moisturizing creams are used to break the dry skin cycle and to maintain the smoothness of the skin. The term 'moisturizer' is often used synonymously with emollient, but moisturizers often contain humectants in order to hydrate the stratum corneum. Dryness is frequently linked to an impaired barrier function observed, for example, in atopic skin, psoriasis, ichthyosis, and contact dermatitis. Dryness and skin barrier disorders are not a single entity, but are characterized by differences in chemistry and morphology in the epidermis. Large differences also exist between moisturizing creams. Moisturizers have multiple functions apart from moistening the skin. Similar to other actives, the efficacy is likely to depend on the dosage, where compliance is a great challenge faced in the management of skin diseases. Strong odor from ingredients and greasy compositions may be disagreeable to the patients. Furthermore, low pH and sensory reactions, from lactic acid and urea for example, may reduce patient acceptance. Once applied to the skin, the ingredients can stay on the surface, be absorbed into the skin, be metabolized, or disappear from the surface by evaporation, sloughing off, or by contact with other materials. In addition to substances considered as actives, e.g. fats and humectants, moisturizers contain substances conventionally considered as excipients (e.g. emulsifiers, antioxidants, preservatives). Recent findings indicate that actives and excipients may have more pronounced effects in the skin than previously considered. Some formulations may deteriorate the skin condition, whereas others improve the clinical appearance and skin barrier function. For example, emulsifiers may weaken the barrier. On the other hand, petrolatum has an immediate barrier-repairing effect in delipidized stratum corneum. Moreover, one ceramide-dominant lipid mixture improved atopic dermatitis and decreased transepidermal water loss (TEWL) in an open-label study in children. In double-blind studies moisturizers with urea have been shown to reduce TEWL in atopic and ichthyotic patients. Urea also makes normal and atopic skin less susceptible against irritation to sodium laurilsulfate. Treatments improving the barrier function may reduce the likelihood of further aggravation of the disease. In order to have optimum effect it is conceivable that moisturizers should be tailored with respect to the epidermal abnormality. New biochemical approaches and non-invasive instruments will increase our understanding of skin barrier disorders and facilitate optimum treatments. The chemistry and function of dry skin and moisturizers is a challenging subject for the practicing dermatologist, as well as for the chemist developing these agents in the pharmaceutical/cosmetic industry.

citations.title: Probiotics for allergy prevention.
citations.abstract: Probiotics, given either as a supplement or in infant foods, have been evaluated in randomised controlled trials for allergy prevention. Here, the aim is to give an overview of the results from these primary prevention studies and to discuss current strategies. In most studies, single strains or a mixture of strains of lactic acid bacteria and bifidobacteria have been used--prenatally, postnatally or perinatally. Several meta-analyses have reported a moderate benefit of probiotics for eczema prevention, and the most consistent effect has been observed with a combined perinatal intervention in infants at high risk of allergic disease due to familial predisposition. In a recent meta-analysis, the use of multi-strain probiotics appeared to be most effective for eczema prevention. No preventive effect has been shown for other allergic manifestations. As long-term follow-up data on later onset allergic conditions (asthma and allergic rhinitis) are available only from a few of the initiated studies, reports from ongoing follow-up studies that are adequately powered to examine long-term outcomes are anticipated to provide more insight. Arguably, the differences in many aspects of study design and the use of different probiotic strains and combinations have made direct comparison difficult. To date, expert bodies do not generally recommend probiotics for allergy prevention, although the World Allergy Organization (WAO) in their recently developed guidelines suggests considering using probiotics in pregnant women, during breastfeeding and/or to the infant if at high risk of developing allergic disease (based on heredity). However, in concordance with other expert bodies, the WAO guideline panel stressed the low level of evidence and the need for adequately powered randomised controlled trials and a more standardised approach before clinical recommendations on specific strains, dosages and timing can be given.

citations.title: Where in the world do bacteria experience oxidative stress?
citations.abstract: Reactive oxygen species - superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals - have long been suspected of constraining bacterial growth in important microbial habitats and indeed of shaping microbial communities. Over recent decades, studies of paradigmatic organisms such as Escherichia coli, Salmonella typhimurium, Bacillus subtilis and Saccharomyces cerevisiae have pinpointed the biomolecules that oxidants can damage and the strategies by which microbes minimize their injuries. What is lacking is a good sense of the circumstances under which oxidative stress actually occurs. In this MiniReview several potential natural sources of oxidative stress are considered: endogenous ROS formation, chemical oxidation of reduced species at oxic-anoxic interfaces, H2 O2 production by lactic acid bacteria, the oxidative burst of phagocytes and the redox-cycling of secreted small molecules. While all of these phenomena can be reproduced and verified in the lab, the actual quantification of stress in natural habitats remains lacking - and, therefore, we have a fundamental hole in our understanding of the role that oxidative stress actually plays in the biosphere.

name: Acesulfame Potassium
scoreRationale: Approved and not metabolized, but long-term human data are thinner than for other sweeteners, it persists in the environment, and WHO discourages sweeteners for weight control.
summary: Ace-K is a zero-calorie sweetener about 200 times sweeter than sugar, often blended with sucralose or aspartame.

overview: Acesulfame potassium is the potassium salt of a small six-membered ring containing oxygen, nitrogen and a sulfonyl group. Its nitrogen sits between a carbonyl group and a sulfonyl group, which makes its N–H strongly acidic, so it readily forms a stable salt with potassium.

It is about 200 times sweeter than sugar, survives baking temperatures, and leaves the body unchanged. It's often blended with sucralose or aspartame because the mix tastes more like sugar than any single sweetener.
profile.function: Sweetens diet drinks and sugar-free foods, masking bitterness when blended with other sweeteners.

mechanisms.title: Sweet with a bitter edge
mechanisms.chemical: Acesulfame potassium, or Ace-K, activates the sweet-taste receptor, the T1R2/T1R3 protein pair, by fitting into a binding pocket and changing the receptor's shape. That makes it about 200 times sweeter than sugar. But Ace-K also fits into some bitter-taste receptors, particularly two called TAS2R31 and TAS2R43. These belong to a large family of receptors that evolved to detect potentially harmful bitter substances. At higher concentrations, Ace-K activates these bitter receptors more strongly.
mechanisms.biological: When both sweet and bitter receptors fire, the brain perceives sweetness with a slightly bitter or metallic aftertaste. Because people carry different versions of the TAS2R31 and TAS2R43 genes, some notice that bitterness far more than others. To mask it, manufacturers often blend Ace-K with other sweeteners such as sucralose or aspartame. Blends also tend to taste more like sugar, because each sweetener has a different sweetness profile and they cover each other's weaknesses. Ace-K's sweetness arrives quickly, which complements sweeteners that build more slowly.

mechanisms.title: Not metabolized
mechanisms.chemical: Ace-K's ring, containing nitrogen, oxygen and sulfur, isn't recognized by any human enzyme. Unlike aspartame, which is broken into amino acids, or sugar, which is digested into glucose, Ace-K passes through the body chemically unchanged. It dissolves easily in water and is absorbed quickly from the small intestine into the blood. From there it is filtered out by the kidneys. Because it is never broken down, it provides no calories or energy.
mechanisms.biological: After absorption, Ace-K circulates in the blood and is filtered out by the kidneys, leaving the body unchanged in urine, mostly within about a day. It doesn't build up because it is removed so efficiently. Since the body doesn't use it for energy, it adds no calories, which makes it useful in diet drinks and sugar-free foods. It is also heat-stable, so it can be used in baked goods. Small amounts pass into breast milk.

reactions.title: Building the ring
reactions.summary: Ace-K is made by building a six-membered ring containing oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur atoms. The process starts with two simple industrial chemicals, sulfamic acid and diketene, and uses sulfur trioxide to close the ring. The final step converts the ring into its potassium salt. Chemists designed this route after the molecule's sweetness was discovered by accident in 1967. The process produces a stable, white crystalline powder.

steps.name: Coupling
steps.text: Sulfamic acid, a small molecule containing nitrogen and a sulfonic acid group, reacts with diketene, a reactive four-carbon molecule. The nitrogen of sulfamic acid attacks diketene and opens its ring, forming an acetoacetamide sulfonic acid. This molecule contains all the atoms needed for the final ring.

steps.name: Cyclization
steps.text: Sulfur trioxide (SO₃), a powerful dehydrating agent, is added. It helps the molecule join its own ends into a ring by connecting the end of the chain to the sulfur group, removing a water molecule in the process. The result is a six-membered ring containing one oxygen, one nitrogen and one sulfur atom.

steps.name: Neutralization
steps.text: The ring has an acidic hydrogen on its nitrogen, made acidic because the neighboring carbonyl and sulfonyl groups pull electrons away from it. Potassium hydroxide removes this hydrogen and forms the potassium salt, acesulfame potassium.

reactions.result: The salt form is stable, water-soluble and easy to crystallize. It survives the heat of baking and the acidity of soft drinks without breaking down, which makes it more versatile than aspartame.

regulatory.status: Approved general-purpose sweetener (2003).
ADI 0–15 mg/kg body weight.

hazards.title: Gaps in long-term data
hazards.summary: Acesulfame potassium is approved by regulators around the world, including the U.S. FDA and the European Food Safety Authority, and is considered safe at normal intakes. However, it has been studied less than some other sweeteners, such as aspartame, particularly in long-term human studies. Some scientists have called for more research on its possible effects on gut bacteria and metabolism. In 2023 the World Health Organization advised against using non-sugar sweeteners, Ace-K included, for weight control. That advice was based on weak evidence of long-term benefit, not on proven harm.
hazards.chemical: Because Ace-K isn't broken down, any effects in the body would come from the intact molecule rather than from breakdown products. It is absorbed into the blood and circulates throughout the body before being excreted. In the gut, unabsorbed Ace-K could in theory interact with bacteria. A few laboratory studies have suggested it might affect certain processes in cells, but how relevant that is at normal intakes is unclear. More targeted research is needed to settle the question.
hazards.biological: Some mouse studies found that Ace-K changed the makeup of the gut bacteria and affected body weight, though results vary and may not apply to people. Observational studies in people have linked artificial sweetener use, Ace-K included, to weight gain and health problems, but those links may exist because people who already struggle with weight are more likely to choose sweeteners. The WHO's 2023 guideline concluded that non-sugar sweeteners don't help with long-term weight control. More long-term human research is needed to fully understand Ace-K's effects.

profile.dosage: Diet sodas typically contain tens of milligrams of Ace-K per can, usually blended with other sweeteners. The U.S. FDA and international experts (JECFA) have set an acceptable daily intake of 15 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, about 900 milligrams for a 60-kilogram adult, which is the amount in many cans of diet soda every day. Typical intakes are well below this. Because it isn't metabolized, it contributes no calories. The WHO advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners for weight control and suggests water and less-sweet foods instead.

myths.claim: Ace-K is metabolized into toxic acetoacetamide.
myths.consensus: Acetoacetamide forms only after long storage under harsh conditions; the sweetener is excreted unchanged.

environment.persistence: Highly persistent; used as a tracer for wastewater in groundwater.
environment.biodegradability: Poorly biodegradable, though some treatment plants now degrade it.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Acesulfame potassium was discovered in 1967 by the German chemist Karl Clauss at the company Hoechst, when he licked his finger while working with related chemicals and noticed a sweet taste. It was approved for use in the United States in 1988. Today it is produced in large chemical plants, mainly in China and Germany. The process uses inexpensive industrial chemicals. Ace-K is sold under brand names such as Sunett and Sweet One.
synthesis.mechanism: The process starts with sulfamic acid, which is reacted with diketene in the presence of a base such as triethylamine to form an acetoacetamide intermediate. This intermediate is treated with sulfur trioxide in a solvent, which closes the six-membered ring by joining the molecule's ends and removing water. The ring compound is then neutralized with potassium hydroxide, forming the potassium salt. The crude Ace-K is purified by crystallization, sometimes with activated carbon to remove impurities. The result is a fine white powder.
synthesis.significance: Ace-K is stable enough for baking and survives the acidity of soft drinks, which is why it is so often paired with less stable sweeteners.

citations.title: The Effect of Non-Nutritive Sweetened Beverages on Postprandial Glycemic and Endocrine Responses: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
citations.abstract: Background: There has been an emerging concern that non-nutritive sweeteners (NNS) can increase the risk of cardiometabolic disease. Much of the attention has focused on acute metabolic and endocrine responses to NNS. To examine whether these mechanisms are operational under real-world scenarios, we conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis of acute trials comparing the effects of non-nutritive sweetened beverages (NNS beverages) with water and sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) in humans. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, and The Cochrane Library were searched through to January 15, 2022. We included acute, single-exposure, randomized, and non-randomized, clinical trials in humans, regardless of health status. Three patterns of intake were examined: (1) uncoupling interventions, where NNS beverages were consumed alone without added energy or nutrients; (2) coupling interventions, where NNS beverages were consumed together with added energy and nutrients as carbohydrates; and (3) delayed coupling interventions, where NNS beverages were consumed as a preload prior to added energy and nutrients as carbohydrates. The primary outcome was a 2 h incremental area under the curve (iAUC) for blood glucose concentration. Secondary outcomes included 2 h iAUC for insulin, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), peptide YY (PYY), ghrelin, leptin, and glucagon concentrations. Network meta-analysis and confidence in the network meta-analysis (CINeMA) were conducted in R-studio and CINeMA, respectively. Results: Thirty-six trials involving 472 predominantly healthy participants were included. Trials examined a variety of single NNS (acesulfame potassium, aspartame, cyclamate, saccharin, stevia, and sucralose) and NNS blends (acesulfame potassium + aspartame, acesulfame potassium + sucralose, acesulfame potassium + aspartame + cyclamate, and acesulfame potassium + aspartame + sucralose), along with matched water/unsweetened controls and SSBs sweetened with various caloric sugars (glucose, sucrose, and fructose). In uncoupling interventions, NNS beverages (single or blends) had no effect on postprandial glucose, insulin, GLP-1, GIP, PYY, ghrelin, and glucagon responses similar to water controls (generally, low to moderate confidence), whereas SSBs sweetened with caloric sugars (glucose and sucrose) increased postprandial glucose, insulin, GLP-1, and GIP responses with no differences in postprandial ghrelin and glucagon responses (generally, low to moderate confidence). In coupling and delayed coupling interventions, NNS beverages had no postprandial glucose and endocrine effects similar to controls (generally, low to moderate confidence). Conclusions: The available evidence suggests that NNS beverages sweetened with single or blends of NNS have no acute metabolic and endocrine effects, similar to water. These findings provide support for NNS beverages as an alternative replacement strategy for SSBs in the acute postprandial setting.

citations.title: A Systematic Review of Nonsugar Sweeteners and Cancer Epidemiology Studies.
citations.abstract: Nonsugar sweeteners (NSSs) are added to foods and beverages to provide sweetness in place of sugar while reducing the total caloric content. Reducing sugar intake, and corresponding calories, may decrease the risk of diabetes and other health conditions associated with obesity (e.g., cancer). Numerous observational epidemiology studies have evaluated the effect of NSSs on cancer risk, sometimes focusing on a specific NSS or a specific cancer, other times focusing on all NSSs or all cancers. We conducted a systematic review of epidemiology studies of NSS intake (of all types in aggregate and individually) and the risks of all types of cancer published through Fall 2024 [preregistered with Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/gc8v6)]. We considered how major study quality concerns might have impacted the interpretation of individual study results, as well as the evidence as a whole. We identified 90 studies of acesulfame potassium (ace-K), aspartame, cyclamate, saccharin, sucralose, or nonspecific NSSs in aggregate [e.g., diet sodas, artificially sweetened beverages], and 17 specific types of cancer. We found no consistent associations between any NSS or NSSs in aggregate and any cancer overall, and no evidence for dose-response. NSS intake information was always self-reported, rendering exposure misclassification an ongoing challenge in all studies, and recall bias remains a significant possibility in all case-control studies. Many studies also did not fully account for potential confounders. Experimental animal and mechanistic evidence for NSSs does not support human-relevant carcinogenicity or any biologically plausible mechanisms by which NSSs could cause genotoxicity or cancer in humans. Overall, the epidemiology evidence does not support associations between any NSS and any cancer type.

citations.title: Biological fate of low-calorie sweeteners.
citations.abstract: With continued efforts to find solutions to rising rates of obesity and diabetes, there is increased interest in the potential health benefits of the use of low- and no-calorie sweeteners (LNCSs). Concerns about safety often deter the use of LNCSs as a tool in helping control caloric intake, even though the safety of LNCS use has been affirmed by regulatory agencies worldwide. In many cases, an understanding of the biological fate of the different LNSCs can help health professionals to address safety concerns. The objectives of this review are to compare the similarities and differences in the chemistry, regulatory status, and biological fate (including absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) of the commonly used LNCSs: acesulfame potassium, aspartame, saccharin, stevia leaf extract (steviol glycoside), and sucralose. Understanding the biological fate of the different LNCSs is helpful in evaluating whether reports of biological effects in animal studies or in humans are indicative of possible safety concerns. Illustrations of the usefulness of this information to address questions about LNCSs include discussion of systemic exposure to LNCSs, the use of sweetener combinations, and the potential for effects of LNCSs on the gut microflora.

citations.title: Artificial sweeteners and risk of cardiovascular diseases: results from the prospective NutriNet-Santé cohort.
citations.abstract: Objectives: To study the associations between artificial sweeteners from all dietary sources (beverages, but also table top sweeteners, dairy products, etc), overall and by molecule (aspartame, acesulfame potassium, and sucralose), and risk of cardiovascular diseases (overall, coronary heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease). Design: Population based prospective cohort study (2009-21). Setting: France, primary prevention research. Participants: 103 388 participants of the web based NutriNet-Santé cohort (mean age 42.2±14.4, 79.8% female, 904 206 person years). Dietary intakes and consumption of artificial sweeteners were assessed by repeated 24 h dietary records, including brand names of industrial products. Main outcomes measures: Associations between sweeteners (coded as a continuous variable, log10 transformed) and cardiovascular disease risk, assessed by multivariable adjusted Cox hazard models. Results: Total artificial sweetener intake was associated with increased risk of cardiovascular diseases (1502 events, hazard ratio 1.09, 95% confidence interval 1.01 to 1.18, P=0.03); absolute incidence rate in higher consumers (above the sex specific median) and non-consumers was 346 and 314 per 100 000 person years, respectively. Artificial sweeteners were more particularly associated with cerebrovascular disease risk (777 events, 1.18, 1.06 to 1.31, P=0.002; incidence rates 195 and 150 per 100 000 person years in higher and non-consumers, respectively). Aspartame intake was associated with increased risk of cerebrovascular events (1.17, 1.03 to 1.33, P=0.02; incidence rates 186 and 151 per 100 000 person years in higher and non-consumers, respectively), and acesulfame potassium and sucralose were associated with increased coronary heart disease risk (730 events; acesulfame potassium: 1.40, 1.06 to 1.84, P=0.02; incidence rates 167 and 164; sucralose: 1.31, 1.00 to 1.71, P=0.05; incidence rates 271 and 161). Conclusions: The findings from this large scale prospective cohort study suggest a potential direct association between higher artificial sweetener consumption (especially aspartame, acesulfame potassium, and sucralose) and increased cardiovascular disease risk. Artificial sweeteners are present in thousands of food and beverage brands worldwide, however they remain a controversial topic and are currently being re-evaluated by the European Food Safety Authority, the World Health Organization, and other health agencies. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03335644.
