name: Sodium Citrate
scoreRationale: The sodium salt of citric acid; safe and biodegradable, contributing a small amount of sodium.
summary: Sodium citrate buffers pH, keeps melted cheese smooth, and softens water in eco-friendly detergents.

overview: Sodium citrate (trisodium citrate) is citric acid with all three acidic protons replaced by sodium ions. The citrate ion carries three negative charges on its carboxylate groups, which makes it a strong chelator of calcium and magnesium and a mild base.

In solution it forms a buffer with citric acid, holding pH steady. Those two talents explain its odd range of jobs: smooth cheese sauces, anticoagulant in blood bags, and a phosphate-free water softener in detergents.
profile.function: Buffers acidity in drinks, emulsifies processed cheese, and binds calcium and magnesium in detergents.

mechanisms.title: Smooth melted cheese
mechanisms.chemical: Cheese is built mainly from casein proteins held together in a network, partly by calcium phosphate bridges in which calcium ions link negatively charged spots on neighboring protein molecules. When cheese is heated, this network can tighten and squeeze out fat, leaving the cheese rubbery and greasy. Sodium citrate is a chelator: it grabs calcium ions with its three negatively charged carboxylate groups. By pulling calcium out of those bridges, it loosens the casein network. The freed casein proteins can then move more freely and mix with both water and fat.
mechanisms.biological: Once released from their calcium bridges, casein proteins act as natural emulsifiers, with parts that attract water and parts that attract fat. They coat fat droplets and keep them evenly spread, so melted cheese stays smooth, glossy and stretchy instead of separating into clumps and oil. This is how processed cheese and nacho cheese sauce are made. Home cooks can add a pinch of sodium citrate to make perfectly smooth sauces from almost any cheese. It is also why processed cheese slices melt so evenly.

mechanisms.title: Keeping donated blood liquid
mechanisms.chemical: Blood clotting is a cascade of chemical reactions involving many proteins called clotting factors, and several of the steps need calcium ions (Ca²⁺) to work. Calcium helps clotting factors attach to the surfaces of platelets and to each other. Sodium citrate binds calcium ions tightly, forming calcium citrate complexes. With the calcium locked away, the clotting factors can't do their jobs. The clotting process is stopped before it starts.
mechanisms.biological: Donated blood is collected into bags containing a citrate solution, which keeps it from clotting while it is stored. This lets blood be kept for weeks and transfused to patients who need it. After a transfusion, the recipient's liver quickly breaks the citrate down through the Krebs cycle, releasing the calcium so normal clotting can resume. Citrate is also used in some blood tests and dialysis machines. Without anticoagulants like citrate, modern blood banking wouldn't be possible.

mechanisms.title: Preventing kidney stones
mechanisms.chemical: Most kidney stones are made of calcium oxalate, which forms when calcium and oxalate ions in urine combine into insoluble crystals. Citrate in urine binds calcium ions into soluble complexes, so less calcium is free to pair up with oxalate. Citrate also sticks to the surfaces of tiny crystals, stopping them from growing and clumping together. In addition, when the body metabolizes citrate, it produces bicarbonate, which raises the pH of urine. Higher urine pH keeps uric acid dissolved, which helps prevent uric acid stones too.
mechanisms.biological: People with low citrate levels in their urine, a condition called hypocitraturia, are more likely to form kidney stones. Doctors often prescribe potassium citrate or sodium citrate to people prone to stones, which raises urine citrate and lowers the chance of new stones. Lemon juice and other citrus juices can raise urine citrate a little as well. Drinking plenty of water remains one of the most important ways to prevent stones. Potassium citrate is usually preferred, because extra sodium can increase the amount of calcium in urine.

reactions.title: Calcium chelation
reactions.summary: Chelation is when one molecule grabs a metal ion and holds it from several sides at once, like a claw. Citrate is a good chelator because its three carboxylate groups can surround a calcium ion. That stops the calcium from reacting with other substances. Chelation is used in foods, medicine and cleaning products. The word comes from the Greek chele, meaning claw.

steps.name: Dissolving
steps.text: When sodium citrate is added to water, it dissolves and separates into sodium ions (Na⁺) and citrate ions. Each citrate carries three negative charges on its three carboxylate groups. The sodium ions take no further part.

steps.name: Binding
steps.text: Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) carry two positive charges and are drawn to citrate's negative carboxylate groups. Citrate can wrap around a calcium ion so that several of its oxygen atoms bond to it at once. That makes the bundle much more stable than if only one group were attached.

steps.name: Complex
steps.text: The calcium is now held in a soluble calcium citrate complex. It can't easily react with other substances, such as soap, carbonate, or the proteins in blood and cheese. The complex stays dissolved.

reactions.result: The same reaction softens hard water in detergents, where it stops calcium from reacting with soap and forming scum; keeps stored blood from clotting; and makes cheese sauces smooth. It is one simple chemical idea with a remarkably wide range of uses.

reactions.title: The citrate buffer
reactions.summary: A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its partner base that resists changes in pH when acid or base is added. Citric acid and sodium citrate together form a citrate buffer. Because citric acid can release three protons, the citrate buffer works across a wide range of pH values, from about 3 to 6. Buffers matter in foods, drinks, medicines and laboratory work. They keep products tasting the same and chemically stable.

steps.name: Acid partner
steps.text: Citric acid can release hydrogen ions (H⁺). If a base is added to the mixture, citric acid donates protons that neutralize it. This stops the pH from rising sharply.

steps.name: Base partner
steps.text: Citrate ions can accept hydrogen ions. If an acid is added, citrate soaks up the extra protons and turns back into citric acid. This stops the pH from dropping sharply.

steps.name: Balance
steps.text: With both forms present, the mixture can absorb either acid or base, and the pH stays close to a set value as long as both partners remain. The ratio of citric acid to citrate decides the exact pH.

reactions.result: Soft drinks and candies use this buffer to keep their tartness consistent, and medicines and intravenous fluids use citrate buffers to keep their active ingredients stable. Even a small amount of buffer can make a big difference to how stable a product is.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Authorized as E331 at quantum satis.

hazards.title: Very low toxicity
hazards.summary: Sodium citrate has very low toxicity and is considered safe in the amounts used in food and drinks. The body handles citrate easily, since it is a normal part of energy metabolism. Concerns arise mainly in medical settings, when large amounts enter the bloodstream directly, such as during massive blood transfusions or some types of dialysis. Taken by mouth in large amounts it can cause mild stomach upset. People on low-sodium diets should remember that it contributes sodium.
hazards.chemical: Citrate's main chemical action in the body is binding calcium. When a lot of citrate enters the bloodstream quickly, for example from many units of transfused blood, it can bind enough calcium to lower the level of free, active calcium in the blood. Normally the liver breaks citrate down in the Krebs cycle and the calcium is released again. But if citrate arrives faster than the liver can process it, or the liver isn't working well, free calcium can drop. This is called citrate toxicity.
hazards.biological: Calcium is essential for nerve signals, muscle contraction and a steady heart rhythm. When free calcium in the blood drops too low, a condition called hypocalcemia, it can cause tingling around the mouth and fingers, muscle cramps and spasms, and in severe cases an irregular heartbeat. During massive transfusions, doctors monitor calcium and give supplements when needed. None of this happens with the small amounts of sodium citrate in food. In foods, the main thing to consider is its sodium.

profile.dosage: Foods use under 1 percent sodium citrate, usually to control acidity, to act as an emulsifying salt in processed cheese, or to stabilize drinks. International experts (JECFA) have given citrates an acceptable daily intake of “not specified,” reflecting their very low toxicity, and the U.S. FDA considers sodium citrate generally recognized as safe. The body processes citrate as part of normal metabolism. Larger doses are used medically, under a doctor's supervision, to treat kidney stones and acidosis. Each gram of sodium citrate contains roughly 250 milligrams of sodium, which counts toward daily sodium limits.

myths.claim: Sodium citrate is just salt.
myths.consensus: It is a citrate salt with far less sodium per gram than table salt and different functions.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low; a green replacement for phosphate builders.

synthesis.title: Neutralizing citric acid
synthesis.summary: Sodium citrate is made by neutralizing citric acid with a sodium-containing base. The citric acid itself is almost always made by fermentation with the mold Aspergillus niger. Neutralization is a simple acid–base reaction, much like what happens when baking soda meets lemon juice. The product is crystallized into a white powder or granules. Depending on how much base is added, manufacturers can make monosodium, disodium or trisodium citrate, with trisodium citrate the most common.
synthesis.mechanism: Citric acid, which has three acidic hydrogen atoms on its carboxylic acid groups, is dissolved in water, and sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate is slowly added. Each hydroxide ion removes a hydrogen ion from a carboxylic acid group, forming water, while a sodium ion takes its place as the partner of the now negatively charged carboxylate. When three sodium ions have replaced all three acidic hydrogens, the product is trisodium citrate. The solution is concentrated by evaporation and cooled, so sodium citrate crystals form. These are separated, dried and sieved.
synthesis.significance: Citrate anticoagulant, introduced around 1914, made stored blood transfusions practical.

citations.title: Sodium citrate targeting Ca2+/CAMKK2 pathway exhibits anti-tumor activity through inducing apoptosis and ferroptosis in ovarian cancer.
citations.abstract: Introduction: Ovarian cancer (OC) is known for its high mortality rate. Although sodium citrate has anti-tumor effects in various cancers, its effect and mechanism in OC remain unclear. Objectives: To analyze the inhibitory effect of sodium citrate on ovarian cancer cells and the underlying mechanism. Methods: Cell apoptosis was examined by TUNEL staining, flow cytometry, and ferroptosis was examined intracellular Fe2+, MDA, LPO assays, respectively. Cell metabolism was examined by OCR and ECAR measurements. Immunoblotting and immunoprecipitation were used to elucidate the mechanism. Results: This study suggested that sodium citrate not only promoted ovarian cancer cell apoptosis but also triggeredferroptosis, manifested as elevated levels of Fe2+, LPO, MDA andlipid ROS production. On one hand, sodium citrate treatment led to a decrease of Ca2+ content in the cytosol by chelatingCa2+, which further inhibited the Ca2+/CAMKK2/AKT/mTOR signaling, thereby suppressing HIF1α-dependent glycolysis pathway and inducing cell apoptosis. On the other hand, the chelation of Ca2+ by sodium citrate resulted in inactivation of CAMKK2 and AMPK, leading to increase of NCOA4-mediated ferritinophagy, causing increased intracellular Fe2+ levels. More importantly, the inhibition of Ca2+/CAMKK2/AMPK signaling pathway reduced the activity of the MCU and Ca2+ concentration within the mitochondria, resulting in an increase in mitochondrial ROS. Additionally, metabolomic analysis indicated that sodium citrate treatment significantly increased de novo lipid synthesis. Altogether, these factors contributed to ferroptosis. As expected, Ca2+ supplementation successfully reversed the cell death and decreased tumor growth induced by sodium citrate. Inspiringly, it was found that coadministration of sodium citrate increased the sensitivity of OC cells to chemo-drugs. Conclusion: These results revealed that the sodium citrate exerted its anti-cancer activity by inhibiting Ca2+/CAMKK2-dependent cell apoptosis and ferroptosis. Sodium citrate will hopefully serve as a prospective compound for OC treatment and for improvingthe efficacy of chemo-drugs.

citations.title: Characteristics of Ureaplasma urealyticum urease.
citations.abstract: Sonication of Ureaplasma urealyticum cells grown in a dialysate growth medium effectively separated the cytoplasmic fraction from the membrane fraction, with both fractions relatively free from exogenous contaminating proteins. The urease activity was associated with the cytoplasmic fraction, and the ureaplasmal urease exhibited a specific activity higher than that of crystalline jack bean urease. The enzymatic activity of the ureaplasmal enzyme was optimum at pH 7.5 and was resistant to the chelating agents EDTA and sodium citrate. Sulfhydryl-blocking agents such as HgCl2 and Pb(NO3)2 inhibited the ureaplasmal urease, which was also shown to be particularly sensitive to flurofamide and, to a much lesser extent, to acetohydroxamic acid. Electrophoretic analysis of the proteins of the ureaplasmal cell fractions combined with Western immunoblot with an antiserum to the ureaplasmal urease indicated that the urease constitutes a major component of the cytoplasm and is composed of several 70-kilodalton polypeptides. Clinical characteristics: Mitochondrial DNA-associated Leigh syndrome spectrum (mtDNA-LSS) is part of a continuum of progressive neurodegenerative disorders caused by abnormalities of mitochondrial energy generation, which includes the overlapping phenotypes mtDNA-associated Leigh syndrome and mtDNA-associated Leigh-like syndrome. Mitochondrial DNA-LSS is characterized by onset of manifestations typically between ages three and 12 months, often following an intercurrent illness (usually viral) or metabolic challenge (vaccinations, surgery, prolonged fasting). Decompensation (often with elevated lactate levels in blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid) is typically associated with developmental delay and/or regression. Neurologic features include hypotonia, spasticity, seizures, movement disorders, cerebellar ataxia, and peripheral neuropathy. Brain stem dysfunction may manifest with respiratory symptoms, swallowing difficulties, ophthalmoparesis, and abnormalities in thermoregulation. Extraneurologic manifestations may include poor weight gain, cardiomyopathy, and conduction defects. Up to 50% of individuals die by age three years, most often from respiratory or cardiac failure. Diagnosis/testing: The diagnosis of mtDNA-LSS is established in a proband fulfilling clinical diagnostic criteria for LSS by identification of a heteroplasmic or homoplasmic pathogenic variant in one of the 15 mtDNA genes known to be involved in mtDNA-LSS. Management: Treatment of manifestations: Treatment is supportive. Sodium bicarbonate or sodium citrate for significant acidosis (THAM may be used if there is hypernatraemia); anti-seizure medication for seizures; dystonia therapy with benzhexol, baclofen, tetrabenazine, or gabapentin alone or in combination, or by botulinum toxin injection; treatment of respiratory compromise per pulmonologist; caloric and nutritional supplementation and feeding therapy as needed; developmental and educational support; physical therapy and occupational therapy; standard treatment of eye movement disorders; medical management of cardiomyopathy; treatment of constipation as needed; treatment of liver failure per hepatologist; treatment of electrolyte abnormalities per nephrologist; hearing aids or cochlear implants for sensorineural hearing loss; speech therapy and hearing support services as needed; management of diabetes mellitus and adrenal insufficiency per endocrinologist; standard treatments for anxiety and/or depression; psychological support and care coordination for the affected individual and family. Surveillance: Affected individuals should be followed at regular intervals to monitor for progression of disease and associated complications. Neurologic assessment for ataxia and seizures at each visit along with an assessment of pulmonary issues, growth, nutrition, and gastrointestinal manifestations. Development, educational, and cognitive assessment and assessment of mobility and self-help skills at least annually. Ophthalmology assessment every six to 12 months or as advised by ophthalmologist. Annual blood pressure, EKG, and echocardiogram or as advised by cardiologist. Liver function tests, urinalysis, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, urine amino acids, serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, complete blood count, and fasting glucose annually. Annual audiology assessment. Assessment of care coordination and family psychosocial needs at each visit. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Sodium valproate, medications that cause acidosis, and dichloroacetate should be avoided or used with caution; administration of anesthesia requires careful consideration to avoid aggravation of respiratory symptoms and precipitation of respiratory failure. Genetic counseling: Mitochondrial DNA-LSS is transmitted by maternal inheritance. The mother of a proband may have the mtDNA pathogenic variant and may exhibit mild clinical manifestations of mtDNA-LSS. Many affected individuals have no known family history of mtDNA-LSS or other mitochondrial disorder. The explanation for apparently simplex cases may be absence of a comprehensive and/or reliable family history, a maternal heteroplasmy level below the disease threshold (i.e., the minimum level of heteroplasmy expected to result in mitochondrial disease), or a de novo mtDNA pathogenic variant in the proband. If the mother of the proband has the mtDNA pathogenic variant identified in the proband, all sibs of the proband are at risk of inheriting the pathogenic variant. Sibs may inherit the pathogenic variant at varying heteroplasmy levels due to the bottleneck effect and variant-specific segregation patterns. The risk to a sib of developing clinical manifestations is difficult to determine and depends on heteroplasmy level, the variation in heteroplasmy levels among different tissues, and the disease threshold for the specific variant. Recurrence risk assessment and prenatal testing for disorders caused by pathogenic variants in mtDNA is challenging due to the intricacies of mtDNA transmission and the inherent challenge in using prenatal genetic test results to predict clinical outcome. Reproductive options for the family members of a proband with an mtDNA pathogenic variant may include prenatal testing, preimplantation genetic testing, and oocyte donation.

citations.title: Nutrition of lead.
citations.journal: Comp Biochem Physiol A Comp Physiol
citations.abstract: At the levels to which human beings are exposed in the workplace as well as in the general environment, lead has been shown to be a toxic element in most of its chemical forms, whether it is inhaled or ingested in water or food. The four main sources of contamination of food are soil, industrial pollution, agricultural technology and food processing. Reasonable quantities of the metal can be stored by humans in a relatively inert form in bone; lead has an affinity for bone and acts by replacing calcium. Gastrointestinal lead absorption and retention, the major pathway of lead intake, has been shown to vary widely depending on the chemical environment of the gastrointestinal lumen, age and iron stores (nutritional status of the subject). Studies in animals have shown that certain substances bind lead and increase its solubility, thus enhancing its absorption. These dietary components consist of sodium citrate, ascorbate, amino acids, vitamin D, protein and fat, and lactose. Data suggest a three-compartmental pool for lead metabolism: (1) blood; (2) soft tissue (hair, nails, sweat, salivary, gastric, pancreatic and biliary secretions); and (3) skeleton. Lead absorption occurs primarily in the duodenum where lead enters the epithelial mucosal cells. The total bodily amount of lead does not affect lead absorption; lead does not have a feedback mechanism which limits absorption. In the adult rat, lead absorption from the intestinal lumen appears to proceed by both active transport and passive diffusion. Bile is an important route of excretion in the gut.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 250 WORDS)

citations.title: Fluorometric assessment of gram-negative bacterial permeabilization.
citations.abstract: Uptake of the fluorescent probe 1-N-phenylnaphthylamine (NPN), as adapted to an automated spectrofluorometer enabling multiwell reading of microtitre plates, was applied to determine permeability changes in Gram-negative bacteria. An intact outer membrane is a permeability barrier, and excludes hydrophobic substances such as NPN but, once damaged, it can allow the entry of NPN to the phospholipid layer, resulting in prominent fluorescence. With Escherichia coli O157, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Salmonella typhimurium as test organisms and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid and sodium hexametaphosphate as the model permeabilizers, quantitative and highly reproducible NPN uptake levels were obtained that differed characteristically between the test bacteria. Furthermore, citric acid was shown to be a potent permeabilizer at millimolar concentrations, its effect being partly (Ps. aeruginosa, Salm. typhimurium) or almost totally (E. coli O157) abolished by MgCl2, suggesting that part of the action occurs by chelation. Sodium citrate induced weak NPN uptake, which was totally abolished by MgCl2. In conclusion, the NPN uptake assay with the automated spectrofluorometer serves as a convenient method in analysing and quantifying the effects of external agents, including potential food preservatives, on Gram-negative bacteria.

name: Glycerin
scoreRationale: One of the best-studied, gentlest moisturizing ingredients; the only notable caution is very high amounts in slush drinks for young children.
summary: Glycerin draws water into the skin and keeps foods moist. It's a gentle, versatile ingredient found in nearly every moisturizer.

physical.solubility: Miscible with water and alcohol; insoluble in oils

overview: Glycerin (glycerol) is a three-carbon chain with a hydroxyl (–OH) group on every carbon: propane-1,2,3-triol. Three –OH groups on such a small molecule make it intensely attracted to water. It mixes with water in any proportion and even pulls moisture from the air (it is hygroscopic).

Glycerol is also the backbone of every fat and oil: a triglyceride is glycerol with three fatty acids attached. That's why glycerin appears as a byproduct whenever fats are turned into soap or biodiesel.
profile.function: Attracts and holds water in the skin's outer layer, softens formulas, keeps baked goods and candies moist, and prevents toothpaste from drying out.

mechanisms.title: Drawing water into the skin
mechanisms.chemical: Glycerin is a small molecule with three hydroxyl (–OH) groups packed onto just three carbon atoms. Each –OH group can form hydrogen bonds with water, weak attractions between a hydrogen atom on one molecule and an oxygen atom on another. That means each glycerol molecule can hold several water molecules around itself at once. Substances that attract and hold water like this are called humectants. When glycerin is applied to skin, it settles into the outer layer, the stratum corneum, and keeps water there instead of letting it evaporate.
mechanisms.biological: A well-hydrated outer layer of skin is softer, smoother and more flexible, so it is less likely to crack, flake or feel tight. Because glycerin holds water in place, it slows the rate at which water escapes from the skin, which dermatologists measure as transepidermal water loss. Clinical studies show that moisturizers containing glycerin improve skin hydration and help a damaged skin barrier recover faster. That is why glycerin appears in a huge range of lotions, cleansers and soaps. It works especially well alongside occlusive ingredients like petrolatum, which seal the water in.

mechanisms.title: Aquaporin-3 and barrier repair
mechanisms.chemical: Cell membranes are made of fatty molecules that block most water-soluble substances, so cells use special channel proteins to move water in and out. Aquaporins are a family of these channels, and aquaporin-3 is found in the cells of the skin's outer layers. Unlike aquaporins that carry only water, aquaporin-3 also lets glycerol through. It works like a tunnel through the membrane, shaped so that water and glycerol fit but larger molecules don't. This lets skin cells take up glycerol from their surroundings.
mechanisms.biological: Scientists discovered how important glycerol is for skin by studying mice bred without aquaporin-3. These mice had dry skin that lost water easily and healed slowly after damage. When researchers gave them extra glycerol, either on the skin or in their diet, their skin hydration and barrier repair returned to normal. This suggested that glycerol isn't just an added cosmetic ingredient but one of the skin's own natural moisturizers. It helps explain why glycerin works so well in skincare.

mechanisms.title: Used for energy
mechanisms.chemical: If glycerol is swallowed, it is absorbed into the blood and taken up mainly by the liver. There, an enzyme called glycerol kinase attaches a phosphate group to it, forming glycerol-3-phosphate. A second enzyme converts this into dihydroxyacetone phosphate, a molecule that sits right in the middle of glycolysis, the pathway that breaks down sugar. From there it can be burned for energy or built up into glucose. Glycerol is also used as the backbone for building new fat molecules.
mechanisms.biological: Because the body handles glycerol through the same pathways as sugar, it can be used for energy and provides about 4.3 calories per gram, similar to sugar. In foods, glycerin keeps products moist and adds sweetness; it is about 60 percent as sweet as sugar. It raises blood sugar less than sugar does, so it is sometimes used in products for people with diabetes, though it still provides calories. The body also releases glycerol naturally whenever it breaks down stored fat. During fasting, that glycerol helps the liver make glucose.

reactions.title: Released when soap is made
reactions.summary: Soapmaking, or saponification, is the reaction of a fat or oil with a strong base such as lye (sodium hydroxide). Every fat molecule is built from one glycerol molecule linked to three fatty acids. When the base breaks those links, the fatty acids become soap and the glycerol is released. In traditional soapmaking the glycerin stays in the soap; in commercial production it is often separated and sold. It is one of the oldest chemical reactions people have used on purpose.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: Hydroxide ions (OH⁻) from the lye attack the ester bonds that connect each fatty acid to the glycerol backbone. The carbon atom in each ester bond is slightly positive because it is attached to two oxygen atoms. The hydroxide bonds to that carbon and the ester bond breaks.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: As each of the three ester bonds breaks, a fatty acid is cut free from the glycerol. Once all three are gone, glycerol is left as its own molecule with three –OH groups. One glycerol is released for every fat molecule.

steps.name: Products
steps.text: The fatty acids, now negatively charged, pair with sodium ions to become soap molecules. In handmade soap the glycerol simply stays mixed in. In industrial soapmaking, salt is added to separate the soap, and the glycerol-rich liquid is collected and purified.

reactions.result: Handmade soaps keep their glycerin, which is why they often feel less drying than some commercial bars. Recovered glycerin is purified and used in cosmetics, foods and medicines. For a long time, soapmaking was the main source of glycerin.

reactions.title: Nitration to nitroglycerin
reactions.summary: Glycerol's three –OH groups can be swapped for nitrate groups, creating a very different molecule: nitroglycerin. This reaction, called nitration, was first carried out in 1847 by the Italian chemist Ascanio Sobrero. Nitroglycerin is a powerful explosive because each molecule contains both fuel (carbon and hydrogen) and the oxygen needed to burn it. Surprisingly, it is also an important heart medicine. The story shows how a small chemical change can transform a molecule's properties.

steps.name: Nitronium ion
steps.text: Concentrated nitric acid is mixed with concentrated sulfuric acid. The stronger sulfuric acid helps nitric acid lose a water molecule, forming the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺), a highly reactive positive ion. The mixture has to be kept cold to control the reaction.

steps.name: Esterification
steps.text: Glycerol is added slowly to the acid mixture. Each of its three –OH groups reacts with a nitronium ion, forming a nitrate ester group (–ONO₂). It is like ordinary ester formation, but with nitric acid in place of a carboxylic acid.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: Once all three –OH groups have reacted, the result is nitroglycerin, an oily liquid. Its molecules are packed with energy and unstable, because breaking them apart releases large volumes of gas extremely quickly.

reactions.result: Alfred Nobel tamed nitroglycerin in 1867 by soaking it into a soft, porous rock called diatomaceous earth, creating dynamite, and later used his fortune to found the Nobel Prizes. In tiny doses, nitroglycerin is also a medicine for chest pain caused by heart disease: the body converts it into nitric oxide, which relaxes and widens blood vessels.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Safe as used in cosmetics.
Advises that slush-ice drinks containing glycerol should not be given to children under 4.

hazards.title: Glycerol intoxication in young children
hazards.summary: Glycerin is extremely safe in cosmetics and in the small amounts used in food. However, some slush ice drinks use large amounts of glycerol to keep them from freezing solid, and young children who drank them have occasionally become ill. Reported cases in the U.K. and Ireland involved children who became unwell soon after a slush drink. As a result, the U.K. Food Standards Agency advised in 2023 that children under four shouldn't have these drinks at all. Children aged four to ten are advised to have no more than one a day.
hazards.chemical: A slush drink can contain a lot of glycerol, sometimes tens of grams in a large serving. When it is drunk quickly, the glycerol is absorbed rapidly into the blood. Because glycerol is a small dissolved molecule, a large amount raises the concentration of dissolved particles in the blood, which affects how water moves between the blood and the body's cells. The liver also has to process the glycerol, which may interfere with its normal control of blood sugar. A small child's body is less able to cope with a sudden large dose.
hazards.biological: In reported cases, children developed headache, nausea and sleepiness and, more seriously, low blood sugar, shock and loss of consciousness, usually within an hour of drinking. These symptoms are thought to come from rapid shifts in fluid balance and blood sugar. Most children recovered quickly with treatment. Because younger children weigh less, the same drink gives them a much higher dose per kilogram of body weight. That is why the advice is based on age.

profile.dosage: Cosmetics typically contain about 2 to 10 percent glycerin, and some moisturizers contain more. It is one of the least toxic substances used in consumer products: in rats, the oral dose needed to cause death is more than 12 grams per kilogram of body weight. The U.S. FDA considers it generally recognized as safe in food, and international experts haven't set any limit on daily intake. In food it is used in small amounts to keep products moist and add sweetness. The one notable caution is the large amount in some slush drinks given to young children.

myths.claim: Glycerin pulls moisture out of your skin.
myths.consensus: In extremely dry air, pure glycerin could draw water from deeper skin, but at typical 3–10% in formulas it hydrates skin.

myths.claim: Vegetable glycerin is healthier than synthetic glycerin.
myths.consensus: They are the same molecule; source matters for sustainability and dietary preferences, not safety.

synthesis.title: Byproduct of biodiesel and soap
synthesis.summary: Most glycerin today is a byproduct of making biodiesel, a fuel made from vegetable oils or animal fats. For every 10 kilograms of biodiesel produced, about 1 kilogram of crude glycerin is made. The rapid growth of the biodiesel industry in the 2000s flooded the market with glycerin and made it cheap. Some glycerin also comes from soapmaking and from splitting fats to produce fatty acids. A smaller amount is made synthetically from propylene, a petroleum chemical.
synthesis.mechanism: In biodiesel production, vegetable oils or fats, which are triglycerides, are mixed with methanol and a catalyst such as sodium hydroxide. The methanol takes glycerol's place in the fat molecules in a reaction called transesterification, forming fatty acid methyl esters, which are biodiesel. Each triglyceride releases one glycerol molecule. Because glycerol is denser and doesn't mix with biodiesel, it settles as a separate layer at the bottom. This crude glycerin is drained off, neutralized to remove the catalyst and purified by distillation to the high purity needed for medicines and cosmetics.
synthesis.significance: Finding new uses for surplus glycerin, from animal feed to plastics, has become a goal of green chemistry.

synthesis.title: Biological production
synthesis.summary: Glycerol is a natural part of life. Every fat molecule in plants and animals, and many of the molecules in cell membranes, contain glycerol as part of their structure. Living things constantly build and break down fats, releasing and reusing glycerol as they go. Yeast also makes glycerol during fermentation to keep its internal chemistry in balance. Some commercial glycerin is produced by fermentation, though most comes from fats.
synthesis.mechanism: When your body needs energy, for example between meals or during exercise, fat cells break down stored triglycerides in a process called lipolysis. Enzymes called lipases cut the fatty acids away from glycerol, and both are released into the blood. Muscles and other tissues burn the fatty acids as fuel, while the glycerol travels to the liver, where it can be turned into glucose. During alcoholic fermentation, yeast cells make glycerol from an intermediate of glycolysis, which helps them recycle the helper molecule NAD⁺. This matters most when yeast is stressed, for example in very sugary surroundings.
synthesis.significance: Wine contains a few grams of glycerol per liter, which contributes to its smooth, full body.

citations.title: Three enzyme systems for galactoglycerolipid biosynthesis are coordinately regulated in plants.
citations.abstract: Galactoglycerolipids, in which galactose is bound at the glycerol sn-3 position in O-glycosidic linkage to diacylglycerol, are abundant in plants and photosynthetic bacteria, where they constitute the bulk of the polar lipids of the photosynthetic membranes. Galactoglycerolipid biosynthesis in plants is highly compartmentalized involving enzymes at the endoplasmic reticulum and the two chloroplast envelopes. This peculiar organization requires extensive trafficking of lipid precursors. It is now increasingly apparent that there are three different sets of lipid galactosyltransferases capable of galactoglycerolipid biosynthesis in the model plant Arabidopsis. Two enzymes, MGD1 and DGD1, provide the bulk of galactoglycerolipids in the chloroplast and in photosynthetic tissues in general. Under phosphate-limited growth conditions and in non-photosynthetic tissues MGD2/3 and DGD2 are highly active. Moreover, galactoglycerolipids produced by this second pathway are often found in extraplastidic membranes. Although these galactosyltransferases use UDP-Gal as the galactose donor, a third pathway involves a processive enzyme, which transfers galactose from one galactolipid to another.

citations.title: Indole-3-Glycerol Phosphate Synthase From Mycobacterium tuberculosis: A Potential New Drug Target.
citations.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by the pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis, affects millions of people worldwide. Several TB drugs have lost efficacy due to emerging drug resistance and new anti-TB targets are needed. Recent research suggests that indole-3-glycerol phosphate synthase (IGPS) in M. tuberculosis (MtIGPS) could be such a target. IGPS is a (β/α)8 -barrel enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of 1-(o-carboxyphenylamino)-1-deoxyribulose 5'-phosphate (CdRP) into indole-glycerol-phosphate (IGP) in the bacterial tryptophan biosynthetic pathway. M. tuberculosis over expresses the tryptophan pathway genes during an immune response and inhibition of MtIGPS allows CD4 T-cells to more effectively fight against M. tuberculosis. Here we review the published data on MtIGPS expression, kinetics, mechanism, and inhibition. We also discuss MtIGPS crystal structures and compare them to other IGPS structures to reveal potential structure-function relationships of interest for the purposes of drug design and biocatalyst engineering.

citations.title: Sugar-Phosphate Toxicities.
citations.abstract: Accumulation of phosphorylated intermediates during cellular metabolism can have wide-ranging toxic effects on many organisms, including humans and the pathogens that infect them. These toxicities can be induced by feeding an upstream metabolite (a sugar, for instance) while simultaneously blocking the appropriate metabolic pathway with either a mutation or an enzyme inhibitor. Here, we survey the toxicities that can arise in the metabolism of glucose, galactose, fructose, fructose-asparagine, glycerol, trehalose, maltose, mannose, mannitol, arabinose, and rhamnose. Select enzymes in these metabolic pathways may serve as novel therapeutic targets. Some are conserved broadly among prokaryotes and eukaryotes (e.g., glucose and galactose) and are therefore unlikely to be viable drug targets. However, others are found only in bacteria (e.g., fructose-asparagine, rhamnose, and arabinose), and one is found in fungi but not in humans (trehalose). We discuss what is known about the mechanisms of toxicity and how resistance is achieved in order to identify the prospects and challenges associated with targeted exploitation of these pervasive metabolic vulnerabilities.

citations.title: Aquaporins in the Skin.
citations.authors: Patel, Kevin Heard, Chen et al.
citations.abstract: The skin is the largest organ of the body, serving as an important barrier between the internal milieu and the external environment. The skin is also one of the first lines of defense against microbial infection and other hazards, and thus, the skin has important immune functions . This organ is composed of many cell types, including immune-active dendritic cells (epidermal Langerhans cells and dermal dendritic cells), connective tissue-generating dermal fibroblasts and pigment-producing melanocytes. Comprising the outer skin layer are the epidermal keratinocytes, the predominant cell of this layer, the epidermis , which provides both a mechanical barrier and a water -permeability barrier. Recent data suggest that aquaporins, a family of barrel-shaped proteins surrounding internal pores that allow the passage of water and, in some family members, small solutes such as glycerol , play critical roles in regulating various skin parameters. The involvement of different aquaporin family members in skin function is discussed.

citations.title: Mitochondrial generation of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide as the source of mitochondrial redox signaling.
citations.abstract: This review examines the generation of reactive oxygen species by mammalian mitochondria, and the status of different sites of production in redox signaling and pathology. Eleven distinct mitochondrial sites associated with substrate oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation leak electrons to oxygen to produce superoxide or hydrogen peroxide: oxoacid dehydrogenase complexes that feed electrons to NAD+; respiratory complexes I and III, and dehydrogenases, including complex II, that use ubiquinone as acceptor. The topologies, capacities, and substrate dependences of each site have recently clarified. Complex III and mitochondrial glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase generate superoxide to the external side of the mitochondrial inner membrane as well as the matrix, the other sites generate superoxide and/or hydrogen peroxide exclusively in the matrix. These different site-specific topologies are important for redox signaling. The net rate of superoxide or hydrogen peroxide generation depends on the substrates present and the antioxidant systems active in the matrix and cytosol. The rate at each site can now be measured in complex substrate mixtures. In skeletal muscle mitochondria in media mimicking muscle cytosol at rest, four sites dominate, two in complex I and one each in complexes II and III. Specific suppressors of two sites have been identified, the outer ubiquinone-binding site in complex III (site IIIQo) and the site in complex I active during reverse electron transport (site IQ). These suppressors prevent superoxide/hydrogen peroxide production from a specific site without affecting oxidative phosphorylation, making them excellent tools to investigate the status of the sites in redox signaling, and to suppress the sites to prevent pathologies. They allow the cellular roles of mitochondrial superoxide/hydrogen peroxide production to be investigated without catastrophic confounding bioenergetic effects. They show that sites IIIQo and IQ are active in cells and have important roles in redox signaling (e.g. hypoxic signaling and ER-stress) and in causing oxidative damage in a variety of biological contexts.

name: Sodium Lauryl Sulfate
scoreRationale: Not carcinogenic, but a well-documented skin irritant that strips barrier lipids; better tolerated in rinse-off products than leave-on.
summary: SLS is a powerful foaming cleanser in shampoos, toothpastes and cleaners. It's safe but can irritate sensitive skin and mouths.

physical.solubility: Soluble in water; forms micelles above about 8 mM
physical.phStability: Stable pH 4–10; hydrolyzes in strong acid

overview: Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS, also called sodium dodecyl sulfate) is a classic surfactant: a 12-carbon hydrocarbon tail that repels water, attached to a negatively charged sulfate head that loves water. One molecule, two personalities.

Above a threshold called the critical micelle concentration (about 8 millimolar), SLS molecules cluster into micelles: spheres with their tails inside and heads outside. Oil and grease dissolve into the oily cores and wash away with water, and the same molecules stabilize the thin films of bubbles, which is why SLS foams so well.
profile.function: Lowers surface tension so water can lift oils and dirt, and creates rich foam.

mechanisms.title: Lifting oil and dirt
mechanisms.chemical: Water alone can't remove grease because oil and water don't mix: water molecules cling strongly to each other and push oil molecules away. Sodium lauryl sulfate has a long tail of 12 carbon atoms that is attracted to oil and a charged sulfate head that is attracted to water. When SLS is added to water, the tails burrow into oily dirt while the heads stay in the water. This lowers the surface tension between the oil and the water, making it easier for water to work its way between the oil and the surface. Eventually the oil is lifted off and wrapped up inside clusters of SLS molecules called micelles.
mechanisms.biological: Inside a micelle, the oil is hidden in the center, surrounded by tails, while the charged heads face outward into the water. Because the outside of the package is water-loving, the whole thing rinses away. This is how shampoo removes sebum, the natural oil made by the scalp, along with dirt and styling products. In toothpaste, SLS helps loosen food particles and plaque and spreads the paste around the mouth. The foam it makes isn't needed for cleaning, but people tend to associate it with a product working.

mechanisms.title: Stripping the skin barrier
mechanisms.chemical: The outer layer of skin, the stratum corneum, is made of flattened dead cells filled with a protein called keratin and surrounded by layers of fatty substances called lipids. SLS doesn't just remove oil from the skin's surface; its molecules can also work their way into this layer. Their charged heads bind to keratin proteins, and their tails can pull lipids out from between the cells. At higher concentrations SLS can even make keratin proteins unfold, a process called denaturation. All of this damages the structure that keeps water in and irritants out.
mechanisms.biological: When the skin barrier is disrupted, water evaporates from the skin more quickly, making it dry and tight. Irritants and microbes can also get in more easily, triggering inflammation that causes redness, itching and sometimes flaking. SLS is so reliable at causing this kind of irritation that dermatologists use it as the standard test irritant in research, to study how skin reacts and how well treatments repair it. The effect is stronger at higher concentrations, with longer contact and on skin that is already sensitive. Rinse-off products limit the contact time.

mechanisms.title: Canker sores
mechanisms.chemical: The inside of the mouth is lined with a moist tissue called the oral mucosa, protected by a thin layer of mucin, a slippery protein that forms a barrier. Some researchers think SLS in toothpaste may dissolve or disturb this protective layer. Without it, the cells underneath are more exposed to irritants, bacteria and food acids. SLS might also irritate the mucosal cells directly. The exact mechanism hasn't been pinned down.
mechanisms.biological: Canker sores, also called aphthous ulcers, are small, painful sores inside the mouth. Their cause isn't fully known, but triggers include minor injuries, stress, certain foods and possibly toothpaste ingredients. In some clinical trials, people who often got canker sores had fewer and less painful ones after switching to a toothpaste without SLS. Not every study agrees, though, and SLS doesn't seem to affect people who aren't prone to them. For people who get them often, trying an SLS-free toothpaste is a simple experiment.

reactions.title: Micelle formation
reactions.summary: Surfactant molecules like SLS spontaneously organize themselves into tiny spheres called micelles once there are enough of them in water. This self-assembly needs no outside help; it is driven by the way water molecules interact with each other. The concentration at which micelles start to form is called the critical micelle concentration, or CMC. For SLS it is about 8 millimoles per liter, roughly 0.24 percent. Micelles are what allow detergents to dissolve oil in water.

steps.name: Surface first
steps.text: When a little SLS is added to water, the molecules first head to the surface, where their oily tails can stick out into the air and escape the water. They line up side by side with their heads in the water. This lowers the water's surface tension.

steps.name: Saturation
steps.text: Once the surface is full, any extra SLS molecules have to stay inside the water. But their oily tails disrupt the network of hydrogen bonds between water molecules, which water resists. The molecules need another way to hide their tails.

steps.name: Assembly
steps.text: About 60 SLS molecules cluster together with their tails pointing inward, away from the water, and their charged heads facing out. This forms a micelle, a sphere a few nanometers across with an oily core. Oil and grease can dissolve into that core.

reactions.result: This self-assembly, driven by what scientists call the hydrophobic effect, is also how cell membranes form, except that membrane molecules arrange themselves into double layers instead of spheres. Above the CMC, adding more surfactant simply makes more micelles.

reactions.title: Sulfation and neutralization (how it's made)
reactions.summary: SLS is made by attaching a charged sulfate group to lauryl alcohol, a fatty alcohol with a 12-carbon chain. This turns a molecule that barely dissolves in water into a powerful detergent. The reaction uses sulfur trioxide, a very reactive gas, followed by neutralization with a base. The same basic approach is used to make many detergents. It is carried out in specialized reactors that remove the heat the reaction gives off.

steps.name: Sulfation
steps.text: Lauryl alcohol is exposed to sulfur trioxide (SO₃) gas, usually diluted with air, in a thin-film reactor. The oxygen of the alcohol's –OH group attacks the sulfur atom of SO₃ and forms a new bond. The reaction releases a lot of heat, so it has to be cooled.

steps.name: Acid intermediate
steps.text: This creates lauryl sulfuric acid, which has an –OSO₃H group at the end of its chain. It is a strong acid and not very stable, so it is neutralized quickly to stop it breaking down.

steps.name: Neutralization
steps.text: Sodium hydroxide removes the acidic hydrogen and replaces it with a sodium ion. The result is sodium lauryl sulfate, with a negatively charged sulfate head and a sodium partner. It is sold as a powder, paste or solution.

reactions.result: The same pattern, a fatty tail plus a charged head, underlies most synthetic detergents. Changing the length of the tail or the type of head produces surfactants with different strengths and properties.

regulatory.status: Safe in rinse-off products; leave-on products should contain no more than 1%.
Permitted as a direct food additive, e.g., as a whipping aid for egg whites.
Listed among safer surfactants for cleaning products.

hazards.title: Skin irritation
hazards.summary: SLS is an irritant, meaning it can directly damage the skin barrier and cause redness and dryness, but it isn't an allergen, and despite widespread online claims it doesn't cause cancer. How irritating it is depends on concentration, how long it stays on the skin and the condition of the skin. Rinse-off products like shampoo limit contact time, so most people tolerate them well. People with eczema or very sensitive skin are more likely to react. Many brands now offer SLS-free products for them.
hazards.chemical: SLS molecules work their way into the outermost layer of skin, where their tails pull out the lipids that fill the spaces between dead skin cells. Their charged heads bind to keratin proteins, and at higher concentrations make those proteins unfold and swell. Both effects weaken the skin barrier. Because SLS is a small molecule with a strongly charged head, it penetrates skin more easily than larger, milder surfactants. The higher the concentration and the longer the contact, the more damage it does.
hazards.biological: A damaged barrier lets more water escape, causing dryness, tightness and flaking. It also lets irritants and microbes in, which makes skin cells release inflammatory signals called cytokines. These cause redness, itching and sometimes a burning feeling. In people with eczema, whose barrier is already weak, SLS can trigger flare-ups. The irritation usually settles once exposure stops and the skin has time to repair itself.

hazards.title: Eye irritation
hazards.summary: Shampoo stings when it gets in your eyes mainly because of surfactants like SLS. The eyes are especially sensitive because they lack the protective dead-cell layer that covers the rest of the skin. The stinging is temporary and doesn't usually cause lasting damage. Rinsing with clean water quickly relieves it. Baby shampoos labeled “tear-free” use milder surfactants that sting much less.
hazards.chemical: The surface of the eye is covered by the tear film, a thin layer made of water and mucus topped with an oily layer that slows evaporation. Surfactants like SLS can dissolve that oily layer and disturb the mucus. They can also reach the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye, and disrupt the membranes and proteins of its surface cells. With those protective layers disturbed, the eye's sensitive nerve endings are exposed. SLS's small size and strong charge make it particularly irritating.
hazards.biological: The cornea is one of the most densely innervated tissues in the body, packed with pain-sensing nerve endings. When surfactants disturb its surface, these nerves fire, producing intense stinging. The eye responds by making tears and blinking to flush the irritant out, and its blood vessels widen, turning it red. Because corneal surface cells regenerate quickly, a brief exposure usually heals within hours. “Tear-free” formulas replace SLS with milder surfactants and adjust the pH to match tears.

profile.dosage: Shampoos typically contain about 10 to 20 percent SLS or related surfactants, and toothpastes about 1 to 2 percent. Because these products are rinsed off quickly, most people tolerate them well. Irritation becomes more likely at higher concentrations, with longer contact and in leave-on products; safety reviewers recommend keeping SLS below 1 percent in products meant to stay on the skin. People with eczema, sensitive skin or frequent canker sores may prefer SLS-free alternatives. Despite online rumors, no major regulatory or scientific body considers SLS a carcinogen.

myths.claim: SLS causes cancer.
myths.consensus: This traces to a 1998 chain email; SLS is not classified as a carcinogen by IARC, NTP or any regulator.

myths.claim: Sodium coco-sulfate is a gentler natural alternative.
myths.consensus: It is mostly the same molecule with a slightly broader chain-length mix, and similarly irritating.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Harmful to aquatic life at elevated concentrations before treatment.

synthesis.title: From coconut or palm kernel oil
synthesis.summary: Most SLS is made from coconut or palm kernel oil, which are naturally rich in lauric acid, a fatty acid with a 12-carbon chain; that is where the “lauryl” in its name comes from. The oil goes through several chemical steps to become lauryl alcohol, which is then turned into SLS. Products made this way are often marketed as “plant-derived” or “from coconut.” However, the final SLS molecule is made by chemical reactions and is identical whatever its source. Only the origin of its carbon atoms differs.
synthesis.mechanism: First, coconut or palm kernel oil is reacted with methanol, which replaces the glycerol in its fat molecules and produces fatty acid methyl esters. These are separated by distillation to collect the 12-carbon methyl laurate. Next, the methyl laurate is reacted with hydrogen gas at high pressure over a copper-based catalyst, which converts the ester group into an alcohol group, giving lauryl alcohol. The lauryl alcohol is then reacted with sulfur trioxide to attach a sulfate group, forming lauryl sulfuric acid. Finally, sodium hydroxide neutralizes it to sodium lauryl sulfate.
synthesis.significance: Coconut and palm kernel oils are unusual among plant oils in having mostly 12- and 14-carbon chains, which is why they are the preferred source for foaming cleansers.

synthesis.title: From petroleum (the Ziegler process)
synthesis.summary: SLS can also be made from petroleum, using ethylene, a simple gas, as the building block. This method grew out of the Nobel Prize–winning work of the German chemist Karl Ziegler in the 1950s and builds fatty alcohols by joining ethylene molecules together. The lauryl alcohol it produces is chemically identical to the alcohol made from coconut oil. Petroleum-based and plant-based SLS are used interchangeably. The choice mainly comes down to cost and marketing.
synthesis.mechanism: Ethylene gas is reacted with triethylaluminum, a compound in which an aluminum atom is bonded to three ethyl groups. Ethylene molecules insert themselves one at a time between the aluminum and the growing carbon chain, adding two carbons each time. This chain growth produces straight hydrocarbon chains of various lengths. The aluminum compound is then treated with oxygen and water, which converts the chains into fatty alcohols. These are separated by distillation to collect lauryl alcohol, which is sulfated and neutralized as usual.
synthesis.significance: Plant-derived and petroleum-derived SLS are the same molecule; only the source of the carbon differs.

citations.title: [Allergic contact dermatitis].
citations.abstract: Clinical definition of eczema is based on the presence of multiform erythematous, papular and vesicular lesions which are followed by marked desquamation. When the underlying mechanism is allergic, skin lesions are mediated by inflammatory Th1 lymphocytes recognizing hapten determinants, i.e. IVth allergic mechanism in allergic contact dermatitis. This mechanism is responsible also for allergy to bacterial proteins in nummular eczema, or to fungal and bacterial proteins, atopens and nickel in dyshidrotic eczema. Eczematous lesions can develop after damage to the skin barrier by toxic chemical or irritating substances, as non-allergic irritation eczema. These substances non-specifically stimulate the Langerhans cells and keratinocytes to produce numerous cytokines inducing expression of adhesion molecules on the endothelial cells. This is responsible for non-specific mobilization of Th1 cells to the skin. A model example is dermatitis induced by mercury salts and/or sodium lauryl sulfate. Intermediate position between allergic and non-allergic eczema is occupied by atopic dermatitis/eczema. In addition to classical IgE-dependent mechanism leading to degranulation of mast cells, there is generation of specific population of Th2 lymphocytes recognizing food and air-borne atopens. This reaction is responsible for skin inflammation in the late-phase response, in which allergic process started by Th2 cells switches to non-specific migration of Th1 cells attracted by cytokines released from eosinophils, keratinocytes and Th2 lymphocytes.

citations.title: Different types of emollient cream exhibit diverse physiological effects on the skin barrier in adults with atopic dermatitis.
citations.abstract: Background: Eczema (atopic dermatitis; AD) is a very common itchy skin condition affecting 1 in 5 children and up to 1 in 10 adults worldwide. The skin of eczema sufferers is prone to redness, irritation and dryness because it does not form an effective barrier, i.e. the ability of the skin to stop irritants, allergens and microorganisms getting into the body. Skin barrier dysfunction is a hallmark of AD. The regular and liberal (600 g/week for an adult) use of emollients is recommended for all patients with eczema), even between episodes of itching and redness, to soften and soothe the skin. In England alone, almost 9 million prescriptions for emollient creams were issued in 2018, at a cost of over £50 million. Despite this widespread use, relatively little is known about how commonly prescribed emollient creams affect the skin's barrier, and thus the role of moisturizers in AD development and progression remains unclear. We set out to compare three different types of emollient cream and a no-treatment control. Aim: To compare the barrier-strengthening properties of a new moisturizer containing urea and glycerol (urea-glycerol cream; UGC), with those of a glycerol-containing moisturizer (glycerol cream; GC), a simple paraffin cream (PC) with no humectant, and a no-treatment control (NTC). Methods: This was an observer-blinded prospective Phase 2 within-subject multilateral single-centre randomized controlled trial in adults with AD (Clinical Trials #NCT03901144). The intervention involved 4 weeks of treatment, twice daily, with the three products applied to one of four areas on the forearms the (the fourth area was the untreated control, randomized allocation). Skin properties [dryness, transepidermal water loss (TEWL), hydration and natural moisturizing factor (NMF) levels] were assessed before, during and after treatment to see what happened to the skin's barrier. The primary outcome was skin sensitivity to the irritant sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) after treatment. We performed tests on the skin before and after treatment to see what happened to the skin's barrier. Results: In total, 49 patients were randomized, completed treatment and included in the analysis. UGC significantly reduced the response to SLS as indicated by a reduction in TEWL compared with NTC (-9.0 g/m2 /h; 95% CI -12.56 to -5.49), with PC (-9.0 g/m2 /h; 95% CI -12.60 to -5.44) and with GC -4.2 g/m2 /h; 95% CI 7.76 to -0.63). Skin moisturization improved at sites treated with UGC compared with NTC and PC, and this was accompanied by concordant changes in dryness and NMF levels. Subgroup analysis suggested FLG-dependent enhancement of treatment effects. Conclusion: The study showed that not all emollient creams for eczema are equal. The simple paraffin-based emollient, which represents the most widely prescribed type of emollient cream in England, had no effect on the skin's barrier and reduced the skin's NMF. UGC markedly improved the skin's barrier and protected against irritation. GC performed better than PC, but not as well as UGC. UGC strengthened the skin barrier through a mechanism involving increased NMF levels in the skin, and imparted protection from SLS-induced irritation. By helping correct a major pathophysiological process, UGC has the potential to improve the long-term control of AD. The results show that different emollient creams have different effects on our skin, and only certain types have the ability to improve the skin's barrier and protect against irritants that trigger eczema.

citations.title: Allergic contact dermatitis.
citations.abstract: Allergic contact dermatitis is a frequent inflammatory skin disease. The suspected diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms, a plausible contact to allergens and a suitable history of dermatitis. Differential diagnoses should be considered only after careful exclusion of any causal contact sensitization. Hence, careful diagnosis by patch testing is of great importance. Modifications of the standardized test procedure are the strip patch test and the repeated open application test. The interpretation of the SLS (sodium lauryl sulfate) patch test as well as testing with the patients' own products and working materials are potential sources of error. Accurate patch test reading is affected in particular by the experience and individual factors of the examiner. Therefore, a high degree of standardization and continuous quality control is necessary and may be supported by use of an online patch test reading course made available by the German Contact Dermatitis Research Group. A critical relevance assessment of allergic patch test reactions helps to avoid relapses and the consideration of differential diagnoses. Any allergic test reaction should be documented in an allergy ID card including the INCI name, if appropriate. The diagnostics of allergic contact dermatitis is endangered by a seriously reduced financing of patch testing by the German statutory health insurances. Restrictive regulations by the German Drug Law block the approval of new contact allergens for routine patch testing. Beside the consistent avoidance of allergen contact, temporary use of systemic and topical corticosteroids is the therapy of first choice.

citations.title: Salmeterol Xinafoate.
citations.journal: Profiles Drug Subst Excip Relat Methodol
citations.abstract: Salmeterol xinafoate is a potent and a long-acting β2-adrenoceptor agonist. It is prescribed for the treatment of severe persistent asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Different methods were used to prepare (R)-(-)-salmeterol such as: mixing a sample of 4-benzyloxy-3-hydroxymethyl-ω-bromoacetophenone with sodium lauryl sulfate and the mixture was added to the microbial culture of Rhodotorula rubra, treatment of p-hydroxyacetophenone with Eschenmoser's salt and carbonate exchange resin followed by a sequence of supported reagents and scavenging agents or via Rh-catalyzed asymmetric transfer hydrogenation. The enantioselective synthesis of (S)-salmeterol was achieved via asymmetric reduction of the azidoketone 4 by Pichia angusta yeast. Physical characteristics of salmeterol xinafoate were confirmed via: X-ray powder diffraction pattern, thermal analysis and UV, vibrational, nuclear magnetic resonance, and mass spectroscopical data. Initial improvement in asthma control may occur within 30 min following oral inhalation of salmeterol in fixed combination with fluticasone propionate. Clinically important improvements are maintained for up to 12 h in most patients. It is extensively metabolized in the liver by hydroxylation, thus increased plasma concentrations may occur in patients with hepatic impairment.

citations.title: Maintaining Supersaturation of Nimodipine by PVP with or without the Presence of Sodium Lauryl Sulfate and Sodium Taurocholate.
citations.abstract: Amorphous solid dispersion (ASD) is one of the most versatile supersaturating drug delivery systems to improve the dissolution rate and oral bioavailability of poorly water-soluble drugs. PVP based ASD formulation of nimodipine (NMD) has been marketed and effectively used in clinic for nearly 30 years, yet the mechanism by which PVP maintains the supersaturation and subsequently improves the bioavailability of NMD was rarely investigated. In this research, we first studied the molecular interactions between NMD and PVP by solution NMR, using CDCl3 as the solvent, and the drug-polymer Flory-Huggins interaction parameter. No strong specific interaction between PVP and NMD was detected in the nonaqueous state. However, we observed that aqueous supersaturation of NMD could be significantly maintained by PVP, presumably due to the hydrophobic interactions between the hydrophobic moieties of PVP and NMD in aqueous medium. This hypothesis was supported by dynamic light scattering (DLS) and supersaturation experiments in the presence of different surfactants. DLS revealed the formation of NMD/PVP aggregates when NMD was supersaturated, suggesting the formation of hydrophobic interactions between the drug and polymer. The addition of surfactants, sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) or sodium taurocholate (NaTC), into PVP maintained that NMD supersaturation demonstrated different effects: SLS could only improve NMD supersaturation with concentration above its critical aggregation concentration (CAC) value while not with lower concentration. Nevertheless, NaTC could prolong NMD supersaturation independent of concentration, with lower concentration outperformed higher concentration. We attribute these observations to PVP-surfactant interactions and the formation of PVP/surfactant complexes. In summary, despite the lack of specific interactions in the nonaqueous state, NMD aqueous supersaturation in the presence of PVP was attained by hydrophobic interactions between the hydrophobic moieties of NMD and PVP. This hydrophobic interaction could be disrupted by surfactants, which interact with PVP competitively, thus hindering the capability of PVP to maintain NMD supersaturation. Therefore, caution is needed when evaluating such ASDs in vitro and in vivo when various surfactants are present either in the formulation or in the surrounding medium.

name: Sodium Laureth Sulfate
scoreRationale: Milder than SLS, but ethoxylation can leave traces of 1,4-dioxane, a possible carcinogen now strictly limited in some states.
summary: SLES is the main foaming cleanser in most shampoos and body washes. It's gentler than SLS; the concern is a manufacturing contaminant, not the surfactant itself.

identity.composition: C12–C14 alkyl chains with an average of 1–3 ethylene oxide units, capped with a sodium sulfate group.

overview: Sodium laureth sulfate (SLES) is SLS with a short chain of ethylene oxide units (–CH₂CH₂O–), usually one to three, inserted between the fatty tail and the sulfate head. The “-eth” in laureth refers to these ether links.

That spacer makes the water-loving head larger and more flexible. SLES forms bigger, more stable micelles, binds skin proteins less and is noticeably milder than SLS while still foaming richly, which is why it's the main cleanser in most shampoos and body washes.
profile.function: Produces dense lather and removes oil in shampoos, body washes, hand soaps and dish detergents.

mechanisms.title: Gentler cleansing
mechanisms.chemical: SLES has the same 12-carbon tail as SLS, but between the tail and the sulfate head it has a short chain of ethylene oxide units, usually one to three. This spacer makes the water-loving head of the molecule larger and more flexible. Bigger heads make micelles form more easily, so at any given concentration, a larger share of SLES molecules are tucked into micelles. The molecules left floating freely, called monomers, are the ones that penetrate and irritate skin. SLES therefore leaves fewer free monomers available to cause irritation.
mechanisms.biological: Because fewer free SLES molecules are available to soak into the skin, it binds less to skin proteins and strips out fewer protective lipids. As a result, skin and scalp tolerate it better than SLS, making it more suitable for daily use. Studies comparing the two find that SLES causes less redness, dryness and water loss from the skin. That is why SLES is the main cleansing ingredient in most shampoos, body washes and liquid soaps. It still foams well and removes oil effectively.

mechanisms.title: Thickening with salt
mechanisms.chemical: In water, SLES molecules normally form small spherical micelles. The negatively charged sulfate heads on the outside of these micelles repel each other, which keeps the micelles small. When salt (sodium chloride) is added, its positive sodium ions cluster around the negative heads and shield them from each other, an effect called charge screening. With less repulsion, the heads can pack closer together, and the micelles grow from little spheres into long, flexible, worm-like shapes. These long micelles tangle together like spaghetti.
mechanisms.biological: The tangled network of worm-like micelles makes the liquid much thicker, which is why manufacturers add salt to shampoo and body wash to give them a rich, gel-like texture. People often associate a thicker product with better quality. But adding too much salt makes the micelles change shape again, branching and breaking up, and the product turns thin. Formulators carefully adjust the salt to reach the right thickness, following what they call the salt curve. A shampoo that suddenly seems runny may simply have too much salt.

reactions.title: Ethoxylation
reactions.summary: Ethoxylation is the process of adding ethylene oxide units to a molecule such as a fatty alcohol. Ethylene oxide is a small, highly reactive molecule shaped like a three-membered ring of two carbons and one oxygen. The ring is strained, meaning its bond angles are squeezed, so it springs open easily when attacked. Each opening adds a –CH₂CH₂O– unit to the chain. Ethoxylation is used to make many of the surfactants and emulsifiers in cosmetics and cleaning products.

steps.name: Activation
steps.text: A base catalyst, such as potassium hydroxide, removes the hydrogen from lauryl alcohol's –OH group, forming an alkoxide ion. This negatively charged oxygen is far more reactive than the original alcohol. It is now ready to attack.

steps.name: Ring opening
steps.text: The alkoxide attacks one of the carbon atoms of an ethylene oxide ring. The ring opens, releasing its strain, and the ethylene oxide unit becomes attached to the chain as –CH₂CH₂O⁻. The new end is again an alkoxide.

steps.name: Chain growth
steps.text: The new alkoxide end can attack another ethylene oxide molecule and add another unit. This continues until the ethylene oxide is used up. Because each chain grows at random, the product is a mixture of molecules with different numbers of units.

reactions.result: The average number of units added, written for example as “laureth-2,” is controlled by the ratio of ethylene oxide to alcohol. More units make the molecule more water-loving and milder.

reactions.title: Formation of 1,4-dioxane
reactions.summary: During ethoxylation, a small amount of an unwanted byproduct called 1,4-dioxane can form. It is a small ring-shaped molecule made of four carbons and two oxygens. 1,4-Dioxane is a concern because it is classified as a possible human carcinogen and is hard to remove from water once released into the environment. It isn't added on purpose, but it can remain as a trace contaminant in products. Manufacturers remove most of it with a process called vacuum stripping.

steps.name: Side reaction
steps.text: Instead of attaching to the growing fatty-alcohol chain, two ethylene oxide units can link to each other. This is more likely under acidic conditions, including during the later sulfation step. The two units join end to end.

steps.name: Ring closure
steps.text: The linked units curl around and close into a six-membered ring with two oxygen atoms opposite each other. This is 1,4-dioxane. It is very stable and doesn't break down easily.

steps.name: Removal
steps.text: Because 1,4-dioxane is volatile, meaning it evaporates fairly easily, manufacturers remove it by heating the finished surfactant under reduced pressure, which is vacuum stripping. This brings 1,4-dioxane down to trace amounts.

reactions.result: New York State now caps 1,4-dioxane in personal-care and cleaning products at a few parts per million, pushing manufacturers to strip it more thoroughly. Some have also changed their processes to make less of it in the first place.

regulatory.status: Safe as used when formulated to be non-irritating.
Caps 1,4-dioxane at 1 ppm in household cleaning and personal-care products and 10 ppm in cosmetics.
1,4-Dioxane (the impurity) is Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic.

hazards.title: 1,4-dioxane impurity
hazards.summary: The main concern about SLES isn't the surfactant itself but a contaminant called 1,4-dioxane that can be left over from manufacturing. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies 1,4-dioxane as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), based on animal studies. Levels in well-made SLES are very low, and exposure from rinse-off products is brief. It is also an environmental concern because it contaminates sources of drinking water. Regulations in some places now set strict limits.
hazards.chemical: 1,4-Dioxane is a small ether molecule that dissolves completely in water and evaporates fairly easily. When products containing it go down the drain, it passes through wastewater treatment plants largely unchanged, because it neither sticks to sludge nor breaks down easily. It can then reach rivers and groundwater that may be used for drinking water. Removing it from water is difficult and expensive. This persistence in the environment is a major reason regulators target it.
hazards.biological: In animal studies, rats and mice that drank water containing high concentrations of 1,4-dioxane for their whole lives developed liver tumors, and some developed tumors elsewhere. Those doses were far higher than anything people encounter from cosmetics. At high concentrations it can also irritate the eyes and airways. Evidence in people is limited. Because it is a possible carcinogen that lingers in water, regulators aim to minimize exposure from every source.

hazards.title: Irritation at high concentration
hazards.summary: SLES is much milder than SLS, but it is still a detergent designed to remove oils, so it can dry or irritate skin under some conditions. This is more likely with very frequent washing, high concentrations or leaving the product on the skin for a long time. People with eczema or sensitive skin may notice dryness. Most people use SLES-based products every day without problems. Moisturizing ingredients and milder co-surfactants reduce irritation further.
hazards.chemical: Even though SLES forms micelles more readily than SLS, some free SLES molecules, called monomers, are always present in solution. These monomers can penetrate the skin's outer layer and pull out lipids from between its cells. At higher concentrations there are more monomers available to do this. Repeated exposure gradually depletes the skin's protective lipids. The effect is similar to SLS's but less intense.
hazards.biological: When lipids are removed faster than the skin can replace them, the barrier weakens. Water evaporates more quickly, leaving skin dry, rough and tight, and irritants get in more easily, causing redness or itching. People who wash their hands many times a day, such as healthcare workers, can develop irritant hand dermatitis this way. Using lukewarm instead of hot water and putting on moisturizer after washing helps protect the skin. Formulas with added glycerin or oils also reduce dryness.

profile.dosage: Shampoos and body washes commonly contain about 10 to 20 percent SLES, often combined with milder co-surfactants such as cocamidopropyl betaine. Because these products are rinsed off within a minute or two, skin exposure is brief. Well-made SLES contains only trace amounts of 1,4-dioxane, and several places now regulate the maximum; New York State, for example, limits it to a few parts per million in finished products. People with very sensitive or eczema-prone skin may prefer sulfate-free cleansers. For most people, SLES-based products are safe for daily use.

myths.claim: SLES contains cancer-causing chemicals.
myths.consensus: The surfactant is not carcinogenic; the concern is a removable impurity that regulators now limit.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic to aquatic life before wastewater treatment.

synthesis.title: Ethoxylation, sulfation and neutralization
synthesis.summary: SLES is made from lauryl alcohol in three main chemical steps. The lauryl alcohol can come from coconut or palm kernel oil or from petroleum. First, ethylene oxide units are added; then a sulfate group is attached; and finally the product is neutralized with a base. A last purification step removes the unwanted byproduct 1,4-dioxane. The whole process runs on a vast scale, since SLES is one of the most widely used surfactants in the world.
synthesis.mechanism: Lauryl alcohol is first reacted with ethylene oxide in the presence of a base catalyst, which adds an average of one to three –CH₂CH₂O– units to the end of each molecule; this is ethoxylation.
