Conclusiones de los autores: En la actualidad se carece de evidencia de ECA para guiar la toma de decisiones sobre la efectividad de la limpieza de heridas en comparación con ninguna limpieza y los enfoques óptimos para la limpieza de las úlceras venosas de la pierna. A partir de los cuatro estudios identificados, no hay evidencia suficiente para demostrar si el uso de la solución PHMB en comparación con el suero fisiológico; el peróxido de oxígeno acuoso en comparación con el agua estéril; la betaína propil y la polihexanida en comparación con un suero fisiológico; o el OHP en comparación con la solución de Ringer supone alguna diferencia en el tratamiento de las úlceras venosas de la pierna. La evidencia de tres de los estudios es de certeza muy baja, debido a las limitaciones de los estudios y a la imprecisión. Un estudio no presentó datos para los desenlaces principales ni secundarios. Podría ser importante realizar más estudios bien diseñados que aborden desenlaces clínicos, de calidad de vida y económicos importantes, sobre la base de la prioridad clínica y para el paciente de esta falta de certeza.

name: Methylparaben
scoreRationale: Methylparaben is considered safe at permitted levels, but parabens as a class have weak estrogenic activity and longer-chain parabens face tighter limits.
summary: Methylparaben is a long-used, low-allergy preservative. Longer-chain parabens raised hormone questions that led to limits; methylparaben is the least concerning of the group.

overview: Methylparaben is the methyl ester of para-hydroxybenzoic acid: a benzene ring with an –OH group at one end and a methyl ester (–COOCH₃) directly opposite. “Para” describes that opposite arrangement on the ring.

Parabens form a family (methyl, ethyl, propyl, butyl) that differ only in the length of the ester chain. Longer chains are more fat-soluble and more antimicrobial but also bind estrogen receptors more strongly, which is why rules are stricter for propyl- and butylparaben than for methylparaben.
profile.function: Prevents mold and bacterial growth in creams, lotions and some foods.

mechanisms.title: Stopping microbial growth
mechanisms.chemical: Methylparaben is a small molecule with a benzene ring, an –OH group at one end and a methyl ester group at the other. Its partly oily structure lets it dissolve into the fatty membranes of microbes. There, it disturbs the proteins embedded in the membrane, including the ones that carry nutrients into the cell. It also interferes with the buildup of hydrogen ions across the membrane, which the microbe needs to make energy in the form of ATP. Some research suggests parabens can also interfere with the making of DNA and RNA.
mechanisms.biological: With nutrient transport and energy production disrupted, molds, yeasts and Gram-positive bacteria can't grow in the product. Parabens are less effective against Gram-negative bacteria, which have an extra outer membrane that keeps them out. That is why products often combine several parabens, or parabens with other preservatives, to cover a wider range of microbes. Methylparaben works best against molds and yeasts, while longer-chain parabens are better against bacteria. Together they keep lotions, creams and some foods safe to use for months.

mechanisms.title: Weak estrogen mimicry
mechanisms.chemical: Estrogen hormones such as estradiol work by binding to estrogen receptors, proteins inside cells that switch genes on and off. Part of estradiol's structure is a benzene ring with an –OH group, called a phenol. Parabens have this same para-hydroxyphenyl group, which lets them fit loosely into the estrogen receptor's binding pocket. The rest of the paraben molecule fits poorly, though, so it binds thousands of times more weakly than estradiol. Longer ester chains fit somewhat better, which is why butylparaben is more estrogen-like than methylparaben.
mechanisms.biological: In laboratory tests using cells that respond to estrogen, parabens can cause weak estrogen-like effects at high concentrations. In animal studies, very high doses of some parabens have affected the uterus and reproductive organs. Methylparaben is the weakest member of the family in these tests. Because the body's own estrogen is far more potent and normal paraben exposure is low, the extra estrogen-like effect from cosmetics is considered very small. This concern is still the reason regulators set stricter limits on the longer-chain parabens.

mechanisms.title: Rapid breakdown
mechanisms.chemical: Methylparaben is an ester, a type of molecule formed by joining an acid and an alcohol. Enzymes called esterases, found in the skin, liver and blood, break ester bonds by adding water, a reaction called hydrolysis. This splits methylparaben into para-hydroxybenzoic acid (PHBA) and methanol. PHBA is then attached to other molecules, such as glycine or glucuronic acid, a process called conjugation. The conjugated forms dissolve much more easily in water.
mechanisms.biological: The conjugated PHBA is filtered out by the kidneys and excreted in urine, usually within hours to a day. Because esterases in the skin start breaking methylparaben down as soon as it is absorbed, much of it is metabolized before it ever reaches the bloodstream. That means it doesn't build up much in the body with normal use. Studies have found small amounts of intact parabens in human urine and tissues, so some does get through. Those amounts are far below the doses that cause effects in animal studies.

reactions.title: Kolbe–Schmitt carboxylation and esterification
reactions.summary: Parabens are made in two main steps. First, a carboxylic acid group is attached to phenol to make para-hydroxybenzoic acid (PHBA), using a reaction called the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction. Developed by Hermann Kolbe and Rudolf Schmitt in the 1800s, it uses carbon dioxide as a building block. Then PHBA is joined with an alcohol to make the paraben ester. The alcohol chosen decides which paraben is made.

steps.name: Carboxylation
steps.text: Phenol is converted into potassium phenoxide by reacting it with potassium hydroxide. The potassium phenoxide is then heated with carbon dioxide under high pressure at about 200 °C. The carbon dioxide attaches to the ring opposite the oxygen, forming a carboxylate group, and acidifying the product gives para-hydroxybenzoic acid.

steps.name: Esterification
steps.text: PHBA is heated with methanol in the presence of an acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid. The methanol's oxygen attacks the carbon of PHBA's carboxylic acid group. This is Fischer esterification, the same reaction used to make fruity-smelling esters.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: As the ester bond forms, a water molecule is released, and removing that water pushes the reaction forward. The product is methylparaben. It is purified by crystallization into white crystals.

reactions.result: Swapping methanol for propanol or butanol gives the other parabens. Using potassium phenoxide rather than sodium phenoxide favors attaching the carboxyl group opposite the oxygen, the “para” position that gives parabens their name.

reactions.title: Hydrolysis in the body
reactions.summary: Once methylparaben enters the body, it is broken down by the reverse of the reaction used to make it. Enzymes called esterases split the ester bond, releasing para-hydroxybenzoic acid and methanol. This process, called hydrolysis, uses a water molecule to break the bond. It happens quickly in the skin and liver. The products are then prepared for removal from the body.

steps.name: Binding
steps.text: Esterase enzymes in the skin, liver and blood recognize methylparaben's ester group and hold it in their active site. The enzyme positions a water molecule right next to the ester bond. That makes the bond much easier to break.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: The water molecule attacks the carbon of the ester group, breaking the bond between that carbon and the oxygen attached to the methyl group. The products are para-hydroxybenzoic acid (PHBA) and methanol. The amount of methanol released is tiny.

steps.name: Excretion
steps.text: Other enzymes attach PHBA to glycine or glucuronic acid, which makes it more water-soluble. The kidneys filter this conjugated PHBA out of the blood, and it leaves the body in urine.

reactions.result: Fast hydrolysis is one reason regulators consider methylparaben low-risk at permitted levels. PHBA itself is found naturally in many fruits and vegetables.

regulatory.status: Methyl- and ethylparaben allowed; propyl- and butylparaben capped at 0.14% combined and banned in leave-on diaper-area products; five other parabens banned (2014).
Methylparaben is GRAS in food.
Safe at present practices of use.

hazards.title: Endocrine questions
hazards.summary: Parabens have been controversial since a 2004 study detected them in breast tumor tissue, raising fears that they might contribute to breast cancer by mimicking estrogen. However, that study didn't show the parabens caused the tumors, and it didn't compare tumors with healthy tissue. Extensive research and regulatory reviews since then have found no causal link between parabens and breast cancer. Methylparaben is the weakest estrogen mimic in the family and is considered safe at permitted levels. Regulators have restricted the longer-chain parabens, which are more estrogen-like.
hazards.chemical: Parabens bind weakly to estrogen receptors because their para-hydroxyphenyl group resembles part of the estradiol molecule. Binding strength increases as the ester chain gets longer: methyl, then ethyl, propyl and butyl. Even the strongest parabens bind thousands of times more weakly than the body's own estrogen. Parabens are also broken down quickly by esterase enzymes, which reduces how much can reach estrogen receptors at all. Some parabens may also weakly block androgen receptors.
hazards.biological: In laboratory and animal studies, parabens cause weak estrogen-like effects only at doses far higher than people get from cosmetics. Even so, the European Union restricted propylparaben and butylparaben to a combined maximum of 0.14 percent, banned them from leave-on diaper-area products for children under three, and banned several less-studied parabens outright. Methylparaben and ethylparaben remain permitted at up to 0.4 percent each. No study has shown that parabens at normal exposure cause cancer or hormonal disorders in people.

hazards.title: The “paraben paradox” allergy
hazards.summary: Parabens rarely cause allergies on healthy skin, but people with damaged skin, for example from eczema or leg ulcers, sometimes become allergic. Curiously, many of these people can use paraben-containing products on healthy skin elsewhere without any reaction. The dermatologist Alexander Fisher called this the “paraben paradox.” Overall, parabens are among the least allergenic preservatives. That is one reason some dermatologists consider them safer than many of their replacements.
hazards.chemical: On damaged skin, parabens can penetrate more deeply and in larger amounts than through healthy skin. There they may bind to skin proteins and act as haptens, small molecules that make proteins look foreign to the immune system. Damaged skin also has more immune activity going on, which makes sensitization more likely. On intact skin, the barrier limits how much paraben gets in at all. That difference in penetration may explain the paradox.
hazards.biological: In sensitized people, applying paraben-containing creams to damaged skin can trigger allergic contact dermatitis, with itching, redness and a worsening of the existing rash. This was especially relevant for medicated creams used on eczema or leg ulcers, many of which contained parabens. Yet the same people may have no trouble with paraben-containing cosmetics on healthy skin. Patch testing finds paraben allergy in only about 1 percent or fewer of people tested for cosmetic allergies. That is a remarkably low rate for such widely used preservatives.

profile.dosage: Cosmetics typically use 0.1 to 0.3 percent methylparaben, often combined with other preservatives. In the European Union, methylparaben and ethylparaben are each permitted at up to 0.4 percent, and up to 0.8 percent when combined with other parabens, while stricter limits apply to propyl- and butylparaben. Studies measuring parabens in urine show that typical human exposure is far below the doses that cause hormonal effects in animals. Methylparaben is also used in some foods and medicines. People with eczema who react to paraben-containing creams should talk to a dermatologist.

myths.claim: Parabens cause breast cancer.
myths.consensus: A 2004 study detected parabens in tumor tissue but did not test healthy tissue or show causation; no causal link has been established.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Methylparaben is made in chemical plants from phenol, carbon dioxide and methanol, which are produced from petroleum and natural gas. Parabens were first used as preservatives in the 1920s and became popular because they are effective, cheap, stable and have little smell or color. Methylparaben is one of the most widely used preservatives in cosmetics, medicines and foods. It is often paired with propylparaben to cover more kinds of microbes. Together they protect a product against both molds and bacteria.
synthesis.mechanism: First, phenol is reacted with potassium hydroxide to form potassium phenoxide. This is heated with carbon dioxide under pressure in the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction, which attaches a carboxyl group to the ring opposite the oxygen, and the product is acidified to give para-hydroxybenzoic acid (PHBA). PHBA is then heated with methanol and an acid catalyst, which joins them into the methyl ester and releases water. The crude methylparaben is purified by crystallization and washing, producing fine white crystals. It is tested for purity before sale.
synthesis.significance: Methylparaben occurs naturally too: it's found in blueberries and is a component of the honeybee queen's pheromone.

citations.title: Xiaoyaosan improves depression-like behaviours in mice with post-stroke depression by modulating gut microbiota and microbial metabolism and regulating P2X7R/NLRP3 inflammasome.
citations.abstract: Background: Post-stroke depression (PSD) represents the most prevalent complication of stroke and has been reported to be associated with an imbalance in the gut microbiota. Clinically, Xiaoyaosan (XYS) alleviates depressive symptoms in patients with PSD. However, the existing literature does not provide sufficient evidence to ascertain whether XYS can alleviate these symptoms by modulating gut microbiota. Purpose: This study aims to investigate the potential mechanism of XYS to improve depression-like behavior in mice with PSD by regulating intestinal flora and microbial metabolism. Study design: The authors assessed the effect of XYS on the behaviour of PSD mice and evaluated the effects of XYS on structure and metabolism of gut microbiota, the protein expression levels of P2X7 and NLRP3, and associated inflammatory factors in PSD mice. In addition, by performing faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) on PSD mice with faecal bacteria treated with XYS, the authors further clarified the relationship between intestinal flora disorder, the onset of PSD, and the intervention effect of XYS. Methods: To investigate the ameliorative effect of XYS on behavioural abnormalities and clarify the important role of intestinal flora regulation in the improvement of PSD by XYS in diseased mice, the authors employed various methodologies, including the PSD model, behavioural tests, haematoxylin and eosin staining, ultrastructural morphology, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, western blotting, 16S rRNA sequencing, metabolomic analyses, and FMT. Results: Oral administration of XYS effectively alleviated depression-like behaviours in PSD mice and repaired the damaged colonic mucosa. XYS inhibited inflammatory factors in serum and hippocampus and regulated the protein expression levels of P2X7 and NLRP3 in the colon and hippocampus of PSD mice. Moreover, XYS restored the gut microbiota and modulated intestinal metabolites in PSD mice. It effectively reduced the abundances of microbes including Ligullacoccus, Streptococcus, and Staphylococcus, while significantly increased the abundances of microbes including Faecalibaculum, Allobaculum, and Monolobus. Furthermore, XYS effectively regulated intestinal metabolites such as methylparaben, valproic acid (Depakene), and disulfiram. More importantly, faecal transplants from the PSD models reproduced depression-like behaviours in normal mice, while XYS-FMT effectively alleviated depression-like behaviours in PSD mice. Conclusion: Our findings indicate that XYS improves depression-like behaviours in mice with PSD by modulating the gut microbiota and microbial metabolism, and regulating the P2X7R/NLRP3 inflammasome.

citations.title: [Effect of the Metabolic Modification of Environmental Chemicals on Endocrine-disrupting Activity].
citations.abstract: The endocrine-disrupting activities of various environmental chemicals are metabolically activated. For example, diphenyls, styrene oligomers, chalcones, trans-stilbene and 2-nitrofluorene are not estrogens, but after incubation with liver microsomes, their metabolites show estrogenic activities. Thus, these chemicals are estrogenically activated by the cytochrome P450 system. In contrast, the antiandrogenic activity of fenthion, an organophosphorus insecticide, is abolished after metabolism to sulfoxide and sulfone derivatives. Structural requirements of twenty bisphenol A related compounds, as well as various benzophenones, for estrogenic and antiandrogenic activities have been investigated. The estrogenic and antiandrogenic activities of Benzophenone 3, a representative UV absorbant, are activated by oxidative metabolism. Parabens (used as antimicrobial agents) exhibit estrogenic activity, and their potency shows a bell-shaped curve between C1 (methylparaben) and C12 (dodecylparaben) parabens. The AhR ligand activity of indirubin is decreased by metabolism. Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE) are activated by hydroxylation to show estrogenic and thyroid hormone-disrupting activities. Halogen adjacent to a hydroxyl group is essential for thyroid hormone-disrupting activity. Tetrabromobisphenol A, tetrachlorobisphenol A and tetramethylbisphenol A also exhibit thyroid hormone-disrupting activity. Amphibian metamorphosis of tadpoles to frogs is affected by hydroxylated PCB, hydroxylated PBDE and bisphenol A derivatives. These chemicals suppress thyroid hormone-dependent metamorphosis, acting as antagonists of thyroid hormone. Thus, metabolic modification can have a dramatic impact on the endocrine-disrupting activities of environmental chemicals.

citations.title: True Allergy to Amide Local Anesthetics: A Review and Case Presentation.
citations.abstract: Adverse reactions to local anesthetics are usually a reaction to epinephrine, vasovagal syncope, or overdose toxicity. Allergic reactions to local anesthetics are often attributed to additives such as metabisulfite or methylparaben. True allergic reactions to amide local anesthetics are extremely rare but have been documented. Patients with true allergy to amide local anesthetics present a challenge to the dental practitioner in providing adequate care with appropriate intraoperative pain management. Often, these patients may be treated under general anesthesia. We report a case of a 43-year-old female patient that presented to NYU Lutheran Medical Center Dental Clinic with a documented history of allergy to amide local anesthetics. This case report reviews the use of 1% diphenhydramine with 1:100,000 epinephrine as an alternative local anesthetic and reviews the relevant literature. Ipecac, or syrup of ipecac, is a medication that was once widely used to induce vomiting. The medical use of the drug has largely disappeared and is no longer recommended for managing toxic ingestion. However, the misuse of syrup of ipecac as a purgative in eating disorders is on the rise. Ipecac is commonly derived from the alcohol extraction of plants such as Cephaelis acuminata and Cephaelis ipecacuanha. The extract is often combined with glycerin, sugar (syrup), and methylparaben. The active components are plant alkaloids, cephaeline, and methyl-cephaeline (emetine). Paradoxically, ipecac is inherently toxic. However, its rapid induction of vomiting typically mitigates concerns about its poisonous properties. Notably, emetine is one of ipecac's active components, and it exhibits antihelminthic and antiamoebic properties.

citations.title: Understanding allergic reactions to local anesthetics.
citations.abstract: Objective: To review the pharmacology and mechanisms by which local anesthetics cause allergic reactions. Recommendations concerning appropriate use of local anesthetics and alternative therapies in patients with documented local anesthetic allergies are given. Data source: A MEDLINE search of English-language literature identified pertinent clinical studies, case reports, and reviews. The periods of review were Med1, 1990-present, and Med2, 1985-1989, using the MeSH terms drug hypersensitivity and anesthetics. References from the selected studies, case reports, and reviews were reviewed. Study selection: Controlled and uncontrolled prospective studies and case reports pertaining to local anaesthetic allergies were reviewed. The selection focused on information pertaining to the etiology and diagnosis of allergic reactions to local anesthetics and alternative therapies for patients with local anesthetic allergies. Data synthesis: Local anesthetics are classified as either ester or amide compounds. Esters are associated with a higher incidence of allergic reactions, due to a p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite. Amide agents do not undergo such metabolism. However, preservative compounds (methylparaben) used in the preparation of amide-type agents are metabolized to PABA. Patients who are allergic to ester local anesthetics should be treated with a preservative-free amide local anesthetic. If the patient is not allergic to ester local anesthetics, these agents may be used in amide-sensitive patients. In the rare instance that hypersensitivity to both ester and amide local anesthetics occurs, or if skin testing cannot be performed, than alternative therapies including diphenhydramine, opioids, general analgesia, or hypnosis can be used. Conclusions: A true immunologic reaction to a local anesthetic is rare. Intradermal skin testing of local anesthetic compounds, methylparaben, and metabisulfite should be performed in patients when a thorough history does not rule out a possible allergic reaction to local anesthetics and future local anesthesia is necessary. Skin testing enables the clinician to identify autonomic responses to minor surgical procedures and toxic reactions to anesthetics so that patients are not incorrectly labeled as "caine" allergic. Diphenhydramine can be used as an alternative to ester and amide local anesthetics in minor procedures of short duration.

name: Fragrance
scoreRationale: The leading cause of cosmetic contact allergy; formulas are trade secrets, so consumers can't see which of dozens of chemicals are inside.
summary: "Fragrance" can hide dozens of scent chemicals under one word. It's the most common cause of allergic reactions to cosmetics.

identity.composition: Undisclosed blends of essential oils and synthetic aroma chemicals (for example limonene, linalool, citronellol, musks), often with solvents.

overview: “Fragrance” (or parfum) on a label stands for a blend that can contain dozens to hundreds of aroma molecules: terpenes such as limonene and linalool from citrus and flowers, aldehydes, esters, musks and woody notes, plus solvents. Recipes are trade secrets, so they're listed as a single word.

Perfumers build blends in layers: volatile top notes (citrus) that evaporate within minutes, heart notes (florals) that last hours, and heavy base notes (musks, woods) that linger. The same reactive molecules that make a fragrance pleasant also make it the most common cause of allergic reactions to cosmetics.
profile.function: Gives products a pleasant scent and masks the odor of other ingredients.

mechanisms.title: How we smell a fragrance
mechanisms.chemical: A fragrance is a mixture of volatile molecules, meaning they evaporate easily at skin temperature and drift into the air. When you breathe in, these molecules reach the olfactory epithelium, a small patch of tissue high inside the nose that carries about 400 different types of odorant receptors. Each receptor is a protein with a pocket that fits certain features of molecules, such as their size, shape and the groups of atoms they carry. One receptor responds to many different molecules, and each molecule activates several receptors. So every scent produces its own combination of activated receptors, a bit like a chord played on a piano.
mechanisms.biological: Each activated receptor makes its nerve cell fire, and the signals travel to the olfactory bulb at the front of the brain. The brain reads the overall pattern of signals as a particular smell, such as rose or vanilla. Unlike the other senses, smell signals reach the amygdala and hippocampus, brain areas involved in emotion and memory, without first passing through the thalamus, the brain's usual relay station. That direct route explains why a scent can instantly bring back a vivid memory or a strong feeling. It also helps explain why fragrance preferences are so personal.

mechanisms.title: Allergic contact dermatitis
mechanisms.chemical: Some fragrance molecules are reactive enough to form chemical bonds with proteins in the skin. Others only become reactive after they react with oxygen in the air, forming oxidized products such as hydroperoxides. Small molecules that become allergens by attaching to proteins are called haptens. A fragrance molecule bonded to a skin protein creates a shape the immune system has never seen before. That new shape is what can trigger an allergy.
mechanisms.biological: Immune cells in the skin called Langerhans cells pick up the altered proteins and carry them to nearby lymph nodes, where they teach T cells to recognize them. This first stage, called sensitization, causes no symptoms. On later exposures, the memory T cells recognize the altered proteins and set off inflammation, usually one to three days after contact. The result is an itchy, red, sometimes blistering rash wherever the fragrance touched the skin. Fragrance allergy affects roughly 1 to 4 percent of people and is among the most common causes of cosmetic allergy.

mechanisms.title: Fixatives and lasting scent
mechanisms.chemical: Small, light fragrance molecules evaporate quickly, while larger, heavier ones evaporate slowly. How quickly a molecule evaporates depends on its vapor pressure, which reflects how strongly its molecules cling to each other. Heavy molecules such as musks and resins have a low vapor pressure. When mixed with lighter molecules, they hold onto them through weak attractions between molecules, slowing their evaporation. These heavy ingredients are called fixatives.
mechanisms.biological: Because lighter molecules evaporate first, a perfume changes over time after it is applied. The first impression, the top notes, often citrus or herbal, fades within minutes. The heart notes, often floral, last a few hours, and the base notes, such as woods, vanilla and musks, can linger for many hours. Fixatives slow the whole process down, so the scent lasts longer on skin. Perfumers design a fragrance so that this slow change is pleasant from start to finish.

reactions.title: Autoxidation of fragrance terpenes
reactions.summary: Many fragrance ingredients, especially terpenes such as limonene from citrus and linalool from lavender, slowly react with oxygen in the air. This process, called autoxidation, happens on its own over weeks or months and is sped up by light and warmth. Its products include hydroperoxides, molecules with an –O–O–H group. Hydroperoxides are much more likely to cause skin allergy than the original molecules. That is why old perfumes and essential oils are more likely to cause rashes.

steps.name: Initiation
steps.text: Light, heat or a trace of a reactive molecule pulls a hydrogen atom off a carbon next to a carbon–carbon double bond, where hydrogens are relatively easy to remove. This leaves a radical, a molecule with an unpaired electron. The chain reaction is now started.

steps.name: Oxygen capture
steps.text: The radical quickly reacts with an oxygen molecule from the air, which attaches to it. This forms a peroxy radical, carrying an –O–O• group. It is highly reactive.

steps.name: Chain reaction
steps.text: The peroxy radical takes a hydrogen atom from another terpene molecule, becoming a hydroperoxide (–O–O–H) and creating a new radical. That new radical reacts with oxygen and the chain continues. A single starting event can produce many hydroperoxides.

reactions.result: Hydroperoxides of limonene and linalool are much stronger skin sensitizers than the fresh molecules, so old perfumes and essential oils are more likely to cause rashes. Adding antioxidants, storing products somewhere cool and dark, and keeping lids closed all slow this process down.

reactions.title: Reactions with indoor ozone
reactions.summary: When fragrance molecules evaporate into indoor air, they can react with ozone, a reactive form of oxygen that drifts indoors from outside, especially on smoggy days. Ozone attacks carbon–carbon double bonds, which many fragrance molecules contain. These reactions break the fragrance molecules into smaller pieces, some of which are irritating. Some of the products clump together into tiny particles floating in the air. Scientists have only studied this kind of indoor air chemistry in detail in recent decades.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: An ozone molecule (O₃) adds across a carbon–carbon double bond in a terpene such as limonene. This forms an unstable ring-shaped intermediate called an ozonide. The reaction is fast because ozone is so reactive.

steps.name: Fragmentation
steps.text: The ozonide breaks apart, splitting the original molecule where the double bond was. This creates smaller oxidized molecules, including aldehydes, ketones and formaldehyde, along with reactive radicals. Some of these are irritants.

steps.name: Particles
steps.text: Some of the larger, heavier oxidation products barely evaporate at all, so they condense into tiny particles suspended in the air. These ultrafine particles can be breathed deep into the lungs.

reactions.result: Heavy use of scented sprays, air fresheners or cleaning products on smoggy days can briefly raise indoor levels of formaldehyde and fine particles. Opening windows and using fragranced products sparingly reduces the effect.

regulatory.status: 26 fragrance allergens must be named on labels above 0.001% in leave-on or 0.01% in rinse-off products; a 2023 update expands this to about 80 allergens.
Requires FDA to issue a rule for fragrance allergen labeling.
Industry standards restrict or ban specific fragrance materials.

hazards.title: Skin allergy
hazards.summary: Fragrance is the leading cause of allergic reactions to cosmetics. Because a single fragrance can contain dozens of molecules, people often don't know which one they are allergic to. Once someone becomes allergic to a particular fragrance molecule, the allergy usually lasts for life. To help people avoid their triggers, the European Union requires the most common fragrance allergens to be named individually on labels when they are present above set levels. People with fragrance allergy often need to choose fragrance-free products.
hazards.chemical: The molecules responsible include both reactive fragrance ingredients, such as cinnamal and isoeugenol, and molecules that become reactive after oxidizing in air, such as limonene and linalool. These haptens form covalent bonds with skin proteins, often at the amino acids lysine or cysteine. The immune system then treats the modified proteins as foreign. Once someone is sensitized, even tiny amounts can trigger a reaction. Products labeled “unscented” may still contain masking fragrance, so “fragrance-free” is the safer choice.
hazards.biological: In sensitized people, exposure triggers allergic contact dermatitis, typically one to three days after contact. Common sites include the neck, face, hands and underarms, where perfumes, deodorants and lotions are applied. The rash may be itchy, red, scaly or blistered. Dermatologists identify fragrance allergy with patch testing, using standard mixtures of the most common fragrance allergens. Avoiding the specific allergen is the main treatment, along with creams that calm the inflammation.

hazards.title: Airway symptoms in sensitive people
hazards.summary: Some people, especially those with asthma, migraines or sensitive airways, report coughing, wheezing, headaches or nausea around strong scents. These reactions usually aren't true allergies but responses to irritation. Strong fragrances in perfumes, air fresheners and cleaning products are common triggers. The effects can make shared spaces such as classrooms and offices difficult for some people. Some workplaces and schools have adopted fragrance-free policies for this reason.
hazards.chemical: Fragrances release volatile organic compounds (VOCs), carbon-based molecules that evaporate into the air. Some of these, and the products formed when they react with ozone, such as aldehydes, can irritate nerve endings in the nose and airways. Those nerve endings act as detectors that trigger protective reflexes when they sense an irritant. In people with sensitive airways, the reflexes are stronger. Both the concentration of fragrance in the air and the person's sensitivity matter.
hazards.biological: When airway nerves are irritated, they can trigger coughing, sneezing and a runny nose, and they can make the muscles around the airways tighten, which causes wheezing in people with asthma. Strong smells are also a well-known migraine trigger, though exactly why isn't clear. Surveys find that a meaningful share of people report health complaints from fragranced products. These reactions vary greatly from person to person. Moving into fresh air usually relieves the symptoms.

profile.dosage: Perfumes contain 10 to 30 percent fragrance oils, while lotions, shampoos and cleaning products usually contain less than 1 percent. Fragrance ingredients are assessed by the industry's Research Institute for Fragrance Materials, and the International Fragrance Association sets standards that restrict or ban certain ingredients. The European Union requires known fragrance allergens to be named on labels when they exceed trace levels, so people with allergies can avoid them. In the United States, fragrance ingredients can still be listed simply as “fragrance.” People with fragrance allergy should choose products labeled “fragrance-free” rather than “unscented.”

myths.claim: "Unscented" means fragrance-free.
myths.consensus: Unscented products may contain masking fragrance; "fragrance-free" is the better choice for allergies.

myths.claim: Natural essential oils are safer than synthetic fragrance.
myths.consensus: Essential oils contain the same allergens, such as limonene and linalool, and are common causes of dermatitis.

environment.persistence: Varies; some synthetic musks are persistent.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Some components (like musks) are toxic to aquatic life.

synthesis.title: Natural extraction
synthesis.summary: Many fragrance ingredients come from plants: flowers, leaves, fruit peels, wood, roots, seeds and resins. These natural materials, often called essential oils or absolutes, each contain dozens to hundreds of aroma molecules. Some are extremely expensive because so much plant material is needed; it takes several thousand kilograms of rose petals to make a single kilogram of rose oil. Different plants need different extraction methods. Natural extracts give perfumes depth, but they can vary from one harvest to the next.
synthesis.mechanism: Steam distillation passes steam through plant material such as lavender, mint or eucalyptus; the volatile aroma molecules evaporate along with the steam and separate from the water as an oil when cooled. Cold pressing squeezes oil out of citrus peels, where it is stored in tiny pockets near the surface. Delicate flowers such as jasmine, which heat would damage, are extracted with solvents like hexane that dissolve the aroma molecules; the solvent is evaporated, and the waxy residue is washed with alcohol to give an absolute. Newer methods use supercritical carbon dioxide, which dissolves aroma molecules without heat or toxic solvents. Each method captures a slightly different set of molecules.
synthesis.significance: The smell of a natural extract depends on the method used, which is why the same flower can yield several different oils.

synthesis.title: Synthetic aroma chemicals
synthesis.summary: Most modern fragrances rely heavily on aroma molecules made in laboratories. Some are identical to molecules found in nature, like vanillin or linalool, while others are new creations with no natural equivalent. Synthetic molecules let perfumers create scents that are consistent, affordable and sometimes impossible to get from nature, such as the smell of fresh air or the sea. They also reduce the need to harvest rare plants and animals. A typical modern perfume contains mostly synthetic ingredients.
synthesis.mechanism: Chemists design and make aroma molecules using organic chemistry reactions such as esterification, oxidation and condensation. Some start from natural materials, for example turpentine from pine trees, while others start from petroleum chemicals. Important synthetic families include aldehydes, which add a bright, sparkling quality; synthetic musks, which replaced musk taken from animals; and woody molecules that imitate sandalwood and cedar. Each molecule is purified and tested for safety. Perfumers then blend dozens of synthetic and natural materials into a final formula.
synthesis.significance: Chanel No. 5 (1921) was among the first perfumes built on synthetic aldehydes, launching modern perfumery.

citations.title: Simultaneous sensitivity to fragrances.
citations.authors: Buckley, Basketter, Smith Pease et al.
citations.abstract: Background: Cinnamal/cinnamic alcohol and isoeugenol/eugenol are pairs of related fragrance chemicals found in Fragrance Mix I (FM I), and thus are routinely tested in combination with other fragrances in the European standard patch test series. Their close structural similarity makes the occurrence of simultaneous sensitivity within these chemical pairs likely, although at present there are no robust data to support this hypothesis. Objectives: To establish the frequency of simultaneous reactions to these fragrance chemicals in patients with suspected fragrance allergy attending a contact dermatitis clinic; to provide evidence in support of proposed metabolic pathways; and to determine whether including all four separately in FM I is necessary to avoid missing a diagnosis of fragrance allergy. Methods: We analysed retrospectively the records of patients patch tested to the European standard series during the 15-year period 1984-98 for positive reactions to FM I. In a subset of patients tested to the constituents of FM I, positive reactions to cinnamal, cinnamic alcohol, isoeugenol and eugenol were sought. Data were analysed using 2x2 contingency tables (Fisher's exact test). Results: During this period, 23,660 patients were tested to the European standard series, of whom 1811 (7.7%) had positive reactions to FM I. Of the 1112 patients tested to the constituents of FM I, 934 had positive reactions to at least one constituent (total 1324 positive reactions to constituents). Of these 934, 826 also had positive reactions to FM I itself; 108 were negative to FM I but reacted to one or more of its constituents. One hundred and seventy-eight patients did not react to any of the breakdown constituents of FM I; 34 of these had positive reactions to FM I itself. Of 139 patients allergic to cinnamic alcohol, 87 were also allergic to cinnamal (63%), compared with 108 (11.1%) of 973 cinnamic alcohol-negative patients (P<0.00001). Of 231 patients allergic to isoeugenol, 50 were also allergic to eugenol (22%), vs. 109 (12.4%) of 881 isoeugenol-negative patients (P=0.0002). Conclusions: These data support in vitro experiments indicating that cinnamal and cinnamic alcohol may generate a common hapten and are consistent with the view that simultaneous sensitization to isoeugenol and eugenol occurs to a limited extent, despite their being metabolized via different pathways. In view of the substantial number of isolated reactions to each of these fragrance chemicals, all four should continue to be included separately as constituents of FM I.

citations.title: CD8+ T cells are effector cells of contact dermatitis to common skin allergens in mice.
citations.abstract: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) to strong experimental haptens is mediated by specific CD8+ T cells. Here, we show that similar mechanisms occur for weak haptens, which comprise the vast majority of chemicals responsible for human ACD. We used a model of ACD, that is, the contact hypersensitivity reaction, to test for the allergenicity of three weak haptens involved in fragrance allergy. ACD to weak haptens could not be induced in normal mice. In contrast, mice acutely depleted in CD4+ T cells developed a typical ACD reaction to the three weak fragrance allergens that peaked 24 hours after challenge. Priming of CD8+ T cells was observed in draining lymph nodes 5 days after sensitization and development of ACD was associated with the infiltration of activated CD8+ T cells in the challenged skin. CD8+ T cells were effectors of the ACD reaction as in vivo treatment with depleting anti-CD8 mAbs abrogated the ACD responses and as purified CD8+ T cells could adoptively transfer ACD to naive recipients. In conclusion, our data demonstrate a dominant role of CD8+ T cells as initiators of ACD to weak haptens, and suggest that CD8+ T cells may represent potential targets for preventing or treating ACD.

citations.title: Recognizing and Managing Allergic Contact Dermatitis: Focus on Major Allergens.
citations.abstract: Patch testing is the reference standard for the diagnosis of allergic contact dermatitis. Identification and avoidance of culprit allergens are essential in the treatment of this disease. Each year, new allergens are identified as emerging or important. The authors discuss allergens that are common, enduring, emergent, incompletely recognized, and controversial for the practicing allergist and dermatologist. This Clinical Management Review will encompass a review of fragrances, preservatives, rubber, acrylates, metals, and medications; their common sources of exposure; controversies in diagnosis and patch testing; management and how to avoid those allergens. This review will also include practical aspects of diagnosis and management and will provide resources that can be used as guidance for physicians and patients on nickel, methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone, and fragrance, the most common allergens positive on patch testing.

citations.title: [How common is fragrance allergy really?].
citations.abstract: Background: Fragrances are regarded as the most common contact allergens after nickel. In this context, the frequency of positive patch test reactions to fragrance mix is often presented as proof. According to EU regulation No. 1223/2009, 26 fragrances that are regarded as significant allergens have to be declared on cosmetic products. Objectives: The frequency of patch test reactions to fragrances and differentiation between frequently and rarely sensitizing fragrances were evaluated. Materials and methods: Data from the Information Network of Departments of Dermatology (IVDK), mostly of the years 2016-2018, were retrospectively analyzed. Results: Frequency of positive reactions to fragrance mix I in the departments of dermatology joining the IVDK reached a historical low of 5.4% in 2018. Since 2013, positive reactions to fragrance mix II have been declining, yielding 3.2% in 2018. Of fragrance mix I, the allergen with the most positive test reactions is no longer oakmoss absolute, but isoeugenol. In fragrance mix II, hydroxyisohexyl 3‑cyclohexene carboxaldehyde (HICC) is still leading. Only 11 of the 26 fragrances subject to mandatory declaration elicited allergic test reactions in more than 1% of the patients tested. Discussion: The decline of positive test reactions to the fragrance mixes is mainly due to the reduced use of oakmoss containing atranol and chloroatranol, and HICC. Use of these substances in cosmetic products was prohibited within the EU starting in August 2019. Therefore, a further decline of the sensitization frequencies can be expected. A differentiated consideration of the individual fragrances under allergological aspects is urgently required.

citations.title: North American Contact Dermatitis Group Patch Test Results: 2021-2022.
citations.abstract: Background: Patch testing is an important diagnostic tool for the assessment of allergic contact dermatitis (ACD). Objective: This study documents the North American Contact Dermatitis Group (NACDG) patch testing results from 2021 to 2022. Methods: At 12 centers in North America, patients were tested in a standardized manner with a screening series of 80 allergens. Results: Overall, 3056 patients were tested; 2200 (72.0%) had at least 1 positive/allergic patch test reaction and 1412 patients (46.6%) had a primary diagnosis of ACD. The most commonly positive allergens were nickel sulfate hexahydrate 5% and 2.5% petrolatum (24.9% and 22.1%, respectively), methylisothiazolinone (MI) (11.5%), hydroperoxides of linalool (10.1%), cobalt chloride hexahydrate (9.2%), and methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone (9.0%). Compared with 2019-2020, prevalence of the top 20 allergens statistically increased for nickel (P < 0.001), cobalt (P < 0.01), gold (P < 0.001), hydroperoxides of limonene (P < 0.001), oleamidopropyl dimethylamine (P < 0.01), dimethylaminopropylamine (P < 0.01), and ammonium persulfate (P < 0.001). MI positivity continued to decrease from its peak in 2017-2018. More than one-fifth of patients (n = 640, 21.1%) had at least one clinically relevant reaction to an allergen/substance not present in the NACDG screening series. Conclusions: The epidemic of MI contact allergy in North America appears to continue its descent. Fragrance allergy is still very common, but the composition of fragrance allergy markers appears to be changing. Patch testing using a robust screening series, and supplemental allergens as indicated, is necessary for the comprehensive evaluation of ACD.

name: Hyaluronic Acid
scoreRationale: A molecule the body makes itself; extremely well tolerated with a strong hydration record.
summary: Hyaluronic acid is a natural skin molecule that binds water and plumps the skin's surface. It's one of the gentlest actives available.

identity.composition: Linear polysaccharide of repeating D-glucuronic acid and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine units; cosmetic grades range from about 5 kDa to 2,000 kDa.

overview: Hyaluronic acid is a polysaccharide made of repeating pairs of two sugars, glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine, linked into chains that can contain tens of thousands of units. Sodium hyaluronate is its salt form, used in skincare because it's more stable.

Each repeating unit carries a negative charge and several hydroxyl groups, so the chain attracts water and swells into a gel. In your body it fills the spaces between skin cells, lubricates joints and gives the eye's vitreous humor its jelly-like structure.
profile.function: Hydrates and plumps the skin's surface, improves texture, and gives serums a smooth glide.

mechanisms.title: Binding water
mechanisms.chemical: Hyaluronic acid is a very long chain of repeating sugar pairs, and each pair carries a negatively charged carboxylate group and several hydroxyl (–OH) groups. These groups form hydrogen bonds with water molecules and hold them close. At the same time, the negative charges along the chain repel each other, pushing the chain to stretch out into a large, loose coil. The space inside the coil fills up with water. A single hyaluronic acid molecule can hold a great deal of water compared with its own weight, which is why it forms a gel.
mechanisms.biological: Applied to the skin, hyaluronic acid forms a thin, water-holding film on the surface, which hydrates the outer layer and makes skin feel smoother and more supple. That hydration can temporarily plump up fine lines and make them less noticeable. In the body, hyaluronic acid fills the spaces between cells in the skin and gives it volume. In joints, it is a major part of the fluid that lubricates and cushions cartilage, helping joints move smoothly. The amount in skin falls with age, which contributes to drier, less plump skin.

mechanisms.title: Molecular size matters
mechanisms.chemical: Hyaluronic acid comes in different sizes, measured by molecular weight in kilodaltons (kDa). High-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid, over 1,000 kDa, is made of very long chains that are too big to pass through the skin's outer layer. Low-molecular-weight fragments, below about 50 kDa, are small enough to get into the upper layers of the skin. Manufacturers can break long chains into shorter ones using enzymes or other treatments. A molecule's size affects not only where it goes but also how cells respond to it.
mechanisms.biological: Large hyaluronic acid stays on the skin's surface, forming a film that holds in moisture and reduces water loss. Smaller fragments can penetrate deeper and may hydrate the skin from within. Laboratory studies suggest small fragments can also act as signals that influence the skin cells involved in repair and inflammation, although very small fragments may sometimes encourage inflammation. Because of these different effects, many serums blend several sizes. Evidence comparing the sizes in people, however, is still limited.

mechanisms.title: Signaling through CD44
mechanisms.chemical: Cells have receptor proteins on their surfaces that recognize particular molecules outside the cell. CD44 is one of them, found on skin cells, immune cells and many others, and hyaluronic acid is its main partner. When hyaluronic acid binds to CD44, it changes the receptor's shape. That change sends signals inside the cell that affect its internal skeleton and its activity. Different sizes of hyaluronic acid can bind CD44 differently and trigger different signals.
mechanisms.biological: Through CD44, hyaluronic acid influences how cells move, multiply and respond to injury. During wound healing, hyaluronic acid levels rise, and its signals help cells migrate into the wound and help keep inflammation in check. That is why hyaluronic acid is being studied for wound dressings and treatments for skin injuries. It also plays roles in development and in the immune system. These findings come mainly from laboratory studies, and how much skincare products influence these signals isn't well understood.

reactions.title: Built inside the cell membrane
reactions.summary: Hyaluronic acid is made by enzymes called hyaluronan synthases, which sit in the cell membrane. Most large sugar chains, called polysaccharides, are assembled inside the cell in a compartment called the Golgi apparatus and then shipped out. Hyaluronic acid is unusual because it is built right at the cell surface and pushed out as it grows. That lets cells make extremely long chains. The process uses sugars made from glucose.

steps.name: Building blocks
steps.text: Inside the cell, enzymes convert glucose into two activated sugars: UDP-glucuronic acid and UDP-N-acetylglucosamine. The UDP part is a high-energy tag that makes each sugar ready to be linked. These are the raw materials for hyaluronic acid.

steps.name: Alternating addition
steps.text: Hyaluronan synthase, embedded in the membrane, takes the activated sugars and adds them to the growing chain, alternating between glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine. Each addition releases the UDP tag. The enzyme can add thousands of sugars to a single chain.

steps.name: Extrusion
steps.text: As the chain grows, it is threaded out through a pore in the membrane into the space around the cell. This lets it grow far longer than the cell itself. Outside, it binds water and becomes part of the gel-like material between cells.

reactions.result: Unlike most polysaccharides, it is made at the cell surface rather than inside the Golgi apparatus. This lets cells produce large amounts of hyaluronic acid quickly when they need to, for example during wound healing.

reactions.title: Breakdown by hyaluronidase
reactions.summary: The body is constantly making and breaking down hyaluronic acid, so its supply is always being renewed. Enzymes called hyaluronidases cut the long chains into shorter pieces. This is hydrolysis, because water is used to break each bond. Hyaluronic acid turns over remarkably fast: in skin, about half of it is replaced within a day or two. Doctors also use hyaluronidase as a medicine, for example to dissolve hyaluronic acid fillers when something goes wrong.

steps.name: Binding
steps.text: Hyaluronidase enzymes, found in tissues, blood and inside cells, bind to the hyaluronic acid chain. Each enzyme has an active site shaped to fit the sugar pairs. It positions a water molecule next to a bond between sugars.

steps.name: Hydrolysis
steps.text: The water molecule attacks the bond between an N-acetylglucosamine and the next glucuronic acid, breaking it. This cuts one long chain into two shorter ones. Repeated cuts produce smaller and smaller fragments.

steps.name: Turnover
steps.text: The fragments are taken up by cells, especially in the lymph nodes and liver, and broken down further into single sugars. These sugars can be reused or burned for energy. This keeps the hyaluronic acid in tissues fresh.

reactions.result: About a third of the body's hyaluronic acid is replaced every day. This constant renewal lets tissues adjust their hyaluronic acid quickly. And because hyaluronidase breaks down injected fillers, doctors can use it to reverse a filler treatment if a problem occurs.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Regulated as a device in dermal fillers and joint injections.

hazards.title: Very low hazard
hazards.summary: Hyaluronic acid is one of the safest skincare ingredients, because it is a molecule the body makes itself and uses in skin, joints and eyes. Allergic reactions to products applied to the skin are very rare. Cosmetic-grade hyaluronic acid is usually made by bacterial fermentation and purified to remove impurities. The risks people hear about come mainly from injected fillers, which are medical procedures, not from serums and creams. As with any product, a few people may react to other ingredients in the formula.
hazards.chemical: Hyaluronic acid in skincare is chemically identical to the hyaluronic acid naturally found in human skin and connective tissue. Because the molecule is familiar, the immune system doesn't treat it as foreign. It is also broken down by the body's own hyaluronidase enzymes into simple sugars. Products made by fermentation are purified to remove bacterial proteins and other contaminants that could cause reactions. Injected fillers, by contrast, use hyaluronic acid that has been chemically cross-linked so it lasts for months.
hazards.biological: Applied to skin, hyaluronic acid hydrates the surface and is gradually broken down, with no known harmful effects. Some people find that a hyaluronic acid serum feels tight in very dry air; layering a moisturizer on top helps. Injected fillers can, rarely, block a blood vessel, causing tissue damage or even vision loss if injected in the wrong place. Those risks belong to medical procedures and depend on the injector's skill. They don't apply to skincare products.

profile.dosage: Skincare serums typically contain about 0.1 to 2 percent sodium hyaluronate, often a blend of different molecular sizes. Higher concentrations don't necessarily work better and can feel sticky. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review has concluded that hyaluronic acid and its salts are safe as used in cosmetics. Oral supplements and medical joint injections use different amounts and forms. Because the body makes it naturally, no maximum daily limit has been set for use on the skin.

myths.claim: Hyaluronic acid holds 1,000 times its weight in water.
myths.consensus: It binds a lot of water, but this marketing number doesn't reflect what happens on skin.

myths.claim: HA dries out skin in dry climates.
myths.consensus: It works best with an occlusive moisturizer on top, but it doesn't dehydrate skin.

synthesis.title: Bacterial fermentation
synthesis.summary: Most hyaluronic acid used in cosmetics and medicine today is made by bacteria through fermentation. Certain bacteria naturally make hyaluronic acid as a protective outer coat called a capsule. By growing them in large tanks, manufacturers can produce large amounts of pure hyaluronic acid. The bacterial product is chemically identical to the hyaluronic acid in the human body. This method replaced extraction from animal tissue.
synthesis.mechanism: Bacteria such as Streptococcus zooepidemicus, or engineered Bacillus subtilis strains that are safer to handle, are grown in tanks of glucose, nutrients and water. They use their hyaluronan synthase enzymes to build long hyaluronic acid chains and release them into the surrounding broth, which turns thick and stringy. After fermentation, the bacteria are filtered out. Alcohol is added so the hyaluronic acid comes out of solution, and it is collected and purified to remove bacterial proteins and other impurities. It can then be broken into smaller pieces to make different molecular weights and dried into a white powder.
synthesis.significance: It was once harvested from rooster combs; fermentation gives a purer, animal-free product.

citations.title: Hyaluronic acid skin penetration evaluated by tape stripping using ELISA kit assay.
citations.abstract: Hyaluronic Acid (HA) is an endogenous skin matrix component with moisturizing and anti-inflammatory and healing properties. Cosmetic formulations containing HA aim to enhance skin structure, hydrate skin and reduce wrinkles. Therefore, the skin diffusion of HA into stratum corneum after application of a formulation containing two different size of HA, High Molecular weight (HMW-HA) and Low Molecular Weight (LMW-HA)) was evaluated. Ex vivo human skin samples were used to validate an ELISA assay measuring HA in the stratum corneum (SC), viable epidermis and dermis, and to identify optimal washing and extraction methods. These methods were used to measure HA levels in the SC of subjects before and after daily topical application of an HA-containing formulation for 7 days. Samples of SC (5 tape strips) were taken before and 2 h after the application on D0, D1 and D7. The ELISA assay was suitable for measuring HA in the SC but not epidermal or dermal layers. The upper and lower limits of quantitation were the same for both sizes of HA (200 and 3.1 ng/ml, respectively). In both ex vivo human skin and human volunteers, the "dry method" of removing the formulation led to much higher levels of HA in the SC samples, whereas the "wet method" involving one cotton swab soaked with an aqueous solution containing 10% soap and a second cotton swab for drying, was effective in removing the formulation and more relevant to simulate washing/showering. In the clinical study, the amount of HA in SC layers 3-5 were used to represent the HA level in the SC, whereas layers 1 and 2 were considered as surface "residual film". After each application, there was a significantly higher amount of HA compared to the amount before application, which was observed using both wash methods. The residual level 24 h after the first application was at least 8 times higher than before the first application and at least 31 times higher after 7 applications. In conclusion, these investigations validated the use of the ELISA method for the measurement of HA in SC samples. The ex vivo experiments provided recommendations for the clinical study, including the preferred cleansing and optimal sampling methods. The clinical study demonstrated the diffusion, accumulation and maintenance of HA levels in the SC after repeated application of the formulation containing HMW-HA and LMW-HA.

citations.title: Influence of hyaluronic acid on wound healing using composite porcine acellular dermal matrix grafts and autologous skin in rabbits.
citations.abstract: This study aims to explore the influence of hyaluronic acid (HA) on wound healing during xenogeneic porcine acellular dermal matrix (PADM) composite skin grafting. The results will facilitate the development of methods for improving graft contracture and poor elasticity of composite transplantation. Exogenous HA was added to composite PADM grafts and to thin autologous skin grafts during rabbit full-thickness skin wound repair. The influence of HA on wound healing was evaluated according to its contracture rate and its expression of collagen types I and III. The possible mechanism was then explored based on HA metabolism and vascularisation in the skin graft. The results show that exogenous HA relieves graft contracture on rabbit wound surfaces, increases collagen I and III expression and decreases the ratio between collagen types. HA stimulates the generation of more CD44 receptors to strengthen its enzymolysis. The resulting metabolites promote the vascularisation of the wound surface, which are conducive for mitigating graft contracture, and further improve the composite grafting effect.

citations.title: Animal-based hyaluronic acid fillers: scientific and technical considerations.
citations.abstract: Background: Successful clinical application of dermal filler products requires an understanding of their physical characteristics and in vivo behavior. This study reviewed the data for hyaluronic acid dermal filler products derived from an animal source--the rooster comb. Methods: A review of the hyaluronic acid literature was performed. Clinical experience with the animal-derived hyaluronic acid products was evaluated. Results: The source of the hyaluronic acid has not been demonstrated to be a clinically important point of differentiation among filler products. Hypersensitivity reactions are rare and are also present in the products derived from bacteria. Variations that effect the hyaluronic acid products' physical characteristics and clinical performance are more closely related to cross-linking and formulation. Hyaluronic acid gel derived from animal sources is cross-linked by a sulfonyl-bis-ethyl bond and is a soft gel compared with other hyaluronic acid products. There is minimal gel swelling, which results in modest postinjection edema. Optimal clinical application favors patients who desire quick recovery and minimal palpability. Conclusions: Hyaluronic acid skin filler products derived from an animal source are safe and effective. Successful clinical application should be based on an understanding of the patient's goals and the choice of a hyaluronic acid product with the optimal characteristics.

citations.title: Migrating granulomatous chronic reaction from hyaluronic acid skin filler (Restylane): review and histopathological study with histochemical stainings.
citations.abstract: Background: A unique case is presented in whom an allergic reaction to Restylane filler, associated with migrating granulomas, persisted despite medical interventions. A histopathological study was requested for evidence at court. Methods: Hematoxylin-eosin, alcian blue and colloidal iron staining were applied to skin sample biopsies obtained 5 months and 3 years after the hyaluronic acid (HA) injection. Results: The histological staining highlighted the presence of the filler inside the foreign body granuloma and in the derma of a biopsy obtained after 5 months; a small amount of filler was discovered within a granulomatous reaction 3 years after the injection. Conclusions: Smaller fragments of HA display inflammatory, angiogenic and immune-stimulatory activities. Intradermal skin testing before the start of HA filler therapy, and before each subsequent injection, may prevent legal implications for the plastic surgeon. Informed consent to skin tests should be obtained.

name: Niacinamide
scoreRationale: A vitamin with strong evidence for barrier and pigmentation benefits and a wide safety margin; high percentages can cause mild flushing.
summary: Niacinamide is a form of vitamin B3 that strengthens the skin barrier, evens tone and calms redness. It's gentle and well researched.

overview: Niacinamide (nicotinamide) is a form of vitamin B3: a pyridine ring, a benzene-like ring containing one nitrogen, with an amide group (–CONH₂) attached. It is small, very water-soluble and stable to heat and light, which makes it easy to formulate.

Inside cells it becomes part of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, coenzymes that shuttle electrons in hundreds of reactions, from making ATP to repairing DNA. On skin, it strengthens the barrier and evens tone, with one of the strongest evidence records of any cosmetic active.
profile.function: Improves barrier function, reduces hyperpigmentation and redness, and fortifies foods as vitamin B3.

mechanisms.title: Repairing the skin barrier
mechanisms.chemical: The outer layer of skin is held together by fatty molecules, including ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids, which form layers between the dead skin cells like mortar between bricks. Ceramides are made through a series of enzyme reactions, and the first step is controlled by an enzyme called serine palmitoyltransferase. Niacinamide increases the activity of this enzyme and the production of other barrier lipids. That leads to higher levels of ceramides and free fatty acids in the skin. It may also help skin cells make more of the proteins needed to build a strong barrier.
mechanisms.biological: A strong barrier holds water inside the skin, reducing water loss and keeping skin hydrated and smooth. It also keeps irritants and allergens out, making skin less reactive. Clinical studies have shown that applying niacinamide reduces dryness, redness and water loss from the skin. It helps people with dry or sensitive skin and conditions such as rosacea and eczema. Niacinamide is also very well tolerated, which makes it a popular choice for daily use.

mechanisms.title: Fading dark spots
mechanisms.chemical: Skin color comes from melanin, a pigment made by cells called melanocytes. Melanocytes pack melanin into small sacs called melanosomes and hand them over to neighboring skin cells, called keratinocytes, which make up most of the skin's outer layer. Niacinamide reduces this hand-over of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes. Unlike some other brightening ingredients, it doesn't block the production of melanin itself. Instead it reduces how much pigment ends up in the visible skin cells.
mechanisms.biological: With less melanin delivered to the outer skin cells, dark spots such as sun spots and marks left by acne gradually fade as the pigmented cells are shed. Clinical studies show visible improvement within four to eight weeks at concentrations of 2 to 5 percent. Because niacinamide works differently from ingredients like vitamin C or hydroquinone, it is often combined with them. Its effect is reversible, so spots can return if use stops or skin gets more sun. Daily sunscreen is essential to prevent new pigmentation.

mechanisms.title: Supporting DNA repair
mechanisms.chemical: Ultraviolet light from the sun damages the DNA in skin cells, and cells fix it with repair systems that use a lot of energy. One key molecule in this process is NAD⁺, which is needed by enzymes that detect and repair DNA damage, such as PARP. UV exposure uses up NAD⁺ and lowers the cell's ATP, its energy supply, which can slow DNA repair. Niacinamide is a building block for NAD⁺, so it helps restore NAD⁺ and ATP levels after UV exposure. That supports the cell's ability to repair the damage.
mechanisms.biological: By supporting DNA repair and reducing the way UV suppresses the skin's immune defenses, niacinamide may help protect against skin cancer. In the ONTRAC trial, published in 2015, people at high risk of skin cancer took 500 milligrams of oral nicotinamide twice a day for a year. They developed 23 percent fewer new non-melanoma skin cancers, such as basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas, than those on placebo. The benefit disappeared after they stopped. Nicotinamide isn't a substitute for sunscreen, but doctors may recommend it for high-risk patients.

reactions.title: Becoming NAD⁺
reactions.summary: Niacinamide's main job in the body is to become part of NAD⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide), a coenzyme, meaning a helper molecule that enzymes need in order to work. NAD⁺ takes part in hundreds of reactions, from breaking down sugar for energy to repairing DNA. When enzymes use NAD⁺, they often release niacinamide, which cells then recycle back into NAD⁺. This recycling route is called the salvage pathway. It is the main way cells keep up their NAD⁺ supply.

steps.name: First step
steps.text: An enzyme called NAMPT attaches a ribose-phosphate group, taken from a molecule called PRPP, to niacinamide. This forms nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN. It is the slowest step in the pathway, so it controls how much NAD⁺ is made.

steps.name: Second step
steps.text: Another enzyme, NMNAT, attaches an AMP unit taken from ATP to NMN. This completes the NAD⁺ molecule. NAD⁺ now has two nucleotides joined together, which is why it is called a dinucleotide.

steps.name: In action
steps.text: In many metabolic reactions, NAD⁺ accepts a hydride ion (H⁻), a hydrogen atom carrying an extra electron, and becomes NADH. NADH carries those electrons to the mitochondria, where they are used to make ATP. NAD⁺ is regenerated and ready to accept more electrons.

reactions.result: This salvage pathway lets cells reuse the niacinamide released when NAD⁺ is used up, for example by DNA repair enzymes. Without enough niacinamide or its precursors, NAD⁺ levels fall and the deficiency disease pellagra can develop.

reactions.title: Hydrolysis to niacin
reactions.summary: Under harsh conditions, such as strong acid, strong base or high heat, niacinamide's amide group can be broken off by water. This converts niacinamide into nicotinic acid, also called niacin, another form of vitamin B3. Both forms count as vitamin B3, but niacin has a very different effect on skin: it causes flushing. Formulators keep conditions in products mild to prevent this conversion. It is a textbook example of amide hydrolysis.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: A water molecule attacks the carbon atom of niacinamide's amide group (–CONH₂), which is slightly positive. Strong acid, strong base or heat speed this up enormously. Under mild conditions it is extremely slow.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: The bond between that carbon and the amide's nitrogen breaks. The nitrogen leaves as ammonia (NH₃). The carbon is left holding an –OH group.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: The result is nicotinic acid (niacin), with a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) where the amide used to be. Niacin is still vitamin B3, but it interacts with the body differently.

reactions.result: Niacin causes skin flushing by activating receptors that release prostaglandins, which widen blood vessels. To avoid this, formulas keep the pH between about 5 and 7, where the conversion is negligible. Old advice warned against mixing niacinamide with vitamin C for this reason, but at normal pH and temperature the effect is minimal.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a nutrient.
Safe as used.

hazards.title: Tingling or flushing at high strength
hazards.summary: Niacinamide is generally very well tolerated, but some people get mild tingling, warmth or redness, especially at high concentrations of 10 percent or more. These reactions are usually brief. People with very sensitive skin may be more prone to them. Research suggests that 2 to 5 percent provides most of the benefit with fewer side effects. Starting with a lower concentration and working up helps the skin adjust.
hazards.chemical: At high concentrations, niacinamide itself can mildly irritate the skin. Products can also contain small amounts of nicotinic acid (niacin), either as an impurity or formed from niacinamide over time, especially if the product's pH is very low or very high. Niacin activates a receptor called GPR109A on skin cells, which triggers the release of prostaglandins. Prostaglandins are signaling molecules that widen blood vessels. Even small amounts of niacin can have this effect.
hazards.biological: When prostaglandins widen blood vessels in the skin, more blood flows to the surface, causing warmth, redness and sometimes tingling or itching. It is the same flushing that happens when people take high doses of niacin as a cholesterol medicine. In skincare it is usually mild and fades within minutes to an hour. It isn't an allergic reaction and doesn't damage the skin. Choosing lower concentrations and products with a stable pH reduces the chance of it happening.

hazards.title: Very high oral doses
hazards.summary: Oral niacinamide supplements are generally safe at moderate doses, such as the 500 milligrams twice a day used for skin cancer prevention. Very high doses, however, above about 3 grams a day, have been linked to side effects. These include nausea, vomiting and signs of stress on the liver. Such doses are far higher than what is needed for good health or found in foods and skincare. Anyone considering high-dose supplements should talk to a doctor.
hazards.chemical: When large amounts of niacinamide are swallowed, the liver has to process the excess. One way the body gets rid of niacinamide is by attaching a methyl group to it, drawing on a supply of methyl groups that is also needed for other important reactions. At very high doses, this can drain that supply. The liver also produces breakdown products that must be excreted. Over time, these demands can stress liver cells.
hazards.biological: Doses above about 3 grams a day have been linked to nausea, vomiting and, rarely, signs of liver damage in blood tests. High doses may also affect blood sugar control. Unlike niacin, niacinamide doesn't usually cause flushing even at high oral doses. Adults need only about 14 to 16 milligrams of vitamin B3 a day, easily supplied by food. Niacinamide applied to the skin is absorbed only in small amounts and doesn't cause these effects.

profile.dosage: Skincare serums typically contain 2 to 10 percent niacinamide, with studies showing most of the benefit at 2 to 5 percent. It is considered safe for daily use and suits most skin types, including sensitive skin. Adults need about 14 to 16 milligrams of vitamin B3 a day from food, while oral nicotinamide at 500 milligrams twice a day has been used under medical supervision to help prevent skin cancer. Doses above about 3 grams a day may stress the liver. Niacinamide is found naturally in meat, fish, nuts, mushrooms and whole grains.

myths.claim: Never combine niacinamide with vitamin C.
myths.consensus: Conversion to flushing niacin requires high heat over time; modern formulas can be combined safely.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis from tryptophan
synthesis.summary: The human body can make its own vitamin B3 from tryptophan, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. So vitamin B3 deficiency usually happens only when a diet is low in both niacin and tryptophan. The conversion happens mainly in the liver through a long series of enzyme reactions. It isn't very efficient, though. Most people get their vitamin B3 partly from food and partly from tryptophan.
synthesis.mechanism: Tryptophan is broken down through a series of enzyme steps called the kynurenine pathway. Along the way, the tryptophan molecule's ring structure is broken open and rearranged, eventually forming a molecule called quinolinic acid. Quinolinic acid is converted into nicotinic acid mononucleotide, which is then built into NAD⁺. As NAD⁺ is used, cells release niacinamide from it. On average, about 60 milligrams of tryptophan yields just 1 milligram of niacin equivalent, so a lot of tryptophan is needed.
synthesis.significance: Pellagra, B3 deficiency, struck populations eating mostly untreated corn, which is low in both niacin and tryptophan. Traditional Mexican cooking avoided it by soaking corn in an alkaline solution, which frees its bound niacin.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Most niacinamide used in supplements, fortified foods and cosmetics is made in factories through a combination of chemistry and biology. The process starts with a petrochemical called 3-methylpyridine, a ring molecule similar to benzene but containing a nitrogen atom. A chemical step turns it into a nitrile, and then an enzyme from bacteria converts the nitrile into niacinamide. Pairing chemical and enzyme steps like this is an example of green chemistry. It is efficient and produces very pure niacinamide.
synthesis.mechanism: First, 3-methylpyridine is reacted with ammonia and oxygen at high temperature over a metal-oxide catalyst, a process called ammoxidation. This converts its methyl group (–CH₃) into a nitrile group (–C≡N), producing 3-cyanopyridine. Next, the 3-cyanopyridine is mixed with water and cells of Rhodococcus bacteria, which contain an enzyme called nitrile hydratase. The enzyme adds a water molecule across the nitrile's triple bond, turning it into an amide group (–CONH₂) and forming niacinamide. The product is then purified and crystallized.
synthesis.significance: The enzyme step stops cleanly at the amide, avoiding over-hydrolysis to niacin.

citations.title: Niacinamide - mechanisms of action and its topical use in dermatology.
citations.abstract: Niacinamide, an amide of vitamin B3 (niacin), is a hydrophilic endogenous substance. Its effects after epicutaneous application have long been described in the literature. Given a sufficient bioavailability, niacinamide has antipruritic, antimicrobial, vasoactive, photo-protective, sebostatic and lightening effects depending on its concentration. Within a complex metabolic system niacinamide controls the NFκB-mediated transcription of signalling molecules by inhibiting the nuclear poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP-1). Niacinamide is a well-tolerated and safe substance often used in cosmetics. Clinical data for its therapeutic use in various dermatoses can increasingly be found in the literature. Although the existing data are not sufficient for a scientifically founded evaluation, it can be stated that the use of niacinamide in galenic preparations for epicutaneous application offers most interesting prospects.

citations.title: Niacinamide: a review on dermal delivery strategies and clinical evidence.
