citations.abstract: Niacinamide, an active form of vitamin B3, is recognised for its significant dermal benefits including skin brightening, anti-ageing properties and the protection of the skin barrier. Its widespread incorporation into cosmetic products, ranging from cleansers to serums, is attributed to its safety profile and proven efficacy. Recently, topical niacinamide has also been explored for other pharmaceutical applications, including skin cancers. Therefore, a fundamental understanding of the skin permeation behaviour of niacinamide becomes crucial for formulation design. Given the paucity of a comprehensive review on this aspect, we provide insights into the mechanisms of action of topically applied niacinamide and share the current strategies used to enhance its skin permeation. This review also consolidates clinical evidence of topical niacinamide for its cosmeceutical uses and as treatment for some skin disorders, including dermatitis, acne vulgaris and actinic keratosis. We also emphasise the current exploration and perspectives on the delivery designs of topical niacinamide, highlighting the potential development of formulations focused on enhancing skin permeation, particularly for clinical benefits.

citations.title: Topical Treatments for Melasma and Their Mechanism of Action.
citations.abstract: Objective: We conducted a review of topical agents currently used in melasma, discussing their mechanism of action, efficacy, safety, and tolerability, with an update on newer treatments. Methods: A systematic review from PubMed database was performed, using PRISMA guidelines. The search was limited to English and Spanish studies that were double or single blinded, prospective, controlled or randomized clinical trials, reviews of literature, and meta-analysis studies. Results: 348 studies were analyzed; 80 papers met inclusion criteria. Triple combination (TC) therapy and hydroquinone (HQ) are still the most well-studied agents with strong evidence-based recommendation. TC therapy remains the gold standard of care based on efficacy and patient tolerability. Evidence has shown ascorbic acid, azelaic acid, glycolic acid, kojic acid, salicylic acid, and niacinamide to be effective as adjuvant therapies with minimal side effects. Tranexamic acid (TA) and cysteamine have become recent agents of interest due to their good tolerability, however more trials and studies are warranted. Less evidence exists for other topical agents, such as linoleic acid, mulberry extract oil, rucinol, 2% undecylenoyl phenylalanine, and epidermal growth factors agents. Limitations: Some studies discussed represented a low sample size, and there is an overall lack of recent studies with larger populations and long-term follow up. Conclusions: TC therapy continues to be the gold standard of care. Topical cysteamine and TA are newer options that can be incorporated as adjuvant and maintenance treatments into a patient's regimen. Cysteamine and topical TA have no known severe adverse effects. Evidence comparing other topical adjuvant treatments to HQ, maintains HQ as the gold standard of care.

citations.title: The effect of niacinamide on reducing cutaneous pigmentation and suppression of melanosome transfer.
citations.abstract: Background: Cutaneous hyperpigmentation occurs in multiple conditions. In addition, many Asian women desire a lighter skin colour. Thus, there is a need for the development of skin lightening agents. Niacinamide is a possible candidate. Objectives: To investigate the effects of niacinamide on melanogenesis in vitro and on facial hyperpigmentation and skin colour in vivo in Japanese women. Methods: Melanin production was measured in a purified mushroom tyrosinase assay, cultured melanocytes, a keratinocyte/melanocyte coculture model, and a pigmented reconstructed epidermis (PREP) model. The clinical trials included 18 subjects with hyperpigmentation who used 5% niacinamide moisturizer and vehicle moisturizer in a paired design, and 120 subjects with facial tanning who were assigned to two of three treatments: vehicle, sunscreen and 2% niacinamide + sunscreen. Changes in facial hyperpigmentation and skin colour were objectively quantified by computer analysis and visual grading of high-resolution digital images of the face. Results: Niacinamide had no effect on the catalytic activity of mushroom tyrosinase or on melanogenesis in cultured melanocytes. However, niacinamide gave 35-68% inhibition of melanosome transfer in the coculture model and reduced cutaneous pigmentation in the PREP model. In the clinical studies, niacinamide significantly decreased hyperpigmentation and increased skin lightness compared with vehicle alone after 4 weeks of use. Conclusions: The data suggest niacinamide is an effective skin lightening compound that works by inhibiting melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes.

name: Salicylic Acid
scoreRationale: An effective, FDA-recognized acne active, but it can irritate, and large-area use is not advised for young children or in pregnancy at high strength.
summary: Salicylic acid is an oil-soluble exfoliant that clears pores and treats acne. Effective at 0.5–2%, but it can dry or irritate skin.

physical.solubility: Slightly soluble in water (about 2 g/L); soluble in ethanol and oils

overview: Salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) is a benzene ring with a carboxylic acid group and a hydroxyl group on neighboring carbons. Because the –OH sits right next to the acid group, the two form an internal hydrogen bond, making salicylic acid more fat-soluble than most acids.

That oil-friendliness is its superpower in skincare. Unlike water-soluble alpha-hydroxy acids, salicylic acid, a beta-hydroxy acid, dissolves into the oily sebum inside pores and exfoliates from within, which is why it's a go-to acne treatment.
profile.function: Exfoliates inside pores, reduces acne lesions and treats dandruff, warts and calluses.

mechanisms.title: Unclogging pores
mechanisms.chemical: Most skincare acids, such as alpha-hydroxy acids, dissolve well in water but poorly in oil. Salicylic acid is different: its –OH and –COOH groups sit next to each other and form a hydrogen bond with each other, hiding some of their water-loving character. That makes salicylic acid lipophilic, meaning it dissolves in oils such as sebum, the oily substance made inside hair follicles. Because it dissolves in sebum, it can travel down into pores. Inside the pore, it weakens desmosomes, the protein connections that hold the cells lining the pore together.
mechanisms.biological: Acne starts when dead skin cells and sebum clump together and clog a pore, forming a plug called a comedo. Open comedones are blackheads and closed ones are whiteheads. By loosening the cells that line the pore, salicylic acid helps them shed normally instead of sticking together and blocking it. That prevents new blackheads and whiteheads and helps loosen existing ones. It is especially useful for oily and acne-prone skin.

mechanisms.title: Calming inflammation
mechanisms.chemical: Salicylic acid is a close chemical relative of aspirin, which is acetylsalicylic acid. Inside cells, salicylic acid can reduce the production of prostaglandins, signaling molecules that promote inflammation. It also dampens a key inflammation pathway called NF-κB, which switches on genes for inflammatory proteins. Unlike aspirin, salicylic acid doesn't permanently block the COX enzymes that make prostaglandins, but it can lower their output by other routes. These effects have been seen mainly in laboratory studies.
mechanisms.biological: Inflammation is what makes acne spots red, swollen and painful. By reducing inflammatory signals, salicylic acid may help red, swollen pimples settle faster. Together with its pore-clearing action, that makes it a common ingredient in acne treatments. It is also used in dandruff shampoos and products for other flaky scalp conditions, where it helps loosen scales. Evidence for its anti-inflammatory effect in acne specifically comes mostly from the lab.

mechanisms.title: A plant immune hormone
mechanisms.chemical: In plants, salicylic acid works as a hormone, a chemical signal that coordinates responses throughout the plant. When a plant is infected by a pathogen such as a bacterium or virus, it makes more salicylic acid. Salicylic acid binds to receptor proteins called NPR proteins. That binding changes the receptors and allows them to switch on genes that produce defense proteins. Some of those proteins attack the invaders directly.
mechanisms.biological: When one part of a plant is infected, salicylic acid levels rise and signals spread through the plant, preparing other parts to defend themselves. This is called systemic acquired resistance, and it resembles in some ways how the human immune system remembers infections. Plants that can't make or respond to salicylic acid are much more vulnerable to disease. Some farmers use chemicals that mimic salicylic acid to help protect crops. This role in plants is why many of them, willow included, contain salicylic acid or related compounds.

reactions.title: Kolbe–Schmitt carboxylation
reactions.summary: The Kolbe–Schmitt reaction attaches a carbon dioxide molecule directly to a benzene ring, turning phenol into salicylic acid. Hermann Kolbe developed it in 1860, and Rudolf Schmitt improved it in 1885. It is unusual because carbon dioxide is normally quite unreactive, but the electron-rich phenoxide ion is reactive enough to grab it. The reaction needs high temperature and pressure. It is still the main way salicylic acid is made today.

steps.name: Phenoxide
steps.text: Phenol, a benzene ring with an –OH group, is reacted with sodium hydroxide. This removes the hydrogen from the –OH, forming sodium phenoxide. The negatively charged oxygen pushes electrons into the ring, making the ring more reactive.

steps.name: Carboxylation
steps.text: The sodium phenoxide is heated with carbon dioxide at about 125 °C and roughly 100 atmospheres of pressure. The electron-rich ring attacks the carbon of CO₂, attaching it at the position right next to the oxygen. The sodium ion helps hold the CO₂ near that spot.

steps.name: Acidification
steps.text: The product, sodium salicylate, is treated with sulfuric acid. This adds hydrogen ions, converting the salt into salicylic acid. Salicylic acid is less soluble in water, so it comes out as crystals.

reactions.result: Hermann Kolbe's 1860 synthesis made salicylic acid cheap enough to become aspirin's starting material. Using potassium instead of sodium shifts where the carboxyl group attaches, producing para-hydroxybenzoic acid, the starting material for parabens.

reactions.title: Acetylation to aspirin
reactions.summary: Salicylic acid itself was used for pain and fever in the 1800s, but it badly irritated the stomach. In 1897, chemists at the German company Bayer, including Felix Hoffmann, found that adding an acetyl group to salicylic acid made it gentler. The result was acetylsalicylic acid, sold as aspirin. The reaction is an esterification, forming an ester bond between salicylic acid and an acetyl group. Aspirin went on to become one of the most widely used medicines in history.

steps.name: Reagent
steps.text: Acetic anhydride, made by joining two acetic acid molecules with the loss of water, is a reactive source of acetyl groups (CH₃CO–). It reacts far more readily than acetic acid itself. A little acid catalyst is often added.

steps.name: Esterification
steps.text: The –OH group on salicylic acid's ring attacks one of the carbonyl carbons of acetic anhydride. A new bond forms, attaching an acetyl group to that oxygen and creating an ester. The other half of the anhydride leaves as acetic acid.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: The products are acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) and acetic acid. The aspirin is purified by crystallization, usually from cold water, in which it dissolves poorly.

reactions.result: In the body, aspirin transfers its acetyl group to the COX enzyme, permanently blocking it, and becomes salicylic acid again. Blocking COX reduces the production of prostaglandins, which cause pain, fever and inflammation, and of thromboxane, which helps blood clot; that second effect is why low-dose aspirin is used to prevent heart attacks.

regulatory.status: OTC acne drug monograph.
Allowed as a preservative and for other uses; not for children under 3 except in shampoos.
regulatory.limit: Up to 2% (3% in rinse-off hair products)

hazards.title: Dryness and irritation
hazards.summary: The most common side effect of salicylic acid in skincare is dryness, peeling or mild irritation. It happens because the acid exfoliates the skin and the products have a low pH. It is more likely when salicylic acid is used often, at high concentrations, or together with other exfoliants or retinoids. People with dry or sensitive skin are more prone to it. Using a moisturizer and starting with less frequent application helps.
hazards.chemical: Salicylic acid loosens the connections between cells in the skin's outer layer, so dead cells shed faster. Products containing it are also usually kept at a low pH, to keep the acid in its active, uncharged form. Both effects can weaken the skin barrier, especially alongside other acids or retinoids that also speed up cell turnover. A weaker barrier lets more water escape and lets irritants penetrate. Salicylic acid can also directly irritate nerve endings in the skin.
hazards.biological: When the barrier is weakened, water loss increases and skin feels dry, tight and flaky. Peeling happens as dead cells shed faster than usual. Irritation can cause stinging, burning or redness, especially on sensitive areas around the nose and mouth. These effects are usually mild and settle when use is cut back. Using salicylic acid every other day, applying moisturizer and wearing sunscreen all help protect the skin.

hazards.title: Salicylate toxicity from large-area use
hazards.summary: Salicylic acid in spot treatments and face washes is very safe, but applying high-strength products to large areas of skin, especially broken skin, can let enough be absorbed to cause poisoning. This is called salicylate toxicity, or salicylism. It is a particular concern for young children, who have a lot of skin relative to their body weight, and for people with kidney or liver problems. Cases have occurred with treatments for skin conditions such as psoriasis that covered large areas. Products for large areas are usually used under medical supervision.
hazards.chemical: Salicylic acid can pass through the skin into the bloodstream, where it travels as salicylate. The amount absorbed rises with the concentration, the area covered, how long it stays on, and whether the skin is damaged or covered by a dressing. In the blood, salicylate interferes with several processes, including energy production in mitochondria and the body's acid–base balance. It also directly stimulates the brain's breathing center. The kidneys remove salicylate, but slowly when levels are high.
hazards.biological: Early signs of salicylate toxicity include ringing in the ears (tinnitus), nausea, vomiting and dizziness. As levels rise, breathing becomes fast and deep and the body's acid–base balance is thrown off. Severe cases can cause confusion, seizures and organ damage and can be life-threatening. Treatment means stopping the exposure and, in hospital, helping the body get rid of the salicylate. Using salicylic acid only on small areas and following label directions prevents the problem.

profile.dosage: Over-the-counter acne products in the United States contain 0.5 to 2 percent salicylic acid, and the European Union generally limits it to 2 percent in leave-on cosmetics, with lower limits for some product types. Wart and callus removers can contain up to 40 percent but are meant only for small areas. Under EU rules, products containing it shouldn't be used on children under three, except shampoos. People with aspirin allergy should avoid salicylic acid. Daily sunscreen is a good idea, since exfoliation can increase sun sensitivity.

myths.claim: Willow bark extract works the same as salicylic acid.
myths.consensus: Willow bark contains salicin and very little free salicylic acid, so it's much weaker.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Almost all salicylic acid made today is produced from phenol using the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction. The phenol itself is made from petroleum chemicals. The process is efficient and has run on an industrial scale for more than a century. Most of the world's salicylic acid is turned into aspirin. The rest goes into skincare, dandruff shampoos, food preservatives and other products.
synthesis.mechanism: Phenol is reacted with sodium hydroxide to make sodium phenoxide, which is dried carefully because water interferes with the next step. The dry sodium phenoxide is heated with carbon dioxide gas at about 100 atmospheres and 125 °C. The carbon dioxide attaches to the ring next to the oxygen, forming sodium salicylate. This is dissolved in water and acidified with sulfuric acid, so salicylic acid crystallizes out. It is then purified by recrystallization or sublimation to the standard needed for medicines and cosmetics.
synthesis.significance: Most of the world's salicylic acid becomes aspirin, one of the most widely used medicines ever made.

synthesis.title: From willow bark
synthesis.summary: Long before modern chemistry, people used willow bark to treat pain and fever. Ancient Sumerian and Egyptian texts describe willow remedies, and the Greek physician Hippocrates recommended willow leaves. Willow bark contains salicin, a natural compound the body converts into salicylic acid. In the 1800s, scientists isolated salicin and then salicylic acid from willow and from other plants such as meadowsweet. Those discoveries led directly to aspirin.
synthesis.mechanism: Salicin is a molecule made of salicyl alcohol joined to a glucose sugar. When willow bark is eaten, enzymes in the intestine remove the glucose, releasing salicyl alcohol, which is absorbed and then oxidized in the liver to salicylic acid. In 1828 Johann Buchner isolated salicin from willow bark, and in 1838 the Italian chemist Raffaele Piria converted salicin into salicylic acid in the lab. He did it by splitting off the sugar and oxidizing what remained. Salicylic acid was also obtained from meadowsweet, whose old Latin name, Spiraea, gave aspirin the “spir” in its name.
synthesis.significance: Willow bark remedies for pain and fever date back thousands of years, to ancient Sumer and Egypt.

citations.title: Complete biosynthesis of salicylic acid from phenylalanine in plants.
citations.abstract: Salicylic acid (SA) is a pivotal phytohormone for plant responses to biotic and abiotic stresses. Plants have evolved two pathways to produce SA: the isochorismate synthase and phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL) pathways1. Whereas the isochorismate synthase pathway has been fully identified2-4, the PAL pathway remains incomplete. Here we report the full characterization of the PAL pathway for SA biosynthesis via functional analysis of rice (Oryza sativa) SA-DEFICIENT GENE 1 (OSD1) to OSD4. The cinnamoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) ligase OSD1 catalyses the conversion of trans-cinnamic acid to cinnamoyl-CoA, which is subsequently transformed to benzoyl-CoA via the β-oxidative pathway in peroxisomes. The resulting benzoyl-CoA is further converted to benzyl benzoate by the peroxisomal benzoyltransferase OSD2. Benzyl benzoate is subsequently hydroxylated to benzyl salicylate by the endoplasmic reticulum membrane-resident cytochrome P450 OSD3, which is ultimately hydrolysed to salicylic acid by the cytoplasmic carboxylesterase OSD4. Evolutionary analyses reveal that the PAL pathway was first assembled before the divergence of gymnosperms and has been conserved in most seed plants. Activation of the PAL pathway in rice significantly enhances salicylic acid levels and plant immunity. Completion of the PAL pathway provides critical insights into the primary salicylic acid biosynthetic pathway across plant species and offers a precise target for modulating crop immunity.

citations.title: Roles of the reactive oxygen species-generating peroxidase reactions in plant defense and growth induction.
citations.abstract: Extracellularly secreted plant peroxidases (POXs) are considered to catalyze the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) coupled to oxidation of plant hormone indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) and defense-related compounds salicylic acid (SA), aromatic monoamines (AMAs) and chitooligosaccharides (COSs). This review article consists of two parts, which describe H(2)O(2)-dependent and H(2)O(2)-independent mechanisms for ROS generation, respectively. Recent studies have shown that plant POXs oxidize SA, AMAs and COSs in the presence of H(2)O(2) via a conventional POX cycle, yielding the corresponding radical species, such as SA free radicals. These radical species may react with oxygen, and superoxide (O(2)(.-)) is produced. Through the series of reactions 2 moles of O(2)(.-) can be formed from 1 moles of H(2)O(2), thus leading to oxidative burst. It has been revealed that the ROS induced by SA, AMAs and COSs triggers the increase in cytosolic Ca(2+) concentration. Actually POXs transduce the extracellular signals into the redox signals that eventually stimulate the intracellular Ca(2+) signaling required for induction of defense responses. On the other hand, IAA can react with oxygen and plant POXs in the absence of H(2)O(2), by forming the ternary complex enzyme-IAA-O(2), which readily dissociates into enzyme, IAA radicals and O(2)(.-). This article covers the recent reports showing that extracellularly produced hydroxy radicals derived from O(2)(.-) mediate the IAA-induced cell elongation. Here a novel model for IAA signaling pathway mediated by extracellular ROS produced by cell-wall POXs is proposed. In addition, possible controls of the IAA-POX reactions by a fungal alkaloid are discussed.

citations.title: Treatment of seborrheic dermatitis: a comprehensive review.
citations.abstract: Seborrheic dermatitis (SD) is a chronic, recurring inflammatory skin disorder that manifests as erythematous macules or plaques with varying levels of scaling associated with pruritus. The condition typically occurs as an inflammatory response to Malassezia species and tends to occur on seborrheic areas, such as the scalp, face, chest, back, axilla, and groin areas. SD treatment focuses on clearing signs of the disease; ameliorating associated symptoms, such as pruritus; and maintaining remission with long-term therapy. Since the primary underlying pathogenic mechanisms comprise Malassezia proliferation and inflammation, the most commonly used treatment is topical antifungal and anti-inflammatory agents. Other broadly used therapies include lithium gluconate/succinate, coal tar, salicylic acid, selenium sulfide, sodium sulfacetamide, glycerin, benzoyl peroxide, aloe vera, mud treatment, phototherapy, among others. Alternative therapies have also been reported, such as tea tree oil, Quassia amara, and Solanum chrysotrichum. Systemic therapy is reserved only for widespread lesions or in cases that are refractory to topical treatment. Thus, in this comprehensive review, we summarize the current knowledge on SD treatment and attempt to provide appropriate directions for future cases that dermatologists may face.

citations.title: Erythema nodosum.
citations.abstract: Erythema nodosum is an acute inflammatory dermatosis characterized by painful nodules which are generally symmetrical and non ulcerative and are mainly located to the extensor surface of the lower legs. The nodules, due to septal panniculitis, are often accompanied by fever and resolve without permanent sequelae. Arthralgia occurs in more than 50% of patients and begins during the eruptive phase or precedes the eruption by 2-4 weeks. Erythema nodosum is presumed to be a hypersensitivity reaction and may occur in association with several systemic diseases or drug therapies, or it may be idiopathic. The most common cause of erythema nodosum is streptococcal infection in children and streptococcal infection and sarcoidosis in adults. Peak incidence occurs at age 18-34 years. Age and sex distributions vary according to etiology and race; women are affected more often than men. It is possible to distinguish between an acute and a chronic form of erythema nodosum; in the acute form, an early stage and a late stage can be detected, both clinically and histologically. Laboratory and instrumental examinations to be performed in case of erythema nodosum are varied and are intended to identify any underlying trigger disease. Erythema nodosum is a self-limited disease, so the therapy is often only symptomatic. Even if the erythema nodosum quickly responds to systemic steroids, in most cases their use is not recommended, nor necessary; is usually sufficient to use NSAIDs (eg, acetyl salicylic acid, ibuprofen, naproxen, indomethacin).

citations.title: Nitric oxide molecular targets: reprogramming plant development upon stress.
citations.abstract: Plants are sessile organisms that need to complete their life cycle by the integration of different abiotic and biotic environmental signals, tailoring developmental cues and defense concomitantly. Commonly, stress responses are detrimental to plant growth and, despite the fact that intensive efforts have been made to understand both plant development and defense separately, most of the molecular basis of this trade-off remains elusive. To cope with such a diverse range of processes, plants have developed several strategies including the precise balance of key plant growth and stress regulators [i.e. phytohormones, reactive nitrogen species (RNS), and reactive oxygen species (ROS)]. Among RNS, nitric oxide (NO) is a ubiquitous gasotransmitter involved in redox homeostasis that regulates specific checkpoints to control the switch between development and stress, mainly by post-translational protein modifications comprising S-nitrosation of cysteine residues and metals, and nitration of tyrosine residues. In this review, we have sought to compile those known NO molecular targets able to balance the crossroads between plant development and stress, with special emphasis on the metabolism, perception, and signaling of the phytohormones abscisic acid and salicylic acid during abiotic and biotic stress responses.

name: Retinol
scoreRationale: One of the best-proven anti-aging actives, but it commonly irritates, increases sun sensitivity, and is advised against in pregnancy; the EU capped concentrations in 2024.
summary: Retinol is a vitamin A derivative that speeds skin renewal and builds collagen. It works, but start slowly, use sunscreen and skip it in pregnancy.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in oils
physical.phStability: Unstable to light, air and heat; needs protective packaging

overview: Retinol is vitamin A in its alcohol form: a six-membered ring (the β-ionone ring) attached to a long chain of four alternating double bonds, ending in an –OH group. That long conjugated chain absorbs light, making retinol pale yellow and very sensitive to UV light and oxygen.

In skin, retinol is converted step by step into retinoic acid, which acts like a hormone, switching genes on and off inside cell nuclei. That's why retinoids are among the few cosmetic ingredients with strong evidence for reducing wrinkles.
profile.function: Reduces fine lines, evens texture and pigmentation, and treats acne.

mechanisms.title: Switching genes through nuclear receptors
mechanisms.chemical: Retinol itself is inactive; skin cells first have to convert it into retinoic acid. Retinoic acid travels into the cell's nucleus, where the DNA is kept. There it binds to proteins called retinoic acid receptors (RARs), which pair up with a second kind of receptor called retinoid X receptors (RXRs). These receptor pairs sit on specific stretches of DNA called retinoic acid response elements. When retinoic acid binds, the receptors change shape and switch nearby genes on or off.
mechanisms.biological: The genes controlled by retinoic acid govern how skin cells grow, divide and mature. Retinoids speed up skin-cell turnover, so old, damaged cells at the surface are replaced more quickly. They also increase production of collagen, the protein that keeps skin firm, and reduce the activity of enzymes called matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that break collagen down, especially after sun exposure. Over months of use, this can smooth fine lines, improve texture and even out skin tone. Retinoids are among the few cosmetic ingredients with strong scientific evidence for reducing wrinkles.

mechanisms.title: Vision
mechanisms.chemical: In the retina at the back of the eye, light is detected by a molecule called retinal, the aldehyde form of vitamin A. Retinal is held inside a protein called opsin, and together they form rhodopsin in the rod cells. In the dark, retinal has a bent shape, called 11-cis-retinal, because one of its double bonds is in a cis arrangement. When retinal absorbs a photon of light, the energy flips that double bond into the straight trans arrangement. Retinal goes from bent to straight in trillionths of a second.
mechanisms.biological: When retinal straightens, it no longer fits snugly inside opsin, so the protein changes shape. That sets off a chain of reactions inside the rod cell that ends with a nerve signal sent to the brain. Rod cells handle vision in dim light, so they depend especially heavily on vitamin A. Vitamin A deficiency first causes night blindness, an inability to see in dim light. Severe deficiency can damage the cornea and cause permanent blindness, and it remains a major cause of preventable blindness in children worldwide.

mechanisms.title: Treating acne
mechanisms.chemical: In acne, the cells lining the hair follicles grow and shed abnormally. Instead of falling away, they stick together and mix with sebum, clogging the pore. Retinoids bind to retinoic acid receptors in these cells and change the activity of genes that control how they mature and detach. This makes shed cells less sticky and brings the follicle lining's renewal back to normal. Retinoids also calm inflammation by affecting immune signals.
mechanisms.biological: With fewer sticky cells clogging pores, fewer blackheads and whiteheads (comedones) form, and comedones are the starting point of every acne spot. Existing ones are loosened and cleared. Because they target the root cause, dermatologists consider retinoids a first-line treatment for most types of acne. Prescription retinoids such as tretinoin and adapalene are stronger than cosmetic retinol. Adapalene 0.1 percent is now sold without a prescription in many countries.

reactions.title: Stepwise oxidation in skin
reactions.summary: Retinol is a precursor: it has to be converted into retinoic acid before it can switch on genes. This happens in two oxidation steps inside skin cells, each carried out by a different enzyme. Each step removes hydrogen atoms or adds oxygen, changing the group at the end of the molecule. Because each step is slow, only a fraction of the retinol becomes retinoic acid. That explains why retinol is gentler but slower-acting than prescription retinoids.

steps.name: Step 1
steps.text: The enzyme retinol dehydrogenase removes two hydrogen atoms from retinol's –CH₂OH end, converting it into an aldehyde group (–CHO). This makes retinal, also called retinaldehyde. This step can run in both directions, so retinal can be turned back into retinol.

steps.name: Step 2
steps.text: The enzyme retinal dehydrogenase adds an oxygen atom to retinal's aldehyde group, converting it into a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). This makes retinoic acid. This step only runs one way.

steps.name: Action
steps.text: Binding proteins carry retinoic acid into the nucleus, where it attaches to retinoic acid receptors (RARs) and switches genes on and off. Extra retinoic acid is broken down by enzymes called CYP26, so it doesn't build up.

reactions.result: Each conversion step limits how much reaches the active form, which is why retinol is gentler and slower than prescription retinoic acid (tretinoin). Retinal, sold in some products as retinaldehyde, is one step closer to the active form and works somewhat faster than retinol.

reactions.title: Light-triggered isomerization (how you see)
reactions.summary: Vision depends on one of the fastest chemical reactions in biology: a light-triggered change in the shape of retinal. When retinal absorbs light, one of its double bonds flips from a bent (cis) arrangement to a straight (trans) one. This change, called isomerization, takes about 200 femtoseconds, which is 200 millionths of a billionth of a second. It is the first step in turning light into a nerve signal. Afterward, the retinal has to be reset to its bent form.

steps.name: Resting state
steps.text: In the dark, 11-cis-retinal sits inside a protein called opsin, and together they form rhodopsin in the retina's rod cells. The cis double bond at position 11 gives the retinal chain a bent shape. That bent shape fits snugly inside the protein.

steps.name: Absorption
steps.text: When a photon strikes, its energy is absorbed by retinal's conjugated double bonds. This briefly loosens the double bond at position 11, so that part of the molecule can rotate. The chain straightens into all-trans-retinal.

steps.name: Signal
steps.text: The straightened retinal no longer fits inside opsin, so the protein changes shape. This activates a protein called transducin, starting a chain of reactions that changes the rod cell's electrical state and sends a signal along the optic nerve to the brain.

reactions.result: The used all-trans-retinal is released and recycled back into the 11-cis form by a series of enzymes. The same light sensitivity is why retinol products come in opaque packaging and are used at night: UV and visible light break down retinol's chain of double bonds.

regulatory.status: Caps vitamin A in cosmetics.
regulatory.limit: 0.05% retinol equivalent in body lotions; 0.3% in face and hand products

regulatory.status: Cosmetic ingredient; prescription retinoids (tretinoin) are drugs.

hazards.title: Irritation (“retinization”)
hazards.summary: When people first start using retinol, it is common to go through a period of irritation called retinization. Symptoms include redness, dryness, peeling and sometimes stinging. They usually start within the first week or two and settle within about four to six weeks as the skin adapts. Stronger products and more frequent use make it more likely. Starting slowly, with a low concentration a few nights a week, helps the skin adjust.
hazards.chemical: Retinoic acid formed from retinol speeds up skin-cell turnover and changes the production of the lipids and proteins that make up the skin barrier. During the adjustment period, the outer layer becomes thinner and the barrier lipids are temporarily disrupted. That lets more water escape and more irritants get in. Retinoids also trigger the release of inflammatory signals in the skin. These changes are part of how retinoids work, but they also cause irritation.
hazards.biological: With the barrier temporarily weakened, skin loses more water and becomes dry, flaky and tight. Faster cell turnover causes peeling. Inflammatory signals cause redness and sometimes burning or stinging. Over several weeks the skin adapts: cells adjust their gene activity and the barrier recovers. A gentle moisturizer, avoiding other harsh products and using retinol every other night at first make the process more comfortable.

hazards.title: Pregnancy caution
hazards.summary: Standard medical advice is to avoid retinoids during pregnancy. The caution comes from oral retinoids such as isotretinoin, a powerful acne medicine that can cause severe birth defects. Retinol in cosmetics is absorbed in very small amounts, and there is no clear evidence it harms a developing baby. But because the consequences could be serious, doctors recommend avoiding it as a precaution. Pregnant people can use other ingredients, such as azelaic acid, for acne or pigmentation.
hazards.chemical: Retinoic acid plays a crucial role in the developing embryo, switching genes on and off in precise patterns that guide how organs and limbs form. The amount of retinoic acid in each part of the embryo has to be tightly controlled. When there is too much, especially early in pregnancy, those signals are scrambled and organs can form abnormally. Oral isotretinoin is a form of retinoic acid that reaches high levels in the blood. Retinol on the skin is absorbed far less and converted to retinoic acid only slowly.
hazards.biological: Oral isotretinoin can cause severe birth defects affecting the brain, heart, face and ears, as well as miscarriage, so people taking it must use reliable contraception and have regular pregnancy tests. Studies of retinoids applied to the skin haven't shown a clear increase in birth defects, because blood levels stay very low. Even so, avoiding them during pregnancy and breastfeeding is recommended as a precaution. Vitamin A from food, in normal amounts, is essential for a healthy pregnancy.

hazards.title: Sun sensitivity
hazards.summary: Retinoids can make skin more sensitive to sunlight, so it burns more easily. That is why retinol products are usually used at night, with sunscreen every morning. The extra sensitivity is greatest in the first weeks of use. Retinol itself also breaks down in sunlight, so it works less well if applied in the morning. Consistent sun protection also helps retinoids show their full benefits.
hazards.chemical: Retinoids speed up shedding of the dead cells in the outermost layer of skin, the stratum corneum, making it thinner. This layer normally helps scatter and absorb ultraviolet light before it reaches living cells. With a thinner layer, more UV gets through to the living cells beneath. On top of that, retinol's long chain of double bonds absorbs UV light, which breaks the molecule apart. So sunlight both weakens retinol and makes the skin more vulnerable.
hazards.biological: With more UV reaching living skin cells, skin burns more easily and suffers more DNA damage. Sunburn cells, damaged skin cells that self-destruct, form more readily. Over time, extra UV damage could cancel out the anti-aging benefits of retinoids, since UV is the main cause of skin aging. Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen and limiting sun exposure protect the skin. Many dermatologists suggest pausing retinoids for a few days before intense sun, such as a beach vacation.

profile.dosage: Cosmetic retinol products typically contain 0.01 to 1 percent retinol, while prescription retinoids such as tretinoin are stronger. The European Union has set limits of 0.3 percent retinol equivalent for face and hand products and 0.05 percent for body lotions, to keep total vitamin A exposure safe when combined with diet. Starting with a low concentration two or three nights a week and increasing slowly helps avoid irritation. Retinoids should be avoided during pregnancy as a precaution. Daily sunscreen is essential while using them.

myths.claim: Retinol thins your skin.
myths.consensus: It thins the outermost dead layer slightly but thickens the living epidermis and increases collagen over time.

myths.claim: You can't use retinol in summer.
myths.consensus: You can, with daily sunscreen; it increases sensitivity to sunburn.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis from beta-carotene
synthesis.summary: Animals, including humans, can't make vitamin A from scratch, but they can make it from beta-carotene and other carotenoids found in plants. Beta-carotene is the orange pigment in carrots, sweet potatoes, pumpkins and many leafy greens. Plants make carotenoids to help capture light and protect themselves from light damage. When we eat these plants, enzymes in the intestine convert beta-carotene into vitamin A. Animal foods such as liver, eggs and dairy contain ready-made vitamin A.
synthesis.mechanism: Beta-carotene is a long molecule with a ring at each end and a chain of 11 conjugated double bonds between them. In the cells lining the intestine, an enzyme called beta-carotene oxygenase 1 (BCO1) cuts the molecule exactly in the middle. This produces two molecules of retinal, each with one ring and half of the chain. Retinal is then reduced to retinol by adding hydrogen atoms. Retinol is attached to fatty acids to form retinyl esters, which are packaged with dietary fat and carried to the liver, where most of the body's vitamin A is stored.
synthesis.significance: Carrots don't contain vitamin A itself, but their beta-carotene becomes vitamin A in your body.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Most of the vitamin A in supplements, fortified foods, animal feed and cosmetics is made synthetically by chemical companies such as BASF and DSM. The challenge is building a 20-carbon molecule with a ring and four conjugated double bonds in exactly the right arrangement. Chemists solve it by joining two smaller pieces together. The final product is usually retinyl acetate or retinyl palmitate, more stable forms that the body converts to retinol. Synthetic vitamin A is chemically identical to vitamin A from food.
synthesis.mechanism: In BASF's route, chemists start from β-ionone, a ring-shaped molecule with a short side chain that also gives violets their scent. It is extended and converted into a 15-carbon molecule carrying a phosphorus group, called a phosphonium salt. This salt is reacted with a 5-carbon aldehyde in a Wittig reaction, which joins the two pieces by forming a new carbon–carbon double bond. The result is retinyl acetate, with all 20 carbons in place. It is purified by crystallization and protected from light and oxygen.
synthesis.significance: The Wittig reaction, which joins molecules with a C=C bond, earned Georg Wittig a share of the 1979 Nobel Prize.

citations.title: Molecular Basis for Vitamin A Uptake and Storage in Vertebrates.
citations.abstract: The ability to store and distribute vitamin A inside the body is the main evolutionary adaptation that allows vertebrates to maintain retinoid functions during nutritional deficiencies and to acquire new metabolic pathways enabling light-independent production of 11-cis retinoids. These processes greatly depend on enzymes that esterify vitamin A as well as associated retinoid binding proteins. Although the significance of retinyl esters for vitamin A homeostasis is well established, until recently, the molecular basis for the retinol esterification enzymatic activity was unknown. In this review, we will look at retinoid absorption through the prism of current biochemical and structural studies on vitamin A esterifying enzymes. We describe molecular adaptations that enable retinoid storage and delineate mechanisms in which mutations found in selective proteins might influence vitamin A homeostasis in affected patients.

citations.title: Retinol Dehydrogenases Regulate Vitamin A Metabolism for Visual Function.
citations.abstract: The visual system produces visual chromophore, 11-cis-retinal from dietary vitamin A, all-trans-retinol making this vitamin essential for retinal health and function. These metabolic events are mediated by a sequential biochemical process called the visual cycle. Retinol dehydrogenases (RDHs) are responsible for two reactions in the visual cycle performed in retinal pigmented epithelial (RPE) cells, photoreceptor cells and Müller cells in the retina. RDHs in the RPE function as 11-cis-RDHs, which oxidize 11-cis-retinol to 11-cis-retinal in vivo. RDHs in rod photoreceptor cells in the retina work as all-trans-RDHs, which reduce all-trans-retinal to all-trans-retinol. Dysfunction of RDHs can cause inherited retinal diseases in humans. To facilitate further understanding of human diseases, mouse models of RDHs-related diseases have been carefully examined and have revealed the physiological contribution of specific RDHs to visual cycle function and overall retinal health. Herein we describe the function of RDHs in the RPE and the retina, particularly in rod photoreceptor cells, their regulatory properties for retinoid homeostasis and future therapeutic strategy for treatment of retinal diseases.

citations.title: Functions of Intracellular Retinoid Binding-Proteins.
citations.abstract: Multiple binding and transport proteins facilitate many aspects of retinoid biology through effects on retinoid transport, cellular uptake, metabolism, and nuclear delivery. These include the serum retinol binding protein sRBP (aka Rbp4), the plasma membrane sRBP receptor Stra6, and the intracellular retinoid binding-proteins such as cellular retinol-binding proteins (CRBP) and cellular retinoic acid binding-proteins (CRABP). sRBP transports the highly lipophilic retinol through an aqueous medium. The major intracellular retinol-binding protein, CRBP1, likely enhances efficient retinoid use by providing a sink to facilitate retinol uptake from sRBP through the plasma membrane or via Stra6, delivering retinol or retinal to select enzymes that generate retinyl esters or retinoic acid, and protecting retinol/retinal from excess catabolism or opportunistic metabolism. Intracellular retinoic acid binding-proteins (CRABP1 and 2, and FABP5) seem to have more diverse functions distinctive to each, such as directing retinoic acid to catabolism, delivering retinoic acid to specific nuclear receptors, and generating non-canonical actions. Gene ablation of intracellular retinoid binding-proteins does not cause embryonic lethality or gross morphological defects. Metabolic and functional defects manifested in knockouts of CRBP1, CRBP2 and CRBP3, however, illustrate their essentiality to health, and in the case of CRBP2, to survival during limited dietary vitamin A. Future studies should continue to address the specific molecular interactions that occur between retinoid binding-proteins and their targets and their precise physiologic contributions to retinoid homeostasis and function.

citations.title: Dermatological Safety of Cosmetic Products Marketed to Children: Insights on the Sephora Kids Phenomenon.
citations.abstract: The "Sephora Kids" trend, where children, especially tweens and teens, are increasingly using makeup and skincare products marketed by beauty retailers, presents notable dermatological challenges. Although these products can facilitate self-expression and teach self-care, their safety and efficacy for young users are largely unverified. This review examines 4 key ingredients commonly found in these products,retinol, exfoliating acids (AHA and BHA), and vitamin C, to assess their implications for pediatric skincare. Current literature and FDA-approved guidelines indicate that these ingredients have not been thoroughly tested in children. Consequently, using these products without medical supervision can pose risks such as skin redness, irritation, heightened sun sensitivity, dermatitis, and other potential adverse effects. This review underscores the importance of cautious use and highlights the need for further research to ensure the safety of these ingredients in young populations. By informing healthcare providers and consumers of these risks, we aim to promote safer skincare practices among children.

citations.title: Retinoic Acid Synthesis and Degradation.
citations.abstract: Retinoic acid (RA) was identified as the biologically active form of vitamin A almost 70 years ago and work on its function and mechanism of action is still of major interest both from a scientific and a clinical perspective. The currently accepted model postulates that RA is produced in two sequential oxidative steps: first, retinol is oxidized reversibly to retinaldehyde, and then retinaldehyde is oxidized irreversibly to RA. Excess RA is inactivated by conversion to hydroxylated derivatives. Much is left to learn, especially about retinoid binding proteins and the trafficking of the hydrophobic retinoid substrates between membrane bound and cytosolic enzymes. Here, background on development of the field and an update on recent advances in our understanding of the enzymatic pathways and mechanisms that control the rate of RA production and degradation are presented with a focus on the many questions that remain unanswered.

name: Zinc Oxide
scoreRationale: One of only two sunscreen filters the FDA proposes as generally safe and effective; gentle on sensitive skin. Avoid inhaling sprays and powders.
summary: Zinc oxide is a mineral sunscreen that blocks UVA and UVB and soothes diaper rash. It's very gentle on skin.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; dissolves in acids
physical.phStability: Amphoteric; dissolves in strong acids and bases

overview: Zinc oxide (ZnO) is an inorganic mineral that crystallizes in the wurtzite structure, where each zinc ion sits inside a tetrahedron of four oxygen ions. It's a white, insoluble powder gentle enough for diaper creams.

It's also a semiconductor with a band gap of about 3.3 electron volts. Photons with more energy than that, meaning UV light shorter than about 380 nm, are absorbed, so zinc oxide blocks UVB and most UVA, the broadest coverage of any single sunscreen filter.
profile.function: Provides broad-spectrum UV protection, protects and soothes irritated skin, and adds opacity.

mechanisms.title: Broad-spectrum UV protection
mechanisms.chemical: Zinc oxide is a semiconductor, a material whose electrons need a certain minimum amount of energy, called the band gap, to jump to a higher energy level. For zinc oxide the band gap is about 3.3 electron volts, which matches light with a wavelength of about 380 nanometers. Ultraviolet light has shorter wavelengths and more energy than that, so it is absorbed as it kicks electrons across the gap. Visible light has longer wavelengths and less energy, so it isn't absorbed. Zinc oxide particles also scatter and reflect some light.
mechanisms.biological: The absorbed UV energy is released mostly as a tiny amount of heat, which harmlessly dissipates. By absorbing UV before it reaches living skin cells, zinc oxide stops it from damaging DNA and other molecules. It protects against both UVB rays, which cause sunburn, and most UVA rays, which penetrate deeper, age the skin and contribute to skin cancer. Zinc oxide gives the broadest protection of any single sunscreen ingredient approved in the U.S. It is often recommended for sensitive skin and children because it rarely irritates.

mechanisms.title: Soothing irritated skin
mechanisms.chemical: Applied to skin, zinc oxide forms a thick physical barrier that shields the skin from moisture, friction and irritants such as urine and stool in the diaper area. Because zinc oxide dissolves slightly in acid, the skin's mildly acidic surface releases small amounts of zinc ions (Zn²⁺) from it. Zinc is an essential trace element that many enzymes in the body need. Some of those enzymes are involved in repairing wounds. Zinc ions also have mild antimicrobial effects.
mechanisms.biological: The physical barrier keeps irritants off damaged skin so it can heal. The zinc ions may support the enzymes that repair tissue and help calm inflammation, and zinc's mild antibacterial and antifungal effects can help prevent infection in broken skin. That is why zinc oxide is the key ingredient in diaper rash creams, calamine lotion and many treatments for minor skin irritation. The U.S. FDA recognizes zinc oxide as a skin protectant. It is gentle enough for newborns.

mechanisms.title: Staying on the surface
mechanisms.chemical: Sunscreen makers often use nano-sized zinc oxide particles, smaller than 100 nanometers, because they look clear on the skin instead of leaving a white cast. Some people have worried that such small particles might soak into the skin. In practice, nanoparticles tend to clump together into larger clusters called aggregates. These clusters are too big to pass through the tightly packed outer layer of skin. Even single nanoparticles are blocked by the structure of the stratum corneum.
mechanisms.biological: Studies using sensitive techniques, including tracing zinc with special isotopes, found that zinc oxide nanoparticles stay in the outermost layer of dead skin cells, in skin folds and in hair follicles. Very little, if any, reaches living skin cells or the bloodstream through intact skin. A tiny amount of zinc may be absorbed as zinc ions, but that is small next to the zinc in a normal diet. The European Union's scientific safety committee has concluded that nano zinc oxide is safe in sunscreens applied to healthy skin. Sprays and powders are a different matter, because they could be breathed in.

reactions.title: Amphoteric behavior
reactions.summary: Zinc oxide is amphoteric, meaning it can react as either a base or an acid. With acids, it acts as a base and dissolves to form zinc salts. With strong bases, it acts as an acid and dissolves to form zincate ions. Most metal oxides behave only as bases, so this two-sided behavior is unusual. It explains some of zinc oxide's behavior in skin products and in industry.

steps.name: With acid
steps.text: Hydrogen ions (H⁺) from an acid react with the oxide ions in zinc oxide, forming water and releasing zinc ions (Zn²⁺) into solution. For example, zinc oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form zinc chloride and water. Here zinc oxide is acting as a base.

steps.name: With base
steps.text: In strong hydroxide solutions, such as concentrated sodium hydroxide, zinc oxide reacts with hydroxide ions to form zincate ions, [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻. Here zinc oxide is acting as an acid. This doesn't happen at the pH of skin.

steps.name: In skin products
steps.text: Skin's surface is mildly acidic, with a pH of about 4.5 to 5.5. At that pH a tiny amount of zinc oxide dissolves, releasing a small number of zinc ions. These may contribute to its soothing and antimicrobial effects.

reactions.result: Being amphoteric means zinc oxide can act as either an acid or a base, depending on its surroundings. Industry uses this property too, for example to scrub acidic gases out of exhaust and to make zinc salts.

reactions.title: The French process
reactions.summary: The French process is one of the oldest ways of making very pure zinc oxide. It works by boiling zinc metal into vapor and burning that vapor in air. It was popularized in France in the 1840s. The method produces a fine, pure white powder suitable for paints, cosmetics and medicines. The size of the particles can be controlled by adjusting the conditions.

steps.name: Vaporizing
steps.text: Zinc metal is heated in a furnace above its boiling point, about 907 °C, turning it into a gas. Starting from pure zinc metal guarantees a pure product. The zinc vapor flows into a combustion chamber.

steps.name: Combustion
steps.text: The zinc vapor reacts with oxygen in the air, burning with a bright, bluish-white flame. Each pair of zinc atoms combines with an oxygen molecule to form zinc oxide. The reaction gives off a lot of heat.

steps.name: Collection
steps.text: The zinc oxide forms as a fine white smoke of tiny particles, which are cooled and caught in bag filters. The particles can be sorted by size. Cosmetic grades are often coated to help them spread smoothly on skin.

reactions.result: Alchemists called the fluffy white product “philosopher's wool” because it looked like cotton. The French process remains the main source of high-purity zinc oxide.

regulatory.status: Generally recognized as safe and effective sunscreen active.
Safe as a UV filter, including nano forms, except in sprayable products that may be inhaled.

hazards.title: Inhaling powder or fumes
hazards.summary: Zinc oxide in creams and lotions is very safe, but breathing in zinc oxide powder or fumes can be harmful. For consumers, the main concern is breathing in sprayed or powdered sunscreen. For workers, the bigger risk is fresh zinc oxide fumes formed when zinc-coated (galvanized) metal is welded or cut. Those fumes can cause an illness called metal fume fever. Avoiding inhalation is the key precaution.
hazards.chemical: When zinc-coated metal is heated to very high temperatures during welding, the zinc vaporizes and instantly reacts with oxygen in the air, forming tiny particles of fresh zinc oxide. These particles are extremely small, often only nanometers across, so they can be breathed deep into the lungs, down to the tiny air sacs called alveoli. Fine powders from sprays and loose cosmetics can also reach the lungs, though they are usually larger. In the lungs, the particles interact with immune cells and with the airway lining. Fresh fumes are far more reactive than the powder in a lotion.
hazards.biological: Metal fume fever causes flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, cough and a metallic taste, usually starting a few hours after exposure. It comes from an inflammatory response in the lungs, in which immune cells release signals that cause fever. Symptoms usually clear within a day or two. Curiously, workers become tolerant over the working week and lose that tolerance over the weekend, so symptoms can be worst on Mondays, earning it the nickname “Monday fever.” Good ventilation and masks prevent it.

hazards.title: Zinc in waterways
hazards.summary: When people swim in sunscreen or wash it off, some zinc oxide can end up in rivers, lakes and oceans. At high concentrations, zinc can harm some aquatic life, including algae, fish and coral. This is mainly a local concern in heavily used swimming spots. Zinc oxide is often considered more reef-friendly than some chemical UV filters, but it isn't entirely free of environmental impact. Researchers are still studying its effects in real-world conditions.
hazards.chemical: In water, zinc oxide particles slowly dissolve, especially under slightly acidic conditions, releasing zinc ions (Zn²⁺). Zinc ions can interfere with how aquatic animals move other ions, such as calcium, across their membranes, particularly in fish gills. Zinc oxide nanoparticles may also generate reactive oxygen molecules in sunlight, which can damage cells. How toxic it is depends on the zinc concentration, the water chemistry and the species. Coatings on the particles may reduce these effects.
hazards.biological: Fish gills rely on moving ions in and out to absorb oxygen and control their salt and calcium levels. When zinc disrupts that, fish can struggle to breathe and to keep their body chemistry in balance. Some studies have found that high concentrations of zinc oxide nanoparticles can harm coral and the algae living inside it, contributing to coral bleaching. Those effects were mostly seen in laboratory studies with high concentrations. Using sunscreen sensibly and covering up with clothing reduces the environmental impact.

profile.dosage: Sunscreens typically contain 5 to 25 percent zinc oxide, and the U.S. FDA allows up to 25 percent; in 2019 it proposed recognizing zinc oxide as safe and effective. Diaper rash creams contain 10 to 40 percent. On intact skin, it isn't absorbed into the body in meaningful amounts. Avoid breathing in sprayed or powdered sunscreen, and spray it onto your hands first before applying it to your face. Zinc oxide is also used as a zinc supplement in fortified foods, where it provides an essential nutrient.

myths.claim: Nano zinc oxide enters the bloodstream.
myths.consensus: Studies show nanoparticles remain on the outer skin layers.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Zinc ions are toxic to some aquatic organisms at elevated concentrations.

synthesis.title: French process
synthesis.summary: The French process, also called the indirect process, starts with pure zinc metal and produces very pure zinc oxide. It is the main method for the zinc oxide used in cosmetics, medicines and high-quality paints. It is called indirect because it uses refined zinc metal rather than ore. It was popularized in France in the 1840s. The size and shape of the particles can be carefully controlled.
synthesis.mechanism: Pure zinc metal is melted and then boiled in a furnace, becoming zinc vapor at about 907 °C. The vapor is directed into a combustion chamber, where it reacts with oxygen in the air and burns with a bright flame. Each zinc atom combines with an oxygen atom, forming zinc oxide particles that cool and solidify into a fine white powder. By controlling the temperature, airflow and cooling rate, manufacturers control the particle size. The powder is collected, sorted by size and, for cosmetics, often coated with materials such as silica to improve how it performs and reduce its reactivity.
synthesis.significance: Controlling the burn controls the particle size, which decides whether zinc oxide looks chalky white or nearly clear on skin.

synthesis.title: American process
synthesis.summary: The American process, also called the direct process, makes zinc oxide straight from zinc ore without first refining it into pure zinc metal. It was developed in the United States in the 1850s. It is cheaper than the French process but gives less pure zinc oxide, which may carry traces of other metals from the ore. This grade goes mainly into rubber, ceramics and other industrial uses. Most of the world's zinc oxide is used in rubber manufacturing.
synthesis.mechanism: Zinc ore, usually zinc sulfide or zinc carbonate, is first roasted in air to turn it into impure zinc oxide. This is mixed with coal and heated strongly. The carbon in the coal strips oxygen from the zinc oxide, producing zinc vapor and carbon monoxide. The zinc vapor is then immediately burned in air within the same process, forming zinc oxide again, now as a finer, cleaner powder. Impurities from the ore can be carried along, so the product is less pure than French-process zinc oxide.
synthesis.significance: Rubber manufacturing, not cosmetics, uses most of the world's zinc oxide; it helps cure the rubber in car tires.

citations.title: Hybrid Enzymatic/Photocatalytic Degradation of Antibiotics via Morphologically Programmable Light-Driven ZnO Microrobots.
citations.abstract: Antibiotics are antimicrobial substances that can be used for preventive and therapeutic purposes in humans and animals. Their overdose usage has led to uncontrolled release to the environment, contributing significantly to the development of antimicrobial resistance phenomena. Here, enzyme-immobilized self-propelled zinc oxide (ZnO) microrobots are proposed to effectively target and degrade the released antibiotics in water bodies. Specifically, the morphology of the microrobots is tailored via the incorporation of Au during the synthetic process to lead the light-controlled motion into having on/off switching abilities. The microrobots are further modified with laccase enzyme by physical adsorption, and the immobilization process is confirmed by enzymatic activity measurements. Oxytetracycline (OTC) is used as a model of veterinary antibiotics to investigate the enzyme-immobilized microrobots for their removal capacities. The results demonstrate that the presence of laccase on the microrobot surfaces can enhance the removal of antibiotics via oxidation. This concept for immobilizing enzymes on self-propelled light-driven microrobots leads to the effective removal of the released antibiotics from water bodies with an environmentally friendly strategy.

citations.title: Enhanced anticancer potency using an acid-responsive ZnO-incorporated liposomal drug-delivery system.
citations.abstract: The development of stimuli-responsive nanocarriers is becoming important in chemotherapy. Liposomes, with an appropriate triggering mechanism, can efficiently deliver their encapsulated cargo in a controlled manner. We explored the use of acid-sensitive zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZNPs) as modulators of the responsive properties of liposomes. Nanocomplexes formed by the incorporation of ZNPs in liposomes (ZNP-liposomes) were designed to demonstrate the pH-responsive release of a drug (daunorubicin) without premature drug leakage and with the maintenance of the relevant therapeutic concentrations. The nanocomplexes were spherical in shape with a narrow size distribution and showed a high drug-encapsulating efficiency. Under acidic conditions, the ZNP-liposome nanocomplexes released the loaded drug more rapidly than bare liposomes. Using flow cytometry, confocal microscopy and an MTT assay, we demonstrated that these nanocomplexes were readily taken up by cancer cells, resulting in significantly enhanced cytotoxicity. On exposure to the acidic conditions inside cancer cells, the ZNPs rapidly decomposed, releasing the entrapped drug molecules from the ZNP-liposome nanocomplexes, producing widespread cytotoxic effects. The incorporated ZNPs were multimodal in that they not only resulted in a pH-responsive drug-delivery system, but they also had a synergistic chemo-photodynamic anticancer action. This design provides a significant step towards the development of multimodal liposome structures.

citations.title: Sunscreens part 2: Regulation and safety.
citations.authors: Abdel Azim, Bainvoll, Vecerek et al.
citations.abstract: The second part of this CME article discusses sunscreen regulation and safety considerations for humans and the environment. First, we provide an overview of the history of the US Food and Drug Administration's regulation of sunscreen. Recent Food and Drug Administration studies clearly demonstrate that organic ultraviolet filters are systemically absorbed during routine sunscreen use, but to date there is no evidence of associated negative health effects. We also review the current evidence of sunscreen's association with vitamin D levels and frontal fibrosing alopecia, and recent concerns regarding benzene contamination. Finally, we review the possible environmental effects of ultraviolet filters, particularly coral bleaching. While climate change has been shown to be the primary driver of coral bleaching, laboratory-based studies suggest that organic ultraviolet filters represent an additional contributing factor, which led several localities to ban certain organic filters.

citations.title: Dermatological and environmental toxicological impact of the sunscreen ingredient oxybenzone/benzophenone-3.
citations.abstract: Oxybenzone (Benzophenone-3) is an emerging human and environmental contaminant used in sunscreens and personal care products to help minimize the damaging effects of ultraviolet radiation. The Center for Disease Control fourth national report on human exposure to environmental chemicals demonstrated that approximately 97% of the people tested have oxybenzone present in their urine, and independent scientists have reported various concentrations in waterways and fish worldwide. Oxybenzone can also react with chlorine, producing hazardous by-products that can concentrate in swimming pools and wastewater treatment plants. Moreover, adverse reactions could very well be increased by the closed loop of ingesting fish contaminated with oxybenzone and/or washing the ingredient off our bodies and having it return in drinking water as treatment plants do not effectively remove the chemical as part of their processing protocols. In humans, oxybenzone has been reported to produce contact and photocontact allergy reactions, implemented as a possible endocrine disruptor and has been linked to Hirschsprung's disease. Environmentally, oxybenzone has been shown to produce a variety of toxic reactions in coral and fish ranging from reef bleaching to mortality. Lastly, with the rise in skin cancer rates and the availability of more effective sunscreen actives such as micronized zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, serious doubts about the relative prevention benefit of personal care products containing oxybenzone must be raised and compared with the potential negative health and environmental effects caused by the accumulation of this and other chemicals in the ecosystem.

citations.title: Implication of Nanoparticles to Combat Chronic Liver and Kidney Diseases: Progress and Perspectives.
citations.abstract: Liver and kidney diseases are the most frequently encountered problems around the globe. Damage to the liver and kidney may occur as a result of exposure to various drugs, chemicals, toxins, and pathogens, leading to severe disease conditions such as cirrhosis, fibrosis, hepatitis, acute kidney injury, and liver and renal failure. In this regard, the use of nanoparticles (NPs) such as silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), gold nanoparticles (AuNPs), and zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnONPs) has emerged as a rapidly developing field of study in terms of safe delivery of various medications to target organs with minimal side effects. Due to their physical characteristics, NPs have inherent pharmacological effects, and an accidental buildup can have a significant impact on the structure and function of the liver and kidney. By suppressing the expression of the proinflammatory cytokines iNOS and COX-2, NPs are known to possess anti-inflammatory effects. Additionally, NPs have demonstrated their ability to operate as an antioxidant, squelching the generation of ROS caused by substances that cause oxidative stress. Finally, because of their pro-oxidant properties, they are also known to increase the level of ROS, which causes malignant liver and kidney cells to undergo apoptosis. As a result, NPs can be regarded as a double-edged sword whose inherent therapeutic benefits can be refined as we work to comprehend them in terms of their toxicity.

name: Methylisothiazolinone
scoreRationale: A potent skin sensitizer that caused an allergy epidemic in the 2010s; banned from leave-on cosmetics in the EU and tightly limited elsewhere.
summary: MIT is a strong preservative in cleaners and some rinse-off products. It is one of the most common causes of contact allergy.

overview: Methylisothiazolinone (MIT) is a small five-membered ring in which sulfur and nitrogen are bonded directly to each other, next to a carbonyl group. That N–S bond is weak and electron-poor, which makes the molecule eager to react with sulfur atoms in proteins.

That reactivity makes MIT a powerful preservative at parts-per-million levels, and it's the same property that makes it one of the most common causes of allergic contact dermatitis. The EU banned it from leave-on cosmetics in 2017.
profile.function: Kills bacteria and fungi in water-based products at parts-per-million levels.

mechanisms.title: Disabling microbial enzymes
mechanisms.chemical: MIT's five-membered ring contains a sulfur atom bonded directly to a nitrogen atom, and that N–S bond is weak and electron-poor. Many enzymes inside microbes contain the amino acid cysteine, which carries a thiol group (–SH), a sulfur atom with a hydrogen attached. The thiol's sulfur is drawn to MIT's electron-poor sulfur and attacks it, breaking the N–S bond. This forms a new sulfur–sulfur bond, called a disulfide, tying the enzyme to the opened-up MIT molecule. With its cysteine blocked, the enzyme can no longer work.
mechanisms.biological: Many of the enzymes microbes need for respiration and energy production, such as dehydrogenases, depend on cysteine thiols in their active sites. When MIT blocks those thiols, energy production shuts down. Bacteria and fungi stop growing within minutes and die within hours. Because the reaction targets such a basic feature of proteins, MIT works against a wide range of microbes, including bacteria, yeasts and molds. That makes it a powerful preservative even at a few parts per million.

mechanisms.title: Sensitizing human skin
mechanisms.chemical: The same reaction that disables microbial enzymes also happens with proteins in human skin. Skin proteins contain cysteine, and their thiol groups can attack MIT's N–S bond and form disulfide links. This attaches MIT fragments to skin proteins, a process called haptenation. The modified proteins have new shapes the immune system has never seen before. MIT is small and slips into skin easily, which makes it efficient at this.
mechanisms.biological: Immune cells in the skin called Langerhans cells pick up the modified proteins and present them to T cells in the lymph nodes, teaching those T cells to recognize them. Once a person is sensitized, later exposures trigger allergic contact dermatitis, an itchy, red, sometimes blistering rash. Sensitized people can react to tiny amounts, just a few parts per million. Some even react to MIT evaporating from freshly painted walls. The allergy usually lasts for life.

reactions.title: Thiol attack and ring opening
reactions.summary: MIT works by reacting with thiol groups, the –SH groups on the amino acid cysteine in proteins. The reaction opens MIT's ring and fastens it to the protein through a sulfur–sulfur bond. Chemists call this thiol–disulfide exchange. The same reaction explains both how MIT kills microbes and how it causes allergies in people. It is a clear example of a single chemical property having both useful and harmful effects.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: The sulfur atom of a cysteine thiol in a protein has spare electrons, and it is drawn to the sulfur in MIT's ring, which is electron-poor because it is bonded to an electron-hungry nitrogen. The thiol sulfur attacks MIT's sulfur and starts forming a new bond.

steps.name: Ring opening
steps.text: As the new sulfur–sulfur bond forms, the weak nitrogen–sulfur bond in MIT's ring breaks. The ring opens up into a chain. The nitrogen picks up a hydrogen.

steps.name: Disulfide
steps.text: The protein is now linked to the opened MIT through a disulfide bond (S–S). The cysteine's thiol is blocked and can no longer do its job in the protein. The protein is permanently altered.

reactions.result: Any protein with an exposed cysteine can be modified, whether it is a bacterial enzyme or a skin protein. That lack of selectivity is exactly what makes MIT both a powerful preservative and a strong allergen.

reactions.title: Making the ring
reactions.summary: MIT is made by forming a ring that includes a sulfur–nitrogen bond. The starting material contains a sulfur atom and an amide group, and the ring is closed by linking that sulfur to the amide's nitrogen. This needs a chlorinating agent to activate the sulfur. The reaction often produces a mixture of MIT and a closely related chlorinated molecule, methylchloroisothiazolinone (MCI). The mixture is sometimes sold as a preservative blend.

steps.name: Precursor
steps.text: The starting material is N-methyl-3-mercaptopropionamide, a small molecule with a thiol group (–SH) at one end and an amide group with a methyl on its nitrogen at the other. Sometimes its disulfide, two molecules joined through their sulfur atoms, is used instead. It contains every atom the ring needs.

steps.name: Chlorination
steps.text: A chlorinating agent, such as chlorine or sulfuryl chloride, reacts with the sulfur atom and attaches chlorine to it. That makes the sulfur electron-poor and reactive. It is now ready to bond with the nitrogen.

steps.name: Cyclization
steps.text: The amide's nitrogen attacks the activated sulfur, forming a nitrogen–sulfur bond and closing the five-membered ring, and a double bond forms in the ring as well. Some molecules pick up an extra chlorine on the ring, which gives MCI.

reactions.result: MCI and MIT are often sold together as a blend, which is an even stronger sensitizer. The ratio of MIT to MCI can be adjusted by changing the reaction conditions.

regulatory.status: Banned in leave-on cosmetics since 2017.
Mixtures with 15 ppm or more must warn that they may produce an allergic reaction.
Allergen of the Year 2013.

hazards.title: Allergic contact dermatitis
hazards.summary: MIT is one of the most common causes of allergic contact dermatitis, a skin allergy caused by direct contact. Allergy rates rose dramatically in the 2010s after manufacturers began using MIT on its own at higher concentrations to replace older preservatives. The American Contact Dermatitis Society named it Allergen of the Year in 2013. In response, the European Union banned MIT from leave-on cosmetics in 2017 and capped its concentration in rinse-off products. Allergy rates in Europe have since fallen.
hazards.chemical: MIT reacts with cysteine thiols in skin proteins, fastening itself to them through disulfide bonds. Because it is small, penetrates skin easily and reacts readily, it modifies skin proteins very efficiently. The more MIT in a product and the longer it stays on the skin, the greater the chance of sensitization. Leave-on products such as lotions and wet wipes keep MIT on the skin for hours, so they are especially likely to cause it. Rinse-off products cause much less exposure.
hazards.biological: Once sensitized, a person's immune system reacts to MIT whenever they meet it, causing an itchy, red, sometimes blistering eczema where products touch the skin. Common sites include the hands, face, eyelids and, in children, the diaper area, from wet wipes. The rash usually appears one to three days after exposure. Because MIT turns up in cosmetics, cleaning products, paints and glues, avoiding it can be challenging. Dermatologists confirm the allergy with patch testing.

hazards.title: Airborne exposure
hazards.summary: MIT is used as a preservative in water-based paints, glues and cleaning products, and it can evaporate into the air from them. People who are already allergic to MIT can develop skin reactions just from being in a freshly painted room, without touching anything. This is called airborne contact dermatitis. It can be severe and hard to trace to its cause. MIT-free paints are available for people who are sensitized.
hazards.chemical: MIT is a small molecule that evaporates fairly readily at room temperature. As paint dries, water evaporates and carries some of the MIT with it. MIT levels in the air of a freshly painted room can stay raised for weeks. The airborne MIT settles on exposed skin, especially the face and eyelids. It then reacts with skin proteins in the usual way.
hazards.biological: In sensitized people, airborne MIT causes allergic reactions on exposed skin, usually the face, eyelids and neck. The rash is often itchy and swollen and can be mistaken for other conditions. Some people also get respiratory symptoms, such as a runny nose or difficulty breathing. Symptoms continue as long as the person stays in that environment, which can be weeks after painting. Ventilating rooms, avoiding newly painted spaces and choosing MIT-free paint prevent reactions.

profile.dosage: In the European Union, MIT is banned from leave-on cosmetics and limited to 15 parts per million (0.0015 percent) in rinse-off products, while cleaners and paints may contain tens of parts per million. Once someone is sensitized, reactions can occur at just a few parts per million, including from paint fumes. In the United States it is still allowed in leave-on products, although many manufacturers have reduced or dropped it. People with MIT allergy should check labels for both methylisothiazolinone and methylchloroisothiazolinone. Patch testing can confirm the allergy.

myths.claim: Rinse-off products with MIT are completely safe.
myths.consensus: Rinse-off exposure is lower, but people already sensitized can still react.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: MIT is made in chemical plants by closing a ring that contains a sulfur–nitrogen bond. Isothiazolinones were developed as preservatives and biocides in the 1960s and 1970s.
