MIT is often produced together with MCI, a related chlorinated molecule, and the two can be separated or sold as a mixture. Besides cosmetics, isothiazolinones are used in paints, adhesives, cooling water, fuels and cleaning products. Their power at very low concentrations made them popular.
synthesis.mechanism: The starting material, N-methyl-3-mercaptopropionamide or its disulfide, is reacted with a chlorinating agent such as chlorine gas or sulfuryl chloride in a solvent. The chlorinating agent activates the sulfur atom, making it electron-poor. The amide's nitrogen then attacks that sulfur, forming a nitrogen–sulfur bond and closing the five-membered ring. Depending on the conditions, the product is a mixture of MIT and MCI, which carries an extra chlorine on the ring. The two are separated by distillation or crystallization, and the MIT is purified for use.
synthesis.significance: When MIT alone was allowed at higher levels in the 2000s, allergy rates rose sharply, a lesson in how dose drives sensitization.

citations.title: Importance of porins for biocide efficacy against Mycobacterium smegmatis.
citations.abstract: Mycobacteria are among the microorganisms least susceptible to biocides but cause devastating diseases, such as tuberculosis, and increasingly opportunistic infections. The exceptional resistance of mycobacteria to toxic solutes is due to an unusual outer membrane, which acts as an efficient permeability barrier, in synergy with other resistance mechanisms. Porins are channel-forming proteins in the outer membrane of mycobacteria. In this study we used the alamarBlue assay to show that the deletion of Msp porins in isogenic mutants increased the resistance of Mycobacterium smegmatis to isothiazolinones (methylchloroisothiazolinone [MCI]/methylisothiazolinone [MI] and octylisothiazolinone [2-n-octyl-4-isothiazolin-3-one; OIT]), formaldehyde-releasing biocides {hexahydrotriazine [1,3,5-tris (2-hydroxyethyl)-hexahydrotriazine; HHT] and methylenbisoxazolidine [N,N'-methylene-bis-5-(methyloxazolidine); MBO]}, and the lipophilic biocides polyhexamethylene biguanide and octenidine dihydrochloride 2- to 16-fold. Furthermore, the susceptibility of the porin triple mutant against a complex disinfectant was decreased 8-fold compared to wild-type (wt) M. smegmatis. Efficacy testing in the quantitative suspension test EN 14348 revealed 100-fold improved survival of the porin mutant in the presence of this biocide. These findings underline the importance of porins for the susceptibility of M. smegmatis to biocides.

citations.title: Cosmetic Preservatives: Hazardous Micropollutants in Need of Greater Attention?
citations.abstract: In recent years, personal care products (PCPs) have surfaced as a novel class of pollutants due to their release into wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) and receiving environments by sewage effluent and biosolid-augmentation soil, which poses potential risks to non-target organisms. Among PCPs, there are preservatives that are added to cosmetics for protection against microbial spoilage. This paper presents a review of the occurrence in different environmental matrices, toxicological effects, and mechanisms of microbial degradation of four selected preservatives (triclocarban, chloroxylenol, methylisothiazolinone, and benzalkonium chloride). Due to the insufficient removal from WWTPs, cosmetic preservatives have been widely detected in aquatic environments and sewage sludge at concentrations mainly below tens of µg L-1. These compounds are toxic to aquatic organisms, such as fish, algae, daphnids, and rotifers, as well as terrestrial organisms. A summary of the mechanisms of preservative biodegradation by micro-organisms and analysis of emerging intermediates is also provided. Formed metabolites are often characterized by lower toxicity compared to the parent compounds. Further studies are needed for an evaluation of environmental concentrations of preservatives in diverse matrices and toxicity to more species of aquatic and terrestrial organisms, and for an understanding of the mechanisms of microbial degradation. The research should focus on chloroxylenol and methylisothiazolinone because these compounds are the least understood.

citations.title: Novel insights into contact dermatitis.
citations.abstract: Contact dermatitis is a common disease that is caused by repeated skin contact with contact allergens or irritants, resulting in allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) and/or irritant contact dermatitis. Attempts have been made to identify biomarkers to distinguish irritant and allergic patch test reactions, which could aid diagnosis. Some promising candidates have recently been identified, but verification and validation in clinical cases still need to be done. New causes of ACD are constantly being recognized. In this review, 10 new contact allergens from recent years, several relating to anti-aging products, have been identified. Frequent allergens causing considerable morbidity in the population, such as the preservative methylisothiazolinone, have been regulated in the European Union. A significant drop in the number of cases has been seen, whereas high rates are still occurring in other areas such as North America. Other frequent causes are fragrance allergens, especially the widely used terpenes and acrylates found in medical devices for control of diabetes. These represent unsolved problems. Recent advances in immunology have opened the way for a better understanding of the complexity of contact dermatitis, especially ACD-a disease that may be more heterogenous that previous understood, with several subtypes. With the rapidly evolving molecular understanding of ACD, the potential for development of new drugs for personalized treatment of contact dermatitis is considerable.

citations.title: Recognizing and Managing Allergic Contact Dermatitis: Focus on Major Allergens.
citations.abstract: Patch testing is the reference standard for the diagnosis of allergic contact dermatitis. Identification and avoidance of culprit allergens are essential in the treatment of this disease. Each year, new allergens are identified as emerging or important. The authors discuss allergens that are common, enduring, emergent, incompletely recognized, and controversial for the practicing allergist and dermatologist. This Clinical Management Review will encompass a review of fragrances, preservatives, rubber, acrylates, metals, and medications; their common sources of exposure; controversies in diagnosis and patch testing; management and how to avoid those allergens. This review will also include practical aspects of diagnosis and management and will provide resources that can be used as guidance for physicians and patients on nickel, methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone, and fragrance, the most common allergens positive on patch testing.

citations.title: [Preservative allergy : An enduring issue].
citations.abstract: Background: Preservatives in cosmetics are often suspected as contact sensitizers and hence frequently patch tested in dermatitis patients. Exposure in this field has changed over the course of years. Objective: To describe the frequency of contact sensitization to various preservatives. Materials and methods: Retrospective data analysis from the Information Network of Departments of Dermatology (IVDK) for the years 2009-2018. Results: Frequency of sensitization to methylisothiazolinone (MI) has increased from 2.0% in 2009 to 7.2% in 2013. Since 2014, the rate has been falling again. Increasing the patch test concentration of methyldibromo glutaronitrile (MDBGN) in 2016 has caused a sudden rise in positive patch test reactions from 2.0% to more than 4.5%. Allergic reactions to other preservatives occurred in less than 1% of the patients tested. Discussion: Since 2014, the worldwide "epidemic" of sensitization to MI has been subsiding in Central Europe, thanks to corresponding restrictions on use. Since 2008, there is no longer any widespread exposure to MDBGN; the new, higher test concentration elicits many false-positive test reactions and explains the sudden rise in positive patch test reactions since 2016. Despite widespread use, phenoxyethanol, benzoates, benzyl alcohol, parabens and sorbates rarely cause allergic reactions. Therefore, they can be recommended for cosmetics from the epidemiological-allergological point of view.

name: Cetearyl Alcohol
scoreRationale: A gentle fatty alcohol, not a drying alcohol; rare contact allergy is the only notable caution.
summary: Cetearyl alcohol is a waxy fatty alcohol that thickens creams and softens skin. Despite the name, it isn't drying like rubbing alcohol.

identity.composition: Mixture of cetyl alcohol (C16) and stearyl alcohol (C18).

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in oils

overview: Cetearyl alcohol is a blend of two fatty alcohols: cetyl alcohol (16 carbons) and stearyl alcohol (18 carbons). Each is a long, straight hydrocarbon chain ending in a single –OH group, so the molecules are waxy solids at room temperature.

Despite the word “alcohol”, they behave nothing like drinking or rubbing alcohol. A small –OH head on a long oily tail makes them gentle emulsifiers and thickeners that give creams their rich, cushiony body and leave skin soft rather than dry.
profile.function: Thickens and stabilizes emulsions and conditions skin and hair.

mechanisms.title: Building cream structure
mechanisms.chemical: Cetyl and stearyl alcohol molecules each have a long oily tail and a small water-loving –OH head, so they are weakly attracted to both oil and water. On their own they don't mix well with water. But when they are combined with an emulsifier and heated in water, they arrange themselves into stacked double layers called lamellae, with their tails tucked inward and their heads facing the water. Water gets trapped between these layers, forming a thick gel network that also holds oil droplets in place. This structure is remarkably similar to the layered lipids between cells in the skin's own outer layer.
mechanisms.biological: The lamellar gel network gives creams and lotions their thick, smooth, rich texture, so they feel luxurious and spread easily. It also keeps oil and water from separating, so the product stays stable on the shelf for years. On the skin, the cream softens slightly and spreads evenly. Because its structure resembles the skin's own lipid layers, it can feel natural and comfortable. That is why cetearyl alcohol is one of the most common ingredients in creams, conditioners and lotions.

mechanisms.title: Softening skin
mechanisms.chemical: Cetearyl alcohol molecules are long, straight, waxy chains that act as emollients, substances that soften and smooth the skin. When applied, they fill the tiny gaps between rough, flaking skin cells on the surface, like grout filling the spaces between tiles. They also form a thin, light film on the skin. That film slows the evaporation of water from the surface without sealing it completely. Unlike short-chain alcohols such as ethanol, fatty alcohols don't dissolve the skin's own lipids.
mechanisms.biological: By filling gaps and smoothing the surface, cetearyl alcohol makes dry, rough skin feel softer right away. The thin film reduces water loss, helping skin stay hydrated longer. In hair conditioners, it coats strands, making them smoother, softer and easier to comb. Because it doesn't strip natural oils, it suits dry and sensitive skin. Many people are surprised to learn that some of the “alcohols” in skincare are actually moisturizing.

reactions.title: Hydrogenation of plant fatty acids
reactions.summary: Cetearyl alcohol is made from the fatty acids in plant oils such as coconut or palm oil, through a process called hydrogenation. Hydrogenation means adding hydrogen to a molecule; here it converts the carbonyl group (C=O) of a fatty acid ester into an alcohol group (–CH₂OH). That turns a fatty acid into a fatty alcohol. The reaction needs high pressure, high temperature and a metal catalyst. The same kind of reaction makes many other fatty alcohols for detergents and cosmetics.

steps.name: Esters
steps.text: First, coconut or palm oil, which is made of triglycerides, is reacted with methanol to produce fatty acid methyl esters and glycerin. Methyl esters are easier to hydrogenate than the oil itself. They are separated by distillation.

steps.name: Hydrogenation
steps.text: The methyl esters are mixed with hydrogen gas at high pressure, around 200 to 300 atmospheres, and heated over a copper-based catalyst. The catalyst helps hydrogen atoms add across the ester's carbon–oxygen double bond. This is called reduction because the molecule gains hydrogen.

steps.name: Products
steps.text: The reaction produces fatty alcohols, with the ester group turned into a –CH₂OH group, and releases methanol, which is recycled. The fatty alcohols are separated by distillation into different chain lengths. The 16-carbon cetyl alcohol and 18-carbon stearyl alcohol fractions are then blended to make cetearyl alcohol.

reactions.result: Reducing a carbonyl group to an alcohol is one of the core reactions of organic chemistry. The same process produces other fatty alcohols, such as lauryl alcohol, which is used to make detergents like SLS.

reactions.title: Forming a lamellar gel network
reactions.summary: When a cream is made, its thick texture forms as it cools, much the way jelly sets. That happens because cetearyl alcohol and emulsifiers arrange themselves into a structured network called a lamellar gel network. Getting this structure right is the key to a cream with the right texture and stability. Manufacturers carefully control temperature, mixing speed and cooling rate. Small changes can make a cream thicker, thinner or grainy.

steps.name: Hot mixing
steps.text: Cetearyl alcohol and an emulsifier are melted together, typically above about 70 °C, and mixed with hot water and oils. At that temperature the fatty alcohol is liquid and mixes easily. The emulsifier breaks the oil into tiny droplets.

steps.name: Swelling
steps.text: As the mixture starts to cool, emulsifier and fatty alcohol molecules pair up and line up into flat, layered sheets. Water is drawn in between the layers, which swell. This creates a structured, water-filled gel.

steps.name: Cooling
steps.text: As cooling continues, the fatty alcohol chains in the layers become more ordered and crystallize, locking the structure in place. The network traps water and oil droplets so they can't separate. The cream thickens into its final consistency.

reactions.result: Cooling speed and stirring change the network, which is why manufacturers control them precisely. Cooling too fast or too slowly can make a cream grainy or thin, and the network can slowly change in storage, which is why some creams thicken or thin over time.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Permitted as an indirect and direct food additive in specific uses.

hazards.title: Rare contact allergy
hazards.summary: Cetearyl alcohol is used in a huge number of creams, lotions and conditioners, and allergic reactions to it are uncommon. When they happen, they are usually mild. People with damaged skin, for example from eczema or leg ulcers, or who use many medicated creams, are more likely to react. Some reactions may be caused by impurities in lower-quality material. For most people, cetearyl alcohol is gentle and non-irritating.
hazards.chemical: Fatty alcohols aren't very reactive, so they rarely bind to skin proteins. Some batches, however, may contain small amounts of impurities, such as shorter-chain alcohols or oxidation products. These, or occasionally the fatty alcohols themselves, can act as haptens, small molecules that bond to skin proteins and make them look foreign to the immune system. Damaged skin lets more of these molecules in. Higher-purity cetearyl alcohol lowers the risk.
hazards.biological: In a sensitized person, immune cells recognize the modified skin proteins and trigger inflammation on later exposures. This causes allergic contact dermatitis, with itchy, red, scaly patches where the product was applied, usually one to two days after contact. Reactions are more common on skin that is already damaged, such as around leg ulcers treated with creams. Patch testing by a dermatologist can identify the allergy. Switching to products without cetearyl alcohol usually solves the problem.

profile.dosage: Creams and lotions typically contain about 1 to 5 percent cetearyl alcohol, and conditioners often more. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review has concluded that cetearyl alcohol and related fatty alcohols are safe in cosmetics, and the U.S. FDA also allows cetyl and stearyl alcohols in small amounts in food and medicines. Unlike short-chain alcohols such as ethanol, it isn't drying. People with damaged skin who react to many different creams may benefit from patch testing.

myths.claim: All alcohols in skincare dry out skin.
myths.consensus: Fatty alcohols are waxy emollients unrelated to ethanol's solvent action.

synthesis.title: From plant oils
synthesis.summary: Most cetearyl alcohol today is made from plant oils, especially coconut and palm oil. These oils are rich in fatty acids with 12 to 18 carbon atoms. The fatty acids are converted to fatty alcohols by hydrogenation and then separated by chain length. Cetearyl alcohol can also be made from petroleum, though plant sources are more common. The result is a white, waxy solid, usually sold as flakes or pellets.
synthesis.mechanism: Coconut or palm oil is first split into fatty acids or converted into fatty acid methyl esters by reaction with methanol. These are hydrogenated with hydrogen gas at high pressure over a copper catalyst, which turns the acid or ester group into an alcohol group (–CH₂OH). The resulting mixture of fatty alcohols is separated by distillation, which sorts chains of different lengths by their boiling points. The 16-carbon (cetyl) and 18-carbon (stearyl) fractions are collected. They are blended in the desired ratio, typically about half and half, and solidified into flakes.
synthesis.significance: Cetyl alcohol was first isolated in 1817 from spermaceti, a waxy oil from sperm whales; its name comes from cetus, Latin for whale.

citations.title: Radiolysis characterization of cetostearyl alcohol by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry.
citations.abstract: Methods for sample preparation, assay test and impurity test were established. Degrees of cetostearyl alcohol (CSA) radiolyses in pure state, ointment base and in chloramphenicol eye ointment (CAPEO) were determined at doses of 25 and 50 kGy. Radiolyses of CSA occur in all cases. The degrees are directly proportional to the irradiation dose in each case. Forty-two impurities and radiolysis products were identified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. The radiolysis products were assigned to be n-alkane, n-aldehyde and 2-methyl-1-alcohol. Accordingly, the degradation pathways of cetosteary alcohol were elucidated. Radiolysis behaviors of CSA in pure state, eye ointment base and CAPEO were studied by assay and impurity analyses. The influence of eye ointment matrixes is modest and chloramphenicol molecule exhibits slight scavenger function for cetostearyl. Both qualitative and quantitative data confirm that the radiolysis products of CSA do not cause safety concerns for human use.

citations.title: Evaluation of hydrophobic materials as matrices for controlled-release drug delivery.
citations.abstract: The present study was undertaken to evaluate the effect of different insoluble and erodable wax-lipid based materials and their content level on the release profile of drug from matrix systems. Matrix tablets of theophylline were prepared using carnauba wax, bees wax, stearic acid, cetyl alcohol, cetostearyl alcohol and glyceryl monostearate as rate-retarding agents by direct compression process. The release of theophylline from these hydrophobic matrices was studied over 8-hours in buffer media of pH 6.8. Statistically significant difference was found among the drug release profile from different matrices. The release kinetics was found to be governed by the type and content of hydrophobic materials in the matrix. At lower level of wax matrices (25%), a potential burst release was observed with all the materials being studied. Bees wax could not exert any sustaining action while an extensive burst release was found with carnauba wax at this hydrophobic load. Increasing the concentration of fat-wax materials significantly decreased the burst effect of drug from the matrix. At higher hydrophobic level (50% of the matrix), the rate and extent of drug release was significantly reduced due to increased tortuosity and reduced porosity of the matrix. Cetostearyl alcohol imparted the strongest retardation of drug release irrespective of fat-wax level. Numerical fits indicate that the Higuchi square root of time model was the most appropriate one for describing the release profile of theophylline from hydrophobic matrices. The release mechanism was also explored and explained with biexponential equation. Application of this model indicates that Fickian or case I kinetics is the predominant mechanism of drug release from these wax-lipid matrices. The mean dissolution time (MDT) was calculated for all the formulations and the highest MDT value was obtained with cetostearyl matrix. The greater sustaining activity of cetostearyl alcohol can be attributed to some level of swelling and erosion within this matrix at lower fat-wax level which is also supported by release exponent values and Fickian fraction release against time profile of this agent. The results generated in this study showed that proper selection of these hydrophobic materials based on their physico-chemical properties is important in designing wax matrix tablets with desired dissolution profile.

citations.title: Allergic Contact Dermatitis from Topical Acyclovir: Case Series.
citations.abstract: Background: Despite the widespread use of oral or topical acyclovir, allergic contact dermatitis caused by it has been rarely reported, with fewer than 20 case studies published in the English literature to date. Case reports: A diagnosis of allergic contact dermatitis from acyclovir cream was established in a 62-year-old female patient who had been continuously using acyclovir cream for 3 weeks after systemic therapy for herpes zoster with acyclovir, and in a 35-year-old female patient, who had undergone liver transplantation in 2008 and subsequently developed a severe form of herpes zoster treated orally with 4 g/day acyclovir and prolonged topical administration of acyclovir cream. In both cases, patch tests were performed with extended European Baseline Series, with the excipients of acyclovir cream (propylene glycol, sodium lauryl sulfate, cetostearyl alcohol, dimethyl sulfoxide) and commercial cream containing acyclovir 2%. Positive reactions were obtained only with the commercial cream with acyclovir 2%. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: Allergic contact dermatitis caused by acyclovir is rarely reported and frequently misdiagnosed, despite the wide use of oral or topical acyclovir. Allergic contact dermatitis due to acyclovir applied topically is a clinical problem with which health care providers should be familiar, and which prompts patch testing in suspected patients. Knowledge and education focused on allergens are important to clinicians in daily practice.

citations.title: Contact dermatitis from cetostearyl alcohol.
citations.abstract: Emulsifiers are an uncommon cause of allergic contact dermatitis. Five cases of allergic contact dermatitis to cetostearyl alcohol are presented. In all five cases, multiple positive reactions to other allergens were present, usually topical corticosteroid creams.

name: Propylene Glycol
scoreRationale: Low toxicity with decades of use, but it can irritate or sensitize some people and was the 2018 Allergen of the Year.
summary: Propylene glycol keeps products moist and dissolves other ingredients. It's low in toxicity but can irritate sensitive skin.

physical.solubility: Miscible with water, ethanol and acetone

overview: Propylene glycol (propane-1,2-diol) is a three-carbon molecule with two –OH groups, on the first and second carbons. The second carbon is chiral, so it has two mirror-image forms; commercial propylene glycol is a 50:50 mix.

Two hydroxyls on a small backbone let it mix with water, alcohol and many oils. It holds moisture, dissolves flavors and active ingredients, and lowers water's freezing point, which is why it appears in everything from cake frosting to aircraft de-icer.
profile.function: Retains moisture, dissolves flavors and actives, enhances penetration, and lowers the freezing point.

mechanisms.title: Humectant and solvent
mechanisms.chemical: Propylene glycol has two hydroxyl (–OH) groups on a small three-carbon backbone, plus a methyl group (–CH₃). The hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, attracting and holding moisture, which makes it a humectant. Its small oily methyl group, meanwhile, lets it dissolve molecules that don't dissolve well in water alone. That balance means propylene glycol mixes with water, alcohol and many oils. It acts as a bridge that helps different ingredients stay mixed.
mechanisms.biological: In skincare, propylene glycol carries active ingredients such as vitamins or medicines, keeping them dissolved and spreading them evenly. Its humectant action also draws water to the skin's surface, helping keep it hydrated. In food, it keeps flavors, colors and other additives evenly dissolved and helps baked goods and frostings stay moist. It is also used in medicines to dissolve active ingredients that won't dissolve in water. That versatility makes it one of the most widely used ingredients across many industries.

mechanisms.title: Helping ingredients penetrate
mechanisms.chemical: The outermost layer of skin, the stratum corneum, contains tightly packed layers of lipids that form a barrier. Propylene glycol can slip into these lipid layers and temporarily loosen their orderly packing. It also changes the chemical environment inside the skin, affecting how easily other ingredients move out of a product and into the skin, a process called partitioning. Acting as a solvent within the skin, it can carry other molecules along with it. The result is a skin barrier that is temporarily more permeable.
mechanisms.biological: Because propylene glycol helps other ingredients get in, it is often used in medicated creams, such as steroid creams, to make them work better. In cosmetics, it can help active ingredients reach deeper layers of the skin. The flip side is that it can also increase the penetration of irritating ingredients, which may cause stinging or redness. The effect is temporary, and the barrier returns to normal once the product is gone. Formulators balance these effects when designing products.

mechanisms.title: Metabolized to lactic acid
mechanisms.chemical: When propylene glycol is swallowed or absorbed, it is carried to the liver. There, the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes one of its hydroxyl groups, converting propylene glycol into lactaldehyde. A second enzyme, aldehyde dehydrogenase, then oxidizes lactaldehyde into lactic acid. These are the same kinds of enzymes that break down drinking alcohol. A large share of an absorbed dose, nearly half, is also excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
mechanisms.biological: Lactic acid is a normal part of the body's metabolism; muscles make it during exercise. It is either burned for energy or turned back into glucose by the liver. So at normal exposures, propylene glycol is handled easily and safely. Only very large amounts, typically from high-dose intravenous medicines in hospital, can produce lactic acid faster than the body clears it. That can lead to lactic acidosis, a condition in which the blood becomes too acidic.

reactions.title: Hydration of propylene oxide
reactions.summary: Propylene glycol is made industrially by adding water to propylene oxide, a reactive three-membered ring of two carbons and an oxygen with a methyl group attached. A reaction that adds water to a molecule is called hydration. The ring opens, and the water's atoms are split between the two carbons. The reaction is efficient and gives mostly propylene glycol. It is the main way propylene glycol is made worldwide.

steps.name: Ring strain
steps.text: Propylene oxide's three-membered ring has bond angles of about 60 degrees, far tighter than the usual 109.5 degrees for carbon. This squeezed shape stores energy, called ring strain, which makes the ring eager to open. It is much more reactive than an ordinary ether.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: Water attacks one of the ring's carbon atoms, often helped by a little acid or by high temperature and pressure. The acid adds a hydrogen to the ring oxygen, making the carbons more attractive targets. Water's oxygen forms a bond with a ring carbon.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: As that new bond forms, a carbon–oxygen bond in the ring breaks and the ring opens. The water's H and OH end up spread across the two carbons, each of which now carries an –OH group. The product is propylene glycol.

reactions.result: Excess water is used so the product doesn't react further into larger glycols, such as dipropylene glycol, which form when propylene glycol reacts with more propylene oxide. Those byproducts are separated by distillation and have their own commercial uses.

reactions.title: Metabolism in the body
reactions.summary: When propylene glycol enters the body, it is broken down by the same enzymes that process alcohol. It goes through two oxidation steps, each removing hydrogen and changing the molecule's structure. The end product is lactic acid, which the body uses as an ordinary fuel. This harmless breakdown is why propylene glycol is considered far safer than its close cousin, ethylene glycol. Following the pathway shows exactly why the two are treated so differently.

steps.name: Oxidation 1
steps.text: In the liver, alcohol dehydrogenase removes two hydrogen atoms from propylene glycol's secondary –OH group, the one on the middle carbon, turning it into a carbonyl group (C=O). This produces lactaldehyde. The helper molecule NAD⁺ accepts the hydrogen.

steps.name: Oxidation 2
steps.text: Aldehyde dehydrogenase adds an oxygen to lactaldehyde's aldehyde group, converting it into a carboxylic acid. This produces lactic acid. Again, NAD⁺ takes the hydrogen.

steps.name: Recycling
steps.text: Lactic acid enters normal metabolism: it is either converted to pyruvate and burned for energy in the mitochondria or turned back into glucose by the liver. These are pathways the body uses every day.

reactions.result: This harmless pathway is why propylene glycol, not toxic ethylene glycol, is used in “pet-safe” antifreeze. The same enzymes turn ethylene glycol into oxalic acid and other toxic products that damage the kidneys.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
ADI 25 mg/kg body weight; EU food use limited to carrier roles.
Allergen of the Year 2018.

hazards.title: Irritation and allergy
hazards.summary: Propylene glycol is generally safe in cosmetics, but it can irritate some people's skin and, less often, cause a true allergy. The American Contact Dermatitis Society named it Allergen of the Year in 2018 to raise awareness, since it appears in so many cosmetics, medicines and foods. Irritant reactions such as stinging and redness are much more common than true allergy. They are more likely at high concentrations or on broken skin. People with eczema may be especially sensitive.
hazards.chemical: At high concentrations, propylene glycol can draw water out of the skin and disturb the lipid layers of the barrier. That lets it, and other ingredients, penetrate more deeply and irritate the skin. In some people propylene glycol can act as an allergen, possibly by binding to skin proteins or through its breakdown products, though the exact mechanism isn't well understood. Irritation is a direct chemical effect. Allergy, by contrast, involves the immune system.
hazards.biological: Irritant reactions cause stinging, burning, redness or dryness soon after application, especially on sensitive areas or broken skin, and usually settle once the product is stopped. True allergic reactions cause itchy, red, scaly eczema that appears one to two days after exposure. Rarely, people allergic to propylene glycol react to foods or medicines containing it, with a widespread rash. Patch testing helps tell irritation apart from allergy. Choosing products without it resolves either problem.

hazards.title: Very high intravenous doses
hazards.summary: Propylene glycol is safe in food and cosmetics, but very large doses given into a vein in hospital can cause problems. Some medicines, such as intravenous lorazepam and certain other sedatives, contain large amounts of propylene glycol as a solvent. Patients who receive high doses of these medicines for long periods, especially in intensive care or with kidney or liver problems, can develop toxicity. Doctors watch for this and adjust treatment if needed. It is not a concern for everyday consumers.
hazards.chemical: When propylene glycol is infused straight into the blood in large amounts, the liver converts it into lactic acid. If it arrives faster than the body can clear that lactic acid, the acid builds up in the blood. At the same time, unchanged propylene glycol accumulates, raising the concentration of dissolved particles in the blood, a condition called hyperosmolality. People with kidney or liver problems clear both more slowly. Infants are also more vulnerable because their enzymes are immature.
hazards.biological: Lactic acidosis, too much acid in the blood, can cause rapid breathing, confusion, low blood pressure and, if severe, organ damage. High propylene glycol levels can also affect the kidneys and nervous system. Doctors watch for warning signs in blood tests in patients on high-dose infusions. Switching to a medicine without propylene glycol usually fixes the problem. These effects require doses far higher than anyone gets from food or skincare.

profile.dosage: Cosmetics use propylene glycol at about 1 to 20 percent, and foods use small amounts as a carrier for flavors and colors. International experts (JECFA) have set an acceptable daily intake of 25 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, and the U.S. FDA considers it generally recognized as safe in food. Typical intake from food is well below that limit. In medicine, very high intravenous doses require monitoring. People with eczema who notice irritation may prefer products without it.

myths.claim: Propylene glycol is antifreeze.
myths.consensus: Toxic antifreeze is ethylene glycol; propylene glycol is used in "pet-safe" antifreeze because it's far less toxic.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Low, though large de-icing runoff can deplete oxygen in streams.

synthesis.title: From propylene
synthesis.summary: Most propylene glycol is made from propylene, a gas obtained from petroleum refining and natural gas processing. The propylene is first converted into propylene oxide, which is then reacted with water to make propylene glycol. Millions of tonnes are produced every year for foods, cosmetics, medicines, antifreeze and plastics. Pharmaceutical and food grades must meet strict purity standards. Industrial grades go into antifreeze and serve as a chemical building block.
synthesis.mechanism: Propylene gas is first oxidized to propylene oxide, either by reacting it with hydrogen peroxide over a catalyst or through older processes that use chlorine or organic peroxides. The propylene oxide, a strained three-membered ring, is then mixed with excess water and heated under pressure. Water opens the ring, putting an –OH group on each of two carbons and producing propylene glycol. Larger glycols formed as byproducts are separated by distillation. The propylene glycol is distilled further to reach pharmaceutical or food grade.
synthesis.significance: The hydrogen peroxide route to propylene oxide, introduced in the 2000s, produces only water as a byproduct, a cleaner alternative to older chlorine-based methods.

synthesis.title: From glycerin
synthesis.summary: Propylene glycol can also be made from glycerin, the byproduct of biodiesel production. Because biodiesel plants produce a large surplus of glycerin, turning it into useful chemicals is both economical and environmentally sensible. This route makes bio-based propylene glycol, chemically identical to the petroleum version. Several companies now produce it this way. It is a good example of turning waste into something valuable.
synthesis.mechanism: Glycerin, which has three –OH groups, is reacted with hydrogen gas at high temperature and pressure over a copper-based catalyst. The catalyst helps break one of glycerin's carbon–oxygen bonds and replace that –OH group with a hydrogen atom, a reaction called hydrogenolysis. Removing the –OH from an end carbon leaves a methyl group, so glycerin becomes propylene glycol, which has only two –OH groups. Water is released as a byproduct. The propylene glycol is then purified by distillation.
synthesis.significance: Turning a waste stream into a useful chemical is a core idea of green chemistry.

citations.title: Etomidate revisited.
citations.abstract: The major advantage of etomidate is its lack of cardiovascular side effects. In addition, etomidate is supposed to be neuroprotective. The side effects of etomidate include adrenal suppression and myocloni. A review of the recent literature on etomidate, its clinical use, its side effects and its mechanism of action was performed. Among others, major recent advances include a new drug preparation devoid of propylene glycol and its side effects, a new pretreatment technique that may reduce the incidence of myocloni, and the identification of its site of action in the central nervous system.

citations.title: An overview on the conversion of glycerol to value-added industrial products via chemical and biochemical routes.
citations.authors: Lima, da Silva, Neto et al.
citations.abstract: Glycerol is a common by-product of industrial biodiesel syntheses. Due to its properties, availability, and versatility, residual glycerol can be used as a raw material in the production of high value-added industrial inputs and outputs. In particular, products like hydrogen, propylene glycol, acrolein, epichlorohydrin, dioxalane and dioxane, glycerol carbonate, n-butanol, citric acid, ethanol, butanol, propionic acid, (mono-, di-, and triacylglycerols), cynamoil esters, glycerol acetate, benzoic acid, and other applications. In this context, the present study presents a critical evaluation of the innovative technologies based on the use of residual glycerol in different industries, including the pharmaceutical, textile, food, cosmetic, and energy sectors. Chemical and biochemical catalysts in the transformation of residual glycerol are explored, along with the factors to be considered regarding the choice of catalyst route used in the conversion process, aiming at improving the production of these industrial products.

citations.title: Toxic Alcohols.
citations.abstract: This article reviews the background, metabolism, clinical effects, and treatment of toxic alcohols, specifically ethylene glycol, methanol, diethylene glycol, propylene glycol, and isopropyl alcohol. This article also reviews the importance of an anion gap metabolic acidosis in relation to toxic alcohols and explores both the utility and the limitations of the osmole gap in patient management.

citations.title: Propylene Glycol.
citations.abstract: Propylene glycol (PG), an emollient and emulsifier found in cosmetics, medications, and food, has been granted the dubious honor of being named the American Contact Dermatitis Society's Allergen of the Year for 2018. Allergic and irritant contact dermatitis and systemic cutaneous reactions to PG, which has become an increasingly common ingredient, have been documented. Propylene glycol is as contentious as it is ubiquitous because it acts as both a weak sensitizer and an irritant, confounding the results of positive patch tests. This report serves to increase awareness about PG sensitization and appropriate testing and evaluation of PG patch tests.

citations.title: Amphiphilic transdermal permeation enhancers: structure-activity relationships.
citations.abstract: Transdermal drug delivery offers numerous advantages over conventional routes of administration; however, poor permeation of most drugs across the skin barrier constitutes a serious limitation of this methodology. One of the approaches used to enlarge the number of transdermally-applicable drugs uses permeation enhancers. These compounds promote drug permeation through the skin by a reversible decrease of the barrier resistance. Enhancers can act on the stratum corneum intracellular keratin, influence desmosomes, modify the intercellular lipid domains or alter the solvent nature of the stratum corneum. Even though, hundreds of substances have been identified as permeation enhancers to date, yet our understanding of the structure-activity relationships is limited. In general, enhancers can be divided into two large groups: small polar solvents, e.g. ethanol, propylene glycol, dimethylsulfoxide and amphiphilic compounds containing a polar head and a hydrophobic chain, e.g. fatty acids and alcohols, 1-dodecylazepan-2-one (Azone), 2-nonyl-1,3-dioxolane (SEPA 009), and dodecyl-2-dimethylaminopropanoate (DDAIP). In this review we have focused on structure-activity relationships of amphiphilic permeation enhancers, including the properties of the hydrophobic chains, e.g. length, unsaturation, and branching, as well as the polar heads characteristics, e.g. hydrogen bonding ability, lipophilicity, and size. We present over 180 examples of enhancers with different polar head to illustrate the structural requirements and the possible role of the polar head. We have given an overview of the methods used for investigation of the mechanisms of permeation enhancement, namely differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), infrared (IR) and Raman spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction and future perspectives in this field. Furthermore, biodegradability and chirality of the enhancers are discussed.

name: Panthenol
scoreRationale: A provitamin with excellent tolerance and evidence for barrier repair and soothing.
summary: Panthenol (provitamin B5) hydrates, soothes and helps skin and hair repair. It's gentle enough for babies.

physical.state: Clear viscous liquid (D-form) or white powder (DL-form)
physical.solubility: Freely soluble in water and alcohol

overview: Panthenol is the alcohol form of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5): pantoic acid joined by an amide bond to 3-aminopropanol. Its several hydroxyl groups make it a viscous, water-loving liquid.

The name pantothenic comes from the Greek pantothen, “from everywhere”, because the vitamin is found in almost all foods. In skin and hair care, panthenol is a provitamin: skin enzymes convert it into pantothenic acid, which cells use to build coenzyme A.
profile.function: Moisturizes, calms irritation, supports healing, and adds shine to hair.

mechanisms.title: Coenzyme A and barrier lipids
mechanisms.chemical: Once panthenol has been converted into pantothenic acid in the skin, cells use it to build coenzyme A (CoA), an essential helper molecule. Coenzyme A carries acyl groups, the building blocks of fats, through many metabolic reactions. It is especially important for making fatty acids, which are assembled two carbons at a time from acetyl-CoA. Those fatty acids are then used to make ceramides and other lipids. Without enough coenzyme A, cells can't make these lipids efficiently.
mechanisms.biological: The skin uses fatty acids and ceramides to build and repair its barrier, the protective lipid layer between the cells of the outermost layer. A healthy barrier keeps water in and irritants out. Clinical studies show that applying dexpanthenol, the active form of panthenol, improves skin hydration and reduces water loss through the skin. That helps dry, rough or irritated skin recover. It is common in moisturizers and products for sensitive skin.

mechanisms.title: Soothing and healing
mechanisms.chemical: Laboratory studies show that panthenol and pantothenic acid support the multiplication of fibroblasts, the cells in the deeper layer of skin that make collagen and other structural proteins. They also help skin cells migrate, or move, which is essential for closing a wound. Pantothenic acid may also influence genes involved in wound healing and dampen some inflammatory signals. Together these effects support the skin's natural repair processes. The exact mechanisms are still being worked out.
mechanisms.biological: Because it supports repair, dexpanthenol is widely used in Europe in ointments for minor cuts, burns, scrapes, sunburn and diaper rash. Some studies have found that it helps these wounds heal faster with less redness and irritation. It is also used to soothe skin after procedures such as laser treatments and tattoos. It is gentle enough for babies and sensitive skin. The evidence supports a benefit, though results vary with the type of wound.

mechanisms.title: Hair conditioning
mechanisms.chemical: Panthenol is a small molecule with several hydroxyl groups, which form hydrogen bonds with water. When applied to hair, it soaks into the hair shaft, the visible part of each hair. There it attracts and holds water, acting as a humectant inside the hair. That raises the hair's moisture content. It also leaves a light film on the hair's surface.
mechanisms.biological: With more moisture inside, hair strands become more flexible and less likely to snap. The extra water makes each shaft swell slightly, which can make hair look and feel fuller. The surface film adds shine and smoothness. However, panthenol doesn't reach the follicle under the skin where hair is made, so it doesn't make hair grow faster or prevent hair loss. Its effects are cosmetic and wash out over time.

reactions.title: Activation in skin
reactions.summary: Panthenol is a provitamin, meaning the body converts it into an active vitamin. When applied to skin, panthenol is absorbed and then converted into pantothenic acid, vitamin B5. The conversion is an oxidation reaction carried out by enzymes in the skin. Using panthenol rather than pantothenic acid itself helps the vitamin get into the skin. It is a clever way of delivering a nutrient right where it's needed.

steps.name: Absorption
steps.text: Panthenol is small and uncharged, so it passes through the skin's outer layers more easily than pantothenic acid, which carries a charge at skin pH. It moves into the living layers of the skin. There it meets enzymes that can activate it.

steps.name: Oxidation
steps.text: Enzymes in skin cells oxidize the alcohol group (–CH₂OH) at the end of panthenol's chain, first into an aldehyde and then into a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). Oxygen is added and hydrogen removed. The molecule is now pantothenic acid.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: Cells take up the pantothenic acid and use it to make coenzyme A, through a series of enzyme steps that add phosphate and other building blocks. Coenzyme A then takes part in many reactions, including making the lipids that build the skin barrier.

reactions.result: Panthenol penetrates skin better than pantothenic acid, which is why it is used as the delivery form. Once inside, the body treats it exactly like vitamin B5 from food.

reactions.title: Amide coupling (how it's made)
reactions.summary: Panthenol is made by joining two building blocks, D-pantolactone and 3-aminopropanol, with an amide bond. An amide bond is a strong link between a carbonyl carbon and a nitrogen, the same kind of bond that holds proteins together. D-pantolactone is a ring-shaped molecule called a lactone, which is an ester whose two ends are joined into a ring. The reaction opens the ring and forms the amide in a single step. It is efficient and clean.

steps.name: Lactone
steps.text: Pantolactone is made from simple starting materials, including isobutyraldehyde and formaldehyde. It is produced as a mix of two mirror-image forms, D and L, and the D-form is separated out. Only the D-form is useful.

steps.name: Ring opening
steps.text: 3-Aminopropanol, a small molecule with an amine group (–NH₂) at one end and an –OH group at the other, is mixed with D-pantolactone. The amine's nitrogen attacks the lactone's carbonyl carbon. This breaks the ester bond and opens the ring.

steps.name: Amide
steps.text: As the ring opens, a new amide bond forms between the carbonyl carbon and the nitrogen, and the oxygen that was part of the ring becomes an –OH group. The product is D-panthenol, with three –OH groups and an amide bond.

reactions.result: Only the D-form converts to active vitamin B5, so manufacturers isolate the correct mirror image. A mixture of D and L forms, sold as DL-panthenol, is cheaper, but only half of it is active.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Dexpanthenol ointments are widely approved for minor wounds and diaper rash.

hazards.title: Rare allergy
hazards.summary: Panthenol is one of the gentlest ingredients in skin and hair care. Even though it appears in a wide range of products, including baby care and wound ointments, allergic reactions are rare. When they do occur, they are usually seen in people using dexpanthenol ointments on damaged skin. Most people use panthenol without any problems at all. It is often recommended for sensitive skin.
hazards.chemical: In rare cases, panthenol or one of its breakdown products may act as a hapten, binding to skin proteins and making them look foreign to the immune system. Damaged skin lets more panthenol penetrate, raising the chance of this. Some reported reactions may actually be caused by other ingredients in the same product. The exact mechanism of panthenol allergy isn't well understood. Its low chemical reactivity explains why allergy is so uncommon.
hazards.biological: In sensitized people, panthenol can cause allergic contact dermatitis, with itchy, red, sometimes blistering skin where it was applied. Rarely, it causes contact urticaria, a hive-like reaction that appears within minutes. Reactions are more common when dexpanthenol is used on wounds, eczema or other broken skin. Patch testing can confirm the allergy. Avoiding products containing panthenol resolves it.

profile.dosage: Cosmetics and hair care products typically contain 0.5 to 5 percent panthenol, and wound-healing ointments often contain 5 percent dexpanthenol. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review has concluded that panthenol is safe in cosmetics. Vitamin B5 is found in almost all foods, and adults need about 5 milligrams a day. No upper limit has been set because toxicity from food or supplements is very rare. Panthenol is suitable for babies and sensitive skin.

myths.claim: Panthenol makes hair grow thicker.
myths.consensus: It coats and hydrates hair, making it look fuller, but it doesn't increase hair growth.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis of vitamin B5
synthesis.summary: Plants and many bacteria can make pantothenic acid, vitamin B5, but animals, including humans, can't. That is why it counts as a vitamin for us: we have to get it from food. Fortunately it is in almost every food, and gut bacteria make some too. Deficiency is extremely rare and usually seen only in severe malnutrition. Its name, from the Greek pantothen, “from everywhere,” reflects how widespread it is.
synthesis.mechanism: Bacteria and plants build pantothenic acid from two parts. The first, pantoate, is made from the amino acid valine through a series of enzyme reactions that add a carbon atom and then reduce a carbonyl group. The second, β-alanine, is made by removing a carboxyl group from the amino acid aspartate. An enzyme called pantothenate synthetase then joins pantoate and β-alanine with an amide bond, using energy from ATP. The resulting pantothenic acid is used to make coenzyme A.
synthesis.significance: Because we can't make it, we rely on food and gut bacteria for vitamin B5.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Most panthenol used in cosmetics and supplements is made by chemical synthesis rather than extracted from nature. The process starts with simple chemicals derived from petroleum and builds the molecule in several steps. A key challenge is producing the correct mirror-image form, D-panthenol, since only that form is active. Manufacturers use techniques that separate out or selectively make the D-form. Both pure D-panthenol and a cheaper DL-mixture are sold.
synthesis.mechanism: First, isobutyraldehyde and formaldehyde are combined in an aldol reaction and then treated with hydrogen cyanide and acid to form pantolactone, a ring-shaped molecule. This gives a mixture of D and L forms, which are separated by a process called resolution, often by forming salts with a chiral compound so the two forms crystallize differently. The D-pantolactone is then mixed with 3-aminopropanol, which opens the ring and forms an amide bond, producing D-panthenol. The product is purified to pharmaceutical grade. Some manufacturers use enzymes to make the D-form selectively.
synthesis.significance: Roger J. Williams discovered pantothenic acid in 1933.

citations.title: Telogen Effluvium: A Review of the Literature.
citations.abstract: Telogen effluvium is one of the most common causes of alopecia. It is a scalp disorder characterized by excessive shedding of hair. Several factors such as drugs, trauma, and emotional and physiological stress can lead to the development of telogen effluvium. Multiple alterations in the hair cycle have been proposed as the underlying mechanism. Telogen effluvium can present as acute or chronic hair fall with symptoms such as trichodynia. Diagnostic tests that can be used include hair wash test, trichogram, phototrichogram, and scalp biopsy. In the treatment of telogen effluvium, it is essential to identify and remove the causative factors and to use drugs such as corticosteroids, minoxidil, and novel treatments such as CNPDA (caffeine, niacinamide, panthenol, dimethicone, and an acrylate polymer). Herein, we discuss the presentation, diagnostic approaches, and effective treatment options available for telogen effluvium.

citations.title: Sensitive skin: Active ingredients on the spotlight.
citations.abstract: Objective: Sensitive skin is characterized by self-reported sensory perceptions in response to stimuli that should not provoke unpleasant sensations. Cosmetic products for sensitive skin are designed to minimize these symptoms. This study aimed to unveil the most used active ingredients for sensitive skin in facial care products from the pharmacy and parapharmacy channel. Methods: A pool of products from the pharmacy and parapharmacy channel whose label included the expressions 'sensitive skin', 'reactive skin' or 'intolerant skin' were analysed. The active ingredients were identified from product compositions and ranked in descending order of occurrence. The scientific evidence regarding the mechanism of action and efficacy of each ingredient was also compiled. Results: Eighty-eight products from 19 multinational brands were included. Niacinamide leads the top, followed by Avena sativa, allantoin, glycyrrhetinic acid and derivatives and Laminaria ochroleuca. Ingredients that can reduce skin inflammation and act on the skin barrier were used in more than half of the products analysed. The clinical studies regarding the active ingredients used in these products remain sparse and lack methodological quality. Among the top ingredients, niacinamide, panthenol and acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester were the only ones studied on volunteers having sensitive skin, while acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester and palmitoyl tripeptide-8 were designed to act on the molecular targets involved in this condition. Conclusion: This study reveals the most used active ingredients in cosmetic products for sensitive skin, as well as the scientific evidence supporting their efficacy and the mechanisms of action. This insight is meaningful for dermatologists and other health professionals to provide customized advice based on the symptomatology of individuals with sensitive skin, and for the formulation of cosmetic products and design of new active ingredients. Objectif: La peau sensible se caractérise par des perceptions sensorielles autorapportées en réponse à des stimuli qui ne devraient pas provoquer de sensations désagréables. Les produits cosmétiques pour peaux sensibles sont conçus pour minimiser ces symptômes. Cette étude visait à dévoiler les principes actifs les plus utilisés pour les peaux sensibles dans les produits de soins du visage de la pharmacie et de la chaîne de parapharmacie. MÉTHODES: Un ensemble de produits de la chaîne pharmacie et parapharmacie, dont l’étiquette comportait les expressions « peau sensible », « peau réactive » ou « peau intolérante » ont été analysés. Les principes actifs ont été identifiés à partir des compositions du produit et classés par ordre décroissant d’occurrence. Les preuves scientifiques concernant le mécanisme d’action et l’efficacité de chaque ingrédient ont également été compilées. RÉSULTATS: Quatre-vingt-huit produits provenant de 19 marques multinationales ont été inclus. Le niacinamide est en tête, suivi de l’Avena sativa, de l’allantoïne, de l’acide glycyrrhétinique et de ses dérivés et de Laminaria ochroleuca. Des ingrédients pouvant réduire l’inflammation cutanée et agir sur la barrière cutanée ont été utilisés dans plus de la moitié des produits analysés. Les études cliniques concernant les principes actifs utilisés dans ces produits restent rares et manquent de qualité méthodologique. Parmi les principaux ingrédients, le niacinamide, le panthénol et l’ester de dipeptide acétyl-1 ont été les seuls étudiés sur des volontaires ayant une peau sensible, tandis que l’ester de dipeptide acétyl-1 et le tripeptide palmitoyl-8 ont été conçus pour agir sur les cibles moléculaires qui interviennent dans cette affection. Conclusion: Cette étude révèle les principes actifs les plus utilisés dans les produits cosmétiques pour les peaux sensibles, ainsi que les preuves scientifiques étayant leur efficacité et les mécanismes d’action. Cet éclairage est important pour les dermatologues et autres professionnels de la santé pour apporter des conseils personnalisés basés sur la symptomatologie des personnes ayant la peau sensible, et pour la formulation de produits cosmétiques et la conception de nouveaux principes actifs.

citations.title: The Effectiveness and Safety of a Skin Care Product With Centella asiatica Leaf Extract, Ceramide NP, and Panthenol in Subjects With Sensitive Skin: A Prospective, Observational Study.
citations.abstract: Background: Sensitive skin is a hyperreactive condition with rising prevalence. A holistic skin care routine is crucial for management. Selecting appropriate skin care products is of great concern in clinical practice. Aims: To assess the effectiveness and safety of a facial cream containing Centella asiatica leaf extract, ceramide NP, and panthenol in Chinese females with sensitive skin. Methods: In this single-center, prospective, self-controlled study, 88 female participants applied the cream on their whole face, with follow-ups at Day 2, Weeks 1, 2, and 4. The primary endpoint was the change rate of the SS-10 global score at Week 2. Non-invasive skin parameters and subject self-assessment were conducted. Adverse events (AEs) were monitored. Results: Mean SS-10 scores dropped by 66% and 76% after 2 and 4 weeks. Four symptoms (skin irritation, tautness, itching, and redness) were significantly reduced. TEWL decreased at Weeks 1 and 2, and skin pH at Week 1 and Weeks 2 and 4. SCH increased at all time points and sebum secretion at Week 4. EI, a* value, and facial red area rapidly decreased. Greater improvements were seen in the sensitive skin group compared with the slightly sensitive skin group. All AEs were mild and self-limiting. Conclusions: This study showed the facial cream was effective and safe for 4-week use. It provided immediate relief of facial redness and discomfort, strengthened skin barrier, and modulated pH and sebum secretion, indicating favorable soothing and barrier-repairing properties for sensitive skin.

citations.title: Common cosmeceuticals.
citations.abstract: In the cosmetic arena, many materials are used commercially and claim to provide skin effects (eg, antiaging effects) when used topically. Considering there are so many such materials and many skin appearance effects are encompassed, this short contribution must, by necessity, be selective in terms of the number of materials discussed and the depth with which any particular material is overviewed. This presentation, therefore, focuses on only 10 types of cosmeceutical agents: five vitamins (A, B(3), C, E, panthenol), peptides, hydroxyl acids, sugar amines, ceramides, and metals. In particular, this contribution concentrates on those materials for which there are available clinical data that support a reported skin appearance improvement effect.

citations.title: Scalp application of antioxidants improves scalp condition and reduces hair shedding in a 24-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
citations.abstract: Objective: Increasing hair fullness is a global unmet need for many men and women. An approach to the problem is to decrease hair fall or shedding by reducing scalp stratum corneum oxidation and barrier damage to increase hair retention. This study evaluated a combination of functional antioxidants and barrier-enhancing cosmetic ingredients to improve scalp condition thereby enabling stronger hair anchorage and longer retention. Methods: Male and female subjects with normal scalp condition and self-perceived hair thinning participated in a 24-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical study assessing either a regimen of treatment shampoo and leave-on treatment containing functional antioxidant and barrier-enhancing agents or an identical placebo chassis shampoo control. The functional ingredients were piroctone olamine, zinc pyrithione, zinc carbonate, niacinamide, panthenol and caffeine. At baseline and after 8, 16 and 24 weeks of product use, several measurements were taken: hair shedding, total hair count (by phototrichogram), hair samples, TEWL and evaluation of biomarkers of scalp and hair conditions. Subjects also completed self-assessment questionnaires. Results: Statistically significant effects for functional ingredient-containing treatment regimen versus a placebo control shampoo formulation were observed for reduced hair shedding, increased total hair count, reduced TEWL and improvement in scalp biomarker values. Subjects also noticed these improvements assessed via self-assessment questionnaires. Conclusions: These results establish that the use of functional antioxidant and barrier-enhancing agents to further improve scalp condition can enable a reduction in hair shedding and thus an increase in perceived hair fullness. The underlying improvements in scalp condition suggest the hair benefits were achieved as a result of improved scalp skin barrier and scalp condition leading to a viable preventative approach for hair thinning.

name: Aloe Vera
scoreRationale: Decolorized inner-leaf gel is gentle and soothing; whole-leaf extracts containing aloin carry a possible-carcinogen classification.
summary: Aloe vera gel soothes and hydrates skin. The purified inner gel used in cosmetics is gentle; unpurified whole-leaf extracts are a different story.

identity.composition: About 99% water, with polysaccharides (acemannan), glycoproteins, vitamins and minerals.

physical.phStability: Oxidizes and loses activity over time

overview: Aloe vera gel comes from the clear inner tissue of the thick leaves of Aloe barbadensis Miller. It's about 99% water; the rest is a mix of polysaccharides (especially acemannan, an acetylated chain of mannose sugars), glycoproteins, enzymes, vitamins, minerals and small molecules.

The leaf's outer rind holds a bitter yellow latex rich in anthraquinones such as aloin, a strong laxative. Cosmetic aloe is decolorized to remove most of it, which matters because aloin is behind aloe's main safety concern.
profile.function: Soothes, hydrates, and provides a cooling feel in after-sun and sensitive-skin products.

mechanisms.title: A hydrating film
mechanisms.chemical: Aloe vera gel is about 99 percent water, held in place by long sugar chains called polysaccharides, especially acemannan, a chain of mannose sugars with acetyl groups attached. These long chains form hydrogen bonds with water molecules and trap the water in a gel-like network. When the gel is applied to skin, the water slowly evaporates and leaves behind a thin film of polysaccharides. That film holds some moisture against the skin. The gel's high water content also gives immediate hydration.
mechanisms.biological: As water evaporates from the gel, it takes heat with it, creating a cooling feeling that is soothing on sunburned or irritated skin. The polysaccharide film helps keep the skin's surface hydrated and may reduce water loss for a while. That is why aloe vera is a popular after-sun product and appears in many moisturizers. The soothing effect is real and immediate. Aloe doesn't, however, repair sun damage or prevent the long-term effects of sunburn.

mechanisms.title: Possible burn and wound support
mechanisms.chemical: Laboratory studies have found that some components of aloe vera gel, including acemannan and glycoproteins, affect skin cells. They may stimulate fibroblasts, the cells that make collagen, and encourage cells to multiply. Some components also seem to reduce inflammatory signals, such as certain cytokines and prostaglandins. Aloe contains small amounts of vitamins, minerals and enzymes too. Its composition, however, varies a lot from product to product.
mechanisms.biological: These laboratory effects suggest aloe might help wounds and burns heal faster. Some clinical trials found that aloe gel shortened healing time for minor burns, such as first- and second-degree burns. Other studies found no benefit, and a few found that aloe slowed the healing of surgical wounds. Reviews of the evidence conclude that the results are mixed and better studies are needed. Aloe is reasonable for soothing a minor burn but shouldn't replace medical care for a serious one.

mechanisms.title: Aloin's laxative effect
mechanisms.chemical: Aloin is an anthraquinone glycoside, a three-ring molecule attached to a sugar, found in the yellow latex just under the leaf's outer skin. When swallowed, aloin passes through the stomach and small intestine without being absorbed. In the colon, gut bacteria snip off the sugar and convert aloin into aloe-emodin anthrone. That molecule is the actual laxative. It acts on the cells lining the colon.
mechanisms.biological: Aloe-emodin anthrone makes the colon's muscles contract more strongly, speeding stool along. It also makes the colon secrete more water and salts and absorb less, so stools become loose. The result is cramping, abdominal pain and diarrhea. Aloe latex was once sold as a laxative medicine, but in 2002 the U.S. FDA removed it from approved over-the-counter laxatives because manufacturers didn't provide evidence of its safety. Long-term use can upset the body's salt balance and damage the colon.

reactions.title: Decolorization with activated charcoal
reactions.summary: To make aloe products safer, manufacturers remove most of the aloin and other anthraquinones from aloe juice, a process called decolorization. It uses activated charcoal, a form of carbon with an enormous internal surface area. Aloin molecules stick to the charcoal's surface and are removed when the charcoal is filtered out. The process also removes the yellow color, which is where its name comes from. Decolorized aloe is used in most cosmetics and drinks.

steps.name: Mixing
steps.text: Aloe juice or gel extract is stirred with activated charcoal. Activated charcoal is made by heating carbon-rich materials such as coconut shells with steam or chemicals, which carves out a maze of tiny pores. A single gram can have a surface area of several hundred square meters.

steps.name: Adsorption
steps.text: Flat, ring-shaped molecules like aloin and other anthraquinones are drawn to the flat carbon surfaces inside the charcoal and stick to them, a process called adsorption. Unlike absorption, the molecules cling to the surface rather than soaking in. Large polysaccharides such as acemannan stick far less, so they stay in the juice.

steps.name: Filtering
steps.text: The charcoal, with the aloin attached, is filtered out. What remains is a clear aloe juice containing much less aloin. The process can be repeated to reach the purity required.

reactions.result: Decolorized aloe typically contains less than 10 parts per million of aloin, the industry's safety specification for products meant to be eaten or drunk. This removes the laxative effect and the cancer concerns linked to whole-leaf extract.

regulatory.status: Whole-leaf aloe extract (non-decolorized) is Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic, based on a rat drinking-water study.
Removed aloe as an approved OTC laxative ingredient.
Safe in cosmetics when anthraquinone (aloin) levels are limited.

hazards.title: Whole-leaf extract and aloin
hazards.summary: The main safety concern about aloe vera involves whole-leaf extract that hasn't been decolorized, especially when swallowed. This kind of extract contains aloin and other anthraquinones from the leaf's latex. In a two-year study by the U.S. National Toxicology Program, rats that drank water containing whole-leaf aloe extract developed tumors in the large intestine. As a result, in 2015 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified non-decolorized whole-leaf aloe extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B). Decolorized aloe and the inner-leaf gel used in cosmetics aren't covered by that classification.
hazards.chemical: Once gut bacteria convert aloin and related anthraquinones into aloe-emodin and similar molecules, these can irritate the lining of the colon. In laboratory tests, aloe-emodin has shown some ability to damage DNA. Long-term exposure means repeated irritation and faster cell turnover in the colon. Over time, that could increase the chance of harmful mutations. Removing the anthraquinones by decolorization eliminates this concern.
hazards.biological: In the rat study, long-term exposure led to inflammation, overgrowth of the cells lining the colon and eventually tumors. In people, long-term use of aloe latex as a laxative has been linked to a darkening of the colon lining called melanosis coli, although its connection to cancer is unclear. Human evidence overall is limited. Putting aloe gel on the skin isn't considered a cancer risk. Choosing decolorized aloe products for drinking avoids the concern entirely.

hazards.title: Allergy
hazards.summary: Allergic reactions to aloe vera are uncommon but do happen. They are more likely in people who are allergic to related plants once grouped with aloe in the lily family, such as garlic, onions and tulips. Reactions can include skin rashes from creams and gels or digestive upset from products that are swallowed. Testing a small amount on the skin before using a new product can reveal a sensitivity. Most people use aloe without any trouble.
hazards.chemical: Allergies are usually triggered by specific proteins or other molecules that the immune system mistakes for threats. Aloe contains plant proteins that can cause allergic reactions in sensitive people. Anthraquinones from the latex, if present, can also act as allergens or irritants. People who are already allergic to similar plants may react because their immune systems recognize similar molecules, a phenomenon called cross-reactivity. Decolorized products contain fewer anthraquinones.
hazards.biological: Skin reactions can include redness, itching, hives or eczema where the product was applied, and occasionally more widespread rashes. Swallowing aloe products can cause abdominal cramps or diarrhea, which may be irritation rather than allergy. People with known allergies to related plants should be cautious. Stopping the product usually resolves the symptoms. A doctor can help confirm the cause if reactions keep happening.

profile.dosage: Cosmetic aloe vera products contain anything from a few percent of aloe gel to nearly pure gel, and cosmetic grades are decolorized so that aloin is typically below 50 parts per million. Aloe products meant to be eaten or drunk should be decolorized to below 10 parts per million aloin, according to industry standards. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review has concluded that aloe ingredients are safe in cosmetics when aloin is kept low. Whole-leaf, non-decolorized aloe shouldn't be swallowed regularly. Aloe latex laxatives are no longer approved in the U.S.

myths.claim: Aloe heals burns completely.
myths.consensus: It can soothe minor sunburn, but evidence for faster healing is mixed, and it shouldn't be used on serious burns.

synthesis.title: Harvesting and processing
synthesis.summary: Aloe vera gel is extracted from the leaves of the aloe plant rather than made in a laboratory. The plants are grown on farms in warm, dry regions such as Mexico, Texas, the Caribbean and parts of Africa and Asia. They take about three years to mature before their leaves are harvested. The thick leaves store water in a clear gel, which helps the plant survive drought. Processing has to be fast, because the gel starts breaking down soon after harvest.
synthesis.mechanism: Mature leaves are cut from the plant and washed. They are stood upright so the yellow, aloin-rich latex can drain out. The tough green rind is then removed, leaving the clear inner fillet of gel. The gel is crushed and blended, filtered to remove fibers, and treated with activated charcoal to strip out the remaining aloin. Finally, stabilizers such as vitamin C and citric acid or preservatives are added to slow spoilage, and the gel may be concentrated or dried into a powder.
synthesis.significance: Aloe appears in the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus, written around 1550 BCE.

citations.title: Pharmacological Update Properties of Aloe Vera and its Major Active Constituents.
citations.abstract: Aloe vera has been traditionally used to treat skin injuries (burns, cuts, insect bites, and eczemas) and digestive problems because its anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and wound healing properties. Research on this medicinal plant has been aimed at validating traditional uses and deepening the mechanism of action, identifying the compounds responsible for these activities. The most investigated active compounds are aloe-emodin, aloin, aloesin, emodin, and acemannan. Likewise, new actions have been investigated for Aloe vera and its active compounds. This review provides an overview of current pharmacological studies (in vitro, in vivo, and clinical trials), written in English during the last six years (2014-2019). In particular, new pharmacological data research has shown that most studies refer to anti-cancer action, skin and digestive protective activity, and antimicrobial properties. Most recent works are in vitro and in vivo. Clinical trials have been conducted just with Aloe vera, but not with isolated compounds; therefore, it would be interesting to study the clinical effect of relevant metabolites in different human conditions and pathologies. The promising results of these studies in basic research encourage a greater number of clinical trials to test the clinical application of Aloe vera and its main compounds, particularly on bone protection, cancer, and diabetes.

citations.title: Aloe Vera Gel and Rind-Derived Nanoparticles Mitigate Skin Photoaging via Activation of Nrf2/ARE Pathway.
citations.abstract: Background: Skin aging is the primary external manifestation of human aging, and long-term exposure to ultraviolet radiation is the leading cause of photoaging, which can lead to actinic keratosis and skin cancer in severe cases. Traditional treatments may pose safety risks and cause side effects. As an emerging research direction, plant-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (PDNPs) show promise in combating aging. Aloe vera, known for its natural active ingredients that benefit the skin, aloe-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (ADNPs) have not yet been studied for their potential in delaying skin aging. Methods: In this study, nanoparticles were isolated from two different sites, aloe vera gel and aloe vera rind (gADNPs and rADNPs), and characterized by TEM, SEM, AFM, NTA and BCA. The effects were evaluated by constructing in vitro and in vivo models and using RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence, and histopathological analysis. Results: The results first revealed the exceptional anti-aging effects of ADNPs. We found that ADNPs promoted the nuclear translocation of Nrf2, alleviated oxidative stress and DNA damage induced by UV exposure, and inhibited the elevation of β-gal and SASP. In vivo, ADNPs reduced MDA and SOD levels in mouse skin tissue and delayed skin photoaging. Moreover, safety assessments confirmed the excellent biocompatibility of ADNPs. Conclusion: ADNPs delay skin photoaging through the Nrf2/ARE pathway, holding potential clinical application value, and may provide new therapeutic strategies for future medical cosmetology and skin disease prevention.

citations.title: Treatment of seborrheic dermatitis: a comprehensive review.
citations.abstract: Seborrheic dermatitis (SD) is a chronic, recurring inflammatory skin disorder that manifests as erythematous macules or plaques with varying levels of scaling associated with pruritus. The condition typically occurs as an inflammatory response to Malassezia species and tends to occur on seborrheic areas, such as the scalp, face, chest, back, axilla, and groin areas. SD treatment focuses on clearing signs of the disease; ameliorating associated symptoms, such as pruritus; and maintaining remission with long-term therapy. Since the primary underlying pathogenic mechanisms comprise Malassezia proliferation and inflammation, the most commonly used treatment is topical antifungal and anti-inflammatory agents. Other broadly used therapies include lithium gluconate/succinate, coal tar, salicylic acid, selenium sulfide, sodium sulfacetamide, glycerin, benzoyl peroxide, aloe vera, mud treatment, phototherapy, among others. Alternative therapies have also been reported, such as tea tree oil, Quassia amara, and Solanum chrysotrichum. Systemic therapy is reserved only for widespread lesions or in cases that are refractory to topical treatment. Thus, in this comprehensive review, we summarize the current knowledge on SD treatment and attempt to provide appropriate directions for future cases that dermatologists may face.

citations.title: Aloe Barbadensis Miller (Aloe Vera).
citations.abstract: Aloe Barbadensis Miller (Aloe Vera, AV) is a widely recognized for its diverse health-promoting, skin care, and medicinal properties.
