This narrative review provides a comprehensive overview of AV's bioactive compounds, pharmacological activities, potential applications, its toxic and adverse effects, as well as the clinical evidence supporting AV's efficacy in disease prevention. AV contains over 200 bioactive compounds, with the inner clear gel of the leaves containing the majority of these compounds. These include phenolic acids (274.5-307.5 mg/100 g), flavonoids. (3.63-4.70 g/kg), polysaccharides (3.82-6.55 g/kg), saponins, alkaloids, terpenoids, and anthraquinone derivatives. Findings from clinical studies involving both humans and animals highlight the therapeutic potential of AV across diverse health domains. The studies demonstrate AV's efficacy in reducing blood glucose levels, exhibiting antioxidant and immunomodulatory effects, inducing apoptosis in cancer cells, protecting the liver from damage, and displaying antimicrobial properties. In the fields of dermatology and dentistry, AV has also been observed to promote skin and oral health. However, it is imperative to acknowledge potential risks, adhere to recommended dosages, and seek guidance from healthcare experts before employing AV as a natural therapeutic option. Moreover, considering safety concerns, further well-designed randomized controlled trials are necessary to substantiate the potential benefits of AV and comprehensively assess any associated risks.

citations.title: Antiseptics for burns.
citations.abstract: Background: Burn wounds cause high levels of morbidity and mortality worldwide. People with burns are particularly vulnerable to infections; over 75% of all burn deaths (after initial resuscitation) result from infection. Antiseptics are topical agents that act to prevent growth of micro-organisms. A wide range are used with the intention of preventing infection and promoting healing of burn wounds. Objectives: To assess the effects and safety of antiseptics for the treatment of burns in any care setting. Search methods: In September 2016 we searched the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid MEDLINE (In-Process & Other Non-Indexed Citations), Ovid Embase, and EBSCO CINAHL. We also searched three clinical trials registries and references of included studies and relevant systematic reviews. There were no restrictions based on language, date of publication or study setting. Selection criteria: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that enrolled people with any burn wound and assessed the use of a topical treatment with antiseptic properties. Data collection and analysis: Two review authors independently performed study selection, risk of bias assessment and data extraction. Main results: We included 56 RCTs with 5807 randomised participants. Almost all trials had poorly reported methodology, meaning that it is unclear whether they were at high risk of bias. In many cases the primary review outcomes, wound healing and infection, were not reported, or were reported incompletely.Most trials enrolled people with recent burns, described as second-degree and less than 40% of total body surface area; most participants were adults. Antiseptic agents assessed were: silver-based, honey, Aloe Vera, iodine-based, chlorhexidine or polyhexanide (biguanides), sodium hypochlorite, merbromin, ethacridine lactate, cerium nitrate and Arnebia euchroma. Most studies compared antiseptic with a topical antibiotic, primarily silver sulfadiazine (SSD); others compared antiseptic with a non-antibacterial treatment or another antiseptic. Most evidence was assessed as low or very low certainty, often because of imprecision resulting from few participants, low event rates, or both, often in single studies. Antiseptics versus topical antibioticsCompared with the topical antibiotic, SSD, there is low certainty evidence that, on average, there is no clear difference in the hazard of healing (chance of healing over time), between silver-based antiseptics and SSD (HR 1.25, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.67; I2 = 0%; 3 studies; 259 participants); silver-based antiseptics may, on average, increase the number of healing events over 21 or 28 days' follow-up (RR 1.17 95% CI 1.00 to 1.37; I2 = 45%; 5 studies; 408 participants) and may, on average, reduce mean time to healing (difference in means -3.33 days; 95% CI -4.96 to -1.70; I2 = 87%; 10 studies; 979 participants).There is moderate certainty evidence that, on average, burns treated with honey are probably more likely to heal over time compared with topical antibiotics (HR 2.45, 95% CI 1.71 to 3.52; I2 = 66%; 5 studies; 140 participants).There is low certainty evidence from single trials that sodium hypochlorite may, on average, slightly reduce mean time to healing compared with SSD (difference in means -2.10 days, 95% CI -3.87 to -0.33, 10 participants (20 burns)) as may merbromin compared with zinc sulfadiazine (difference in means -3.48 days, 95% CI -6.85 to -0.11, 50 relevant participants). Other comparisons with low or very low certainty evidence did not find clear differences between groups.Most comparisons did not report data on infection. Based on the available data we cannot be certain if antiseptic treatments increase or reduce the risk of infection compared with topical antibiotics (very low certainty evidence). Antiseptics versus alternative antisepticsThere may be some reduction in mean time to healing for wounds treated with povidone iodine compared with chlorhexidine (MD -2.21 days, 95% CI 0.34 to 4.08). Other evidence showed no clear differences and is of low or very low certainty. Antiseptics versus non-antibacterial comparatorsWe found high certainty evidence that treating burns with honey, on average, reduced mean times to healing in comparison with non-antibacterial treatments (difference in means -5.3 days, 95% CI -6.30 to -4.34; I2 = 71%; 4 studies; 1156 participants) but this comparison included some unconventional treatments such as amniotic membrane and potato peel. There is moderate certainty evidence that honey probably also increases the likelihood of wounds healing over time compared to unconventional anti-bacterial treatments (HR 2.86, 95% C 1.60 to 5.11; I2 = 50%; 2 studies; 154 participants).There is moderate certainty evidence that, on average, burns treated with nanocrystalline silver dressings probably have a slightly shorter mean time to healing than those treated with Vaseline gauze (difference in means -3.49 days, 95% CI -4.46 to -2.52; I2 = 0%; 2 studies, 204 participants), but low certainty evidence that there may be little or no difference in numbers of healing events at 14 days between burns treated with silver xenograft or paraffin gauze (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.59 to 2.16 1 study; 32 participants). Other comparisons represented low or very low certainty evidence.It is uncertain whether infection rates in burns treated with either silver-based antiseptics or honey differ compared with non-antimicrobial treatments (very low certainty evidence). There is probably no difference in infection rates between an iodine-based treatment compared with moist exposed burn ointment (moderate certainty evidence). It is also uncertain whether infection rates differ for SSD plus cerium nitrate, compared with SSD alone (low certainty evidence).Mortality was low where reported. Most comparisons provided low certainty evidence that there may be little or no difference between many treatments. There may be fewer deaths in groups treated with cerium nitrate plus SSD compared with SSD alone (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.99; I2 = 0%, 2 studies, 214 participants) (low certainty evidence). Authors' conclusions: It was often uncertain whether antiseptics were associated with any difference in healing, infections, or other outcomes. Where there is moderate or high certainty evidence, decision makers need to consider the applicability of the evidence from the comparison to their patients. Reporting was poor, to the extent that we are not confident that most trials are free from risk of bias.

name: Shea Butter
scoreRationale: A gentle plant fat with a long history of use; refined shea contains almost no nut protein.
summary: Shea butter is a rich plant fat that softens and protects dry skin. It's gentle and supports women's cooperatives in West Africa.

identity.composition: Triglycerides of stearic and oleic acids plus 5–10% unsaponifiables (triterpene esters, phytosterols, vitamin E).

overview: Shea butter is the fat pressed from the nuts of the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), which grows wild across Africa's Sahel. Chemically it's mostly triglycerides rich in stearic acid (a straight, saturated 18-carbon chain) and oleic acid (an 18-carbon chain with one kink).

That balance makes it solid at room temperature but able to melt on skin. Shea also has an unusually large unsaponifiable fraction, up to about 10%: triterpene alcohols and esters, plant sterols and vitamin E. These components can't be turned into soap and are linked to shea's soothing reputation.
profile.function: Softens and occludes dry skin, adds richness to balms and creams, and conditions hair.

mechanisms.title: Sealing in moisture
mechanisms.chemical: Shea butter is mostly triglycerides, fat molecules made of glycerol and three fatty acids. Its main fatty acids are stearic acid, which is saturated and straight, and oleic acid, which is unsaturated and kinked. That mix makes shea butter solid at room temperature but soft enough to melt at about body temperature. On skin, it melts and spreads into a thin film that fills the gaps between dry skin cells. The film is semi-occlusive, meaning it slows water loss without sealing the skin completely.
mechanisms.biological: By forming a protective film, shea butter slows the evaporation of water from the skin, keeping it hydrated for longer. Filling the gaps between rough skin cells makes the surface feel smoother and softer straight away. That is why shea butter is often recommended for very dry skin, cracked heels, chapped lips and eczema-prone skin. Some studies have found that moisturizers containing shea improve eczema symptoms. It is also used in hair care to soften and protect hair.

mechanisms.title: Anti-inflammatory triterpenes
mechanisms.chemical: Shea butter contains an unusually large share of unsaponifiables, components that don't turn into soap when treated with lye, up to about 10 percent. These include triterpene alcohols and their esters, such as lupeol cinnamate and amyrin cinnamate. In laboratory studies, these triterpenes blocked enzymes involved in inflammation, such as cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), and reduced signaling through inflammatory pathways like NF-κB. They may also act as antioxidants. The amounts vary between shea butters from different regions.
mechanisms.biological: These triterpenes may help explain shea butter's reputation for soothing irritated skin, reducing redness and calming minor inflammation. Traditional healers in West Africa have long used shea butter for skin problems, sprains and small wounds. Most of the evidence for its anti-inflammatory effect, however, comes from laboratory and animal studies. Good-quality human studies are limited. Highly refined shea butter may contain less of these compounds than unrefined shea.

reactions.title: Saponification and the unsaponifiables
reactions.summary: When fats and oils are mixed with a strong base like lye, they undergo saponification, the reaction that makes soap. Most of the fat in shea butter, the triglycerides, turns into soap. But shea butter contains an unusually large amount of other substances, called unsaponifiables, that don't react. These stay in the soap unchanged. That is one reason soap makers value shea butter.

steps.name: Soap formation
steps.text: Hydroxide ions from the lye attack the ester bonds linking fatty acids to glycerol in the triglycerides. Each ester bond breaks, releasing glycerol and turning the fatty acids into their sodium salts. Those salts are soap molecules.

steps.name: Leftovers
steps.text: Triterpene alcohols, sterols and the other unsaponifiables either lack the same kind of ester bonds or have bonds that barely react under soapmaking conditions. Some triterpene esters react only very slowly. So these molecules don't become soap.

steps.name: Result
steps.text: The unsaponifiables remain in the finished bar as separate molecules mixed among the soap. They are oily and don't dissolve in water. They can make the soap feel softer and more conditioning on skin.

reactions.result: Shea soaps keep some of shea's unsaponifiable components, which soap makers prize. Measuring the unsaponifiable content is also one way to check the quality and authenticity of shea butter.

reactions.title: Crystallization and graininess
reactions.summary: Sometimes shea butter develops a grainy texture, with small, gritty lumps, even though it is still perfectly usable. That happens because of the way its fats crystallize after melting and cooling. Fats can crystallize in several different forms, called polymorphs, each with its own structure and melting point. Unstable crystal forms can grow into large grains. The same problem affects chocolate, which can develop a whitish bloom.

steps.name: Melting
steps.text: Shea butter melts at around body temperature, so it can melt during shipping or storage in hot weather. Once melted, all its fat molecules move freely. The orderly crystal structure is lost.

steps.name: Slow cooling
steps.text: As it cools slowly, the triglycerides richest in stearic acid, which melt at higher temperatures, crystallize first, ahead of the others. They may form unstable crystal types. These first crystals act as seeds.

steps.name: Grains
steps.text: Over time those early crystals grow larger, forming gritty lumps scattered through the softer butter. The grains melt on contact with skin, so they don't affect how it works, but they change the texture.

reactions.result: Tempering, controlled heating and cooling as done with chocolate, keeps shea butter smooth. Manufacturers melt it completely and then cool it quickly, sometimes while stirring, so that small, stable crystals form evenly. Grainy shea butter can be fixed at home the same way.

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Shea is one of six vegetable fats allowed in chocolate up to 5%.

hazards.title: Very low hazard
hazards.summary: Shea butter is one of the safest ingredients in skincare. Botanically, shea is a tree nut, which raises questions for people with tree-nut allergies. However, refined shea butter contains almost no protein, and allergies are triggered by proteins. Allergic reactions to shea butter applied to the skin are very rare, even among people with tree-nut allergies. Allergy specialists generally consider refined shea butter low-risk for them.
hazards.chemical: Food allergies are caused by specific proteins that the immune system mistakes for threats. Shea nuts contain proteins, but when shea butter is extracted and refined, the fat is separated from almost all of them. Refined shea butter contains only trace amounts of protein, often too little to detect. Unrefined shea butter may contain slightly more. The fat molecules themselves don't trigger allergy.
hazards.biological: Because the allergy-triggering proteins are largely removed, shea butter rarely causes allergic reactions on the skin. Studies have found no detectable shea proteins in many refined shea butters. People with severe tree-nut allergies who are worried can choose refined shea butter or ask their allergist. Shea butter is generally considered gentle enough for babies and unlikely to clog pores. Very occasionally, someone may experience mild irritation.

profile.dosage: Shea butter is used at every concentration from a few percent in lotions to 100 percent in pure shea balms. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review has concluded that shea butter is safe as used in cosmetics. It is also a food: an ingredient in chocolate and a cooking fat in West Africa, and in the European Union it is one of six vegetable fats allowed to replace up to 5 percent of the cocoa butter in chocolate. Even people with tree-nut allergies rarely react to refined shea butter. There is no meaningful upper limit for use on the skin.

myths.claim: Shea butter clogs pores.
myths.consensus: It rates low on comedogenicity scales, though very heavy use can feel greasy on oily skin.

environment.notes: Shea trees grow wild and are not plantation-farmed; the trade provides income for millions of women in the Sahel.

synthesis.title: Traditional extraction
synthesis.summary: In West Africa, shea butter has been made by hand for centuries, mainly by women, who often work together in cooperatives. The shea tree grows wild across the Sahel, from Senegal to Sudan, and its nuts are gathered from the ground after the fruit falls. Making shea butter by hand is hard work that takes many hours. Much of the world's shea butter still passes through these women's hands. It is an important source of income in rural communities.
synthesis.mechanism: The fallen fruits are collected and their fleshy pulp is removed. The nuts are boiled, dried in the sun and cracked open to free the kernels inside. The kernels are roasted and ground into a thick paste, which the women knead by hand with water for a long time until the fat separates and rises to the surface as a creamy mass. The fat is skimmed off and boiled to drive off water and impurities. It is then filtered and left to cool and set into shea butter.
synthesis.significance: The shea trade provides income for millions of women in the Sahel, earning shea the nickname “women's gold”.

synthesis.title: Industrial refining
synthesis.summary: For cosmetics, chocolate and food, shea butter is often refined in factories. Refining removes its natural smell, yellowish color and impurities, producing a white, odorless fat. Industrial extraction can also use mechanical presses or solvents to recover more fat from the kernels. Refined shea butter is more consistent, but some of its beneficial unsaponifiable compounds may be reduced. Both refined and unrefined shea butter are sold.
synthesis.mechanism: Shea kernels are crushed and pressed in mechanical expellers, or the fat is dissolved out with a solvent such as hexane, which is then evaporated. The crude shea butter is refined in several steps. Free fatty acids are removed, and the fat is bleached with special clays that soak up pigments and impurities. It is then deodorized by passing steam through it at high temperature under vacuum, which carries away odor-causing molecules. Some shea butter is also fractionated, split into softer and harder portions for different uses.
synthesis.significance: In the EU, shea is one of six vegetable fats allowed in chocolate, up to 5%.

citations.title: Vegetable Butters and Oils as Therapeutically and Cosmetically Active Ingredients for Dermal Use: A Review of Clinical Studies.
citations.abstract: While the chemical composition of vegetable butters and oils has been studied in detail, there is limited knowledge about their mechanisms of action after application on the skin. To understand their dermal effects better, 27 clinical studies evaluating 17 vegetable oils (almond, argan, avocado, borage, coconut, evening primrose, kukui, marula, mustard, neem, olive, rapeseed, sacha inchi, safflower, shea butter, soybean and sunflower oils) were reviewed in this research. The reviewed studies focused on non-affected skin, infant skin, psoriasis, xerosis, UVB-induced erythema, atopic dermatitis, molluscum contagiosum, tungiasis, scars, striae and striae gravidarum. We conclude that in inflammation-affected skin, vegetable oils with a high content of oleic acid, together with the lack of or a low linoleic acid content, may cause additional structural damage of the stratum corneum, while oils high in linoleic acid and saturated fatty acids may express positive effects. Non-affected skin, in contrast, may not react negatively to oils high in oleic acid. However, the frequency and duration of an oil's use must be considered an important factor that may accelerate or enhance the negative effects on the skin's structural integrity.

citations.title: Distinct triterpene synthases in the laticifers of Euphorbia lathyris.
citations.abstract: Euphorbia lathyris was proposed about fifty years ago as a potential agroenergetic crop. The tremendous amounts of triterpenes present in its latex has driven investigations for transforming this particular biological fluid into an industrial hydrocarbon source. The huge accumulation of terpenes in the latex of many plant species represent a challenging question regarding cellular homeostasis. In fact, the enzymes, the mechanisms and the controllers that tune the amount of products accumulated in specialized compartments (to fulfill ecological roles) or deposited at important sites (as essential factors) are not known. Here, we have isolated oxidosqualene cyclases highly expressed in the latex of Euphorbia lathyris. This triterpene biosynthetic machinery is made of distinct paralogous enzymes responsible for the massive accumulation of steroidal and non-steroidal tetracyclic triterpenes. More than eighty years after the isolation of butyrospermol from shea butter (Heilbronn IM, Moffet GL, and Spring FS J. Chem. Soc. 1934, 1583), a butyrospermol synthase is characterized in this work using yeast and in folia heterologous expression assays.

citations.title: Complementary and alternative medicine treatments for common skin diseases: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
citations.abstract: Background: Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) treatments are growing in popularity as alternative treatments for common skin conditions. Objectives: To perform a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the tolerability and treatment response to CAM treatments in acne, atopic dermatitis (AD), and psoriasis. Methods: PubMed/Medline and Embase databases were searched to identify eligible studies measuring the effects of CAM in acne, AD, and psoriasis. Effect size with 95% confidence interval (CI) was estimated using the random-effect model. Results: The search yielded 417 articles; 40 studies met the inclusion criteria. The quantitative results of CAM treatment showed a standard mean difference (SMD) of 3.78 (95% CI [-0.01, 7.57]) and 0.58 (95% CI [-6.99, 8.15]) in the acne total lesion count, a SMD of -0.70 (95% CI [-1.19, -0.21]) in the eczema area and severity index score and a SMD of 0.94 (95% CI [-0.83, 2.71]) in the scoring of atopic dermatitis score for AD, and a SMD of 3.04 (95% CI [-0.35, 6.43]) and 5.16 (95% CI [-0.52, 10.85]) in the Psoriasis Area Severity Index score for psoriasis. Limitations: Differences between the study designs, sample sizes, outcome measures, and treatment durations limit the generalizability of data. Conclusions: Based on our quantitative findings we conclude that there is insufficient evidence to support the efficacy and the recommendation of CAM for acne, AD, and psoriasis.

citations.title: Heptapeptide-loaded solid lipid nanoparticles for cosmetic anti-aging applications.
citations.abstract: The cosmetic industry requires more and more expensive actives and ingredients such as retinol, coenzyme Q10, proteins, peptides and biotechnologically produced molecules. In this study, we demonstrate the development of a cost effective formulation of a nanostructured lipid carrier (NLC) or solid lipid nanoparticles (SLN) improving peptide delivery into skin. NLC or SLN are very suitable vehicles for the delivery of active ingredients into skin. The SLN, produced by using hot high pressure homogenization method combine advantages such as physical stability, protection of incorporated labile actives and controlled release. By the used method we dispersed the amorphous heptapeptide DEETGEF in shea butter and homogenized this pre-dispersion at 60°C together with the water phase using a Microfluidizer at 1000bar. The analysis of the obtained SLN-P7 showed a particle size of 173nm, incorporated peptide of 0.014%, entrapment efficiency of 90.8%, melting peak (DSC) of the core lipid of 27°C and a zeta potential of -54mV. By an ex vivo study with skin explants we could stimulate NQO1 (NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase), HMOX1 (Heme oxygenase-1) and PRDX1 (Peroxiredoxin-1) genes all of which are cell protecting enzymes. In a multicellular protection against UV induced stress study with skin explants we detected the formation of sun burn cells and the number and morphology of Langerhans cells. The application of our SLN-P7 formulation on skin explants led to a significant and dose dependent protection against UV irradiation. In the clinical suction blister study, irradiation with UVA light for two hours after final product application led to a statistically significant increase of the 8-OhdG (8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine) concentration in the human epidermis. The skin treated with our verum formulation showed a statistically significant 20% decrease in DNA damage compared to placebo. In conclusion, it was demonstrated that SLN technology enabled peptide delivery into skin allowing it to perform protective functions.

name: Disodium EDTA
scoreRationale: Safe at cosmetic and food levels, but poorly biodegradable, persisting in waterways and mobilizing heavy metals.
summary: EDTA traps metal ions so products stay stable and preservatives work better. Safe for people, but it lingers in the environment.

physical.phStability: Stable; binding strength depends on pH

overview: EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is built from two nitrogen atoms and four acetate arms. Disodium EDTA is its salt with two of the four acid groups neutralized.

In solution, EDTA wraps around a metal ion using six binding sites at once (two nitrogens and four carboxylates), forming an exceptionally stable cage-like complex called a chelate. It grabs calcium, magnesium, iron and copper, metals that would otherwise discolor products, weaken preservatives or speed spoilage.
profile.function: Binds calcium, magnesium and trace metals to prevent rancidity, color changes and scum, and boosts preservatives and cleaners.

mechanisms.title: Locking up metal ions
mechanisms.chemical: EDTA has six atoms that can bond to a metal ion: two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms from its carboxylate groups. When it meets a metal ion, the EDTA molecule wraps around it and forms six bonds at once, arranged in an octahedral shape like a cage. A molecule that grabs a metal ion from several points is called a chelator, from the Greek word for claw. Because one EDTA molecule holds on from six points, the complex is far more stable than if six separate molecules each formed one bond. Chemists call this the chelate effect.
mechanisms.biological: Metal ions such as iron and copper speed up oxidation, which makes oils go rancid, colors fade and fragrances change. Calcium and magnesium from hard water react with soap to form scum and reduce cleaning power. By locking these metal ions away, EDTA prevents all of these problems. Products stay stable, clear and effective for longer. That is why EDTA turns up in shampoos, soaps, creams and some foods, such as canned beans and mayonnaise.

mechanisms.title: Boosting preservatives
mechanisms.chemical: Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane coated with molecules called lipopolysaccharides (LPS), which are held together partly by calcium and magnesium ions that bridge neighboring LPS molecules. These bridges keep the outer membrane tight and resistant to many chemicals. EDTA grabs those calcium and magnesium ions and pulls them out of the membrane. Without the bridges, LPS molecules come loose, and the outer membrane becomes disorganized and leaky. It is like removing the mortar from a brick wall.
mechanisms.biological: With a leaky outer membrane, Gram-negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas and E. coli become much more vulnerable to preservatives that would otherwise struggle to get in. That means lower concentrations of preservative can protect a product. This teamwork matters because Gram-negative bacteria are among the most common contaminants of cosmetics. EDTA isn't a strong antimicrobial on its own, but it greatly boosts other preservatives. That is why it is called a preservative booster.

mechanisms.title: Treating lead poisoning
mechanisms.chemical: EDTA binds different metals with different strengths, and it holds lead much more tightly than calcium. In calcium disodium EDTA, each EDTA molecule is already holding a calcium ion. When it meets lead in the body, the lead pushes the calcium out, because EDTA prefers lead. The result is a lead–EDTA complex that is very stable and dissolves in water. Using the calcium form stops EDTA from pulling calcium out of the blood.
mechanisms.biological: The lead–EDTA complex is filtered out by the kidneys and leaves the body in urine, taking the lead with it. This treatment, called chelation therapy, is used under medical supervision for people with high blood lead levels, which can damage the brain, nerves and kidneys. It is especially important for children, whose developing brains are vulnerable to lead. Giving the wrong form, disodium EDTA instead of calcium disodium EDTA, has caused deaths by dangerously lowering blood calcium. Chelation therapy is used only for confirmed metal poisoning, not as a general “detox.”

reactions.title: Chelation
reactions.summary: Chelation is a reaction in which one molecule binds a metal ion from several points at once. EDTA is one of the most powerful chelators known, gripping a metal ion through six atoms. The reaction is fast and forms a very stable complex. It is the basis of EDTA's uses in cosmetics, food, medicine and laboratories. Chemists even use EDTA to measure how much calcium and magnesium are in water, which is what “water hardness” means.

steps.name: Deprotonation
steps.text: EDTA has four carboxylic acid groups, each of which can release a hydrogen ion (H⁺). In solution, especially at neutral or higher pH, these groups lose their protons and become negatively charged carboxylates. Disodium EDTA has already lost two of them.

steps.name: Wrapping
steps.text: When EDTA meets a metal ion such as calcium (Ca²⁺), its two nitrogen atoms and four carboxylate oxygens close around the metal, forming six bonds. The molecule folds into a cage that surrounds the ion completely. The metal is now trapped.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: As the remaining acid groups bind to the metal, they release their protons into the solution, which becomes slightly more acidic. The finished complex carries an overall negative charge.

reactions.result: Chelation is why EDTA is used in blood-collection tubes: removing calcium stops the blood from clotting, so the sample can be tested. It is also the basis of a lab method called complexometric titration, used to measure water hardness.

reactions.title: Synthesis
reactions.summary: EDTA is made in chemical plants from three main starting materials: ethylenediamine, formaldehyde and sodium cyanide. The process attaches four acetate arms to ethylenediamine's two nitrogen atoms. It uses a type of reaction related to the Strecker synthesis, a classic method for making amino acids. The process gives tetrasodium EDTA, which can be partly acidified to make disodium EDTA. Large amounts are made every year for industrial and consumer uses.

steps.name: Addition
steps.text: Ethylenediamine, a small molecule with two amine groups (–NH₂), reacts with formaldehyde and sodium cyanide in water. Each of the four hydrogen atoms on its two nitrogens is replaced by a –CH₂CN group, a carbon attached to a cyanide group. This is a Strecker-type reaction.

steps.name: Hydrolysis
steps.text: The cyanide groups (–CN), called nitriles, are hydrolyzed in a basic solution. Water attacks each carbon–nitrogen triple bond, turning the nitrile into a carboxylate group (–COO⁻) and releasing ammonia. The product is tetrasodium EDTA.

steps.name: Adjustment
steps.text: Tetrasodium EDTA is partly acidified, turning two of its four carboxylate groups back into carboxylic acids. This gives disodium EDTA, which is crystallized and dried.

reactions.result: Four acetate arms are added in one process, creating the six-armed chelator. The ammonia released is captured and reused or removed.
reactions.equation: H2NCH2CH2NH2 + 4 CH2O + 4 NaCN + 4 H2O → Na4EDTA + 4 NH3

regulatory.status: Safe as used.
Calcium disodium EDTA permitted in foods with limits.
ADI 0–2.5 mg/kg body weight (as calcium disodium EDTA).

hazards.title: Low toxicity in products
hazards.summary: Disodium EDTA is considered safe at the concentrations used in cosmetics and foods. It is poorly absorbed through both the skin and the gut, so very little reaches the bloodstream from these sources. Concerns arise mainly with intravenous use in medicine, where it can lower blood calcium. Environmentally, EDTA is a concern because it breaks down slowly and can carry metals around in waterways. In everyday products, it poses very little risk to people.
hazards.chemical: EDTA's strongly charged structure makes it hard for it to cross the fatty layers of the skin and the gut lining; only about 5 percent or less of a swallowed dose is absorbed. When EDTA does reach the blood in large amounts, it binds calcium and magnesium and lowers the levels of these free ions available to the body. The body doesn't break EDTA down, so any absorbed EDTA leaves unchanged in urine. In the environment, it also resists breakdown by bacteria. That persistence is the main environmental worry.
hazards.biological: Calcium is essential for nerve and muscle function, including the heartbeat. When EDTA lowers blood calcium quickly, as can happen with intravenous disodium EDTA, it can cause muscle spasms, an irregular heartbeat and, in extreme cases, cardiac arrest. That is why chelation therapy is done only under medical supervision with the safer calcium disodium form. At cosmetic and food levels, none of this happens. Environmental concerns have led some manufacturers to switch to biodegradable alternatives.

profile.dosage: Cosmetics typically contain about 0.05 to 0.2 percent disodium EDTA. In foods, calcium disodium EDTA is used in small amounts in products such as mayonnaise, salad dressings and canned foods to prevent spoilage and discoloration. International experts (JECFA) have set an acceptable daily intake of 2.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight for calcium disodium EDTA. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review has concluded that EDTA salts are safe in cosmetics at current levels. Medical chelation therapy uses much higher doses, and only under supervision.

myths.claim: EDTA is a penetration enhancer that drags toxins into your body.
myths.consensus: At cosmetic levels it has minimal effect on skin penetration.

environment.persistence: Persistent; one of the most abundant synthetic chemicals in European surface waters.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Low direct toxicity, but it can remobilize heavy metals from sediments.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: EDTA was first developed in 1935 by the German chemist Ferdinand Münz, who was looking for a substitute for citric acid in textile dyeing, where metal ions in the water interfered with dyes. Today it is made from ethylenediamine, formaldehyde and sodium cyanide. It is one of the most widely used chelating agents in the world. It goes into detergents, papermaking, photography, medicine, food and cosmetics. Most is produced as tetrasodium EDTA.
synthesis.mechanism: Ethylenediamine is reacted with formaldehyde and sodium cyanide in water under carefully controlled conditions. The reaction attaches a –CH₂CN group to each of the four nitrogen–hydrogen positions. As the reaction continues in the basic solution, the nitrile groups are hydrolyzed into carboxylate groups, releasing ammonia gas, which is removed. The product is tetrasodium EDTA. To make disodium EDTA, the tetrasodium form is partly acidified, and the disodium salt is crystallized and dried.
synthesis.significance: Because EDTA breaks down so slowly in nature, chemists have developed biodegradable chelators such as GLDA and MGDA to replace it in some products.

citations.title: The subcellular distribution and storage form of renin in human kidney cortex.
citations.abstract: An assay with the cation exchange resin Dowex 50 WX2 was developed and validated for the measurement of renin activity in subcellular fractions of kidney cortex. After differential centrifugation, renin was found predominantly in the soluble (SOL) fraction (70%) and to a lesser extent in the heavy mitochondrial (HM) extract (17%). Neither acid pH nor trypsin treatment increased renin activity in these fractions. Discontinuous and continuous sucrose concentration gradients were used to partially resolve renin-containing organelles in the granular moiety from marker enzymes for mitochondria, lysosomes, plasma membranes and peroxisomes. The molecular weight (MW) of renin in both the SOL and HM was approximately 45 000. No acid or trypsin-activatable forms of renin were found after gel filtration of these extracts. When renal cortical tissue was extracted in the presence of the proteolytic enzyme inhibitors N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), aprotinin, phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), benzamidine and pepstatin, renin activity was not increased by added trypsin. After gel filtration of the homogenates, the MW of renin activity was 45 000. Protease inhibitors did not appear to preserve high molecular weight (HMW) forms and no trypsin-activatable renin was found. These results suggest that in man renal renin is stored within mechanically fragile granules and that the major storage form is of low molecular weight (LMW).

citations.title: Methemoglobin reduction by NADH-cytochrome b(5) reductase in Propsilocerus akamusi larvae.
citations.journal: Comp Biochem Physiol B Biochem Mol Biol
citations.abstract: For oxygen respiration, a methemoglobin (metHb) reduction system is needed in the cell because metHb cannot bind oxygen. We examined the insect Propsilocerus akamusi larvae to elucidate the metHb reduction system in an organism that inhabits an oxygen-deficient environment. NADH-dependent reduction of metHb in coelomic fluid suggested the coexistence of cytochrome b5 reductase (b5R) and cytochrome b5 with hemoglobin in the fluid and that these proteins were involved in physiological metHb reduction in the larvae. The presence of b5R was revealed by purifying b5R to homogeneity from the midge larvae. Using purified components, we showed that larval metHb was reduced via the NADH-b5R (FAD)-cytochrome b5-metHb pathway, a finding consistent with that in aerobic vertebrates, specifically humans and rabbits, and b5R function between mammal and insect was conserved. b5R was identified as a monomeric FAD-containing enzyme; it had a molecular mass of 33.2 kDa in gel-filtration chromatography and approximately 37 kDa in SDS-PAGE analysis. The enzyme's optimal pH and temperature were 6.4 and 25 °C, respectively. The apparent Km and Vmax values were 345 μM and 160 μmol min(-1) mg(-1), respectively, for ferricyanide and 328 μM and 500 μmol min(-1) mg(-1), respectively, for 2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol. The enzyme reaction was inhibited by benzoate, p-hydroxymercuribenzoate, iodoacetamide, and iodoacetate, and was not inhibited by metal ions or EDTA.

citations.title: EDTA and Salts.
citations.abstract: The Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety reviewed newly available studies since their original assessment in 1998, along with updated information regarding product types and concentrations of use and confirmed that EDTA and certain salts are safe as cosmetic ingredients in the practices of use and concentration as described in this report.

citations.title: Propofol: therapeutic indications and side-effects.
citations.abstract: Propofol (2, 6-diisopropylphenol) is a potent intravenous hypnotic agent which is widely used for the induction and maintenance of anesthesia and for sedation in the intensive care unit. Propofol is an oil at room temperature and insoluble in aqueous solution. Present formulations consists of 1% or 2% (w/v) propofol, 10% soybean oil, 2.25% glycerol, and 1.2% egg phosphatide. Disodium edetate (EDTA) or metabisulfite is added to retard bacterial and fungal growth. Propofol is a global central nervous system depressant. It directly activates GABA(A) receptors. In addition, propofol inhibits the NMDA receptor and modulates calcium influx through slow calcium ion channels. Propofol has a rapid onset of action with a dose-related hypnotic effect. Recovery is rapid even after prolonged use. Propofol decreases cerebral oxygen consumption, reduces intracranial pressure and has potent anti-convulsant properties. It is a potent antioxidant, has anti-inflammatory properties and is a bronchodilator. As a consequence of these properties propofol is being increasingly used in the management of traumatic head injury, status epilepticus, delirium tremens, status asthmaticus and in critically ill septic patients. Propofol has a remarkable safety profile. Dose dependent hypotension is the commonest complication; particularly in volume depleted patients. Hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis are uncommon complications. Allergic complications, which may include bronchospasm, have been reported with the formulation containing metabisulfite. In addition, this formulation has been demonstrated to result in the generation of oxygen free radicals. High dose propofol infusions have been associated with the "propofol syndrome"; this is a potentially fatal complication characterized by severe metabolic acidosis and circulatory collapse. This is a rare complication first reported in pediatric patients and believed to be due to decreased transmembrane electrical potential and alteration of electron transport across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

citations.title: Biodegradation of EDTA.
citations.abstract: The chelating agent ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA) is not degraded by conventional biological and physicochemical methods for the treatment of wastewater and the purification of drinking water. Of the measurable organic compounds it is the one present at the highest concentration in many surface and drinking waters. In recent years, however, studies have demonstrated that EDTA can be degraded by specially enriched bacterial cultures and in wastewater treatment plants receiving EDTA-containing effluents. The amounts of EDTA released into the aquatic environment could thus be reduced by establishing appropriate biological wastewater treatment plants. This article describes the degradation of EDTA and its metal chelates by different bacterial cultures, catabolic steps in EDTA degradation, and biological methods for the removal of this chelating agent from wastewaters.
