name: Oxybenzone
scoreRationale: Absorbed into the body well above FDA's threshold, a known photoallergen, restricted in the EU and banned in Hawaii over coral concerns.
summary: Oxybenzone is a chemical sunscreen filter. It works, but it's absorbed into the body, can cause allergies, and is linked to coral reef harm.

physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in oils

overview: Oxybenzone (benzophenone-3) is two benzene rings joined by a carbonyl group (a ketone), with a hydroxyl group and a methoxy group on one ring. The –OH sits next to the carbonyl, forming an internal hydrogen bond that is key to how the molecule handles UV light.

It absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA and was one of the first broader-spectrum chemical filters. But it's absorbed through skin into the bloodstream, can cause photoallergies and has been linked to harm in corals, so its use is now restricted in several places.
profile.function: Absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA radiation in sunscreens and protects products from UV degradation.

mechanisms.title: Turning UV into heat
mechanisms.chemical: Oxybenzone has two benzene rings joined by a carbonyl group (C=O), forming a conjugated system that absorbs ultraviolet light. One ring carries a hydroxyl group (–OH) right next to the carbonyl, and the two are linked by an internal hydrogen bond. When the molecule absorbs a UV photon, that energy makes the hydrogen jump from the hydroxyl oxygen to the carbonyl oxygen in femtoseconds, a process called excited-state intramolecular proton transfer. This briefly rearranges the molecule into an unstable form. The molecule then relaxes, the hydrogen jumps back, and the absorbed energy is released as heat.
mechanisms.biological: By converting UV energy into harmless heat, oxybenzone keeps UV light from reaching skin cells and damaging their DNA. It absorbs UVB, which causes sunburn, and short-wavelength UVA, which contributes to skin aging and cancer. The tiny amount of heat released is negligible. Because the molecule returns to its original form, it can repeat the cycle many times. It still breaks down gradually in sunlight, though, so sunscreens need reapplying.

mechanisms.title: Absorption into the body
mechanisms.chemical: Oxybenzone is a small, fairly fat-soluble molecule, so it can pass through the fatty layers of the skin's outer barrier into the deeper layers, where blood vessels carry it away. Once in the bloodstream, it travels throughout the body. The liver converts some of it into other molecules, such as benzophenone-1, and attaches sugars to some of it to help excretion. It leaves the body mainly in urine. National surveys have found oxybenzone in the urine of most people tested.
mechanisms.biological: In clinical trials run by the U.S. FDA in 2019 and 2020, people who applied sunscreen as directed had oxybenzone levels in their blood hundreds of times higher than the threshold at which the FDA asks for additional safety testing. That doesn't mean it is harmful, only that more study is needed. Oxybenzone has also been found in breast milk and amniotic fluid. Its long-term health effects in people aren't fully known. The FDA has asked manufacturers for more safety data.

mechanisms.title: Hormone activity in lab studies
mechanisms.chemical: Oxybenzone and its breakdown product benzophenone-1 have shapes that let them bind weakly to estrogen receptors, the proteins that respond to estrogen hormones. They can also block androgen receptors, which respond to male hormones such as testosterone. In laboratory tests on cells, they produce weak hormone-like effects. Benzophenone-1 is more active than oxybenzone itself in these tests. The binding is much weaker than that of the body's own hormones.
mechanisms.biological: In animal studies using high doses of oxybenzone, researchers have seen effects on reproductive organs and hormone levels. Some observational studies in people have hinted at links between oxybenzone exposure and changes in hormone levels or birth outcomes, but studies like these can't prove cause and effect. The animal doses were often much higher than what people get from sunscreen. Overall, how much these findings matter for people is uncertain. Some choose mineral sunscreens as a precaution.

reactions.title: Excited-state proton transfer
reactions.summary: Oxybenzone protects against UV through a remarkable molecular trick called excited-state intramolecular proton transfer (ESIPT). When it absorbs light, a proton shifts within the molecule, letting the absorbed energy be released safely. The whole cycle takes less than a trillionth of a second. This lets one molecule absorb many photons without being destroyed. Many UV filters, and some natural molecules, use similar tricks.

steps.name: Absorption
steps.text: Oxybenzone's conjugated rings and carbonyl group absorb a UV photon. The energy lifts an electron to a higher energy level, putting the molecule into an excited state. In that state its electrons are rearranged.

steps.name: Proton hop
steps.text: In the excited state, the carbonyl oxygen becomes more attractive to protons and the hydroxyl oxygen less so. The proton on the –OH group, already hydrogen-bonded to the carbonyl, jumps across to the carbonyl oxygen in femtoseconds.

steps.name: Relaxation
steps.text: The rearranged molecule quickly sheds its extra energy as heat by vibrating, settling back into its lowest-energy state. The proton then jumps back to where it started. The molecule is restored and ready to absorb another photon.

reactions.result: Because the molecule resets itself, one oxybenzone molecule can absorb many photons, although it still degrades slowly in sunlight. That is why sunscreens containing it need to be reapplied, typically every two hours.

reactions.title: Synthesis
reactions.summary: Oxybenzone is made in chemical plants in two main steps. The first builds a benzophenone with two hydroxyl groups, using resorcinol and benzotrichloride. The second converts one of those hydroxyl groups into a methoxy group while leaving the other alone. The key is to keep the hydroxyl group next to the carbonyl, because that is essential for UV protection. The product is a pale yellow powder.

steps.name: Acylation
steps.text: Resorcinol, a benzene ring with two –OH groups, reacts with benzotrichloride, a benzene ring carrying three chlorine atoms on one carbon. In the presence of water, the trichloride behaves like an acid chloride and attaches a benzoyl group to resorcinol's ring. This forms 2,4-dihydroxybenzophenone.

steps.name: Selective methylation
steps.text: 2,4-Dihydroxybenzophenone has two –OH groups. The one at position 4, away from the carbonyl, is more reactive, while the one at position 2 is held in place by its hydrogen bond to the carbonyl. A methylating agent such as dimethyl sulfate converts the 4-hydroxyl into a methoxy group (–OCH₃).

steps.name: Purification
steps.text: The crude product is crystallized to remove leftover starting materials and byproducts, such as molecules in which both –OH groups were methylated. The result is pure oxybenzone.

reactions.result: Leaving the –OH next to the carbonyl untouched preserves the internal hydrogen bond that makes it a UV filter. If both –OH groups were methylated, the molecule would no longer protect against UV effectively.

regulatory.status: Not yet generally recognized as safe and effective; more data requested.
Restricted.
regulatory.limit: 6% in face, hand and body products; 0.5% in other products

regulatory.status: Sale of sunscreens with oxybenzone and octinoxate banned since 2021.

hazards.title: Photoallergy
hazards.summary: Oxybenzone is one of the most common causes of allergic reactions to sunscreen. These reactions are often photoallergies, meaning they happen only when the skin is exposed to both oxybenzone and sunlight. The American Contact Dermatitis Society named benzophenones Allergen of the Year in 2014. Photoallergy can be confusing, because people may think they are reacting to the sun itself. Patch testing combined with a dose of UV light, called photopatch testing, can identify the cause.
hazards.chemical: When oxybenzone absorbs UV light, it normally releases the energy safely as heat. Occasionally, though, a molecule is converted into a reactive form or breakdown product. That reactive molecule can bond to proteins in the skin, acting as a hapten. The modified proteins are then recognized as foreign by the immune system. Because UV light is needed to create the reactive form, the allergy shows up only on sun-exposed skin.
hazards.biological: In sensitized people, putting on oxybenzone sunscreen and then going into the sun causes an itchy, red, sometimes blistering rash, usually one to two days later. The rash is limited to skin that was both covered in sunscreen and exposed to sunlight, such as the face, neck and arms. Some people also react without sunlight, as an ordinary contact allergy. Switching to sunscreens without oxybenzone, such as mineral sunscreens, usually solves the problem. Dermatologists can confirm the cause with photopatch testing.

hazards.title: Coral reef concerns
hazards.summary: In 2018, Hawaii became the first U.S. state to pass a law banning the sale of sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate to protect coral reefs, and the ban took effect in 2021. Other places, including the U.S. Virgin Islands and the Pacific nation of Palau, have passed similar restrictions. The concern comes from laboratory studies showing that oxybenzone can harm corals. Scientists debate how much real-world sunscreen pollution matters compared with major threats such as ocean warming. Still, many beachgoers now choose reef-friendly sunscreens.
hazards.chemical: When people swim or shower with sunscreen on, oxybenzone washes off into the water. Near crowded beaches, oxybenzone in coastal water can reach measurable, though usually very low, concentrations. Corals can absorb it into their tissue. In sunlight, oxybenzone inside corals can be converted into reactive products, some of them attached to sugars, that may be toxic to coral cells. These reactions may increase oxidative stress in the coral.
hazards.biological: Laboratory studies have found that oxybenzone can damage the DNA of coral larvae, deform their growth and promote coral bleaching, in which corals expel the algae living in their tissues that give them color and food. Bleached corals are more likely to die. However, many of these studies used higher concentrations than are found on most reefs. Ocean warming, pollution and overfishing are considered far greater threats to coral reefs. Restrictions on oxybenzone are seen as a precaution.

profile.dosage: In the United States, sunscreens may contain up to 6 percent oxybenzone; in the European Union it is limited to 6 percent in face and hand products and 2.2 percent in body products and sprays. Applying sunscreen generously over the whole body, as recommended, leads to measurable absorption into the blood, and the U.S. FDA has asked for more safety data. People with sunscreen allergies or concerns about absorption can choose mineral sunscreens with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide. Several places, including Hawaii, restrict its sale to protect coral reefs. Despite these questions, wearing sunscreen remains far safer than unprotected sun exposure.

myths.claim: Because of oxybenzone, sunscreen is more dangerous than sun.
myths.consensus: UV causes skin cancer; mineral or newer filters offer protection without oxybenzone.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic to coral larvae and algae in laboratory studies.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Oxybenzone is made in chemical plants from resorcinol, a petroleum-derived chemical. It was one of the first broader-spectrum UV filters, coming into wide use in sunscreens in the 1980s. Before then, sunscreens mainly protected against UVB, which causes sunburn. Oxybenzone extended protection into part of the UVA range. It is also used in plastics, paints and nail polish to keep them from fading in sunlight.
synthesis.mechanism: Resorcinol is reacted with benzotrichloride, which attaches a benzoyl group to the resorcinol ring, forming 2,4-dihydroxybenzophenone. This intermediate has two –OH groups on one ring. It is then treated with a methylating agent, such as dimethyl sulfate or methyl chloride, under carefully controlled conditions that selectively convert the –OH at position 4 into a methoxy group. The –OH at position 2, held by its hydrogen bond to the carbonyl, is left alone. The crude oxybenzone is purified by crystallization.
synthesis.significance: Mineral filters (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) and newer organic filters offer protection without oxybenzone.

citations.title: Melatonin protects against oxybenzone-induced deterioration of mouse oocytes during maturation.
citations.abstract: Oxybenzone (OBZ), an ultraviolet light filter that is widely used in sunscreens and cosmetics, is an emerging contaminant found in humans and the environment. Recent studies have shown that OBZ has been detected in women's plasma, urine, and breast milk. However, the effects of OBZ exposure on oocyte meiosis have not been addressed. In this study, we investigated the detrimental effects of OBZ on oocyte maturation and the protective roles of melatonin (MT) in OBZ-exposed mouse models. Our in vitro and in vivo results showed that OBZ suppressed oocyte maturation, while MT attenuated the meiotic defects induced by OBZ. In addition, OBZ facilitated H3K4 demethylation by increasing the expression of the Kdm5 family of genes, elevating ROS levels, decreasing GSH, impairing mitochondrial quality, and disrupting spindle configuration in oocytes. However, MT treatment resulted in significant protection against OBZ-induced damage during oocyte maturation and improved oocyte quality. The mechanisms underlying the beneficial roles of MT involved reduction of oxidative stress, inhibition of apoptosis, restoration of abnormal spindle assembly and up-regulation of H3K4me3. Collectively, our results suggest that MT protects against defects induced by OBZ during mouse oocyte maturation in vitro and in vivo.

citations.title: Sunscreens: UV filters to protect us: Part 2-Increasing awareness of UV filters and their potential toxicities to us and our environment.
citations.abstract: Background: Sunscreens are topical preparations containing one or more compounds that filter, block, reflect, scatter, or absorb ultraviolet (UV) light. Part 2 of this review focuses on the environmental, ecological effects and human toxicities that have been attributed to UV filters. Methods: Literature review using NIH databases (eg, PubMed and Medline), FDA and EPA databases, Google Scholar, the Federal Register, and the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). Limitations: This was a retrospective literature review that involved many different types of studies across a variety of species. Comparison between reports is limited by variations in methodology and criteria for toxicity. Conclusions: In vivo and in vitro studies on the environmental and biological effects of UV filters show a wide array of unanticipated adverse effects on the environment and exposed organisms. Coral bleaching receives considerable attention from the lay press, but the scientific literature identifies potential toxicities of endocrine, neurologic, neoplastic and developmental pathways. These effects harm a vast array of aquatic and marine biota, while almost no data supports human toxicity at currently used quantities (with the exception of contact allergy). Much of these data are from experimental studies or field observations; more controlled environmental studies and long-term human use data are limited. Several jurisdictions have prohibited specific UV filters, but this does not adequately address the dichotomy of the benefits of photoprotection vs lack of eco-friendly, safe, and FDA-approved alternatives.

citations.title: Sunscreen Safety and Efficacy for the Prevention of Cutaneous Neoplasm.
citations.abstract: Sunscreen is widely used for ultraviolet radiation protection. Studies validate sun protection factors (SPFs) to prevent ultraviolet (UV)-induced skin changes such as melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Few studies examine sunscreen's impact on endocrine and immune system dysregulation, the production of radical oxygen species, and whether the ingredients deteriorate under prolonged exposure. We present an investigation of sunscreen labels and how ingredients impact sun safety and human health. A review of the literature was conducted using Embase and PubMed to examine sunscreen safety, efficacy, and use to prevent UV-induced skin damage. Increasing sunscreen reapplication, wearing protective clothing, and limiting exposure can reduce the incidence of skin cancer. Inorganic sunscreens form barriers to block UV light, but without titanium dioxide (TiO2), they may not be advantageous due to their low UVA protection. Organic sunscreens absorb into the skin and provide a better feeling after application. Octocrylene and avobenzone are stable and provide UVA and UVB protection with minimal adverse effects. Oxybenzone is harmful to the neuroendocrine system and should be avoided. Titanium dioxide works for broad-spectrum UV protection and offers minimal adverse effects. Octocrylene and avobenzone are organic sunscreen ingredients that also provide a better feeling on the skin after application, which enables higher rates of use. Oxybenzone should be avoided.

citations.title: Dermatological and environmental toxicological impact of the sunscreen ingredient oxybenzone/benzophenone-3.
citations.abstract: Oxybenzone (Benzophenone-3) is an emerging human and environmental contaminant used in sunscreens and personal care products to help minimize the damaging effects of ultraviolet radiation. The Center for Disease Control fourth national report on human exposure to environmental chemicals demonstrated that approximately 97% of the people tested have oxybenzone present in their urine, and independent scientists have reported various concentrations in waterways and fish worldwide. Oxybenzone can also react with chlorine, producing hazardous by-products that can concentrate in swimming pools and wastewater treatment plants. Moreover, adverse reactions could very well be increased by the closed loop of ingesting fish contaminated with oxybenzone and/or washing the ingredient off our bodies and having it return in drinking water as treatment plants do not effectively remove the chemical as part of their processing protocols. In humans, oxybenzone has been reported to produce contact and photocontact allergy reactions, implemented as a possible endocrine disruptor and has been linked to Hirschsprung's disease. Environmentally, oxybenzone has been shown to produce a variety of toxic reactions in coral and fish ranging from reef bleaching to mortality. Lastly, with the rise in skin cancer rates and the availability of more effective sunscreen actives such as micronized zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, serious doubts about the relative prevention benefit of personal care products containing oxybenzone must be raised and compared with the potential negative health and environmental effects caused by the accumulation of this and other chemicals in the ecosystem.

citations.title: Sunscreens part 2: Regulation and safety.
citations.authors: Abdel Azim, Bainvoll, Vecerek et al.
citations.abstract: The second part of this CME article discusses sunscreen regulation and safety considerations for humans and the environment. First, we provide an overview of the history of the US Food and Drug Administration's regulation of sunscreen. Recent Food and Drug Administration studies clearly demonstrate that organic ultraviolet filters are systemically absorbed during routine sunscreen use, but to date there is no evidence of associated negative health effects. We also review the current evidence of sunscreen's association with vitamin D levels and frontal fibrosing alopecia, and recent concerns regarding benzene contamination. Finally, we review the possible environmental effects of ultraviolet filters, particularly coral bleaching. While climate change has been shown to be the primary driver of coral bleaching, laboratory-based studies suggest that organic ultraviolet filters represent an additional contributing factor, which led several localities to ban certain organic filters.

name: Sodium Hypochlorite
scoreRationale: A highly effective disinfectant, but corrosive to skin, eyes and lungs, and dangerous when mixed with acids or ammonia.
summary: Bleach kills germs and whitens by oxidation. Use it diluted, ventilated, and never mix it with ammonia or acidic cleaners.

physical.state: Pale greenish-yellow liquid (3–8% in household bleach)
physical.phStability: Alkaline (pH 11–13); decomposes with heat, light and acid

overview: Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) is a salt of hypochlorous acid. In the hypochlorite ion, chlorine is bonded to oxygen in the +1 oxidation state, which makes it hungry for electrons: a strong oxidizing agent.

Household bleach is a 3–8% solution kept alkaline (pH 11–13) with a little sodium hydroxide for stability. When diluted, part of the hypochlorite becomes hypochlorous acid (HOCl), the form that actually kills microbes, and the same molecule your white blood cells use to destroy bacteria.
profile.function: Disinfects surfaces and water, removes stains and mildew, and whitens laundry.

mechanisms.title: Killing microbes by oxidation
mechanisms.chemical: When bleach is diluted in water, part of the hypochlorite (OCl⁻) picks up a hydrogen ion and becomes hypochlorous acid (HOCl). HOCl is small and carries no electric charge, so it can slip through the fatty membranes of bacteria and the outer layers of viruses. Once inside, it acts as a strong oxidizing agent, meaning it grabs electrons from other molecules. It oxidizes the thiol groups (–SH) in proteins, attaches chlorine atoms to amino groups and damages the bases of DNA. These reactions happen fast and hit many targets at once.
mechanisms.biological: When their proteins are oxidized and chlorinated, bacteria and viruses stop working. Proteins unfold and clump together, enzymes shut down and membranes are damaged. At the correct dilution, bleach kills most bacteria and viruses within seconds to minutes, which is why it is used to disinfect surfaces, drinking water and swimming pools. Because it attacks so many targets at once, microbes find it very hard to become resistant. Dirt and organic matter use bleach up, though, so surfaces should be cleaned before they are disinfected.

mechanisms.title: Whitening stains
mechanisms.chemical: Many stains, such as those from wine, coffee, grass or fruit, contain colored molecules called chromophores. Chromophores have long chains of alternating single and double bonds, called conjugated systems, that absorb particular wavelengths of visible light, which is what gives them color. Hypochlorite, a strong oxidizer, attacks these double bonds, adding oxygen or chlorine atoms and breaking the long chains into shorter pieces. Shorter conjugated systems absorb ultraviolet rather than visible light. So the molecules lose their color.
mechanisms.biological: Once stain molecules stop absorbing visible light, they become colorless and the fabric looks white again. The stain molecules are still there; they are just invisible. That is why bleach works so well on white cotton. Bleach also attacks the dyes in colored fabrics, causing fading, and it can weaken fibers made of protein, such as wool and silk. Always check the care label before bleaching clothes.

mechanisms.title: Your immune system's bleach
mechanisms.chemical: White blood cells called neutrophils contain an enzyme called myeloperoxidase. It combines hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), which neutrophils make, with chloride ions (Cl⁻), which are abundant in the body, to produce hypochlorous acid (HOCl). That is the very same active molecule that forms when household bleach is diluted. Neutrophils store myeloperoxidase in small compartments called granules. When they need it, the granules release it.
mechanisms.biological: When neutrophils swallow bacteria, they trap them inside a small compartment called a phagosome. The neutrophil then fills the phagosome with a burst of reactive molecules, hypochlorous acid among them, a process called the oxidative or respiratory burst. The hypochlorous acid oxidizes the bacteria's proteins and membranes and kills them. This is one of the immune system's most powerful weapons against infection. Myeloperoxidase is also what gives pus its greenish tint.

reactions.title: The hypochlorous acid equilibrium
reactions.summary: Bleach's power to disinfect depends strongly on pH, because hypochlorite exists in two forms: the hypochlorite ion (OCl⁻) and hypochlorous acid (HOCl). The two are in equilibrium, constantly converting back and forth, with the balance set by pH. Hypochlorous acid is by far the more powerful disinfectant, killing bacteria something like 80 to 100 times faster. The hypochlorite ion, however, is more stable in storage. This balance explains how bleach is sold and how it should be used.

steps.name: Dilution
steps.text: Household bleach is sold at a high pH, around 11 to 13, thanks to a little sodium hydroxide. When it is diluted with water, the pH drops toward neutral. That shifts the balance between the two forms.

steps.name: Protonation
steps.text: As the pH falls, hypochlorite ions pick up hydrogen ions and become hypochlorous acid. The pKa is about 7.5, meaning that at pH 7.5 half is in each form. Below that pH, HOCl dominates.

steps.name: Activity
steps.text: Because HOCl is uncharged, it passes easily through microbial membranes, while the negatively charged OCl⁻ is largely kept out. So HOCl kills microbes much faster.

reactions.result: That is why diluted bleach disinfects well, and why bleach is sold alkaline: OCl⁻ is more stable in the bottle and breaks down more slowly. Lowering the pH too far, below about 5, risks forming dangerous chlorine gas.

reactions.title: Chlorine gas when mixed with acids
reactions.summary: Mixing bleach with acidic cleaners is one of the most common and dangerous household chemical accidents. Acidic products include toilet bowl cleaners, some bathroom cleaners, rust removers and vinegar. Adding acid to bleach releases chlorine gas, a toxic yellow-green gas that was used as a chemical weapon in World War I. Even a small amount in a closed bathroom can cause serious breathing problems. Never mix bleach with any other cleaning product.

steps.name: Acid added
steps.text: An acidic cleaner floods the bleach with hydrogen ions (H⁺), and the pH drops sharply. Bleach always contains some chloride ions (Cl⁻) left over from its manufacture. The conditions are now set for a reaction.

steps.name: Conversion
steps.text: Under acidic conditions, hypochlorite (or hypochlorous acid) reacts with chloride ions and hydrogen ions. The chlorine atoms from the hypochlorite and the chloride combine. This forms chlorine gas (Cl₂) and water.

steps.name: Gas release
steps.text: Chlorine gas doesn't stay dissolved in acidic water, so it bubbles out and fills the air. Its sharp, choking smell is a warning sign.

reactions.result: Chlorine gas reacts with the moisture in the eyes, nose and lungs to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid, which damage those tissues. If you mix them by accident, leave the area at once, get fresh air and call a poison control center. Never mix bleach with acids.

reactions.title: Chloramines when mixed with ammonia
reactions.summary: Another dangerous mistake is mixing bleach with products containing ammonia, such as some glass cleaners, or with urine, which contains ammonia-related compounds. This combination produces toxic gases called chloramines. Like chlorine gas, chloramines irritate the eyes and lungs and can cause serious breathing problems. Chloramines are also behind the typical “chlorine” smell of indoor pools, where chlorine reacts with sweat and urine. Never mix bleach with ammonia.

steps.name: Mixing
steps.text: Bleach meets ammonia (NH₃) from a glass cleaner, a multipurpose cleaner or urine. Hypochlorite and ammonia can react directly. The reaction starts immediately.

steps.name: Substitution
steps.text: Chlorine atoms from hypochlorite replace hydrogen atoms on ammonia, one at a time. Replacing one gives monochloramine (NH₂Cl), replacing two gives dichloramine (NHCl₂), and replacing all three gives nitrogen trichloride (NCl₃).

steps.name: Gas release
steps.text: These chloramines evaporate easily and escape into the air as irritating vapors. With extra bleach present, highly toxic nitrogen trichloride can form.

reactions.result: Chloramines irritate the eyes and lungs and can cause coughing, shortness of breath, chest pain and fluid in the lungs. If exposed, leave the area and get fresh air. Never mix bleach with ammonia or ammonia-containing products.

regulatory.status: Registered disinfectant under FIFRA when making germ-kill claims.
Danger: causes severe skin burns and eye damage; very toxic to aquatic life (concentrated).
Labels must warn: "Do not use together with other products. May release dangerous gases (chlorine)."

hazards.title: Toxic gases when mixed
hazards.summary: Mixing bleach with other cleaners is a common cause of household chemical injuries. Every year, U.S. poison control centers receive thousands of calls about people exposed to gases from mixing cleaners. The most dangerous combinations are bleach with acids, which makes chlorine gas, and bleach with ammonia, which makes chloramines. Injuries range from mild irritation to life-threatening lung damage. The simplest rule is never to mix bleach with anything except water.
hazards.chemical: Acids turn hypochlorite into chlorine gas by supplying the hydrogen ions that drive its reaction with chloride. Ammonia reacts with hypochlorite to form chloramines, in which chlorine atoms replace hydrogen atoms on nitrogen. Both chlorine and chloramines are reactive gases that dissolve readily in water. When they dissolve in the moist lining of the airways, they form acids and other reactive compounds. These damage the cells lining the respiratory tract.
hazards.biological: Dissolving into the moist surfaces of the eyes, nose, throat and lungs, these gases cause irritation and burns. Symptoms include burning eyes, coughing, wheezing, chest pain and shortness of breath. Higher exposures can damage the tiny air sacs in the lungs so that fluid leaks in, a serious condition called pulmonary edema that can appear hours later. People with asthma are especially vulnerable. Anyone exposed should get to fresh air and seek medical help if symptoms continue.

hazards.title: Corrosive to skin and eyes
hazards.summary: Household bleach is strong enough to irritate skin and seriously damage the eyes. Undiluted bleach can cause burns, especially with prolonged contact. Splashes in the eyes are particularly dangerous and can cause lasting injury if not rinsed immediately. Wearing gloves while cleaning protects the hands. Diluting bleach properly before use reduces the risk.
hazards.chemical: Bleach harms tissue in two ways. First, hypochlorite is a strong oxidizer that attacks the proteins in skin and eyes and damages their structure. Second, household bleach is strongly alkaline, with a pH around 11 to 13. At that pH, hydroxide ions break down the fats in cell membranes by saponification, the same reaction that makes soap. That combination of oxidation and alkaline attack makes bleach especially harsh on delicate tissue.
hazards.biological: On skin, bleach can cause redness, irritation, dryness and, with prolonged contact, chemical burns. Bleach on the skin often feels slippery because it is turning skin oils into soap. In the eyes, it can damage the cornea, the clear front layer, causing pain, redness and blurred vision, and alkaline damage keeps spreading if it isn't washed away. Eye splashes need immediate rinsing with clean water for at least 15 minutes. Medical attention should follow.

hazards.title: Asthma with frequent use
hazards.summary: Regular, frequent use of bleach and other cleaning sprays has been linked to asthma, especially in people who clean for a living, such as janitors, housekeepers and healthcare workers. Studies have also found links between frequent home use of cleaning sprays and asthma in adults. The risk seems greatest with sprays, which create fine droplets that can be breathed in. Using bleach in well-ventilated areas and choosing non-spray products may lower the risk. Occasional use isn't a major concern for most people.
hazards.chemical: When bleach is used, especially as a spray, small amounts of chlorine-containing gases and droplets get into the air. Hypochlorous acid and chlorine can also react with organic matter on surfaces and in the air, forming irritating compounds such as chloramines and chlorinated organic molecules. These are reactive and can damage the airway lining. Repeated exposure over months and years causes ongoing irritation. That is different from a single accidental exposure.
hazards.biological: Repeatedly breathing in irritants can inflame the airways, making them more sensitive and more prone to narrowing, which are the hallmarks of asthma. In some people this leads to new asthma, called occupational asthma when work is the cause. A large European study found that adults who used cleaning sprays at least once a week had a higher risk of developing asthma. Symptoms include wheezing, coughing and shortness of breath. Better ventilation, masks and safer cleaning methods help protect workers.

profile.dosage: Household bleach contains about 3 to 8 percent sodium hypochlorite. For disinfecting surfaces, health agencies typically recommend diluting it to about 0.1 to 0.5 percent, roughly 1 part bleach to between 10 and 50 parts water depending on the bleach's strength. Diluted bleach loses strength within about a day, so make it fresh. Swallowing a small amount of household bleach usually causes only irritation of the mouth and stomach, but poison control centers receive thousands of calls a year about people exposed to gases from mixing bleach with other cleaners. Always use bleach with good ventilation and never mix it with other products.

myths.claim: More bleach cleans better.
myths.consensus: Bleach disinfects and whitens but doesn't remove dirt; clean first, then disinfect at the labeled dilution.

myths.claim: Bleach is "toxic waste" that persists in the environment.
myths.consensus: It breaks down quickly to salt and water, though it can form chlorinated by-products with organic matter.

environment.aquaticToxicity: Very toxic to aquatic life in concentrated form; can form trihalomethanes and other by-products.

synthesis.title: Chlorine into lye
synthesis.summary: Most sodium hypochlorite is made by reacting chlorine gas with sodium hydroxide solution. Both chemicals come from the same source: the electrolysis of salt water, called the chlor-alkali process. So bleach is essentially made from salt, water and electricity. The first liquid bleach, Eau de Javel, was made near Paris in 1789 and named after the district where it was produced. Today it is one of the most widely used disinfectants in the world.
synthesis.mechanism: Chlorine gas is bubbled into a cold solution of sodium hydroxide. In this reaction chlorine undergoes disproportionation, a reaction in which the same element is both oxidized and reduced. One chlorine atom gains an electron and becomes a chloride ion (Cl⁻), while the other loses electrons and becomes part of a hypochlorite ion (OCl⁻). The result is a solution of sodium chloride and sodium hypochlorite in water. A small excess of sodium hydroxide is left in to keep the pH high, which keeps the bleach stable.
synthesis.significance: Keeping the solution cold matters; heating converts hypochlorite into chlorate.

synthesis.title: Electrochlorination
synthesis.summary: Some facilities make sodium hypochlorite on the spot using only salt, water and electricity, a process called electrochlorination. This avoids transporting and storing large amounts of dangerous chlorine gas or concentrated bleach. It is used in swimming pools, water treatment plants, ships and hospitals. “Saltwater” swimming pools use this method to make their own chlorine. The bleach it produces is dilute, which makes it safer to handle.
synthesis.mechanism: Salt water is passed through an electrolytic cell, where an electric current flows between two electrodes. At the positive electrode, the anode, chloride ions lose electrons and form chlorine. At the negative electrode, the cathode, water gains electrons and forms hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions. Unlike the industrial chlor-alkali process, there is no membrane between the electrodes. So the chlorine reacts straight away with the hydroxide in the solution, producing dilute sodium hypochlorite directly.
synthesis.significance: Swimming pools and water-treatment plants use this to avoid storing chlorine gas.

citations.title: The clinical toxicology of sodium hypochlorite.
citations.abstract: Introduction: Sodium hypochlorite is used as a bleaching and disinfecting agent and is commonly found in household bleach. Objective: The objective is to review critically the epidemiology, mechanisms of toxicity, clinical features, diagnosis, and management of hypochlorite poisoning. Methods: PubMed was searched from January 1950 to June 2018 using the terms "Hypochlorite", "Sodium Hypochlorite", "Sodium Oxychloride", "Hypochlorous Acid", "Bleach", "Chlorine Bleach", in combination with the keywords "poisoning", "poison", "toxicity", "ingestion", "adverse effects", "overdose", and "intoxication". In addition, bibliographies of identified articles were screened for additional relevant studies including non-indexed reports. Non-peer-reviewed sources were also included. These searches produced 110 citations which were considered relevant. Epidemiology: There is limited information regarding statistical trends on world-wide poisoning from sodium hypochlorite. In the United States of America, poison control center data have shown that enquiries regarding hypochlorite bleaches have ranged from 43,000 to 46,000 per year over the period 2012-2016. Mechanisms of toxicity: Hypochlorite's potential to cause toxicity is related to its oxidizing capacity and the pH of the solution. Toxicity arises from its corrosive activity upon contact with mucous membranes and skin. Features following ingestion: While small accidental ingestions are very unlikely to cause clinically significant toxicity, large ingestions may cause corrosive gastrointestinal injury and systemic effects, including metabolic acidosis, hypernatremia, and hyperchloremia. Features following dental exposure: Hypochlorite is used extensively by dentists for cleaning root canals and is safe if the solution remains within the root canal. Extrusions into the periapical area can result in severe pain with localized large and diffuse swelling and hemorrhage. Features following skin exposure: Prolonged or extensive exposure may cause skin irritation and damage to the skin or dermal hypersensitivity. Such exposures can result in either immediate or delayed-type skin reactions. High concentration solutions have caused severe chemical skin burns. Features following inhalation: Although there are only limited data, inhalation of hypochlorite alone is likely to lead to no more than mild irritation of the upper airways. Features following ocular exposure: Corneal injuries from ocular exposure are generally mild with burning discomfort and superficial disturbance of the corneal epithelium with recovery within 1 or 2 days. With higher concentration solutions, severe eye irritation can occur. Diagnosis: The diagnosis can typically be made on the basis of a careful history, including details of the specific product used, its hypochlorite concentration, and the amount involved. As hypochlorite bleach produces a characteristic smell of chlorine, this may provide a diagnostic clue. In severe cases, corrosive injury is suggested on presentation because of hypersalivation, difficulty swallowing, retrosternal pain or hematemesis. Management: Symptom-directed supportive care is the mainstay of management. Gastrointestinal decontamination is not beneficial. Local corrosive injury is the major focus of treatment in severe cases. Fiberoptic endoscopy and CT thorax/abdomen are complimentary and have been shown to be useful in corrosive injuries in assessing the severity of injury, risk of mortality and risk of subsequent stricture formation and should be performed as soon as possible after ingestion. Dental periapical extrusion injuries should be left open for some minutes to allow bleeding through the tooth and to limit hematoma development in tissue spaces. Once the bleeding has ceased, the canal can be dressed with non-setting calcium hydroxide and sealed coronally. Conclusions: Accidental ingestion of household bleach is not normally of clinical significance. However, those who ingest a large amount of a dilute formulation or a high concentration preparation can develop severe, and rarely fatal, corrosive injury so prompt supportive care is essential as there is no specific antidote. Treatment primarily consists of symptom-directed supportive care.

citations.title: Mechanism and clinical aspects of sodium hypochlorite accidents: A narrative review.
citations.abstract: Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) solution is a widely used irrigant in endodontics. However, it is highly cytotoxic and can have destructive effects on surrounding tissues when it is not confined to the root canal during irrigation. The extrusion of NaOCl beyond the confines of the root canal into the surrounding tissues or anatomical spaces is known as a NaOCl accident. The NaOCl accident is a serious iatrogenic mishap that can lead to severe tissue damage and complications, which can be life-threatening and/or cause long-term or permanent consequences with medico-legal implications. Therefore, this narrative review was conducted to provide clinicians with a comprehensive understanding of the mechanism and clinical aspects of NaOCl accidents. A literature search was conducted in various online databases using specific Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and key search terms. The review included all categories of articles dealing with the NaOCl accident and available as full text. Additionally, a manual method of search was conducted by screening references of the included articles. Duplicate articles and articles available only as abstracts were excluded from the review. The included articles were reviewed, analyzed and discussed according to the following sections: causative factors; mechanism; clinical categorization; clinical manifestations; diagnosis, including history, clinical assessment and examination, clinical investigation, and differential diagnoses; and treatment planning of NaOCl accidents. This would enable clinicians to recognize and manage NaOCl accidents in the best possible manner and minimize their serious consequences. Future research should prioritize the identification of solutions or measures to address the challenges associated with conducting clinical or in vivo studies on NaOCl irrigation and extrusion.

citations.title: Chlorhexidine gluconate.
citations.abstract: The aim of root canal treatment is to eliminate bacteria from the infected root canal and to prevent reinfection. Biomechanical cleaning and shaping greatly reduces the number of bacteria. Nevertheless, due to anatomical complexity of the root canal system, residues and bacteria cannot be removed completely. Therefore, various substances have been used during canal preparation to remove debris, necrotic tissue, bacteria and smear layer. The most common irrigant of choice is sodium hypochlorite (NaOCI): it is an effective antimicrobial agent and tissue solvent. However, NaOCI can be toxic. Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHX) is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent. As a root canal irrigant and intracanal medicament, CHX has an antibacterial efficacy comparable to that of NaOCI, and is effective against resistant bacterial strains. CHX may result in residual antimicrobial activity of the dentine surface after prolonged exposure of the root canal to CHX. CHX also has a low grade of toxicity. In this review CHX will be discussed in detail.

citations.title: Peroxide-sensing transcriptional regulators in bacteria.
citations.abstract: The ability to maintain intracellular concentrations of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) within safe limits is essential for all aerobic life forms. In bacteria, as well as other organisms, ROS are produced during the normal course of aerobic metabolism, necessitating the constitutive expression of ROS scavenging systems. However, bacteria can also experience transient high-level exposure to ROS derived either from external sources, such as the host defense response, or as a secondary effect of other seemingly unrelated environmental stresses. Consequently, transcriptional regulators have evolved to sense the levels of ROS and coordinate the appropriate oxidative stress response. Three well-studied examples of these are the peroxide responsive regulators OxyR, PerR, and OhrR. OxyR and PerR are sensors of primarily H(2)O(2), while OhrR senses organic peroxide (ROOH) and sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl). OxyR and OhrR sense oxidants by means of the reversible oxidation of specific cysteine residues. In contrast, PerR senses H(2)O(2) via the Fe-catalyzed oxidation of histidine residues. These transcription regulators also influence complex biological phenomena, such as biofilm formation, the evasion of host immune responses, and antibiotic resistance via the direct regulation of specific proteins.

name: Sodium Hydroxide
scoreRationale: Severely corrosive in drain and oven cleaners; in cosmetics and soaps it is neutralized and harmless.
summary: Lye dissolves grease and clogs and makes soap. In drain cleaners it's dangerous; in finished soaps and lotions it has been fully neutralized.

physical.state: White pellets or flakes; also sold as solution
physical.solubility: Very soluble in water, releasing much heat

overview: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), also called lye or caustic soda, dissolves completely into sodium ions and hydroxide ions (OH⁻), making it a strong base. A 1% solution has a pH around 13.

Dissolving it releases a lot of heat, and its hydroxide ions attack fats and proteins aggressively. That makes it a powerful drain and oven cleaner, and, in tiny neutralized amounts, an everyday ingredient for adjusting pH in cosmetics and for making soap.
profile.function: Breaks down fats and proteins in drain and oven cleaners, adjusts pH in cosmetics, and turns oils into soap.

mechanisms.title: Dissolving grease (saponification)
mechanisms.chemical: Grease and fats are made of triglycerides, molecules in which three fatty acids are attached to glycerol by ester bonds. Sodium hydroxide releases hydroxide ions (OH⁻), strong bases that attack the carbon atom of each ester bond. This breaks the bond, releasing glycerol and turning the fatty acids into their sodium salts. Those fatty-acid salts are soap molecules. The reaction is called saponification, from the Latin word sapo, meaning soap.
mechanisms.biological: The soap formed from greasy clogs and oven grime dissolves in water, while the original grease didn't. So sticky, water-repelling grease becomes something that rinses away. That is how sodium hydroxide clears greasy drain clogs and cleans burnt-on grease in ovens. The reaction also releases heat, which helps melt any remaining fat. In effect, it is making soap inside your drain.

mechanisms.title: Breaking down hair and protein
mechanisms.chemical: Hair is made mainly of keratin, a tough protein whose chains are linked by peptide bonds and strengthened by disulfide bonds, bridges between sulfur atoms on different parts of the protein. Hydroxide ions attack both. They hydrolyze peptide bonds, chopping the protein chains into smaller pieces, and they break the disulfide bonds that give hair its strength and shape. As these bonds break, the hair loses its structure. Eventually it dissolves.
mechanisms.biological: This is how sodium hydroxide drain cleaners dissolve hair clogs, a common cause of blocked bathroom drains. The same chemistry is used in some hair relaxers, which break and rearrange the disulfide bonds in curly hair to straighten it. It also explains why lye is so dangerous to skin: the outer layers of your body are made of protein too. Hydroxide dissolves skin proteins the same way it dissolves hair. That is why protective gloves are essential.

mechanisms.title: Why alkali burns are so serious
mechanisms.chemical: When concentrated sodium hydroxide touches skin or eyes, hydroxide ions attack the fats in cell membranes by saponification, turning them into soap. They also denature proteins, making them unfold and stop working. Unlike acids, which make proteins clump into a crust that slows further damage, alkalis turn tissue into a soft, liquid mush. That mush doesn't stop the chemical from going deeper. The damage continues as long as the alkali is there.
mechanisms.biological: Alkali burns cause a kind of tissue death called liquefactive necrosis, in which tissue breaks down and liquefies. With no protective crust, the alkali keeps soaking deeper, so the burn can be much worse than it first looks. In the eye, alkali burns are especially dangerous because they can pass through the cornea to the inner eye within seconds, potentially causing permanent blindness. That is why lye splashes in the eye need immediate rinsing for at least 15 to 30 minutes. Emergency care should follow.

reactions.title: Saponification
reactions.summary: Saponification is the reaction that turns fats and oils into soap using a strong base such as sodium hydroxide. It is one of the oldest chemical processes people have used, going back thousands of years. In soapmaking, the fat and lye are measured carefully so that they react completely. The products are soap and glycerin. In cleaning products, the same reaction breaks down greasy buildup.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: Hydroxide ions (OH⁻) from the sodium hydroxide are drawn to the carbon atom in each ester bond of a triglyceride. That carbon is slightly positive because it is bonded to two oxygen atoms. The hydroxide bonds to it.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: The ester bond breaks, separating a fatty acid from the glycerol backbone. This happens to all three fatty acids on each triglyceride. Glycerol, with three –OH groups, is released.

steps.name: Salt formation
steps.text: Each fatty acid, now carrying a negative charge on its carboxylate group, pairs with a sodium ion. The result is a sodium carboxylate, a soap molecule with a long oily tail and a charged head.

reactions.result: In properly made soap, all the lye is used up, so none remains in the finished bar. Soapmakers add a little extra fat, called superfatting, to make sure no harsh lye is left over.

reactions.title: Neutralization
reactions.summary: Neutralization is the reaction between an acid and a base, producing water and a salt. When sodium hydroxide is used in cosmetics, tiny amounts are added to raise the pH of a formula that would otherwise be too acidic. The sodium hydroxide reacts completely with the acid in the formula, so no free lye remains. That is why seeing sodium hydroxide on a lotion label is no cause for concern. The finished product contains only the resulting harmless salt.

steps.name: Mixing
steps.text: A small, carefully measured amount of sodium hydroxide, usually as a dilute solution, is added to a formula containing acidic ingredients such as fatty acids or certain thickeners. The amount is calculated to hit a target pH.

steps.name: Reaction
steps.text: Hydroxide ions (OH⁻) from the sodium hydroxide combine with hydrogen ions (H⁺) from the acidic ingredients to form water. Removing free hydrogen ions raises the formula's pH.

steps.name: Result
steps.text: The sodium ions pair with the negatively charged parts of the acidic ingredients, forming salts. The formula's pH rises to its target, often about 5 to 7 for skincare, close to the skin's own pH.

reactions.result: When you see sodium hydroxide on a lotion label, it has already been neutralized into a salt. Many thickeners, such as carbomers, only thicken once they have been neutralized, so sodium hydroxide is essential to how they work.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe as a food processing aid.
Safe as a pH adjuster; hair straighteners are limited in concentration.
Danger: causes severe skin burns and eye damage (H314).

hazards.title: Severe chemical burns
hazards.summary: Concentrated sodium hydroxide, found in drain openers and oven cleaners, is one of the most dangerous household chemicals. Drain openers can contain 30 to 50 percent lye. Contact with skin or eyes can cause severe chemical burns that may not hurt at first but deepen over time. Gloves and eye protection are essential when using these products. If contact happens, rinse immediately with large amounts of water.
hazards.chemical: Concentrated sodium hydroxide attacks the fats in cell membranes by saponification and denatures proteins, breaking down tissue on contact. Dissolving in water, including the moisture on skin, releases a lot of heat, which can add a heat burn to the chemical burn. Because alkalis liquefy tissue instead of forming a protective crust, the chemical keeps penetrating. The longer it stays in contact, the deeper the damage. Even dilute solutions can harm the eyes.
hazards.biological: Lye burns may feel slippery and hurt surprisingly little at first, because the chemical damages nerve endings, which leads people to underestimate the injury. Over minutes to hours, the burn deepens, with redness, blistering and tissue death. In the eyes, lye can badly damage the cornea and inner eye within seconds, causing permanent vision loss. First aid means rinsing with large amounts of water for at least 15 to 30 minutes and getting emergency care. Never try to neutralize a lye burn with acid, because that reaction produces even more heat.

hazards.title: Swallowing (a danger to children)
hazards.summary: Swallowing lye-containing products is a serious danger, especially for young children who may mistake them for drinks. Drain cleaners and some dishwasher detergents contain sodium hydroxide. Swallowing them can cause severe burns to the mouth, throat and esophagus. Children under five are most at risk. Keeping these products out of reach, in their original containers with child-resistant caps, prevents most accidents.
hazards.chemical: When concentrated sodium hydroxide is swallowed, it immediately attacks the tissues of the mouth, throat and esophagus. It saponifies the fats in cell membranes and denatures proteins, liquefying the tissue, and the heat released as it dissolves adds to the damage. Because the esophagus is narrow and the chemical stays in contact with its walls, burns there are often the worst. Liquid products are especially dangerous because they go down before the person can react.
hazards.biological: Swallowing lye causes immediate pain, drooling, vomiting and difficulty swallowing, though symptoms are sometimes delayed. The burns can perforate the esophagus or stomach, which is a medical emergency. As the burns heal, scar tissue can narrow the esophagus, a condition called a stricture, making swallowing difficult for life and sometimes requiring repeated surgery. People who have had lye burns also face a higher risk of esophageal cancer years later. Never induce vomiting; call poison control or emergency services immediately.

profile.dosage: Drain openers can contain 30 to 50 percent sodium hydroxide, and oven cleaners also contain significant amounts; these need gloves, eye protection and good ventilation, and must be stored out of children's reach. In cosmetics, sodium hydroxide is used in tiny amounts to adjust pH and is completely neutralized, so no free lye remains. Soap is made with lye, but properly made soap contains none. Food processing uses it in small, controlled amounts, for example to give pretzels their deep brown crust and to cure olives.

myths.claim: Handmade soap made with lye is harsh and toxic.
myths.consensus: All true soap is made with lye; saponification consumes it, leaving none in properly made soap.

environment.persistence: Neutralized quickly by carbon dioxide and acids in the environment.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Harmful by raising pH when spilled.

synthesis.title: Chlor-alkali electrolysis
synthesis.summary: Almost all sodium hydroxide is made by the chlor-alkali process, which uses electricity to split concentrated salt water. It produces three valuable chemicals at once: sodium hydroxide, chlorine gas and hydrogen gas. Tens of millions of tonnes of sodium hydroxide are made this way every year. It goes into paper, aluminum, soap, textiles and many other chemicals. The process uses a great deal of electricity.
synthesis.mechanism: Concentrated, purified salt water, called brine, flows into an electrolysis cell divided by a special membrane that lets positive ions through but blocks negative ones. At the positive electrode, the anode, chloride ions lose electrons and form chlorine gas. At the negative electrode, the cathode, water molecules gain electrons, forming hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions. Sodium ions pass through the membrane from the anode side to the cathode side, where they pair with the hydroxide ions. The resulting sodium hydroxide solution is concentrated by evaporation and can be dried into solid pellets or flakes.
synthesis.significance: Modern membrane cells replaced older mercury cells, which released toxic mercury into the environment.

synthesis.title: Historical lye
synthesis.summary: Before modern chemistry, people made their own lye for soap from wood ashes. This homemade lye was mostly potassium hydroxide, a close relative of sodium hydroxide that is also a strong base. Soap made with potassium hydroxide tends to be soft, while soap made with sodium hydroxide is hard. The process was simple but took time and skill. Soap made from fat and wood-ash lye has been produced for thousands of years.
synthesis.mechanism: Wood ash contains potassium carbonate, sometimes called potash, which is left behind when wood burns. Soapmakers packed ashes into a barrel with straw at the bottom and slowly dripped water through them, dissolving the potassium carbonate and collecting the liquid at the bottom. To strengthen it, they added slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, made by heating limestone and adding water. The calcium hydroxide reacted with the potassium carbonate, forming solid calcium carbonate that settled out and leaving potassium hydroxide in solution. This strong lye was then boiled with animal fat to make soap.
synthesis.significance: Soap has been made from fat and ash-derived lye for thousands of years.

citations.title: Low-temperature mineralization of perfluorocarboxylic acids.
citations.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent, bioaccumulative pollutants found in water resources at concentrations harmful to human health. Whereas current PFAS destruction strategies use nonselective destruction mechanisms, we found that perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) could be mineralized through a sodium hydroxide-mediated defluorination pathway. PFCA decarboxylation in polar aprotic solvents produced reactive perfluoroalkyl ion intermediates that degraded to fluoride ions (78 to ~100%) within 24 hours. The carbon-containing intermediates and products were inconsistent with oft-proposed one-carbon-chain shortening mechanisms, and we instead computationally identified pathways consistent with many experiments. Degradation was also observed for branched perfluoroalkyl ether carboxylic acids and might be extended to degrade other PFAS classes as methods to activate their polar headgroups are identified.

citations.title: Feline panleukopenia. ABCD guidelines on prevention and management.
citations.abstract: Overview: Feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) infects all felids as well as raccoons, mink and foxes. This pathogen may survive in the environment for several months and is highly resistant to some disinfectants. Infection: Transmission occurs via the faecal-oral route. Indirect contact is the most common route of infection, and FPV may be carried by fomites (shoes, clothing), which means indoor cats are also at risk. Intrauterine virus transmission and infection of neonates can occur. Disease signs: Cats of all ages may be affected by FPV, but kittens are most susceptible. Mortality rates are high - over 90% in kittens. Signs of disease include diarrhoea, lymphopenia and neutropenia, followed by thrombocytopenia and anaemia, immunosuppression (transient in adult cats), cerebellar ataxia (in kittens only) and abortion. Diagnosis: Feline panleukopenia virus antigen is detected in faeces using commercially available test kits. Specialised laboratories carry out PCR testing on whole blood or faeces. Serological tests are not recommended, as they do not distinguish between infection and vaccination. Disease management: Supportive therapy and good nursing significantly decrease mortality rates. In cases of enteritis, parenteral administration of a broad-spectrum antibiotic is recommended. Disinfectants containing sodium hypochlorite (bleach), peracetic acid, formaldehyde or sodium hydroxide are effective. Vaccination recommendations: All cats - including indoor cats - should be vaccinated. Two injections, at 8-9 weeks of age and 3-4 weeks later, are recommended, and a first booster 1 year later. A third vaccination at 16-20 weeks of age is recommended for kittens from environments with a high infection pressure (cat shelters) or from queens with high vaccine-induced antibody levels (breeding catteries). Subsequent booster vaccinations should be administered at intervals of 3 years or more. Modified-live virus vaccines should not be used in pregnant queens or in kittens less than 4 weeks of age.

citations.title: Pretreatment methods for bioethanol production.
citations.abstract: Lignocellulosic biomass, such as wood, grass, agricultural, and forest residues, are potential resources for the production of bioethanol. The current biochemical process of converting biomass to bioethanol typically consists of three main steps: pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, and fermentation. For this process, pretreatment is probably the most crucial step since it has a large impact on the efficiency of the overall bioconversion. The aim of pretreatment is to disrupt recalcitrant structures of cellulosic biomass to make cellulose more accessible to the enzymes that convert carbohydrate polymers into fermentable sugars. This paper reviews several leading acidic, neutral, and alkaline pretreatments technologies. Different pretreatment methods, including dilute acid pretreatment (DAP), steam explosion pretreatment (SEP), organosolv, liquid hot water (LHW), ammonia fiber expansion (AFEX), soaking in aqueous ammonia (SAA), sodium hydroxide/lime pretreatments, and ozonolysis are intensively introduced and discussed. In this minireview, the key points are focused on the structural changes primarily in cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin during the above leading pretreatment technologies.

citations.title: Synthesis and Characterization of Gd3+ Doped HfO₂ Nanoparticles for Radiotherapy Applications.
citations.abstract: Synthesis of pure Hafnium Oxide (HfO₂), and HfO₂ doped with Gadolinium (1, 3, 5 and 7 mol%) nanoparticles (NPs) had been carried out by Precipitation and co-precipitation method using the precursor solution of Hafnium (IV) chloride (HfCl₄) and Gadolinium(III) chloride hexahydrate (GdCl₃·6H₂O) with Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) which was dissolved in deionized water. The synthesized compound was characterized and analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM), Energy dispersive X-ray analysis (EDX), UV-visible spectrophotometer, Photoluminescence (PL), Fourier Transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy. The result from X-ray diffraction showed that the Gd3+ concentration for 7 mol% had attended directly crystalline phase of Cubic HfO₂ structure. Morphology and element analysis of the samples were analyzed using FESEM and EDX, which indicated cluster formation, fluffy and voids with highly agglomerated particles and EDX exhibited no extra peaks with other than constituent elements present in extrinsic HfO₂. From UV Spectra it was observed that the optical band gap of both Intrinsic and extrinsic of HfO2 NPs were found to be 5.74 eV, 3.62 eV, 3.69 eV, 3.78 eV and 4.19 eV. The Photoluminescence Spectra showed the 313 nm emission line which might be due to 6P7/2→8S7/2 transition and the Raman Spectra clearly represented the monoclinic structure by showing the presence of Ag and Bg Modes and cubic structure because of the presence of F2g mode.
