name: Hydrogen Peroxide
scoreRationale: Breaks down into water and oxygen and is mild at 3%, but stronger solutions burn skin and are dangerous to swallow.
summary: Hydrogen peroxide disinfects, whitens and removes stains, then breaks down into water and oxygen. Keep strong grades away from skin and mouths.

physical.state: Colorless liquid (3% household, up to 35% industrial)
physical.phStability: Stabilized in slightly acidic solution; decomposes with light, heat and metals

overview: Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is water with an extra oxygen: two hydrogens attached to an oxygen–oxygen single bond. That O–O bond is weak, so the molecule readily breaks apart, releasing oxygen and making H₂O₂ a strong oxidizer.

Household bottles contain 3% in water, kept slightly acidic and in dark plastic because light and metals speed its breakdown. Your own cells make small amounts of it, both as a weapon against bacteria and as a signaling molecule.
profile.function: Disinfects surfaces, whitens teeth and laundry, lightens hair and removes organic stains.

mechanisms.title: Oxidative killing
mechanisms.chemical: Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) has a weak oxygen–oxygen single bond that breaks easily. That makes it a strong oxidizing agent: it readily takes electrons from other molecules. It can oxidize the fats in cell membranes, the amino acids in proteins and the bases in DNA. When metal ions such as iron or copper are present, hydrogen peroxide forms hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which are even more reactive and attack almost any molecule they touch. Together, these reactions cause widespread damage to a microbe's structures.
mechanisms.biological: With their membranes, proteins and DNA damaged, bacteria, viruses and fungi can no longer survive or reproduce. That makes hydrogen peroxide an effective disinfectant for surfaces, medical equipment and contact lenses. A big advantage is that it breaks down into nothing but water and oxygen, leaving no harmful residue. Some bacteria make an enzyme called catalase that destroys hydrogen peroxide, giving them some resistance, so higher concentrations or longer contact may be needed. Hydrogen peroxide vapor is used to sterilize entire hospital rooms.

mechanisms.title: Bleaching
mechanisms.chemical: The colored molecules in stains, hair and teeth, called chromophores, contain conjugated systems, chains of alternating single and double bonds that absorb visible light. Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes these chromophores, breaking up the conjugated chains by adding oxygen atoms or breaking double bonds. In hair, the pigment is melanin, a large molecule with many conjugated rings. Peroxide, especially when boosted by an alkaline ingredient such as ammonia, breaks melanin into smaller, colorless pieces. With shorter conjugated systems, the molecules no longer absorb visible light.
mechanisms.biological: When chromophores are broken down, stains on fabric become invisible and hair becomes lighter as its melanin is destroyed. Hair bleaches often contain 6 to 12 percent hydrogen peroxide combined with an alkaline booster. Teeth-whitening products use hydrogen peroxide, or carbamide peroxide, which releases it, to oxidize stain molecules inside the enamel. Overuse can make teeth temporarily sensitive and irritate the gums. Bleaching also damages hair proteins, which is why bleached hair becomes more brittle.

mechanisms.title: Cell signaling
mechanisms.chemical: Inside cells, hydrogen peroxide is made in small amounts as a normal part of metabolism. At these low concentrations, it can act as a messenger. It reacts with particular cysteine amino acids in certain proteins, oxidizing their thiol groups (–SH). That changes the protein's shape and activity, switching it on or off. Enzymes such as catalase and peroxiredoxins quickly mop up any excess to keep levels under control.
mechanisms.biological: This signaling helps regulate many processes, including cell growth, division and responses to stress. When tissue is wounded, cells release hydrogen peroxide as a signal that draws immune cells to the injury, a discovery first made in zebrafish. The body keeps hydrogen peroxide in careful balance: too little disrupts signaling, while too much causes oxidative damage. That double role, messenger and potential poison, shows how the same molecule can help or harm depending on the amount. Scientists are still discovering new roles for it.

reactions.title: Decomposition (the fizz)
reactions.summary: When you pour hydrogen peroxide on a cut, it fizzes and foams. That happens because an enzyme in blood and tissue, called catalase, rapidly breaks hydrogen peroxide down into water and oxygen gas. Hydrogen peroxide also breaks down slowly on its own, especially when exposed to light, heat or metals. That is why it is sold in dark bottles. The foaming isn't a sign that germs are being killed, only that catalase is present.

steps.name: Catalyst
steps.text: Catalase is an enzyme found in nearly every living cell, including blood cells and bacteria, and its job is to protect cells from hydrogen peroxide. When hydrogen peroxide touches tissue, catalase grabs it in its active site, which contains an iron atom.

steps.name: Splitting
steps.text: Catalase converts two hydrogen peroxide molecules into two water molecules and one oxygen molecule. The iron in the enzyme helps by accepting and passing on oxygen atoms. The enzyme itself is unchanged and ready for more.

steps.name: Foam
steps.text: The released oxygen gas forms tiny bubbles. Because catalase works so fast, a lot of oxygen is released in a short time, creating the visible foam.

reactions.result: Catalase is one of the fastest enzymes known, processing millions of hydrogen peroxide molecules per second. The foaming on a cut comes mostly from catalase in your own cells, not from bacteria being killed.

reactions.title: The Fenton reaction
reactions.summary: The Fenton reaction, discovered by the British chemist Henry Fenton in the 1890s, happens when hydrogen peroxide meets iron ions. It produces hydroxyl radicals, among the most reactive molecules known. The reaction matters in biology, where it can cause damage inside cells, and in industry, where it is used to destroy pollutants. It shows how a relatively mild chemical can become far more powerful in the presence of a catalyst. Here, iron is the trigger.

steps.name: Electron transfer
steps.text: Ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) gives one of its electrons to a hydrogen peroxide molecule and becomes ferric iron (Fe³⁺). The hydrogen peroxide now has an extra electron, which destabilizes it.

steps.name: Bond breaking
steps.text: The extra electron makes the weak oxygen–oxygen bond snap. One oxygen becomes a hydroxide ion (OH⁻), and the other becomes a hydroxyl radical (•OH) with an unpaired electron. The radical is extremely reactive.

steps.name: Damage
steps.text: Hydroxyl radicals react with almost any molecule they meet within nanoseconds, including fats, proteins and DNA. They steal electrons and set off chain reactions of damage. They react so quickly that they can't travel far from where they form.

reactions.result: This is why cells keep free iron tightly locked up inside proteins such as ferritin, and why peroxide plus iron is used to destroy pollutants in wastewater. The iron can be recycled back to Fe²⁺, keeping the reaction going.

regulatory.status: Registered disinfectant active; on EPA's list for many pathogens.
Teeth whitening limited.
regulatory.limit: 0.1% over the counter; up to 6% via dentists

regulatory.status: Concentrated solutions: harmful if swallowed, causes serious eye damage.

hazards.title: Tissue damage at high concentration
hazards.summary: The 3 percent hydrogen peroxide sold in drugstores is a mild irritant, but stronger solutions are dangerous. Concentrations of 35 percent, sometimes marketed as “food grade,” have caused serious injuries and deaths when swallowed, often by people who believed false health claims. Even the 10 to 12 percent solutions used for hair bleaching can burn skin. The danger rises steeply with concentration. High-strength peroxide must be handled with gloves and eye protection.
hazards.chemical: Concentrated hydrogen peroxide is a powerful oxidizer that rapidly damages the proteins and fats in skin and other tissues. When it meets tissue, catalase breaks it down quickly, releasing large volumes of oxygen gas: one milliliter of 35 percent hydrogen peroxide can release more than 100 milliliters of oxygen. In a confined space like the stomach or a blood vessel, that sudden release of gas is dangerous. The heat released adds to the tissue damage. The stronger the solution, the faster and more violent this becomes.
hazards.biological: On skin, concentrated hydrogen peroxide causes white patches, stinging and blisters, and in the eyes it can cause serious injury. When swallowed, it burns the mouth, throat and stomach, and the released oxygen can swell the stomach painfully. Oxygen bubbles can also enter blood vessels, forming gas embolisms that block blood flow to the brain, heart or other organs and cause strokes or heart attacks. There is no health benefit to drinking hydrogen peroxide. Anyone who swallows concentrated peroxide needs emergency care.

hazards.title: Slower wound healing
hazards.summary: Many people were taught to clean cuts with hydrogen peroxide, but doctors now advise against it. While it does kill some bacteria, it also damages the healthy cells needed for healing. Studies have found that it can slow wound healing. Rinsing a minor cut with clean running water and mild soap is better. Medical professionals still use peroxide in specific situations, such as cleaning heavily contaminated wounds.
hazards.chemical: Hydrogen peroxide doesn't tell bacteria and human cells apart: it oxidizes the membranes, proteins and DNA of every cell it touches. Fibroblasts, which make collagen to rebuild tissue, and keratinocytes, which regrow the skin's surface, are particularly sensitive to it. The foaming caused by catalase may also physically disturb newly forming tissue. At the concentrations used on wounds, it can kill more healthy cells than bacteria. This is a case of a disinfectant being too harsh for the job.
hazards.biological: When healthy cells in a wound are damaged, healing slows because fewer cells are left to rebuild the tissue. Studies in animals and in cell cultures have shown that hydrogen peroxide can delay wound healing. It also doesn't kill all bacteria, since some produce catalase. For minor cuts and scrapes, rinsing with clean water removes dirt and most bacteria without harming healthy tissue. Covering the wound and keeping it clean helps it heal.

profile.dosage: Drugstore hydrogen peroxide is 3 percent, a mild irritant that is fine for surface disinfection and some household uses. Hair bleaching products typically use 6 to 12 percent, and teeth-whitening products sold directly to consumers in the European Union are limited to 0.1 percent, with stronger treatments only through dentists. Concentrations of 35 percent, sometimes sold as “food grade,” are dangerous and have caused severe injuries and deaths when swallowed. Never drink hydrogen peroxide, and keep it out of children's reach. Store it in its original dark bottle, away from heat.

myths.claim: Pouring peroxide on cuts helps them heal.
myths.consensus: It kills bacteria but also damages healthy cells and can slow healing; rinsing with water is better.

myths.claim: Drinking diluted food-grade peroxide detoxifies the body.
myths.consensus: This is dangerous and unsupported.

environment.persistence: Very low; decomposes to water and oxygen.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Toxic at high concentrations but short-lived.

synthesis.title: The anthraquinone process
synthesis.summary: Almost all hydrogen peroxide made today comes from the anthraquinone process, developed by German chemists in the 1930s. It is a clever catalytic cycle that combines hydrogen and oxygen indirectly. A carrier molecule, 2-ethylanthraquinone, picks up hydrogen and then hands it over to oxygen. Because the carrier is recycled, the overall reaction simply joins hydrogen and oxygen. Millions of tonnes are made every year, mainly for bleaching paper and textiles.
synthesis.mechanism: First, 2-ethylanthraquinone, dissolved in an organic solvent, is mixed with hydrogen gas over a palladium catalyst. Hydrogen atoms add to the molecule, turning it into 2-ethylanthrahydroquinone. Next, air is bubbled through the solution, and oxygen takes those hydrogen atoms from the hydroquinone. This forms hydrogen peroxide and turns the carrier back into 2-ethylanthraquinone. The hydrogen peroxide is extracted with water, purified and concentrated, while the anthraquinone solution goes back to the start.
synthesis.significance: The carrier molecule is recycled endlessly, so the net reaction is simply hydrogen plus oxygen.

synthesis.title: Biological production
synthesis.summary: Hydrogen peroxide isn't just an industrial chemical; your body makes it constantly. It is a natural byproduct of breathing oxygen and making energy inside cells. Immune cells also make it on purpose to fight infection. Because it can be harmful in large amounts, cells have enzymes that break it down quickly. Many other organisms, from bacteria to plants, also make and use hydrogen peroxide.
synthesis.mechanism: When cells use oxygen to make energy in their mitochondria, a small share of oxygen molecules accidentally pick up a single extra electron, forming superoxide radicals (O₂•⁻). These are dangerous, so an enzyme called superoxide dismutase quickly converts pairs of superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. The hydrogen peroxide is then broken down by catalase into water and oxygen, or used by enzymes called peroxidases to oxidize other molecules. Some enzymes, called oxidases, make hydrogen peroxide directly when they react with oxygen. Immune cells use an enzyme called NADPH oxidase to make large amounts of it to kill bacteria.
synthesis.significance: Honey's antibacterial activity comes partly from an enzyme that slowly generates hydrogen peroxide.

citations.title: Enzymatic hydroxylation of aromatic compounds.
citations.abstract: Selective hydroxylation of aromatic compounds is among the most challenging chemical reactions in synthetic chemistry and has gained steadily increasing attention during recent years, particularly because of the use of hydroxylated aromatics as precursors for pharmaceuticals. Biocatalytic oxygen transfer by isolated enzymes or whole microbial cells is an elegant and efficient way to achieve selective hydroxylation. This review gives an overview of the different enzymes and mechanisms used to introduce oxygen atoms into aromatic molecules using either dioxygen (O(2)) or hydrogen peroxide (H(2)O(2)) as oxygen donors or indirect pathways via free radical intermediates. In this context, the article deals with Rieske-type and alpha-keto acid-dependent dioxygenases, as well as different non-heme monooxygenases (di-iron, pterin, and flavin enzymes), tyrosinase, laccase, and hydroxyl radical generating systems. The main emphasis is on the heme-containing enzymes, cytochrome P450 monooxygenases and peroxidases, including novel extracellular heme-thiolate haloperoxidases (peroxygenases), which are functional hybrids of both types of heme-biocatalysts.

citations.title: Catalase, a remarkable enzyme: targeting the oldest antioxidant enzyme to find a new cancer treatment approach.
citations.abstract: This review is centered on the antioxidant enzyme catalase and will present different aspects of this particular protein. Among them: historical discovery, biological functions, types of catalases and recent data with regard to molecular mechanisms regulating its expression. The main goal is to understand the biological consequences of chronic exposure of cells to hydrogen peroxide leading to cellular adaptation. Such issues are of the utmost importance with potential therapeutic extrapolation for various pathologies. Catalase is a key enzyme in the metabolism of H2O2 and reactive nitrogen species, and its expression and localization is markedly altered in tumors. The molecular mechanisms regulating the expression of catalase, the oldest known and first discovered antioxidant enzyme, are not completely elucidated. As cancer cells are characterized by an increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and a rather altered expression of antioxidant enzymes, these characteristics represent an advantage in terms of cell proliferation. Meanwhile, they render cancer cells particularly sensitive to an oxidant insult. In this context, targeting the redox status of cancer cells by modulating catalase expression is emerging as a novel approach to potentiate chemotherapy.

citations.title: MicroRNA and heme oxygenase-1 in allergic disease.
citations.abstract: Background: Cumulative evidence suggests that in allergic diseases, oxidative stress and inflammation could often be detected. Therefore, the antioxidant/anti-inflammatory heme oxygenase (HO)-1 was recognized as a protective factor in allergic disorders. However, the precise underlying mechanisms of HO-1-based protection are not yet completely understood. In addition, miRNAs, a class of non-coding RNA, have been confirmed to associate with immunologic and inflammatory disorders in allergy recently. In addition, abundant studies have verified there is a complex connection between HO-1 and miRNAs. Thus, in this review, the combination of HO-1 and miRNAs (e.g. miR-155) in anti-allergy would be introduced. Methods: To further confirm our hypothesis, GEO sequencing datasets of atopic dermatitis children were analyzed. The miR-548a-3p might regulate the cellular response to hydrogen peroxide through HO-1 and HIF-1pathway. Meanwhile, this article reviews the latest knowledge and studies on the protective mechanisms of miRNA-HO-1 in allergy. Results: In brief, we supposed that miRNAs/HO-1 could mediate allergy through oxidative stress pathways, transcription factors and immune cell functions such as mast cell maturation, chemokine expression in T cell and dendritic cell degranulation. Although the detailed mechanism needs further research, this review may reveal the potential application of miRNAs and HO-1 in genetic therapies of allergic disease and provide new biomarkers. Conclusion: This article examines the latest knowledge and studies on the protective roles and mechanisms of miRNA-HO-1 in allergy. Moreover, via bioinformatics analysis of GEO dataset, it was demonstrated that miRNAs (e.g. miR-205, miR-203, and miR-483-5p) could regulate allergy process through HO-1.

citations.title: Excessive Production of Hydrogen Peroxide in Mitochondria Contributes to Atopic Dermatitis.
citations.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a complex disease characterized by chronic recurring eczema and pruritus. In addition, patients with AD display increased cutaneous and systemic levels of oxidative damage markers, whose source remains elusive. In this study, we investigated oxidative and mitochondrial stress in AD epidermis. The levels of superoxide dismutase 2 and hydrogen peroxide are augmented in the mitochondria of flaky tail (ft/ft) mouse keratinocytes, which is associated with the inhibition of the glutathione system and catalase. Furthermore, reduced levels of glutathione peroxidase 4 are associated with accumulation of malondialdehyde, 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal, and oxidized phosphatidylcholines in ft/ft epidermis. Cytochrome c is markedly increased in ft/ft epidermis, hence showing mitochondrial stress. Topical application of MitoQ, which is a mitochondrial-targeting antioxidant, to ft/ft mouse skin reduced damage to macromolecules and inflammation and restored epidermal homeostasis. Absence of alteration in the expression of superoxide dismutase 2, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase 4 and limited lipid peroxidation as well as oxidized phosphatidylcholines in the epidermis of Flg-/- mice suggest that FLG deficiency marginally contributes to oxidative stress in ft/ft epidermis. Increased superoxide dismutase 2, lipid peroxidation, and cytochrome c in the epidermis of patients with AD, associated with reduced antioxidant response in primary AD keratinocytes, corroborate mitochondrial dysfunction and lack of cellular adjustment to oxidative stress in AD epidermis.

citations.title: Oxidative eustress: On constant alert for redox homeostasis.
citations.abstract: In the open metabolic system, redox-related signaling requires continuous monitoring and fine-tuning of the steady-state redox set point. The ongoing oxidative metabolism is a persistent challenge, denoted as oxidative eustress, which operates within a physiological range that has been called the 'Homeodynamic Space', the 'Goldilocks Zone' or the 'Golden Mean'. Spatiotemporal control of redox signaling is achieved by compartmentalized generation and removal of oxidants. The cellular landscape of H2O2, the major redox signaling molecule, is characterized by orders-of-magnitude concentration differences between organelles. This concentration pattern is mirrored by the pattern of oxidatively modified proteins, exemplified by S-glutathionylated proteins. The review presents the conceptual background for short-term (non-transcriptional) and longer-term (transcriptional/translational) homeostatic mechanisms of stress and stress responses. The redox set point is a variable moving target value, modulated by circadian rhythm and by external influence, summarily denoted as exposome, which includes nutrition and lifestyle factors. Emerging fields of cell-specific and tissue-specific redox regulation in physiological settings are briefly presented, including new insight into the role of oxidative eustress in embryonal development and lifespan, skeletal muscle and exercise, sleep-wake rhythm, and the function of the nervous system with aspects leading to psychobiology.

name: Benzalkonium Chloride
scoreRationale: An effective disinfectant but an irritant, linked to occupational asthma and eye-surface damage, toxic to aquatic life, and a contributor to antimicrobial resistance.
summary: Benzalkonium chloride is a "quat" disinfectant in wipes, sprays and some hand sanitizers. It works, but can irritate lungs, eyes and skin.

identity.composition: Mixture of alkylbenzyldimethylammonium chlorides with C12, C14 and C16 alkyl chains.

physical.state: White powder or gel; usually sold as solution
physical.phStability: Stable across a wide pH range

overview: Benzalkonium chloride (BAC) is a mixture of quaternary ammonium compounds, or “quats”. Each has a nitrogen atom bonded to four carbon groups (two methyls, a benzyl ring and a long 12–16-carbon tail), giving it a permanent positive charge, balanced by a chloride ion.

A positively charged head with a long oily tail makes BAC a cationic surfactant. Bacterial membranes are negatively charged, so BAC is drawn to them and breaks them open, which is why it's in disinfecting wipes, sprays and some eye drops.
profile.function: Kills bacteria and enveloped viruses on surfaces; preserves eye drops and nasal sprays.

mechanisms.title: Breaking bacterial membranes
mechanisms.chemical: Benzalkonium chloride molecules have a positively charged nitrogen head and a long oily tail. The outer surfaces of bacteria are covered with negatively charged molecules, such as phospholipids and proteins, so BAC's positive heads are drawn to them like magnets. Once attached, the oily tails push into the bacterial membrane, which is made of two layers of fatty molecules. This disrupts the membrane's orderly arrangement, opening gaps and holes. Many BAC molecules working together can break the membrane apart.
mechanisms.biological: Once the membrane is damaged, important contents of the cell, such as potassium ions and small molecules, leak out, and the cell can no longer keep its internal environment stable. The bacterium dies. BAC also works against enveloped viruses, such as influenza and coronaviruses, whose fatty outer layer it can disrupt. It is less effective against non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus, which lack that fatty layer. That is why BAC disinfectants work on some germs but not all.

mechanisms.title: Selecting for resistance
mechanisms.chemical: When bacteria are exposed to BAC at concentrations too low to kill them, called sub-lethal levels, some survive better than others. The survivors often have efflux pumps, proteins in their membranes that actively pump BAC back out before it can do damage. Bacteria can also change the makeup of their membranes to make them less vulnerable. Repeated exposure favors these tougher bacteria, which then multiply. Genes for some efflux pumps can even be passed between bacteria.
mechanisms.biological: Some of the efflux pumps that remove BAC can also pump out certain antibiotics, so bacteria that become resistant to BAC may also become less sensitive to those antibiotics. This is called cross-resistance. Laboratory studies have shown it can happen, raising concern that overusing quaternary ammonium disinfectants could add to antimicrobial resistance, a major global health threat. Using disinfectants at the correct concentration and contact time, and only when needed, helps reduce the risk. How much this happens outside the lab is still being studied.

mechanisms.title: Damage to the eye's surface
mechanisms.chemical: BAC is used as a preservative in many eye drops, at low concentrations of about 0.004 to 0.02 percent. It doesn't only attack bacterial membranes, though; it can also disrupt the membranes of human cells, which are made of lipids too. The cells on the surface of the cornea and conjunctiva are directly exposed to eye drops. BAC can also disturb the tear film, the protective layer of fluid covering the eye. These effects are stronger with frequent or long-term use.
mechanisms.biological: With repeated use, especially in people who use eye drops daily for years, for example to treat glaucoma, BAC can damage the cells on the surface of the eye. This can cause dryness, redness, burning, a gritty feeling and inflammation, sometimes called ocular surface disease, and can make eyes more sensitive. For this reason, preservative-free drops, packaged in single-use vials or special bottles, are recommended for people who need drops often. Occasional use of preserved drops is generally safe. An eye doctor can advise which type suits a given condition.

reactions.title: The Menshutkin reaction (how it's made)
reactions.summary: Benzalkonium chloride is made using the Menshutkin reaction, described by the Russian chemist Nikolai Menshutkin in 1890. It converts a neutral amine, a nitrogen atom bonded to three carbon groups, into a quaternary ammonium salt with four carbon groups and a permanent positive charge. It is a type of nucleophilic substitution reaction. The reaction is simple and efficient. It is used to make many quaternary ammonium compounds, known as quats.

steps.name: Nucleophile
steps.text: A long-chain alkyldimethylamine has a nitrogen atom bonded to two methyl groups and a long oily chain. The nitrogen also carries a lone pair, two electrons not involved in bonding. That makes it a nucleophile, a molecule that seeks out electron-poor atoms.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: The nitrogen's lone pair attacks the carbon atom in benzyl chloride that is bonded to chlorine. That carbon is electron-poor because chlorine pulls electrons toward itself. As the new nitrogen–carbon bond forms, the chlorine leaves as a chloride ion.

steps.name: Quaternary salt
steps.text: The nitrogen is now bonded to four carbon groups: two methyls, a benzyl group and the long chain. Having used its lone pair, it carries a permanent positive charge, balanced by the chloride ion.

reactions.result: Quaternary ammonium salts stay charged at any pH, unlike ordinary amines, which can gain or lose a proton. That permanent charge is what lets them cling to negatively charged surfaces, bacteria included, and it is also why quats are used in fabric softeners and hair conditioners.

regulatory.status: Registered disinfectant active ingredient.
Permitted in consumer antiseptics; FDA deferred final rulemaking pending more data.
Danger: corrosive when concentrated; very toxic to aquatic life.

hazards.title: Skin and eye irritation
hazards.summary: Benzalkonium chloride is safe at the low concentrations used in wipes and sprays, but concentrated solutions can be corrosive to skin and eyes. Even at low concentrations, frequent use can irritate the skin, especially on the hands. Occasionally BAC causes allergic contact dermatitis. People who use disinfectant wipes many times a day, such as healthcare and cleaning workers, are most likely to notice irritation. Gloves and moisturizer help protect the skin.
hazards.chemical: BAC damages cell membranes by pushing its oily tail into their lipid layers and binding its positive head to negatively charged molecules. That isn't specific to bacteria; it also affects the cells of human skin and eyes. At high concentrations it can damage the skin's outer barrier and the cells beneath it. It can also strip protective lipids from the skin's surface. In a few people it acts as an allergen, though that is less common.
hazards.biological: Irritation shows up as redness, dryness, itching and sometimes cracking, particularly on the hands of frequent users. In the eyes, concentrated BAC can cause serious damage, so splashes must be rinsed immediately. Rarely, people develop an allergy to BAC, with an itchy rash wherever it touches. Disinfectant wipes can leave a residue on the hands, so washing hands after use helps. Gloves are recommended for prolonged use.

hazards.title: Work-related asthma
hazards.summary: Studies have linked frequent use of quaternary ammonium compounds, BAC included, to asthma in people who use them regularly at work, such as cleaners and healthcare workers. The risk appears higher with sprays, which produce fine droplets that can be breathed in. Some studies have found more asthma symptoms and new cases of asthma among these workers. The evidence is still developing. Using wipes instead of sprays and keeping rooms well ventilated may reduce the risk.
hazards.chemical: When BAC is sprayed, it forms tiny droplets, an aerosol, that can be breathed into the airways. Because BAC disrupts cell membranes, it can damage the cells lining the airways. It may also trigger inflammatory responses or act as an allergen in some people. Repeated exposure over time causes ongoing irritation. The exact mechanisms are still being studied.
hazards.biological: Repeated irritation and inflammation can make the airways more sensitive and more likely to narrow, producing asthma symptoms such as wheezing, coughing and shortness of breath. In some workers, quats seem to trigger an allergy-type asthma. Studies of healthcare workers have found that regular use of quat disinfectants is associated with asthma. People who already have asthma may find their symptoms get worse. Workplaces can cut exposure by choosing non-spray products and improving ventilation.

profile.dosage: Disinfecting wipes and sprays typically contain about 0.1 to 0.3 percent benzalkonium chloride, antiseptic hand products about 0.1 to 0.13 percent, and eye drops much less, about 0.004 to 0.02 percent. Use disinfectants as the label directs, including the contact time, the time a surface must stay wet for the germs to be killed. Concentrated solutions require gloves and eye protection. People who use eye drops frequently may benefit from preservative-free versions. Using disinfectants only when they are needed helps limit resistance.

myths.claim: Disinfecting wipes clean and disinfect in one swipe.
myths.consensus: Most labels require the surface to stay visibly wet for several minutes to disinfect.

environment.persistence: Adsorbs strongly to sludge and sediments.
environment.biodegradability: Biodegradable under aerobic conditions but inhibits microbes at high concentrations.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: Benzalkonium chloride is made in chemical plants from fatty amines, which are derived from fatty alcohols that come from coconut or palm oil or from petroleum. It was introduced in 1935 by the German scientist Gerhard Domagk, who later won a Nobel Prize for discovering the first sulfa antibiotics. Since then it has become one of the most widely used disinfectants and preservatives. It is found in disinfectant wipes, sprays, hand sanitizers, eye drops and some cosmetics. Its use rose sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic.
synthesis.mechanism: Fatty alcohols with 12 to 16 carbon atoms are first converted into alkyldimethylamines by reacting them with dimethylamine, a small nitrogen-containing molecule. These amines are then mixed with benzyl chloride, which contains a reactive carbon–chlorine bond. In the Menshutkin reaction, each amine's nitrogen attacks the carbon of benzyl chloride, forming a new bond and pushing out a chloride ion. This produces a mixture of quaternary ammonium chlorides with different chain lengths, which together make up benzalkonium chloride. The product is diluted with water into a stable solution.
synthesis.significance: Because the product is a mixture of chain lengths, its germ-killing strength depends on the blend; the 12- and 14-carbon chains are usually the most effective.

citations.title: TFOS DEWS II iatrogenic report.
citations.abstract: Dry eye can be caused by a variety of iatrogenic interventions. The increasing number of patients looking for eye care or cosmetic procedures involving the eyes, together with a better understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms of dry eye disease (DED), have led to the need for a specific report about iatrogenic dry eye within the TFOS DEWS II. Topical medications can cause DED due to their allergic, toxic and immuno-inflammatory effects on the ocular surface. Preservatives, such as benzalkonium chloride, may further aggravate DED. A variety of systemic drugs can also induce DED secondary to multiple mechanisms. Moreover, the use of contact lens induces or is associated with DED. However, one of the most emblematic situations is DED caused by surgical procedures such as corneal refractive surgery as in laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) and keratoplasty due to mechanisms intrinsic to the procedure (i.e. corneal nerve cutting) or even by the use of postoperative topical drugs. Cataract surgery, lid surgeries, botulinum toxin application and cosmetic procedures are also considered risk factors to iatrogenic DED, which can cause patient dissatisfaction, visual disturbance and poor surgical outcomes. This report also presents future directions to address iatrogenic DED, including the need for more in-depth epidemiological studies about the risk factors, development of less toxic medications and preservatives, as well as new techniques for less invasive eye surgeries. Novel research into detection of early dry eye prior to surgeries, efforts to establish appropriate therapeutics and a greater attempt to regulate and oversee medications, preservatives and procedures should be considered.

citations.title: The cGAS-STING pathway-dependent sensing of mitochondrial DNA mediates ocular surface inflammation.
citations.abstract: The innate immune response is the main pathophysiological process of ocular surface diseases exposed to multiple environmental stresses. The epithelium is central to the innate immune response, but whether and how innate immunity is initiated by ocular epithelial cells in response to various environmental stresses in ocular surface diseases, such as dry eye, is still unclear. By utilizing two classic experimental dry eye models-a mouse ocular surface treated with benzalkonium chloride (BAC) and a mouse model with surgically removed extraorbital lachrymal glands, as well as dry eye patient samples-along with human corneal epithelial cells (HCE) exposed to hyperosmolarity, we have discovered a novel innate immune pathway in ocular surface epithelial cells. Under stress, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) was released into the cytoplasm through the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) and further activated the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway, aggravating downstream inflammatory responses and ocular surface damage. Genetic deletion or pharmacological suppression of STING and inhibition of mtDNA release reduced inflammatory responses, whereas mtDNA transfection supported cytoplasmic mtDNA-induced inflammatory responses by activating the cGAS-STING pathway. Our study clarified the cGAS-STING pathway-dependent sensing of mitochondrial DNA-mediated ocular surface inflammation, which elucidated a new mechanism of ocular surface diseases in response to multiple environmental stresses.

citations.title: Allergic Conjunctivitis Management: Update on Ophthalmic Solutions.
citations.abstract: Purpose of review: The aim of this review, is to present an updated revision of topical management of SAC and PAC, based on the available scientific evidence and focused on the impact of ophthalmic solution formulations on eye surface. Recent findings: Physicians treating ocular allergy should be aware of tear film and tear film disruption in SAC and PAC, and how eye drop composition and additives affect the physiology of the allergic eye. Seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC) are the most frequent causes of ocular allergy (OA), and both conditions are underdiagnosed and undertreated. SAC and PAC are immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated hypersensitivity reactions. The additional tear film disruption caused by the release of inflammatory mediators increases and exacerbates the impact of signs and symptoms and may trigger damage of the ocular surface. Comorbidities are frequent, and dry eye disease in particular must be considered. Clinical guidelines for the management of SAC and PAC recommend topical therapy with antihistamines, mast cells stabilizers or dualaction agents as first-line treatment, but care should be taken, as many medications contain other compounds that may contribute to ocular surface damage.

citations.title: Allergy to ophthalmic preservatives.
citations.abstract: Purpose of review: The purpose of the present review is to examine the hypersensitivity reactions to preservatives in topical ophthalmic therapies. Recent findings: Ocular hypersensitivity reactions to different types of preservatives in different chemical classes of topical ophthalmic treatments reviewed in the literature include IgE-mast cell mediated, cell mediated and toxic. Quaternary ammoniums (benzalkonium chloride) are most commonly (8% reported cases in OVID and PubMED based searches) associated with irritant toxic reactions whereas the organomercurials (thimerosal) and the alcohols (chlorobutanol) have the highest association (19% of OVID and 14% of PubMED based searches and 20% of OVID and 11% of PubMED searches), respectively, with allergic responses although the term allergy for the 'alcohols' appears to be actually an irritant effect whereas the organomercurials appear to truly interact with the immune system as neoantigens. Summary: A large number of clinical and experimental studies reveal that preservatives in topical ophthalmic medications have been demonstrated to produce effects from inflammation/ hypersensitivity to permanent cytotoxic effects involving all structures of the eye.

citations.title: State of the art etch-and-rinse adhesives.
citations.abstract: Objectives: The aim of this study was to explore the therapeutic opportunities of each step of 3-step etch-and-rinse adhesives. Methods: Etch-and-rinse adhesive systems are the oldest of the multi-generation evolution of resin bonding systems. In the 3-step version, they involve acid-etching, priming and application of a separate adhesive. Each step can accomplish multiple goals. Acid-etching, using 32-37% phosphoric acid (pH 0.1-0.4) not only simultaneously etches enamel and dentin, but the low pH kills many residual bacteria. Results: Some etchants include anti-microbial compounds such as benzalkonium chloride that also inhibits matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in dentin. Primers are usually water and HEMA-rich solutions that ensure complete expansion of the collagen fibril meshwork and wet the collagen with hydrophilic monomers. However, water alone can re-expand dried dentin and can also serve as a vehicle for protease inhibitors or protein cross-linking agents that may increase the durability of resin-dentin bonds. In the future, ethanol or other water-free solvents may serve as dehydrating primers that may also contain antibacterial quaternary ammonium methacrylates to inhibit dentin MMPs and increase the durability of resin-dentin bonds. The complete evaporation of solvents is nearly impossible. Significance: Manufacturers may need to optimize solvent concentrations. Solvent-free adhesives can seal resin-dentin interfaces with hydrophobic resins that may also contain fluoride and antimicrobial compounds. Etch-and-rinse adhesives produce higher resin-dentin bonds that are more durable than most 1 and 2-step adhesives. Incorporation of protease inhibitors in etchants and/or cross-linking agents in primers may increase the durability of resin-dentin bonds. The therapeutic potential of etch-and-rinse adhesives has yet to be fully exploited.

name: Sodium Carbonate
scoreRationale: A simple, biodegradable cleaning mineral; its alkalinity irritates eyes and skin.
summary: Washing soda softens water and cuts grease in laundry and cleaners. It's a mineral workhorse; just keep it out of your eyes.

overview: Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃), known as washing soda or soda ash, is the salt of carbonic acid with two sodium ions. The carbonate ion pulls protons from water, producing hydroxide ions, so its solutions are strongly alkaline (about pH 11.5 at 1%).

That alkalinity helps break down greasy soils, and carbonate ions grab calcium and magnesium from hard water, precipitating them so detergents can work. It's one of the oldest industrial chemicals and, together with sand, the main ingredient of glass.
profile.function: Softens water so detergents work, saponifies grease, and raises pH in laundry products.

mechanisms.title: Softening hard water
mechanisms.chemical: Hard water contains dissolved calcium ions (Ca²⁺) and magnesium ions (Mg²⁺), picked up from rocks such as limestone and dolomite that the water flowed through. Sodium carbonate dissolves into sodium ions and carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻). The carbonate ions combine with the calcium and magnesium ions to form calcium carbonate and magnesium carbonate. These compounds are insoluble, meaning they don't dissolve in water. So they come out of solution as tiny solid particles, a process called precipitation.
mechanisms.biological: Calcium and magnesium ions interfere with soaps and detergents, reacting with them to form insoluble scum: the gray film on bathtubs and the dullness on washed clothes. That wastes detergent and leaves residue behind. By removing these ions, sodium carbonate lets soaps and detergents lather better and clean more effectively. That is why washing soda is added to laundry as a booster, especially where the water is hard. The tiny calcium carbonate particles simply rinse away with the wash water.

mechanisms.title: Alkaline cleaning
mechanisms.chemical: When sodium carbonate dissolves in water, carbonate ions take hydrogen ions from water molecules, producing hydroxide ions (OH⁻). This makes the solution strongly alkaline, about pH 11.5 for a 1 percent solution. At that pH, hydroxide ions can partly break down fats by saponification, turning them into soap-like molecules. The alkaline conditions also help dissolve acidic stains and loosen proteins. Sodium carbonate is milder than sodium hydroxide but still effective.
mechanisms.biological: The high pH helps lift grease off fabrics, dishes and surfaces so it rinses away more easily. That makes washing soda useful for heavily soiled laundry, greasy pans and stained surfaces. It also neutralizes acidic odors. Because it is much less caustic than lye, it is safer to use at home, though it still deserves care. It is often recommended as an environmentally friendlier cleaning ingredient because it contains no phosphates.

mechanisms.title: Irritation
mechanisms.chemical: Healthy skin has a slightly acidic surface, with a pH of about 4.5 to 5.5, protected by a so-called acid mantle of natural oils and acids. Sodium carbonate solutions are strongly alkaline. When they touch skin, they disturb this acid mantle and start breaking down skin oils by saponification. They can also loosen the proteins of the skin's outer layer. The eyes have no protective dead-cell layer at all, so alkaline solutions can damage their surface cells directly.
mechanisms.biological: On skin, concentrated sodium carbonate can cause dryness, redness and irritation, especially with prolonged contact or repeated use. Hands may feel slippery as skin oils are turned into soap. In the eyes, splashes cause pain and redness and can do serious damage, so they must be rinsed immediately. Breathing in the powder can irritate the nose and throat. Wearing gloves and keeping it away from the eyes minimizes these risks.

reactions.title: Making water alkaline
reactions.summary: Sodium carbonate makes water alkaline through a reaction called hydrolysis, in which carbonate ions react with water. Carbonate is the partner base of a weak acid, bicarbonate, so it has a strong tendency to take hydrogen ions from water. That leaves behind hydroxide ions, which raise the pH. This reaction is why washing soda is an effective cleaner. It is also why it should be handled with some care.

steps.name: Proton grab
steps.text: When sodium carbonate dissolves, it separates into sodium ions and carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻). Carbonate ions are drawn to the hydrogen atoms of water molecules. Each carbonate ion can take one hydrogen ion (H⁺) from a water molecule.

steps.name: Hydroxide
steps.text: A water molecule that loses a hydrogen ion becomes a hydroxide ion (OH⁻), while the carbonate becomes bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). The solution now has more hydroxide ions than hydrogen ions.

steps.name: pH rises
steps.text: The extra hydroxide ions make the solution alkaline; a 1 percent solution reaches a pH of about 11.5. That is far more alkaline than baking soda, which gives a pH of about 8.3.

reactions.result: This is why washing soda feels slippery: it begins to saponify the oils on your skin, turning them into soap. It is also why washing soda cleans more strongly than baking soda, though it is harsher on skin.

reactions.title: Glassmaking
reactions.summary: Most of the world's sodium carbonate goes into making glass. Pure sand, made of silicon dioxide, melts at about 1,700 °C, a temperature that is very hot and expensive to reach. Adding sodium carbonate lowers the melting temperature a lot. That makes glassmaking practical and affordable. Glassmakers have used soda ash this way for thousands of years.

steps.name: Mixing
steps.text: Sand (silica, SiO₂), soda ash (sodium carbonate) and limestone (calcium carbonate) are mixed together, often with recycled glass called cullet. The exact recipe determines the properties of the finished glass.

steps.name: Melting
steps.text: The mixture is heated in a furnace to about 1,500 °C. At this temperature, sodium carbonate reacts with silica, releasing carbon dioxide gas and forming sodium silicate. The gas bubbles out of the melt.

steps.name: Glass
steps.text: The sodium ions break up silica's strong network of silicon–oxygen bonds, lowering its melting point and making it easier to work. Calcium from the limestone makes the glass more durable and water-resistant. The molten glass is shaped and cooled.

reactions.result: Most window and bottle glass is “soda-lime” glass made this way. Without the lime, sodium silicate glass would slowly dissolve in water; that dissolvable form is actually sold separately as “water glass.”

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Warning: causes serious eye irritation (H319).

hazards.title: Eye and skin irritation
hazards.summary: Sodium carbonate is far safer than sodium hydroxide, but it is still an alkaline chemical that can irritate skin and seriously irritate eyes. Washing soda powder and concentrated solutions are the main concern. Most problems come from splashes in the eyes or prolonged skin contact. Gloves for heavy cleaning and keeping it away from children prevent most accidents. It should never be swallowed.
hazards.chemical: In solution, sodium carbonate produces hydroxide ions, making it strongly alkaline. At high pH, hydroxide ions break down the fats in cell membranes and loosen the proteins of the skin's outer layer. In the eye, which lacks skin's protective dead-cell layer, these reactions quickly damage the surface cells of the cornea. The powder can also pull moisture out of skin and eyes, concentrating its alkaline effect. The higher the concentration, the greater the damage.
hazards.biological: Skin contact can cause dryness, redness and irritation, especially for people with sensitive skin or eczema. Eye splashes cause stinging, redness and tearing and can damage the cornea if not rinsed promptly; rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes and get medical advice. Swallowing washing soda irritates the mouth, throat and stomach, causing pain and vomiting. Keeping laundry products in their original containers and out of children's reach prevents accidents. Store the powder dry and sealed.

profile.dosage: Laundry products and washing-soda boosters can contain 10 to 40 percent sodium carbonate or be nearly pure washing soda, and typical use is a few tablespoons per load. It is classified as an eye irritant, so gloves for heavy use and care around the eyes are advised. In food, small amounts are used as an acidity regulator, for example in ramen noodles, where alkaline salts give them their springy texture. Unlike phosphates, it doesn't feed algae blooms in waterways. It should be kept away from young children.

myths.claim: Washing soda and baking soda are the same.
myths.consensus: Washing soda (carbonate) is far more alkaline and not for cooking or skin.

environment.persistence: Part of the natural carbonate cycle.

synthesis.title: The Solvay process
synthesis.summary: The Solvay process, developed by the Belgian chemist Ernest Solvay in the 1860s, is a major way to make sodium carbonate. It uses inexpensive raw materials: salt, limestone and ammonia, which is recycled. The process first makes sodium bicarbonate, which is then heated to give sodium carbonate. It replaced the older Leblanc process, which produced huge amounts of toxic waste. It is still widely used in many countries.
synthesis.mechanism: Limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated to release carbon dioxide and form lime (calcium oxide). Concentrated salt water is saturated with ammonia gas, and the carbon dioxide is bubbled through it. Sodium bicarbonate, the least soluble product, crystallizes out and is filtered off. It is then heated to about 200 °C, which drives off water and carbon dioxide and leaves sodium carbonate. The leftover ammonium chloride is treated with the lime to recover the ammonia for reuse, producing calcium chloride as a byproduct.
synthesis.significance: The process's main waste, calcium chloride, is sold for road de-icing and dust control, so even its byproduct is useful.

synthesis.title: Mining trona
synthesis.summary: In the United States, sodium carbonate is mostly produced from natural trona ore rather than by the Solvay process. The world's largest trona deposit lies in Wyoming's Green River Basin, left by an ancient lake that dried up about 50 million years ago. Mining trona uses less energy and produces less waste than the Solvay process. The U.S. is one of the world's largest producers and exporters of soda ash. Natural deposits are also found in Turkey, Kenya and elsewhere.
synthesis.mechanism: Trona, a natural mineral containing both sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate, is mined from deep underground beds. The ore is crushed and heated in a kiln, a step called calcination, which converts the sodium bicarbonate into sodium carbonate and releases water and carbon dioxide. The crude soda ash is dissolved in water, and insoluble rock and clay are filtered out. The purified solution is evaporated so that sodium carbonate crystals form. These are dried and heated again to give pure, water-free soda ash.
synthesis.significance: Ancient Egyptians used natron, a natural sodium carbonate mixture, to mummify the dead.

citations.title: Intermolecular binding of blueberry pectin-rich fractions and anthocyanin.
citations.abstract: Pectin was extracted from blueberry powder into three fractions of water soluble (WSF), chelator soluble (CSF) and sodium carbonate soluble (NSF). The fractions were incubated with cyanidin-3-glucoside (C3G), a mixture of five anthocyanidins (cyanidin, pelargonidin, malvidin, petunidin and delphinidin) or blueberry juice at pH 2.0-4.5. Free anthocyanins and bound anthocyanin-pectin mixtures were separated by ultrafiltration. WSF bound the least amount of anthocyanin at all pH values. CSF had stronger anthocyanin binding ability at pH 2.0-3.6, while NSF had stronger anthocyanin binding ability at pH 3.6-4.5. The pectin and anthocyanin binding was lowest at pH 4.5 and higher at pH 2.0-3.6. Nearly doubling C3G pigment content increased bound anthocyanin percentage by 16-23% at pH 3.6, which favored anthocyanin aromatic stacking, compared to 3-9% increase at pH 2.0. Ionic interaction between anthocyanin flavylium cations and free pectic carboxyl groups, and anthocyanin stacking may be two major mechanisms for pectin and anthocyanin binding.

citations.title: Influence of Chemical Species on Polyphenol-Protein Interactions Related to Wine Astringency.
citations.abstract: One of the most accepted mechanisms of astringency consists of the interaction between polyphenols and some specific salivary proteins. This work aims to obtain further insights into the mechanisms leading to a modulation of astringency elicited by polyphenols. The effect of the presence of different chemical species (present in food and beverages as food additives) on the polyphenol-protein interaction has been evaluated by means of techniques such as sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and cell cultures using a cell-based model of the oral epithelium. Results obtained showed that several chemicals, particularly sodium carbonate, seem to inhibit polyphenol binding to salivary proteins and to oral epithelium. These results point out that polyphenol-saliva protein interactions can be affected by some food additives, which can help to better understand changes in astringency perception.

citations.title: Uptake and Removal of Uranium by and from Human Teeth.
citations.abstract: Uranium-238 (238U), a long-lived radiometal, is widespread in the environment because of both naturally occurring processes and anthropogenic processes. The ingestion or inhalation of large amounts of U is a major threat to humans, and its toxicity is considered mostly chemical rather than radiological. Therefore, a way to remove uranium ingested by humans from uranium-contaminated water or from the air is critically needed. This study investigated the uranium uptake by hydroxyapatite (HAP), a compound found in human bone and teeth. The uptake of U by teeth is a result of U transport as dissolved uranyl (UO22+) in contaminated water, and U adsorption has been linked to delays in both tooth eruption and development. In this present work, the influence of pH, contact time, initial U concentration, and buffer solution on the uptake and removal of U in synthetic HAP was investigated and modeled. The influence of pH (pH of human saliva, 6.7-7.4) on the uptake of uranyl was negligible. Furthermore, the kinetics were extremely fast; in one second of exposure, 98% of uranyl was uptaken by HAP. The uptake followed pseudo-second-order kinetics and a Freundlich isotherm model. A 0.2 M sodium carbonate solution removed all the uranyl from HAP after 1 h. Another series of in vitro tests were performed with real teeth as targets. We found that, for a 50 mg/L U in PBS solution adjusted to physiological pH, ∼35% of the uranyl was uptaken by the tooth after 1 h, following pseudo-first-order kinetics. Among several washing solutions tested, a commercially available carbonate, as well as a commercially available fluoride solution, enabled removal of all the uranyl taken up by the teeth.

citations.title: Research Advances of Prevention and Control of Hydrogen Sulfide in Coal Mines.
citations.abstract: Sudden emission and casualty accidents caused by abnormal enrichment of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) in coal mines are becoming frequent increasingly, causing major casualties and environmental pollution. Scholars in various countries have developed various measuring devices for hydrogen sulfide content in coal and rock formations and their calculation methods. The existing prevention and control technologies of H2S in coal mines were summarized in various countries. According to the distribution characteristics, occurrence modes, and emission forms of H2S in coal mines, the prevention and control technologies of H2S in coal-bearing strata, airflow in tunnel, and underground water body are mainly introduced. Analyzed the effects of different ventilation systems on prevention and control of H2S, which include conventional ventilation system, partial homotropal ventilation system, and full homotropal ventilation system. The methods used mainly include neutralization by injecting alkalizer through drilling in coal seams with high pressure, spraying alkalizer in tunnel, attenuation by increasing wind amount, changing the ventilation method, pumping, dredging, and blocking the water that contains H2S as well as comprehensive prevention and control method. The basic agents adopted mainly include sodium carbonate (the mass percentage concentration is about 0.5% ~ 3.0%) and sodium bicarbonate solution, and some basic solution is added by an additive, such as surfactant, Fenton reagent, sodium dodecyl benzene sulfonate, sodium hypochlorite, or chloramine-T. The treatment effect and the main problems of each prevention and control technology are analyzed, and a comprehensive method of prevention and control techniques of H2S in coal mines is proposed. According to current technological level as well as the cost, the effective prevention and control techniques of H2S should take the occurrence, distribution, and emission forms of H2S in coal mines as well as the content into consideration.

citations.title: Inactivating SARS-CoV-2 by electrochemical oxidation.
citations.abstract: Fully inactivating SARS-CoV-2, the virus causing coronavirus disease 2019, is of key importance for interrupting virus transmission but is currently performed by using biologically or environmentally hazardous disinfectants. Herein, we report an eco-friendly and efficient electrochemical strategy for inactivating the SARS-CoV-2 using in-situ formed nickel oxide hydroxide as anode catalyst and sodium carbonate as electrolyte. At a voltage of 5 V, the SARS-CoV-2 viruses can be rapidly inactivated with disinfection efficiency reaching 95% in only 30 s and 99.99% in 5 min. Mass spectrometry analysis and theoretical calculations indicate that the reactive oxygen species generated on the anode can oxidize the peptide chains and induce cleavage of the peptide backbone of the receptor binding domain of the SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein, and thereby disables the virus. This strategy provides a sustainable and highly efficient approach for the disinfection of the SARS-CoV-2 viruliferous aerosols and wastewater.
