name: Alcohol
scoreRationale: An excellent solvent and disinfectant, but flammable, drying at high skincare concentrations, and toxic when swallowed by children.
summary: Alcohol dissolves ingredients, kills germs and evaporates fast. It's effective, but high amounts can dry skin, and it's flammable.

physical.solubility: Miscible with water and most solvents

overview: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is a two-carbon chain with a hydroxyl group: small and polar enough to mix completely with water, yet oily enough to dissolve many fats and fragrances. That dual nature makes it one of the world's most useful solvents.

It's the alcohol in drinks, the active ingredient in most hand sanitizers, and, as “alcohol denat.”, a common cosmetic ingredient made undrinkable with bitter additives. Yeasts have produced it by fermentation for hundreds of millions of years.
profile.function: Dissolves fragrances and actives, preserves, gives a quick-drying feel, and disinfects hands and surfaces.

mechanisms.title: Killing germs
mechanisms.chemical: Proteins only work when they are folded into precise three-dimensional shapes. Those shapes are held in place by weak attractions such as hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, where oily parts of the chain huddle together away from water. Ethanol is small enough to slip between the folded chains, and because it is partly oily and partly water-like, it competes with both kinds of attraction, loosening the protein until it unfolds. This is called denaturation. Ethanol also dissolves the fatty molecules that make up cell membranes and the outer envelope of some viruses. Surprisingly, 60 to 80 percent ethanol works better than pure ethanol, because water helps it soak into cells and is itself needed for proteins to unfold; pure ethanol also evaporates before it can finish the job.
mechanisms.biological: Most bacteria and enveloped viruses, those wrapped in a fatty outer layer, such as influenza and coronaviruses, are inactivated within seconds of contact with a properly made sanitizer. That is why health agencies recommend sanitizers with at least 60 percent alcohol when soap and water aren't available. Ethanol works poorly against norovirus, the stomach bug that spreads on cruise ships, because it has no fatty envelope to dissolve and a tough protein shell. It also can't kill bacterial spores, such as those of Clostridioides difficile, which have thick protective coats. Sanitizer doesn't remove dirt either, so washing with soap and water is still best for visibly dirty hands.

mechanisms.title: Effects on the brain
mechanisms.chemical: When someone drinks alcohol, ethanol is absorbed from the stomach and small intestine into the blood. Because it dissolves in both water and fat, it easily crosses into the brain. There it changes how nerve cells communicate by acting on receptors, proteins that respond to chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. Ethanol boosts the activity of GABA-A receptors, which respond to GABA, the brain's main “calm down” signal, letting more negatively charged chloride ions into nerve cells and making them less likely to fire. At the same time, it blocks NMDA receptors, which respond to glutamate, the brain's main “go” signal.
mechanisms.biological: With nerve signals slowed, a person who drinks first feels relaxed and less inhibited, then loses coordination, balance and judgment. At high blood levels they can become confused, vomit, pass out or stop breathing. Blocking NMDA receptors also disrupts the formation of new memories, which explains alcohol “blackouts.” The brain keeps developing until the mid-20s, especially the prefrontal cortex, which handles planning and self-control, and studies suggest the teenage brain is more vulnerable to alcohol's effects on learning and memory. Ethanol also triggers the release of dopamine in the brain's reward circuits, which is part of why drinking can become a habit.

mechanisms.title: Drying skin
mechanisms.chemical: The outermost layer of skin, the stratum corneum, works like a brick wall. Flattened dead cells are the bricks, and a mixture of fats, including ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids, is the mortar. These fats keep water in and irritants out. Ethanol can dissolve some of these fats and carry them away as it evaporates, and its fast evaporation also briefly pulls water from the skin's surface. With repeated use, the “mortar” thins and the barrier becomes leaky.
mechanisms.biological: People who use hand sanitizer many times a day, such as nurses and doctors, can develop dry, rough, cracked hands. Interestingly, hospital studies have found that alcohol rubs containing moisturizers are often less irritating than frequent washing with soap and water, which strips skin fats too. That is why sanitizers add glycerin or other humectants, ingredients that attract and hold water in the skin. Cracked skin can harbor more bacteria and stings when sanitizer is applied, so using hand cream regularly helps. A true allergy to ethanol on the skin is rare.

reactions.title: Fermentation
reactions.summary: Fermentation is how yeasts, single-celled fungi, turn sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide when they don't have enough oxygen. With plenty of oxygen, yeast would burn sugar completely, which releases far more energy. Without it, they use fermentation as a backup to keep making a small amount of energy. People have used this process for thousands of years to make bread, beer and wine, long before anyone understood the chemistry. In the 1850s and 60s, Louis Pasteur showed that living yeast cells are responsible.

steps.name: Glycolysis
steps.text: Inside the yeast cell, a series of ten enzyme-driven reactions splits each glucose molecule, which has six carbons, into two molecules of pyruvate, which has three. This releases a little energy that the cell stores as ATP, its energy currency. Along the way, a helper molecule called NAD⁺ picks up electrons and becomes NADH.

steps.name: Decarboxylation
steps.text: An enzyme called pyruvate decarboxylase removes a carbon dioxide molecule from each pyruvate. That leaves acetaldehyde, a two-carbon molecule. The carbon dioxide escapes as gas bubbles.

steps.name: Reduction
steps.text: An enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase transfers electrons from NADH to acetaldehyde, turning it into ethanol. This regenerates NAD⁺. Without that recycling, glycolysis would stall, because the cell has only a limited supply of NAD⁺.

reactions.result: The carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise and gives beer and sparkling wine their fizz; in bread, the ethanol bakes off. Most yeasts stop working when ethanol reaches about 12 to 15 percent, because it becomes toxic to them, which is why stronger spirits must be distilled.

reactions.title: Metabolism in the liver
reactions.summary: When you drink alcohol, your body treats ethanol as a toxin and works to get rid of it, mainly in the liver. The liver breaks ethanol down in two steps, each controlled by a different enzyme. It can only process a limited amount per hour, roughly the alcohol in one standard drink or a little less, and nothing, not coffee or cold showers, speeds this up. The intermediate product, acetaldehyde, is more toxic than ethanol itself. How quickly a person clears it depends partly on their genes.

steps.name: Step 1
steps.text: Alcohol dehydrogenase, an enzyme in liver cells, removes two hydrogen atoms from ethanol, oxidizing it to acetaldehyde. The hydrogens are passed to NAD⁺, forming NADH. In people who drink heavily, another enzyme system, CYP2E1, takes on more of this work.

steps.name: Step 2
steps.text: Aldehyde dehydrogenase, mainly a form called ALDH2 found in mitochondria, oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetic acid, the same acid found in vinegar. This step normally happens quickly, keeping acetaldehyde levels low.

steps.name: Final
steps.text: The acetic acid is attached to a carrier molecule to form acetyl-CoA, which enters the same energy-producing pathways used for food. It ends up as carbon dioxide, which you breathe out, and water.

reactions.result: Acetaldehyde is toxic and carcinogenic. Many people of East Asian descent carry a less active form of ALDH2, so acetaldehyde builds up and causes facial flushing, nausea and a racing heart after drinking, along with a higher risk of esophageal cancer if they drink regularly.

regulatory.status: Hand sanitizers must contain 60–95% ethanol.
Denatured alcohol for cosmetics must contain bittering or denaturing agents to prevent drinking.
Alcoholic beverages are Group 1 carcinogens when consumed; topical use is not linked to cancer.

hazards.title: Flammable
hazards.summary: Ethanol is highly flammable, which is why hand sanitizers, alcohol sprays and perfumes carry flame warnings. Its vapor can catch fire from a spark, a candle, a gas stove or even static electricity. Fires have happened when people used sanitizer and then went near a flame before it had fully dried. Large stocks, such as those kept in hospitals and schools, are covered by fire-safety rules. Store alcohol-based products away from heat and flames, and let sanitizer dry completely before going near any flame.
hazards.chemical: A liquid's flash point is the lowest temperature at which it gives off enough vapor to form a mixture with air that can ignite. Pure ethanol's flash point is about 13 °C, below normal room temperature, so it is always releasing enough vapor to burn; a 70 percent solution's flash point is only slightly higher, at about 21 °C. When ethanol burns, it reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water, releasing a lot of heat. Its flame is pale blue and can be almost invisible in daylight. Ethanol vapor is also heavier than air, so it can pool low and drift toward a flame.
hazards.biological: The main danger from alcohol-based products isn't poisoning but burns from fire. Because the flame can be nearly invisible, a person may not realize their hands or clothes are burning until they feel pain. Burns from sanitizer fires have been reported, including in children who held sanitizer-covered hands near candles or stoves. Rubbing sanitizer in until the hands are completely dry, which takes about 20 seconds, lets the ethanol evaporate and removes the hazard. Spills should be wiped up and the area aired out before lighting anything.

hazards.title: Poisoning if swallowed
hazards.summary: Swallowing hand sanitizer is a real danger for young children, who may be drawn to fruity scents, bright colors or the gel's look. Most sanitizers contain 60 to 95 percent alcohol, far stronger than beer, wine or most spirits; a 70 percent sanitizer is nearly twice as strong as vodka. Even a small amount can give a toddler a dangerous blood alcohol level. Poison control centers receive many calls every year about children swallowing sanitizer. Store sanitizers out of reach and supervise young children who use them.
hazards.chemical: Ethanol is absorbed quickly from the stomach and intestines into the blood, where it depresses the central nervous system, the brain and spinal cord, slowing breathing and reflexes. In the liver, breaking down ethanol uses up NAD⁺, a helper molecule the liver also needs to make new glucose, a process called gluconeogenesis. Young children have only small stores of glycogen, the stored form of sugar. So when their glucose production stalls, their blood sugar can fall dangerously low. And because their bodies are small, the same amount of alcohol produces a much higher blood level in a child than in an adult.
hazards.biological: A child who swallows sanitizer may become drowsy, unsteady and confused, may vomit, or may become difficult to wake. Low blood sugar can cause seizures, and very high alcohol levels can slow breathing dangerously. Symptoms usually appear within 30 minutes to an hour. Anyone who suspects a child has swallowed sanitizer should call a poison control center right away, even if the child seems fine. With prompt treatment, most children recover fully.

hazards.title: Alcoholic drinks and cancer
hazards.summary: Drinking alcoholic beverages is a well-established cause of several cancers, including cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, liver, colon and breast. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies alcoholic beverages as a Group 1 carcinogen, its highest category, meaning there is strong evidence they cause cancer in humans. The risk rises with how much and how often a person drinks, and no level of drinking is known to be completely free of cancer risk. This concern applies to drinking alcohol. Using ethanol on the skin, in sanitizers or cosmetics, isn't linked to cancer.
hazards.chemical: When the body breaks down ethanol, the first product is acetaldehyde, a reactive molecule. Acetaldehyde can bind directly to DNA, forming DNA adducts, chemical attachments that cause errors when the DNA is copied. It can also damage the proteins that repair DNA. Breaking down ethanol also creates reactive oxygen species that cause oxidative damage. In addition, alcohol raises estrogen levels, which helps explain its link to breast cancer, and it acts as a solvent that helps other carcinogens, such as those in tobacco smoke, get into the cells of the mouth and throat.
hazards.biological: Over years, DNA damage that isn't repaired can lead to mutations, changes in the genes that control cell growth. If enough mutations build up, cells may begin dividing uncontrollably and form a cancer. People who both drink and smoke face a much higher risk of mouth and throat cancers than people who do only one. Skin products are different: very little ethanol is absorbed through the skin, and it evaporates quickly, so it isn't linked to cancer. Drinking less lowers the risk over time.

profile.dosage: Hand sanitizers contain about 60 to 95 percent alcohol; health agencies recommend at least 60 percent for it to work, and a coin-sized amount rubbed in until dry is enough. In cosmetics, ethanol, often listed as “alcohol denat.”, is used as a solvent and to help products dry quickly. Using it on the skin is low risk, while swallowing sanitizer can poison a young child, so keep it out of reach. For drinking, health authorities advise that less is better, and most countries set a minimum legal drinking age partly because alcohol is especially harmful to the developing brain.

myths.claim: Any alcohol in skincare ruins your skin barrier.
myths.consensus: High levels can be drying with frequent use, but low levels in well-formulated products have modest effects.

environment.notes: A volatile organic compound that contributes to smog formation.

synthesis.title: Fermentation and distillation
synthesis.summary: Fermentation is the oldest way of making ethanol, and it is still how alcoholic drinks and most fuel ethanol are made. The United States makes most of its fuel ethanol from corn, while Brazil uses sugar cane, and the ethanol is blended into gasoline. The sugar source varies: grapes for wine, barley for beer, and corn, wheat or potatoes for many spirits. Starchy grains first need their starch broken down into sugar by enzymes. Distillation is then used when a higher concentration is needed.
synthesis.mechanism: Yeast ferment sugar from sugar cane, corn or grain mash into a weak alcohol solution, usually around 10 to 15 percent ethanol. In distillation, this mixture is heated. Ethanol boils at 78 °C, lower than water's 100 °C, so the vapor that rises is richer in ethanol than the liquid left behind. The vapor is cooled and condensed back into a liquid with more ethanol, and repeating this many times, usually in a tall column, concentrates it to about 95 percent. In fuel plants, the leftover grain solids are sold as animal feed.
synthesis.significance: Ethanol and water form an azeotrope at about 95%, so ordinary distillation can't go higher. Fuel ethanol is dried the rest of the way with molecular sieves, materials with pores just the right size to trap water molecules.

synthesis.title: Hydration of ethylene
synthesis.summary: Some industrial ethanol isn't made by yeast at all but from ethylene, a gas obtained from petroleum and natural gas. This synthetic ethanol is chemically identical to fermented ethanol. It is mainly used as an industrial solvent and for making other chemicals, not in drinks. Whether this route or fermentation is cheaper depends on the prices of oil and crops. Scientists can tell the two kinds apart by measuring carbon-14, which is present in recently living plants but absent from fossil fuels.
synthesis.mechanism: Ethylene (C₂H₄) has a carbon–carbon double bond. It is mixed with steam and passed over a catalyst of phosphoric acid on a porous support, at about 300 °C and around 60 to 70 times atmospheric pressure. The acid gives a hydrogen ion to the double bond, creating a positively charged carbon, which a water molecule then attacks. When the water gives up a hydrogen ion, an –OH group is left on the carbon, forming ethanol. Only a small fraction of the ethylene reacts on each pass, so the unreacted gas is recycled many times.

citations.title: Vanillyl alcohol oxidase.
citations.abstract: This review presents a historical outline of the research on vanillyl alcohol oxidase (VAO) from Penicillium simplicissimum, one of the canonical members of the VAO/PCMH flavoprotein family. After describing its discovery and initial biochemical characterization, we discuss the physiological role, substrate scope, and catalytic mechanism of VAO, and review its three-dimensional structure and mechanism of covalent flavinylation. We also explain how protein engineering provided a deeper insight into the role of certain amino acid residues in determining the substrate specificity and enantioselectivity of the enzyme. Finally, we summarize recent computational studies about the migration of substrates and products through the enzyme's structure and the phylogenetic distribution of VAO and related enzymes.

citations.title: Transketolase: observations in alcohol-related brain damage research.
citations.abstract: Thiamin, or vitamin B1, is crucial for brain function. In its active form, thiamin pyrophosphate (TPP), it is a co-enzyme for several enzymes, including transketolase. Transketolase is an important enzyme in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), a pathway responsible for generating reducing equivalents, which is essential for energy transduction and for generating ribose for nucleic acid synthesis. Transketolase also links the PPP to glycolysis, allowing a cell to adapt to a variety of energy needs, depending on its environment. Abnormal transketolase expression and/or activity have been implicated in a number of diseases where thiamin availability is low, including Wernicke-Korsakoff's Syndrome and alcoholism. Yet, the precise mechanism by which this enzyme is involved in the pathophysiology of these disorders remains controversial.

citations.title: Facial and neck erythema associated with dupilumab treatment: A systematic review.
citations.abstract: Background: Neither dupilumab-associated facial erythema nor neck erythema was reported in phase 3 clinical trials for the treatment of atopic dermatitis, but there have been a number of reports of patients developing this adverse event in clinical practice. Objective: To outline all cases of reported dupilumab-associated facial or neck erythema to better characterize this adverse event, and identify potential etiologies and management strategies. Methods: A search was conducted on EMBASE and PubMed databases. Two independent reviewers identified relevant studies for inclusion and performed data extraction. Results: A total of 101 patients from 16 studies were reported to have dupilumab-associated facial or neck erythema. A total of 52 of 101 patients (52%) had baseline atopic dermatitis facial or neck involvement and 45 of 101 (45%) reported different cutaneous symptoms from preexisting atopic dermatitis, possibly suggesting a different etiology. Suggested etiologies included rosacea, allergic contact dermatitis, and head and neck dermatitis. Most commonly used treatments included topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and antifungal agents. In the 57 patients with data on the course of the adverse events, improvement was observed in 29, clearance in 4, no response in 16, and worsening in 8. A total of 11 of 101 patients (11%) discontinued dupilumab owing to this adverse event. Limitations: Limited diagnostic testing, nonstandardized data collection and reporting across studies, and reliance on retrospective case reports and case series. Conclusion: Some patients receiving dupilumab develop facial or neck erythema that differs from their usual atopic dermatitis symptoms. Prompt identification and empiric treatment may minimize distress and potential discontinuation of dupilumab owing to this adverse event.

citations.title: Corticosteroid allergy.
citations.abstract: Allergy to corticosteroids is becoming increasingly recognized. Diagnosis is difficult because of frequently false-negative patch tests. The optimum concentration and vehicle for patch testing with pure corticosteroid has still not been established. The patch test results of 19 patients with allergy to corticosteroids seen at the Skin and Cancer Foundation in Sydney, Australia, were analysed. It was found that patch testing with the patient's corticosteroid in the commercial cream base gave a greater yield of positive results than testing with the commercial corticosteroid ointment or with the pure corticosteroid in either petrolatum or in alcohol. Tixocortol pivalate, and to a lesser extent budesonide, were useful for detecting allergy to hydrocortisone, but not necessarily other corticosteroids. Delayed positive patch tests were often seen, showing the importance of carrying out a late reading. The repeat open application test (ROAT) with the patient's own corticosteroid was found to be a simple, useful diagnostic test.

citations.title: Alcohol-induced oxidative stress.
citations.abstract: Alcohol-induced oxidative stress is linked to the metabolism of ethanol involving both microsomal and mitochondrial systems. Ethanol metabolism is directly involved in the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS). These form an environment favourable to oxidative stress. Ethanol treatment results in the depletion of GSH levels and decreases antioxidant activity. It elevates malondialdehyde (MDA), hydroxyethyl radical (HER), and hydroxynonenal (HNE) protein adducts. These cause the modification of all biological structures and consequently result in serious malfunction of cells and tissues.

name: Isopropyl Alcohol
scoreRationale: Effective disinfectant and solvent, but flammable, irritating to eyes, and more toxic than ethanol if swallowed.
summary: Rubbing alcohol disinfects and cleans glass and electronics. It evaporates fast but is flammable and poisonous to drink.

physical.state: Clear, volatile liquid with sharp odor

overview: Isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol) is a three-carbon chain with its hydroxyl group on the middle carbon, which makes it a secondary alcohol. It's slightly less polar than ethanol, so it dissolves oils and residues well and evaporates quickly without streaks.
Rubbing alcohol is usually 70% isopropanol in water. Like ethanol, it denatures proteins, but it is more toxic if swallowed, because the liver converts it into acetone.
profile.function: Disinfects, dissolves oils and residues, and evaporates quickly without streaks.

mechanisms.title: Disinfecting
mechanisms.chemical: Like ethanol, isopropyl alcohol kills germs by denaturing proteins, making them unfold and lose their working shape, and by dissolving the fatty molecules in cell membranes. Water plays a key role. At around 70 percent, the water helps the alcohol soak through the cell wall and membrane, and water is itself needed for proteins to unfold properly. The water also slows evaporation, so the alcohol stays on a surface long enough to work. That is why 70 percent is usually the best concentration for disinfecting.
mechanisms.biological: Seventy percent isopropyl alcohol inactivates most bacteria and enveloped viruses within seconds to minutes, which is why it is used to wipe skin before injections and to clean medical equipment. Higher concentrations, 91 to 99 percent, evaporate too fast and are thought to harden the proteins on the outside of a bacterial cell into a protective shell that spares the inside. Isopropanol is somewhat better than ethanol against some bacteria but weaker against viruses without a fatty envelope. Like ethanol, it can't kill bacterial spores. High-purity 99 percent isopropanol is preferred for cleaning electronics because it contains so little water.

mechanisms.title: Cooling skin
mechanisms.chemical: Turning a liquid into a gas takes energy, called the heat of vaporization. When isopropyl alcohol evaporates from skin, it takes that energy from the skin in the form of heat. Because it evaporates much faster than water, it pulls heat away quickly. This is the same reason sweating cools you down, only faster. The chill is noticeable within seconds.
mechanisms.biological: Skin feels cold, which is why rubbing alcohol feels chilly and why it was once used in sponge baths to bring down fevers. Doctors no longer recommend this. Children can absorb isopropyl alcohol through their skin and breathe in its vapor, especially when it is applied over a large area, and some have been poisoned this way. Rapid cooling can also cause shivering, which actually raises body temperature. Fever is better treated with fever-reducing medicines and fluids, following a doctor's advice.

mechanisms.title: Metabolized to acetone
mechanisms.chemical: Isopropyl alcohol is a secondary alcohol, meaning its –OH group sits on a carbon attached to two other carbons. In the liver, the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase removes two hydrogen atoms from it, converting it into acetone, a ketone with a C=O group. Unlike the acetaldehyde made from ethanol, acetone can't easily be oxidized further into an acid. Instead, it lingers in the body and is slowly breathed out or removed in urine. That explains why isopropanol poisoning looks different from poisoning with other alcohols.
mechanisms.biological: Both isopropanol and acetone depress the central nervous system, so poisoning causes drowsiness, confusion, poor coordination and, at high doses, coma. Isopropanol is roughly twice as potent as ethanol in its effect on the brain, and its effects last longer because acetone hangs around. Acetone also gives the breath a fruity smell. Unlike methanol and antifreeze, which are converted into toxic acids, isopropanol doesn't cause severe acidosis, a dangerous buildup of acid in the blood. It does irritate the stomach, causing pain and vomiting, sometimes with bleeding.

reactions.title: Hydration of propene
reactions.summary: Isopropyl alcohol is made by adding water across the double bond of propene, a three-carbon gas from petroleum, in what is called a hydration reaction. Because propene isn't symmetrical, water could in principle add in two ways: the –OH group could end up on the middle carbon or on an end carbon. A rule described by the Russian chemist Vladimir Markovnikov in 1870 predicts which one forms. The answer depends on which intermediate is more stable. This reaction is a staple of high school and college chemistry.

steps.name: Protonation
steps.text: An acid catalyst gives a hydrogen ion (H⁺) to propene's double bond. The hydrogen attaches to the end carbon, leaving the positive charge on the middle carbon, which forms the more stable secondary carbocation (Markovnikov's rule). It is more stable because its two neighboring carbon groups push electrons toward the positive charge, helping to share the burden.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: A water molecule, whose oxygen has spare pairs of electrons, is drawn to the positively charged middle carbon. The oxygen forms a bond with that carbon. For a moment, the oxygen carries the positive charge.

steps.name: Deprotonation
steps.text: The oxygen gives up one of its hydrogen ions, which returns to the catalyst so it can be reused. That leaves a neutral –OH group on the middle carbon. The product is isopropanol.

reactions.result: Markovnikov's rule predicts that the –OH ends up on the middle carbon rather than the end, which is why this reaction gives propan-2-ol rather than propan-1-ol. The rule is a shortcut for remembering that reactions follow the path through the most stable intermediate.

reactions.title: Oxidation to acetone
reactions.summary: Oxidizing an alcohol means removing hydrogen atoms from it, and what happens next depends on the type of alcohol. Primary alcohols, with the –OH on an end carbon, oxidize to aldehydes and then on to carboxylic acids. Secondary alcohols like isopropanol oxidize to ketones and stop there. Tertiary alcohols, whose –OH carbon is attached to three other carbons, resist oxidation altogether. This reaction happens both in the laboratory and in the human liver.

steps.name: Oxidation
steps.text: An oxidizing agent in the lab, such as acidified potassium dichromate, or the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase in the body, removes two hydrogen atoms. One comes from the –OH group and one from the carbon it is attached to. In the body, the hydrogens are handed to the helper molecule NAD⁺.

steps.name: Carbonyl
steps.text: With those two hydrogens gone, the carbon and oxygen form a double bond, so the C–OH becomes a C=O group, called a carbonyl. A carbonyl on a middle carbon makes the molecule a ketone. Here the product is acetone, the solvent in many nail polish removers.

steps.name: Stops there
steps.text: Ketones resist further oxidation, unlike aldehydes. To be oxidized again, the carbonyl carbon would need a hydrogen attached, and in a ketone it has only carbon neighbors. Breaking a carbon–carbon bond takes much harsher conditions.

reactions.result: This is the same reaction your liver performs, and a classic way to tell primary from secondary alcohols. In school labs, orange dichromate turns green when it oxidizes a primary or secondary alcohol, while a tertiary alcohol leaves it orange.

regulatory.status: Antiseptic hand rubs may contain 70–91.3% isopropyl alcohol.
Danger: highly flammable (H225), causes serious eye irritation (H319), may cause drowsiness (H336).

hazards.title: Flammable
hazards.summary: Isopropyl alcohol is highly flammable, and its vapor ignites easily at room temperature. Rubbing alcohol, alcohol wipes and some cleaning sprays all carry fire risks. Fires have started when people used it near candles, stoves, heaters or cigarettes, or when vapor built up in a closed space. Like ethanol, it burns with a pale flame that can be hard to see. Store it somewhere cool, away from heat and flames, and use it in a ventilated area.
hazards.chemical: Isopropanol's flash point is about 12 °C for the pure liquid and around 20 °C for a 70 percent solution, at or below room temperature, so there is always enough vapor above it to catch fire. Its vapor is about twice as heavy as air, so it can pool near the floor and travel some distance to a flame. Air containing roughly 2 to 12 percent isopropanol vapor can burn. When it burns, it reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water, releasing a lot of heat. A spark of static electricity can be enough to ignite it.
hazards.biological: The main injuries from isopropyl alcohol fires are burns to the skin, hands or face. Because the flame can be nearly invisible, people may not notice something is burning. Keep it away from flames and sparks, and don't use it near heaters. When cleaning electronics, let it evaporate completely before switching them back on. Wipe up large spills, air out the room and keep containers tightly closed.

hazards.title: Poisoning if swallowed
hazards.summary: Isopropyl alcohol is more toxic than ethanol, so swallowing it is more dangerous than swallowing the same amount of drinking alcohol. Young children may drink rubbing alcohol by mistake, and some people drink it as a substitute for alcoholic drinks. Rubbing alcohol is usually 70 to 91 percent isopropanol, so even a small amount is concentrated. For a small child, as little as about 1 milliliter per kilogram of body weight, a couple of teaspoons for a toddler, can be dangerous. If someone swallows it, call a poison control center right away.
hazards.chemical: Isopropanol is absorbed quickly from the gut, and it can also be absorbed through skin or breathed in as vapor. It depresses the central nervous system more strongly than ethanol, and its metabolite acetone adds to the effect. Because acetone is cleared slowly, the effects can last a day or more. Isopropanol also irritates the lining of the stomach. In severe poisoning, it can lower blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels and weakening the heart's pumping.
hazards.biological: Symptoms include drowsiness, dizziness, slurred speech, unsteady walking, vomiting and stomach pain, and the breath may smell fruity from acetone. Severe poisoning can cause coma, slowed breathing and low blood pressure, which can be fatal. Doctors give supportive care, such as fluids and help with breathing, and in severe cases use dialysis to filter it from the blood. Because it doesn't cause severe acid buildup, the outlook with treatment is generally good. Keeping rubbing alcohol out of children's reach prevents most poisonings.

profile.dosage: Rubbing alcohol is usually 70 percent isopropanol, with 91 and 99 percent versions sold for cleaning, and 70 percent is the most effective for disinfecting. Alcohol prep pads used before injections are also about 70 percent. It is meant only for skin and surfaces, never for drinking, and shouldn't be used for sponge baths. For a small child, swallowing as little as about 1 milliliter per kilogram of body weight can be dangerous. Use it in well-ventilated areas, away from flames.

myths.claim: Higher-percentage alcohol always disinfects better.
myths.consensus: 70% often works better than 91–99% because water helps it penetrate cells.

synthesis.title: Hydration of propene
synthesis.summary: Isopropyl alcohol is made from propene, a gas produced when petroleum is refined and cracked. Propene was once a nuisance byproduct of refineries, and turning it into isopropanol was one of the first ways chemists made useful chemicals from petroleum. Millions of tonnes are made every year. Most goes into solvents, disinfectants and the manufacture of other chemicals. A smaller amount is made by adding hydrogen to acetone.
synthesis.mechanism: There are two main methods. In the older indirect method, propene reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to form sulfate esters, molecules in which the propyl group is attached to the acid, and water is then added to split them, releasing isopropanol. In the direct method, propene and steam are passed over a solid acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure, adding water across the double bond in a single step. Either way, the –OH ends up on the middle carbon, as Markovnikov's rule predicts. The crude mixture of alcohol and water is then purified by distillation.
synthesis.significance: First produced commercially in 1920, isopropanol is considered the first petrochemical.

citations.title: Isopropanol poisoning.
citations.abstract: Introduction: Isopropanol is a clear, colorless liquid with a fruity odor and a mild bitter taste. Most commonly found domestically as rubbing alcohol, isopropanol is also found in numerous household and commercial products including cleaners, disinfectants, antifreezes, cosmetics, solvents, inks, and pharmaceuticals. Aim: The aim of this review is to critically review the epidemiology, toxicokinetics, mechanisms of toxicity, clinical features, diagnosis, and management of isopropanol poisoning. Methods: OVID MEDLINE and ISI Web of Science were searched to November 2013 using the words "isopropanol", "isopropyl alcohol", "2-propanol", "propan-2-ol", and "rubbing alcohol" combined with the keywords "poisoning", "poison", "toxicity", "ingestion", "adverse effects", "overdose", or "intoxication". These searches identified 232 citations, which were then screened via their abstract to identify relevant articles referring specifically to the epidemiology, toxicokinetics, mechanisms of toxicity, clinical features, diagnosis, and management of isopropanol poisoning; 102 were relevant. Further information was obtained from book chapters, relevant news reports, and internet resources. These additional searches produced eight non-duplicate relevant citations. Epidemiology: The majority of isopropanol exposures are unintentional and occur in children less than 6 years of age. Although isopropanol poisoning appears to be a reasonably common occurrence, deaths are rare. Toxicokinetics: Isopropanol is rapidly absorbed following ingestion with peak plasma concentrations occurring within 30 min. It can also be absorbed following inhalation or dermal exposure. Isopropanol is widely distributed with a volume of distribution of 0.45-0.55 L/kg. Isopropanol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetone, acetol and methylglyoxal, propylene glycol, acetate, and formate with conversion of these metabolites to glucose and other products of intermediary metabolism. The elimination of isopropanol is predominantly renal, though some pulmonary excretion of isopropanol and acetone occurs. In one case 20% of the absorbed dose was eliminated unchanged in urine, with the remainder excreted as acetone and metabolites of acetone. The elimination half-life of isopropanol is between 2.5 and 8.0 h, whereas elimination of acetone is slower with a half-life following isopropanol ingestion of between 7.7 and 27 h. Mechanisms of toxicity: While the exact mechanism of action of isopropanol has not been fully elucidated, brain stem depression is thought to be the predominant mechanism. While the clinical effects are thought to be mostly due to isopropanol, acetone may also contribute. Clinical features: The major features of severe poisoning are due to CNS and respiratory depression, shock, and circulatory collapse. The most common metabolic effects are an increased osmol (osmolal) gap, ketonemia, and ketonuria. Diagnosis. Poisoning can be diagnosed using the measurement of isopropanol serum concentrations, though these may not be readily available. Diagnosis is therefore more typically made on the basis of the patient's history and clinical presentation. An osmol gap, ketonemia, and/or ketonuria without metabolic acidosis, along with a fruity or sweet odor on the breath and CNS depression support the diagnosis. Management. Supportive care is the mainstay of management with primary emphasis on respiratory and cardiovascular support. Hemodialysis enhances elimination of isopropanol and acetone and should be considered in very severe poisoning. Conclusions: Severe isopropanol poisoning results in CNS and respiratory depression and circulatory collapse. Treatment primarily consists of symptom-directed supportive care. Although hemodialysis increases the elimination of isopropanol and acetone substantially, it should only be considered in severe life-threatening poisonings. Patients usually make a full recovery provided they receive prompt supportive care. Antiseptics are chemical agents applied to the skin to reduce the microbial count and reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs). SSIs are defined as an infection occurring at the surgical site within 30 days of the procedure and represent one of the most common complications of dermatologic surgery. Broad-spectrum antiseptics generally cover more pathogens and subsequently are some of the most popular in dermatologic surgery. Antiseptic agents in dermatologic surgery commonly include chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, chloroxylenol, isopropyl alcohol, hexachlorophene, benzalkonium chloride, and hydrogen peroxide. They should be used for most, if not all, procedures that enter the dermis of the skin or deeper. This activity outlines the indications, mechanism of action, methods of administration, important adverse effects, contraindications, and monitoring of skin antiseptics, so providers can direct patient therapy where they are indicated as part of the interprofessional team.

citations.title: Toxic Alcohols.
citations.abstract: This article reviews the background, metabolism, clinical effects, and treatment of toxic alcohols, specifically ethylene glycol, methanol, diethylene glycol, propylene glycol, and isopropyl alcohol. This article also reviews the importance of an anion gap metabolic acidosis in relation to toxic alcohols and explores both the utility and the limitations of the osmole gap in patient management.

citations.title: Toxic Alcohol Poisoning.
citations.abstract: This article reviews the background, metabolism, clinical effects, and treatment of toxic alcohols, specifically ethylene glycol, methanol, diethylene glycol, propylene glycol, and isopropyl alcohol. This article also reviews the importance of an anion gap metabolic acidosis in relation to toxic alcohols and explores both the utility and the limitations of the osmol gap in patient management.

name: Ammonia
scoreRationale: Corrosive, irritating to airways, and forms toxic gases when mixed with bleach.
summary: Ammonia cuts grease and leaves glass streak-free. Its fumes irritate lungs, and it must never be mixed with bleach.

physical.solubility: Ammonia is highly soluble in water

overview: Household ammonia is ammonia gas (NH₃) dissolved in water. Ammonia is a pyramid-shaped molecule with a lone pair of electrons on its nitrogen; that lone pair grabs protons from water, forming ammonium (NH₄⁺) and hydroxide (OH⁻) ions, so the solution is alkaline (pH about 11–12).

Because ammonia is volatile, it evaporates completely from glass and leaves no residue, the secret behind streak-free window cleaners. The same volatility explains why its sharp smell reaches your nose so quickly.
profile.function: Removes grease and evaporates without residue in glass cleaners; opens hair cuticles in permanent hair dyes.

mechanisms.title: Streak-free grease cutting
mechanisms.chemical: Household ammonia cleaners make water alkaline: ammonia (NH₃) takes hydrogen ions from water and leaves hydroxide ions (OH⁻) behind. These hydroxide ions break down thin, greasy films, such as fingerprints and cooking residue, partly by saponification, turning fats into soap-like molecules that dissolve in water. Ammonia itself is a gas at room temperature, so as the cleaner dries, the ammonia evaporates along with the water. Many glass cleaners also contain a little alcohol to speed drying. Unlike soap or detergent, nothing solid is left behind.
mechanisms.biological: Windows and mirrors are left clean, with nothing behind to leave streaks. Soaps and detergents often leave a thin residue that dries into visible smears, which is why ammonia became a favorite in glass cleaners. The same property makes it useful on chrome and stainless steel. However, ammonia can damage some surfaces, such as tinted car windows and certain painted or coated finishes. Its strong smell is the price of its streak-free results.

mechanisms.title: Irritating the airways
mechanisms.chemical: Ammonia is extremely soluble in water: a single liter of water can dissolve hundreds of liters of ammonia gas. When ammonia vapor reaches the moist surfaces of the eyes, nose and throat, it dissolves at once in that moisture. There it reacts with water to form ammonium ions and hydroxide ions, making the surface strongly alkaline. The hydroxide ions damage the fats and proteins of the cells lining these tissues. Because ammonia dissolves so readily, most of it is caught in the upper airways before it can reach deep into the lungs.
mechanisms.biological: This causes burning eyes, a stinging nose, coughing and watery eyes. We can smell ammonia at about 5 parts per million (ppm), well below harmful levels; workplace air limits are set at about 25 to 50 ppm. So the sharp smell works as a built-in warning, prompting people to leave before damage occurs. At very high levels, as in industrial accidents, ammonia can cause severe burns to the airways and lungs. People with asthma may react to even low levels.

mechanisms.title: Opening hair for dye
mechanisms.chemical: Each hair is covered by a cuticle, overlapping layers of flat cells arranged like roof shingles that protect the inner part, called the cortex. Permanent hair dyes contain ammonia, which raises the pH to around 9 to 11. At this high pH, the cuticle swells and its scales lift slightly, opening gaps. Ammonia also activates hydrogen peroxide, the other half of a permanent dye kit. Together they let chemicals get inside the hair shaft.
mechanisms.biological: With the cuticle opened, small dye-precursor molecules and hydrogen peroxide can enter the cortex. The peroxide lightens the hair's natural pigment, melanin, and also makes the small dye molecules link together into larger colored molecules. These are too big to escape back through the cuticle, so the color is permanent and lasts until the hair grows out. Repeated dyeing damages the cuticle, leaving hair dry and brittle. “Ammonia-free” dyes usually use a related chemical called ethanolamine, which does the same job with less smell.

reactions.title: Acting as a base
reactions.summary: Ammonia makes water alkaline by acting as a base, a substance that accepts hydrogen ions (H⁺). This comes from the structure of the ammonia molecule. Ammonia has one nitrogen atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms, arranged like a short pyramid, plus a spare pair of electrons on the nitrogen. That pair of electrons is free to form a new bond. This reaction is why a bottle of ammonia solution is often labeled “ammonium hydroxide.”

steps.name: Lone pair
steps.text: Nitrogen has five outer electrons. Three are shared with hydrogen atoms in bonds, and the other two form an unshared pair, called a lone pair. A lone pair is attracted to positive charges such as hydrogen ions.

steps.name: Proton grab
steps.text: When ammonia meets water, its lone pair forms a bond with one of water's hydrogen atoms and pulls it away as a hydrogen ion. The nitrogen now holds four hydrogens and carries a positive charge. This is an ammonium ion (NH₄⁺).

steps.name: Hydroxide
steps.text: The water molecule that lost a hydrogen ion keeps the electrons from that bond, becoming a hydroxide ion (OH⁻). Hydroxide ions are what make a solution alkaline. The more there are, the higher the pH.

reactions.result: Only a small fraction reacts at any moment (ammonia is a weak base), but enough to give pH 11–12. Because the reaction is reversible, ammonia can turn back into gas and escape, which is why an open bottle slowly loses strength while its smell fills the room.

reactions.title: Chloramines (never mix with bleach)
reactions.summary: Mixing ammonia with bleach produces chloramines, toxic gases that irritate the eyes and lungs. It is one of the most common dangerous mixing accidents at home. It can happen when someone uses an ammonia glass cleaner after cleaning with bleach, or mixes the two thinking it will make a stronger cleaner. Bleach can also react with urine in toilets or litter boxes, because urine contains ammonia-related compounds. The reaction starts immediately.

steps.name: Mixing
steps.text: Ammonia (NH₃) meets sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) from bleach. Hypochlorite, and the hypochlorous acid it forms in water, holds a chlorine atom that is easily handed to other molecules.

steps.name: Substitution
steps.text: Chlorine atoms replace hydrogen atoms on ammonia. One swap gives monochloramine (NH₂Cl); with more bleach, dichloramine (NHCl₂) and nitrogen trichloride (NCl₃) can form. Which ones form depends on the ratio of bleach to ammonia and on the pH.

steps.name: Toxic vapors
steps.text: Chloramines evaporate easily and escape into the air. In a small, closed space such as a bathroom, they can quickly reach harmful levels.

reactions.result: Chloramine vapors cause coughing, chest pain and breathing problems. If you are exposed, leave the area, get fresh air and call a poison control center; never mix bleach with any other cleaner.

regulatory.status: Danger: causes severe skin burns (H314), may cause respiratory irritation (H335), very toxic to aquatic life (H400).
Workplace exposure limit 50 ppm (8-hour average).

hazards.title: Corrosive when concentrated
hazards.summary: Household ammonia is 5–10%; industrial solutions are much stronger, often 25 to 30 percent, and can cause severe burns. Even household strength can irritate skin and seriously irritate the eyes. Most home injuries come from splashes in the eyes or from breathing vapor in poorly ventilated spaces. Gloves protect the skin during heavy cleaning. Keep ammonia in its original container, out of children's reach.
hazards.chemical: Ammonia solutions are alkaline because they contain hydroxide ions, which damage proteins and lipids on contact. Hydroxide breaks down the fats in cell membranes by saponification and makes proteins unfold. Like other alkalis, ammonia causes liquefactive necrosis, a kind of damage in which tissue softens and liquefies, letting the chemical sink deeper. Ammonia gas also dissolves into the moisture on skin, eyes and airways, forming hydroxide right on the tissue. Concentrated solutions release large amounts of gas, adding a breathing hazard.
hazards.biological: Concentrated ammonia burns skin and eyes; use household strength with ventilation. On skin, household ammonia can cause redness and irritation, while concentrated ammonia causes burns and blisters. In the eyes, it can damage the cornea, and because alkali burns keep penetrating, injuries can be severe unless the eye is rinsed immediately for at least 15 minutes. Swallowing ammonia burns the mouth, throat and esophagus. Breathing concentrated vapor can damage the airways and cause fluid to build up in the lungs.

hazards.title: Toxic gas with bleach
hazards.summary: Never combine ammonia and bleach. Together they form chloramines, toxic gases that can cause serious lung injury. The mistake often happens by accident, for example when a bathroom is cleaned with bleach and then with a glass cleaner, or when bleach is used to clean up urine. Poison control centers handle many such cases every year. Using one cleaner at a time and rinsing surfaces between products prevents it.
hazards.chemical: Chloramines form immediately: chlorine atoms move from hypochlorite to ammonia, replacing its hydrogens and forming compounds such as monochloramine (NH₂Cl). They evaporate readily and fill the air. Once breathed in, they dissolve in the moist lining of the airways. There they break down into reactive chemicals, including hypochlorous acid and ammonia, which damage cell membranes and proteins. The stronger the mixture and the smaller the room, the higher the exposure.
hazards.biological: Inhaling them inflames the lungs and can cause fluid buildup. Symptoms include coughing, shortness of breath, chest pain, watery eyes and wheezing. In serious cases, fluid fills the lungs' tiny air sacs, a condition called pulmonary edema, which can appear hours after exposure and can be life-threatening. People with asthma or other lung conditions are especially at risk. Anyone exposed should get to fresh air immediately and seek medical help if symptoms continue.

profile.dosage: Household ammonia cleaners contain about 5 to 10 percent ammonia, while industrial solutions are around 25 to 30 percent and far more dangerous. Most people can smell ammonia at about 5 parts per million, well below the 25 to 50 ppm limits set for workplace air, so a strong smell is a signal to ventilate. Permanent hair dyes contain a few percent, and the EU caps ammonia in cosmetics at 6 percent. Never mix ammonia with bleach, and use it with windows open or a fan running.

myths.claim: Mixing ammonia and bleach makes a stronger cleaner.
myths.consensus: It makes toxic chloramine gas; never combine them.

environment.persistence: Low; converted by bacteria to nitrate.
environment.biodegradability: Nitrified by soil and water bacteria.

synthesis.title: The Haber–Bosch process
synthesis.summary: Almost all ammonia is made by the Haber–Bosch process, developed in Germany in the early 1900s by the chemist Fritz Haber and the engineer Carl Bosch. It takes nitrogen, which makes up 78 percent of the air but is very unreactive, and turns it into a useful compound. Before this, the main sources of nitrogen for fertilizer were natural deposits such as Chilean saltpeter and bird droppings called guano. Today well over 150 million tonnes of ammonia are made each year, mostly for fertilizer. The process uses roughly 1 to 2 percent of the world's energy.
synthesis.mechanism: Hydrogen is made from natural gas, mostly methane, by reacting it with steam, while nitrogen comes from the air. The two gases are compressed to very high pressure, roughly 100 to 300 times atmospheric pressure, and passed over an iron-based catalyst at 400 to 450 °C. Nitrogen's triple bond is one of the strongest in chemistry, and the catalyst's surface helps break it, letting nitrogen atoms combine with hydrogen. Only part of the gas reacts on each pass, so the ammonia is cooled until it condenses into a liquid, and the leftover gases are recycled. For household cleaners, the ammonia is then dissolved in water.
synthesis.significance: Ammonia made this way feeds roughly half the world's population through fertilizer; Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch both won Nobel Prizes for it.

citations.title: Urea cycle disorders-update.
citations.abstract: The urea cycle is a metabolic pathway for the disposal of excess nitrogen, which arises primarily as ammonia. Nitrogen is essential for growth and life-maintenance, but excessive ammonia leads to life-threatening conditions. The urea cycle disorders (UCDs) comprise diseases presenting with hyperammonemia that arise in either the neonatal period (about 50% of cases) or later. Congenital defects of the enzymes or transporters of the urea cycle cause the disease. This cycle utilizes five enzymes, two of which, carbamoylphosphate synthetase 1 and ornithine transcarbamylase are present in the mitochondrial matrix, whereas the others (argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase and arginase 1) are present in the cytoplasm. In addition, N-acetylglutamate synthase and at least two transporter proteins are essential to urea cycle function. Severity and age of onset depend on residual enzyme or transporter function and are related to the respective gene mutations. The strategy for therapy is to prevent the irreversible toxicity of high-ammonia exposure to the brain. The pathogenesis and natural course are poorly understood because of the rarity of the disease, so an international registry system and novel clinical trials are much needed. We review here the current concepts of the pathogenesis, diagnostics, including genetics and treatment of UCDs.

citations.title: Neurobiology of ammonia.
citations.abstract: Hyperammonemia resulting from inherited urea cycle enzyme deficiencies or liver failure results in severe central nervous system dysfunction including brain edema, convulsions and coma. Neuropathologic evaluation in these disorders reveals characteristic alterations of astrocyte morphology ranging from cell swelling (acute hyperammonemia) to Alzheimer Type II astrocytosis (chronic hyperammonemia). Having no effective urea cycle, brain relies on glutamine synthesis for the removal of excess ammonia and the enzyme responsible, glutamine synthetase, has a predominantly astrocytic localization. Accumulation of ammonia in brain results in a redistribution of cerebral blood flow and metabolism from cortical to sub-cortical structures. In addition to changes in astrocyte morphology, increased brain ammonia concentrations result in alterations in expression of key astrocyte proteins including glial fibrillary acidic protein, glutamate and glycine transporters and "peripheral-type" (mitochondrial) benzodiazepine receptors. Such changes result in alterations of astrocytic volume and increased extracellular concentrations of excitatory and inhibitory substances. In addition, the ammonium ion has direct effects on excitatory-inhibitory transmission via distinct mechanisms involving cellular chloride extrusion and postsynaptic receptor function. Acute ammonia exposure leads to activation of NMDA receptors and their signal transduction pathways. Chronic hyperammonemia also results in increased concentrations of neuroactive L-tryptophan metabolites including serotonin and quinolinic acid. Therapy in hyperammonemic syndromes continues to rely on ammonia-lowering strategies via peripheral mechanisms (reduction of ammonia production in the gastrointestinal tract, increased ammonia removal by muscle).

citations.title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis exaggerates ammonia-induced tracheal injury Via TLR4 signaling pathway.
citations.abstract: Ammonia is a toxic air pollutant that causes severe respiratory tract injury in animals and humans. Gut microbiota dysbiosis has been found to be involved in the development of respiratory tract injury induced by air pollutants, however, the specific mechanism requires investigation. Here, we found that, inhaled ammonia induced tracheal injury by reducing expression of claudin-1, increasing expression of muc5ac, TLR4, MyD88, NF-κB and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and IL-10), and also altering tracheal microbiota composition. Spearman correlation analysis indicated that gut microbiota dysbiosis positively correlated with TLR4 level in the trachea. Antibiotic depletion intestinal microbiota treatment reduced the severity of ammonia-induced tracheal injury via TLR4 signaling pathway. Microbiota transplantation induced the tracheal injury via TLR4 signaling pathway even without the ammonia exposure. These results indicate that gut microbiota dysbiosis exaggerates ammonia-induced tracheal injury via TLR4 signaling pathway. In addition, the [Ruminococcus]_torques_group, Faecalibacterium, unclassified_f_Lachnospiraceae may be the key gut microbiota contributing to the alterations of tracheal microbiota composition.

citations.title: Ammonia-Induced Glial-Inflammaging.
citations.abstract: Astrocytes are functionally diverse glial cells that maintain blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, provide metabolic and trophic support, and react to pathogens or harmful stimuli through inflammatory response. Impairment of astrocyte functions has been implicated in hepatic encephalopathy (HE), a neurological complication associated with hyperammonemia. Although hyperammonemia is more common in adults, ammonia gliotoxicity has been mainly studied in cultured astrocytes derived from neonate animals. However, these cells can sense and respond to stimuli in different ways from astrocytes obtained from adult animals. Thus, the aim of this study was to investigate the direct effects of ammonia on astrocyte cultures obtained from adult rats compared with those obtained from neonate rats. Our main findings pointed that ammonia increased the gene expression of proteins associated with BBB permeability, in addition to cause an inflammatory response and decrease the release of trophic factors, which were dependent on p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK)/nuclear factor κB (NFκB) pathways and aquaporin 4, in both neonatal and mature astrocytes. Considering the age, mature astrocytes presented an overall increase of the expression of inflammatory signaling components and a decrease of the expression of cytoprotective pathways, compared with neonatal astrocytes. Importantly, ammonia exposure in mature astrocytes potentiated the expression of the senescence marker p21, inflammatory response, activation of p38 MAPK/NFκB pathways, and the decrease of cytoprotective pathways. In this regard, ammonia can trigger and/or accelerate the inflammaging of mature astrocytes, a phenomenon characterized by an age-related chronic and low-grade inflammation, which may be implicated in HE neurological symptoms.
