name: Vinegar
scoreRationale: Household vinegar is low hazard and biodegradable; concentrated acetic acid is corrosive.
summary: Vinegar (dilute acetic acid) dissolves mineral scale, cuts soap scum and flavors food. It's one of the gentlest cleaners.

physical.state: Clear liquid (5% in table vinegar, 6–10% in cleaning vinegar)

overview: Acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is a two-carbon carboxylic acid: a methyl group attached to a –COOH group. It's a weak acid (pKa 4.76), so in vinegar, which is about 5% acetic acid, only a small fraction of molecules release their proton at any moment.

Pure acetic acid freezes at 16.6 °C into ice-like crystals, which is why it's called glacial acetic acid. Vinegar's sharp smell is acetic acid evaporating; its cleaning power comes from dissolving the alkaline mineral deposits left by hard water.
profile.function: Dissolves limescale and soap scum, deodorizes, and adds sourness and preservation to foods.

mechanisms.title: Dissolving limescale
mechanisms.chemical: Limescale, the chalky white crust in kettles, on faucets and around showerheads, is mostly calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) left behind when hard water evaporates. Calcium carbonate is a base, and it doesn't dissolve in plain water. The acetic acid in vinegar gives hydrogen ions to the carbonate ions, turning them into carbonic acid, which quickly breaks down into water and carbon dioxide gas. The calcium is left as calcium acetate, which does dissolve in water. Soap scum, made of calcium salts of fatty acids, is loosened by the acid in a similar way.
mechanisms.biological: Kettle scale, faucet crust and soap scum loosen and rinse away. You can often see small bubbles of carbon dioxide forming as the reaction runs. Thick deposits may need several hours of soaking. Vinegar shouldn't be used on natural stone such as marble or limestone countertops, which are also made of calcium carbonate and will be etched. With long contact, it can also damage grout and some metal finishes.

mechanisms.title: Preserving food
mechanisms.chemical: Acetic acid is a weak acid, so in vinegar most of its molecules keep their hydrogen and carry no electric charge. Uncharged molecules can slip through the fatty membranes of bacteria and molds, which charged ions can't easily cross. Inside the microbe, where the pH is close to neutral, the acetic acid releases its hydrogen ion, acidifying the cell's interior and leaving acetate ions trapped inside. The microbe then has to spend energy pumping hydrogen ions back out to survive. This trick works because the inside and outside of the cell have different pH levels.
mechanisms.biological: With its interior acidified and its energy drained, a microbe's enzymes stop working properly and it can't grow or multiply. Spoilage and disease-causing bacteria can't grow in pickles and other vinegar-preserved foods. Pickled foods are made acidic enough, at a pH of 4.6 or lower, to stop the growth of Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium behind botulism, a rare but deadly food poisoning. That is why tested canning recipes must be followed carefully. Vinegar doesn't kill every microbe, but it keeps them from multiplying.

mechanisms.title: Blood sugar after meals
mechanisms.chemical: Researchers think acetic acid may affect blood sugar in a few ways. It may slow gastric emptying, the rate at which food passes from the stomach into the small intestine, where most sugar is absorbed. It may also reduce the activity of gut enzymes that break starch and table sugar into glucose, and it may help muscles take up glucose from the blood. Together, these effects would slow the rate at which glucose enters the bloodstream. The exact mechanisms haven't been fully worked out.
mechanisms.biological: Small human trials found that a tablespoon or two of vinegar taken with a meal high in carbohydrates modestly lowered the rise in blood sugar afterward, in both healthy people and people with type 2 diabetes. The effect is modest, and vinegar is no replacement for medical treatment. Drinking vinegar straight can irritate the throat and wear away tooth enamel, so it is best diluted or used in food, such as salad dressing. Larger, longer studies are needed to know whether regular vinegar use improves long-term health. People taking diabetes medicines should talk to a doctor before changing their routine.

reactions.title: Dissolving limescale
reactions.summary: Vinegar dissolves limescale through an acid–carbonate reaction, one of the most common reactions in chemistry. Acids react with carbonates to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. It is the same reaction that makes baking soda and vinegar fizz in a model volcano, and the reason acid rain slowly dissolves marble statues. In cleaning, it turns a hard, insoluble crust into a dissolved salt. With vinegar it is slower than with stronger acids, because acetic acid is weak.

steps.name: Proton transfer
steps.text: Acetic acid molecules donate hydrogen ions (H⁺) to the carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) in the scale. Each carbonate ion can accept two. The acetic acid molecules become acetate ions.

steps.name: Carbonic acid
steps.text: A carbonate ion that has gained two hydrogen ions becomes carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). Carbonic acid is unstable and quickly breaks down into water and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide forms the fizz you can see.

steps.name: Soluble salt
steps.text: The calcium ions, no longer locked in the solid scale, pair with acetate ions. The result is calcium acetate, which dissolves in water and washes away.

reactions.result: Soaking a showerhead in vinegar overnight uses exactly this reaction. Warming the vinegar speeds it up, because molecules move and collide faster at higher temperatures.

reactions.title: Acetic fermentation
reactions.summary: Vinegar is made when bacteria turn alcohol into acetic acid. This process, called acetic fermentation, is technically an oxidation, because the bacteria use oxygen from the air. It is how wine, cider, beer and rice wine have been turned into vinegar for thousands of years. Wine left open to the air turns sour because these bacteria get in. In the 1860s, the French chemist Louis Pasteur showed that living bacteria are responsible.

steps.name: Bacteria
steps.text: Acetobacter bacteria live at the surface of alcoholic liquids, where there's oxygen. They need oxygen to work, which is why vinegar is made in open vessels or in tanks with air pumped through. They can tolerate the acid they produce.

steps.name: Oxidation
steps.text: The bacteria use enzymes to oxidize ethanol to acetaldehyde, then acetaldehyde to acetic acid. The hydrogen they strip off ends up combined with oxygen as water. This releases the energy the bacteria live on.

steps.name: Mother of vinegar
steps.text: Some of these bacteria make cellulose, the same material found in plant cell walls, forming a slimy, jelly-like mat on the surface called the mother of vinegar. A piece of mother can be used to start a new batch.

reactions.result: The French “vin aigre” means sour wine. Because alcohol is needed first, vinegar making is really a two-step process: yeast turn sugar into alcohol, then bacteria turn alcohol into acetic acid.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Vinegar is not a registered disinfectant for germ-kill claims.
Concentrated acetic acid: causes severe skin burns (H314) and is flammable.

hazards.title: Concentrated acid is corrosive
hazards.summary: Household vinegar is safe; 20–30% horticultural vinegar is not. Table vinegar is about 5 percent acetic acid and fine to eat and clean with. “Cleaning vinegar” is often 6 to 10 percent, and horticultural vinegar sold as a weed killer is strong enough to burn skin and badly damage eyes. Glacial acetic acid, which is nearly pure and used in labs and industry, is highly corrosive. The percentage on the label matters a lot.
hazards.chemical: Concentrated acetic acid denatures proteins and burns tissue. At higher concentrations, more molecules are present to release hydrogen ions, and the acid's power to damage tissue rises steeply. Acids make proteins unfold and clump together, a process called coagulation, forming a hard layer of damaged tissue. Because the uncharged acetic acid molecule passes through fatty membranes, it can soak into tissue more easily than many acids. Concentrated acetic acid also gives off a strong, irritating vapor.
hazards.biological: Strong cleaning or weed-killing vinegars require gloves and eye protection. On skin, they can cause redness, pain and burns, and in the eyes they can cause serious, sometimes permanent damage. Swallowing concentrated acetic acid can burn the mouth, throat and stomach. Breathing its vapor irritates the nose and throat. Rinse any splash right away with plenty of water, and keep strong vinegars in labeled containers, away from food vinegar.

hazards.title: Never mix with bleach
hazards.summary: Vinegar is an acid, so it must never be mixed with bleach. Some people combine them believing it makes a stronger cleaner, but the mixture releases chlorine gas. Even a small amount in a closed bathroom can cause harm. The same goes for other acidic cleaners, such as toilet bowl and rust removers. Use one product at a time and rinse surfaces in between.
hazards.chemical: Adding acid to bleach releases chlorine gas. Bleach contains hypochlorite and chloride ions. When an acid such as acetic acid lowers the pH, hypochlorite becomes hypochlorous acid, which reacts with chloride and hydrogen ions to form chlorine gas (Cl₂). Chlorine doesn't stay dissolved in acidic water, so it bubbles out. The lower the pH, the more chlorine is released.
hazards.biological: Chlorine gas irritates and damages the lungs. When it dissolves in the moist lining of the eyes, nose and airways, it forms hydrochloric and hypochlorous acids, which burn tissue. Symptoms include burning eyes, coughing, choking and chest tightness, and severe exposure can cause fluid in the lungs. If you mix them by accident, leave the room, get fresh air and call poison control. Also avoid storing vinegar and hydrogen peroxide together in one container, since they can form peracetic acid, which is corrosive.

profile.dosage: Table vinegar is usually 4 to 8 percent acetic acid, most often 5 percent, and is safe in food; in the United States, a product must contain at least 4 percent to be called vinegar. Cleaning vinegars run about 6 to 10 percent, and horticultural vinegars 20 to 30 percent, which call for gloves and eye protection. Acetic acid is also an approved food additive (E260 in Europe) used for sourness and preservation. If you drink vinegar, dilute it to protect your teeth and throat. Never mix it with bleach.

myths.claim: Vinegar disinfects as well as bleach.
myths.consensus: It reduces some bacteria but doesn't reliably kill many pathogens; use a registered disinfectant when needed.

myths.claim: Vinegar is safe on every surface.
myths.consensus: Its acid can etch marble, granite and some finishes.

synthesis.title: Bacterial fermentation (vinegar)
synthesis.summary: In many countries, a product sold as vinegar must be made by fermentation rather than by diluting synthetic acetic acid. The starting liquid can be wine, cider, malt (unhopped beer), rice wine or diluted distilled alcohol, and it gives each vinegar its flavor. Traditional methods, such as the slow Orléans method using wooden barrels, take weeks to months. Modern factories use the submerged method, which takes a day or two. Traditional balsamic vinegar is different again, made from cooked grape juice aged for many years in wooden barrels.
synthesis.mechanism: Alcohol from fermented fruit, grain or rice is oxidized by Acetobacter bacteria in tanks with vigorous aeration until it reaches about 5% acetic acid. First, yeast ferment the sugars into alcohol. In the submerged method, the alcoholic liquid then sits in a large stainless steel tank called an acetator, with fine air bubbles pumped through so the bacteria always have oxygen. The temperature is held around 30 °C, because the reaction gives off heat and too much would kill the bacteria. When the vinegar is ready, part of it is drawn off and filtered, and fresh alcohol is added to keep the process going.

synthesis.title: Methanol carbonylation (industrial acid)
synthesis.summary: Most of the acetic acid used in industry, well over 10 million tonnes a year, is made from methanol and carbon monoxide. This route was developed by the Monsanto company around 1970 and later improved in BP's Cativa process in the 1990s. It is much cheaper and faster than fermentation. Industrial acetic acid goes into plastics, paints, adhesives and medicines. It is chemically identical to the acetic acid in vinegar, though it is mostly not used in food.
synthesis.mechanism: Methanol and carbon monoxide react over a rhodium or iridium catalyst with an iodide promoter (the Monsanto and Cativa processes). First, methanol reacts with hydrogen iodide to form methyl iodide. The metal catalyst inserts itself into the bond between the methyl group and the iodine, and then a carbon monoxide molecule slips in between the metal and the methyl group. The resulting acetyl group is released as acetyl iodide, which reacts with water to give acetic acid and regenerate hydrogen iodide. The catalyst is then free to repeat the cycle again and again.
synthesis.significance: Industrial acetic acid goes into vinyl acetate for paints and glues, and into PET plastic.

citations.title: New developments in oxidative fermentation.
citations.abstract: Oxidative fermentations have been well established for a long time, especially in vinegar and in L-sorbose production. Recently, information on the enzyme systems involved in these oxidative fermentations has accumulated and new developments are possible based on these findings. We have recently isolated several thermotolerant acetic acid bacteria, which also seem to be useful for new developments in oxidative fermentation. Two different types of membrane-bound enzymes, quinoproteins and flavoproteins, are involved in oxidative fermentation, and sometimes work with the same substrate but produce different oxidation products. Recently, there have been new developments in two different oxidative fermentations, D-gluconate and D-sorbitol oxidations. Flavoproteins, D-gluconate dehydrogenase, and D-sorbitol dehydrogenase were isolated almost 2 decades ago, while the enzyme involved in the same oxidation reaction for D-gluconate and D-sorbitol has been recently isolated and shown to be a quinoprotein. Thus, these flavoproteins and a quinoprotein have been re-assessed for the oxidation reaction. Flavoprotein D-gluconate dehydrogenase and D-sorbitol dehydrogenase were shown to produce 2-keto- D-gluconate and D-fructose, respectively, whereas the quinoprotein was shown to produce 5-keto- D-gluconate and L-sorbose from D-gluconate and D-sorbitol, respectively. In addition to the quinoproteins described above, a new quinoprotein for quinate oxidation has been recently isolated from Gluconobacter strains. The quinate dehydrogenase is also a membrane-bound quinoprotein that produces 3-dehydroquinate. This enzyme can be useful for the production of shikimate, which is a convenient salvage synthesis system for many antibiotics, herbicides, and aromatic amino acids synthesis. In order to reduce energy costs of oxidative fermentation in industry, several thermotolerant acetic acid bacteria that can grow up to 40 degrees C have been isolated. Of such isolated strains, some thermotolerant Acetobacter species were found to be useful for vinegar fermentation at a high temperature such 38-40 degrees C, where mesophilic strains showed no growth. They oxidized higher concentrations of ethanol up to 9% without any appreciable lag time, while alcohol oxidation with mesophilic strains was delayed or became almost impossible under such conditions. Several useful Gluconobacter species of thermotolerant acetic acid bacteria are also found, especially L-erythrulose-producing strains and cyclic alcohol-oxidizing strains. Gluconobacter frateurii CHM 43 is able to rapidly oxidize meso-erythritol at 37 degrees C leading to the accumulation of L-erythrulose, which may replace dihydroxyacetone in cosmetics. G. frateuriiCHM 9 is able to oxidize cyclic alcohols to their corresponding cyclic ketones or aliphatic ketones, which are known to be useful for preparing many different physiologically active compounds such as oxidized steroids or oxidized bicyclic ketones. The enzymes involved in these meso-erythritol and cyclic alcohol oxidations have been purified and shown to be a similar type of membrane-bound quinoproteins, consisting of a high molecular weight single peptide. This is completely different from another quinoprotein, alcohol dehydrogenase of acetic acid bacteria, which consists of three subunits including hemoproteins.

citations.title: Vinegar-processed Schisandra Chinensis enhanced therapeutic effects on colitis-induced depression through tryptophan metabolism.
citations.abstract: Background: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an inflammatory bowel disease characterized by its incurable nature and undefined etiology, which is often accompanied by a high prevalence of comorbid depression. The gut-brain axis has emerged as a promising treatment target in recent years. Purpose: This study aimed to investigate how vinegar-processed Schisandra Chinensis (VSC) enhances therapeutic effects on depressive behavior in chronic UC mice. Methods: A chronic UC model was induced in mice using dextran sulfate sodium. The therapeutic effects of both raw and vinegar-processed Schisandra Chinensis on UC and associated depressive symptoms were assessed. Colonic mucosal damage was evaluated using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Alcian blue staining. The integrity of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and synaptic structures was visualized via transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was employed to quantify inflammatory cytokine levels in the colon, serum, and brain, while western blotting was performed for protein expression analysis. Additionally, metagenomic analysis was conducted to investigate gut microbiota composition. Nissl staining and immunofluorescence were used to assess hippocampal neuronal damage, and behavioral assessments including the morris water maze, open field test, forced swimming test and tail suspension test, were implemented to evaluate depressive states. Serum metabolites were analyzed using UPLC-MS/MS. Results: Both raw and vinegar-processed Schisandra Chinensis significantly upregulated aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), inhibited NF-κB p-p65 activation, and reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokine. These treatments also enhanced the expression of tight junction proteins, restored colonic mucosal and BBB integrity, alleviated damage to hippocampal neurons, and improved synaptic structure. Behavioral assessments indicated that VSC was particularly effective in ameliorating depressive-like behaviors in chronic UC mice. In the gut, both treatments reshaped the gut microbial composition, restoring the relative abundance of Duncaniella, Candidatus_Amulumruptor, Alistipes, Parabacteroides, Lachnospiraceae_bacterium, uncultured_Bacteroides_sp., Candidatus_Amulumruptor_caecigallinarius, with VSC showing more pronounced effects. Serum metabolomics revealed an increase in tryptophan levels and a decrease in kynurenine and xanthurenic acid levels with VSC, indicating that tryptophan metabolism shifted from the kynurenine pathway to the 5-HT or indole pathway. However, this phenomenon did not occur with Schisandra Chinensis (SC). Conclusion: This study demonstrated that the disruption of tryptophan metabolic balance served as a biological mechanism underlying the occurrence of depressive behaviors induced by UC. The application of SC following vinegar processing enhanced its regulatory effects on gut microbiota and tryptophan metabolism. This findings provided a new insight for the clinical management of gut-brain comorbidities.

citations.title: Gustatory Processing in Drosophila melanogaster.
citations.abstract: The ability to identify nutrient-rich food and avoid toxic substances is essential for an animal's survival. Although olfaction and vision contribute to food detection, the gustatory system acts as a final checkpoint control for food acceptance or rejection. The vinegar fly Drosophila melanogaster tastes many of the same stimuli as mammals and provides an excellent model system for comparative studies of taste detection. The relative simplicity of the fly brain and behaviors, along with the molecular genetic and functional approaches available in this system, allow the examination of gustatory neural circuits from sensory input to motor output. This review discusses the molecules and cells that detect taste compounds in the periphery and the circuits that process taste information in the brain. These studies are providing insight into how the detection of taste compounds regulates feeding decisions.

citations.title: Safety and side effects of apple vinegar intake and its effect on metabolic parameters and body weight: a systematic review.
citations.abstract: Introduction: Apple vinegar (AV) has been proclaimed to have different health benefits, such as a weight loss, the ability to lower blood glucose levels, and reducing the risk of heart diseases. Studies on animals have demonstrated effects of AV consumption, deepening our knowledge of the beneficial effects and side effects. Aim: The aims of this study were to evaluate the evidence of the effect of AV on metabolic parameters and body weight in humans, furthermore, to evaluate the safety and side effects of ingesting AV, and additionally to evaluate the evidence of the effect of AV on metabolic parameters, safety, and side effects of AV from studies performed on animals (mammals). Methods: A systematic literature search was performed. The databases PubMed (MEDLINE), PsycInfo (Ebsco), CINAHL (Ebsco), and Embase (Ovid) were searched for relevant articles. Primary outcomes were glycated hemoglobin, postprandial glucose, and synonyms for blood glucose. Secondary outcomes were waist circumference, visceral fat, high-density lipoprotein, low-density lipoprotein, triglycerides, and total cholesterol. Studies performed on humans and animals were included. The included studies performed on humans were quality assessed for risk of bias using a version of the Cochrane Collaboration's tool. Results: A total of 487 papers were identified in the literature search. Of these, 13 studies performed on humans and 12 studies performed on animals were included. There may be beneficial health effects from the consumption of AV. The risk of side effects when ingested in recommended quantities and in recommended ways seems inconsiderable. Conclusion: Due to inadequate research of high quality, the evidence for the health effects of AV is insufficient. Therefore, more large-scale, long-term clinical studies with a low risk of bias are needed before definitive conclusions can be made.

citations.title: The therapeutic importance of acid-base balance.
citations.abstract: Baking soda and vinegar have been used as home remedies for generations and today we are only a mouse-click away from claims that baking soda, lemon juice, and apple cider vinegar are miracles cures for everything from cancer to COVID-19. Despite these specious claims, the therapeutic value of controlling acid-base balance is indisputable and is the basis of Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for constipation, epilepsy, metabolic acidosis, and peptic ulcers. In this narrative review, we present evidence in support of the current and potential therapeutic value of countering local and systemic acid-base imbalances, several of which do in fact involve the administration of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate). Furthermore, we discuss the side effects of pharmaceuticals on acid-base balance as well as the influence of acid-base status on the pharmacokinetic properties of drugs. Our review considers all major organ systems as well as information relevant to several clinical specialties such as anesthesiology, infectious disease, oncology, dentistry, and surgery.

name: Sodium Percarbonate
scoreRationale: A chlorine-free bleach that breaks down to soda, water and oxygen; the powder can damage eyes and is harmful if swallowed.
summary: Sodium percarbonate is "oxygen bleach": it releases hydrogen peroxide in water to lift stains, then breaks down harmlessly.

physical.solubility: Soluble in water, releasing hydrogen peroxide

overview: Sodium percarbonate is a crystal that holds hydrogen peroxide inside a sodium carbonate lattice, in a ratio of two Na₂CO₃ to three H₂O₂. It's essentially solid hydrogen peroxide: stable as a dry powder, but it separates into its two components as soon as it dissolves.
That gives two cleaning agents in one scoop: hydrogen peroxide to oxidize stains and sodium carbonate to raise the pH and soften the water. It's the active ingredient in “oxygen bleach” boosters.
profile.function: Removes stains, whitens laundry and deodorizes without chlorine.

mechanisms.title: Oxidizing stains
mechanisms.chemical: When sodium percarbonate dissolves, it releases hydrogen peroxide and sodium carbonate. The sodium carbonate raises the pH to about 10 to 11, and in this alkaline water some hydrogen peroxide loses a hydrogen ion to become the perhydroxyl ion (HOO⁻), its more active bleaching form. Colored stain molecules contain chromophores, long chains of alternating single and double bonds that absorb visible light. The released peroxide oxidizes these chromophores, attacking and breaking their double-bond systems. Once the chains are broken up, the molecules no longer absorb visible light.
mechanisms.biological: Coffee, wine and grass stains lose their color without the harshness of chlorine bleach. Oxygen bleach is gentler on most colored fabrics because it attacks many dyes less aggressively than chlorine bleach does. It also breaks down into harmless products: water, oxygen and sodium carbonate. It is weaker than chlorine bleach for disinfecting and on some stubborn stains. Testing on a hidden area first shows whether a fabric's color will hold.

mechanisms.title: Cold-water bleaching with an activator
mechanisms.chemical: Hydrogen peroxide bleaches best at high temperatures, 60 °C or more, and works slowly in cooler water. Detergents solve this by adding a bleach activator, most commonly TAED (tetraacetylethylenediamine). TAED reacts with peroxide in a reaction called perhydrolysis, forming peracetic acid. Peracetic acid is a peroxide with an acetyl group attached, which makes it a much more reactive oxidizer. It bleaches effectively at lower temperatures.
mechanisms.biological: Clothes can be bleached at 30–40 °C instead of 60 °C or more, saving energy. Heating water accounts for most of the energy a washing machine uses, so washing cooler has a real environmental benefit. Peracetic acid also kills many bacteria, helping keep laundry hygienic at low temperatures. TAED has been used for decades in European detergents. After use, it breaks down into harmless products.

reactions.title: Dissolving
reactions.summary: Sodium percarbonate is an unusual crystal: hydrogen peroxide molecules held inside a sodium carbonate lattice by hydrogen bonds. Despite its name, it doesn't contain a true percarbonate ion, and chemists call it sodium carbonate peroxyhydrate. About a third of its weight is hydrogen peroxide. When it dissolves, the crystal comes apart into its two ingredients. That's why it is sometimes described as “solid hydrogen peroxide.”

steps.name: Water
steps.text: When the powder is added to water, water molecules surround the crystal and pull its parts away, breaking up the lattice. The sodium ions, carbonate ions and hydrogen peroxide molecules all dissolve. This happens faster in warm water.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: Hydrogen peroxide and sodium carbonate dissolve separately, and each now acts on its own. The peroxide is the bleaching agent. The carbonate is the alkaline helper.

steps.name: Activation
steps.text: The carbonate raises the pH to around 10 to 11, which helps the peroxide react with stains by forming the more reactive perhydroxyl ion (HOO⁻). The carbonate also softens hard water by removing calcium and magnesium. Both effects improve cleaning.

reactions.result: Oxygen bleach works best in warm water, or with an activator in cool water. As the peroxide works, it slowly breaks down into water and oxygen, which is why oxygen bleach solutions fizz gently.

reactions.title: Perhydrolysis with TAED
reactions.summary: Perhydrolysis is the reaction that turns hydrogen peroxide into peracetic acid inside the washing machine, using the activator TAED. It is what lets detergents bleach well at low temperatures. TAED is stable as a dry powder and only reacts once it dissolves alongside peroxide. Each TAED molecule can release two molecules of peracetic acid. It is a neat example of making a reactive chemical exactly where and when it is needed.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: Perhydroxyl ions (HOO⁻) from peroxide attack TAED's acetyl groups. Each acetyl group has a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, and that carbon is slightly positive, making it a target for the negatively charged perhydroxyl ion.

steps.name: Transfer
steps.text: Acetyl groups transfer to the peroxide as the bond between each acetyl group and TAED's nitrogen breaks. Two of TAED's four acetyl groups react this way.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: Peracetic acid forms, which bleaches effectively at low temperatures. What is left of TAED is DAED (diacetylethylenediamine), which is harmless and biodegradable.

reactions.result: This is why many European detergents clean well at low wash temperatures. Peracetic acid is also used on its own as a disinfectant in food processing and hospitals.

regulatory.status: Danger: may intensify fire (H272), harmful if swallowed (H302), causes serious eye damage (H318).
Accepted as a bleaching agent in eco-labeled detergents.

hazards.title: Serious eye damage
hazards.summary: Sodium percarbonate is generally safe in normal laundry use, but the dry powder is the main hazard: it can seriously damage the eyes. It is classified as causing serious eye damage, the most severe category of eye hazard. Most injuries come from powder flying into the eyes while pouring, or from children getting into the container. It is also harmful if swallowed. Keeping the container closed and out of reach prevents most accidents.
hazards.chemical: When percarbonate powder lands on the moist surface of the eye, it dissolves right there, releasing concentrated hydrogen peroxide and sodium carbonate. Peroxide plus high pH damages the surface of the eye. The peroxide oxidizes the proteins and fats of the cells covering the cornea, while the sodium carbonate makes the area strongly alkaline, damaging cell membranes and proteins further. Together, oxidation and alkalinity do more harm than either would alone. Because there is so little tear fluid to dilute it, the concentration on the eye can be very high.
hazards.biological: Keep powder away from eyes and children; rinse immediately if exposed. Rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical care. Eye exposure can cause pain, redness, blurred vision and damage to the cornea. On skin, the powder may cause mild irritation, especially if the skin is wet. Swallowing it irritates the mouth and stomach and releases gas, which can cause bloating and vomiting.

hazards.title: Oxidizer
hazards.summary: Sodium percarbonate is an oxidizer, meaning it can supply oxygen to a fire and make it burn more intensely. It doesn't burn by itself, but it can make other materials burn faster. Store it away from heat and flammable materials. Moisture and heat make it break down early. Never store dissolved percarbonate in a sealed container.
hazards.chemical: It releases oxygen as it decomposes. The hydrogen peroxide in percarbonate slowly breaks down into water and oxygen gas, and heat, moisture and some metals speed this up. If the powder gets damp or warm, it decomposes faster, releasing both oxygen and heat. Oxygen-rich air makes nearby materials such as paper, cloth or wood burn much more fiercely. Manufacturers coat the particles to slow this breakdown in storage.
hazards.biological: Oxygen can intensify a fire, so the powder shouldn't be stored near fuels. A sealed bottle of dissolved percarbonate can build enough pressure from oxygen gas to burst, spraying caustic liquid, so mix solutions fresh and use them in open containers. Keep the powder in its original container, tightly closed, somewhere cool and dry. Don't mix it with other cleaning chemicals, especially acids or bleach. Damp, clumped powder has lost much of its strength.

profile.dosage: Oxygen-bleach boosters are usually about 50 to 90 percent sodium percarbonate, and many powdered laundry detergents contain some as well. A typical dose is a scoop per load, following the label. In water it breaks down into water, oxygen and sodium carbonate, which is why it is considered an environmentally friendly bleach. The main precautions are avoiding eye contact, keeping it away from children and never storing solutions in sealed containers. Gloves are a good idea for long soaking jobs.

myths.claim: Oxygen bleach is just as harsh as chlorine bleach.
myths.consensus: It works more gently and breaks down to harmless products, though it's slower as a disinfectant.

environment.biodegradability: Breaks down to carbonate, water and oxygen.

synthesis.title: Crystallization
synthesis.summary: Sodium percarbonate is made by combining sodium carbonate and hydrogen peroxide, two chemicals produced in huge amounts. The process doesn't form new chemical bonds between them; it traps hydrogen peroxide inside the carbonate's crystal structure. The main challenge is making crystals that stay stable in storage, since detergent boxes often sit in damp laundry rooms. In Europe, percarbonate has largely replaced an older oxygen bleach, sodium perborate. It is made in large chemical plants and shipped to detergent makers.
synthesis.mechanism: A concentrated sodium carbonate solution is crystallized with hydrogen peroxide under carefully controlled conditions, often with stabilizers such as magnesium compounds or silicates that slow the peroxide's breakdown. As the mixture cools or water is removed, crystals form, with hydrogen peroxide held in the sodium carbonate lattice by hydrogen bonds. Another method sprays the two solutions onto a bed of tumbling particles in a fluid-bed dryer, where they dry into granules. The crystals are then coated, for example with sodium sulfate, to protect them from moisture and from other detergent ingredients and improve storage stability. Finally, the product is dried and sieved to an even size.
synthesis.significance: Percarbonate replaced sodium perborate in many European detergents after perborate was classified as toxic to reproduction because of its boron.

citations.title: Study on the catalytic degradation of Acid Orange 7 and the potential mechanism by ferrous-percarbonate.
citations.abstract: Factors affecting the degradation of Acid Orange 7 (AO7) were evaluated and optimized when ferrous was used to catalyze percarbonate in the present study. The optimized conditions included the initial pH values ranging from 3 to 11 for AO7 solution, the initial level of AO7, sodium percarbonate (SPC), and Fe2+ . Some ions and natural organic materials, which commonly exist in natural water, were also tested to evaluate their potential impacts on the degradation of AO7. The degradation efficiency of AO7 was up to 95% under the optimized test conditions, where the ferrous/percarbonate/AO7 molar ratio was 15/10/1 in the 0.285 mmol/l AO7 aqueous solution. The presence of Cl- , SO4 2- , NO3 - , Na+ , and Mg2+ did not affect the removal of AO7. The addition of HCO3 - significantly inhibited its removal, even when the concentration of HCO3 - was low to 0.6 mmol/l. A slight inhibition effect was observed when the added concentration of humic acid ranged from 0.5 to 5 mg/l, whereas the residue of AO7 was significantly enhanced when the level of humic acid was continually increased from 50 to 100 mg/l. Hydroxyl radicals (•OH) were the main reactive intermediates controlling the oxidation of AO7 in the present Fe2+ /SPC system. The produced intermediates through the degradation of AO7 were identified to include 2-coumaranone, 2-naphthol, phthalic acid, phthalimide, N-methylnaphthylamine, and 2-methylphenol. The proposed degradation pathways are consistent with the radical formation and the identified intermediates. PRACTITIONER POINTS: The ferrous/percarbonate system can remove 95% of AO7 under the optimized conditions. AO7 removal was inhibited by adding HCO3 - and humic acid, but not affected by Cl- , SO4 2- , NO3 - , Na+ , and Mg2+ . Hydroxylation, ring opening, and mineralization driven by the generated hydroxyl radicals were derived as the major processes for degrading AO7.

citations.title: Enhanced degradation of benzene by percarbonate activated with Fe(II)-glutamate complex.
citations.abstract: Effective degradation of benzene was achieved in sodium percarbonate (SPC)/Fe(II)-Glu system. The presence of glutamate (Glu) could enhance the regeneration of Fe(III) to Fe(II), which ensures the benzene degradation efficiency at wider pH range and eliminate the influence of HCO3 (-) in low concentration. Meanwhile, the significant scavenging effects of high HCO3 (-) concentration could also be overcome by increasing the Glu/SPC/Fe(II)/benzene molar ratio. Free radical probe compound tests, free radical scavenger tests, and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) analysis were conducted to explore the reaction mechanism for benzene degradation, in which hydroxyl radical (HO•) and superoxide anion radical (O2 (•-)) were confirmed as the predominant species responsible for benzene degradation. In addition, the results obtained in actual groundwater test strongly indicated that SPC/Fe(II)-Glu system is applicable for the remediation of benzene-contaminated groundwater in practice.

citations.title: A review on percarbonate-based advanced oxidation processes for remediation of organic compounds in water.
citations.abstract: Sodium percarbonate (SPC) is considered a potential alternative to liquid hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) in organic compounds contaminated water/soil remediation due to its regularly, transportable, economical, and eco-friendly features. The solid state of SPC makes it more suitable to remediate actual soil and water with a milder H2O2 release rate. Apart from its good oxidative capacity, alkaline SPC can simultaneously remediate acidized solution and soil to the neutral condition. Conventionally, percarbonate-based advanced oxidation process (P-AOPs) system proceed through the catalysis under ultraviolet ray, transition metal ions (i.e., Fe2+, Fe3+, and V4+), and nanoscale zero-valent metals (iron, zinc, copper, and nickel). The hydroxyl radical (•OH), superoxide radical (•O2-), and carbonate radical anion (•CO3-) generated from sodium percarbonate could attack the organic pollutant structure. In this review, we present the advances of P-AOPs in heterogeneous and homogeneous catalytic processes through a wide range of activation methods. This review aims to give an overview of the catalysis and application of P-AOPs for emerging contaminants degradation and act as a guideline of the field advances. Various activation methods of percarbonate are summarized, and the influence factors in the solution matrix such as pH, anions, and cations are thoroughly discussed. Moreover, this review helps to clarify the advantages and shortcomings of P-AOPs in current scientific progress and guide the future practical direction of P-AOPs in sustainable carbon catalysis and green chemistry.

citations.title: Bleaching of nonvital teeth. A clinically relevant literature review.
citations.abstract: Today, the bleaching of nonvital, discolored teeth is a low-risk routine treatment for improving esthetics. This review article focuses on the etiology of tooth discolorations, different treatment techniques, and risks of bleaching procedures. Some tooth discolorations in endodontically treated teeth are caused by dental treatments. The three most popular techniques for nonvital tooth bleaching are the walking bleach technique, inside/outside bleaching, and in-office bleaching. The walking bleach technique is a relatively reliable, fairly simple technique for dentists and patients. Inside/outside bleaching can be used additionally when internal and external bleaching must be combined. In-office bleaching seems to be a short-term solution, the effects of which can largely be attributed to dehydration of the teeth. There are still some open questions concerning the bleaching agents. Improved safety seems desirable with regard to adding thiourea as a scavenger of radicals or newer materials such as sodium percarbonate. The thermocatalytic technique, insufficient cervical sealing, and high concentrations of bleaching agents should be avoided, as this can increase the risk of cervical root resorptions. Patients should be informed about the low predictability of bleaching success and the risk of recurrent discoloration. The risk of cervical root resorption should be discussed with the patient. There is a strong correlation between root resorption and dental trauma.

citations.title: Advances in Controlled Oxygen Generating Biomaterials for Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Therapy.
citations.abstract: Oxygen (O2) generating biomaterials are emerging as important compositions to improve our capabilities in supporting tissue engineering and regenerative therapeutics. Several in vitro studies demonstrated the usefulness of O2 releasing biomaterials in enhancing cell survival and differentiation. However, more efforts are needed to develop materials that can provide sustained O2 release for the long-term. In this paper, we present different O2 generating sources, including hydrogen peroxide, sodium percarbonate, calcium peroxide and magnesium peroxide, and also cover types of carriers and relevant methods of fabricating O2 generating systems. Then, the applications of O2 generating materials in supporting engineered constructs, supplying high O2 demanding cell transplants, and supporting ischemic tissues are discussed. Moreover, the challenges and future perspectives are highlighted.
