name: Sodium Dodecylbenzenesulfonate
scoreRationale: The world's most-used detergent surfactant: readily biodegradable, but a skin and eye irritant and harmful to aquatic life before treatment.
summary: LAS is the main cleaning agent in most laundry detergents. It biodegrades well but irritates skin and eyes.

physical.state: White to yellow powder or paste
physical.phStability: Stable across pH; tolerant of hard water with builders

overview: Sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate is the most-used member of the linear alkylbenzene sulfonates (LAS), the world's workhorse detergent surfactants. It has a straight 12-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring that carries a negatively charged sulfonate group (–SO₃⁻).

The straight chain matters. Early detergents used branched chains that bacteria couldn't break down, causing mountains of foam on rivers in the 1950s and 60s. Switching to linear chains, which microbes digest from the end, made LAS readily biodegradable.
profile.function: Lifts and suspends oily soils in laundry and dish detergents.

mechanisms.title: Detergency
mechanisms.chemical: Each LAS molecule has two very different ends. The long 12-carbon tail is oily and avoids water, while the sulfonate head (–SO₃⁻) is charged and attracted to water; molecules like this are called surfactants, short for surface-active agents. In wash water, LAS molecules line up at the boundary between water and oily soil, tails in the oil and heads in the water, lowering the interfacial tension, the force that keeps oil and water apart. As the tension drops, oily soil rolls up off the fabric into droplets. Above a certain concentration, LAS molecules also gather into tiny spheres called micelles, with their tails pointing inward, and oil gets trapped inside them.
mechanisms.biological: Greasy stains wash out of clothes, and the negative charges keep removed soil from settling back on fabric. Because every micelle and every LAS-coated dirt particle carries a negative charge, they repel one another and stay suspended until the water drains away. LAS foams well, which people tend to link with cleaning power. It works poorly in very hard water, because calcium binds to it, so detergents add builders such as sodium carbonate or zeolites to remove calcium. LAS is usually blended with other surfactants to tackle a wider range of soils.

mechanisms.title: Biodegradation
mechanisms.chemical: Bacteria in wastewater treatment plants and in the environment start by oxidizing the far end of LAS's straight carbon chain, turning the last carbon into a carboxylic acid group. They then shorten the chain two carbons at a time by beta-oxidation, the same pathway our own cells use to break down fats. Once the chain is short, the bacteria remove the sulfonate group and break open the benzene ring. The final products are carbon dioxide, water and sulfate. Branched chains block this process, because the enzymes can't get past the branch points.
mechanisms.biological: Most LAS is removed in wastewater treatment within days, protecting rivers; well-run plants typically remove more than 99 percent. The older branched surfactants passed through treatment plants untouched, creating huge banks of foam on rivers and even foamy tap water in the 1950s and 60s. Switching to linear chains solved the problem. LAS breaks down poorly where there is no oxygen, such as in some sludges and sediments. Once oxygen is available again, it degrades.

mechanisms.title: Skin and eye irritation
mechanisms.chemical: LAS is an anionic surfactant, meaning its charged head is negative. Like other anionic surfactants, it extracts lipids and binds proteins at the skin surface: it dissolves and carries away the natural fats that form the skin's barrier, much as it lifts grease from clothes. It also binds to proteins in the skin's outer layer, such as keratin, causing them to swell and change shape. In the eye, it can disrupt the membranes of the cells covering the cornea. The damage depends on concentration and contact time.
mechanisms.biological: Undiluted detergent can redden skin and seriously irritate eyes. Repeated contact can leave hands dry, rough and cracked, especially for people who often wash laundry or dishes by hand. At the dilution found in wash water, LAS is much milder, and rinsing removes most of it from clothes. Gloves help people with sensitive skin. Splashes of concentrated detergent in the eyes need prompt rinsing.

reactions.title: Sulfonation
reactions.summary: Sulfonation is the reaction that gives LAS its water-loving head, attaching a charged head to an oily tail. It adds a sulfonic acid group to the benzene ring of linear alkylbenzene, an oily molecule made from petroleum. The reaction uses sulfur trioxide, a very reactive chemical, in special reactors that remove heat quickly, because the reaction releases a lot of it. The resulting sulfonic acid is then neutralized to make the sodium salt. It is a textbook example of electrophilic aromatic substitution.

steps.name: Electrophile
steps.text: Sulfur trioxide (SO₃) is a powerful electrophile, a molecule that seeks electrons. Its sulfur atom is strongly positive because the three oxygens bonded to it pull electrons away. It is drawn to the electron-rich benzene ring.

steps.name: Substitution
steps.text: It attacks the benzene ring of linear alkylbenzene, swapping a hydrogen for a –SO₃H group (electrophilic aromatic substitution). The ring briefly loses its special stability, called aromaticity, as the new bond forms, then regains it by releasing a hydrogen ion. The group usually attaches opposite the carbon chain, at what is called the para position.

steps.name: Neutralization
steps.text: Sodium hydroxide converts the sulfonic acid into its sodium salt. The hydroxide removes the acidic hydrogen, forming water and leaving a negatively charged sulfonate group paired with a sodium ion. The salt is easier to handle and more stable in detergents.

reactions.result: Electrophilic aromatic substitution is one of the main reactions of benzene rings. The same kind of reaction is used to attach nitro groups, chlorine atoms and carbon chains to rings when making dyes, medicines and plastics.

regulatory.status: Surfactants must meet ready-biodegradability criteria, which LAS does.
Warning: harmful if swallowed, causes skin irritation and serious eye damage; harmful to aquatic life.

hazards.title: Eye damage from concentrated detergent
hazards.summary: Concentrated detergent can cause serious eye injuries, and it is especially a risk with liquid detergent pods. Pods hold highly concentrated surfactants, LAS among them, in a thin film that dissolves easily when wet. Young children may squeeze or bite them, squirting detergent into their eyes or mouths, and the bright colors can look like candy. Poison control centers have received thousands of reports of children exposed to laundry pods. Keeping pods in their closed container, out of sight and reach, prevents most injuries.
hazards.chemical: Concentrated surfactant disrupts corneal cells. The oily tails of LAS molecules push into the fatty membranes of the cells on the surface of the cornea, while the charged heads pull them apart, dissolving the membranes. LAS also binds to proteins and makes them unfold. Pods contain far higher concentrations than diluted wash water, so damage happens quickly. Other pod ingredients, such as solvents, add to the effect.
hazards.biological: Eye exposure needs prolonged rinsing; detergent pods should be kept away from young children. Injuries range from irritation and redness to chemical burns of the cornea, causing pain and blurred vision. Rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes and get medical advice. Swallowing pod contents can cause vomiting, drowsiness and breathing problems, and some children have needed hospital care. In the EU, pods must come in opaque packaging and carry a bitter coating to discourage children.

hazards.title: Harm to aquatic life before treatment
hazards.summary: Before treatment, the detergent that goes down our drains can harm aquatic life, but wastewater treatment removes most of it. Problems arise where untreated sewage reaches rivers, or with spills of concentrated product. Because LAS biodegrades readily, it doesn't build up in the environment the way some chemicals do. Even so, it is toxic to fish and small water creatures at fairly low concentrations. That is why treatment matters.
hazards.chemical: Surfactants disrupt the gill membranes of fish and invertebrates. Gills are thin, delicate tissues with a large surface area for absorbing oxygen. LAS's oily tails slip into the fatty membranes of gill cells and its charged heads destabilize them, making them leaky. This interferes with oxygen uptake and with the gills' control of salts. LAS also lowers the surface tension of water, which can affect insects that live on the water's surface.
hazards.biological: Untreated discharges can harm aquatic life, which is why biodegradability is legally required for detergents in the EU. At high enough concentrations, fish struggle to breathe and small invertebrates may die. In rivers below treatment plants, LAS levels are usually far below harmful levels. The EU Detergents Regulation requires surfactants to break down completely in standard tests. Many other countries have similar rules.

profile.dosage: Laundry and dish detergents typically contain about 5 to 25 percent LAS, which is diluted hundreds of times in the wash; pods and concentrates pack much more into each dose. At wash-water dilution it is mild, but undiluted detergent should be kept away from eyes and rinsed off skin. LAS is among the most thoroughly studied chemicals in consumer products, and safety assessments have concluded that normal use is safe for people. Using only the recommended dose gives good results and limits what goes down the drain. Keep pods out of children's reach.

myths.claim: Detergent foam in rivers means detergents don't biodegrade.
myths.consensus: That was true of branched ABS in the 1950s; linear LAS replaced it and degrades within days.

environment.biodegradability: Readily biodegradable (aerobic); persists longer in anaerobic sediments.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Harmful to aquatic life before wastewater treatment.

synthesis.title: From petroleum
synthesis.summary: LAS is built in two main steps from two petroleum-based ingredients: benzene and long, straight-chain hydrocarbons. Millions of tonnes are produced every year, making it one of the most-used surfactants in the world. First the oily tail is attached to the ring, then the charged head is added. The process was redesigned in the 1960s to produce straight chains instead of branched ones. It is cheap to make, which is one reason it remains so widely used.
synthesis.mechanism: Long straight-chain hydrocarbons called normal paraffins, separated from kerosene, are converted into olefins, molecules with one double bond, with 10 to 14 carbons. Benzene is alkylated with these linear olefins in the presence of an acid catalyst, which attaches the chain to the ring and forms linear alkylbenzene (LAB). The LAB is then sulfonated with sulfur trioxide, adding a sulfonic acid group to the ring. Finally, it is neutralized with sodium hydroxide, forming sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate and its close relatives. The product is a mixture of molecules with slightly different chain lengths and attachment points.
synthesis.significance: In 1965 the U.S. detergent industry switched from branched to linear surfactants to end the foam problem on rivers.

citations.title: Characteristics and pH-Responsiveness of SDBS-Stabilized Crude Oil/Water Nanoemulsions.
citations.abstract: Nanoemulsions are colloidal systems with a wide spectrum of applications in several industrial fields. In this study, crude oil-in-water (O/W) nanoemulsions were formulated using different dosages of the anionic sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS) surfactant. The formulated nanoemulsions were characterized in terms of emulsion droplet size, zeta potential, and interfacial tension (IFT). Additionally, the rheological behavior, long-term stability, and on-demand breakdown of the nanoemulsions via a pH-responsive mechanism were evaluated. The obtained results revealed the formation of as low as 63.5 nm average droplet size with a narrow distribution (33-142 nm). Additionally, highly negative zeta potential (i.e., -62.2 mV) and reasonably low IFT (0.45 mN/m) were obtained at 4% SDBS. The flow-ability of the nanoemulsions was also investigated and the obtained results revealed an increase in the nanoemulsion viscosity with increasing the emulsifier content. Nonetheless, even at the highest SDBS dosage of 4%, the nanoemulsion viscosity at ambient conditions never exceeded 2.5 mPa·s. A significant reduction in viscosity was obtained with increasing the nanoemulsion temperature. The formulated nanoemulsions displayed extreme stability with no demulsification signs irrespective of the emulsifier dosage even after one-month shelf-life. Another interesting and, yet, surprising observation reported herein is the pH-induced demulsification despite SDBS not possessing a pH-responsive character. This behavior enabled the on-demand breakdown of the nanoemulsions by simply altering their pH via the addition of HCl or NaOH; a complete and quick oil separation can be achieved using this simple and cheap demulsification method. The obtained results reveal the potential utilization of the formulated nanoemulsions in oilfield-related applications such as enhanced oil recovery (EOR), well stimulation and remediation, well-bore cleaning, and formation fracturing.

citations.title: Ultrahigh-throughput screening system for directed polymer binding peptide evolution.
citations.abstract: Accumulation of plastics in the environment became a geological indicator of the Anthropocene era. An effective reduction of long-lasting plastics requires a treatment with micro-organisms that release polymer-degrading enzymes. Polymer binding peptides function as adhesion promoters and enable a targeted binding of whole cells to polymer surfaces. An esterase A-based Escherichia coli cell surface display screening system was developed, that enabled directed evolution of polymer binding peptides for improved binding strength to polymers. The E. coli cell surface screening system facilitates an enrichment of improved binding peptides from a culture broth through immobilization of whole cells on polymer beads. The polypropylene (PP)-binding peptide liquid chromatography peak I (LCI) was simultaneously saturated at five positions (Y29, D31, G35, E42, and D45; 3.2 million variants) and screened for improved PP-binding in the presence of the anionic surfactant sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (LAS; 0.25 mM). The cell surface system enabled efficient screening of the generated LCI diversity (in total ~10 million clones were screened). Characterization of identified LCI binders revealed an up to 12-fold improvement (eGFP-LCI-CSD-3: E42V/D45H) in PP-binding strength in the presence of the surfactant LAS (0.125 mM). The latter represents a first whole cell display screening system to improve adhesion peptides which can be used to direct and to immobilize organisms specifically to polymer surfaces (e.g., PP) and novel applications (e.g., in targeted plastic degradation).

citations.title: Amended safety assessment of dodecylbenzenesulfonate, decylbenzenesulfonate, and tridecylbenzenesulfonate salts as used in cosmetics.
citations.abstract: Sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate is one of a group of salts of alkylbenzene sulfonates used in cosmetics as surfactant-cleansing agents. Sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate is soluble in water and partially soluble in alcohol, with dermal absorption dependent on pH. Dodecylbenzenesulfonate salts are not toxic in single-dose oral and dermal animal tests, and no systemic toxicities were observed in repeat-dose dermal animal studies. In dermal animal studies, no evidence of reproductive or developmental toxicity was reported. At 15% concentrations, sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate was severely irritating to rabbit skin. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel concluded that the irritant properties of these ingredients are similar to those of other detergents, with severity dependent on concentration and pH. Products containing these ingredients should be formulated to ensure that the irritancy potential is minimized.

citations.title: Organic Acid Sanitizers for Natamycin and Other Fungicides in Recirculating Application Systems for Citrus Postharvest Decay Management.
citations.abstract: Natamycin is a new postharvest biofungicide for citrus and some other fruit crops in the United States that can be effectively used in recycling drench or flooder treatments. These applications necessitate sanitation of the fungicide solution to ensure that it remains free from contamination by bacteria that are potentially human pathogens. During in vitro experiments, heated (48°C) citric acid (1,100 or 2,200 μg/ml) amended with sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS) (60 or 120 μg/ml, respectively) significantly reduced the viability of a nonpathogenic strain of Escherichia coli in natamycin solutions by >5 log10 compared with the control. During laboratory studies with Penicillium digitatum-inoculated lemon fruit, 1,000 μg/ml of natamycin mixed with 1,000 μg/ml of lactic acid or citric acid and with or without SDBS (55 μg/ml) effectively and significantly reduced green mold. Natamycin mixed with lactic acid at ≥2,000 μg/ml, however, caused fruit injury, resulting in browning and rind pitting. Natamycin was incompatible with peroxyacetic acid, resulting in reduced efficacy against green mold. Sodium hypochlorite mixed with natamycin lost its toxicity to E. coli; however, the performance of natamycin was not affected. With heated (average 49°C) drench treatments on an experimental packing line, natamycin (1,000 μg/ml), fludioxonil (300 μg/ml), or azoxystrobin (300 μg/ml) mixed with citric acid (1,000 μg/ml) and SDBS (55 μg/ml) were effective against green mold without fruit injury. At a pH between 3.6 and 3.8, citric acid-SDBS significantly reduced the viability of E. coli by approximately 4 log10 in mixtures with fludioxonil or azoxystrobin, but not with natamycin. However, natamycin at 1,000 μg/ml mixed with 2,000 μg/ml of citric acid and SDBS (55 μg/ml) significantly reduced E. coli counts by >4 log10 within 4 min when the pH was maintained between 3.0 and 3.3, and the efficacy of the fungicide was retained. The use of citric acid with a surfactant can be a viable alternative sanitation method for natamycin in citrus packinghouses utilizing heated recirculating fungicide systems.

citations.title: In Situ Assay of Interfacial Interaction between ZnO Nanoparticles and Live Cell Disturbed by Surfactants.
citations.abstract: The interfacial interaction between pollutants and organisms is a critical process in controlling the environmental fates of pollutants; however, in situ assay of the interaction is still a great challenge. Here, in situ determination of dissociation constants (Kd) for ZnO nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) from live algal cells disturbed by different-charged surfactants was established using microscale thermophoresis (MST). Moreover, in situ measurement of the adhesion force between the ZnO NPs probe and live single cell was performed using an atomic force microscope (AFM). Results showed that the cationic cetyltrimethylammonium chloride (CTAC) and anionic sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS) increased but nonionic Triton X-100 (TX-100) decreased the adhesion of ZnO NPs on cells. However, the force signature exhibited a smooth single retracted peak at short distances in the SDBS- and TX-100-treated groups, distinguished from the "see-saw" pattern peak in the CTAC-treated groups. The extended Derjaguin-Landau-Verway-Overbeek (XDLVO) calculation further confirmed that SDBS and TX-100 mainly disturbed the short-range hydration on the NP-cell interface, while CTAC reduced the long-range electrostatic repulsion. Furthermore, an excellent linear correlation between Zn bioaccumulation and two parameters (Kd and adhesion force) indicated that NP-cell interfacial interactions affected Zn bioaccumulation. Thus, in situ assay provides a quantitative basis for the pollutant-organism interfacial interaction to evaluate the environmental fate and ecological risk of pollutants.

name: Limonene
scoreRationale: A natural citrus solvent, but it oxidizes into skin sensitizers and reacts with indoor ozone to form formaldehyde and fine particles.
summary: Limonene gives cleaners and cosmetics a citrus scent and dissolves grease. Natural, but aged limonene is a common skin allergen.

physical.state: Colorless oily liquid with orange scent
physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; miscible with oils and alcohol

overview: Limonene is a naturally occurring monoterpene (C₁₀H₁₆) and the primary component of essential oils extracted from citrus rinds. As a highly volatile compound, it vaporizes easily at room temperature, which is why peeling an orange instantly releases a strong, distinct scent.

Limonene exists as two mirror-image isomers (enantiomers) that trigger different olfactory receptors in the human nose. (R)-limonene (D-limonene) smells like sweet oranges and is the most abundant form in nature. (S)-limonene (L-limonene) has a harsher, pine-like, or turpentinic odor often associated with lemons, caraway, and pine needles.
profile.function: Dissolves grease, adhesives and tar, and adds a fresh citrus scent.

mechanisms.title: Anti-inflammatory action
mechanisms.chemical: Inflammation inside cells is controlled partly by a protein complex called NF-κB, which acts like a master switch for inflammatory genes. Normally NF-κB sits in the cytoplasm, the fluid outside the cell's nucleus, held in check by an inhibitor protein called IκB, a bit like a dog on a leash. When a cell is stressed or injured, enzymes tag IκB for destruction, which frees NF-κB to travel into the nucleus. In laboratory studies, limonene, which crosses cell membranes easily because it dissolves in fats, interfered with this step and kept IκB from being broken down. With IκB intact, NF-κB stays stuck outside the nucleus.
mechanisms.biological: Because NF-κB can't reach the DNA, it can't switch on the genes that make inflammatory messengers called cytokines, such as TNF-α and IL-6. These messengers normally call in immune cells and cause the redness, heat and swelling of inflammation. In cell and animal studies, limonene reduced these signs of inflammation. Researchers are interested in whether this could help with inflammatory conditions. These results come from the laboratory, though, and it isn't known whether the small amounts people meet in foods or cleaners have any such effect.

mechanisms.title: Antioxidant properties
mechanisms.chemical: Limonene (C₁₀H₁₆) has two carbon–carbon double bonds, regions packed with shared electrons. Free radicals are unstable molecules with an unpaired electron, such as the hydroxyl radical, and they react aggressively with whatever is nearby in order to grab an electron. Limonene's electron-rich double bonds can react with these radicals, either by giving up electrons or by adding the radical across the double bond. Either way, the radical is neutralized. In laboratory tests, this makes limonene a mild antioxidant.
mechanisms.biological: Free radicals can damage cell membranes by stealing electrons from their fat molecules, a chain reaction called lipid peroxidation that leaves membranes leaky. They can also damage proteins and DNA, a state known as oxidative stress. In cell and animal studies, limonene reduced markers of this kind of damage. Whether this matters for human health at normal exposures is unknown. Ironically, the same reactivity with oxygen is what makes limonene form skin-sensitizing products as it ages.

mechanisms.title: Gastrointestinal and reflux relief
mechanisms.chemical: Limonene is lipophilic, meaning it dissolves in fats, and hydrophobic, meaning it doesn't mix with water. It is also lighter than water, with a specific gravity of about 0.84. In the watery, acidic environment of the stomach it doesn't dissolve, so it tends to float on top of the stomach contents, much as oil floats on vinegar in a salad dressing. Some researchers have suggested that this floating layer could act as a barrier. It may also have mild effects on the muscles of the digestive tract.
mechanisms.biological: Heartburn happens when stomach acid splashes up into the esophagus, the tube that carries food to the stomach, and irritates its lining. A small number of studies of D-limonene capsules suggested they might reduce heartburn, possibly by forming a protective layer or by helping the stomach and esophagus move their contents along. However, these studies were small, and their results haven't been confirmed by large, well-designed trials. Limonene isn't an approved treatment for reflux. Anyone with frequent heartburn should see a doctor.

mechanisms.title: Hepatic (liver) enzyme induction
mechanisms.chemical: After limonene is absorbed, it travels to the liver, whose cells process foreign substances. In animal studies, limonene binds to sensor proteins inside liver cells, such as the constitutive androstane receptor (CAR), which detect foreign chemicals. When these sensors are activated, they switch on genes for detoxification enzymes. These include Phase I enzymes, such as cytochrome P450s, which chemically modify foreign molecules, and Phase II enzymes, such as glutathione S-transferases, which attach water-soluble groups to them. Raising enzyme production this way is called enzyme induction.
mechanisms.biological: Detoxification enzymes help the body turn fat-soluble substances into water-soluble forms that the kidneys can flush out in urine. In rodents, limonene increased the activity of these enzymes, and some studies suggested this helped protect against certain cancer-causing chemicals. But enzyme induction can also change how fast the body processes medicines. Whether limonene meaningfully affects human liver enzymes at normal exposures hasn't been established. These findings remain at the laboratory stage.

reactions.title: Autooxidation (reaction with oxygen over time)
reactions.summary: Autoxidation is a slow, spontaneous chain reaction that happens when limonene is exposed to oxygen in the air. Light and heat speed it up by creating the first free radicals. Fresh, pure limonene rarely causes skin allergies, but the products of its autoxidation are well-known contact allergens. That means citrus oils and citrus-scented cleaners can become more irritating as they age. It is the same basic chemistry that makes cooking oils go rancid.

steps.name: Initiation
steps.text: A trace free radical, often produced by ultraviolet light, pulls a hydrogen atom off an allylic carbon on the limonene ring, meaning a carbon right next to a double bond. Hydrogens in that position come off more easily. This leaves a limonene radical with an unpaired electron.

steps.name: Propagation
steps.text: The limonene radical immediately reacts with an oxygen molecule (O₂) from the air. The oxygen attaches to it, forming a peroxy radical (–OO•). This new radical is also highly reactive.

steps.name: Hydroperoxide formation
steps.text: The peroxy radical steals a hydrogen atom from another limonene molecule. That turns it into limonene hydroperoxide (R–OOH) and creates a new limonene radical, which keeps the chain going. One starting event can produce many hydroperoxide molecules.

steps.name: Decomposition
steps.text: Limonene hydroperoxides are unstable and slowly break down into other oxidized products. These include carvone, which smells like spearmint; carveol, an alcohol; and limonene oxide, an epoxide. Several of these are also skin sensitizers.

reactions.result: When an old bottle of citrus essential oil sits on a sunny shelf, its limonene slowly turns into hydroperoxides and carvone, which is why older oils are more likely to cause skin rashes. Keeping oils in dark, tightly closed bottles, using them within a year or so and adding antioxidants all slow this down.

reactions.title: Indoor ozone chemistry (ozonolysis)
reactions.summary: When you use citrus-scented cleaning sprays or air fresheners indoors, the limonene in the air can react with ozone (O₃), a reactive form of oxygen. Ozone drifts in from outdoor smog and is also produced by some air purifiers and older laser printers. The reaction, called ozonolysis, breaks limonene apart at its double bonds. It follows a pathway first described by the German chemist Rudolf Criegee in the 1950s. Its products include irritating gases and tiny airborne particles.

steps.name: Cycloaddition
steps.text: An ozone molecule attacks one of limonene's double bonds, usually the one inside its ring. All three of ozone's oxygen atoms attach across the double bond at once, forming a very unstable five-membered ring called a primary ozonide.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: The primary ozonide immediately falls apart, completely breaking the original carbon–carbon double bond. This creates two pieces: a carbonyl compound, with a C=O group, and a high-energy molecule called a Criegee intermediate, also known as a carbonyl oxide.

steps.name: Secondary reactions
steps.text: The Criegee intermediate is extremely unstable. It quickly reacts with water vapor in the air or rearranges itself, forming a variety of oxygen-containing volatile organic compounds and releasing reactive hydroxyl radicals.

steps.name: Aerosol formation
steps.text: Many of the large, oxygen-rich molecules formed this way barely evaporate, so they don't stay as gases. They condense onto dust particles or clump together into microscopic droplets suspended in the air, forming an aerosol.

reactions.result: The reaction produces secondary organic aerosols, ultrafine particles that can be breathed deep into the lungs, along with small amounts of formaldehyde. That is why atmospheric chemists warn that heavy use of pine or citrus cleaners in a poorly ventilated room on a smoggy day can create a short burst of indoor air pollution. Opening windows helps.

regulatory.status: Must be named on labels above 0.001% (leave-on) or 0.01% (rinse-off) as a fragrance allergen.
Generally Recognized as Safe as a flavoring.
Warning: flammable, skin irritant and sensitizer, very toxic to aquatic life.

hazards.title: Skin sensitization (contact dermatitis)
hazards.summary: Fresh, pure limonene rarely irritates skin or causes allergies; the problem appears as it ages. Once a bottle of citrus oil or cleaner is opened and exposed to air, light and warmth, limonene slowly reacts with oxygen and forms products that are strong skin allergens. Oxidized limonene is now one of the most common fragrance allergens found in patch testing. That is why the European Union requires limonene to be listed on cosmetic labels when it is present above trace amounts. People who are sensitized need to avoid it in many products.
hazards.chemical: Through autoxidation, oxygen from the air attacks limonene next to its double bonds, converting it into limonene hydroperoxides along with carvone and limonene oxide. Limonene hydroperoxides are reactive molecules with an –O–O–H group. Because they are small and dissolve in fats, they slip easily through the skin's outer barrier, the stratum corneum. Once inside, they act as haptens, small molecules that form strong chemical bonds with the skin's own proteins. That creates altered proteins the immune system doesn't recognize.
hazards.biological: Immune cells in the skin called Langerhans cells detect the altered proteins, carry them to the lymph nodes and teach T cells to treat them as threats. This sensitization stage causes no symptoms at first. On later exposures, the memory T cells trigger a delayed, Type IV immune response, usually 24 to 72 hours after contact. The result is allergic contact dermatitis: red, itchy, sometimes blistering skin wherever the product touched. Once someone is sensitized, the allergy usually lasts for life.

hazards.title: Respiratory irritation
hazards.summary: Limonene's citrus smell isn't harmful in itself at normal levels, but it can be a starting material for indoor air pollution. When limonene vapor from cleaning sprays mixes with ozone indoors, it forms formaldehyde and tiny particles that can irritate the airways. This mainly matters with heavy use of citrus or pine cleaners in poorly ventilated spaces. People with asthma may be more sensitive. Good ventilation greatly reduces the effect.
hazards.chemical: When limonene vapor meets ozone in indoor air, ozonolysis breaks the limonene ring apart. This creates formaldehyde, reactive hydroxyl radicals and large, oxygen-rich organic molecules. Because these heavy molecules don't stay as gases, they condense into microscopic droplets called secondary organic aerosols. These particles are ultrafine, far smaller than a grain of dust. How much forms depends on the amounts of limonene and ozone and on how quickly fresh air replaces indoor air.
hazards.biological: When a person breathes this air, the ultrafine particles and formaldehyde can travel deep into the lungs. There they can cause oxidative stress, a buildup of reactive molecules that damages cells and irritates the airway lining. This can trigger coughing, chest tightness, shortness of breath and, in people with asthma, flare-ups. Formaldehyde also irritates the eyes and nose. Opening windows and using fragranced cleaners sparingly, especially on smoggy days, reduces exposure.

hazards.title: Aspiration hazard
hazards.summary: Limonene has very low toxicity when swallowed in small amounts, such as from citrus fruit. But swallowing concentrated limonene, such as pure orange oil or a citrus degreaser, carries a serious risk to the lungs. This is called an aspiration hazard, and it is mainly a danger for young children who might drink cleaning products. The risk comes not from limonene's chemistry in the stomach but from what happens if it reaches the lungs. If someone swallows a limonene product, don't make them vomit; call a poison control center.
hazards.chemical: Limonene is a nonpolar hydrocarbon, made only of carbon and hydrogen, with very low viscosity, meaning it is thin and runny, and low surface tension, meaning it spreads easily. These properties let it flow and spread over moist surfaces very quickly. It is also an excellent solvent for fats and oils. In the lungs, these properties become dangerous. Limonene can dissolve the fatty substances the lungs depend on.
hazards.biological: If a person swallows concentrated limonene and then chokes, coughs or vomits, its low surface tension lets it slip past the vocal cords into the airways and lungs. In the tiny air sacs called alveoli, it dissolves the pulmonary surfactant, a fatty film that keeps the air sacs open. Without surfactant, air sacs collapse, fluid leaks in and the lungs become inflamed, a condition called chemical pneumonitis. This can make breathing very difficult and can be life-threatening. That is why such products carry warnings and child-resistant caps.

hazards.title: Aquatic toxicity
hazards.summary: Limonene is classified as very toxic to aquatic life, so large amounts shouldn't be poured into drains or waterways. Small amounts from household use are usually broken down at wastewater treatment plants. The concern is mainly spills of concentrated limonene or industrial waste. Limonene breaks down fairly quickly in the environment, which limits long-term effects. Still, at high concentrations it can harm fish and other water creatures.
hazards.chemical: Limonene barely dissolves in water and is lighter than water, with a specific gravity of about 0.84. If a large amount is spilled into water, it floats on the surface as an oily film rather than mixing in. Because it is so lipophilic, it readily moves out of the water and into fatty tissue. In aquatic organisms, it moves into the fatty membranes of gills and other cells. Under the global hazard system, limonene is classified as Aquatic Acute 1 and Aquatic Chronic 1, the most toxic categories.
hazards.biological: When limonene builds up in the fatty membranes of fish gills and other cells, it disrupts their structure, making them leaky and interfering with breathing and other vital functions. Small aquatic animals such as water fleas, and fish, are particularly sensitive. Large spills can kill aquatic life in the affected area. However, limonene is readily biodegradable, meaning microbes break it down within days to weeks, so it doesn't linger. Disposing of concentrated products properly prevents harm.

profile.dosage: Citrus cleaners may contain about 1 to 20 percent limonene, while cosmetics usually contain less than 1 percent. In the European Union, limonene must be named on cosmetic labels when it exceeds 0.001 percent in leave-on products or 0.01 percent in rinse-off products, so people with allergies can avoid it, and fragrance-industry standards limit how oxidized it may be. Eating citrus fruit and foods flavored with orange oil provides small amounts that the body handles easily. The main precautions are storing products away from light and heat, keeping them away from children and ventilating rooms while cleaning.

myths.claim: Natural citrus cleaners are completely non-toxic.
myths.consensus: Limonene is natural but still a sensitizer and an aquatic toxin.

environment.notes: A volatile organic compound that contributes to indoor air pollution chemistry.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis (how plants make it)
synthesis.summary: Plants make limonene through a series of enzyme-controlled reactions rather than in one step. In citrus fruit, this happens in tiny oil glands in the peel, the small dots you can see on an orange's skin. Many other plants, including mint, pine and caraway, also make limonene. Plants produce it partly to defend themselves against insects and microbes and partly to attract pollinators. Each plant uses an enzyme that makes one particular mirror-image form.
synthesis.mechanism: Plants build limonene from geranyl pyrophosphate (GPP), a 10-carbon chain that is the starting point for all monoterpenes. An enzyme called limonene synthase holds GPP in a pocket shaped to guide what happens next. The enzyme removes the pyrophosphate group, leaving a positively charged carbon called a carbocation, which is very reactive. The molecule rearranges and curls around so that its tail attacks the positive carbon, closing a six-carbon ring. Finally, the enzyme removes a hydrogen ion, creating a double bond and releasing limonene.
steps: The enzyme strips away the pyrophosphate group, leaving a positively charged, highly reactive carbon (a carbocation).
The unstable molecule rearranges into a different intermediate called the linalyl cation.
The positive charge pulls the tail of the molecule around, forcing it to snap shut into a six-carbon ring (the α-terpinyl cation).
Finally, the enzyme removes a proton (H⁺), forming the last double bond and releasing (R)-limonene.
synthesis.significance: This is a highly stereospecific reaction. Because the enzyme's “pocket” is precisely shaped, it almost exclusively produces the (R)-enantiomer (sweet orange scent) in citrus, whereas a different enzyme in pine trees produces the (S)-enantiomer (pine scent).

synthesis.title: Chemical synthesis (the Diels–Alder reaction)
synthesis.summary: Making limonene from scratch in a laboratory is possible but rarely done commercially, because squeezing orange peels is far cheaper. When chemists do build it, they can use a classic reaction called the Diels–Alder reaction, discovered by Otto Diels and Kurt Alder in 1928, which earned them the 1950 Nobel Prize. This reaction joins two molecules into a ring in a single step. Starting from isoprene, a simple five-carbon molecule, it can form limonene's six-membered ring. It is a favorite example in organic chemistry courses.
synthesis.mechanism: Isoprene is a five-carbon molecule with two double bonds separated by a single bond, a type of molecule called a diene. When isoprene is heated, two of its molecules can react with each other. One acts as the diene, contributing four carbon atoms, and the other acts as the dienophile, contributing two atoms through one of its double bonds. The electrons in their double bonds shift together in a circle, forming two new single bonds and one new double bond at the same moment. This single step, called a [4+2] cycloaddition, zips the two molecules into a six-membered ring, giving limonene.
synthesis.significance: Because no enzyme guides the shape, this heat-driven reaction produces dipentene, a 50:50 mixture of (R)- and (S)-limonene. Dipentene is used as a cheap industrial solvent and in rubber manufacturing, since separating the two mirror-image forms is difficult and expensive.

synthesis.title: Industrial manufacturing (physical extraction)
synthesis.summary: Almost all commercial limonene comes from the orange peels left over from making orange juice, amounting to tens of thousands of tonnes a year. That makes it an upcycled byproduct, turning waste into something valuable. Because the orange tree has already made the limonene, manufacturing only has to separate it from the peel. No chemical reactions are needed. Brazil and the United States, the world's biggest orange juice producers, are major suppliers.
synthesis.mechanism: After oranges are pressed for juice, the leftover peels, which hold most of the fruit's limonene, are crushed or scraped to burst the tiny oil glands. The resulting slurry is sprayed with water and sent through powerful centrifuges, machines that spin very fast. Because limonene is lighter than water and doesn't mix with it, the spinning separates it from the heavier water and plant material, leaving a layer of cold-pressed orange oil. Limonene can also be recovered by steam distillation of the peels, where it evaporates with the steam and is collected as the vapor cools. Cold-pressed orange oil is about 95 percent limonene.
synthesis.significance: For higher purity, the crude oil is distilled under vacuum. Lowering the pressure lowers limonene's boiling point, so it evaporates at a gentler temperature and leaves waxes and pigments behind, giving limonene that is about 99 percent pure.

citations.title: Biotechnological production of limonene in microorganisms.
citations.abstract: This mini review describes novel, biotechnology-based, ways of producing the monoterpene limonene. Limonene is applied in relatively highly priced products, such as fragrances, and also has applications with lower value but large production volume, such as biomaterials. Limonene is currently produced as a side product from the citrus juice industry, but the availability and quality are fluctuating and may be insufficient for novel bulk applications. Therefore, complementary microbial production of limonene would be interesting. Since limonene can be derivatized to high-value compounds, microbial platforms also have a great potential beyond just producing limonene. In this review, we discuss the ins and outs of microbial limonene production in comparison with plant-based and chemical production. Achievements and specific challenges for microbial production of limonene are discussed, especially in the light of bulk applications such as biomaterials.

citations.title: The volatome of Aspergillus fumigatus.
citations.abstract: Early detection of invasive aspergillosis is absolutely required for efficient therapy of this fungal infection. The identification of fungal volatiles in patient breath can be an alternative for the detection of Aspergillus fumigatus that still remains problematic. In this work, we investigated the production of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) by A. fumigatus in vitro, and we show that volatile production depends on the nutritional environment. A. fumigatus produces a multiplicity of VOCs, predominantly terpenes and related compounds. The production of sesquiterpenoid compounds was found to be strongly induced by increased iron concentrations and certain drugs, i.e., pravastatin. Terpenes that were always detectable in large amounts were α-pinene, camphene, and limonene, as well as sesquiterpenes, identified as α-bergamotene and β-trans-bergamotene. Other substance classes that were found to be present in the volatome, such as 1-octen-3-ol, 3-octanone, and pyrazines, were found only under specific growth conditions. Drugs that interfere with the terpene biosynthesis pathway influenced the composition of the fungal volatome, and most notably, a block of sesquiterpene biosynthesis by the bisphosphonate alendronate fundamentally changed the VOC composition. Using deletion mutants, we also show that a terpene cyclase and a putative kaurene synthase are essential for the synthesis of volatile terpenes by A. fumigatus. The present analysis of in vitro volatile production by A. fumigatus suggests that VOCs may be used in the diagnosis of infections caused by this fungus.

citations.title: Botanical solvents.
citations.abstract: Botanical, or plant-derived, solvents such as turpentine, pine oils, and various essential oils are used as environmentally acceptable alternatives to traditional solvents and degreasing agents. This article focuses on three lesser-known botanical solvents: limonene, oleic acid, and linoleic acid. Although data are limited, limonene, linoleic acid, and oleic acid are likely of low toxicity. Mild skin irritation may occur from exposure to these compounds, and oxidation products of limonene may produce dermal sensitization. Limonene, and possibly linoleic and oleic acids, may have irritative and bronchoconstrictive airway effects; however, data are scant and more studies are required.

citations.title: North American Contact Dermatitis Group Patch Test Results: 2021-2022.
citations.abstract: Background: Patch testing is an important diagnostic tool for the assessment of allergic contact dermatitis (ACD). Objective: This study documents the North American Contact Dermatitis Group (NACDG) patch testing results from 2021 to 2022. Methods: At 12 centers in North America, patients were tested in a standardized manner with a screening series of 80 allergens. Results: Overall, 3056 patients were tested; 2200 (72.0%) had at least 1 positive/allergic patch test reaction and 1412 patients (46.6%) had a primary diagnosis of ACD. The most commonly positive allergens were nickel sulfate hexahydrate 5% and 2.5% petrolatum (24.9% and 22.1%, respectively), methylisothiazolinone (MI) (11.5%), hydroperoxides of linalool (10.1%), cobalt chloride hexahydrate (9.2%), and methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone (9.0%). Compared with 2019-2020, prevalence of the top 20 allergens statistically increased for nickel (P < 0.001), cobalt (P < 0.01), gold (P < 0.001), hydroperoxides of limonene (P < 0.001), oleamidopropyl dimethylamine (P < 0.01), dimethylaminopropylamine (P < 0.01), and ammonium persulfate (P < 0.001). MI positivity continued to decrease from its peak in 2017-2018. More than one-fifth of patients (n = 640, 21.1%) had at least one clinically relevant reaction to an allergen/substance not present in the NACDG screening series. Conclusions: The epidemic of MI contact allergy in North America appears to continue its descent. Fragrance allergy is still very common, but the composition of fragrance allergy markers appears to be changing. Patch testing using a robust screening series, and supplemental allergens as indicated, is necessary for the comprehensive evaluation of ACD.

citations.title: Limonene Hydroperoxides.
citations.abstract: Limonene is a fragrance widely used in cosmetics and household products. Until recently, contact allergy to limonene was considered rare because positive patch tests to it were infrequently observed. In recent years, however, it has been demonstrated that exposure of limonene to oxygen (air) results in the formation of a number of oxidation products, of which the hydroperoxides have a far stronger sensitizing potency than the pure compound. By routine testing of patients suspected of contact dermatitis with hydroperoxides of limonene, high frequencies of positive reactions were found, indicating that these chemicals are important fragrance allergens. It should be realized, however, that a number of "positive" reactions may well be false-positive, irritant responses.

name: Protease
scoreRationale: Lets detergents clean at lower temperatures, but enzyme dust is a respiratory sensitizer, so products use encapsulated granules.
summary: Protease enzymes break down protein stains like blood, egg and grass. They're safe in finished detergents but can cause allergies as dust.

identity.composition: Serine protease enzymes (subtilisins) produced by Bacillus bacteria, supplied as encapsulated granules or stabilized liquids.

overview: Proteases are enzymes that cut proteins. The ones in laundry detergents are mostly subtilisins, made by Bacillus bacteria: folded protein molecules whose active site holds a precisely arranged trio of amino acids (serine, histidine and aspartate) called the catalytic triad.
Each enzyme molecule can cut thousands of peptide bonds per minute without being used up, breaking protein stains like blood, egg and grass into small fragments that wash away, even in cold water.
profile.function: Digests protein stains into small, water-soluble peptides, enabling cold-water washing.

mechanisms.title: The catalytic triad
mechanisms.chemical: An enzyme's active site is a small pocket where the reaction takes place. In subtilisin, three amino acids, serine, histidine and aspartate, sit close together there. Aspartate and histidine together pull a proton from serine: aspartate's negative charge holds histidine in position, and histidine takes the hydrogen ion from serine's –OH group. That turns serine's oxygen into a powerful nucleophile, an atom strongly attracted to positive charges, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of a peptide bond, the bond linking amino acids in a protein. The enzyme holds the protein chain in exactly the right position for this attack.
mechanisms.biological: Protein stains are cut into short, water-soluble peptides at mild temperatures, so clothes come clean without hot water. Blood, egg, grass, milk, sweat and food stains all contain proteins that stick tightly to fabric. Once cut into small pieces, they dissolve and are carried away by the surfactants. Because enzymes are catalysts, a tiny amount does a lot of work. Wool and silk are themselves made of protein, so detergents for these fabrics usually leave protease out.

mechanisms.title: Engineered to survive bleach
mechanisms.chemical: Bleach in detergents can oxidize certain amino acids, especially methionine, which contains a sulfur atom that reacts easily with oxygen. In subtilisin, a methionine sits right next to the active-site serine. When bleach oxidizes it, the active site is distorted and the enzyme stops working. In the 1980s, scientists used genetic engineering to replace this easily oxidized methionine with a different amino acid, such as alanine or serine, which can't be oxidized the same way. Changing one chosen amino acid like this is called site-directed mutagenesis.
mechanisms.biological: The enzyme keeps working in detergents that also contain oxygen bleach, an early success of protein engineering. Since then, detergent enzymes have been engineered to work in cold water, tolerate high pH and resist other detergent ingredients. Modern detergents may contain several engineered enzymes, including amylases for starch and lipases for fats. This makes it possible to clean well at low temperatures, saving energy. Protein engineering is now used to design enzymes for many industries.

mechanisms.title: Respiratory allergy
mechanisms.chemical: Proteases are proteins, and the immune system can treat foreign proteins as invaders. When enzyme dust is breathed in, the immune system recognizes it as a foreign protein lining the airways. In some people, it responds by producing IgE antibodies, which recognize that particular enzyme. These antibodies attach to mast cells, immune cells found in the airways. This first stage, called sensitization, causes no symptoms.
mechanisms.biological: People can develop IgE-mediated allergy and asthma, which is why enzymes are sold encapsulated or in liquids, not as loose dust. Once someone is sensitized, breathing in even tiny amounts of the enzyme makes their mast cells release histamine and other chemicals, causing sneezing, a runny nose, watery eyes, wheezing and asthma attacks. This was seen mainly in detergent factory workers in the late 1960s. Studies of people using enzyme detergents at home haven't found a meaningful allergy risk from normal use. Encapsulation, liquid formulas and air monitoring have greatly reduced cases among workers.

reactions.title: Peptide-bond hydrolysis
reactions.summary: Hydrolysis means “splitting with water”: a water molecule is used to break a bond. Peptide bonds are very stable, and without an enzyme they would take years to break in plain water. Subtilisin speeds this up enormously by guiding the reaction through a series of steps. The mechanism is the same as in chymotrypsin, a digestive enzyme in your gut, even though the two enzymes evolved separately. That makes it a famous example of convergent evolution at the molecular level.

steps.name: Acylation
steps.text: Activated serine attacks the peptide bond's carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate. For a moment the carbon is bonded to four groups instead of three, and its oxygen carries a negative charge. A pocket in the enzyme called the oxyanion hole steadies that charge with hydrogen bonds.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: The bond breaks; one fragment leaves while the other stays attached to serine (the acyl-enzyme). Histidine passes the hydrogen it took from serine to the nitrogen of the departing fragment. The first piece of the protein drifts away.

steps.name: Deacylation
steps.text: A water molecule, activated by histidine, attacks the acyl-enzyme. Histidine pulls a hydrogen ion from the water, making its oxygen a strong nucleophile. A second tetrahedral intermediate forms.

steps.name: Reset
steps.text: The second fragment is released and the enzyme is ready for the next bond. Serine gets its hydrogen back, so the active site is restored exactly as it started. The whole cycle takes a tiny fraction of a second.

reactions.result: Enzymes are catalysts: they speed reactions enormously and come out unchanged. That is why a detergent needs only a tiny amount of protease to digest a stain.

regulatory.status: Danger: may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled (H334).
Manufacturers monitor workplace enzyme exposure and encapsulate enzymes to prevent dust.

hazards.title: Respiratory sensitization
hazards.summary: Breathing in enzyme dust is mainly a workplace hazard for detergent manufacturers. In the late 1960s, soon after enzyme detergents appeared, many factory workers developed allergies and asthma from inhaling it. The industry responded by changing how enzymes are made and handled. Today the risk is mainly to people who work with concentrated enzymes, not consumers. Detergent enzymes are classified as respiratory sensitizers under hazard labeling rules.
hazards.chemical: Airborne enzyme protein triggers antibody production in the lungs. Tiny particles of enzyme dust can be breathed deep into the airways, where the immune system meets the foreign protein. In susceptible people, it produces IgE antibodies against it. Proteases may make sensitization more likely because they can break down proteins that hold airway cells together, giving the enzyme easier access to immune cells. The risk depends on how much enzyme is in the air and for how long.
hazards.biological: Allergy and asthma symptoms in exposed workers led the industry to encapsulate enzymes and monitor air levels. Once someone is sensitized, even small exposures can cause sneezing, itchy eyes, chest tightness and asthma attacks. Factories now use dust-free granules and liquids and keep airborne levels extremely low, measured in billionths of a gram per cubic meter. Regular health checks catch sensitization in workers early. Consumers using finished detergents normally aren't exposed to enough enzyme dust to cause problems.

profile.dosage: Laundry and dishwasher detergents contain well under 1 percent active enzyme protein, often a small fraction of a percent, because enzymes are catalysts that work in tiny amounts. In finished products, enzymes are sealed in granules or dissolved in liquids, so consumers breathe in almost none. Workplace air limits for subtilisin are extremely low, around 60 nanograms per cubic meter. Use detergents as directed, avoid breathing in powder dust and keep products away from children. Detergents for wool and silk usually leave protease out.

myths.claim: Enzyme detergents eat your skin.
myths.consensus: They are designed for stains; consumer skin reactions are uncommon at use concentrations.

synthesis.title: Fermentation
synthesis.summary: Detergent enzymes are made by microorganisms, mostly Bacillus bacteria, grown in huge fermentation tanks. Bacillus species naturally release proteases into their surroundings to break down proteins for food. Companies have engineered strains that produce far more enzyme than wild ones. This approach is called industrial biotechnology. The same technology produces enzymes for food processing, textiles and biofuels.
synthesis.mechanism: Engineered Bacillus strains grow in large fermenters, steel tanks holding many thousands of liters of nutrient broth containing sugars and proteins. The tanks are kept sterile, stirred and supplied with air at a controlled temperature and pH, and the bacteria secrete protease into the broth. After a few days, the bacteria are removed by filtration or centrifugation. The enzyme solution is recovered and concentrated, often by ultrafiltration through membranes that let water through but hold back the larger enzyme molecules. Finally, it is encapsulated in dust-free granules for powders or stabilized in liquid for liquid detergents.
synthesis.significance: Otto Röhm made the first enzyme detergent in 1913 using enzymes from animal pancreas; bacterial enzymes took over in the 1960s.
